en: Preface to the *Shishi Tongjian*:
Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, expounded the teachings throughout five periods. At the end, he held up a flower;

had it not been for Kāśyapa’s breaking into a smile and Ānanda’s compilation, then these five thousand and forty-eight fascicles—the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma and the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa—would all have become submerged in oblivion.
Alas! It would cause sentient beings throughout kalpas to fall into the bitter sea of precipices, with no means of escape.
Since the Dharma has been circulated, it is like the waters of the great ocean, which satisfy all according to their capacity.

Beyond the sūtras and śāstras, there subsequently appeared the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), the *Wudeng lu* (Record of the Five Lamps), the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification [of Buddhism]), and the *Zhengzong*.

The *Jì* (Records), the *Sēngbǎo chuán* (Biographies of the Sangha Jewel), the *Línjiān lù* (Forest Records), the *Zōngmén tǒngyào* (Compendium of the Essential Teachings of the School), and the *Dàhuì wǔkù* (Great Wisdom Armory)—all these were produced by those who had attained the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*).

They brought forth the very marrow of the "Yellow-Faced Old Man" (the Buddha) so that those of great capacity and great vessels might attain awakening upon hearing [the Dharma] once and become Buddhas on the spot.
This is indeed the ultimate goal. Guōshān Yī'ān Jué, the Head Seat, from his youth donned...

Master Zhi possessed an air and character that were beyond the mundane. He exhaustively explored the sūtras and śāstras and attained profound mastery in Chan meditation, achieving a subtle elegance of self-realization.

He pierced through those points where ancient masters had failed to reach. Moved by pity for the various scriptures, histories, biographies, and annals, which were not interconnected in their chronological sequences, he [composed this work].

It was not convenient for perusal. Therefore, regarding those divine wonders of successive dynasties that had remained hidden and unmanifest, he sought them out extensively and exhaustively, working by lamplight until his oil was consumed, to compile them into a single work titled the *Shishi Tongjian* (Comprehensive Mirror of the Śākya Clan).
Furthermore, he donated his own funds to carve the woodblocks so as to enlighten future generations.
Were it not for the fact that he possessed the auspicious bones of a former life, how could he have applied himself with such dedication? Fellow seekers of the Way, gentlemen!
If you wish to examine the life stories and deeds of the various sages, worthies, patriarchs, and masters of antiquity and the present, you must first read this collection.

It is like ascending the summit of Mount Sumeru; once the four continents are clearly visible before one’s eyes, one will realize that this collection was compiled with great diligence in its resolve and that its benefit is no small matter.
Having finished reading it, this old monk willingly steps back three paces and adds these few words as a defilement [to its purity].
At the end of the compilation it says:
On the Chrysanthemum Festival of the sixth year of the Xianchun era, Jianfu used the unusual manuscript of Master Cuo to compose the preface to the *Tongjian* of the Śākyamuni School.
Generally speaking, for those who enter the Way, their faculty of faith must be firm and their power of aspiration must be vast.
Such sincere seekers are the most difficult to lead into the Way. This is because the Way has its sovereign lord and its supporting wings; the sovereign lord is the Tathāgata.
To entrust this task to a single person would leave them with more than enough capacity;

yet as for those who serve as its wings and feathers, the sages and worthies of antiquity and the present have employed thousands and hundreds of people, and even then they feared it was insufficient.

Therefore, from the manifestation of traces in the Western Heaven (India) and the display of form in the Eastern Land (China), beyond the thirty-three patriarchs, there have been various manifestations—whether real or provisional—which are inconceivable and beyond deliberation, and cannot be grasped.
Those who have recorded these matters in full detail are all true descendants of the Tathāgata and followers of the path of the orthodox teaching.
Even if one were to cite only one or two individuals, it would still cause people to be inspired upon hearing their reputation.

Now, the Venerable Yiguan composed the *Shishi Tongjian* (General Mirror of the Śākya Clan), following the annalistic style of Confucian histories, beginning from the jiayin year of King Zhao of Zhou and ending with Emperor Gong of the Later Zhou.

From the Gengshen year [of the Zhou dynasty] to the present, a total of one thousand nine hundred and thirty years have passed. The various patriarchs and masters have recorded these matters exhaustively without omission;

their collection is most abundant and their compilation most diligent. These works were not included among the holdings of the Three Palaces or the Four Libraries, nor were they seen in the Dàyǒu or Lángqíng repositories.
Alas! Just as jars, basins, hairpins, and bracelets are all made of the same pure gold, so too are the *guī*, *bì*, *cóng*, and *huáng* jade ornaments of one substance.

There is nothing that is not precious jade; from its roots, branches, trunk, and joints, there is nothing that is not sandalwood. Whether black, white, dark, or yellow, there is nothing that is not the Tamer of Men (the Buddha).
My friend Lan Hanqing once obtained a Song edition of this text in the region of Jingchu; regarding it as an extraordinary book, he kept it with great secrecy and parsimony.

When the Honorable Official Hancheng passed away, my father managed his funeral affairs. Now that the surviving heirs have come from afar to entrust me with his遗书 (posthumous writings), I feel as if a *utpala* flower has appeared once more.
However, upon cataloging these texts, I find there are occasional errors such as those of a pig crossing a river;

furthermore, as many years have passed, the paper has faded and the ink has blurred, resulting in some omissions. It happened that I was convalescing in the mountains, having withdrawn from all worldly affairs.

Having much leisure, I daily examined the scriptural treasury, once again collating and verifying it: I excised redundancies, supplemented omissions, corrected errors, and left doubtful passages as lacunae.
Furthermore, I consulted biographical records and inquired of virtuous teachers until the collection was finally complete.
I venture to reveal this secret from within the curtains and intend to enshrine it within the repositories of the sacred mountains.
I respectfully entrust it to the carvers, hoping that those of like mind may all together achieve the cause for attaining the Way. Thus I speak.
On the day the Buddha appeared in the world during the Bingyin year of the Tianqi era, the lay devotee Chan-ti, Bi Xizhi, respectfully wrote this preface to the *Shishi Tongjian*.

Among the various schools of historiography, none exceed the two forms of annals and biographies. Master Zu Qiu [Zuo] and Master Gu [Gongyang] composed their commentaries based on the classics and then wrote the biographies accordingly.
He compiled this work as an annalistic history. From the era of Longmen onwards, the histories of successive dynasties have all followed the biographical (liezhuan) format.
Master Sima Wenzheng composed the *Tongjian* (Comprehensive Mirror), emulating the style of the *Zuo Zhuan*; it spans several thousand years across dozens of successive courts.

The rise and fall, the preservation and destruction, the worthy and the unworthy, and the gains and losses of successive dynasties can all be grasped in their general outlines by opening a single scroll; those who read history find this advantageous.

Alas, since the rise of historical recording, the annalistic style (biannian) has become prevalent, and as the excellence of events and rhetoric has increased, the Way and its principles have declined.
I cannot conceal this from the historians. Yet, history is not solely for the use of the Confucian school. The Great Canon contains five thousand [volumes].
The remaining volumes record the Three Vehicles, floating like the five carriages of Master Hui; the Dharma surged eastward, its fame gathered in collections that have further increased day by day.
Yet, as for the principles of world-transcendence—the sounds from the beginning of the kalpa—it is not easy to peer behind their barriers.

The golden scrolls are vast and profound, the jade cases are densely layered; they are like the vision of the Sea God Ruo, which those of initial capacity, whose roots of faith are not yet firm, find difficult to fathom.

I truly hope you will not turn back upon reaching the cliffs. During the Song dynasty, there was the Chan Master Jue of Kuoshan, who compiled the Buddhist scriptures and expounded them through Confucian prose.
Adopting the methods of Sima Qian, he authored the *Shishi Tongjian* (Comprehensive Mirror of the Buddhists), spanning from the Western Zhou to the Five Dynasties.

He gathered the sacred truths and divine traces of the past without omission; neither a formal sutra nor a commentary, it stands as a distinct body of work in its own right. It records the sharp, piercing exchanges between the ancient masters.
What is called the essential and subtle is speech devoid of worldly meaning; yet, amidst this, erroneous views have arisen.

Since both the principles and the demonic obstacles have been dispelled, one reaches the depths of both the profound intent and the numinous texts. This is truly a fine historical record for the Buddhist tradition and a great precious raft across the sands of India.
My son, Xi-zhi, has been bedridden with illness for years; he has purified his mind by studying Buddhism and daily examines the Great [Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra].
I kept this collection close at hand, never letting it leave my hands. I happened to obtain these surviving fragments of the Song edition from Lan Hanqing of Min.

Treasuring them like a rare *tanhua* blossom, we planned together to carve them into woodblocks so that all who aspire to the Way might behold the spiritual manifestations and extraordinary wonders of the sages and worthies of successive dynasties, understand their intentions, and collectively serve as wings and feathers for the Patriarchs, together clarifying the causal conditions of this one great matter. Universally...

They deliver sentient beings so that all may ascend to perfect enlightenment; thus they plant the seed of resolute faith, give rise to vast vows, and shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi—these are none other than the various patriarchs and masters appearing in the world.

Long ago, Lord Wang Jing was censured by the Buddhist community for his erroneous interpretation of the term *samādhi*, yet Lord Wang Yanzhou could not avoid [the same fate] regarding the term *bimbamala*.

I have long pondered the meanings of the two characters "Li" (利) and "Hua" (果). Having examined them in the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings), I felt as though I had obtained a ship laden with pearls.
Indeed, one must rely on historical records and commentaries; how much more so when it concerns the Tathāgatas, the World-Honored Ones who guide the ten directions of the Śākya clan?
The three vehicles draw beings upward; their words are vast and grand, enough to startle, and their path is pure and remote, difficult to tread.
Were it not for this book being specially recorded, it would be like seeking a reflection in an inverted mirror.

Thus, this book is indeed a chronicle of former sages who transcended the mundane and realized sainthood, as well as a forest of the successes and failures, gains and losses of previous generations. It is truly sufficient to transmit the lamp and prolong its light.
This work, *Hongming* (Illuminating the Propagation), surpasses the various volumes of the *Zhulin qixian lu* (Record of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove) and the *Baotun* (Precious Exhortations).

Jiǎyīn: The twenty-sixth year of King Zhāo (This is the chronology of the Zhou dynasty; various texts differ. Here, it is compiled according to the *Lìdài niǎnpǔ* following the *Jīngshì shū* of Kāngjié).
There is no need to harbor doubts.
Śākyamuni Buddha was the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. On the eighth day of the fourth month of this year, he manifested his birth in Kapilavastu, in Central India.
That country is the center of the trichiliocosm; therefore, the Buddha was born there.
There, his father was King Śuddhodana and his mother was Queen Māyā. On that day, while the Queen was strolling in the Lumbinī Garden, she reached out her hand to grasp a branch of an *aśoka* tree.
The Prince was born from her right side by a miraculous transformation; he immediately took seven steps and pointed his fingers toward heaven and earth, declaring:
"In all the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored. Then, nine dragons from the sky spat forth water to bathe the Great One.

The father-king named his son Siddhārtha (as seen in the *Śākyapuṭa*; however, various biographical records all state that the Buddha was born in the year Jia-yin of King Zhao’s reign—some identifying it as the twenty-fourth year, others as the ninth.

Now, according to Master Lin’s *Bianzheng lun*, based on the chronicle of the Buddha’s birth by the Sui dynasty scholar Yao Changqian, it is definitively the Jia-yin year, the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao’s reign).
On the day the Buddha was born, the rivers and streams of this region overflowed, springs and wells surged forth, and the great earth shook.
A light of five colors pierced the Taiwei constellation and spread throughout the West. King Zhao, struck with wonder, questioned his ministers.
The Grand Astrologer Suyou reported, "In the west, a sage has been born. The King asked, "What will come of this? Suyou replied, "At present, there is no cause for concern."

One thousand years later, the teachings of the Buddha reached this land. The King then engraved an inscription on stone and erected it as a record, burying it at the southern suburban altar for sacrifice (*as recorded in the *Zhou shu yiji*;

He seized an elephant with his hands and hurled it beyond the city walls, then caught it again with his hands. Within the garden were seven each of golden drums, silver drums, stone drums, and iron drums.

Xinwei and Renshen, the forty-fourth year: the Buddha was nineteen years of age. He went out through the four gates of the city to travel and observe. At the eastern [gate...]

To the southwest, he beheld old age, sickness, and death, and gave rise to a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*). At the northern city gate, he saw a renunciant (*pravrajita*) departing, and gave rise to a mind of joyful aspiration.
On the eighth night of the second month, riding his celestial horse, he leaped over the city walls and ascended into the void.
Arriving at Mount Tāṇḍaka, he used his own precious sword to sever his beard and hair. A deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens offered him a saṃghāṭī robe, which he then donned. He entered [the forest].
At Mount Meru, in the place of Ārāḍa Kālāma, he practiced the concentration of the sphere of nothingness for three years (according to the *Zhengzong ji* and other sources).
In the years Gengyou, Jiaxu, and Yihai—

In meditation for another three years— namely the years Bingzi, Dingchou, and Wuyin— for fifty years,
the World-Honored One resided on Mount Gajaśīrṣa, where he lived together with various non-Buddhist practitioners, subsisting daily on hemp and wheat.
A magpie nested atop his dwelling. Because he was without mental activity and without the practice of sensory reception, the non-Buddhists were subdued;

(Comprehensive Record) ○ The Great Brahmā Heavenly King came to the assembly on Vulture Peak and offered golden sāla flowers to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One held up a flower to show the assembly. Among the hundreds of thousands of beings, both humans and devas, none could fathom it; only the monk Kāṣāyadhara broke into a smile.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate of the signless reality.
I entrust this to Mahākāśyapa. Listen to my verse: "The Dharma is fundamentally no-dharma; no..."

"Dharma, dharmas, and also Dharma. Now, at the time of entrusting the non-Dharma, when has Dharma ever been Dharma? (The picking up of the flower and the transmission of the Dharma appear in the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* [specifically the *Brahmā-rāja-prcchā-buddha-sūtra*];

The year of Ren-shen, the fifty-third [of the Buddha’s era]; the seventy-ninth year since the World-Honored One appeared in the world.

Having completed his work of transformation, on the fifteenth day of the second month, between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, as he was approaching parinirvāṇa, after having preached the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he surveyed the three realms and addressed the great assembly, saying: "With the profound *prajñā*, I have surveyed..."
The three realms are fundamentally detached by nature; they are ultimately quiescent, identical in appearance to empty space, and utterly devoid of anything whatsoever.
Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Those who know this are called world-transcenders; those who do not know this are said to be at the beginning of birth and death.
Thus, he entered meditative absorption three times, emerged from it three times, and spoke three times, finally saying: "For these reasons, I now abide in eternal quiescence."

The light was extinguished; this is called Great Parinirvāṇa. He then lay upon his right side on a jeweled couch. In the middle of the night, in profound stillness and silence, he entered Parinirvāṇa.
The jeweled trees turned white, and humans and devas were struck with grief and lamentation. Kāśyapa came from afar to hasten to the site and pay his respects.
The golden coffin opened of its own accord, and his two feet immediately appeared outside the coffin. After the assembly had paid homage to his feet, they returned and the feet re-entered the coffin.

The Tathāgata himself then leaped forth from his chest and was cremated by fire. Devas and humans each divided the *śarīra* relics and erected stupas (*Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, preceding and succeeding sections).
On this day, a violent wind suddenly arose in this region, damaging houses and breaking trees; the earth shook and the shadows of the trees shifted toward the west.

The Imperial Lord of Zǐtóng descended in spirit and spoke these words: "I have heard the words of those beyond the mundane world, which say:"
In the western lands there was a Great Sage, the Ancient Sovereign (Gu Huang), who viewed life and death as morning and evening, and regarded enmity and resentment as dreaming and waking.
Believing that this floating existence is but brief, he sought the state of non-birth (*anutpāda*). I have long admired him;

having recently encountered a reclusive practitioner who sang of him, I said to him: "I have just heard these wondrous principles, which deeply accord with my humble heart. I pray you will grant me some of your wise maxims."
The hermit sighed and said, “He has pointed out to me the seal of the mind and bestowed upon me the True Dharma.

[Sources include the *Fayuan Zhulin* and the *Hongming Ji*. Regarding the accounts of the dream-vision provided by various scholars, the dates of the vision and the arrival of the scriptures often differ; some claim the dream was experienced in the seventh year and the mission returned in the tenth, while others claim the dream occurred in the second year and [the mission returned] in the seventh.]

An envoy was dispatched. He returned in ten years. If one examines these accounts, they are indeed as stated; yet for a journey of tens of thousands of li, how could it have been completed in the space of three years? Furthermore, according to the *Zizhi Tongjian*, the Buddha had already entered China by the eighth year [of the Han era];

thus, if he sought the teachings only in the seventh year, how could the Buddha have already been present in China by the eighth? One can therefore know with certainty that the account of the envoy being dispatched in the seventh year is incorrect. Based on local gazetteers and other records, it is clear that the account of the Emperor being moved by a dream in the third year to seek the teachings, and returning them in the eighth year, is the correct one.

Yihai, the second year [of the Han era]: Mouzi retired from the world to live in seclusion. He resolved his will upon the Buddha-way and composed thirty-seven chapters on "Reasoning to Dispel Delusions.
In one of these texts, there is a question that says: "The Buddha-way is most supreme and most great. Why did Yao, Shun, King Wen, and Confucius not cultivate it?

"How could he possibly surpass the beauty of the sacred works as recorded in the Classics and Traditions? Mōzi said:
"Books need not be the words of Confucius, and medicines need not be the prescriptions of Bian Que. That which accords with righteousness is followed; that which heals illness is excellent.
A gentleman gathers all manner of goodness from many sources to assist his own person. Zīgòng said: "What constant teachers does the Master have? Yao served Jūnchóu."

Shun’s affairs were successfully accomplished and made manifest; Dan (the Duke of Zhou) studied under Lü Wang, and Qiu (Confucius) studied under Lao Dan; yet none of these are recorded in the Six Classics.
Although these four masters were sages, when compared to the Buddha, they are like common birds and beasts compared to the qilin and the phoenix.

Since even Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius were surpassed by him, how much more so is this true for the Buddha, whose wisdom and insight exhaustively penetrate the profound origins of all phenomena—how could one abandon him?
"If one studies the matters and principles of the Six Classics, there may be points that are not recorded by the Buddha; how is it then anything to be wondered at or doubted? Furthermore, he asked:
'The body, hair, and skin are received from one's parents; one dares not damage them. Now, the śramaṇa shaves his head and differs from the common custom;

The father fell into the water. His son rolled up his sleeves, seized him by the head, and overturned him, causing the water to flow out from his mouth, whereby the father’s life was restored.
Now, to seize someone by the head and overturn them is the greatest act of filial impiety; yet, it was done to preserve the father’s body.

Had he stood with folded hands, merely practicing the ordinary rites of a filial son, the father’s life would have perished in the water. Confucius said: "One may be associated with the Way, but one cannot be associated with its ultimate realization."
"Expediency" refers to what is appropriate for the occasion. When Taibo cut off his hair and tattooed his body, Confucius praised him as possessing "supreme virtue" and never disparaged him.
Viewed from this perspective, if one possesses great virtue, one is not constrained by minor matters.

A śramaṇa renounces family wealth, abandons wife and children, and refrains from listening to music or beholding beautiful forms; this may be called the ultimate form of yielding. How could this be contrary to the sages?
[The Master] said: "Is this not consistent with filial piety? Yu Rang swallowed charcoal and lacquered his body; Nie Zheng covered his face and took his own life;

Lady Bo stepped into the fire; and Gao Xing cut off her own nose. When the gentleman acts with courage and dies for the sake of righteousness, we have never heard of anyone censuring him for destroying or sacrificing himself."
The śramaṇa shaves his hair to advance in virtue; compared to these four types of men, is he not far removed? He asked again: "There is nothing greater in filial impiety than having no descendants.
The śramaṇa abandons his wife and children and discards his wealth and goods; how does this not contradict the practice of filial piety? The Master said:
"That which is long on the left must be short on the right; that which is broad in front must be narrow behind. Wife, children, and wealth are but the remnants of the world."

To keep one’s person pure and non-active is the subtlety of the Dao. The filial son asks: "Between reputation and the person, which is more dear? Between the person and wealth, which is more numerous? It is further said:

"Reciting the Odes and Documents and cultivating ritual propriety, so that one's legacy is transmitted among the villagers and one's reputation spreads far and wide—this is what the scholar of middling capacity practices, but it is of no concern to those who are tranquil and dispassionate.
Thus, Xu You dwelt in a nest upon a tree, and Yi and Qi starved on Mount Shouyang.
Confucius praised his virtue, saying, "He who sought benevolence and attained it. He did not hear [Confucius] criticizing him for lacking descendants or wealth.
A śramaṇa cultivates the Way and its Virtue to replace the pleasures of worldly wandering; he returns to goodness and virtue to substitute for the joys of wife and children.
This is not considered strange; what, then, would be considered strange? Again, he asked: Mencius said, "I have heard that one uses the Xia..."

"One transforms the barbarians; I have never heard of using the barbarians to transform the Chinese. You, sir, study the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, yet you abandon it to study the arts of the barbarians—is this not delusion?
He replied, "You merely see the splendor of ritual regulations while remaining blind to the reality of the Dao and its Virtue."
To peer into the brilliance of a torch is not yet to behold the sun of the celestial court. What Mencius spoke of was merely a critique of one-sidedness.
Formerly, Confucius wished to dwell among the nine tribes of the Yi, saying, "When a gentleman dwells there, what shall be considered uncivilized? Yu emerged from the Western Qiang and became a sage;
Youyu was born among the Di and served as a hostage for Qin. Furthermore, the *Zhuangzi* states that the North Star is the pivot of the heavens.
It is located north of the human realm. Judging from this, it is not necessarily the center of heaven that the land of Han occupies.
Buddhist scriptures maintain that the realms of the ten directions are all encompassed within the Buddha’s transformation, and his Dharma is the source of all phenomena;
therefore, I again revere and study it. Why should one abandon the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius? Gold and jade do not harm each other; they are like the precious jade of Sui.
They do not obstruct one another. This means that people are deluded; they are merely deluding themselves. Question: The Way of the Buddha is unconditioned and tranquil.

Yet, many people of the world revile it, saying its teachings are vast and empty, difficult to apply, and its emptiness (xu-wu) difficult to believe. Why is this? Answer: The ultimate flavor does not accord with the common palate;
the Great Sound does not harmonize with the common ear. When the Xianchi was performed or the Xiao-shao was played, no one [could appreciate them].
It is harmony. When the strings and songs of Zheng, Wei, and Zhang are played with the melodies of the current age, people will surely clap their hands without being prompted.
Yet Han Fei, with his view through a tube, slandered Yao and Shun; and Jieyu, with his preoccupation over the distinction between a hair’s breadth and a cow’s tail, reviled Zhongni.
Both were those who indulged in the trivial while neglecting the great. Indeed, to hear the *qing-shang* scale and call it *jiao* is not merely a matter of plucking strings.
This is the fault of the listener, who lacks keen hearing. It is not that the jade of He is base, but that the observer lacks clear vision.
The Great Way is non-action; it is not what the vulgar perceive. It is not made noble by those who offer praise.
He was not disparaged by those who sought to defame him (the remainder of the text is found in the *Hongming ji* collection).

He was appointed as an assistant to his own officials. Sengzu remained firm in his resolve and did not waver, and consequently met his death. Sengzu’s younger brother, Fazuo, whose virtuous conduct was profound and sincere, was also killed.

Having finished distributing the clothing and provisions, the next day he went to visit Fotucheng (Foguang). His words offended Cheng’s disposition, and Cheng ordered his arrest. Daosheng (Daizu) then said, "I have come to bring this matter to an end.
This is a karmic bond formed over many lifetimes; it is not a matter of today alone. At that time, the Qiang and Hu tribes of the Long Mountains were about to escort him back to the Central Kingdom.
On the road, they heard that he had been killed, and everyone desired to take revenge for Daosheng. They led their cavalry to oppose Fotucheng.

In battle, he captured Kuang alive and executed him. He then divided Zu’s remains and established temples for each portion, where they were venerated with ritual services (according to the *Benzhuan*;
Kuang is also recorded as Fu in some versions).

After Chengyuan had passed away, Daozhen consulted with Chengji and Chenghu regarding the finalization of the texts.
Daozhen himself translated thirty-six fascicles of scriptures.
Guiyou (the first year of Jianxing of Emperor Min of Jin). [3] [3] [6]. Emperor Min ascended the throne in Chang’an.
He established the Tongling and Baima monasteries (*Lidai Fabao Ji*).
In this year, two stone images of the Buddhas Kāśyapa of the Past and Kāśyapa of the Future arrived by sea and entered the Wusong River. They were seen from afar at the mouth of the Hudu estuary.
It drifted away. Daoists and sorcerers went out to meet it, but the wind and waves were surging and tumultuous.

Zhu Ying of Wu County, who had long been devoted to the True Dharma, then went with several others to welcome the image. Thereupon, it came of its own accord along the current. Upon its back was an engraved inscription.
When they took hold of it and boarded their boat, it was as light as a feather. They then enshrined it at Tongxuan Temple. This was indeed from the time of the Buddhas of antiquity.

The teachings of the Dharma likewise flowed and transformed this land (*Fayuan*). ○ As for Zhu Fahu’s translations of one hundred and seventy-five scriptures, it was at this point that his pen was laid down (*Shijiaolu*).
On the day of Jiashu (the second day), [a meteor] fell to the earth, followed by three suns appearing in the west and moving toward the east.

At that time, Shi Le was stationed with his troops at Gepo, where he was solely engaged in slaughter. Fotudeng wished to convert him. Shi Le had a general named Guo Helü, who had long been a devotee of the Buddha-dharma;
Fotudeng went to see him, and Helü subsequently received the five precepts and honored him as his disciple.

During the Battle of Suliao, Fu Jian’s subordinates were engaged in combat. Fo Tucheng predicted the outcome of every victory and defeat in advance. Because Shi Le harbored suspicions regarding Tucheng’s extraordinary insights, he questioned him, saying, "There is a 'Cheng' here.

Shi Le said, "He is a gift from Heaven," and summoned him. Shi Le asked, "How does Buddhism possess such spiritual power? Tucheng knew that Shi Le did not understand the profound principles of the Dharma and could be led along by means of worldly wonders.
He then requested permission to burn incense; he took water in an alms bowl and recited mantras over it. In a short while, [lotuses] grew within it.
The blue lotus flower was radiant and dazzling to the eye; Fu Le revered it for this reason (according to his biography).

over six hundred scrolls of sutras and vinayas were translated, one hundred and eighty monasteries were established, and there were more than three thousand seven hundred monks and nuns.

During the Eastern Jin dynasty of the Sima clan, the capital was Jiankang. There were twelve rulers for a total of one hundred and four years.

Dingchou (the first year of Jianwu under Emperor Yuan [Sima Rui]; the second year of Linjia under Liu Cong of Han; the reign of Shi Le of Later Zhao; the seventh year of Yuheng under Taizong of Cheng; the fifth year of Jianxing under Xiping Yuangong Shi of Liang;
the reign of Gaozu of Yan; and the first year of Yulu under Pingwen Di of Dai):

The śramaṇa Zhu Qian, style name Fahu, possessed profound talent and understanding. Since the beginning of the Yongjia era, he had fled the chaos and crossed the Yangtze River; it was at this time that—
Emperor Yuan, as well as Chancellor Wang Maohong and Grand Marshal Yu Yuangui, all admired his character and virtue,
befriending him with deep respect (as recorded in his biography).
Wu-yin (the first year of Wenxing) &; (Former Zhao) (Liu Yao’s first year of Guangchu) &;&;&; (6) &;&; (2);

Zhu Qian often wore wooden clogs when entering the palace halls. People of the time marveled at his lofty character and moral integrity, for he was initially unaware that there were markets or court audiences.

Emperor Yuán established the Wàguān and Lóngxīng monasteries. He assembled a thousand monks from Dānyáng and Jiànyè (as recorded in the Liùtiē).

Gengchen (the 3rd year). (3) (2) (8) (4). At Waguan Temple in Yangdu, Zhu Sengfu, on account of the prevailing view that the spirit has form—merely being more subtle than the myriad things—composed the "Treatise on the Formlessness of the Spirit.
To refute [this view], he stated in brief: "If there is form, there must be number; if there is number..."
That which has form is finite. Since the spirit is inexhaustible, one knows that those who are formless and invisible are revered and submitted to.
On the day of Xin-si (the fourth), Chenglie Gong (Mao) [and] Huidi (He Zhuanyuan) were present. At that time, Fotucheng said to Shi Le:
"When a ruler’s virtue is spread and his transformation is pervasive, then the four auspicious creatures manifest their omens. Political...

When the path of decadence is extinguished, the spirits of wisdom and prosperity manifest their portents; these are constantly perceived through appearances, and signs of fortune or calamity follow one's actions.
This is a constant testimony throughout antiquity and the present. Shi Le was greatly pleased by this, and those who were condemned to execution were spared eighteen (according to the *Benzhuan*).

Renwu (the first year of Yongchang): [5] [4] [2]. Śrīmitra of India (translated here as Jiyou) formerly abdicated his royal throne to enter the monastic life. He arrived in this land during the Yongjia era and subsequently traveled across the Yangtze River.

Guiwei (the first year of Da’ning, Emperor Shao of the Ming Dynasty). [6] [5].
Emperor Ming was intelligent and possessed the capacity for decisive judgment. Among those who possessed the virtue of a ruler during the Jin dynasty, he alone was such a person.
He frequently honored the practice of fasting and promoted merit by establishing the two monasteries of Huangxing and Daochang (as recorded in the *Liutie*).
Jia-shen (2nd year). [7] [6]. Zhu Fasheng’s spiritual realization was transcendent and his profound discernment surpassed that of others.
He studied under Dharmarakṣa, who held him in high esteem. Later, he went to Dunhuang and established a monastery there.
He attracted his fellow students, causing even wolves and jackals to reform their hearts. The Rong and Di peoples came to know the rites of propriety, and the Great Transformation spread to the West.

The source of the moat for the city walls of Xiangguo suddenly ran dry. Shi Le requested that Fotucheng provide water.

Fotucheng went to the head of the source, which had already been parched like a tortoise shell for a long time. Fotucheng burned incense and recited mantras over it; after three days, the water suddenly began to flow slightly.
The small dragon followed out. After a short while, the waters surged greatly, filling the ditches in terror.
Dinghai (the second day of the month). November: Su Jun incited a rebellion. The Emperor fled to Shitou.

Wuzi (3) (11) [The year of] the extinction of Later Zhao; (Tahe Year 1) [the year of] the destruction of Han Zhao and the seizure of the Central Plains.
Shi Le wished to battle Liu Yao and consulted Fotudeng regarding it. Fotudeng examined the sound of the bell and knew that he would certainly capture Yao.

On the fifth day of the third month of the first year of Jianping (342 CE), during the reign of Shi Le of Zhao, Zhang Xi, a native of Linhai, obtained a gold-copper lotus flower from the sea; its pedestal was then set upon the golden [statue] of Gao Kui.
The Buddha’s footprints were thus solemnly and perfectly manifested. That evening, the sacred image emitted light that reached the heavens, and celestial music resounded clearly;
this ceased after two nights (*Tongji*). In this year, Shi Le proclaimed himself the Heavenly King of the Great Zhao and acted as the Emperor.
He served Fotudeng with ever-increasing devotion and respect; whenever he undertook any matter, he would invariably consult him before acting. He was titled "Great Monk" (Daheshang).

In the *xinmao* year (the sixth year), Shi Le’s beloved son Bin died of illness.

From then on, Shi Le and his sons mostly resided at Tancheng’s temple to be cared for by him.
In the seventh year of the Renchen era (273 CE), the śramaṇas Kang Sengyuan, Kang Fachang, Zhi Mindu, and others all crossed the river. Sengyuan was well-versed in both Buddhist and secular classics;

He maintained a life of purity and frugality. Wang Maohong of Langya mocked him, saying, "Your nose is high and your eyes are deep.

Zhiyuan replied, "The nose is the mountain of the face; the eyes are the abyss of the face. If the mountain were not high, it would lack its spirit; if the abyss were not deep, it would lack its clarity.
At the time, this was considered a brilliant response.

He recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. When Hehuang was saving people from a disaster, someone who had fallen ill requested his assistance. Suddenly, the mountain streams and waters surged in a violent flood.

for the most part, they served the Buddha, vying with one another to construct temples and shave their heads to enter the monastic life. The Director of the Imperial Library, Wang Du, submitted a memorial stating that it would be appropriate to prohibit the people of the country from leaving home to become monks.
Emperor Taiwu issued an edict, saying: "I am unworthy to rule. As for the common people of the various regions who delight in serving the Buddha, I shall allow them to do so specifically."
[The Master] listened. Tancheng possessed the *dhāraṇī* of Dharma-Constancy (*dharmadhātu-dhāraṇī*). His two disciples were thousands of li away; whatever they said, Tancheng knew it all.
Consequently, the people of the country constantly cautioned one another, saying, "Do not give rise to evil thoughts;
the Great Monk knows them all. Wherever Tancheng was, no one among the people dared to spit, urinate, or defecate in that direction.
The way of his spiritual transformation and its resonance with all things was such that, since the Great Teaching first arrived in the East, it reached its height during the time of Fotucheng.

In the year Bingshen (the second year of the era), Kang Fasuī compiled the *Piyujing* (Sūtra of Parables) in ten fascicles (a collection of essential matters from various sūtras; it is currently included in the canon). ○ Zhidao Gen translated sūtras.
Seven fascicles.

Zhu Fayu had long served under Fotudeng. Possessing brilliant talent and extensive learning, he once collaborated with Kang Falang and others to compile [commentaries on] the scriptures.

He used "matching meanings" (*geyi*) to instruct his disciples. At the beginning of his career, Fǎlǎng vowed to travel to the Western Regions. On the road, he encountered a monk suffering from dysentery; Fǎlǎng stayed behind to care for him.
When the seventh day arrived, the entire room was filled with a fragrant scent. Only then did he realize the monk’s extraordinary nature.

Thereupon, he traveled extensively through various kingdoms, thoroughly investigating the sutras and śāstras. Later, while lecturing at Zhōngshān, he had several hundred disciples. Among them was a disciple named Lìng...
Shao was constantly in meditative absorption (dhyāna) and did not emerge for several days.

On the *wùxū* day (the fourth day of the month), during the first year of the Jian’guo era of Shi Yijian (corresponding to the first year of Hanyuan of the Han dynasty, when Li Shou, the Zhongzong of Han, had killed [his predecessor] Qi and changed the era name), Tianpeng of Nanyang—whose family was devoted to the faith—was regularly hosting a monastic assembly (*saṃgha-melaka*).
One day, the food overturned onto the ground, and he was utterly bewildered.

However, he did not keep count of the number [of people]. A monk said, "The poor man’s alms-bowl has provided sufficient food for the entire assembly. After the meal, he threw his bowl into the air and departed.
Immediately, they carved a wooden image of him and worshipped it; it would regularly report matters of misfortune or fortune to his family (from the *Gantong zhuan*).
Jihai (the fifth year). This was the year Wang Dao passed away. Dao was thoroughly versed in Buddhist principles, simple and frugal with few desires.

Having served as a high minister for three reigns, his granaries held no stored grain and his clothing did not include double layers of silk (according to the *Book of Jin*). Dao had a younger brother named Daobao, who renounced worldly glory to become a monk, becoming renowned for his learning and conduct.
[From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*].

In the gengzi year (360), while Emperor Cheng was still a minor, Yu Bing, acting as regent by virtue of being the maternal uncle of the Emperor, submitted a memorial proposing that śramaṇas should perform the full rites of deference toward the sovereign. Shang... [text fragment] ...shou.
The Secretariat Director He Chong and others deliberated that one should not perform the ritual of bowing down; the official evaluation and the discussion of the *boshi* concurred with Chong’s view.

However, the Gate Secretariat (Menxia) followed the imperial will and issued a rebuttal. The Palace Attendants (Puyue), Chu Yi and others, submitted a memorial stating that they would not alter the established method of virtuous practice.
This was intended to harmonize the aspirations of all under heaven and to continue the legacy of the late Emperor; thus, in terms of righteousness, this course of action was deemed superior.
Binggu said, "The 'Exhaustion of Reverence' refers to the ultimate limit of respect, while the 'Regulations for Subordinates' refers to the provisional use of ceremonial attire.

To transcend these by opposing them and to treat secular rites with arrogance—I do not approve of this. Chong and the others again submitted a memorial, stating: "If one order were to require them to prostrate, it would utterly destroy their dharma.

The custom of cultivating goodness would be abandoned during the Age of Sages. Furthermore, the world has passed through three dynasties and people have become increasingly enlightened; yet even now, you do not permit it."

The imperial decree was not rescinded. The King, however, remained unconvinced and issued another edict stating: "If the distinction between the honorable and the humble is not maintained, the royal teachings will not be unified.

To allow two [systems] leads to disorder. Chong and the others submitted three memorials in defense, stating: "From the Han, Wei, and Jin dynasties down to the present, we have heard of no such dissenting opinions.
How could śramaṇas now dare to be negligent regarding the rites of respect? Whenever they burn incense and offer prayers, their vows are always..."
First, regarding the simplicity of the state’s ritual etiquette: this is essentially a matter of adhering strictly to the law.
Therefore, the former sages did not reform it, nor did they require prostrations; thus, there is no deficiency in accordance with the law.

By benefiting others through what is advantageous to them, the sovereign above enjoys the grace of heaven’s covering and earth’s supporting, while below there are those who maintain integrity and cultivate goodness. Consequently, the contentious debate was finally quelled (*Hongming ji*).
In the seventh year of the Xinchou cycle (561), the nun Jingjian of Zhulin Temple saw a celestial maiden holding flowers of five colors come from the sky to welcome her.
She then ascended straight up into the air; the path she traveled appeared like a rainbow stretching directly toward heaven (*Tongji*).
In the fifth month of the Renyin year (8), Emperor Cheng passed away.
This emperor had founded the two monasteries of Zhongxing and Luye and had gathered a thousand monks who were experts in the study of translated scriptures and their meanings (from the *Liutie*).
Gui-mao (the year Jian’an 1 under Emperor Kangdi): At that time, He Zhun, styled Youdao, was noble-minded and had few desires.

Although summoned by both the provincial and metropolitan governments, he did not accept. His elder brother, He Chong, held the weighty position of a high minister, and his influence dominated the age.
Yet Zhun wore his sash loosely at his humble gate, withdrew from worldly affairs, and devoted himself solely to reciting the Buddha’s teachings.
[He was] merely a reciter of the sutras (according to the *Book of Jin*).
Jiǎchén (the Emperor died in the ninth month; Mùdì, the Xìozōng, Lǎn, ascended the throne). [Year] 10: [Guīyì Hóu Shì, Tàihé Year 1]. [Year] 11: Zhú Fǎhuì arrived in Xiāngyáng.
He was able to conceal his body and could know of matters concerning people’s good and ill fortune (according to the *Monastic Biographies*).

In the year Yisi (the first year of Yonghe, under Emperor Mu’s reign), the monk Shandao from Dunhuang wore only coarse hemp clothing and was neither afraid of cold nor heat. He did not lie down day or night, abstained from grain, and subsisted on pine nuts and resin.
He delighted in dwelling in the mountains; however, when mountain spirits manifested their forms to test him, he remained entirely undaunted.
Jusè was the Governor of Fuling. He sent horsemen to meet him, but Kāi traveled on foot.

Bingwu (2), the twelfth month, the first year of Jianning: In the first month, He Chong passed away.
Chong’s courtesy name was Cidao. Previously, Ruan Yu had once jestingly said to him, "Your ambition encompasses the universe, and your courage surpasses that of antiquity.
Chong examined the reason for this remark, and Yu replied, "I am still unable to manage even a commandery of several thousand households."
"Your Excellency plans to become a Buddha—is this not truly magnificent? Thereafter, his family members served the Buddha with great devotion.
His grandson Shangzhi, as well as Dian Yin and others, all established great principles and elucidated the Buddha-dharma (from the *Benzhuan*).
Dingwei (3) [Year 13] (Han 2) [The year of the Jin conquest]; [Reign of] Prince Chonghua, the Jinglie Gong, Year 35.
Viceroy Hu reported to the Grand Astrologer: "A 'Star of the Immortal' has appeared; there must be a man of high character entering our borders.

at that time, Shi Tao sought his treatment, but the result was exactly like that of [the previous] tiger. [The Emperor] commanded Fotucheng to converse with him all day long.

Fotucheng said, "This practitioner observes the rise and fall of the state. If he departs, there will surely be great chaos. In the year Jihyou (379 AD), Daokai crossed south to Xuchang. Shortly thereafter, Ye...

On the wu-shen day (the fourth), [and on] the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the twelfth month, Fotudeng, knowing that the Shi clan was about to perish, said to his disciple Fazuo: "The Shi clan shall..."
"I shall extinguish myself before I fall into disorder; I have already begun my transformation. He then sent a messenger to take his leave of Zhao Jun, the Lord of Qi.
Jun was startled and asked, "Has the Great Monk suddenly abandoned our kingdom because of some calamity? He immediately went to the temple in person to console Fotudeng. Fotudeng said:
To be born and to enter death is the constant way of the world. Longevity and brevity are fixed by destiny; there is no means by which the state can increase or diminish them.

One who sets their heart upon the Buddha-dharma ought to receive blessings from the community; yet, if they administer government with ferocity and cruelty, allowing punishments to overflow indiscriminately, they will specifically violate the sacred scriptures and ultimately receive no blessings or protection.

Only by being able to spread benevolent governance might their reign be prolonged. Ji Long was overcome with grief and lamentation, knowing that [the Emperor] would surely pass away. He immediately...
He had the burial pit excavated and the tomb prepared; on the eighth day, he sat upright and passed away. Fotucheng was eight feet tall, with a dignified and elegant bearing.
He possessed a profound mastery of the deep sutras and was well-versed in secular treatises. His virtuous influence transformed the cruel and violent, and his compassion permeated all living beings.

He was one hundred and seventy years old and had entered the Way for one hundred and nine years. He did not drink wine beyond the age of ten and did not eat after midday, never failing to observe the precepts.
During the Li era, he established eight hundred and ninety-three monasteries, and his disciples who received his teachings numbered in the millions.
Later, a monk came from Yongzhou and reported to Shi Jilong that Fotudeng had entered the Guanzhong region.
Jilong ordered the tomb to be opened, but only a block of stone remained. Jilong sighed and said, "The stone is I myself; the Great Monk has buried me and departed. I am about to die."
Consequently, he fell ill. The following year, Shi Jilong died, and the state fell into great chaos; thus, the Shi clan was indeed extinguished (*Book of Jin*).
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states: When Shi Hu first encoffined Fotudeng, he placed the monk’s bowl and staff inside the coffin. Later, Ran Min ascended the throne.
When the coffin was opened, only the alms bowl and staff remained. Tian Rong’s *Zhao Ji* states: "Before his death, Fo Tucheng personally prepared his own burial vault.

Since Cheng knew the tomb would certainly be opened, and moreover, his corpse had departed by means of transformation, how could he have prepared it in advance? This must be an error on the part of Rong."
Jiyou (the fifth year): [Zhao] (Shi Hu died; the state fell into great chaos; Ran Min established himself as ruler). [Liang] 37. [Yan] Junyuan 12.
Zhu Fotiao had long been a disciple of Tancheng. He resided at Changshan Temple for many years. Sometimes he manifested multiple bodies in other places, or entered the mountains for months on end.
Once, carrying several pecks of dried rice, he returned to Changshan with a surplus remaining. While traveling through the mountains, he encountered snow. Fotiao...

He entered a tiger’s cave to stay the night. When the tiger returned, he lay down with it; later, he himself determined the day of his passing. People from near and far all arrived. Tiao said, "The human body is impermanent.
If one can focus the mind on true purity, though our physical forms eventually diverge, we shall surely share the same realization.
He sat upright and passed away. Later, when a disciple entered the mountains, he saw Tiao upon a cliff. The assembly prostrated and asked, "Is the Master still here? Tiao—
He said, "I am always here, yet you do not see me. The multitude opened the coffin together, and only the robes and shoes remained (according to his biography).
On the gengxu day (the sixth day), [Ran Min changed the state name to Wei and Shi Zhi established himself at Xiang; Fu Hong of Qin occupied Chang'an].

As the shell broke, a chick emerged and walked about, but after a brief moment, both vanished together. Only then did Zhi Dun achieve awakening; from then on, he maintained a vegetarian diet.

For the rest of his life, he maintained "external friendships" with Xie An, Wang Xizhi, Wang Qia, Liu Hui, Yin Hao, Xu Hu, Xi Chao, Sun Chuo, Huan Yanbiao, Wang Jingren, He Chong, and others—all of whom were renowned figures of their generation.

He [Hui]yundun composed an inscription to exhort him, which said: "Be diligent, be diligent! The Ultimate Way is not far off.

Yet within the vast and boundless Three Realms, one remains long bound in a distant exile. Guard the clear prohibitions with care, and set your will upon non-action," and so forth. Later, he moved to Mount Shicheng.

He established Xigu Temple, where he lived on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams, setting his aspirations upon the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Later, he went to Shan-yin and lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*.
Xu Xun served as the presiding host, and they engaged in debates on doctrinal principles several times; those who listened were filled with admiration and submission (according to his biography).

Śramaṇa Dānakāra arrived at the capital. Later, he entered Mount Luofu, where he dwelt alone in a thatched hut in a state of profound detachment.

He passed away at over one hundred years of age beyond the mundane world. By imperial decree, his disciples were instructed to place his remains within a stone chamber. Later, at the beginning of the Xingning era, Yuan Hong...

Senghong said, "The Master’s religious practice was extraordinary among his peers; it is truly like a cicada shedding its shell. He then composed a eulogy for him (as recorded in the *Biographies*).
Gengshen (4) & (2); Emperor You Wei (1st year of Jianxi). Baoke Guang had originally been staying at Shicheng Mountain in Shan since the Yonghe era.
A mountain deity manifested in the forms of a snake and a tiger to terrify him, but Guang remained in peaceful meditation without fear.
The deity then spoke of its own accord, saying it would move to Zhang’an and offer its cave-dwelling to him.
Thereafter, both monastics and laypeople venerated him, and gradually a monastery was established there. Sengguang would often enter meditative absorption and remain without rising for seven days.
He dwelt in the mountains for fifty-three years, reaching an age of one hundred and ten. At the end of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he passed away while sitting upright in meditation.
Xinyou (5th year) [3] (Qin) [Shengping era]; the śramaṇa Yufa Kai was a disciple of Master Lan.
He was skilled in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with its radiating light and was especially proficient in medical arts.
Once he encountered a woman in the fields who was in critical condition. Kai said, "This is easily treated. The host slaughtered a sheep, intending to provide it for his illicit desires.
At the imperial sacrifice, Yao Kai was ordered to take some meat and prepare a broth for the Emperor's consumption. After he had finished, he administered acupuncture to the Emperor.

In an instant, the fetus emerged wrapped in its amnion. That year, Emperor Xiaozong fell ill; Kai examined his pulse and knew he would not recover, so he refused to provide further medical treatment. The Emperor subsequently passed away.

Someone asked the Dharma Master, "Your eminence is lofty, clear-sighted, firm, and simple; why do you keep medical arts in your heart? He replied, "To clarify the six perfections is to eliminate the maladies of the four māras;
to regulate the nine pulses is to treat the ailments of wind and cold. To benefit oneself and others—is this not also permissible?"
Renxu (the first year of Longhe of Emperor Ai, Ping): [4] Zhu Qian withdrew from public view to Mount Shan.

He spent more than thirty years teaching with ease and grace. Among those who threw themselves at his feet as disciples, there were none whose understanding was not comprehensive in both Buddhist doctrine and secular learning.
At this time, Emperor Ai took a great liking to the Buddha-dharma and dispatched an envoy to invite Qian to court. Upon his arrival, he immediately—
He lectured on the *Prajñāpāramitā* at the imperial banquet, and both the Emperor and the court officials praised him highly.

When both of Sengzhao’s parents passed away, and his elder sister Sengdu also died, he suddenly realized the impermanence of life and immediately renounced secular life to become a monk.
After completing his mourning period, Sengzhao wrote a letter to Sengdu, stating that one's hair and skin must not be mutilated and that the ancestral sacrifices must not be abruptly abandoned;

he urged her to heed worldly teachings and revise her far-reaching aspirations, so that her brilliant and radiant talent might flourish during this era of great enlightenment and bring lasting honor to her ancestors.
This spiritual essence provides immediate solace for the human heart’s longings. He also presented five poems, one of which says:

"A human life within this world is as fleeting as the wind passing through a window. Pure sounds may delight the ear; savory flavors may satisfy the palate; fine silks and brocades may adorn the body."
A flower crown may adorn the head; why then do you trouble yourself to shave it? To indulge in emptiness (śūnyatā) while harming existence is not the way for a concubine in a small district;
my concern is merely that you provide for your descendants. Hui-duo replied in a letter: "To serve a ruler to govern a single state is not as good as propagating the Way to save the myriad realms.
To serve one's parents to perfect a single family is not as good as propagating the Way to save the three worlds. As for hair and skin..."
This is merely a colloquial expression used among the laity. Those who have realized the Way know that one must establish oneself and practice the Path.

Furthermore, when one dons the *kāṣāya*, wields the *khakkhara* staff, drinks from clear streams, and chants the *Prajñāpāramitā*, even the robes of kings and dukes, the feasts of the eight delicacies, resounding music, and brilliant splendors cannot compare to this.
If one can reach such profound resonance, then we shall share the same goal in *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, human minds differ as much as faces do. Your lack of delight in the Way is like my own lack of longing for the mundane world.
We, the followers of Yang, shall part forever; our karmic connection spanning ten thousand generations is severed this day. The year draws to a close, and time does not wait for us.
Those who study the Way should take "daily diminution" as their resolve; those who dwell in the world should take "timeliness" as theirs.

"Your Excellency, your years and virtue are both flourishing; you ought to hasten toward some worthy pursuit. Do not let your mind be preoccupied with the Way of men and thus sit idly by while losing the prime of your life.
He further sent five poems in reply, one of which said: "The movement of fate knows no pause; in an instant, the years and seasons pass away."
It is truly because our departure never ceases that it causes the sighs by the river. Have you not heard of Rong Qiqi, who sang a pure song with white hair?
A simple robe can warm the body; who would discuss the adornment of fine silks? Though this world may be called happy, what can one do for those yet to be born?
Sengdu’s resolve was as firm as a rock, such that it could not be turned back; Tiāohuá, having been awakened from her delusions, likewise turned toward the Way.

At that time, he was also preaching the Dharma within the imperial palace.

As Yu Fakai’s practice of the Way had already become renowned, Emperor Ai repeatedly issued edicts. He subsequently departed from the capital to lecture on the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*.

All those of established learning who harbored doubts were without exception enlightened and relieved of their uncertainties. Upon taking his leave to return home, the Emperor generously bestowed money and goods upon him, as did Xie An and Wang Wendu.
He was kind and friendly toward all. He passed away at the age of sixty. Daokai had a disciple named Fawei, who was pure and insightful, possessing a keen and eloquent discernment.
From Hui-lan to Daokai, and from Daokai to Fawei, there were thus three generations who bore a great reputation (from the *Monastic Biographies*).

Hui Dun asked, "How does he compare to Ji Kang? Dao’an replied, "Ji must have exerted great effort to achieve even half [of this]. He asked again, "How does he compare to Yin Hao?
Dao’an said, "In terms of continuous debate and argumentation, he might well rival him; yet as for transcendent excellence and profound origins, Yin Hao possesses a sense of shame."
Later, Chao sent a letter to his old friends, saying: "Master Lin was one who attained the realm of the divine principle; he was profoundly transcendent and uniquely enlightened.

For several hundred years, he alone has sustained and flourished the Great Dharma, ensuring that the True Principle did not perish. This year, he withdrew from official life and submitted a memorial to return to the mountains.

He retired from public life. Subsequently, he withdrew his traces to Mount Shan, where he spent the remainder of his life in the forests and marshes.
He died at the age of fifty-three. Once, someone offered him a horse for the sake of Zhi Dun; Dun accepted it. When some criticized this, Dun said, "I appreciate its divine spirit and fine form;

I am merely keeping it for a while. Later, someone sent him a crane. Dun said, "A crane is a creature that soars toward the heavens; how could it be kept as a mere plaything for the ears and eyes? He then released it.
(Main Biography) During the Qin dynasty, Dharmagupta (translated as Fǎhǎi) from the Western Regions translated three versions of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-mātṛkā*.

When the recitation was finished, the tigers all departed. Shortly thereafter, a great serpent ten spans in girth came racing forward, coiling itself around him and raising its head toward him.
After half a day, it also left. One day, a deity appeared in person and said, "Your disciple [has been here] for the summer retreat."
The son of the Emperor lived in the mountains for over two thousand years. Now, as he was departing for Mount Hanshi, he offered his dwelling to [the Master] as a gift.
Accompanied by the sounding of *bing* drums and the blowing of horns, he ascended into the clouds and departed. Those who practiced meditation and study all went to visit him (from the *Benzhuan*).

"Your Majesty ought to diligently cultivate virtuous governance to block the heavenly reprimand; this humble monk shall, in turn, respond with my utmost sincerity.

In the seventh month, the Emperor passed away. By nature, the Emperor was benevolent and forgiving. He fashioned Buddha images, established vegetarian feasts, ordained monks, and founded monasteries at Changgan Monastery.
A stupa was erected, magnificent and exceptionally grand (*Liutie*). In this year, Dong Zongzhi, a man of Hepu, while fishing in the sea, encountered the circular halo of a Buddha.
He presented it to Gao Kui; the back of the golden Buddha he had obtained fit together perfectly with it. Only after more than forty years was the sacred image complete.

From the Jin through the Sui dynasties—six reigns in total—there were no kings or ministers who did not pay their respects to this numinous image. *Note: The term "li" (靈) refers to a spiritual or numinous manifestation.*
Differing from the One (from the *Jian gantong lu*). ○ During the Former Liang dynasty, the Upāsaka Zhi Shilun of Yuezhi translated the *Sūrata-sūtra* and other scriptures.
Guiyou year (the first year of Ningkang, under Emperor Yao of the Xiaowu era). (9) [Date marker].
Dharma Master Dao’an, since arriving in Xiangyang, has extensively propagated the sutras and their meanings, clarifying them from his own time onward.

He established Tanxi Temple, constructed a stupa, and cast a bronze statue; he was able to initiate these practices himself, and its radiance illuminated the heavens, drawing the entire city to pay their respects and offerings.
The shouts of joy shook the mountains and valleys. Fu Jian, the ruler of Qin, sent a foreign golden image of Maitreya; Dao’an used it as a witness whenever he preached.
One night, the image emitted light that filled the room; upon inspection, it was found that there were *śarīra* relics within its crown.
Xi Zuochi, a distinguished scholar of Xiangyang, first established friendly relations by sending a letter, and subsequently visited Dao’an, introducing himself as "Xi Zuochi of the Four Seas."
Dao’an said, “This is Shi Dao’an, who covers the heavens. They took great delight in meeting one another.

Emperor Xiaowu, admiring the Master’s virtue and wisdom, dispatched an envoy to convey his greetings and issued an edict stating: "Master Dao’an, by means of his virtue and wisdom, illuminates both humans and devas, causing the Great Dharma..."

This became a widespread trend. As a reliance for the common people, it was appropriate that they should receive daily sustenance from the stipends of princes and dukes; the relevant authorities were to provide these at the proper times.

Dao’an firmly declined and would not accept them. Later, when Fu Jian, the ruler of Later Qin, captured Xiangyang, he was delighted to have obtained Dao’an and said to his attendants, "I sent a hundred thousand troops to take Xiangyang, yet I have gained but one person and a half. His attendants asked who this person was.
Tao Kan said: "Master Dao’an is a whole person; Xi Zuochi is but half a person.

Xu Yuan was of refined character and noble discernment. He renounced the glory of high office as a prime minister to don the simple white robes of a monk.

We were just relying on him to propagate the Way and save all living beings when he suddenly passed away; this causes deep sorrow in our hearts. Ten thousand coins shall be granted as funeral expenses to assist in the construction of his burial mound and stupa.
It is decreed that this śramaṇa be accorded a state funeral, beginning with the precedent set by Huiqian. Qian had disciples named Fayou, Fayun, and Fashi.

In that year, he suddenly contracted a wind-illness. He constantly recited the name of Avalokiteśvara, and in a dream, he saw someone cut open his abdomen and wash his intestines.

When life does not burden one's spirit, then that spirit may become darkly unified (*ming*). Because the spirit is darkly unified and one has severed from the realm of extremes, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, although the śramaṇa maintains a protocol of equality with the sovereign of ten thousand chariots and holds his practice in high esteem, he does not accept rank from kings or lords, yet he partakes in their bounty. (4)

At that time, it was acclaimed as a marvelous exposition of the Mahāyāna principles; thus, he was given the title "Mahāyāna" (Mòhēshēn). (From his *Benzhuan*) ○
The monk Sengliang wished to cast a sixteen-foot golden image.

Having heard that the temple of Wu Zixu in Xiangzhou contained many bronze vessels, Sengliang informed the Regional Inspector Zhang Shao, requesting one hundred strong men and seven large ships. Zhang Shao said, "Since the temple is so efficacious, those who violate its sanctity will surely die;
moreover, it is guarded by the Man people—how could you possibly obtain them? Sengliang replied, "If it truly brings blessings..."
As for the merit, it shall be shared with the donor; as for any fault, I shall personally bear it. Yao then provided the man with a boat, and after three days they arrived at the temple.
Before the temple were two cauldrons, each with a capacity of over a hundred hu; within them was a giant serpent more than ten zhang long.
A serpent emerged and blocked the path. Huiliang then took up his monk’s staff and recited incantations over it; the serpent immediately vanished.

Shortly thereafter, a man appeared carrying a ceremonial tablet and said, "I have heard that the Master’s spiritual practice is extraordinary and that your undertaking for the merit of the temple is of great importance. I have come specifically to join you in your joy. He then ordered men to transport the bronze.
Since there was so much copper in the shrine, they took one-tenth of it, yet the boat was already full. Upon returning, they encountered favorable winds and currents.

The various barbarian tribes informed one another, and by the time they pursued him, he was already beyond reach. Upon his return to the capital, the casting of the statue was completed; however, the halo of flames alone remained unfinished.
Emperor Wen had a circular halo made of gold leaf for it and installed it at Pengcheng Temple.
During the Taishi era, Emperor Ming moved the statue to Xianggong Temple (according to the *Monastic Biographies*).
Wu-yin (the fifteenth year); [Year Six]; [The Northern Yan was conquered by the Wei]; [Year Four];
Shi Fasheng of Liang translated the *Sūtra on Casting One’s Body to Feed a Starving Tiger*. Shi Daotai translated the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* and other works.
Buddhabhadra (translated as Juekai) translated the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, completing one hundred fascicles; these were lost when the territory of Liang collapsed into chaos.
40. At present there are only sixty fascicles. Luo Shun was a general of the Pingxi Prefecture and was stationed at Shangming.

While he was hunting hawks in the wild marshes, both the hawk and a pheasant fell. At that time, a fire was burning the wilds, yet a patch of thick grass about three *zhang* in circumference did not catch fire.
Luo Shun then tore through it to search for his hawk and discovered a golden image of a Bodhisattva. The Magistrate of Dingxiang at the time suspected it had been hidden by a thief.
He then descended into the boundary of the talismanic site, where no one lost their image [of the Buddha]. He subsequently collected it and offered it up (*Gantong lu*).

In the year Jīmáo (the sixteenth year), during the Northern Liáng dynasty—which was extinguished by the Wèi—in the fifth year of the Tàiyán era of the Wèi, the monk Shì Dàojiǒng entered a mountain cave to collect stalactites.
His torch went out, and Dàojiǒng was terrified. He then recited the name of Guānyīn. After a short while—
He saw a light like that of a firefly; following it, he was led out [of the water]. Once, while crossing a river on ice at night, the ice broke beneath him midway.
He then called upon Avalokiteśvara, whereupon a certain object suddenly appeared to support his feet, enabling him to reach the opposite bank (from the *Biographies*).

The Dharma Master Lingche (also known as Sengche) passed away. Initially a disciple of Master Huiyuan, Lingche was profoundly versed in the sutras and śāstras and was renowned for his literary talent. He once asked Huiyuan:
The Vinaya prohibits pipes and strings; the precepts forbid song and dance. How could one engage in singing or chanting?
Huiyuan said, "To let thoughts arise upon contact with objects disturbs the emotions and hinders the Way; it is not worth doing.

Consequently, Daocheng abandoned his brush and inkstone and lectured on the Great Dharma, becoming a master revered by his disciples (the *Benzhuan* states he died in the twenty-ninth year). From the Xinchu year of the Yong’an era of Northern Liang until this point...
[The reign of] the second ruler lasted thirty-nine years. Nine persons, both monastics and laypeople, produced over three hundred fascicles of sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras.

In the *gengchen* year (the seventeenth year; the first year of the Taiping Zhenjun era of the Wei dynasty), the śramaṇa Huiguang, who studied under Buddhayaśas, was exceptionally gifted and possessed brilliant insight;
he was then called the "Holy Śrāmaṇera. He composed commentaries and annotated the scriptures.
They were very numerous. Those who entered his gate were like a forest; those who entered his inner chamber numbered nine: the monk Daohui, the Confucian scholar Feng Gun, and others.

○ The śramaṇa Faxi of Mount Zhong, finding no spring at his residence, prayed with utmost sincerity and performed repentance rites, seeking the water of eight virtues from the Anavatapta Lake in the Western Heaven.
After seven days, he dug into the earth and indeed obtained it. ○ Dharma Master Tanshen of Mount Lu revealed [this].
Ji (died at age seventy-nine). Iyepara (translated as "Svāmin" or "Mastery") translated the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* at Pengcheng.
In the year Xinsi (the eighteenth year, the second month), the Indian monk Saṃghadatta arrived at the capital of Song;
while practicing dhyāna in seclusion in the mountains, flocks of birds offered him fruit. In this year, Kang...
The King invited [Dharmamitra]—whose name means "Dharma-Excellence" (Fashou) in Chinese—to reside in Guangling. He was born with joined eyebrows and was skilled in incantations;
he was constantly protected by benevolent deities acting as his guardians. While in the capital, he translated twelve fascicles of *dhyāna* sūtras (*Shijiao lu*).
Renwu (the 19th year): (3) The Western Regions presented Emperor Wen with a fire-cloth (*agni-kṣāra*) *kāṣāya*. At that time, the Emperor himself wore it.
(*Tongji*) ○ In the seventh month, Dharmamitra entered nirvāṇa at Shangsi on Mount Zhong. He was eighty-seven years of age. ○ The Indian monk Saṃghavarman...
Mopa returned to the Western Regions.
On the *gouwei* day (the twentieth) of the ninth month, the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman suddenly passed away at the Jetavana Monastery. He himself spoke of his level of realization.

Regarding the two fruits [of the śrāvaka path], he composed in advance a posthumous text of over a hundred verses, fully explaining his realization that the body is illusory and his attainment of the fruit through diligent cultivation.
At the time of his death, the assembly saw an object resembling a dragon ascend directly from his bed into the air.

In this year, the Dharma Master Shi Huayan passed away at the age of eighty-one. The Emperor issued an edict stating: "Dharma Master Huayan, having completed his cycle of studying the Way, has suddenly departed."
The Emperor granted him fifty thousand coins and fifty bolts of cloth (from his biography). ○ Guṇabhadra translated the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Later, Bodhidharma pointed to this land, saying that only the meaning of this sūtra accords with the direct pointing of the Chan school.
Jiashen (21st year) [5]: Dharmodgata. Twenty-five people traveled through the Western Regions for over twenty years.
All others died, and Dharmodgata alone returned, obtaining the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, which was translated at the capital. Prince Huang of the Wei dynasty was seized by the rebel Cui.
Regarding this slander, Emperor Taizu became suspicious of him. Huáng sought mercy from the śramaṇa Yuán Gāo, who performed the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* repentance ritual for him.
Emperor Taizu then dreamed of his ancestors, who reproached him, saying: "You ought not to harbor suspicion toward the Crown Prince because of slander.

Upon waking, he spoke of this to his ministers, and all the ministers declared that the Crown Prince was without fault; they treated him as before. Cui Hào, fearing that the Crown Prince would not survive, [became apprehensive].
Seeking his own advantage, [Tao] Li said to Emperor Taizu (Taiwu): "The Crown Prince previously indeed harbored a plot;
he allied with Gao through artifice to cause the late Emperor to fear Your Majesty. If he is not eliminated early, he will surely cause great harm. Emperor Taizu was enraged.
In the ninth month of that year, Gao and Huichong were arrested and strangled. Gao’s disciple Yuanchang fled far away to weep for Gao; Gao suddenly opened his eyes.

He said, "Prosperity and decline reside in outward traces; the principle remains eternally serene. Cultivate your own mind well. Having finished speaking, he departed for good. Furthermore, Fada saw Hui Gao in the air.
Fada stepped forward and asked, "Where was Master Hui Gao reborn? Gao replied, "I went to evil realms to save sentient beings;

Hui Chong has returned to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing" (from the *Monk Biographies*). At that time, Chong was the preceptor to Han Wande, the Minister of the Interior; Wande followed Gao, and he too was suspected [of having attained rebirth].
In the year Yiyou (the twenty-second), [year 6]—

the monk Tanyue (alternatively known as Huijue) of the Wei dynasty possessed talent and understanding. He translated the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish) in fifteen fascicles, which fully records parables of good and evil.
In the Bingxu year (the twenty-third), [year] seven, the Wei ruler and Cui Hao both placed their faith in Kou Qianzhi and followed his Way. Hao frequently spoke to the Wei ruler regarding this.

He [the Emperor] believed that because the Buddha-dharma was empty and extravagant, it should be eliminated. When the Wei ruler went to suppress Gai Wu, he arrived at Chang’an and entered a Buddhist temple.
There, the śramaṇas drank wine from his attendants. An official entered their quarters and saw weapons there; he reported this to the Wei ruler, who said in anger:
"This is not something practiced by śramaṇas; it must be a conspiracy with Gai Wu to incite rebellion. He ordered the authorities to investigate and execute all the śramaṇas in the monastery.
Hao then persuaded the Emperor to execute all śramaṇas throughout the empire and destroy all scriptures and images. The Emperor followed his advice.

Kou Qianzhi earnestly remonstrated, deeming it improper; however, Hao did not listen. He first executed the śramaṇas of Chang’an and burned their scriptures and images, sparing only four temples within the capital.
An imperial edict was issued to the four quarters of the realm, strictly following the laws of Chang’an.

Crown Prince Huang, who had long been fond of Buddhism, repeatedly remonstrated against this without success; he then leaked the wording of the decree so that those far and near could take prior notice and each [prepare accordingly].
As a result of these measures, many śramaṇas escaped and were spared, or they concealed scriptures and images;
as for the pagodas and temples within the territory of Wei, none remained at all (Wei Shu).
Dinghai (the twenty-fourth year): [Year 8].

Although the Wei dynasty had suppressed the teachings, they still flourished extensively in the Song. An imperial edict summoned the youth Huiji to enter the palace; the Emperor held him in high esteem.

A great assembly was convened at Qihuan Temple, and the imperial carriage visited the site. The Duke and Ministers gathered to perform the tonsure ceremony for Huiji (Huiji was capable of mastering the sutras).
Zong Bing of Mount Lu passed away at the age of sixty-nine. Bing had once composed the *Míngfó lùn* (Treatise on Clarifying Buddhism), which is now included in the *Hóngmíng jí*.
