Shi Falang was renowned for many miraculous feats. His teacher, Shi Fajin, was also of noble conduct. Falang was able to pass through the door-bolt and keyhole.
When Emperor Wu of Wei suppressed the Dharma, he traveled west to Kucha, where the king treated him with the rites due to a sage. After his death, his body was cremated.
His skeletal remains [showed] the two shoulders and the *jōgen* (涌泉, fontanelle) rising straight toward heaven (*Benzhuan*).
On the *wuzi* day (the twenty-fifth), Shi Fayuan held a lecture on the teachings.
The Regional Inspector Yu Dengzhi once requested him to lecture on the Dharma. Emperor Wen inquired after and sought out his [discourses].

Regarding Master Sengsheng’s doctrine of sudden enlightenment, an imperial edict was issued summoning him to the capital for an audience. Fayuan presented his arguments with such clarity and detail that He Shangzhi sighed in admiration, saying:

"I had thought that with the passing of Master Sengsheng, these subtle teachings would be lost forever. Now, hearing again this discourse on the realm beyond forms, one can truly say that Heaven has not yet allowed these sacred texts to perish.
By imperial decree, he was appointed as the Preceptor of the Five Precepts for Prince Mu of Nanping, Xiao Shuo. Later, during the Tianbao...

The temple was completed, and by imperial decree, Huiyuan was appointed to preside over it. When Wang Jingwen attended one of his lectures, he sighed in admiration, saying: "Everything he presents is unheard of;
everything he points toward transcends the reach of the intellect. He is truly a dragon within the Dharma" (from his *Biography*). ○ Lei Cizong of Mount Lu passed away at the age of eighty.
Jichou (the twenty-sixth year): On the tenth day, Śramaṇa Baoyun passed away.
Yun had traveled extensively through the Western Regions and later returned to Chang’an, where he practiced meditation under Buddhabhadra.
When Buddhabhadra was expelled from the Qin territory, Yun returned to the capital of Yangzhou. There, together with Zhiyan, he jointly translated various scriptures.
On the day of Gengyin (the twenty-seventh), [the eleventh month], the Wei attacked Song.
Emperor Wen dispatched Xiao Bin to resist them. The vanguard commander, Wang Yuemo, was unskilled in managing his troops.
The soldiers were cowed and fled even before the battle had begun. Sengbin was enraged and intended to execute Sengmu.

Sengmu dreamed that a person told him, "If you recite the name of Avalokiteśvara one thousand times, you will be spared. Upon waking, he recited it one thousand times. Just as he was about to face the blade, Wang Qingzhi interceded, saying:

The Wei invaders’ military prowess shook the world; how could [Zhu] Mo have been able to withstand them? Before the battle had even begun, he executed his deputy general, thereby weakening himself—this was not a sound strategy.
Zhu Bin realized this and immediately commuted his death sentence; Mo continued to lead his troops as before (*Nanshi*). When the Wei dynasty suppressed the Buddha-dharma...
Previously, when Kou Qianzhi had contended [with the Emperor], Cui Hao had not followed his advice. Kou said, "You are now shortening your own years and bringing about the extinction of your family.
When it came to this moment, Hao carved the national history he had compiled onto wooden tablets at the sacrificial altar; upon these were inscribed the affairs of the Wei dynasty's ancestors.

Thereupon, both court and commoners reported this to the Emperor, claiming that Hao was publicly exposing the state's evils. The Emperor was enraged and executed Hao along with three generations of his kin, as well as his subordinates and attendants.

There were one hundred and thirty-eight officials. They further ordered Hao to urinate upon [the remains]. Initially, when Hao burned and destroyed scriptures and images, he would invariably urinate on any discarded image he encountered along the road.
When his clan was executed and no one remained to collect the corpses, people likewise urinated upon them, ceasing only when the bodies had rotted away (from the *Weishu*).

In the *xinmao* year (the twenty-eighth year of the reign, the first year of Zhengping), the śramaṇa Huishi (alternatively known as Tanshi) encountered the suppression of the Dharma under the Wei dynasty and went into hiding. Reaching this time, he knew that the Great Dharma was about to flourish once more.
During the [Xiao] Zhao-yuan era, Shi Shi arrived at the palace gate with his staff shaking. An official informed Emperor Taiwu, who said, "Execute him immediately!

When the blade fell, it caused no wound, yet Shi Shi had already reached the steps of the hall. Enraged, Taiwu drew the sword from his girdle and struck him himself, but it likewise could not harm him;
the sword left only a slight mark. At that time, tigers were being kept in a cage in the northern garden, so Taiwu ordered Shi Shi to be fed to them.
The tigers all crouched in submission, not daring to blink. His attendants requested that the Celestial Master test them; the tigers immediately let out a roar. Emperor Taiwu was greatly alarmed.
Daoshi was invited to ascend the hall and prostrate twice. Emperor Taiwu granted his request. (From the *Beishan lu*). Prince Huang of the Wei dynasty passed away.
Shi Huishao stacked firewood and recited the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter. He burned himself until he was extinguished. At the moment of his death...
He said, "At the place where I burned my body, a paulownia tree (*ficus venosa*) shall grow. Three days later, it indeed sprouted there.

In the twenty-ninth year, the *Renchen* year (the first year of King Sejong’s reign, known as Gwangjong’s *Heungan* era), following the destruction of Buddhism by Emperor Wu of Wei, he suffered from a severe illness for two years starting from the beginning of the *Jeongpyeong* era, with sores breaking out over his entire body.
Pus and blood flowed together; thus, the Buddha’s prohibitions gradually relaxed, and there were those among the common people who privately practiced [the religion].
In this year, he was assassinated by Zong’ai, the Palace Attendant, and passed away. Emperor Gaozong Wencheng, named Jun, was the son of [Emperor] Huang. In the tenth month, he ascended the throne.
The various ministers exhorted him to restore the teachings of Śākyamuni, whereupon he issued an edict stating: "As for being an emperor..."

O King, you must surely venerate the enlightened spirits and manifest the Way of Benevolence. Those who are able to bestow grace upon the living people and provide relief and benefit to all classes of beings—though they lived in antiquity, their heroic deeds are still recorded in order.
Thus, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* praises the rites of reverent illumination, and the Ritual Codes record the lineages that have bestowed merit.
How much more so for Śākyamuni Tathāgata, whose merit rescued the great trichiliocosm and whose grace flowed through the realms of dust. Having sought [this truth],...
Regarding "birth and death," it praises its profound insight; regarding those who examine its literary meaning, they value its wondrous gateways.

It assists the prohibitions and laws of royal governance and augments the virtuous nature of benevolence and wisdom. It repels the multitude of heterodoxies and expounds the True Enlightenment. Therefore, since ancient times—
There are none who do not hold them in high esteem; they are also those whom our own nation has always honored and served.

When Emperor Taizu Wudi of the world opened up the remote frontiers and his virtuous bounty spread afar, śramaṇas and daoshi whose conduct was excellent and sincere—such as the likes of Huishì—reached every distant place.
Their integrity and righteousness moved one another, appearing in numbers as dense as a forest. Indeed, within the depths of mountains and seas, strange creatures abound.
Those of lewd and depraved character have found it possible to feign and take refuge within the lecture halls and monasteries, thereby forming criminal factions therein.

For this reason, the previous dynasty took advantage of these vulnerabilities to execute those who were guilty. However, the officials misunderstood the imperial intent and prohibited all such practices. Emperor Jingmu [reinstated them].
I have often felt deep regret over this. However, as the state has been beset by many affairs of war, I have not yet had the leisure to restore these institutions.

Now, having inherited the great legacy and presiding over the myriad realms, I contemplate fulfilling the aspirations of my predecessors to cause this Way to flourish. I now decree that in all prefectures and counties, wherever there are large populations, each shall be permitted to establish one Buddhist monastery.
Furthermore, those who take pleasure in the Dharma and wish to become śramaṇas, whose character and conduct have long been steadfast, and who are from their localities...
What the Prefect clarified was that those permitted to leave the household life would be sufficient to transform evil into good and propagate the Way of the Buddha.

Thereupon, throughout the empire, people followed this wind; before their names were even known at court, the monasteries of former times were all restored, and the scriptures and images were all brought forth.

At that time, the śramaṇa Shi Xian, of the royal lineage of Kaśmīra, had encountered the decline of the teaching and had temporarily relied upon medical arts. Yet he remained steadfast in the Way and did not change his resolve.
On the day the teaching was restored, he immediately became a śramaṇa along with four companions; the Emperor personally shaved their heads.
Xian served as the Sangha- Superintendent (according to the Wei History).
Gui-si (the 30th year), [February, the Emperor passed away].

(2) The Wei court commanded the relevant authorities to cast five statues of Śākyamuni at the Five-Storey Great Temple for the five emperors beginning with Taizu, each one zhang and six chi in height, using two hundred and fifty thousand jin of gold. The śramaṇa Tanyao was honored by the Emperor as...

According to the *Wei Shu*, in the year Jiawu (the first year of Xingguang, the first year of Xiaojian, during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Wei dynasty), Prince Yixuan of Qiao secretly plotted treasonous acts.
Guṇabhadra remonstrated with him, but he would not listen. This occurred at Liangshan.
Upon his defeat, Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict to the army: "Should anyone capture Tuo Luo, dispatch him by relay post. Shortly thereafter, he was captured and sent to Jinling for an audience.
The Emperor questioned him in detail regarding his circumstances and ordered him to reside in the rear hall, providing him with clothing and offerings.
One day, the Emperor asked, "Do you still think of Prince Qiao? He replied, "The ancients did not forget a single meal. Your Majesty fed me for ten years; how could I dare suddenly forget it?"

"I pray that you will request from Your Majesty that [Buddhabhadra] be granted this for the sake of the King’s long-term cultivation of merit in the afterlife. The Emperor, moved with sorrow, changed his expression.

When Zhongxing Temple was completed, an imperial decree ordered him to serve as its abbot. During a banquet at the Eastern Palace where the high officials had all assembled, the Emperor summoned Guṇabhadra.

He responded to the occasion with eloquence, and the Emperor was greatly pleased. Śramaṇa Puming lived in simple clothing and subsisted on vegetarian food, specializing in the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Whenever he reached the "Exhortation" chapter (*Prasādanīya-parivarta*), he would invariably see Samantabhadra standing before him riding upon an elephant;

while reciting the *Vimalakīrti*, he also heard the sound of music from the air. He was also skilled in divine mantras, and all whom he treated were healed. Once, the wife of a certain man fell ill, and she invited Puming to come.
When she cast a spell and entered the gate of a woman’s quarters, the woman immediately fell into a swoon. She saw a raccoon dog emerge from a dog’s den, and because of this, she was cured.
Furthermore, when she once entered a shrine, the deities all fled (as recorded in her biography).

In the second year of Yiwu (the first year of Tai’an), Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict appointing the śramaṇa Daoyou as the presiding master of the Xin'an Zhen Temple. Initially, Emperor Wen had held him in profound esteem.
Reaching this point, he became the Dharma Master for the world, fully meeting the expectations of his time. He passed away during the Yuanhui era at the age of seventy-one.

As for Śramaṇa Baoliang: at the age of twelve, he took refuge under Dao Ming of Qingzhou and left the household life. Once his studies were refined, he later traveled to the capital and resided at Zhongxing Temple.
Yuan Can of the Secretariat, having seen him and marveled at his extraordinary character, sent a letter to his teacher, Dao [Ming].
Ming said briefly: "Recently I have seen Master Liang; he is no ordinary man. Day by day I hear what I have never heard before, and I am unaware that the year is drawing to a close.
Yet, when pearls are produced in Hepu, the people of Wei take them to illuminate their carriages; when jade is found in Handan, the King of Qin requests it to adorn his state.
The treasures of the world cannot be monopolized; they must be shared with others. From this point on, Liang’s fame [spread far and wide]."

Master Shi Sengyu was increasingly revered. He often remarked that the accumulation of karmic burdens in the three realms of suffering arises from emotional attachments; once these emotions are exhausted, the physical form should likewise be relinquished.
In the sixth month of that year, he gathered firewood at Mount Lu to construct a cremation chamber. Once the fire was lit, he entered it and sat upright, reciting the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter.
Even as the flames reached him on all sides, he remained with his palms joined and did not disperse. Both monastics and laypeople alike beheld a purple light.
The vapor ascended into the air. Fourteen days later, twin paulownia trees grew in his chamber, rising up to form a wondrous grove.

On the Bingshen day (the third day of the second month), Shi Yuanchang, who had initially served Yuan Gao, fled to Yangzhou following the suppression of the Dharma under the Wei dynasty; there he profoundly mastered the sutras, vinaya, and dhyāna.

Essentials. Initially, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was vast and profound in both its text and meaning, and no commentaries had yet been produced to explain it. Daochang then extracted its chapters and annotated its phrases; his lectures have been transmitted to this day. Daochang was the pioneer of this tradition.

Furthermore, he was skilled in the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) and became a preeminent master for scholars. Emperor Wen held him in high esteem and requested that he serve as a tutor to the Crown Prince.
Daochang declined the offer three times, but it was only upon the events of the Taichu era that the Emperor finally recognized his foresight. From then on...
He moved to rest at Mount Jingzhou and lectured on the Dharma at Changsha Temple.
In the year Dingyou (the first year of the Daming era), the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, entrusted the Dharma to Bodhidharma with this verse: "The mind-ground contains..."
The various seeds, through the mind, again give rise to the principle; the fruit is fulfilled and Bodhi is perfected. As the flower blooms, the world arises.

Immediately upon his seat, he stood up, extended his left and right hands, and emitted twenty-seven rays of light. He leaped into the void and transformed into fire to consume himself; the *śarīra* relics fell from the sky like rain.
(This was the year of the Jia-wu cycle, the main body of the teaching. Shi Huìjiǎn translated the *Sūtra of the Five Divine Messengers* and other scriptures.
Ten fascicles.
Wuxu (2nd year). At that time, Shi Sengquan was a master who had thoroughly refined the Tripiṭaka;
his transformative influence permeated the region south of the Yangtze River. By nature, he delighted in giving alms and generously provided for the poor and destitute.
He lived without silk or coinage. He frequently fashioned golden images and never ceased his practice of dhyāna and ritual worship.

Meng Yi, Zhang Chang, Zhang Fu, Dai Yong, and Dai Bo all served him as their teacher (*Monk Biography*). The Emperor issued an edict for Dharma Master Tanzong to perform a rite of repentance for his transgressions.

The Emperor then said, "What crime have I committed that troubles you by having you perform this repentance on my behalf? Tanzong replied, "Shun said, 'If I err, you must assist me. Yu said, 'The myriad regions have..."* (The text here is incomplete).
"The fault lies with me alone. Your Majesty treads the Way with humble reflection; how could you alone be exempt from this? The Emperor was greatly pleased (*Tongji*).

On the day Jihai (the third year), Shi Daowang—having initially studied under Master Yuangong and thoroughly mastered the sutras and vinaya—was once traveling on the road to Liangzhou when he was surrounded by Qiang rebels.
Wang Nian was contemplating Avalokiteśvara. After a short while, he felt as though clouds and mist were covering his body; the thief could no longer find him, and thus Wang escaped with his life.
Later, he resided in Chengdu, where he propagated the Dharma throughout Ba and Shu. When Emperor Xiaowu heard of Wang’s virtuous conduct, he welcomed him to serve as the abbot of Zhongxing Temple.
In the second month, the monk Sengqing performed the practice of self-immolation before an image of Vimalakīrti. The assembly saw a single object—
Like a dragon ascending to heaven from a thicket (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
Gengzi (the fourth year) [429] (A triangular ox was offered in Guangzhou and a dancing horse was offered in Henan). (The first year of Heping).
On the eighth day of the tenth month, Empress Dowager Luzhao completed the image of Samantabhadra and established it within the meditation hall of Zhongxing Temple.

During a vegetarian feast, the two hundred invited monks had already assembled when a strange monk suddenly took a seat among them. His appearance was exceptionally refined and radiant, causing the entire assembly to marvel in astonishment.
The host of the feast asked him which monastery he came from; he replied, "Tian'an. While they were still conversing, he suddenly vanished. The assembly then realized he was a divine monk.
At that time, Shi Daowen was appointed by imperial decree as the Chief Administrator of Monks for the capital. Kong, the Governor of Jingzhao—

A spiritual talisman was presented with a memorial regarding these matters. By imperial decree, the meditation hall was renamed Tian'an Temple. Later, when Daowen began lecturing there, he frequently experienced divine wonders, which delighted the Emperor;
he was subsequently granted five hundred thousand coins (from the Biography of Wen). ○ A monk from the Western Regions named Gongde arrived in Jingzhou.
The monk Yuanchang requested that he translate the *Nianfo Sanmei* and other sutras; Yuanchang edited and clarified their textual meanings, and their phrasing and intent were elegant.
Qie. Chang was able to extend his hand and emit fragrance, and water flowed from his palm;
none could fathom these wonders. Xinchou (5) [Year 2]:

Shi Sengjing initially resided in the capital to lecture on the Dharma. Xu Zhanzhi held him in high esteem and requested that he serve as his personal teacher. Later, his transformation of others became pervasive.

His fame spread throughout the Three Wu regions. Emperor Shizu, admiring his reputation, issued an edict for him to reside at Dinglin Monastery, where he frequently established assemblies for the Dharma.

Shi Huitong wielded his fly-whisk with such authority that carriages and canopies filled the streets. Emperor Xiaowu bestowed upon him high honors and rank, issuing an edict appointing him as a companion to the Princes of Hailing and Jianping.
Ren-yin (6): (3) Shi Sengyuan.
Initially, he lectured on the Dharma in Qingzhou, where both monastics and laypeople were filled with joy and submission. Wang Sengda of Langya invited him to reside at Zhongzao Temple.
Sengyuan assisted the poor and relieved those in want; he left no personal wealth behind. He gathered in the dead and comforted the living, bestowing kindness upon them as if they were his own kin.

Prince Xiao Jing honored Prince Luan and established Xin’an Temple; by imperial decree, [Hui]yuan was appointed to reside there. In the ninth month, the Right Court Censor submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your servant has heard that the Buddha disciplines himself through humility and takes loyalty and obedience as his path. The Bhikṣu Bujing would bow to anyone he encountered."

When the Great Being Maudgalyāyana encountered his elder [parents], he immediately prostrated himself; how could it be that the fourfold assembly merely bows their knees, yet they pay special homage to their two parents?

Or how could one who has bowed his forehead to monks of seniority directly bare his body before the Ten-Thousand-Wagon Sovereign? Your servants, having deliberated together, believe that when śramaṇas receive visitors, [they should follow such propriety].

All should adopt an appearance of utmost reverence; thus the court’s splendor will be orderly. Although the Emperor was quite a believer in the Dharma, he remained particularly arrogant and self-indulgent.

On the day the memorial was presented, the Emperor issued an edict granting approval immediately. Huiyuan sighed and said, "I originally left the household life to seek the Way; what concern does this have for emperors?

That very day, he declined his illness as an excuse and brushed off his robes to depart, retiring to Mount Dinglin. (When a principle can be put into practice, it remains unchanging for ten thousand ages; when a principle cannot be practiced, [it is abandoned].)

For a time, communication was difficult; although the imperial decree had been issued, the multitude ultimately did not comply, and after more than a year, they returned to their former ways. ○ Shi Fayao was renowned for his exegesis of the Dharma.

In this year, an imperial edict was issued to the Wuxing Commandery to respectfully summon him to the capital. He resided together with Daoyou at Xinxian Temple, establishing distinct schools of thought for the two types of awakening—sudden and gradual—and expounding upon them as soon as he arrived.
The imperial carriage descended to halt its procession, and the hundred officials attended the assembly (from his *Benzhuan*). ○ Wei.
Shi Tanyao, rejoicing in the restoration of the Triple Gem, translated the *Dharmatrāta-avadāna* (Fu fazang zhuan) and other scriptures at Beitaisi Monastery.
Initially, the Wei Emperor, thirty *li* northwest of Heng’an, carved into a stone cliff on the northern face of Mount Wuzhou to establish Lingyansi Monastery;
its largest niches were over twenty *zhang* high and could accommodate three thousand people, wherein various holy figures were carved.
The images extend for more than thirty li in succession. At the eastern end is a Buddhist monastery that regularly provides sustenance for a thousand people;
although Emperor Taizu destroyed [the temples], this grotto was not destroyed.
In the *guǐmǎo* year (the seventh), there was a great drought throughout the realm.
The Emperor requested Guṇabhadra to pray for rain. Guṇabhadra immediately burned incense and offered prayers;

he abstained from food and drink and silently recited sūtras and dhāraṇīs. At the hour of *bù* (3–5 p.m. the following day, winds shook and clouds gathered, and it rained continuously for several days. An imperial edict was issued to have him appear [at court].
He was comforted and provided with offerings in succession. Shi Huiyi of the Qi dynasty abstained from grains for several years, consuming only fragrant oil.
Vowing to perform self-immolation, on the eighth day of the fourth month of that year, he prepared a cauldron and procured oil at Mount Zhong.

He went in person to the Yunlong Gate to take leave of the Emperor. The Emperor personally came out of his palace gate; Huiyi relied upon the Buddha-dharma to entrust his final wishes and bid farewell. The Emperor also followed him there, accompanied by both monastics and laypeople.
When Fayi was about to enter the cauldron, he wrapped himself in *karpāsa* (cotton) cloth and placed a cap over his head.

He poured oil upon it and, holding a candle in his hand, set the cap ablaze while reciting the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter. When the fire reached his eyes, his voice ceased. At that time, the sound of flutes and pipes was heard from the air, and a wondrous fragrance wafted forth.
That night, the Emperor dreamed that Fayi arrived shaking his monk’s staff and further entrusted him with the Buddha-dharma. The next day, the Emperor...
The place where he established an assembly to save sentient beings by burning his own body is called Yaowang Temple (*Běnzhuan*).
○ Shi Sengqu translated the *Daśabhāṇavāra-karman*.
Jiachen (the eighth year), the fifth month: the Emperor passed away; Crown Prince Ziyè ascended the throne.
(5) An edict was issued restoring the status of the śramaṇas and exempting them from paying homage to the sovereign. (*Tongjian*) ○ Tianzhu Ānàmódìng (translated here as Bǎoyì).
Upon arriving at the capital, he could constantly discern good or bad fortune by rolling over several hundred *baizi* (cowrie shells). He was skilled in divine incantations;
by applying incense to his palms, he could also see people’s past lives. Emperor Shizu gave him a bronze spittoon, which was suddenly stolen.
[Daorong] took a mat, rolled it up empty, and recited incantations over it several times. After three nights had passed, the spittoon was found back inside the mat. Dao[rong].
The common people respected him as extraordinary (from his *Benzhuan*).

In the year Yisi (the first year of Jinghe, the eleventh month), the high ministers deposed the ruler, whereupon they installed Emperor Ming of the Taizong reign; [the era was changed to] the first year of Taishi.

In the sixth month (the fifth month, when the Gaozong passed away and the Xianzong ascended the throne), at Waguan Monastery in Yangzhou, the monk Shi Huiguo was constantly reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*. One day, while in the latrine, he saw a ghost who prostrated and said:

In the past, when he served as the *karmadāna* for a monastic community, he was slightly improper in his conduct and consequently fell into hell. He was subsequently reborn among the *pūti-gandha* (feces-eating) spirits. He prayed, "May the Master rescue me.
He further said, "Formerly, I had three thousand coins buried beneath a persimmon tree; I pray that you take them to create merit.

Indeed, upon being informed by him, [the Master] had the assembly dig up the money and established a ritual assembly for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Later, he saw the spirit in a dream, who said, "I have already attained rebirth in a superior realm."
(Gantong Lu) ○ Shi Hui Liang was renowned for his lecturing halls. Yan Yanzhi sighed in admiration, saying: "Hui'an and Daotai have spat forth pearls and jade before us;
Sengbin and Hui Liang now vibrate with golden sounds behind them. These pure discourses and subtle threads were nearly extinguished, yet they have flourished once more.

At this time, at Zhuangyan Temple, students gathered in great numbers. By imperial decree, Hui Liang and Sengbin were appointed in turn as Dharma Masters. (From the *Benzhuan*) ○ Emperor Gaozong of the Wei Dynasty.
Emperor Cheng reigned until his death in the fifth month. The Emperor ordained over thirty thousand monks and nuns, extensively promoting Buddhism and restoring various monasteries.
Bingwu (the second year of Taishi). [The first year of Tian’an of Wei Xianzu Xuanwen Di]. Together. The first year of Tian’an.
Shi Sengjin: Initially, during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, he was appointed as the Preceptor to Prince Xiangdong (the Prince was later the Taizong).

The Prince followed him and requested the five precepts, treating him with the utmost courtesy and honor. When the Emperor ascended the throne, he issued an edict appointing Jin as the Patriarch of the Monks throughout the realm, providing him with an armed escort, carriages, and a monthly stipend of thirty thousand coins.
By nature, Jin did not hoard gold; he spent it all on meritorious works, establishing the two monasteries of Linggen and Lingji.
[He was buried at] the Monastery. He passed away during the Yuanhui era. The Great Being Baozhi came and went between Mount Xuan and the Jian River;
he had shorn his hair and walked barefoot, wearing a brocade robe. His face was square and as clear and translucent as a mirror; his hands and feet were all webbed with bird-like claws.
Initially, the wife of a man from the Zhu family in Dongyang, Jinling, heard the crying of a child within an eagle’s nest; she climbed the tree and retrieved it, raising it as her own.

At the age of seven, he entered the monastic order under Sengjian at Mount Zhong and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna meditation. It was at this time that his miraculous manifestations became evident.
Carrying a pair of scissors, a ruler, and a whisk suspended from the tip of his staff, he traveled about. When he passed through villages, children would clamor and chase after him;

at times he would beg for a little wine, and at other times he would go without food for several days. Once, encountering someone eating minced fish, he followed them and asked for some; the eater shared a portion with him.
Yet he harbored a frivolous thought and immediately spat them into the water; they all became living fish.
From time to time he composed poems, which at first seemed unintelligible, but later were all proven true (as recorded in his biography).
Dingwei (3) [Regnal Year 1 of Huangxing]: Shi Daomeng.

His learning reached the profound and subtle. Initially residing at a temple in the capital, he was deeply honored and recommended by Xiao Changmao, who was then the Prince of Xiangdong during the reign of Emperor Taizong.
Upon ascending the throne, the Emperor redoubled his courtesy and reception of him. The Emperor established a monastery outside Jianyang Gate and issued an edict appointing Daomeng as its abbot.

Preface. The Emperor said: "A person can broaden the Way; the Way relies on a person to be broadened. Now, the Dharma Master has not only benefited the common people through the Way, but has also brought glory to it.
His reputation is such that he may be looked up to by the world. Let the temple be named Xinghuang. By imperial decree, Sengmeng was ordered to lecture on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* at the temple.
On the day the preface was presented, the Emperor personally visited in person, and the high officials all assembled. After a long while, the Emperor issued an edict, saying: "Meng Fa..."
Master [Seng]feng was widely beneficial to the Way; he was a long-standing friend of mine. I shall grant him a monthly stipend of thirty thousand coins, along with attendants, carriages, and litters.
Sengmeng followed suit in acquiring wealth, which he entirely bestowed upon the poor and used to build temples. He passed away in the third year of the Yuanhui era. *Śramaṇa Zhilin.*

An imperial edict from the Song dynasty was issued for the monasteries in the capital to lecture upon and clarify the meaning of the Two Truths (*satyadvaya*). There were three schools with differing views.

At that time, Zhou Yong also composed the *Sanzong lun* (Treatise on the Three Schools), which accorded with the views of Lin [Guang]. Lin then sent a letter to Yong stating: "As for this doctrine, no one has been able to grasp it;
fortunately, you have already elucidated its meaning. It would be well to propagate it widely. Thus, the principles of the Three Schools were transmitted and recorded.

To this day... Zhou Yong, styled Bolen, was successively promoted to serve in the palace chambers as a *zhishì*. When Emperor Ming was cruel and tyrannical, Yong did not dare to offer open remonstrance;

instead, he would recite from the sutras accounts of the causes and conditions of sin and merit. The Emperor was somewhat discouraged by this. To the west of Mount Zhong, Yong established a separate vihāra (*jingśè*);
whenever he took leave for rest or recreation, he would return there, maintaining a vegetarian diet throughout the year. Although he had a wife and children, [he remained detached].
He lived in seclusion in a mountain hermitage. When the Chancellor Wang Jian asked him, "What do you eat in the mountains? he replied, "Red rice, white salt, green chives, and purple dock.
Xiao Zixian jokingly asked, "Among vegetarian dishes, which flavor is best? Yong replied, "Early chives at the beginning of spring;

late *shung* (a type of wild vegetable) at the end of autumn. Such was his refined character. He retired from office during the height of his career to dwell in the mountains, where he lived out his life until his death.
(Main Biography) ○ During the Wei dynasty, the Yongning Temple was built at the Northern Terrace in Chang’an. Its seven-story pagoda stood over three hundred feet high.
Furthermore, at the Tiangong Temple, a great statue was fashioned, forty-three feet in height, using one hundred thousand catties of copper and six hundred catties of gold (*Tongjian*).
Wu-shen (the fourth day), the second month of the first year:
Gunabhadra of India took his leave of the Son of Heaven at court. The high officials remarked that he was about to manifest his passing into extinction.

The Emperor came in person to bid him farewell. Gunabhadra passed away with a smile. He was seventy-five years of age. Gunabhadra maintained a vegetarian diet and carried an incense burner for the rest of his life.
He never let [the scriptures] leave his hand. Whenever he ate, he would invariably share some with the birds; the birds would all gather at his hands to take the food.

He prayed for the translation of fifty-two treatises and commentaries in one hundred and thirty-four fascicles. Emperor [Wu] built Xianggong Monastery; once its construction was completed, he opened a grand lecture hall and carefully selected eminent monks.
By imperial decree, Fayuan was invited to serve as the Dharma Master. The Emperor descended from his carriage to attend the dharma assembly. [The Duke...]
"You, Excellency, please take your seat. This was a moment of great splendor, and those who witnessed it were filled with honor (from the *Monastic Biographies*).

In the year Jiyou (the fifth year), Śramaṇa Hongchong’s thoughts entered the profound and subtle, and his eloquence was as celestial and transcendent as it was brilliant. Both the sovereign and his ministers held him in high esteem. Emperor Ming established [the monastery] at Xiang...

He was invited to serve as the head of the Gongsì Monastery. At that time, there was also Faxian at Xiánggōng Monastery; he was intelligent, wise, and influential, and his reputation was equal to that of Sengchong.
Shì Chāojìn was summoned to the capital by imperial decree, where he lectured on the *Fagǔ jīng* (Dharmadruma-sūtra).
Later, he returned to Kuaiji, where he passed away during the Yuánhuí era at the age of ninety-four. In the seventh month, Zhào Tài died. Ten days later, he revived and said: "There were two men."
Hong entered the Black Gate and saw men dressed in crimson robes. They called out names one by one and questioned them regarding their deeds during life. The overseer said:
"I constantly dispatch messengers into the human world to record the good and evil of people so as to examine them upon death.

There are three evil realms; those who kill living beings for sacrifices are the most grievous. Those who uphold the Buddha’s virtuous precepts will, upon death, reside in the House of Fortune. Otherwise, they shall go to hell."

As he went on his rounds of inspection, he saw that Tai’s parents and younger brother were in the Niraya hell. He further saw those who, having already received their retribution for their offenses in prison, were undergoing further transformative punishments.
He also saw those who, by making offerings to the Buddha and cultivating merit, had attained liberation from rebirth.

Then, entering the Gate of Radiant Light, he saw the Buddha delivering beings from the various hells until the hells became empty. Tai then asked: "How far apart are the Path of Heaven and the Gate of the Hell Path?"
He said, "The Path of Heaven and the Path of Hell are gates that face one another. He asked again, "Among those who have died, which is the most joyful?

He replied, "Only those who have honored the Buddha and maintained the precepts find joy. He asked further, "If one committed transgressions before honoring the Buddha, are those faults removed now that they honor the Buddha?
He replied, "They are all removed. The Overseer then summoned the Registrar and asked, "How did Tai die? He ordered him to take up the registers to examine them; there was more to follow.
When he was thirty years old, he was seized by a ghost; the ghost was made to release him and send him back.

Because of this, the entire family resolved their minds to serve the Buddha, and for the sake of their grandparents and younger brother, they prepared banners and canopies and held merit-making assemblies.
Gengxu (the sixth day), Year 4:
He Jingshu of the Eastern Sea had served the Dharma since his youth. Having obtained some sandalwood, he fashioned it into an image, yet it lacked a halo.
Having sought it repeatedly without success, he dreamed of a śramaṇa with a staff who said, "The donor cannot be found here;
you should seek it at the He family's place behind the county seat. The next morning, he went to purchase it from them. He asked, "I have never shown this to anyone before;

how did you come to know of it? Jing’s uncle told him what had happened. The He family was filled with joy and wonder, and they presented it to him to fashion into a mirror. Later, he served as a magistrate of Xiangfu.
[Recorded in] the *Sheng* (Excerpts) as a dream-vision (*gantong*).
Xinhai (the seventh year; the first year of Yanxing of Emperor Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty).

Emperor Xianzu of the Wei had been on the throne for six years. He was intelligent and sagacious from early youth, possessed a resolute and firm character, and held deep faith in the Śākya clan (Buddhism).

In his studies, he frequently invited court officials and śramaṇas to discuss profound principles together. He held wealth and honor in low esteem and constantly harbored a desire to transcend the mundane world.
In the sixth month, he abdicated the throne to his heir apparent, Hong, who became Emperor Xiaowen of the Gaozu era.
When Hong was five years old, he enshrined his grandfather as the Taishang Huangdi (Supreme August Emperor).

The Retired Emperor moved his residence to Chongguang Palace, located within the Northern Garden. He also constructed Luye Monastery on the western mountains of the garden, where he resided together with the monks.
At that time, he discussed the principles of Chan (Beishi).
On the *renzi* day of the fourth month in the first year of Taiyu (472), Emperor Taizong passed away.
He had occupied the throne for eight years. His governance was peaceful and his rule prosperous. He commissioned a sixteen-foot golden statue and partook of a single morning meal.
He maintained constant fasting and recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* daily; consequently, he was moved by the appearance of śarīra relics, and he constructed Hongpu Temple (*Liutie*).
(From the *Lidai fabao ji*) During the Wei dynasty, the Western Region monk Jiayiye (translated as Yanke) translated twenty-four fascicles of scriptures, including the *Ratnakūṭa*.
Gui-chou (the first year of Yuanhui under Emperor Cangwu): [3] The śramaṇa Shao Shuo was a native of Kangju.
He was the closest friend of Master Zhi. Whether entering or leaving, walking or practicing meditation, he did not inquire whether it was night or day.
Whenever people sought him out, he would depart to travel to Yizhou, using humorous and witty speech to provoke laughter in others.
He exhorted them toward goodness, and every household rejoiced in this. Whenever he went to sleep on the floor of a person’s house, that family would inevitably suffer a death.

He was able to manifest his body in several places at once; the Regional Inspector Liu Mengming held him in high esteem. One day, he suddenly appeared before Mengming wearing a cloth cap, and shortly thereafter, Mengming passed away.
Previously, Mengming’s Chief Secretary, Shen Zhongyu, had revised the regulations for flogging and caning, making them more severe than the standard code.
Shi said to Zhongyu: "The world is in a state of clamor arising from this; if you can remove the scourge of the *biange* (the oppressive official), you shall become a Provincial Governor (*cishi*).

Zhongyu removed it, and by the following morning, he had indeed passed away. Zhongyu then proceeded to govern the province. In the ninth month of that year, as he was about to die, he said to the śramaṇa Fajin:
"I wish for my remains to be exposed beneath the pines, but my feet must wear sandals. Fajin consented, and subsequently he passed away. They carried his body...

He exposed the corpse, but when he went to look for it the next day, its location was lost. Shortly thereafter, someone arriving from Pí County said, "Yesterday I saw Master Shu wearing only a single shoe walking through the market.
He said, 'Tell Master Jìn for me: the boy deceived me; I only want my one shoe back.
Jìn asked in astonishment, and the novice replied, "When the corpse was being carried away, one shoe fell off while walking; we were in such haste that we did not have time to retrieve it."
Bound. Jia-yin (2);
Yi-mao (3) [A woman from Dongguan, wife of Xu Yuan, was pregnant; the child in her womb cried] (4); (5).
Shi Tanbin was renowned for his skill in expounding the Dharma. At the beginning of the Xiaojian era, he was commanded by Wang Mu to travel from the capital to reside at Xin’an Temple.
There he lectured on the principles of the sudden and gradual teachings, and everyone of the time was delighted and won over by him. He passed away at this time (according to his biography).
Bingchen (the fourth year); (Chengming Year 1: the Emperor Taishanghuang passed away).

Wei established Jianming Temple. Thereafter, temples were built for merit and monks were ordained in great numbers. On the Northern Terrace alone, there were over one hundred temples with two thousand monks and nuns.
Throughout the four quarters, there were over six thousand temples with seventy-seven thousand monks and nuns.
[Other sources (Beishi):
Ding-si (5th month, July), the Emperor Cangwu was assassinated; Emperor Shun was established as regent. [Reigned] (Shengming Year 1) & (Tahé Year 1).
At that time, the recluse Gu Huan still adhered to the teachings of Huang-Lao. Regarding the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism, scholars were mutually disparaging them; thus, [Gu Huan]...
He composed the *Yixia lun* (Treatise on Barbarians and Chinese). It states in brief: "The Way is the Buddha; the Buddha is the Way.

Their sanctity accords, yet their traces diverge. Sometimes they harmonize their light to manifest the near; sometimes they radiate their brilliance to reveal the far. Because the Way saves all under heaven, there is no place it does not enter.
Because wisdom encompasses all things, there is nothing it does not do. Their modes of entry differ, yet that which they do..."
They must be different. Each establishes its own nature and does not alter its practices. Thus, the formal robes and sash-belt are the attire of the Central Kingdom;

the shorn hair and loose garments are the dress of the Western Regions. To preserve one's physical form is the custom for maintaining propriety and continuing the goodness of human nature; to disfigure the face and alter the appearance is [the practice of the West].
The study of severing evil extends throughout the inexhaustible worlds. Sages arise in succession; some illuminate the Five Classics, while others propagate the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
To the Chinese, they transform them through the Chinese language; to the barbarians, they seek them through the barbarian tongue. Although the Way of the Sages is the same, the methods differ:

Nirvana and the transformation into an immortal are each distinct arts. Buddhism is called the "Correct and True" (Zhengzhen), while Daoism is termed the "Correct and One" (Zhengyi). Both return to the Non-being (Wu).

Death is, in truth, non-arising (*anutpāda*). In name, they are opposites; in reality, they are unified. However, the teaching of non-arising is remote, while the transformation of deathlessness is immediate.
The immediate Dharma can be used for advancement; the remote Dharma can be used for retreat. Buddhism is ornate and vast; Daoism is substantial and refined.
Being refined means that only a person of singular excellence can master it; being vast means that even a person of common capacity can be widely transformed by it.
The Buddha’s words are flowery yet expansive; the Daoist words are substantial yet restrictive. The Buddhist scriptures are voluminous yet manifest; the Daoist scriptures are concise yet obscure.
Being obscure, the wondrous gate is difficult to perceive; being manifest, the correct path is easy to follow. This is the distinction between these two teachings.

The Sage Craftsman has no fixed method, yet square and round vessels have their own forms. Since the vessels differ, the application of the teachings must also vary. The Buddha’s method is that which destroys evil.
The Way is the art of promoting goodness; when goodness is promoted, one naturally becomes exalted. When evil is destroyed, valorous effort is prized. The traces of the Buddha are grand and luminous;

they are suited for transforming others. The traces of the Way are subtle and profound; they are suited for cultivation within oneself. This is the distinction between their relative superiority and inferiority.
The general outline is as follows: Although [Huan] Huan and [Wang] Xun shared the same two teachings, Huan’s intent favored the Way of the Sage (Daoism).

Minister Yuan Can wrote a critique of this, stating in brief: "The teachings of Confucius and Laozi take worldly engagement as their foundation; the teachings of Śākyamuni take transcendence from the world as their principle.

Since their starting points differ, their ultimate goals also diverge. Furthermore, the immortalization of the *xian* tradition prizes the transformation of the physical form, whereas *nirvāṇa* prioritizes the cultivation of the spirit."
Those who transform their bodies may have white hair and exhaustively investigate the profound mysteries, yet they remain unable to transcend death.

Those who refine their spirits daily diminish their worldly delusions until they abide in a state of serene stillness—this is the Way of Nirvana, the realm where there is no death. If the refinement of the spirit is such as this, how can it be said that [the Buddhist and Daoist teachings] are identical?
At that time, the Court Attendant Chen Zhenzhi observed the harmonious coexistence of these two teachings and found it deeply unjust; he therefore sent a letter to [Huiyuan].
Huan wrote a passionate letter stating that Daoism was insufficient to rival the teachings of the Śākya clan (Buddhism). He then sent another letter, in which he said briefly:
"When the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) divided, form and consciousness became erroneously manifest; consciousness flows and is defiled due to causes, while form is bound by attachment due to conditions.

When one sinks into desire and is submerged in the waves, one touches the shore and thinks of salvation. To seek salvation is to pray for goodness; to pray for goodness is to receive the response of the Sage. Who is this Sage?"

It is that which is moved and thereby attains penetration. Now, penetration does not penetrate itself; movement does not move itself. Movement always resides here, while penetration always occurs there.
Speaking from the perspective of "there," it is like a mirror suspended high in a hall; speaking from the perspective of "here," all myriad forms return to it.

Thus we know that India is the center of the land, and within the great chiliocosm, there is this movement and penetration toward the Supreme Sage. Since the Sage’s response lies there, his voice [reaches us].
Thus, this Way was practiced as a moving cloud; its teaching was spread like rain over the land of China. The Way is one, while form is two. The Way is the true, while form is the mundane.
To exhaust duality and attain unity, one should unify the Dharma. To extinguish the mundane and return to the true, one must necessarily depart from worldly custom.
Therefore, Confucius preserved his physical form to maintain ancestral sacrifices and extended his kindness to his six kin; Laozi, however, focused on the cultivation of life.

In terms of its inherent nature, [the Chinese system] excels over external objects; yet it cannot be said to be entirely perfect, for it is a limited regulation that has not yet reached the ultimate goal.
How, then, can it be compared to the Way of Bodhi or equated with the Sage Muni?

At that time, there was also Zhu Changshi Zhaozuo, who composed the *Nanyixia lun* (Treatise on the Difficulties of China and the Barbarians), and Zhu Guangzuo, who composed the *Zixiyialun* (Consultation on China and the Barbarians); both are divided into chapters.

[He] composed a treatise to refute [the opposing view], yet his joy was obscured by superficiality. Zhou Yong of Runan and the eminent monk Huitong both authored refutations of the "Discourse on Barbarians and Chinese" (Yixialun).
Consequently, Senghuang’s work proved no more than a collection of errors. Furthermore, there was the Dharma Master Shaoping.

He authored the *Zhèngjiào lùn* (Treatise on the Correct Teaching). It states in brief: "The Buddha clarifies the fundamental principle (*zōng*), while the Dao completes one's life. Those who cling to life remain obstructed;
those who clarify the fundamental principle attain penetration," and so forth (*Nánshǐ*).
Wu-wu (2): In the fourth month of the third year of the Shengming era, Emperor Shun abdicated the throne to the Qi dynasty, [founded by] Wang Xiao Daocheng.
During the sixty years of the Song dynasty, there were one thousand nine hundred thirteen monasteries, thirty-six thousand monks and nuns, and two translators.

Thirteen persons [were involved]. The translated sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras amounted to four hundred and ninety fascicles. The teaching of Śākyamuni flourished, and those of sincere faith increased manifold (according to the local gazetteers).
The Qi dynasty, surnamed Xiao, had its capital at Jiankang (seven rulers for twenty-four years; they abdicated to the Liang). [This was contemporary with] the Wei.
Jiwei (the first year of the Jianyuan era of Emperor Taizu Gao [Gao Daocheng], corresponding to the third year of Taihe):
In the fourth month, the Taizu of Qi ascended the imperial throne. He revered the Three Jewels and extensively saved all living beings, applying his mind with benevolence.

"Exercising Transformation through Frugality" (Six Categories). At Songwang Monastery in Pengcheng, there was a golden image eighteen feet tall. Whenever military unrest arose in the northern borders, the image would break into a sweat.

In that year, the image suddenly began to perspire. In winter, the Wei invaders attacked the Huai River region; at that time, the monks of Yanzhou were being coerced into assisting the Wei army in battle and defense.
The Wei forces falsely accused them of aiding the rebellion and were about to execute them. At that moment, the image broke into a profuse sweat, and it flowed across the ground.
The Wei Regional Inspector of Xuzhou was Prince Liang, who upheld the Dharma. When the prince sent several people to wipe [the bowl] with silk, it continued to emerge without end.
The prince then prostrated himself and said, "The assembly of monks is without fault; I vow to personally protect them and shall certainly not inflict punishment.

If my profound sincerity moves the divine, may the wiping stop immediately as it occurs. Having spoken, he wiped it himself; it became dry at the touch of his hand. The prince submitted a detailed report of this event, and an imperial edict was issued.
"All were seen to be pardoned" (from the *Gantong lu*). ○ Wang Yan had long venerated a golden image of Guanyin. Initially, it was kept at Nanjian Temple in Yangdu.
One night, Yan suddenly dreamed that the image was standing in the corner of his seat; he immediately hurried to welcome it back.

That same evening, more than ten images were missing from Nanjian Temple, having been stolen by thieves who melted them down to mint coins. In the seventh year of the Daming era of the Song dynasty, the image emitted light three feet high, and the entire family [experienced its spiritual power].
They beheld it together. Later, this image was entrusted to Daobao Temple. Yan traveled to the Jing and Chu regions for ten years and did not know the location of the image.
Upon his return to the capital of Yangdu, he dreamed that he was at the eastern side of the temple hall; early the next morning, he went to the temple and found it exactly as he had dreamed.
This was on the tenth day of the seventh month of that year (*Yan Mingxiang ji*). Shi Yuanchang departed for Chengdu at the end of the Song dynasty; in this year, he reached Minling Qi.
At Mount Hou, he harbored the ambition to spend his final years there. On the twenty-third day of the fourth month, he established a site and founded a temple named Qixing (Arising Together).

This was precisely the moment when the ancestral patriarch received his mandate; thus, the celestial timing and human affairs coincided perfectly from ten thousand *li* away. At that time, Fu Yan was stationed in Chengdu;

admiring [Hui]chang’s character and conduct, he treated him with the respect due to a teacher. Consequently, Yan reported Chang’s achievements to the throne, and by imperial decree, one hundred households were exempted from taxes.
Households were assigned to provide his stipend (according to his biography).

On the gengshen day, the second month, the fourth year [of the reign], the monk Senghui lectured on the Dharma and was revered as a master by those studying in the West. At this time, by imperial decree, he was appointed as the Monastic Head (Sengzhu) of Jingzhou. He was advanced in years.

He frequently traveled to lectures by carriage; onlookers called him "The Bald Head. His official status was equal to that of Yuan Chang, and people of the time spoke of them as the "Two Heroes in Black Robes.
At that time, at the Viye Monastery in Fanyu, there was a large stone image from Funan.
It required seventy or eighty men to lift it before it would budge. When this monastery was threatened by fire, three or four nuns attempted to carry it away, and it floated off.

However, when it was moved, the image did so as well, and the house was subsequently consumed by fire. It constantly manifested divine light, and whenever a bandit appeared, it would shed tears and sweat.
Later, Guangzhou sent it out to the capital, where it was enshrined in a temple in Jiangzhou (Gantong). Emperor Wei issued an edict appointing Sengxian as the Metropolitan Superintendent of Śramaṇas.
Xinyou (the third year), [year 3] & (the fifth year):
Shi Sengyuan of the Wei dynasty was of magnificent stature, with a waist girth of ten spans. He was renowned for his profound understanding of the Dharma.
Liu Yinzhi donated the mountain where he resided to provide him with a vihāra. His disciples Huiji and Daodeng were both held in high esteem by Emperor Wen.
In this year, Huiyuan passed away (according to his biography). Furthermore, Shi Daohui, who possessed wisdom in the study of the Dharma, also passed away this year.

At that time, a eunuch of the capital lamented his own status as a physical remnant of punishment and submitted a petition requesting permission to enter the mountains to practice the Way. The Emperor granted his request; he then took the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with him and recited it day and night, performing rites of repentance without ceasing.
Suddenly, a beard and mustache grew, and he attained the physical marks of a man. When he reported this situation to the Emperor, the Emperor was greatly astonished.

[The people] marveled at this. The entire kingdom revered the *Avataṃsaka*. (From the *Gantong lu*) ○ During the Qi dynasty, Dharmagatayaśas of India (translated as Fasheng) produced the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*).

In the first month of the fourth year of the Renxu cycle (461 CE), Emperor Gaozu visited Zhuangyan Temple to listen to Dharma Master Xingyuan’s lecture on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. The high officials and nobles were all assembled there.

Because the Emperor was seated somewhat far away, he could not hear the sound of the Dharma. Zhang Xu of the Secretariat advised Xingyuan to move his seat closer to the Emperor. [The Emperor] moved back.
He did not wait for even a moment. The Emperor himself moved his seat to sit near him. In the third month, Emperor Gao died; he had occupied the throne for four years.
He constantly recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* and transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. On the eighth day of the fourth month, he regularly cast golden images.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he universally provided alms-basins at the temples and made offerings to three hundred monks. He established the Zhiqu and Zhengguan monasteries. The Emperor often said: "May I govern..."
In ten years, throughout the world, gold shall become equal in value to soil. Alas, his life was not long;
he lived to the age of fifty-six (Fang Zhi et al.). Emperor Wu (Wei), the World-Honored One, ascended the throne.

On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, the Crown Prince gathered Mahayana monks at Xuānpǔ to observe the ninety-day summer retreat (*an-jū*) and lecture on the Dharma, concluding on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
The lecture concluded with the relinquishing of his body; from the carriage and ceremonial cap down to the sash, there were ninety-nine items in total.

He vowed that by the power of this act, may its benefits universally reach both the hidden and the manifest worlds, so that those submerged in the ocean of suffering may attain awakening through the realization of principle.
Guihai (the first year of Yongming of Emperor Wu of the World-Honored One):

[7] On the eighth day of the second month, Prince Jingling of the Qi dynasty established a lecture hall at Fayun Vihāra in the Imperial Residence, extensively gathering a multitude of monks to expound the Dharma for six nights (*Hongming ji*).
○ Shi Sengzhong was skilled in the Three Treatises and possessed eloquence; he resided at Zhong...
The Xing Temple was established. In this year, the Wei envoy Li Daogu came to court. The Emperor summoned Zhong to serve as his host and converse with Daogu.
When midday had passed, Zhong did not eat. Daogu asked, "Why do you not eat? Zhong replied, "According to the bequeathed Dharma of the former Buddha, one does not eat after noon.
Daogu said, "Are you not then a śrāvaka? Zhong replied, "Those who are to be saved by means of the śrāvaka vehicle [should be so perceived]."
He would then manifest as a śrāvaka; when preaching the Dharma, he used names as his interlocutors. Thereafter, he remained there, and crowds gathered to lecture and listen.
Prince Wenhui and Prince Jingling repeatedly invited him. He served in the southern capital for seven years before passing away.
Both Prince Wenhui and Prince Wenxuan of Jingling, Ziliang, were refined in Buddhist principles, though Ziliang was particularly profound in his understanding.
He frequently invited renowned monks to lecture on the Buddha-dharma; the grandeur of the assembly, comprising both clergy and laity, was unprecedented in the region south of the Yangtze River.
On occasion, he personally served food and distributed water to the monks, for which the world at large considered him to have lost the dignity of a Chancellor.
Yet, Ziliang’s faith remained ever more profound (Nanshi).
Jiazi (2) & (8): Shi Sengyuan.
Having secluded himself at Dinglin Mountain, he directed his mind toward the garden of the Dharma and longed for the realm beyond the mundane world. He was a renowned scholar of the time.
Zhou Yong, Wu Bao, Zhang Rong, and others all threw themselves at his feet to receive his instructions on the precepts and models of conduct.

When Emperor Taizu of the Qi dynasty was about to ascend the throne, he went into the mountains to seek out Huiyuan. Huiyuan firmly declined, citing his old age and illness such that his feet did not even reach the edge of his bed;

nevertheless, Taizu personally descended to pay his respects and consulted him in full detail. Upon his accession to the imperial position, Taizu again arrived in person by imperial carriage to visit Huiyuan’s quarters, intending to go to his room. However—
The quarters were so narrow that they could not accommodate a palanquin. When Emperor Taizu wished to see Huiyuan, Huiyuan maintained his composure and did not move.

The Emperor then dispatched an envoy to offer greetings before turning his carriage away; Huiyuan had never deigned to show him such courtesy. Later, when he was bedridden with illness, Emperors Wenhui and Wenxuan received him with the etiquette due to a teacher and visited him several times to inquire after his health.
At that time, high-ranking officials and nobles came and went without ceasing. For over fifty years, Huiyuan had subsisted on a vegetarian diet.
In this year, he lived by drinking from mountain streams for over twenty years. On the first month of this year, he passed away. The Emperor sent a letter to Faxian, saying:
"I have learned that Master Yuan has met his end. As a disciple, I already knew of it in the middle of the night. Master Yuan’s departure is truly to a most excellent place."
"I have seen the Dharma Master belatedly; we may now discuss the auspicious dream. I am currently performing meritorious deeds on his behalf, and you may provide whatever is required.
Later, Prince Wenxuan of Jingling wrote again, saying: "Dharma Master Yuan is a man of renowned virtue for this entire era; his reputation is enjoyed throughout the four seas."

I, your disciple, am dull-witted and ignorant, yet I have mistakenly received the guidance of your teacherhood. Just as I was about to look up to your benevolent transformation in order to wash away my troubled thoughts, I did not expect that you would suddenly pass into another world;
how can I bear this grief? Since your master’s deeds and practices were rare and unsurpassed, it is fitting that they should manifest in response: you have come to dwell amidst the monastic tombs.
A separate small territory should be established; the tree-stūpa marks its uniqueness. Stone was carved to commemorate his virtue. He then had a tomb constructed on the southern side of the mountain.

Wang Jian composed the stele inscription (according to the *Benzhuan*). In the eleventh month, the monk Yuan Chang, taking advantage of Emperor Wu’s favorable disposition, was summoned by both Prince Wenxuan and Crown Prince Wenhui.
Thereupon, he traveled eastward by boat (the *Benzhuan* states that he died shortly after arriving in the capital at the age of sixty-nine). Furthermore, at the Dharma...

[The *Xu gaoseng zhuan*] records that Daochang passed away at the beginning of the Jianwu era, at the age of seventy-five. However, since both monastic biographies (*sengzhuan*) were produced by the same hand—Huijiao—yet these two accounts differ in this way, was there truly only one Daochang, or were there perhaps two Daochangs? (This is a question posed by Ren Zhengtong.)

In the year Yichou (the third), [the Emperor] issued an edict appointing the śramaṇas Faxian and Yuanchang as joint Monastic Chiefs (*sengzhu*), assigning them respectively to the northern and southern banks.

Master Xian was pure and refined in his observance of the Vinaya, and his virtue served as a model for all beings. Initially, he traveled west to Khotan, where he obtained a Buddha-tooth relic, sacred texts, and images.
Huan Chang was also pure and disciplined in his observance of the precepts. Crown Prince Wenhui appointed him as his preceptor for the precepts (*śīla-ācārya*).

After Emperor Xian received the imperial decree to travel through the Three Wu regions to carefully select members of the two assemblies (monks and nuns), Huan Chang also traveled eastward to once again propagate the method of receiving the precepts.

Huan Chang passed away at the beginning of the Jianwu era at the age of seventy-five. Emperor Xian died at the end of the Jianwu era at the same age as Huan Chang. (Biographies of Eminent Monks) ○ Shi Fa...

Fadu arrived in the capital at the end of the Song dynasty. The eminent scholar Ming Sengshao was living in seclusion on Mount Lingshan in Langya; he donated his residence to establish the Qixia Vihāra and invited Fadu to dwell there. Previously, there had been a Daoist who wished to use the temple grounds as a retreat, but those who stayed there invariably died.

Later, when it became a monastery, Fadu resided there himself, and all the malevolent spirits ceased their disturbances. One day, a deity appeared and announced its name, saying: [The deity said: "I am the spirit of this mountain. I have long watched over this place. Because of my devotion to the Buddha-dharma, I have protected the site for many years. Now that you have established this monastery here, I shall serve as your guardian.

Fadu replied, "If you truly wish to protect this place, you must not harm sentient beings. The deity bowed and withdrew. From then on, the mountain was peaceful and free from calamities. Fadu remained there until his death, after which he was buried on the mountain. His remains were later enshrined in the monastery, where they remain to this day. People who visit the site often report hearing the sound of his voice or seeing his shadow. Those who pray with sincerity receive his protection and blessings. Thus, his spiritual power continues to manifest even today.
Jin Shang said, "My disciple Wang has possessed this mountain for over seven hundred years. As you, Dharma Master, are one to whom the Way and Virtue turn, I respectfully offer it to you as a gift.

Furthermore, I pray that you will confer upon me the five precepts. Huidu replied, "The lay donor’s ancestral sacrifices involve the consumption of blood; this is the most strictly prohibited among the precepts.
Shang said, "If you are prepared to accept me as a follower, I shall first cease all killing. He then took his leave. After several days, he returned again, bringing money as an offering.
He prepared offerings and prostrated together with the assembly. He ordained [Fadu] and received the precepts for him, after which Fadu departed for Mount Nie.

The temple sorceress dreamed that a deity told her: "I have already received the ordination and the Dharma Master’s precepts; henceforth, do not slaughter animals when sacrificing to me. From then on, the temple offerings consisted only of vegetables and dried meat.
Later, when Fadu fell ill, the deity again offered him medicinal water, and his illness was cured.

In the third month of the Bingyin year (the tenth year), there was a large stone that floated from the sea into the river. It was taken and presented [to the authorities], who carved it into a statue;
the seated height is over three feet (according to the *Sanbao ji*). ○ Shi Senghui passed away at the age of seventy-nine. From Fotudeng to Dao’an... Dao’an... [text fragment].
It reached Huiyuan; from Yüan it passed to Tanshun; from Shun it reached Senghui.

For five generations, their reputation was so highly esteemed that emperors and kings were moved by their influence, and their deeds were recorded in the historical annals (*Beishan lu*). ○ Senghui had a disciple named Sengxiu, who was also distinguished for his learning.
There was also one named Huichang, whose aspirations and conduct were pure and upright; he succeeded Senghui as the head of the monastic community (*Sengshi*). ○ Shi Hongming of Kuaiji.
He passed away at the age of eighty-four. He was clear in his recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* and took the practice of meditation and repentance rituals as his vocation.
Every morning, his water jar would fill itself; a celestial youth served him as his attendant. Tigers would often enter his room and prostrate before his bed, departing only after a long time.
Furthermore, mountain spirits came to disturb him; Ming bound one with his waist-cord, and only released it when the ghost apologized.
*Dingmao* (the fifth year), [Month] 11:
In the first month, Jiaozhou presented a pearl two inches in height, which contained within it an image of the Buddha; its pedestal, dais, brows, and eyes were all complete (*Sanbao ji*).
○ Meng Jingyi, a Daoist of Wuxing, composed the *Zhengyi lun*. Its summary states: "The Buddha, by means of one..."
The vehicle is the Dharma. For the Laozi, it takes "embracing the One" as its model; for the Buddha, it is the *dharmatā* (true mark); for the Dao, it is the Mysterious Female (*xuanpin*).

The Great Image of the Dao is precisely the Dharmakāya of the Buddha. Zhang Rong, the Minister of Education and General of the Household, composed the *Menlü* (Regulations on the Gate), which states in brief:
"The Dao and the Buddha reach the ultimate limit without distinction. He showed this to Zhou Yong of Runan, who challenged it, saying: "The Dharma of Emptiness and the [Dharma of] Existence..."
"Although their nature is identical in its quiescence, the principles regarding the methods for attaining quiescence in various stages differ," and so forth (Nan shi).

○ Shi Jingdu abstained from grain and consumed pine resin. He was capable of lecturing on and reciting the sūtras, dhyāna, and vinaya. Once, while reciting the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, he fell ill and passed away halfway through the text.
His attendant took his place [in the meditation]. After he had finished reading through it, he passed away. People saw a precious horse in the sky carrying his coffin as it departed.
(Wuchen—Year 6; [Year 12] [Jizhou sends a nine-tailed fox;
general amnesty]) Shi Tandu was profoundly versed in the study of the *śāstras* and was peerless in his time. Emperor Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty dispatched an envoy to invite him to Pingcheng.
He opened a grand lecture hall. The Emperor paid his respects by descending from his seat to join the assembly and personally inquired into the subtleties of the doctrine.

Consequently, the number of disciples flourished. He passed away that year. Śramaṇa Daosheng was skilled in exposition and debate; initially, both Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty and Xie Chaozong held him in profound esteem as their teacher.
The Qi Emperor issued an edict appointing him as the successor to Tandu as the Head of the Sangha (Sengzhu). Dharma Master Baoliang was the Prince Wenxuan of Jingling during the Qi dynasty.
Upon hearing his name, the King went in person to the monk’s quarters and invited him to serve as a Dharma master. Later, he moved to Lingwei Monastery to lecture on the sutras.
His sharp eloquence was as transcendent as the heavens; he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* eighty-four times, the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra* forty-two times, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*.

He recited the *Tattvasiddhi*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Large Version), the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Small Version), the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, and others nearly ten times each.
His disciples, both ordained and lay, numbered over three thousand, and those who sought instruction from him were beyond counting (from his biography).

Śramaṇa Puheng constantly practiced dhyāna and was on friendly terms with Master Tao of Shu. He once entered the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) and beheld the karmic deeds of his previous lives.
Regarding matters such as retribution, he later passed away while seated in meditation. ○ Saṃghabhadra (translated here as Sengxian) produced the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* in eighteen fascicles.
○ In the sixth month, Dongyang presented a six-eyed tortoise; there were characters inscribed on its belly.
Furthermore, the banner-pole of Chanling Temple emitted light (from the *Sanbao ji*).

When Sengcheng, the Monastic Head (*Sengtong*) of Xuzhou under the Wei dynasty, passed away, the Emperor issued an edict to Xuzhou to bestow three hundred rolls of silk and to provide a vegetarian feast for five thousand people as an offering for his posthumous merit.
In the year Jisi (the seventh year of the cycle), [the thirteenth day], the Emperor was incensed that the Great Being Baozhi was deluding the masses. He was arrested and imprisoned in Jiankang.

On this day, people saw the Great Being walking through the markets and streets, yet upon inspection, he remained within the prison. That evening, he said to the officials, "Outside the gate, there are two litters."

She was eating rice from a golden bowl; "You may take it," she said. Subsequently, Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince Jingling sent offerings to Jiankang and ordered Lü Wenxian to report this to the Emperor.
The Emperor expressed regret and apologized, welcoming her into the inner palace. Shortly thereafter, while the Emperor was feasting with the ladies of the harem, Baozhi briefly went outside.
Yet, a moment later, she was still seen walking in meditation at the Xianyang Hall. Startled, the Emperor dispatched an official to go and inquire.

The official reported that Daozhi had been out for a long time and was now back in the palace. The Emperor’s divine reverence for him increased all the more. Later, Daozhi manifested supernatural power;

he appeared before Emperor Wu in the underworld, where the Emperor was undergoing the suffering of being pricked by needles and knives. From that time on, the Emperor permanently abandoned the use of needles and knives.

Daozhi’s miraculous manifestations and his transformation of people were not limited to a single instance (from the *Benzhuan*). There was a miraculous stone that floated across the sea and entered the territory of Wu. Zhu Fa... [text fragment] ...was there.

Ranghuo presented [the statue] at court. At that time, the Emperor was constructing Chanling Temple; he therefore had a stone Buddha image carved, over six feet in height, and venerated it with solemnity (*Zulin*).
In this year, the monk Sengzhong passed away. When Zhong first met Emperor Wu at the Qianhe Hall, he addressed him as "I, the poor monk.
At that time, Chang Xian also had an audience with the Emperor; he always addressed him by name and did not take a seat. The Emperor then questioned him...

The former Minister of State Wang Jian asked: "When śramaṇas meet with emperors and kings, what titles do they use? And are they permitted to participate in formal court assemblies? Wang Jian replied:

"During the Eastern Jin dynasty, monks from various regions all referred to themselves as 'poor practitioners' (pindao) and were permitted to participate in court assemblies. In the middle period, Yu Bing and Huan Yuan wished to compel monks to pay full obeisance;

however, the court debates were so tumultuous that these matters were all ultimately abandoned. From the Song dynasty until the present, [monks] have mostly been permitted to participate in such assemblies."

[The Emperor] addressed him as "the Poor Man" (pindao). The Emperor said, "If even these two monks, Xiang and Xian, whose monastic accomplishments (*daoye*) are such as this, still address themselves by name, how much more so should others?
To bow down to them would be excessive; there is no cause for objection in addressing them by name.

From that time on, monks addressed emperors by name; this began with [the monks] Xiang and Xian. (From the *Monk Biographies*, *Sengzhuan*) Śramaṇa Faqi left the household life at Zhizhuan Monastery. He recited the sutras and maintained his simple integrity. One...
During the day, he returned to his former residence, then went to Dinglin Temple, and subsequently returned to Zhishou Monastery.

Examining these three locations later, it was found that he had been partaking of the midday meal at all three places simultaneously; thus, though there were three locations, it was truly one and the same time. That evening, he passed away suddenly.

His corpse was remarkably fragrant and supple, leading the assembly to realize that he had attained the fruit of sainthood. This was reported to the Emperor, who personally visited the site and provided a monastic feast in his honor.
Wen-hui and Wen-xuan both came to pay their respects and assisted in arranging the funeral rites. Offerings and donations gathered like clouds;
with that money, they constructed a stupa at Zhijuan Temple (according to the *Monastic Biographies*).
Gengwu (the eighth day of the month):
(14) The Central Asian Dharma-ti (translated here as Fayi), who translated the *Devadatta-sūtra* and other texts in two fascicles during the Qi dynasty—
Shi Fadao once entered meditative absorption and ascended to the Inner Court, where he beheld Maitreya, who emitted light from his navel that illuminated the sufferings of the three evil realms.
He devoted himself to the Path with such diligence that he remained in a constant sitting posture without lying down; at his death, his complexion, which had been dark, turned white.
Shi Huiji was renowned for his scholarship. The śramaṇas Zhizang, Sengmin, Fayun, and others all approached him to request instruction.

Wenhui and Wenxuan both revered him with the etiquette due to a teacher. In this year, while lecturing on the *Śata-śāstra*, when he reached the "Chapter on Refuting Particles," he suddenly passed away.
Shi Huilong was skilled at lecturing and debating. Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty invited him to the Xianggong Monastery to lecture on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

Subsequently, princes, dukes, and other nobles frequently summoned him to give lectures. Whenever there were points in the traditional interpretations that were stubbornly stuck or obscure, Huilong would clarify and elucidate them until they were perfectly understood.
Zhou Yong remarked of him: "Huilong is carefree and refined, like pine and bamboo beneath the frost. He passed away that year.
(Main Biography) ○ Prince Xiao Ziliang of Jingling established the *Jingzhu jingxing famen* (Dharma-gate of Pure Abiding and Pure Conduct).
"Pure abiding" (*jingzhu*) is a translation for *poṣadha*, meaning to abide in accordance with the precepts by purifying body, speech, and mind. As for the "Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct":
