Because all karmas are purified, one transforms and acts within the world; because one has thoroughly understood the various dharma-gates, there are distinctions among their characteristics and natures.

(The text consists of two fascicles; the Monk Shi Tong of Zhongnan Mountain during the Tang Dynasty abridged it into one fascicle. Thus, it serves as the first step for those with a beginner’s mind and marks the preceding tracks for those who strive thereafter. Those who revere and believe in it are called people of pure conduct. To believe and practice it is not to let it perish—the title "Pure Abiding" (*Ningzhu*).

First, the Gate of Distinguishing Virtue through the Sovereign Awakening: because the Buddha-way is supreme, one constantly sets one's will upon the Mahāyāna. Second, the Gate of Opening Beings to Faith: by washing away the defilements of the mind, one then beholds the Dharmakāya. Third, the Gate of Purification...)

1. The Gate of Eliminating the Three Karmas: Since there is nothing that surpasses repentance as the essential means for extinguishing suffering. 2. The Gate of Cultivating the Six Faculties: To adorn the Dharma-body, one must purify the six sense faculties. 3. The Gate of Birth, Old Age, Sickness, and Death: Regarding the great suffering of these four marks, one should give rise to a mind of weary detachment.

4. The Gate of Self-Reproach toward Body and Mind: By examining the three karmas, ensure that no good deed is left unpracticed. 5. The Gate of Examining and Concealing the Three Karmas: Constantly inspecting oneself to see how much one delights in goodness or clings to evil. 6. The Gate of Rebuking and Interrogating the Four Elements.

9. Because the four great elements are shameless, they cause me to suffer. 10. Leaving home follows the gate of goodness, for one knows the faults [of worldly life] and the merit of leaving home is pure and sublime. 11. Remaining at home follows the gate of evil, for the suffering and affliction of desire for those remaining at home are boundless.

11. The Gate of the Sunken and Obscure Hells: because one receives retribution for the three miserable realms, it depends solely upon the three poisons. 12. The Gate of the Renunciant Embracing the Way: because one must constantly restrain [the senses], wondrous practice will surely be accomplished.

13. The Gate of the Layperson Embracing Goodness: because once one knows its afflictions, one should follow the Buddha’s teachings. 14. The Gate of Suffering Within the Three Realms: because worldly phenomena are all suffering; there is nothing therein that can be enjoyed. 15. The Gate of Bliss Beyond the Three Realms: because by cultivating and realizing the Dharma-body, one attains great sovereignty. 16. The Gate of Severing Doubt and Confusion: because with wisdom, confusion is removed. 17.

The Gate of the Ten Kinds of Shame and Remorse: because I lack the karmic work of the Way, I am deeply ashamed and abashed. 18. The Gate of Utmost Great Shame and Remorse: Internally and externally...

19. The Gate of Self-Examination and Utmost Shame: by means of constant mutual admonition. 20. The Gate of Precepts Governing Life: by means of generating virtuous qualities through the precepts. 21. The Gate of Ending the Old and Stopping the New: by means of various forms of self-congratulation. 22.

The Gate of Great Patience Toward Adverse Conditions: by means of the greatness of the power of patience. 23. The Gate of Unimpeded Engagement with Objects: by means of practicing the Dharma of liberation. 24. The Gate of Single-Minded Diligence: by means of courageous and vigorous cultivation.

25. Paying homage to the Śarīra stupas. 26. Reverencing and honoring the True Dharma. 27. Supporting and nourishing the field of the Sangha: by means of constant reverence for the Three Jewels. 28. The Gate of Exhortation and Entreaty for Progress: twenty.

The ninth is the gate of rejoicing in ten thousand virtues; the thirtieth is the gate of dedicating [merit] toward the Buddha-way; the thirty-first is the gate of making vows for adornment—all of these accomplish pure conduct. All these gates have extensive expositions; they are seen in detail in the *Hongming ji* (Collection on Propagating and Clarifying [the Dharma]).
○ During the Wei dynasty, the śramaṇa Yingtong was granted by imperial decree an annual allotment of three hundred bolts of silk.
Xinwei (the ninth year, the fifteenth day):

Guṇavidi (translated here as Anjin) from the Western Regions was thoroughly versed in all internal and external scriptural studies. He participated in the translation of scriptures during the Qi dynasty.
In the *renshen* year (the tenth year), [Emperor] summoned the recluse He Dian to serve as Vice Director of the Secretariat.
Dian did not go. The Dian family had served the Buddha with great devotion for generations.
Together with Zhang Rong and Kong Zhiqi, they formed a circle of "square" (non-secular) friendships, attracting eminent companions to engage in refined discourse and compose poetry.
He wandered about in self-contentment. When the Chancellor Wang Jian and Prince Yi of Yuzhang went to visit him, they were both unable to see him.

Later, when Daodian was at Falun Temple, Prince Ziliang of Jingling went to see him. Daodian put on his horned cap and ascended the seat; Prince Ziliang sat opposite him, feeling an inexhaustible sense of joy.
In his youth, Daodian had once suffered from thirst that did not cease for many years. Later, while he was in Wucheng... [at] Shifo...
At a Buddhist temple, while preaching the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* in the lecture hall, he fell asleep during the day and dreamed that a strange monk bestowed upon him a handful of medicinal pellets.

Upon consuming them in his dream, he was immediately cured. At that time, it was considered to have been moved by his pure virtue. Subsequently, the Wei dynasty issued an edict decreeing that on the eighth day of the fourth month every year, [the Buddha’s birthday]...

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, it was decreed that one hundred persons from a large prefecture, fifty from a medium prefecture, and twenty from a small prefecture might become monks or nuns;
this was established by imperial edict as a permanent regulation. Shi Chaobian resided at Dinglin Temple in the capital.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* once every day, and with whatever strength remained, he prostrated before the Thousand Buddhas more than one million five hundred thousand times, never venturing outside his room.

He remained at the gate for over thirty years. In this year, he manifested his passing. As for the monk Tanchao, who propagated the teachings of the Chan path, he resided at Lingyuan Mountain in Qiantang.
After entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) for several days, he suddenly saw a person come and pay him homage, saying:

"Your disciple lives seven *li* away, being a native of Fuyang County. I excavated the foot of the mountain, thereby encroaching upon and destroying the dragon’s dwelling. The dragons were enraged and swore an oath three times."
"It has not rained for a hundred days; now that the hundred days have passed, the fields and ponds are parched and dry. We wish to entreat you, whose virtue and Way are profound, to go before them;
you will surely be able to evoke moistening rains and bring benefit to the common people, such that the merit may be attributed to you. Daochao granted his permission. The spirit then departed.

Daochao traveled south for five days until he reached Mount Chiting, where he offered prayers for the dragons. When night fell, the dragons manifested as human beings and came to pay their respects to him. Daochao...

He further preached the Dharma, whereupon [the dragon] returned to seek the Three Refuges and identified himself as a dragon. He requested that Xuāocháo bring down rain, but they looked at one another in silence.
That night, he appeared in Xuāocháo’s dream and said: "I originally made this vow out of anger; since you have now guided me toward the good, I dare not disobey your command.
At the hour of *bù* tomorrow, rain shall fall. When the time arrived, the rain fell in abundance, and the harvest for the year was secured. This year, the Master...

End of [the main biography]. Emperor Wei issued an edict to the Governor of Xuzhou to bestow three hundred rolls of silk and to provide a vegetarian feast for five hundred people, thereby honoring the deceased with further merit.
Guiyou (the eleventh year; in the seventh month, the Emperor passed away and Emperor Zhaoye of Yulin ascended the throne). (Seventeen) In the seventh month, Emperor Wu passed away.
He had occupied the throne for twelve years. He greatly promoted the teachings of the Dharma and constructed the two monasteries of Zhaoxian and Youxuan (according to local gazetteers).
Initially, when the Great Being Baozhi was at Hualin Garden, he suddenly donned a three-peaked cloth cap over his existing one.
Before long, the Emperor passed away, followed in succession by the death of Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince of Yuzhang;

thus it was exactly as the prophecy had foretold. Wang Zhongxiong asked, "What office shall I hold? He did not answer the question directly, but instead gave him a left-hand cord from the end of his staff.

Later, Zhongxiong indeed reached the rank of Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs (*shàngshū zuǒchéng*). When Xu Ling was a child, his father took him to visit [Seng]zhi. Zhi rubbed the crown of his head and said: "This..."
"The boy is a stone qilin from the heavens. Later, Ling indeed became prominent in the world. Shi Sengbian was skilled in Sanskrit chanting.
Once, while he was reading a sutra, a flock of cranes descended and gathered before his steps; when the recitation ended, they departed. He passed away that year.

Jiaxu (the first month, Emperor Yulin changed the era name to Longchang; in the seventh month, he was assassinated; Prince Zhao-wen of Hailing ascended the throne and changed the era name to Yuanxing; in the tenth month, Emperor Gaozong Mingdi ascended the throne) [changed the era name to Jianwu];
(Year 18) [the capital was moved to Luoyang];
the monk Sengrou. In his youth, he ascended the lecture hall. He had a dream of Mount Lingjiu in Shan. The monk Sengxu [was visited by] a divine person at night holding a banner.
The local gentry welcomed him as he filled the mountains. Emperor Tai Zu and all the princes, including Wen Xuan, established monasteries and gathered monks for him;

because he was renowned for his gentle virtue and long-standing reputation, imperial summons arrived year after year. Despite being invited repeatedly by the Princes Wen Xuan and others, he finally left the capital and stayed at Dinglin Monastery, where he personally served as the master craftsman.

Those from near and far looked up to him with reverence; both Princes Wen Hui and Wen Xuan followed his teachings and entered his inner circle, while he constantly vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peace (Sukhāvatī).
During his years of cultivation, his body was free from any further ailment. Facing west, he performed his devotions with profound reverence and suddenly passed away.

Śramaṇa Huìyuè possessed a refined character and virtue from his youth. Both Chǔ Yuǎn, the Grand Chancellor and Duke Wénjiǎn, and Wáng Jiǎn, the Grand Marshal, both requested him to lecture on the Dharma.

When Chǔ Yuǎn fell ill, he dreamed of a deity who said, "A Bodhisattva is coming. Shortly thereafter, Huìyuè arrived, and Yuǎn’s illness was immediately cured. He served as a Palace Attendant (Jíshìzhōng).

Liu Youyu was a descendant of Shen Yue’s clan ancestor. Every time he saw him, he would rise to pay his respects. Someone asked, “Since you are a junior member of this master’s clan, why are you so respectful?
Youyu replied, “When a Bodhisattva appears in the world, he becomes a teacher to all under heaven; how could it be merely that I, an old man, am paying my respects?

When Shen Yue was subsequently assigned to an external post, Youyu accompanied him to the commandery. There, he took delight solely in meditation and recitation, and a wondrous fragrance [pervaded the area].
He entered the chamber; fierce beasts became docile at the steps. A Daoist practitioner descended and resided in the guest house with virtuous tranquility.
It was rumored that he had been afflicted by a mountain spirit. Xu Bichao, the Magistrate of Changshan, invited him to reside there, and the malevolent spirits were pacified.

Later, two women dressed in green emerged from the mountain stream and paid their respects, saying: "Our karmic obstructions have been deep and heavy, causing us to fall as spirits of this water. We have been distressed day and night."
[When] Nao [saw this], he immediately conferred the precepts upon him. From that time on, calamities and anomalies were forever eliminated (according to the *Benzhuan*).

In the year Yihai (the second year of Jianwu, the nineteenth year of the sexagenary cycle), He Yin, the younger brother of [He] Dian, was a man of profound learning with a great reputation. He once entered Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhongshan to listen to [lectures].

He was thoroughly proficient in the inner scriptures (Buddhist texts). Upon reaching this point, he was appointed as Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhongshu Ling). Shortly thereafter, he submitted a memorial to resign from his post.
Because Kuaiji was rich in numinous wonders, Daoyin went there to travel and reside at Yunmen Monastery on Mount Ruoye.

Since he had retired together with his elder brother, they were known at the time as Dadian, the "Great Mountain," and Daoyin, the "Small Mountain. He subsequently moved his residence to Qinwang Mountain, where he established a lecture hall within a forest.
The Founding of the Monastery. His lofty character influenced the whole world. The śramaṇa Huian was an eight-year-old novice when he resided at Jiangling Temple.

Whenever it was his turn to sit in the assembly, he would invariably rise to serve water; he would always carry an empty pitcher, yet as he moved from the top to the bottom of the hall, the water never ran out.
The assembly marveled at this. After he received full ordination, his spiritual wonders became even more manifest. Once, he ascended the hall together with the śramaṇa Huiji.

During the *poṣadha* ceremony, before the doors of the hall had even opened, Dao’an emerged from the wall without obstruction. Huiji was struck with awe. Later, he traveled to Xiang along with a merchant caravan; on the way, he passed away.
As he was about to die, he said to the merchant, "After I die, expose my corpse upon the riverbank;

there is no need for a coffin. The merchant followed his instructions and cast the body onto the bank. That night, flames issued forth from its body, and the merchant was greatly terrified. When [the merchant] arrived...
When the boat reached the region of Xiang, Dao'an had already arrived there beforehand; when [Huiyuan] wished to approach him to speak, he had already vanished from his location.

Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty visited the White Pagoda Temple in Xuzhou. The temple housed the Dharma Master Daodeng, who was profoundly devoted to the study of Buddhist doctrine. The Emperor held him in high regard and rewarded him with great favor.

He constantly attended as a lecturer within the inner palace. Upon his death, the Emperor issued an edict expressing deep sorrow and grief, bestowing one thousand bolts of silk and providing a vegetarian feast for the entire community of monks.
For seven days in the capital city, ritual practices were performed. (Weishu) ○ Liu Qiu, a recluse from Jingzhou, during the Taishi era of the Song dynasty.
He served as the Magistrate of Dangyang and later as the Vice-Governor of Nanjun. He first began his practice of casting off worldly robes at the age of thirty-two.

Thereafter, he abstained from grains and cereals, subsisting on wood-shavings. He wore garments of hempen cloth, sandals of straw, and lived in a thatched hut. He attended the ceremonial curtains to perform liturgical recitations, maintaining a perpetual fast throughout the six periods of the day.

He did not neglect the conventional truths of the world, yet he completely set aside all calligraphy and the arts, devoting himself exclusively to the profound study of Buddhist principles. He provided commentaries and lectures on various [sutras].

Throughout the world, none did not hold his character in high esteem. At the beginning of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as a Tongzhi Sanqishi Lang, but he did not accept.
At the beginning of the Jianwu era, he served briefly as a Guozibo Shi. That winter, he moved to stay at Baiyun (White Cloud) in Jiangzhou.
A strange fragrance lingered about him, and the sounds of bells and Buddhist chants resonated from the air. He subsequently passed away at the age of [blank].
60. During the Datong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, he was posthumously titled Master Wenfan (Hongming ji).
Bingzi (the third year of the Tianjian era), [Day] 20:
Shi Huiji once received two imperial edicts from the Song Emperor; declining on the grounds of illness, he did not travel, but instead remained at Mount Gui in Huaiyi.
He established the Baolin Vihāra, where Zhou Yong and Zhang Rong both extended the rites of a teacher to him. Furthermore, he composed a commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra* for King Wenxuan.
As his virtue spread throughout the Three Wu regions and his reputation resounded across the four seas, an imperial edict appointed him as the Chief Monk (*Sengzhu*) to oversee ten cities.
Those from afar followed his lead like the wind, and the fivefold assembly submitted to his authority. Zhiyi’s character was stern yet capable of warmth; he was pure and—
Because [Sengchou] was so profoundly reverent, none among his disciples failed to feel a sense of awe and trepidation. In the eleventh month of that year, he passed away at the age of eighty-five.

○ Shi Sengzong was skilled at lecturing on the sutras, yet he followed his own nature with unrestrained abandon; whenever he found a point that pleased him, he would act upon it immediately, regarding no such conduct as an impediment.
Prince Wenhui was about to expel him, but after receiving a profound response in a dream, he changed his mind and returned to him.

Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty admired his character and virtue from afar and repeatedly sent letters requesting that he open a lecture series. Emperor Gaozu of the Qi dynasty, however, did not permit him to travel outside;
thus, Huiyuan remained at the capital, supporting himself through offerings of faith and establishing Taichang Temple. He passed away in this year (according to the *Benzhuan*).
Dingchou (the fourth year) [21]:

The Indian Buddhist Master Buddhabhadra (translated here as "The Awakened One") first arrived at Northern Tai’an in Wei during the reign of Emperor Xiaowen. The Emperor provided him with special provisions and support.
Later, when the Emperor moved south and established the capital at Yiluo, he again established a quiet monastery for him to reside in; however, his heart’s desire was to love the Song Mountains.
Emperor Wu issued an imperial decree for him to establish a monastery on Mount Shaoshi; this is the present-day Shaolin Monastery.

He ordained his disciples Huiguang and Sengchou, both of whom were deeply devoted to the practice of meditative concentration. A benevolent deity constantly followed them like a shadow to protect them. Later, when his life was nearing its end, he reported [to the Emperor]:
He painted images of deities on the walls himself (Biography). On the eighth day of the fifth month, Fu Dashi was born in Yiwu County, Wuzhou;
his name was Xi and his courtesy name was Xuānfēng. In the eighth month, the monk Jing Fǎshī of Lúshān passed away. This master had long since ceased eating grain;
he was once attended by two spirits standing in service (Hongming ji). Dharma Master Fǎyún lectured on the sutras at the age of thirty.
His excellence was peerless in his time (according to his biography).

In the year Wuyi (the first year of Yongtai, the seventh month), the Emperor passed away and the Prince of Donghun, Baojuan, ascended the throne. On the twenty-second day, the Ming Emperor passed away.
He had occupied the throne for five years. He constantly observed the six fast days and devoted himself to cultivating the ten wholesome deeds, reciting the Dharma.
He transcribed the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras, copied all the scriptures, established a temple for taking refuge, and commissioned a golden statue worth a thousand pieces of gold (*fangzhi*).

○ Shi Fajian possessed a reputation for wisdom from his youth; by the time he reached the age of twenty, he had already become a master of the Dharma. Wenxuan He Yin was a renowned scholar of his time.

He was thoroughly versed in both the literary and doctrinal aspects of the teachings. He passed away that year. As for the monk Fayan: he was skilled in ritual chanting and guidance (*cangdao*), and was also adept at physiognomy and divination.

Princes, dukes, scholars, and commoners alike took him as their teacher to receive the precepts. At that time, the monastery was situated near a site prone to fires; whenever a fire broke out nearby, it invariably reached the temple.

When his disciples wished to carry Fayan out of the temple, Fayan said, "If the Buddha is to be consumed by fire, what use would I have for living? Thereupon, he applied himself with diligent heart to recollecting the Buddha.
These three halls were consumed by fire, yet only the temple itself remained unburnt (according to the *Benzhuan*).
In the Jǐmǎo year (the first year of the Yongyuán era of Emperor Dōnghūnhóu, the twenty-third year), Śramaṇa Sēngyìn appeared.
His learning spanned many scriptures, but he was particularly renowned for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. During the Dàmíng era of the Song dynasty, Hé Diǎn...
He requested that [Wang] Yin be appointed as a Dharma Master. Listeners gathered there in great numbers; both Wenxuan and Xu Xiaosi revered his character. He passed away that year.
Shi Huitong had, since the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, spoken of future events that were all proven true.
That year, he suddenly asked someone for wine, saying, "I wish to travel far to bid farewell to my acquaintances; you all should diligently cultivate goodness. He then passed away.
First, after finishing his wine, he went to the edge of the wall and lay upon the ground. When they went to look at him, he was already dead. Later, others saw him there again (from the *Benzhuan*).
In the fourth month, Emperor Gaozu Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty passed away. The Emperor had occupied the throne for twenty-nine years. He once built Anxiang Monastery in Ye;
he never let go of his books, and in his leisure time, he personally lectured on them for the ladies of the six palaces, all of whom observed the six fasts.
He was diligent in reciting the sutras and encouraged those who aspired to the Way to leave the household life. He provided abundant and generous offerings to the various monastics.

The monks and nuns he ordained numbered fourteen thousand (as recorded in the *Bianzheng lun* and other texts). In this month, Emperor Shizong Xuanwu (Ke) ascended the throne and issued an edict stating:
"Since the clergy and the laity differ, their laws and regulations also differ; thus, the Way of the Buddha is manifest both in the hidden and the visible realms."
Prohibitions and exhortations each have their appropriate application. Regarding monks who commit crimes such as murder and above, they shall be adjudicated according to secular codes;
all other offenses shall be referred to the Office of Imperial Clergy (Zhaoxuan) to be judged by internal monastic law and regulations (*Weishu*).
Gengchen (the second year); [the first year of Jingming under Emperor Xuanwu].
Shi Fadu and Fashao were then known as the "Two Sages of the Northern Mountains. Shao’s religious practice was pure and austere, and his reputation equaled that of Fadu.

Yet he excelled them in learning and understanding. Both were held in high esteem and venerated as teachers by Prince Ziliang of Jingling and others. Sengdu once received the precepts from the mountain deity of Langya.
Furthermore, he constantly vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), and thus specialized in lecturing on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.

He passed away that year (*Biographies of Eminent Monks*). *Śramaṇa Senghou*: At the beginning of the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he came to the capital and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Prabhāsa* sūtras. He constantly...
Twice a day he would eat once; in this manner, for over sixty years, he maintained a vegetarian diet and refrained from eating after midday.

In that year, he passed away while in *añjali* (palms joined), at the age of eighty-nine. As for the monk Senghui: Initially, Liu Qiu of Nanyang established Zheshan Temple and invited him to reside there.
Senghui constantly desired to cross the Yangtze River, but the ferrymen, because their boat was small, had not yet allowed him to pass. Senghui—
He had already reached the other shore. Furthermore, he would visit the homes of the sick; those who met with his anger would surely die, while those who received his joy would surely recover.

He was also able to manifest multiple bodies simultaneously to attend people's offerings. That year, he passed away, leaving behind many miraculous manifestations (from the *Benzhuan*). Regarding Emperor Donghun:
at Waguan Temple, he dismantled the statue of King Vaideha to grind its hairpins and bracelets for his favorites, using them as grand ornaments. This was the destruction wrought by Emperor Donghun.
This is a jade statue. Initially, its two arms were cut off and fashioned into hairpins. When the Emperor died, the sword-bearer Huang [wielded] his blade;
during the Taiping era, he injured his knee with that blade at night and fell to the ground, whereupon he met his own end. How swift was the retribution!
Xinsi (Emperor He; Baorong; the third month marked the start of the Zhongxing era; in the twelfth month, the Prince of Donghun was assassinated and died).
[2] Imperial decree appointing Shi Huiqiu as the Monastic Head (Sengzhu) of Jingzhou. His merit in instructing and exhorting [the clergy] earned him renown in his time.
He died in the third year of the Tianjian era. ○ Lishi Zhicheng preached the Dharma for over forty years. He was revered by both monastics and laypeople. He died in this same year.

(Hongming). In the second or third month of the Renwu year, Emperor He abdicated the throne to Xiao Yan, the Prince of Liang. Thus ended the twenty-four years of the seven successive rulers of the Qi dynasty.
There were twenty translators who produced seventy-two works in three hundred and fifty fascicles from the sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras.
There were two thousand and fifteen monasteries, with more than thirty-two thousand monks and nuns.
*Comprehensive Chronicle of Buddhism through the Successive Dynasties*, Volumes Four and Five.
Compiled by the monk Benjue of Yishan Yian of the Song Dynasty.
Verified by the Layman Ming Ruru, Bi Xicai. The Southern Dynasties (Nanbeichao):
Liang. Capital:
Jiankang. Four rulers. A total of fifty-six years. Abolished [by the Chen].

During the Chen and Wei dynasties, the Yuan clan split into Eastern and Western branches during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu (Eastern Wei was based in Ye; one ruler reigned for seventeen years before abdicating to the Qi.
Western Wei was based in Chang’an; three rulers reigned for twenty-three years before abdicating to the Zhou).
Renwu (the first year of Tianjian of Emperor Wu of Liang) [equivalent to the third year of Jingming of Emperor Shizong of Wei]:
In the fourth month, Emperor Wu of Liang ascended the throne. At that time, he was thirty-seven years old. Having attained the imperial position, the Emperor reflected upon the common people.

He attained the same realization as the Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-sambodhi) and joined the assembly of the All-Knowing One (Sarvajña). With hands folded in ease, he presided over the court and extensively propagated the teachings of the Sūtras.
He widely invited those of ancient learning and gathered scattered texts from all quarters. He fanned the pure winds [of virtue] for the benefit of both the clergy and the laity (*Sanbao ji*).

The Emperor summoned Baozhi to the palace and treated him with great honor and favor. Consequently, he issued an edict stating: "Master Baozhi’s traces reside within the mundane world, yet his spirit wanders in the profound stillness. Like water..."
Fire cannot burn it, nor can water submerge it; snakes and tigers cannot invade it. When one speaks of its Buddhist principles, it surpasses the level of the Śrāvakas;
when one discusses its esoteric doctrines, even the most exalted recluses and immortals are eclipsed. How can one allow the ordinary sentiments of a worldly person to needlessly constrain it?
"From now on, you may travel and teach as you please; do not be restricted again. Because of this, Sengzhi frequently entered and left the inner palace (from his *Benzhuan*).

The Vice President of the Secretariat, Shen Yue, submitted a memorial requesting that Emperor [Wu] invite Dharma Master Huiyue to reside within the government offices to provide for him, where he would then lecture on the Dharma.
An imperial edict appointed Shi Hui-chao as the Great Sangzheng (Chief Rectifier of the Monks). Hui-chao was over eight chi tall, and his waistband was ten spans in circumference.
Virtue of the precepts is cultivated within, while majestic deportment is purified without. All members of the monastic community follow these established instructions.

The Son of Heaven provides provisions such as official passes, sheep-carts, swift-footed attendants, and clothing. From the time his voice and teachings first reached this land, these have served as the constitutional statutes for the five schools of Buddhism.

All received his influence. Thus, once during a break between lectures, he suddenly saw a powerful benevolent deity who said, "You should gather those with a common affinity and come together to partake of this meal.
On the day the lecture was held, they suddenly filled the seats; their appearances were magnificent and extraordinary, such that no one could recognize them.
Only when the session had concluded did they disperse. Such were the signs of his majestic traces and miraculous manifestations (from his biography). ○ In winter, Zhongduan and Qunana...

Vidi died. His disciples traveled to the region between the Yangtze and Huai rivers, where he translated essential scriptures. Princes and dukes honored his work, establishing monasteries and nurturing disciples;
his virtuous achievements were highly renowned (Shilu). ○ The monk Zhizhao of Tianzhu came from the Western Regions, sailing by ship to the land of Han.

Tracing the current upstream, he arrived at Shaoshan, at the mouth of the Caoxi Brook. Smelling its fragrance, he cupped his hands to taste its flavor and said, "There is a superior site upstream on this water;
I shall seek it out. He subsequently cleared the mountain and established Baolin Monastery, declaring:
"One hundred and seventy years from now, there shall be the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure that will expound the Dharma here. This is the present Sixth Patriarch of Nanhua" (from the *Shiwen*).
[Included in the *Leiju* (Classified Collection)]. Guiwei (the second year); [Day] (fourth).
The Kingdom of India presented an imperial coral Buddha statue to the Emperor of Liang (*Tongji*). ○ Master Yun Guang of Fayun Temple lectured on the sutras.

The heavens rained down flowers. The Emperor took this as a sign of divine verification. That night, in the Hanguang Hall, he burned incense and offered a petition to invite Baozhi, while providing a vegetarian feast for the two masters Fayun and Yun Guang.
On the following day, Baozhi arrived alone; Yun Guang did not yet know that the Emperor held Baozhi in such high esteem (*Monastic History*).
One day, the Emperor summoned Master Zhigong to the palace and granted him a seat in the private hall. Suddenly, Baozhi knit his brows and frowned. He drew—
He sighed deeply from his neck. The Emperor questioned him with surprise, and Sengzhi replied, "An enemy has been born. The Emperor could not fathom this;
it was because that year Hou Jing was born at the Huaisu Garrison in the Xianbei region—he was the latter incarnation of the Prince of Donghun.
(From the *Yinzilun*) The śramaṇa Mandara (translated here as "Weak Voice") produced eleven fascicles of the *Ratnamegha* and other sutras. Initially, the Emperor’s consort, Lady Xi, had married...
The Emperor had three daughters. While the Emperor served as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Yongzhou, one of his consorts passed away. She was by nature cruel and jealous;
having transformed into a giant python, she entered the inner palace and appeared to the Emperor in a dream, seeking merit to rescue her from suffering.

The Emperor examined the Great Canon and composed the *Compassionate Way-Place Repentance Method* (*Cibei daochang chanfa*). He commissioned monks to perform prostrations before the Buddha and repent for her sins. Soon thereafter, she transformed back.
The Heavenly Being (tianren). In mid-air, he thanked Emperor Wudi for his meritorious deeds, saying that he had already attained rebirth in heaven.

The Emperor did not again discuss the appointment of a Queen for the remainder of his life (*from the Nan shi*). ○ Dharma Master Fayun was held in high esteem by the Emperor, who issued an edict permitting him to enter and exit the various palaces.

There, he frequently expounded the essentials of the Dharma; once, while lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*, he moved the heavens so that celestial flowers fell like snow. Master Zhigong respected him and addressed him as "Dashi" (Great Master).

On the eighth day of the fourth month of the year Jiashen (the first year of the Zhengshi era), Emperor [Wu] led more than twenty thousand monastics and laypeople to ascend the Chongyun Hall. There, he renounced the Daoist path and took refuge in the Buddha. (From the "Biography of Dharma Master Lin," Main Tradition)
The Emperor composed this preface himself. It states in brief: "I, the disciple, Xiao Yan, the Emperor of the Liang State, prostrate myself and pay homage.

I have humbly observed the teachings of the Triple Gem of the Buddhas, Dharmas, and Sangha throughout the ten directions. As the sutras state: 'He who gives rise to the bodhicitta is one whose mind is the Buddha-mind; no other virtues can serve as a metaphor for it.
This mind is able to emerge from the gate of suffering within the triple world and enter the supreme path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). I, the disciple..."
In the past, we were deluded and ignorant, indulging in the teachings of Laozi. For generations, we have inherited this adherence to heterodox doctrines.

Now, we renounce our former habits and take refuge in the True Awakening. We vow that in future lives, those born as boys shall leave the household life, extensively transform sentient beings, and together attain Buddhahood.
It would be better to remain long within the True Dharma even if it meant falling into the evil realms, than to delight in following the teachings of Laozi even if it were to yield temporary gain.
[They] were reborn in heaven. They ascended the causes for the Mahāyāna and were forever freed from false views. On the eleventh day, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "Edict to the Gatekeepers:
Among the great scriptures, it is said that there are ninety-six kinds of paths. Only the single path of the Buddha is the True Path; all others are heterodox paths.
I have abandoned heterodox paths to serve the Tathāgata. If the high officials are able to enter into this vow, each may [proclaim it]."
Regarding the bodhicitta: although Laozi, Confucius, and others were disciples of the Tathāgata, they taught only worldly virtues for the sake of conversion;

they were unable to transform the ordinary into the sagely. High officials, ministers, dukes, kings, and their clansmen ought to turn away from the false toward the true, and abandon the heterodox to enter the orthodox.
As the sūtras and śāstras state: "If one serves non-Buddhist paths while holding the Buddha-dharma dear in one's heart, yet holds it lightly..."

This is a false view. If the mind is uniform and of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), yet the mind that serves the Buddha is strong while the mind [toward] Laozi is weak, this constitutes "Pure Faith" (*qingxin*).
"Pure" means that both the internal and external are pure; such faith is correct and not deviant.
Therefore, one is called a "Disciple of the Buddha with Pure Faith. All other forms of goodness are false views and cannot be termed "Correct Faith. [Your] Excellency, act swiftly.
The rites were performed. On the fourteenth day, the high officials submitted a memorial, and [the Emperor] complied with the imperial decree. The Emperor replied in a handwritten edict:

"To be able to turn back from delusion and enter the Way of Orthodoxy may be called having planted roots of goodness in former lives; you should apply yourself with even greater vigor. (From the *Bianzheng lun*) An edict was issued to the recluse He Dian.

Upon meeting the Emperor, Dian was specially appointed as Palace Attendant (*Shizhong*), but he did not accept. The Emperor issued another edict to appoint He [Tianzhi] as Minister of Works (*Sikong*) to establish the Huqiu [Monastery].
Yin. When Yin failed to arrive, an imperial decree was issued to grant him the status of a layman (*baiyi*). The Minister Lu Yin declined and would not accept it.
Dian and Yin both established great principles and propagated the Buddha-dharma (*Nanshi*). ○ The śramaṇa Sengsheng produced the *Jie biqiu jing* (Sūtra on the Precepts for Bhikṣus).

Furthermore, Dao Huan produced the *Zhongjing yaolan* (Essential Survey of Various Scriptures; *Sanbao jing*). ○ The Emperor established Guangzhai Monastery at his own residence and cast a gilded bronze statue one *zhang* in height.

Regarding the eight statues: as the artisan was about to cast them, he suspected that the copper would be insufficient and was just about to submit a request to his superiors when, suddenly, a messenger arrived leading fifteen carts of copper, saying, "I have been sent by imperial decree to deliver this to the temple.
They immediately proceeded with the melting and casting; it was completed in a single pour.

Upon noticing that they were exceptionally large and tall, they measured them and found them to be two zhang and two chi. When this report was submitted to the throne, the Imperial Decree stated: "We did not originally send any copper; this is surely..."
The spirit manifested in response to his invocation. He subsequently carved a flower-base (pedestal) as a record of this spiritual event (*Gantong lu*).
In the year Yiyou (the fourth year), there was a great harvest, and rice was sold at thirty coins per *hu*.

At first, the Emperor dreamed that a divine monk told him: "The six realms and four modes of birth are undergoing great suffering and distress. Why do you not create [a relief] for them through water?"
He fasted for six days and rescued her. The Emperor asked, "The śramaṇa Master Zhigong urged me to seek out the scriptures; there must surely be a karmic cause for this.

He then had the Tripitaka brought forth and personally examined it, subsequently composing the ritual texts. After three years, they were completed. At night, he held the texts and extinguished the candles, praying to the Buddha:
"If the principles of these texts accord with the Holy One, then may this lamp shine of its own accord whenever anyone prostrates before it."
In some cases, when the ritual procedures were not yet detailed, the lamps would remain as dark as at the beginning; once the words were finished, [the practitioner] prostrated himself on the ground.

Upon rising from the first prostration, the lamps and candles were all brightly illuminated. On the fifteenth day of the second month, at Jinsan Temple, the rites were performed according to the protocol.

The Emperor personally attended the site, and by imperial decree, Vinaya Master You was commissioned to proclaim the texts. Thus, benefit reached both the realms of the unseen and the seen (Weijiang ji). ○ Qianshan in Shuzhou is most...
The site was secluded and the foothills were particularly magnificent. Master Zhìgōng and the Immortal White Crane both desired it, so they reported the matter to Emperor Wŭdì.
Since both men possessed supernatural powers, the Emperor ordered each to mark the location with an object; whoever claimed it would be the one to reside there.
The Daoist said, "I shall take the place where the crane alights as my mark. Master Zhigong said, "I shall take the place where my monk’s staff (*zhixi*) strikes the ground as my mark.
Shortly thereafter, the crane flew off first; as it was about to settle at the foot of the mountain, the sound of the staff flying through the air was suddenly heard from above.
Master Zhigong’s staff then struck and remained fixed at the base of the mountain, while the crane, startled, settled elsewhere. The Daoist was displeased, yet he had to abide by his previous words.

"It must not be eaten. Thereupon, each built a dwelling according to what they knew (*Shiwen Leiju*). On the seventeenth day of the third month, Shi Zhong Xiao Lun submitted a memorial, stating in brief:
"Your servant has heard that the Tathāgata sent down clouds of compassion and bestowed rains of ambrosia.

It coincides with the time when Your Majesty, a Bodhisattva, responds to Heaven and governs all things, transforming the people through the Dharma. As you expound the Way and transmit the scriptures, your virtuous fame fills our ears."
"Your servant now discloses his delusions and knows the direction toward which he must turn. Having received the Bodhisattva Great Precepts, I shall restrain my body and mind;

I renounce the heterodox winds of Laozi and enter the true teachings of the Dharma-stream. I prostrate myself, praying that Your Majesty’s compassionate grace will graciously grant me this permission.
From then on, all the officials abandoned heterodoxy and returned to the orthodox path (*Bianzheng lun*). ○ Jiang Mi, a Doctor of the Imperial Academy, had a daughter who was young...
He left the household life and was named Sengqieqi. In the first year of the Yongyuan era, at the age of eight, he would sit in meditation with his eyes closed and recite newly translated scriptures.
By the time he reached the age of sixteen that same year, he had recited twenty-one scriptures totaling thirty-five fascicles, all of which had not been transmitted in the world before.
This was surely because his past habitual practice had remained so unforgotten. Once, while he was...

In the Huaguang Hall, he personally appeared before Emperor Wu and recited a heterodox scripture. The monastics and laity of the Yangdu capital all proclaimed it to have been divinely bestowed (*Sanbao ji*).
○ Shi Sengrong resided at Donglin Temple in Jiujiang. In Jiangling, he exhorted a family to receive the precepts and serve the Buddha.
Previously, they had maintained a shrine to a spirit, but they no longer honored it. Seven days later, the host’s mother saw a ghost attempting to bind her.
His mother grew afraid and requested a monk to recite the sutras; the ghostly disturbances then ceased. Later, when Daorong returned to Mount Lu, he stayed at an inn where there were many ghosts.
They addressed Daorong, saying, "Why do you claim that ghosts and spirits have no spiritual power? Drag us down to the ground quickly!
As the ghosts were about to lay hands upon him, Daorong silently recited the name of Avalokiteśvara. He then saw a celestial general holding a vajra and brandishing it toward them. The ghosts—

He was then startled and dispersed [the assembly] (from the *Monk Biographies*). ○ During the Wei dynasty, Dharmaruci (translated as Fashi) produced eight fascicles of sutras, including the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*.
In the Bingxu year (the fifth), Dharma Master Sengmin arrived at the capital.
The Emperor descended from his seat to receive him with ritual courtesy; from then on, his honored position flourished daily.
○ The Śramaṇa Saṃghabala (translated as Sengyang, or alternatively Zhongkai) of Funan was summoned by imperial decree of the Liang Emperor to Shouguang Temple in Yangdu.
In five locations, including the Palace [Hall], the oral translations were being conducted. During the winter, a drought occurred and the rituals for rain (*yujì*) were performed to the utmost;

yet, rain did not fall. Sengzhi requested that a lecture on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* be held to pray for rain. The Emperor immediately ordered Dharma Master Fayun to lecture on the *Śrīmālā* in the Huaguang Hall.

When the lecture concluded, it snowed heavily throughout the night. Sengzhi further said, "A basin of water must be prepared with a knife placed upon it. Immediately, a great rain fell, drenching both the high and the low lands.
All were satisfied.

On the day of Dinghai (the sixth), the Emperor, through the supernatural power of Master Bao, beheld the suffering of the hells. He asked how they might be saved. Master Bao replied: "In former lives..."
Karmic actions that have already produced their results cannot be extinguished all at once; only upon hearing the sound of the bell does their suffering momentarily cease.

Thereupon, the Emperor issued an edict to all monasteries throughout the realm, commanding that the sound of the bells be struck slowly and leisurely, intending thereby to allow the suffering to linger and subside.
At this time, Dharmaruci (translated as Fǎxī) of the Wei dynasty ceased his work on thirty-five translated scriptures. The Emperor also composed a commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The Emperor commissioned the five Dharma masters, including Sengmin, to lecture on this sutra. From then on, the Emperor invited Sengmin to serve as his domestic preceptor (*kula-guru*), providing him with the four requisites.
He further issued an edict for [Sengmin] to lecture on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* in the Huilun Hall. Meanwhile, the Master Xiang resided at Qingcheng Mountain Temple in Yizhou.
At that time, according to local custom, whenever the third month arrived, people would invariably go to the mountain to enjoy the scenery, often bringing wine and meat to indulge themselves.
Lè (Lè) and Xiāng repeatedly urged him [to eat], but he would not desist. Later, during the third month, as before, they gathered again.
Xiāng ordered people to dig a pit about ten feet square. Suddenly he said, "Donors, you have always eaten and drunk for yourselves and never given to others;
today I must take one meal. Everyone vied with one another to offer delicacies and wine. As soon as they were received, they were exhausted, as if filling a vast chasm. By evening, he said, "I—"
He was intoxicated and satiated. They supported him to a pit so that he would not soil the ground. When they reached the pit, he opened his mouth and vomited profusely;
pheasant meat came out of his mouth and immediately flew away crying, while mutton came out of his mouth and immediately ran off. The wine and food emerged in a chaotic jumble.
As he was about to fill the pit, fish, pickled fish, geese, and ducks swam and frolicked amidst one another; everyone was struck with wonder and sighed in admiration, vowing to cease all slaughter.
From then on, wine and meat were forever excluded from the mountain. This was the virtuous influence of this incense. Later, Master Zhigong sent him a message.
He subsequently manifested his transformation within the temple. When his disciples prepared the tomb for his enshrinement, they marveled that the coffin was so light;

upon opening it, they found nothing but a stool and a staff (as recorded in his biography). Śramaṇa Zhishun was empty-minded and tranquil, reverent and meticulous. His physical presence was as if divine.
He resided at Yunmen in Yuxue, where both officials and commoners paid him their respects. Once, there was a thief whose followers were pursuing him; Zhishun allowed the thief to stay the night.
In his quarters, at dawn the next day, [the Emperor] presented him with money and silk, admonishing him before sending him away.
His benevolence and forbearance were such as this. He passed away that year (according to the *Benzhuan*). Wuzi (7) [Yongping 1].
The Emperor commissioned the court painter Zhang Sengyou to paint a portrait of Master Bao. As he began to delineate the master’s face, the image of a twelve-faced Avalokiteśvara emerged;

sometimes compassionate, sometimes majestic. Sengyou was ultimately unable to complete the painting. On another day, while the Emperor and he were by the river, they saw something floating upstream against the current.
Master Bao drew it toward them with his staff, and it turned out to be a piece of purple sandalwood. He immediately carved his own likeness into it.

His spiritual countenance appeared as if alive. The Emperor annotated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and commanded his ministers to have Master Yun lecture upon it. Yun declined on the grounds of illness and did not go.
The Emperor sent an envoy to urge him, saying, "I hope to circulate this teaching; were it not for one of high virtue, there would be no one upon whom to rely."
Yun began to follow him. Yun was proficient in both Confucianism and Buddhism and possessed the greatest reputation; he was held in high esteem by Prince Zhaoming.
Soon, an imperial decree appointed him as the domestic monk (*jiāsēng*), and another edict named him the abbot of Guangzhai Monastery, where he established monastic regulations.

Śramaṇa Huishao left home at the age of twelve and received full ordination. He traveled to the capital to attend lectures, but finding the exegesis shallow, he went on to study under Fazang of Kaishan Monastery.

The Dharma Master delivered a lecture, and he subsequently realized that his reasoning was superior. That evening, he dreamed that he gathered several *hu* of plum fruits and, intending to eat them, first picked up the branches and leaves.
Upon waking, he realized: "My study will surely lead me to the ultimate depths.

Later, when the Prince of Wuling of the Liang dynasty was stationed in Shu, he invited him to preach at Longyuan Temple. There, he saw a deity dressed in blue robes who bowed and said: "I pray that the Dharma Master..."
"I shall always remain here. I will protect and support you as you propagate the Dharma. Having spoken these words, he vanished. Later, his propagation of the Dharma flourished.

In the seventh month of that year, he informed the assembly and passed away while sitting peacefully (from the *Benzhuan*). The Emperor issued an edict to Sengmin and others to compile the *Zhongjing yaocao* (Essential Excerpts from the Various Scriptures) in eighty-eight fascicles.
The Emperor issued an edict for the Dharma Master Fachong to reside at Qilong Xianwu Temple, requesting him to serve as the family preceptor. 4.
The material provisions were abundant and generous. ○ Lei Namoti (translated here as *Ratnamati*) of the Wei dynasty translated śāstras at the Taiji Hall in Luoyang.
○ Bodhiruci (translated here as *Juexi*) translated śāstras at the Ziji Hall. Ruci was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and had wondrous mastery of dhāraṇīs;
he was also proficient in various arts and incantations, such that he could cause water to gush forth from a well.
Jichou (the eighth year): [Section Two].

The Emperor, because Dharma Master Baoliang’s virtue was esteemed by the public, frequently invited him for discourse. Whenever Baoliang addressed the Emperor, he referred to himself only as "this poor monk.
In the fifth month, the Emperor issued an edict to Baoliang to compose a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* totaling over one hundred thousand words. In the ninth month, the commentary was completed.
The Master composed a preface for it, which states: "To summarize the essential points of the sutras, they do not exceed two paths:

Buddha-nature reveals the source of that which is inherently present, and Nirvana clarifies the principle of returning to the ultimate. Even 'emptiness of emptiness' cannot fathom its true limit, and even the 'mystery within mysteries' cannot exhaust its wondrous gate.
Were it not for one whose virtue equals the state of equality and whose mind merges with the non-arising, how could the golden walls and jade chambers ever be entered?"
How easily accessible he was! Indeed, his merit and virtue attracted offerings that accumulated over time. By nature, he did not hoard gold; he distributed it all to cultivate meritorious deeds.
After his passing, no wealth remained in his quarters. On the fourth day of the tenth month, he passed away into nirvana. His disciples, including Fayun and others, [recorded this].
An inscription was erected stating: In the fifth month, the Śramaṇa Fayue commissioned a sixteen-foot image of Amitāyus. By imperial decree, it was to be cast at Xiaozhuangyan Temple.
When the initial calculation of forty thousand *jin* of copper had been exhausted by the melting and pouring, yet the statue had not even reached the chest, another memorial was sent to report this.
An imperial edict granted three thousand *jin* of "merit-copper. Before this copper had even arrived, a sheep-cart had already reached the site of the image.
Copper was loaded [onto carts]. When one casting was completed by the side of the furnace, it filled a man’s cart; suddenly, it all vanished.

Only when the copper was removed from the mold did they realize that what had been sent previously was a manifestation of divine inspiration. Upon opening the mold, [the statue] emerged, standing nineteen feet tall.

In the ninth month of that year, the image was moved to Guangzhai Temple, where there were frequent manifestations of light and spiritual response (from the *Benzhuan*). At the Shiqian Hall, the Wei Ruler [performed rites] for the sake of all...

The monastics and court officials were lecturing on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*. At that time, the Wei court exclusively venerated the teachings of Śākyamuni and did not attend to secular classics.
Pei Yanjun, Secretariat Director, submitted a memorial stating: "Your Majesty has ascended the Dharma seat and personally lectured upon the Great Awakened One;

all who behold and listen have their obscurations cleared away. I humbly pray that you will also peruse the secular scriptures, maintaining both Confucianism and Buddhism, so that the inner and outer realms may be harmonized."
Both the ultimate and conventional truths were fully elucidated. At that time, among the Chinese śramaṇas in Luoyang, there were over three thousand people who had come from the Western Regions.
The Wei ruler established the Yongming Monastery with over a thousand rooms to accommodate them. Influenced by this example, everyone near and far took up the practice of Buddhism.
By the time of the Yanchang era, there were approximately thirteen thousand monasteries throughout the provinces and prefectures, and the number of monks reached...
Two million [cash] (Beishi). Gengyin (the ninth year):
The Emperor, as Taizu Wenhuang, established Daji Jing Temple at the Bamboo Ravine on Mount Zhongshan and provided for one thousand [monks].

The other monks constructed a sandalwood image in the main hall, two zhang and two chi in height. Furthermore, in the Longyuan Auxiliary Hall within the monastery, they fashioned a gilt-bronze image eighteen chi tall.
Additionally, for the Empress Dowager Xian, they established the Dazhidu Monastery on the western bank of the Qingxi River;
its main hall also contained five hundred gilt-bronze images, each eighteen chi high, where nuns performed recitations and lectures during the four seasons.
The Emperor visited Xing’ai Temple and established a feast of unimpeded offerings (*anāvaraṇa-pūjā*). He cast the Buddha’s *śarīra* relics into bowlfuls of water;
among them was one that remained hidden and did not emerge. The Emperor prostrated himself before it, whereupon the *śarīra* emitted light from within the bowl.

As the heavens revolved for a long time, the entire nation marveled at this unprecedented event. By imperial decree, the śramaṇa Baochang compiled the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Mingseng zhuan*) in eight volumes.
11. Shi Zhi-zhan of the Wei Dynasty. A monk from Qi State, he resided at Zhong Temple in the Northern Valley of Mount Tai. He simplified his affairs and spoke little;
even when birds entered his presence, they were not disturbed. No one could fathom him. At the time of his death, Master Zhi (Zhigong) said to Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty:
"A holy *srotāpanna* from the north has entered parinirvāṇa today. This was Zhi-zhan’s passing; he transformed into extinction without affliction (*gantong zhuan*).
Xinmao (the tenth year), the first year of the Tianjian era.

The Emperor dreamed that a sandalwood image had entered the kingdom. He then ordered Hao Qian and seventy-nine others—eighty people in total—to travel to India to invite the Buddha image carved by King Udayana.
That king had, in turn, modeled and carved this single image from red sandalwood.
Faxian and his companions returned. On the fifth day of the fourth month of that year, Faxian and his party arrived at the capital of Yangdu.

The Emperor, together with his hundred officials, traveled forty li on foot to welcome them back to the Taiji Hall. He established a *zhai* (fasting) ceremony to deliver sentient beings, issued a general amnesty, and prohibited killing.
From then on, the Emperor personally adopted a vegetarian diet and renounced carnal desire (*Gantong lu*).
In the year Renchen (the eleventh year, Yuanchang 1), the monk Fatao concealed his traces at Mount Zhong for over thirty years.
He sat in meditation and recited the scriptures with devotion, performing repentance rites with rigorous austerity.
He lectured extensively on various sutras, attracting disciples like clouds. Both Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty and Prince Wenxian, the Chancellor, personally received his instruction.
As for the ritual: at one time, eminent scholars all received the precepts, and there were over seven thousand disciples, both monastic and lay.

In the ninth month of that year, seeing the Buddha arrive, he sought out [the opportunity] to bathe in hot water and passed away (from his own biography). ○ Dharma Master Huiyue was invited by the Emperor to have an audience; the Emperor’s reverence and courtesy were most excellent.
He discussed the Dharma with the Master, often continuing through day and night. From then on, whenever he came or went, the imperial palace granted him rewards.
He met [the Buddha], and his profound faith was peerless. ○ At the age of sixteen, Master Fu Dashi married a woman of the Liu clan named Miaoguang;
they had two sons, named Pujian and Pucheng.

Gui-si (the twelfth year): (2) During the Wei dynasty, Ratnamati from the Western Regions translated six works, including the *Ratnakūṭa-śāstra*, totaling twenty-four fascicles. Emperor Xuanwu invited him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Suddenly, while at the high seat, he saw a celestial deity who said, "The Heavenly Emperor has invited you to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka*. He then [proceeded] with the capital...
The lecturer, the *karmadāna*, and four others passed away simultaneously in their seats. All who heard of or witnessed this marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Bodhiruci translated the ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

In the Jiawu year (the thirteenth year), the Great Being Baozhi had been publicly known for over forty years. As he was about to manifest his passing into nirvana, he went to the inner palace to bid a final farewell.
The Emperor was greatly startled and asked, "How long will my life last? Baozhi did not answer, but pointed with his finger to his throat and neck.

He emerged [with his neck extended—referring to the throat and neck; it means that the spirit had already spoken before any signs appeared]. One account states: A single candle was left burning, and later a palace attendant reported this to the Emperor.
The Emperor said, "The Master will not remain with us anymore. Is he entrusting me with his final affairs?
He returned to the mountain and entered nirvana on the sixth day of the twelfth month, at the age of ninety-three. The Emperor erected a stupa for him on Mount Zhong.
Year Yiwei (the fourteenth year), fourth month (first month of the year when King Sejong passed away and King Soseong, the filial Emperor Ming, was enthroned):
The Kingdom of Panpan presented the Buddha’s tooth relic of Emperor Liang. [The King] issued an edict for Monk Sō to compile the *Sūtra Catalogue* in four fascicles.
In the tenth month, He Gwi of Guangzhou, while gathering medicinal herbs on Mount Huyi in Yuzhang, encountered a strange person who [taught him] the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom (*Huiyin sanmei*).
One scroll of a sutra was bestowed and instructed to be delivered to Prince Jian’an. Upon finishing these words, he vanished (from the *Liang Hongming ji*).
○ Shi Huiji was proficient in the study of Abhidharma (*lunxue*). The Emperor frequently invited him to expound the teachings. He passed away this year (from his *benzhuan*).

○ Dharma Master Zhizang first traveled to the capital, where the Emperor treated him with profound reverence. By this time, the Emperor had built a pagoda and temple for Master Zhi for the sake of Master Zhigong, naming it Kaishan.

The Emperor decreed that he be housed within the palace. At that time, while the imperial palace was open for his unrestricted wandering and access, the imperial throne was reserved solely for the Son of Heaven to ascend.

However, Xuanzang sat there cross-legged and declared, "I am a prince of the Golden Wheel. The Emperor likewise permitted this. Initially, a physiognomist had said that the Master’s lifespan would end at thirty-one;
therefore, Xuanzang exerted himself to the utmost in cultivating the Way, specializing in the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until the year of his destined misfortune arrived.

At dusk, a voice suddenly spoke from the air: "By the power of Prajñā, you shall double your lifespan. After Xuanzang later left the mountains, a physiognomist exclaimed in surprise, "The signs of a short life are now gone.
Xuanzang asked, "To what extent can my life now reach? The man replied, "It may reach sixty-odd years.
Thereupon, monastics and laypeople throughout Jiangzuo vied with one another to recite this sutra, a practice that continues to this day, as its miraculous responses have been repeatedly manifested.
Bingshen (the fifteenth year) [Xihping Year 1 of Emperor Suzong of the Wei Dynasty]: Shi Mingda.
Originally, the barbarians of the Ba Gorges were plundering the prefectures and districts. Mingda exhorted them, but they did not submit.

A thunderstorm struck with such force that the rebels were terrified and sought his mercy, pledging to take refuge in the Triple Gem. The dark gloom cleared instantly, and consequently, the river routes were restored to peace and order.

Furthermore, he wished to erect a wooden pagoda; water flowed of its own accord to the timber. One suffering from lameness was given a staff and immediately set out. He propagated his teachings throughout the regions of Chu and Shu.
He passed away this winter. At Yinyue Temple in Yuezhou, there was a stone Buddha statue. Originally, the monk Senghu had planned to carve a ten-zhang stone Buddha.
During the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, it was nearly completed, but with only the face remaining rough-hewn, he died. Subsequently, the monk Sengshu took up the task.

The work had been underway but was not yet completed. In the sixth year of the Tianjian era, Lu Xian of Wu Commandery dreamed of a monk who said, "The Prince of Jian'an is suffering from an illness that has not yet healed.
If you can complete the stone image at Shan County, he will surely recover. Although Xian gradually forgot this for a year, the monk came again to urge him.
Xian then informed the Prince of Jian'an, who then entrusted the gold to the monk Sengyou, granting him full authority over the project.
The image project was completed over twelve years, finishing this very spring. The pedestal was five *zhang* high, while the Buddha’s body was ten *zhang* tall.

After the image was finished, the King’s illness was immediately cured (*Sengzhuan*). ○ [Emperor] decreed that the śramaṇa Baochang compile the *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Strange Phenomena of Sūtras and Vinaya) in fifty-five fascicles, as well as the *Biqiǔní zhuàn* (Biographies of Bhikṣuṇīs) in four fascicles (both currently extant in the canon). ○ [This was commissioned during the reign of] Empress Hu of the Wei.

There were two temples at the Yongning Stone Caves. In Yongning there was a statue made of pure gold, eighteen feet (one *zhang*) in height—equivalent to the size of an average person—and ten other statues.
It served as the base for a nine-story pagoda, which stood ninety feet high; atop this, the *śikhara* (finial) rose another ten feet.
At night, when all was still, the sound of bells could be heard for ten *li*. The Buddha Hall resembled the Taiji Palace; the triple gate resembled the Duanmen Gate.
There were a thousand columns of monastic quarters, adorned with pearls, jade, brocade, and embroidery that dazzled both the eyes and the mind.

Since the Buddhist Dharma entered China, there has never been such a flourishing state of pagodas and temples. Once the Empress Dowager had taken refuge in Buddhism, many households ceased their secular ties to become *śramaṇas*. Li Zhan submitted [this memorial].

The argument was: "To neglect the rites of supporting one's parents in this present life while seeking benefits in the future—how could one abandon such a magnificent governance to follow the teachings of ghosts?
The Monastic Commander Sengxian and others, indignant that Xuanzang referred to them as 'the teachings of ghosts,' wept and petitioned the Empress Dowager.
The Dowager rebuked Xuanzang, to which he replied: 'Regarding celestial deities, terrestrial spirits, and human ghosts—the Buddha originally emerged from among humans; this is his name.'"
Regarding his being a ghost, I, your servant, say this is not slander. Xian said, "If this is so, then the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are also ghost-teachings.
Thereupon, the Emperor punished Zhang Yan with a fine of one *liang* of gold (*Beishi*).
Dingyou (the sixteenth year): [Day] 2.

An imperial edict was issued to the śramaṇa Baochang to compile the *Zhòngjīng fómiǎn* (Names of Buddhas in Various Scriptures) in three fascicles (*Sānbǎojì*). In the sixth month, an edict was issued to abolish and reduce the number of Daoist monasteries throughout the empire.

Although the Emperor’s affairs were as numerous as the myriad people and his duties were pressing, he never let go of his books; he scrutinized those who were treacherous and heard the pleas of litigants.

[The Emperor] was enlightened. When presiding over divine rites, he did not personally partake of the offerings; for banquets, music was not permitted. The ladies of the inner palace and those in attendance all wore no silk or brocade.

In his private chambers, his clothing and bedding were generally plain; he used cotton quilts and mats of *guǎn* grass, wearing straw sandals and a *gé* cloth cap. Consequently, he issued an edict to the weaving officials.
Brocade may not be used to depict the forms of immortals, birds, or beasts, for its cutting and tailoring violate the principles of benevolence and forbearance.
Even at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, sacrificial animals are made of flour; all other offerings consist entirely of fruits and vegetables.
Wuxu (the seventeenth year) [Shenguī Year 1]: Shi Tánpéi was skilled in rhetoric and debate.
Emperor Yuánjiǎn of the State of Xì and Hé Yìn both invited him to lecture. He passed away that year (Biographies).
○ Lǜshī Sēngyòu extensively propagated the Vinaya teachings from the beginning of the Qi dynasty; Emperor Wǔ of Liáng treated him with profound courtesy and esteem.

Whenever there were doubts regarding monastic affairs, they all came to him for examination and resolution. As he grew old and suffered from foot ailments, an imperial edict permitted him to enter the inner palace in a sedan chair to confer the precepts upon the six palaces.
Over ten thousand people—including kings, dukes, nobles, and relatives, as well as both ordained and lay followers—attended.

On the twenty-sixth day of the fifth month of that year, he passed away at the age of seventy-four. The Master authored the *Sanzang Ji* (Record of the Tripitaka), the *Fayuan Ji* (Record of the Dharma Garden), and the *Shijie* (World).

The *Shijia pu* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni), the *Hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification [of Buddhism]), and other such works all circulate in the world (as recorded in his original biography).
○ Dharma Master Sōngdútu resided among the crags and valleys forty *lǐ* north of Shuanglín in Wùzhōu; Lóuyǎn Chángshì founded Xiāngshān Temple for him.

When the sacred stupa was being erected, ten thousand people from both the monastic and lay communities together pulled on hemp ropes to raise it; suddenly, the ropes snapped in mid-air and those pulling them all fell down.
The Master then said, "What demonic interference has caused this? Thereupon, he filled his alms bowl with pure water.

He grasped it from both inside and out, recited incantations over it, and prostrated. Holding the bowl, he circumambulated the stupa; after one circuit, it stood firm on its own without the aid of human labor.
Later, he went to Mount Lai and established a monastery there. The Master often said, "Mount Lai is a king [of mountains], yet it will not endure for long."

Mount Xiangshan remained without a ruler for a long time; later, it indeed turned out as had been said (Biography). ○ An imperial decree was issued to the śramaṇa Baochang to compile the *Zhòngjīng mù* (Catalogue of All Scriptures) in four fascicles.
○ In the intercalary eighth month, the monk Huimi passed away. Huimi resided at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong; for over thirty years he did not step outside the mountain.
He constantly practiced meditative concentration and recited the *Prajñāpāramitā*, performing prostrations and repentance during the six periods of the day (Monastic Biographies).
Jihai (the eighteenth year), [Year 2]:

The Emperor, taking the Way as a means to assist humanity, propagated its principles without fail. In bestowing responsibilities, he relied upon personal involvement so that the people’s trust might be established.

Dharma Master Huiyao’s virtue transcended the human world, and his influence reached even the unseen realms. On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Emperor personally invited the Master to receive [the precepts].

Regarding the Bodhisattva Precepts, the Emperor invited the Master to the Hall of Equal Enlightenment. He humbled himself as the sovereign of ten thousand chariots to extend the reverence due to one’s elders and superiors.

For a time, he set aside his dragon-robe to reverently don the field-cloth robes of a monk. He proclaimed the rites for ordination with a body bowed low in sincere solemnity. Furthermore, he established a Great Unrestricted Assembly;

the multitude from the court and the countryside, both clergy and laity, numbered over one hundred thousand. The abundance of incense, flowers, music, and ritual ceremonies was such that it has not been seen since antiquity.

There has not yet been such a precedent. Consequently, by imperial decree for a general amnesty throughout the realm, it was stated: "The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says that those who occupy the position of sovereign should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
Therefore, one should know that although one is noble as the Son of Heaven and possesses the wealth of the four seas, one ought to cultivate the body and restrain the mind."
To propagate the Way, I have reflected that if one does not receive the Bodhisattva precepts, how can one give rise to a heart of compassion and practice impartial conduct?
Therefore, I have received and upheld them; the True Dharma now rests with me. Without hesitation, I desire that the hundreds of millions of common people may share in this merit and blessing.
All crimes throughout the empire, whether light or heavy, shall be universally pardoned and removed. Following this, Master Yue was summoned for an audience.

He separately offered a lacquered couch and first performed a prostration before taking his seat. From the Crown Prince downward, including the imperial princesses, monastics and laypeople, and the commoners of both sexes—all sought liberation.
The ministers and subjects of the entire nation paid their respects with utmost reverence.

Among the disciples who had received the registers (*lu*), there were forty-eight thousand people; the Master’s honor reached its zenith (from the *Benzhuan*). After the Emperor himself had received the precepts...

His tastes were completely renounced; he ate but one meal per day, consisting solely of vegetables. Once he reached the age of forty, he ceased all sexual activity and his living quarters became almost identical to those of a śramaṇa.
Among the emperors of antiquity, none were able to do so. Consequently, as this single individual trod the Path, the four quarters were transformed by him;

throughout the realm, everyone observed the six fast days (ṣaḍ-upavāsa), and the myriad people all received the eight precepts (aṣṭāṅga-śīla). [The Emperor] issued an edict... *Note: The original text contains a fragmentary character at the end, likely part of the word "敕" (chì - edict).*
At Zhuangyan Temple, eight Dharma-thrones were established, with five monks taking turns presiding over the lectures, with Sengmin as their leader.
On the days when Min lectured, the entire city flocked to listen; there was not even room for one to stand in the hall.

Huijiao of Kuaiji compiled the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) in fourteen fascicles, covering the period from the Yongping era of the Han dynasty down to this year, totaling some four hundred and fifty [monks].
Total: 257 people; those mentioned incidentally: over 200 (now preserved in the canon). ○ At Quānlín Monastery in Fùyáng County was the monk Shì Dàolín.

He maintained the precepts and recited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and other scriptures. The monastery was haunted by demons and spirits; when Dàolín resided there, they ceased their disturbances.
A disciple’s head was crushed by a collapsing roof and sank into his chest. Dàolín offered prayers on his behalf, and at night he saw two Brahma monks.
He pulled out its head, and by dawn, [the monk] had recovered. Daolin also prepared a vegetarian feast for the Holy Monk (*sengqie*).
He spread new silk upon his bed, and when the feast concluded, he saw human footprints upon the silk, each three feet long. The assembly all marveled at the power of his spiritual resonance.
That year, Daolin passed away. Empress Dowager of the Wei dynasty ordered that a five-story pagoda be constructed in each province, and various princes and high officials each...
A temple was established in Luoyang. The Empress Dowager frequently hosted vegetarian feasts and bestowed gifts upon the monks, numbering in the tens of thousands (Beishi).

On the day of Gengzi (the first year of Putong / the first year of Zhengguang), the Kingdom of Funan presented a miraculous image carved from sandalwood. At the age of twenty-four, Master Fu went upstream to fish.
While he was lingering beneath Jieting Pond, he encountered the dhūta practitioner Sengtou, who said to him, "In the past, you and I made a vow before the Buddha Vipaśyin to deliver sentient beings.
When will you now return to the Tuṣita Heaven? He then instructed him to look at his reflection in the water.

The Great Being then saw a circular halo and a jeweled canopy, whereupon he realized his former causes. He then said, "Delivering sentient beings is urgent; what leisure have I to dwell on other matters?"
"What heavenly palace music! he exclaimed. Thereupon, he cast aside his fishing gear and, taking [the fish] with him, returned to his home. He then inquired about a place for practicing the Way.
Mount Song pointed to the two *tao* trees on Mount Song and said, "This will suffice. This is the present-day Shuanglin Temple.
The Great Being established a hermitage there and styled himself the "Future Liberated Great Being of Wisdom Beneath the Two Trees. He planted fruits and vegetables for...
A man worked as a hired laborer with his wife, Miaoguang. He would work by day and return home at night to expound upon the Buddha-dharma (from the *Benzhuan*).
At that time, Meditation Master Huida attained the water-contemplation samādhi (*āp-samādhi*); whenever he entered meditative absorption, those who peered inside saw the room filled with clear water.

The śramaṇa Daoxian attained the fire-light samādhi (*tejo-samādhi*); in the chamber where he resided, it was brilliantly illuminated even in the deep of night (from the *Tonglun*). During the reign of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty...

The Emperor, having reached the age for the capping ceremony, commanded śramaṇas and Daoist masters to discourse on the Way within the palace. At that time, the śramaṇa Dharmottara debated with the Daoist master Jiang Bin.
The Emperor asked, "Did the Buddha and Laozi appear at the same time? Bin replied, "According to the *Kaitian jing* (Scripture of the Opening of Heaven)..."
Laozi entered the West to convert the Hu, with the Buddha serving as his attendant; this clearly shows they were contemporaries. Sengzhui asked, "In which year of the Zhou dynasty was Laozi born?
Sengbin replied, "He was born in the third year of King Dingwang and died at the age of eighty-six in the first year of King Jingwang, when he entered the West to convert the Hu.
Sengzhui said, "Our Buddha was born in the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao of Zhou and died in the fifty-third year of King Mu."
He entered parinirvāṇa. From the Buddha’s passing until the third year of King Ding’s reign, exactly three hundred and forty-five years elapsed.
It was only then that Laozi was born. By the first year of King Jing’s reign, when Laozi traveled westward, four hundred and thirty-one years had already passed since the Buddha’s nirvāṇa.

The distance between these times is vast; is it not therefore erroneous to claim that [the Buddha] converted the barbarians? Bin asked: "The Buddha was born during the reign of King Zhao of Zhou—what [is the evidence for this]?"

The *Wenji* (Records of Writings) states: "The *Zhou shu yiji* (Extraordinary Records of the Book of Zhou) and the *Han fa ben neizhuan* (Inner Biography on the Origins of the Dharma in the Han) both contain explicit accounts.
