At that time, the Palace Attendant Liu Teng proclaimed an imperial decree, saying: "Jiang Bin’s discourse lacks a central tenet; he should retire from his seat.

He further asked, "From where did you obtain the *Kaitian jing* (Scripture of Opening Heaven)? You may bring it here. When it was brought forth, the Emperor commanded his ministers to examine and determine its authenticity. Xiao Zong and Li... [text continues].

The one hundred and seventy persons, having finished reading it, submitted a memorial of indictment stating: "Laozi composed only the *Wuqianwen* (Five Thousand Words). What Jiang Bin now relies upon consists of vulgar and coarse language;
its fundamental tenets are erroneous and perverse. His crime is that he ought to delude the masses. The imperial decree granted this, and he was to be punished with execution.
Buddhabhadra memorialized for his release, and Bin was specifically banished to Mayi (Wei Shi). On the twenty-first day of the ninth month, Heaven...
The twenty-eighth patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma, arrived at Guangzhou. The Regional Inspector reported this to Emperor Wu.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree to welcome him. On the first day of the eleventh month, he arrived in Jinling. The Emperor asked: "Since I ascended the throne..."
"Building monasteries, relinquishing scriptures, and ordaining monks—these are beyond counting. What merit do they possess? The Master said, "They possess no merit at all.
The Emperor asked, "Why do they possess no merit at all? The Master replied, "These are merely the causes for tainted results within the small fruits of the realms of humans and devas."
Although these were not the truth, the Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Master replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect;
its essence is inherently empty and still. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means. The Emperor then asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?"
The Master said, "Vast and open, there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me? The Master replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not grasp the profound meaning.
Knowing that his opportunity was not met, on the nineteenth day the Master departed from Liangzhou; he broke off a reed and crossed the river. On the twenty-third day—

He headed north toward the borders of Wei and soon arrived at Luoyang. Initially, he stayed at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song, where he sat facing a wall all day long (this is according to the *Sōng Míngjiào Zhèngzōng Jì* and its chronological records;

however, many other biographies such as the *Chuándēng Lù* record that he reached this country in the eighth year [of the reign], which would misalign with subsequent events such as the opening of the tomb by Emperor Xiaozhuang).

According to the *Wǔdēng Huìyuán*, it further states that on the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the seventh year of Pǔtōng (the Bingwù year), he arrived in Guangzhou. The Prefect Xiao Āng reported his arrival to Emperor Wǔ, who dispatched an envoy to invite him. On the first day of the tenth month of the Dingwù year, he arrived in Jinling.

Now, according to the *Pudeng lu*, the *Chuandeng lu* is pointed out as erroneous; we rely on the *Zhengzong ji* as our standard. ○ The Monk Baozhang, of a thousand years’ [lifespan], traveled to Mount Wutai during the Daming era of the Song dynasty.
He successively resided at Zhurong, Huayan, Huangmei, Shuangfeng, and Donglin on Mount Lu. Upon reaching Jianye, he encountered Bodhidharma’s arrival in the Liang kingdom.
The Master approached him to inquire about the essential meaning [of the Dharma]; he attained awakening and realized wisdom. The Emperor held his Way in high esteem.
In the twelfth month, he was invited into the inner court. His subtle triggering of the response was like that of Wu.
Later, he traveled extensively throughout the two Zhe regions (Wudeng Huiyuan).

In the second year of the Xinchou cycle, in the ninth month, the Emperor established Tongtai Temple. At that time, many monks were violating the Vinaya, and the Monastic Rectifier was unable to restrain them.

The Emperor wished to personally conduct the affairs of the *Sengzheng* (Director of Monks) according to the Vinaya. When the imperial edict was issued, only Dharma Master Zhizang did not comply with it.

The Emperor marveled at this and summoned him for an audience to question him. Zhizang replied that the masses from the five directions could not be bound by the personal preferences of a single individual.
The Emperor could not prevail over him and consequently followed his advice. [At that time], the Ruler of Wei constructed Da Jue Temple in Ye.
Ren-yin (the third year): Dharma Master Zhizang.
In his later years, he concealed his identity through the practice of Chan. On the fifteenth day of the ninth month of this year, he manifested parinirvāṇa.
By imperial decree, he was buried at Dulongsan. ○ Saṃghavarman translated the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* and other scriptures in the capital of Yangdu; by this time, seventeen [years] had passed.
In that year, they together produced eleven scriptures in thirty-three fascicles. The Emperor personally presided over the Dharma-seat and transcribed the text with his own hand.
Śramaṇa Minghui extracted the *Bhikṣuṇī-śīla* (Nun’s Precepts) from within the Great Vinaya in one fascicle; it is still in circulation today.
At the beginning of the Xiping era, Empress Dowager Hu of the Wei dynasty dispatched Song Yun and the bhikṣu Huisheng to the Western Regions to seek out [scriptures] not yet obtained.

Upon reaching the [Jing] River, he traveled again for two years to the kingdom of Qianluo. That winter, he returned and arrived at Luoyang, obtaining one hundred and seventy sections of Buddhist scriptures (Beishi).
○ The Dharma Master Mingche was renowned for his scholarly exegesis. During the reign of Emperor Wu, he was invited into the palace.

The Emperor, considering the Vinaya texts to be voluminous and extensive, wished to extract their essential points by category; thus, he issued an edict for him to enter Hualin Garden and compile them at the Baoyun Monastery.
As he was about to complete his compilation, he suddenly fell ill and moved back to his home temple. On the seventh day of the twelfth month of that year, he passed away.
An imperial edict provided the funeral equipment (from the *Benzhuan*).

From the time the Wei dynasty possessed the empire until this period, Buddhist scriptures had circulated and greatly advanced in China, totaling four hundred and fifteen works comprising one thousand nine hundred and nineteen fascicles. This was during the Zhengguang era and thereafter.
Later, as the world became fraught with many anxieties, the monastic community grew increasingly vulgar and corrupt.

In the year Gui-mao (the fourth year), an edict was issued prohibiting the use of the title "Dharma Master" (Fashi) throughout the empire, while bestowing the honorary name "Zhizhe" upon the monk Huiyue. From that time on, it became the custom for *śramaṇas* to adopt honorary names.
At that time, the recluse Ruan Xiaoxu composed the *Qilu* (Seven Records), which catalogued internal and external books and documents.
The first five were called the "Internal Section"; the sixth was the "Buddhist Records," and the seventh was the "Records of the Way of the Immortals"—these were termed the "External Section.

The recluse He Yin had previously been extravagant regarding flavors; it was only upon receiving a letter from Zhou Yong urging him to eat vegetarian food that he changed his ways. He said: "Among the greatest of transformations, there is none greater than..."

One transcends birth and death. Among the things most weighty in life, none surpasses one's very life and nature. Life and nature are of the utmost urgency for that [other world], whereas the flavors of this world may be deferred.
If it were claimed that the principle of the three periods of existence is false, that might be so; but if this principle is indeed true, [then...]

Yet, as the taking of form does not cease, with one departure and one return, birth and death are constant affairs; thus, the tragic conduct that wounds the heart naturally extends even to you, O Elder.

Regarding those of the "blood-flavored" class, though you do not personally tread upon them, as for the morning wild geese and the night carp, how could you avoid having them prepared at the butcher's door?
Even a single coin that has passed through the hands of a thief is discarded by a man of integrity.
The innate nature of one’s birth has already been opened by the golden knife; how could it be something that mere compassion can endure?

Though the *zhōuyú* (a mythical beast) may be hungry, it will not eat grass that has not died of its own accord. Upon hearing of such a character, would it not cause even a venerable elder to feel much shame?

You have long possessed this quality; I have merely offered these few words to bring it forth. From this point on, I, Yin, shall forever sever my attachment to the taste of blood. I once encountered an extraordinary monk and received [his teachings].
Regarding the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, which was unprecedented in the world: late in life he entered Huqiu Mountain to lecture on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

Later, at the time of his death, he dreamed that more than sixty celestial maidens stood in a row before him; upon waking, he still saw them. He immediately prepared for a bath and solemnly donned his robes and cap.
A short while later, he passed away.

In the Jiachen year (the fifth), Dharma Master Fachong was summoned by the Emperor whenever there were assemblies for the discussion of the *Yi* (scriptures). The Emperor invariably treated him with the highest ritual propriety, disregarding his seniority in years since ordination and decreeing that he always sit at the head of the assembly.
He was not addressed by his personal name but was styled "Dharma Master Shangzuo" (Elder). In the third month of this year, he passed away. The Sovereign...
In mourning for him, the Emperor decreed that he be buried at Dinglin Monastery. When the Master was thirty-eight years old, a monk divined his fate and said, "You shall die at forty.
Sengchong looked at himself in a mirror and saw a dark vapor over his face; he thereupon shut himself in his room to perform prostrations and repentance, without ceasing day or night.

When he reached the end of his fortieth year, he felt a swelling and pain in his ears. A person outside the door said, "Your karmic debt of death has already been exhausted; tomorrow the dark vapor will vanish entirely."
[He] removed [the bone]. Two bones grew on his ears. At this time, at the age of seventy-four, he passed away. Shi Sengfu was profound in his contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

Emperor Wu built a residence for him at Kaishan Temple to await his arrival. A mountain deity named Hu Yishan appeared and bestowed the *Huiyin Sanmei* (Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom) upon He Gui, saying:
"You may give this scripture to Prince Nanping; let him observe it as a fast for the sake of his illness."
It was seven days. Not understanding, he questioned his deputy. Upon visiting the deputy, he discovered that it was indeed the ritual practice he had performed.
Nanping then proceeded with the fasting and sacrifice, and his illness was immediately cured. That year, the Master passed away (from the *Benzhuan*).

The monk Shen Guang heard that Bodhidharma was at Shaolin and went there. He attended upon him morning and night, yet received no instruction or exhortation. One night, a great snowfall occurred; Guang—
He stood motionless, with the accumulated snow reaching above his knees. The Master, moved by compassion, asked him, "You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?

Guang replied, "I only pray that Your Great Compassion will open the gate of ambrosia to widely deliver all beings. The Master said, "The wondrous Way of the Buddhas is difficult to encounter even throughout vast kalpas.
How can one hope for the True Vehicle with such meager virtue and limited wisdom, or with a frivolous and arrogant mind?"
In vain he exerted himself with diligent toil. Guangqian secretly took a blade and severed his own arm, placing it before the Master.

The Master said, "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their bodies for the sake of the Dharma. Now that you have severed your arm before me, your seeking is likewise acceptable. He then changed the man's name to Huike.
He may be asked: "May I hear of the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? The Master said: "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.

He said: "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. The Master said: "Bring forth your mind, and I shall grant you peace. He said: "I have sought my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable.
The Master said: "I have finished granting you peace of mind. (According to the *Chuan Deng Lu*, Shen Guang was only forty years old when he visited Bodhidharma; furthermore, he was a high monk.)

The *Chuan* states: "Guang studied under Bodhidharma for six years and thoroughly investigated the One Vehicle; thus, Guang’s period of study under Bodhidharma precisely occurred during this year. ○ Shi Mingchen, though rich in his mastery of the sutras and śāstras...
Yet he harbored a mind intent on raising objections and deeply resented the lecturers of his time. Initially, he devised the "House Method" to entice people;
subsequently, he composed the "Snake-Posture Method" to instruct his students. Once, while staying with two companions beneath a forest grove, Sengchen said, "I am now feeling a feverish heat within.
He then removed his clothes and lay down naked, tossing and turning restlessly. In a short while, his two legs joined together to become the tail of a snake.

He then said, "I have made the discourse on the serpent’s power; now the retribution has arrived. You may climb the tree; if the serpent's heart reaches you, there will be the karmic condition for it to devour you.
His companion immediately climbed the tree. Suddenly, his entire body transformed into that of a serpent, with only his head remaining unchanged.

Striking himself upon the ground, he instantly took the form of a python; its length suddenly reached fifty *zhang*. It raised its head and looked in the four directions, its eyes like sparks of fire. At that time—

The snakes all arrived together and followed one another toward the valley and departed. His companion witnessed this event firsthand and recounted it upon reaching Ye (according to the *Monk Biographies*).
Year Yisi (6), the first year of Xiaochang.

The Emperor issued an edict appointing Dharma Master Fayun as the Great Sangzheng. At Tongtai Temple, he convened a “Thousand-Monk Assembly” and assembled the multitude to perform the ceremonial rites;
all witnessed things they had never heard before. When a Western Region envoy returned, he brought back the Buddha’s fingernails and hair; the hair was a deep azure-black color.
It is extended by means of an object, conforming to the length or shortness of that object; when released, it curls back into a spiral.

[This was translated] by the Wei-period Buddhayaśas (translated as "Awakened Stability"), who was widely learned in both internal and external teachings and was particularly skilled in the arts. He came to the capital to translate scriptures. [Also mentioned is] Master Dharmatrāta.
His moral integrity was so lofty that the assembly of both monastics and laypeople followed him with one accord. As his reputation spread, it eventually reached Emperor Ming.
Although the Emperor issued three successive edicts summoning him, the Master ultimately did not descend from Shaolin.

The Emperor held him in high esteem and subsequently sent two *māṇava* robes, gold, silver, and various utensils as gifts. The Master declined them all three times; however, the Emperor finally bestowed them upon him.
(*Zhengzong ji*).
In the seventh year of the Bingwu cycle, Prince Zhaoming established Huayi Hall in the Eastern Palace and summoned the renowned monks of the empire to reside there; it was called—

The place where the Dharma was compiled was presided over by the Sangha Rectifier Hui-chao. Since the Tianjian era, the Emperor had invited him to serve as his domestic preceptor, and his inquiries regarding the rites were exceptionally numerous.
He once received an imperial decree to receive the Bodhisattva Precepts; although he was repeatedly requested to lecture on the Dharma, he did not yet consent.

The garden of Zhuangyan Monastery bordered the Southern Creek, where he subsequently constructed a multi-storied hall. In his later years, he resigned from his office and retired to his chamber to cultivate his fundamental nature. In this year...
In the fifth month, he passed away (according to his biography). ○ Dharma Master Huichao was appointed by Emperor Wu as a Scholar of Shouguang Academy.

Furthermore, by imperial decree, he served as the scribe for the translation work alongside Saṃghavarman. His lectures on the teachings flourished and transformed the world. He died in this year (according to his biography).
Dingwei (the first year of Datong): [Day] 3.
An imperial edict was issued for Dharma Master Sengmin to reside at Kaishan Temple. While on his way, he fell ill and remained at Zhuangyan Temple.

On the first day of the second month, he passed away in his quarters at the temple at the age of sixty-one. By imperial decree, he was buried at Kaishan on Mount Zhong. The Master was humble by nature.
He was harmonious and fond of releasing living beings and practicing charity. He did not engage in heterodox divination or geomancy, nor did he rely on the supernatural or the extraordinary.

The gentlemen of the realm all admired him; even those who lived by trade or peddling looked upon him with awe and reverence at the mere mention of his name, while the deceitful and the base were instantly reformed (from his biography).
In this spring, the construction of Tongtai Temple was completed. In the third month, the Emperor visited Tongtai Temple to perform the ritual of "offering his body."

Three days later, he finally returned to the palace (*Tongjian*). Shi Daomu first entered Shenshan in Jingzhou when suddenly wind and thunder roared, and snakes and tigers swarmed around him in a chaotic circle.
Daomu remained composed in his mind; he entered meditative absorption for seven days, after which the snakes and tigers finally vanished.

The mountain deity transformed his appearance and apologized for his transgression, saying, "I am Tian Bowang. I came to request the precepts and to receive the ritual methods. All manner of venomous creatures have now hidden away."

He passed away. The offerings of sacrificial meat and pungent herbs were discontinued; yet prayers for blessings were answered by timely clouds and rain. Such miraculous manifestations were not limited to these alone.
Having resided in the mountains for over thirty years, both monastics and laypeople revered his virtue (as recorded in his original biography).
Wu-shen (2) [Year 1 of Yong’an] (Wei Emperor Jingzong Xiaozhuangdi): Fu Dashi practiced asceticism for seven years, and his disciples grew in number daily.
Desiring to guide all classes of beings, he transformed his wife and children and sold himself to assist in the preparation of a great assembly.
There was a śramaṇa named Huìjí who came wishing to become a disciple and assist the Great Master.
Jiaohua (Enlightenment) ○ In the second month, Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty passed away. In the fourth month, Emperor Xiaozhuang ascended the throne.
He constructed five monasteries and carved ten thousand Buddha images. Jǐyǒu (the first year of Zhongdàtōng). 2.
On the twenty-seventh day of the third month, Dharma Master Fayun passed away at the age of sixty-three. Both the palaces were struck with profound grief.
An imperial edict was issued granting him a secret coffin from the Eastern Garden; all funeral arrangements were to be conducted by the royal household.

A further edict ordered that he be buried beside Dinglin Monastery, and a stele inscription was established, which stated: "On the *guisi* day of the ninth month, the Emperor visited Tongtai Monastery and established the Fourfold Assembly."
The Great Assembly was convened. His Majesty removed his court robes and, wearing Dharma robes, practiced the pure and great relinquishment (*mahātyāga*).
He used his private quarters as a temporary residence and ascended the Dharma seat in the lecture hall to expound the title of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the fourfold assembly.

On the day of Guimao, the ministers offered one hundred million coins to pray to the Triple Gem for the redemption of the Emperor. The Bodhisattva Saṃgha silently granted their consent, and the hundreds of officials [celebrated].
He went to the eastern gate of the temple to present a memorial, requesting that the Emperor return to the throne. After three petitions, permission was granted (*Tongjian*).

In the tenth month, he again held a fourfold *anāvaraṇa* (unrestricted) great assembly, attended by fifty thousand monastics and laypeople. When the assembly concluded, in the eleventh month, the Emperor returned to the palace, issued a general amnesty, and changed the era name.

"For over forty years, I have not eaten fish or meat, nor have I dwelt with my consorts and attendants. Since I do not eat sentient beings, I am free from the obstacle of killing;
since I do not take a consort, I am free from the obstacle of lustful evil. Having removed these two obstacles, my mind..."

His consciousness gradually became clear, and he then composed the "Rhapsody on Pure Deeds" (a portion of which reads): "Observing the innate nature of human life, one embraces the wondrous qi and is pure and still.
Yet, moved by external objects, desire arises; the mind clings to conditions and thus becomes afflicted. Encounters with the ordinary constantly manifest through external dust."
Accumulation [of karma] must stem from external objects; harboring a greedy mind without weariness, one lets the internal faculties run wild on their own.
One lingers among silks and bamboo; the eyes shift toward the five colors. Fragrances waft upward, stimulating consciousness upon contact with the nose.

The tongue perceives flavors, savoring them with a sweet mouth as it chews and eats. The body experiences touch, finding therein self-comfort and delight. [One gazes upon] slender waists, delicate hands, and supple limbs.
Plump flesh adheres to the body, fragrant and pure; when touched, it feels like fat. The frantic mind is deluded, and inverted thoughts deceive itself.
Thus, the six sense-objects equally obstruct the path of goodness. They eclipse the purple with the violet, like grass bending before the wind.

Clinging to delusion at birth, one grows old together with them, following ignorance at every turn—nothing but afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, externally purify the objects of the eyes, and internally cleanse the dust of the mind.
Accompanying virtue and dwelling as neighbors with the Way, one beholds the loveliness of pure karma. Taking non-killing as the cause, one cultivates oneself by distancing from desire and evil;
thus, the spirit is unimpeded, afflictions are eliminated, and the obscurations of ignorance are purified.
Like water that has long been settled, like a mirror recently polished, it reflects many images externally while internally revealing all manner of ailments.

Once the adventitious defilements have been removed, one returns to one's own nature; the mind becomes clear as ice and the will pure as snow. When fetters and bonds are eliminated, sorrow and fear are likewise extinguished.
[He] is parted forever from those he loves; looking back upon life and death, they bid him a final farewell (*Hongming ji*).

On the day of Yisi in the third month, the Emperor visited Tongtai Temple to "surrender his body. On the day of Bingzi in the fourth month, the ministers presented silk to redeem him and returned him to the palace.
Upasena entered the Liang dynasty and had an audience with the Emperor; the Emperor retained him to translate scriptures.
Dingmao (the first year of Taicheng): [Day] 13, [Month] 5;
the Emperor went to Tongtai Temple to "surrender his body" (as recorded in the *Tongjian*). Du Bi served Gao Huan and was held in high esteem; he was dispatched as an envoy to Western Wei.

The Wei Emperor learned that Sengbi was profoundly versed in Buddhist principles and questioned him on the meaning of the breadth and narrowness of *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) and *dharmatā* (Dharma-nature).

Sengbi replied, "It is neither broad nor narrow. The Emperor praised this as excellent (*Benzhuan*). As for the monk Sengmiao (from the Western Regions): he presented Buddha-relics (*śarīra*) to the Emperor. The Emperor sent Sengmiao away; as he traveled, the relics atop his head suddenly emitted light at night that illuminated heaven and earth.
The entire city offered praise, and the sound of their acclaim was heard for dozens of li.
In the second *wùchén* (14th day, 6th month), an Indian monk arrived carrying a stone image.
The figure was one foot high and six inches in diameter; it had eight facets and was purple in color, transparent both inside and out.
During the chaos of Hou Jing’s rebellion, it was placed at Xilin Temple on Mount Lu in Jiangzhou. At the crown of the image’s head...

(Later, during the Kaihuang era, Emperor Yang reverently enshrined [the image] in a lacquered casket. Upon his accession to the position of Crown Prince, he sent it to Riyen Temple at Quchi. Within it, various manifestations and radiant signs appeared more than once. In the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, by imperial decree, it was brought into the palace for veneration; this is recorded in the *Gantong lu* and other texts).
In the eighth month, Kuṇāladatta—also known as Paramārtha (translated here as Zhendi, or "True Meaning," and also as Qinyi)—arrived at the capital from the Western Regions.
The Emperor personally prostrated himself before him and made offerings with utmost sincerity at Baoyun Hall. He then requested that he translate the scriptures.
Jisi (the third year, fourth month: the Emperor passed away; Emperor Taizong Jianwen ascended the throne). (15) (7) In the fourth month, the rebel Hou Jing breached the Tai City.
Summoning [officials] became incessant; the Emperor was incensed by this and subsequently fell ill.

Nevertheless, he did not slacken in his fasting and purification, nor did he cease his recitation of the Buddha’s name. In the fifth month, his condition grew critical; he could no longer take food, and after a long time, his mouth became bitter.
Before Sōmitsu had arrived, he uttered "Ho-ho" and subsequently passed away in the Jingju Hall at the age of eighty-six.
Emperor Taizong Jianwen (Gang) then ascended the throne.

(Yinzilun says: Some claim that the Liang dynasty fell because of Buddhism; have they not reflected upon this? Let us compare it with Emperor Wu of Han. Among the rulers of the two Hans and the Southern and Northern dynasties, none reigned for as many years as these two Emperors Wu.

In both their promotion of academies and their cultivation of talent, they were one and the same. One studied the arts of immortality, while the other studied Buddhism; in their personal preferences, they were likewise one and the same. Yet Emperor Wu of Han remained on the throne for fifty-four years.

He honored and patronized fangshi (immortal-seekers), neglected the myriad affairs of state, exhausted his military forces, and indulged in war until the treasury was empty and the people’s hearts turned away. Why did he not perish? It was because the Han had never for a single day laid down its arms. In the final years of Liang, the Emperor gradually distanced himself from them; his generals and aides abandoned their weapons. This is why Liang fell first. —Sōng)

The Duke extensively expounded upon the teachings, saying: "One must not be mired in the teachings; one must not deceive oneself regarding the Way. To go too far and to fall short are equally harmful. Now, there are matters that are appropriate and principles that are ultimate.

To follow what is appropriate and treat it as such is the teaching of the sages. To reach what is ultimate and realize it as such is the Way of the sages. Emperor Wu of Liang and Emperor Wenxuan of Qi reversed what was appropriate while attending to their teachings—was this not being mired in them?

The rulers of Wei and Zhou obscured what was ultimate while claiming to participate in the Way—was this not deceiving themselves? Such was the manner in which these Buddhist disciples did not merely conform to the whims of their sovereigns nor become mired in the Buddha. By this we may verify that Liang’s miring of the teachings was not without justification; for in studying the Buddha, there is indeed a Middle Way."

Although the Liang dynasty lost its way by adhering to the teachings of the mud [i.e., worldly attachments], it did not meet with ruin because of that alone. Its failure lay in the relaxation of military discipline and the neglect of worthy men. In short, the rise and fall of dynasties are determined by fixed destiny; they cannot be prolonged through mere expediency.

From antiquity, instances of treachery between ruler and minister, father and son, or the internal insults of madmen and bandits are beyond counting. Now, you single out the rebellion of Hou Jing to slander Buddhism—why is this?

Consider Gonggong against Fuxi, Chiyou against Huangdi, Yi and Zhurong against the Xia and Chu, the failure of King Zhao to return, Shen Baochen’s role in the murder of King You during the Zhou, Xiang Yu and Wang Lang against Qin, Jia Chong and Cheng Ji against Wei, Liu Yao and Shi Le against Jin, Erzhu Rong against the Northern Wei, and An Lushan against the Tang. All these were matters of human conflict and political upheaval. How can you attribute them solely to the influence of the Buddha?

Regarding Zhu Ci and Huang Chao in the Tang dynasty—what era has not known its own Hou Jing? Furthermore, when one considers your act of patricide, which was as deranged as that of Jing, what would have deterred you from doing it? Although Jing fell into Tai City, he did not commit acts of rebellion against Emperor Wu;
how then could he be subject to reproach? (From *Chuyinzi Lianghou Lun*).
When the Prince of Xiangdong learned of the passing of the High Ancestor, he vacated his palace to establish Tiangong Temple and invited Dhyāna Master Fachong to reside there.
When Fachong first arrived at Mount Sangai, by the White Horse Spring Valley in Xiangyang, he built a hut to dwell in for meditation.

When the Prince of Jin’an of the Liang dynasty came to govern the regions of Xiang and Yong, he heard of the Master’s reputation and went to the mountain; however, his mounted retinue inexplicably retreated, and the prince returned in shame. That night, he was moved by a spiritual vision.
He had a bad dream. When he went back to Matou (Horse-Returning) as before, the King had to purify himself through fasting before he was permitted an audience.

Upon first arriving at the side of the temple, he saw only a valley where a fierce fire blazed intensely. After waiting for a long time, it suddenly transformed into water. As he stood gazing for some time, the water subsided and a hall appeared.
When he inquired about the matter, he learned that [the Master] had entered the meditative concentration of water and fire (*ap-siṃha-samādhi*). Inside the hall was a rope bed.
At the edge [of the pass] were two tigers. Sengcong pressed down their heads and closed their eyes, then summoned the king and ordered him to step forward;
only then could he perform his prostrations. He then informed [the king] that the region was plagued by many tigers. Sengcong immediately entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

In a short while, seventeen tigers arrived, and he granted them the refuge precepts (*śaraṇagamana-śīla*), commanding them not to harm the common people. Consequently, they ceased their depredations. On that day, he led the king to visit the White Horse Spring (*Baimaquan*).
He saw a white tortoise and said, "This is the male dragon. He also came upon a spiritual spring where there was a five-colored carp; Zhi Cong said, "This is the female dragon.
The King subsequently submitted a memorial, and an imperial edict was issued to construct Chanju Temple for him.

Furthermore, he built Lingquan Temple at his place of residence (this temple was later renamed Jinglin during the Zhou dynasty, Jingkong during the Sui, and retained its Sui name during the Tang). Having reached this point, he resided in the Heavenly Palace, but soon returned to his native village. Afterwards, by means of...

In the ninth month of the fifth year of the Dading era, he passed away without illness at the age of ninety-two. The spiritual portents associated with the Master were numerous (as recorded in his biography).
Gengwu (the first year of Emperor Jianwen’s Dabao era; the sixteenth year of Emperor Wenxuan of Qi’s Tianbao era).
In the first year [of his reign], in the fifth month, Emperor Wei Jingshun abdicated the throne to Emperor Jianwen.

The latter surrendered his heart to the wondrous Dharma and extensively studied the profound scriptures. He compiled the *Fajiji* (Records of the Collection of the Dharma) in two hundred fascicles and the *Fabaoliangbi* (Linked Jades of the Dharma Treasure) in over four hundred chapters.
He constructed Zijing and Ba’en Monasteries and transcribed ten sets of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* using his own blood.

However, though his natural endowment was lofty and brilliant, his character was mild and yielding; he was constrained by Hou Jing and unable to establish himself independently, which was also due to the workings of destiny and timing (as recorded in the *Bianzheng lun* and other texts).
In the fifth month, Gao Yang, the Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty and son of Gao Huan, received the abdication of the Wei Emperor Jing and ascended the imperial throne.
This sovereign had cultivated Buddhist wisdom from an early age, and his sagely intelligence was rarely fathomable. Having now attained the Great Treasure [the throne], he promoted it extensively.
He promoted the Buddha-dharma. The Kapiśī śramaṇa Narendrayaśas (translated as "Venerable") translated scriptures at the capital of Ye from the era of Emperor Xiaojing of the Wei dynasty.
Xinwei (2) & (The 17th year) (In the third month, the Emperor passed away; Emperor Qin was enthroned as the abdicated ruler);

(2) From the beginning of creation until this year, there have been a total of two hundred and eighty-three generations, amounting to seven hundred and sixty-one thousand four hundred and fifteen years (*Bianzheng lun*).
○ It has been one thousand five hundred years from the time the World-Honored One manifested his parinirvāṇa until this point.

Emperor Xuanzu of the Qi dynasty issued an edict, saying: "Looking up with reverence to the Compassionate and Enlightened One, who brought peace and stability to the four seas, I rely upon the Perfect Awakening to repay his virtue.
All birds of prey and other creatures that harm living beings should be released into the mountains and forests.

For the sake of the Empress Dowager Taihuang, a precious stupa shall be erected, and the Office of Falconers shall be abolished to establish Baode Monastery. (From *Bianzheng lun*) The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Liang dynasty encountered the decline of the Liang... [text fragment]
Ning then traveled to Fuchun to engage in translation work. There, he and more than twenty other śramaṇas, including Baoqiong, translated seventeen fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
In that same year, at the request of Hou Jing, he returned to receive offerings (from his own biography).

In the seventh month, as Hou Jing pressed upon Emperor Jianwen, the throne was ceded to Zhaoming Taizi’s grandson, Dong. In the eleventh month, Jing usurped the throne and changed the era name to Dashi.

(Yinzi’s Discourse says: "Observing the rise of the Liang dynasty, there was something distinct from that of the Wei and Jin; weighing the governance of the Liang, it was more flourishing than that of the Song and Qi. The historian praises this for its civil virtue and military achievement, beginning with the campaigns of Tang and Wu. )

It ultimately completed the achievements of the eras of Tang and Yu; this is the factual record. How could the Liang dynasty be said to lack virtuous merit? For several decades following Emperor Wu’s accession to the mandate, its rites, music, and cultural artifacts were preeminent among the Southern Dynasties.

This governance of the Liang stood alone above the five dynasties of the South and the eight generations of both the North and South combined. Song Jingwen’s *New History* states: "The Xiao clan of Liang rose in the region east of the Yangtze and truly possessed merit for the people. They ultimately lacked no great evil and perished only through gradual decline. Thus, their residual blessings reached their descendants:

since the rise of the Tang, they have produced eight successive prime ministers. It has never been heard that the Liang was disparaged for having caused its own downfall through a fondness for Buddhism. Wenzhongzi understood this, and thus he recorded in the *Zhongshuo*: "The Liang flourished because it cultivated the observances of fasting and purification..."

The fall of the state was not the fault of Śākyamuni. It was likely because the court historians did not understand the reasons for the Liang’s downfall; they vied with one another to cite superficial signs as evidence to cast blame upon the Buddha. Emperor Wu did not seek out worthy talent but promoted the mediocre and sycophantic.

As his years grew advanced, he devoted himself to ritual sacrifices and became mired in the sentiments of Buddhist doctrine; thus, there were no remonstrating ministers at court. No one knows a son better than his father, yet when three internal parasites had been simultaneously destroyed and only the heir was spared, why did the Emperor not execute those of improper conduct immediately?

Instead, he allowed them to secretly summon the rebellious youth [Hou Jing], who stood before the jade steps only to be reduced to overgrown weeds. This is why Hou Jing was able to raise arms and defy the sovereign: it was because the Liang possessed famous generals whom the Emperor abandoned and failed to employ, and because the officers knew nothing of war—thereby providing an opportunity for the enemy to exploit. Why?

This refers to the generals. The King [of Liang] divined the talents of such men as Yang Shenbian, Hou Tien, Xu Shipu, and Lu Faho; yet the Liang court did not employ them. Du Sengming, Zhou Wenyu, Hou Sengdu, Mai Tiezhang, and others all possessed the talent of generals.

Since the Liang did not utilize them, they instead provided resources for usurping ministers. Xiangdong lacked the way of commanding generals; before Hou Jing was decapitated, the Chen clan had already begun questioning the legitimacy of the throne. The rapid collapse of the Liang house was due to this very fault.

Yet those who debate the matter claim that it was unfortunate that benevolence, righteousness, ritual, music, precepts, and wisdom led to the fall of Liang—this is incorrect. Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music were the means by which Yao, Shun, and the Three Dynasties achieved great order; we have never heard of a case where there was order at the beginning and chaos at the end. What...

As for those who brought disorder, it was merely because their descendants lost their virtue. Regarding the precepts, concentration, and wisdom: Emperor Ming of the Han sought out both the person [the Buddha] and his teachings; they have been transmitted for two hundred years. Emperor Taizong of the Tang greatly promoted them, yet this did not hinder the governance of the Zhenguan era.

Yet its lineage has endured for two hundred generations. In our Song dynasty, the Taizu and Taizong emperors greatly promoted Buddhism; their sagacious sons and divine descendants have all been more virtuous than the three sovereigns of Shang. It is therefore fitting that their reign shall continue without end. To clarify this point:

Buddhism does not act as a parasite upon the royal transformation of the people; on the contrary, it serves to support good governance. As for those who claim that the Dharma perished with the Liang dynasty, such is surely not the correct argument. (Citing the "Discourse on the House of Liang" by Zisi).
Ren-shen (the first year of Emperor Yuanzong Shizu’s reign): [Xie] Yi, [Chengsheng] Year 1. [The deposed Emperor]: [Liu] Qin, [Yuan] Year 3. Third year:
The Chancellor, Prince of Xiangdong, Yi, inflicted a great defeat upon the army of Jing. Jing fled and was subsequently killed by Hou Tien.
In the eleventh month, Yi ascended the throne at Jiangling; this was Emperor Yuanzong Shizu. The Emperor possessed sagely qualities and many talents, penetrating the subtle mysteries.
Lingwu founded the Tianju and Tiangong monasteries. He frequently lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* and provided commentaries on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
In this year, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* and other scriptures at Zhengguan Monastery in Jinling.

In the second year of the Tianbao era of the Qi dynasty, an imperial edict summoned Meditation Master Sengchou to the capital; the Emperor personally led the imperial carriage out of the city to welcome him. Sengchou...
At over seventy years of age, his spirit remained clear and expansive. The Emperor supported him as he entered the inner palace, where he expounded the True Principle (*saddharma*).

The Emperor prostrated himself to receive the Way of Meditation (*dhyāna*). Thereafter, he increasingly relied upon these pure instructions, showing profound and sincere reverence. Consequently, he received from him the Bodhisattva precepts (*bodhisattva-śīla*). Thereupon, he abstained from alcohol and prohibited the consumption of meat;
he released hawks and falcons, abolished official hunting and fishing, and transformed the realm into a land of benevolence. He also prohibited [the sacrifice to] Heaven...
Below, he supervised the slaughter of oxen. For three months, he earnestly exhorted the people to observe the fasts and precepts.

He prohibited all pungent vegetables from both the imperial gardens and private plots, except for those kept within the palace. After more than forty days, he took his leave to return to the mountains.

That year, by imperial decree, Yunmen Monastery was established in Ye City to house him, and he concurrently served as the abbot of the Great Cave Temple (Shikusi). One day, the Emperor visited him on his carriage; at that time, Tanyou was on his bed.
While sitting, he did not rise to welcome [the Emperor]. When someone slandered him to the Emperor, the Emperor intended to enter the monastery to investigate his lack of respect.

Sengchou learned of this and went out twenty *li* in advance to await the Emperor. When the Emperor arrived, he asked why he had come so far out, and Sengchou replied, "I feared that my own blood might be impure."

He defiled the monastery and waited there. The Emperor prostrated himself, filled with endless shame and remorse; he then personally carried Sengchou’s body to the temple. Sengchou would not accept it.
The Emperor said, "As a disciple carrying his master, even if I were to travel throughout the world, it would not suffice to repay my debt of gratitude.
He then asked, "What did you do in your previous life? He replied, "I was a king of rākṣasas; that is why I still have such a [craving for] meat today."

He killed [the man] and immediately cast a spell over water in a basin, ordering the Emperor to observe it for himself. The form [of the man] was indeed there as expected. The Emperor was greatly shocked.

From then on, he practiced seated meditation and the Way with twice the vigor as before. He further issued an edict to all provinces to establish separate meditation centers, ordering those who had attained mastery in concentration and wisdom to go there and provide instruction.
Consequently, the state treasury was divided into three parts: one for the support of the state, one for his own personal use, and one...

He made offerings to the Triple Gem. From that time on, people’s hearts were thoroughly transformed and turned toward the faith; his influence was peerless throughout antiquity. He extensively constructed temples and stupas, and monks and nuns filled every province.

As the Buddha-dharma flowed eastward, it flourished here most magnificently (*Sengshi*). ○ The Dharma Master Fashang possessed a mountain of precepts so lofty and steep, and an ocean of wisdom so profound and deep.
His virtue could serve as a model for others, and his majesty could inspire awe in all beings. Thus, during the Wei and Qi dynasties, he served in succession as...

As the head of the capital, he oversaw nearly two million monks and nuns under his jurisdiction. Having presided over the administration for nearly forty years, during the reign of Emperor Wenxuan, he extensively propagated the Buddhist scriptures.
He bore the total responsibility and ensured all affairs were harmoniously managed; both within and without, he spread the teachings, gaining the full approval of both the ordained and the laity.
Guiyou (the second year); [the second]; [the fourth];
Layman Lu Faho of Jingshan. Initially held in high esteem by Emperor Yuan, he was granted a rank of leisurely retirement.
He always served diligently under śramaṇas, observing the etiquette of a disciple. Upon reaching this point, the Emperor appointed Faho as the Prefectural Governor of Yingzhou (*Nanshi*). ○ Qi Sha.
Master Seng of the Gate arrived at White Tiger Mountain and, having lost his way, heard the sound of a bell and ascended to a temple.
He sat for a long time in the hall when he suddenly saw fifty or sixty monks descending from the sky. They questioned one another, some mentioning Chang’an and others Chengdu.
From Lingnan to Kuaibei, the distance is always thousands of miles. When Sengqi wished to engage in conversation, he suddenly lost his bearings;
sitting alone upon a flat rock, he asked Master Shangtong about it. The Master replied, "This temple was built in the past by Fotudeng.
Sages and worthies have resided here, appearing and disappearing at will, shifting their locations without fixed pattern. (This is a record of spiritual resonance.)
Jiaxu (the third year) [the first year of Emperor Gong’s reign], the fifth month:
The Great Dhyāna Master Huisi of Nanyue. Initially, he dreamed of a strange monk who exhorted him to leave secular life; he then took leave of his parents and entered the Way.

He constantly practiced seated meditation and ate but one meal a day. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than thirty times, whereby he was moved by the fact that the water in his pitcher never ran out and a celestial youth attended upon him.
At that time, Master Huimeng, having first read the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and attained insight into its essential meaning, subsequently paid homage from afar to Nāgārjuna as his teacher.
The Master then went to transmit the Dharma to him. Day and night he restrained his mind, and for seven weeks during the summer retreat, his side did not even touch his mat.
Having attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, he redoubled his vigor and courage. Soon, however, obstacles arose: his four limbs became limp and weak, and he was unable to walk.
He then reflected to himself: "Illness arises from karma; karma originates from the mind. Since the source of the mind is without arising, what form can external objects take?"
The karma of illness and the mind were both like clouds and shadows. Having observed them thus, his physical ease returned as before. When the summer retreat ended, he still had nothing to realize;

leaning his body against a wall, before his back even touched it, he suddenly attained awakening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. He continued to refine and cultivate this for an increasingly long time.

His prior contemplations increased further; once his reputation for practice had spread, disciples arrived daily. Fearing that times were troubled and wishing to travel to a single location to practice the Way in peace, he was suddenly addressed from the air:
"If you wish to transform sentient beings, you should go to Wudang; if you wish to cultivate meditative concentration, you must go to Nanyue.
Upon reaching this point, he led his followers southward. Encountering the chaos of the Liang dynasty, he temporarily stayed at Mount Dasu.

Śramaṇa Huishan was proficient in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. He authored the eight-fascicle *Sanhua lun* (Treatise on Scattering Flowers—so named because it is like a profusion of various flowers being scattered).
That year, he resided at Chonghua Temple in Chang’an. The state minister of the Zhu family provided offerings and requested him to expound the Dharma (*Biographies*). Śramaṇa Sengshi.
He was born with extraordinary marks. During the Taotong era of the Wei dynasty, an imperial edict stated: "The Master’s eyes are beautiful with double pupils, resembling those of Yu Shun;

his back is prominent and hunched, much like that of the Duke of Zhou. His moral character is pure and sublime, and the measure of his conduct is difficult to emulate. He may be appointed as the Sanzang of the Zhaoxuan Monastery."

It is said that he was a treasure of the world (and so forth). In the first year of the Later Yuan era, because the Master’s talent was profound and his virtue great, he was invited to serve as the National Tripitaka Master.

From then on, he transformed and edified the capital, and his influence grew ever more flourishing over time. Initially, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty had commissioned two statues—one of gold and one of silver—which he venerated in the Chongyun Hall for approximately fifty years.
By this time, the region south of the Yangtze River had not yet been pacified, and matters of profit and harm were at stake.

The two [statues] were majestic. King Sengbian then dispatched Du Kan to guard the palace gates. Du Kan was by nature cruel and obstinate; he intended to destroy the two statues to make them into ingots.
He first ordered several men to ascend the Sanxiu Pavilion and command them to chisel at the necks of the Buddhas.

As soon as the hammers and chisels were raised, the two statues simultaneously turned their heads back. The arms of all the men sent could not be lifted; they became mute like those who are drunk. Du Kan likewise...
However, he still saw vajras coming one after another to strike him; his entire body became swollen and festering, and he died with his skin pierced and his bones exposed (Gantong).
In the year Yihai (the first year of Shaotai of Emperor Jing; the first year of Dading of Zhongzong Xiao Chao of the Later Liang; the second year of Emperor Gong of Wei;

the sixth year of Emperor Xianzu of Qi), Lu Fahuo returned to the Qi state following the defeat of Emperor Yuan. The Emperor of Qi enfeoffed him as Grand Marshal and granted him a prime residence. As for Fahuo—

He requested [permission] to establish a monastery. He resided in a separate chamber, daily practicing the Way, burning incense, prostrating before the Buddha, and sitting in meditative concentration. He predicted the date of his own death;
when the time arrived, he sat and passed away, leaving behind many miraculous traces (*Beishi*). ○ Dharma Master Sōngtóuduó subsequently arrived at Jinhua.
He established Longpan Temple. Furthermore, within the boundaries of Longqiu, he established Longqiu Temple. He also entered Wanshan Mountain and established Li luchen Temple.
Again, traveling west to Mengdu Mountain, he established Sancang Temple. At the very beginning of the Master’s departure, he established Xiangshan Temple.

In total, there were seven such locations where he obtained sites of superior topography amidst mountains and rivers, receiving offerings from both the ordained and the laity; even after a long time, these remained flourishing (from the *Benzhuan*).
The Daoist Lu Xiujing and others had initially been rejected by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and subsequently fled to the Wei state. By this time, their followers had become quite numerous.

However, as the Qi Emperor practiced Buddhism, Lu Xiujing and his associates grew envious of him. They went to the imperial palace to request a contest of dharma with the Buddhist monks. (Section Nine)
An imperial decree was issued under the moonlight, summoning ten monks and Daoists to compete in their respective arts. On the appointed day, high officials were assembled in great numbers.

Sengxiu, Jing, and others used incantations and sorcery to cause the robes and alms bowls of the monks, as well as the beams and pillars of the hall, to fly and move. The monks were unable to counter these feats.
Jing and his companions became arrogant and boastful, saying, "When a śramaṇa manifests one thing, we manifest two; we have merely been using minor arts to entice them. The Emperor...
He said to the Emperor: "How could there be no one in the Buddha-dharma? It is simply that we have not yet sought them out thoroughly.

A few days later, he identified the Dharma Master Tánxiǎn as the one to be sought and immediately submitted a memorial requesting that he be brought before the assembly of practitioners to determine who was authentic and who was false.

On the *yǐmǎo* day of the tenth month, they met in the Main Hall with the hundred officials present as witnesses. Tánxiǎn said: "I have heard it said that a śramaṇa has appeared; I am that very person."

"Manifest two," [Xian] asked. "Is it so? Jing replied, "Yes. Xian then raised one foot and said, "I am currently manifesting one; I request that you manifest two. The Daoist remained silent and had no response.
Xian rebuked him, saying, "You have not encountered a formidable opponent in the past, which is why you dare to indulge in such petty arts.

The Way of the Buddha and Laozi is not the private teaching of a single individual; it has existed since the beginning of heaven and earth.
The gentlemen of antiquity employed it to regulate their vital energy and nourish their minds. Its loftiness could not be encroached upon, and its purity could not be defiled.
Heaven, earth, spirits, and humans alike would all look upon them with reverence. This is why the Sage can achieve his goals swiftly without exerting haste.

It remained as it was from of old. Consequently, there were prophecies concerning the abolition of the Dharma and the destruction of the state. Although the Zhou dynasty suppressed the teachings, they did not reach this image.
Later, when the Dharma was restored during the Kaihuang era, a temple was established on the original site. Its spiritual manifestations were manifold (as recorded in the *Gantong lu*).
Renwu (2) [Later Liang Shizong] (ascended to Heaven in Tianbao Year 1); [Tianbao Year 3]; Heqing Year 1: Emperor Wucheng of the Qi dynasty was deeply devoted to the Buddha-vehicle.
He commissioned the construction of precious pagodas, divesting himself of his rare and imperial robes to contribute them all as alms for the Dharma.
He recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* several times every month. On his tiered terraces and separate pavilions, he established monasteries adorned with jade and precious stones.
Pearls and gems were all provided as ritual offerings. He personally performed prostrations and engaged in walking meditation at every occasion.

In the year Guiwei (the third year of the Tianjia era), Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty convened a Great Unobstructed Assembly. Upon its conclusion, he sacrificed himself for seven days in front of the Taiji Hall. At that time, [he] began... (2) ... (4) ... (2).
Furthermore, regarding the third section on the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha: Initially, as he was about to board a ship to return to the West, he encountered a wind that blew him back to Guangzhou.
The Regional Inspector, Ouyang Wei, invited him to reside at Zhizhi Temple, where he translated treatises such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Paramārtha once spread his sitting mat across the river water and crossed over; it was as if he were riding a large boat, yet the mat remained dry. On other occasions, he would break off lotus stalks...
He crossed [the river] by means of his leaves; his divine wonders were exceedingly numerous. At that time, many people painted his likeness and made offerings to it (from the *Benzhuan*).

During the Qi dynasty, Emperor Shizu constructed an altar within the palace and prepared the ritual protocols for requesting instruction on the Way. He invited Dharma Master Daoshang to bestow upon him the *śaraṇagamana* precepts.

The Emperor spread his hair upon the ground and ordered Daoshang to step upon his hair before ascending the seat. Once the Emperor had completed the conferment of the *mahā-śīla*, he next commanded the eight high-ranking ministers.

He also conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the empress, the consorts, and their relatives. He founded Baode Temple and invited Master Shang to take charge of it. Master Shang was by nature frugal and simple;
although he held the high position of National Teacher during the Great Tong era, he wore tattered robes made of coarse cloth and never rode in a palanquin.

For this reason, the world came to hold him in even greater esteem. A popular proverb went: "For the worldly expectations of the four seas, there is Daochang; for the Dharma, there is Fashang. (From his original biography) ○ Zhou Dynasty.

The Chan Master Sengshi was honored with prostrations by both kings and ministers. One day he told the monks, "Quickly perform religious rites and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara to save a temple in the Jiangnan region from the calamity of its hall collapsing.
At that time, in the lecture hall of Yangdu, a formal assembly for the exposition of the Dharma was being held.

The assembly of monastics and laypeople was full. Suddenly, they heard a strange fragrance from the northwest and the sound of celestial music in the air. The entire hall was startled and rushed outside, whereupon the building suddenly collapsed.

Yet, the great multitude remained unhurt. When this was reported to the Prince of Liang, he sent someone to investigate; only then did he realize that [the Master] had truly been protected by divine power.

Consequently, his fame resounded throughout both countries, and his deeds were compared to those of the Supreme Sage. On the eighteenth day of the seventh month of that year, he manifested his passing.
He lived to the age of eighty-eight. The Emperor mourned for him with profound grief and issued an edict to have his portrait painted at Dafutiian Temple (as recorded in his *Benzhuan*).

In the year Jiashen (the fourth year of the [Xianqing] era), the Indian Jñānayaśas (translated here as Zangcheng or alternatively Shengming), together with two disciples, Yaśakūṭa (translated here as Chengzang)...
Jñānagupta (translated as Zhìdé in Chinese), having resolved to travel abroad to propagate the Dharma, first arrived in Cháng'ān during the year Wǔchéng.

By imperial decree, he was invited into the rear garden and received exceptional honors and special provisions. When he petitioned for permission to transmit the teachings, a separate edict was issued to construct the Four Heavenly Kings Temple (Sìtiānwáng Sì) for him.
In that same year, they began translating the scriptures together. In the ninth month, the Dharma Master Hóngyǎn of the Chen [dynasty] said to his disciples: "The world..."
"Human beings are obscured by a greedy mind. When greedy for oneself, one begrudges even a single hair's fall; when greedy for others, one never knows satisfaction.
After death, there is once again a high tomb and a heavy outer coffin—how lamentable this is! After I close my eyes now, I shall offer this humble body as food for the birds and beasts.
Having finished speaking, he joined his palms and passed away. The following day, the disciples acted accordingly.

He was instructed to inter his remains on the eastern ridge of Mount Zhong (Śītavana). Yan’s appearance, deportment, and virtuous conduct were exemplary; his cursive and clerical scripts were both preeminent among the masses.
His contemporaries praised him as possessing the "Four Excellences" (*benzhuan*). ○ During the Qi dynasty, the śramaṇa Fachang was appointed State Preceptor (*tongji*).
○ The layman Wan Tianyi was proficient in Sanskrit script and also skilled in incantations and esoteric arts; under the Qi, he translated the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. ○ Chen dynasty.

As for Dharma Master Huìyǒng, Emperor Wén heard of his reputation and invited him to lecture at the Dàjí Palace. The hundred high officials were present in full array, and the seven assemblies of the faithful gathered together.

Consequently, he was decreed to reside at Dàchánzhòng Monastery. As for Dharma Master Jǐngsháo, when he was initially in Yùzhāng, he requested Paramārtha to translate the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* and other scriptures;
Paramārtha deeply praised his excellence. Later, Emperor Wén issued an edict inviting him back to the capital. Upon his arrival—
At the request of the assembly, he lectured at Baima Temple for over ten years, widely propagating the teachings. Later, he entered a secluded cliff to practice seated meditation for over ten years.
In the tenth month of the first year of Zhide, he passed away in serene stillness.
Yiyou (5) [Year 4] (6) [After the Qi Emperor’s abdication] (Tian Tong Year 1).
In the fourth month, the Qi Wucheng Emperor took the Dharma as his pleasure and transmitted the throne to the Crown Prince (Wei), who became the Later Emperor Wen Gong.
○ In the Chen state, the monk Póshǒunà translated the *Śrīdevī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in seven fascicles. Nà himself...
In the third year of the Taicheng era, he encountered the Sanskrit manuscript. During the chaos of the Hou Jing rebellion, he carried it with him as he traveled east and west;
it was only upon reaching this time that he finally succeeded in translating it. Na-pei had experienced four successive dynasties—Wei, Qi, Liang, and Chen—while translating scriptures.

Dharma Master Baoqiong stood seven chi and five cun tall. His back bore dragon-like markings, and his mouth contained thirty-nine teeth. His extraordinary features were most remarkable and prominent. Under Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty...
The Emperor once summoned him to lecture on the Dharma. He subsequently returned to his hometown and began lecturing at Jian’an Temple, where the miracle of a white dragon appearing occurred.
Later, he again traveled to the capital, where both monastics and laypeople revered him. Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty showed him exceptional respect.

In the summer of the third year of the Yongding era, while he was formally expounding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in the Chongyun Hall, he dreamed of a deity in vermilion robes urging him to lecture more rapidly. When the lecture concluded, [the dreamer]...
Then there was a clap of thunder. Shortly thereafter, Emperor Chen passed away, and it was only then that [the Master] realized his previous warning.

Upon the accession of Emperor Wen, he was appointed by imperial decree as the Great *Sengzheng* (Chief Administrator) of the capital. The Master governed with purity and led with non-action (*wuwei*).

His regulations were not burdensome, and his prohibitions and punishments were always sparing. Monks and nuns were solemnly submissive; since the time of the Liang dynasty, no monk had held this office with such radiant authority, his dignified bearing providing such protective support.
He ranked below the princes and dukes. Officials and soldiers clamored in the halls and corridors, but since the arrival of Lady Qionglin, these former practices were suddenly cast aside.

Both the court and the commoners praised her sincerity and simplicity. The various kingdoms to the east of the sea depicted her image and returned to their own lands to pay homage from afar with prostrations (as recorded in her biography).
Bingxu (1st year of Tiānhé) &; (5) &; (1st year of Tiānkāng) [April, the Emperor passed away and Línhǎi Wáng Bózōng was established] &;

(2) &; In the fourth month, Emperor Wén of the Chen dynasty passed away. This emperor reigned for eight years. He caused the Three Jewels to flourish and propagated the teachings of the Five Vehicles.
He restored sixty old temples and transcribed fifty sets of the Buddhist canon. He ordained twenty thousand monks and nuns (from the *Liùtì*). ○ Qi.
The Mahayana master Sengcan was appointed as a State Preceptor (Guoshi).
(Comprehensive Record of the Three Kingdoms). Dinghai (2nd year); (6th month); (King Linhai) (Guangda Year 1); (3rd month); Shi Wangming.
Initially, the Emperor of Zhou issued an edict appointing him as the Tripitaka Master of Xiazhou and intended to confer official rank upon him. In the fifth month of this year.
The Grand Chancellor, Yuwen Hu, exhorted him with a letter. He replied in name only that he intended to withdraw his traces into the mountain fastnesses and gather his mind beyond the mundane world;
this was his original aspiration. How could he remain muddled and confused, dwelling long in this Jambudvīpa? Thereupon, he composed the "Inscription on the Precious Man," which says:
At fifteen, I was still devoted to literature; at thirty, I came to value power and status. Thereupon, I sighed deeply and said: "Alas!

That which possesses the power to turn back heaven and overturn the sun can wither and fall so prematurely. That which is as firm as Mount Dai and its massive boulders can suddenly be reduced to ashes.

I know for certain that worldly phenomena are impermanent and this floating life is a hollow illusion. Wealth, nobility, and reputation are but a wearying toil for man. Having said this, I cast aside my hairpin.
[He] shaved his beard and hair; he was permitted to wear robes, carry a staff and a mendicant’s bowl, and discourse upon the profound mysteries.

Desiring to make his physical form like withered wood and his mental deliberations like extinguished ashes, he sought to cast off these afflictions and burdens in pursuit of emptiness and stillness. He then composed the "Admonition and Inscription on Ceasing Study and Quieting the Mind," which says:
Within the Dharma-realm there is a person who is a wish-fulfilling jewel. He seals his body with nine layers of silence and inscribes his breast, saying: "Much knowledge leads to much entanglement."

It is better to let the mind rest; much deliberation leads to many errors. It is better to maintain oneness; when deliberations are many, the will is scattered. When knowledge is excessive, the mind is disturbed.

A disturbed mind gives rise to affliction, and a scattered will obstructs the Way. Such "excellent talent and artistry" is actually the mark of folly and exhaustion. (This passage consists of several dozen lines that are extremely poignant;
it is found in the *Monastic Biographies* [Sengzhuan] and the *Verses of the Chan School*. As for the Great Master Nanyue Huisi, from the time he settled at Mount Dasu, ten years passed in total...
Ren. The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "The source of the Way is not far; the ocean of nature is not remote. Seek it only within yourself; do not look for it elsewhere.

If you seek it, you will not find it; even if you were to find it, it would not be the true. On other occasions, he responded to inquiries as they arose. With the offerings provided by both the clergy and the laity, he commissioned the transcription of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras in golden characters.
At that time, the assembly requested that the Master lecture on these two sūtras, and he expounded their meanings in accordance with the text.
He further commanded his disciple Zhiyi to lecture in his stead. When they reached the point where "one mind contains all practices," a doubt arose that he requested to have resolved.
Zhiyi immediately consulted and received the teachings on the practice of the *Lotus Sūtra*, attaining awakening after twenty-one days.
That year, from Mount Dàsù, he led more than forty monks directly toward Mount Nanyuè. Upon arrival, he said to his followers: "I shall reside on this mountain for only ten years. Thus it was.
Later, he was bound to travel far away. The Master said, "In a previous life, I once lived in this place.

Leading my disciples, I ascended the ridge and saw a site where the forest and springs were exceptionally beautiful, saying, 'This is an ancient temple; I lived here in the past. Upon digging the earth, we indeed found monastic utensils and the foundations of the halls.
Furthermore, pointing to two stones, we discovered remains beneath them, for which a stupa was subsequently built. This is the Stupa of the Third Life."
It was so. Furthermore, he built a platform beside the eastern side of Lingyan to lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the assembly;
it was situated exactly at the heart of Daeak Mountain. This is the present-day Prajñā Monastery. Disciples from both the northern and southern regions came there, drawn by his reputation.

The Master suffered from a lack of water, but suddenly saw moisture beneath the cliff. He struck it with his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), and indeed a spring gushed forth. Yet, even this did not yet suffice for all needs.

Next, there were two tigers that led the Master up the ridge; they pawed the ground and roared, causing spring water to gush forth. This is the present-day Tiger-Paw Spring (*Hupao Quan*). Someone asked:
"Why do you not go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings? Why do you instead gaze upward at the clouds and the Milky Way?"
The Master said, "The Buddhas of the three periods have all been swallowed by me in a single mouth; what further sentient beings are there to deliver?

(Biography) In the past, Buddhist studies flourished in the region south of the Yangtze River, where the gates of doctrinal interpretation were extensively studied. Since his crossing from Sishan, he held both meditative concentration and wisdom in equal measure, becoming the preeminent master of his time. (Biography)
In the fifth zi year (the third, seventh, second, and fourth [months]), Ciṇāratirāja arrived, during which time he translated seven scriptures in fifty-one fascicles.
The ruler of Qi appointed him as the Superintendent of the Śramaṇa Community (Zhao Xuan Tong).
With the stipends he received, he constantly engaged in meritorious works: providing meals for the monastic community, bestowing alms upon the poor, and providing relief to prisoners.

He constructed many wells for the benefit of others, personally filtering water to provide for sentient beings, and cared for those afflicted with leprosy, providing them with the four requisites of life.
At You Mountain in Ji County, he established three monasteries and widely encouraged the observance of the fast (his virtuous deeds are fully recorded in his original biography).
In the winter, Sengtou entered nirvana. Dashi Fu said to his disciples: "Master Seng has already returned to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace; I..."

Those who have crossed over sentient beings together with him have all departed. I shall certainly not remain long in this world. He composed twelve stanzas of poetry on "Returning to the Source" (contained in the *Benlu*).
In the eleventh month, at Xiancheng Monastery in Heyang, Zhou, Master Huiming sat in the lotus posture facing west and passed away while the Buddha appeared before him.
This master was equal in fame to Master Sida. There was a renowned scholar from Jibei named Dai... [text ends]
Liu Kui once consulted his teacher; their exchange is recorded in a letter (found in the biography).

On the eleventh day of the first month of the fifth year of Taichen (the fourth year of the Jiachou cycle), during the reign of Emperor Gaozong (Li Yan), Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Chen dynasty, passed away at the age of seventy-one. This was the time Paramārtha arrived here.
A total of twenty-one years. He translated sixty-four scriptures and treatises in two hundred and seventy-eight fascicles (according to his original biography).
During the reign of Emperor Xiaoxuan of the Chen dynasty’s Gaozong, the harvests were bountiful and the people were at peace;

as there was no unrest within the realm, he established Taihuang Temple in Jinzhong Lane in Yangzhou. Furthermore, out of a profound sense of filial piety and longing for his ancestors, he [established a temple] for King Shaolie and Empress Xiaodaifei.
At Taihuang Temple, he constructed a seven-story pagoda, where gold and pearls shone upon one another. He also built Chonghuang Temple (the character "辨" is corrected to "辦").
The Dharma Master Zhou Dao’an was skilled at propagating the Dharma; Emperor Wu paid him reverent homage and issued an edict for him to reside at Dazhongxing Temple.

In the third month of this year, the Emperor summoned a hundred renowned scholars and monks as officials of the Way, and in the main hall, having ascended the imperial throne, he personally weighed the merits of the Three Teachings.
Regarding their relative merits, by the beginning of the fourth month, an imperial edict was issued once more to summon both monastics and laypeople to state their arguments as fully as possible.

Furthermore, an edict was issued for the Grand Master (Dafu) Zhen Luan to examine the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism in detail, determining their chronological order and their respective depths.

Luan subsequently submitted the *Xiaodao lun* (Treatise on Laughing at Daoism) in three fascicles (now preserved in the canon). In the fifth month, the Emperor again assembled his ministers to scrutinize Luan’s treatise, concluding that it undermined the Way.
In the ninth month, Dao’an lamented this matter and composed twelve treatises titled *The Treatise on the Two Teachings* (*Erjiao lun*).

He designated the teaching that governs the physical form as "External" (*wai*) and the teaching that saves the spirit as "Internal" (*nei*). If one discusses the internal and external comprehensively, they encompass both the Chinese and the barbarians;

if one restricts the scope to this land alone, they may be termed Confucianism and Buddhism. This is because the Nine Schools, including Confucianism and Daoism, all belong to the Confucian tradition.
He regarded non-Buddhist teachings as external and those that exhaustively investigate principles and fully realize human nature as internal teachings.

He elaborated upon the correct meaning in detail and presented it to the court (the text is now preserved in the canon). The Emperor had Zhang Bin compose a panegyric with the intent of excluding Buddhism;
however, upon reading Da’an’s treatise, the proposal was subsequently abandoned (*Monk Biographies*). In the fourth month, Dashi Fu announced to his two sons, the Dharma Masters Pu Jian and Pu Cheng:
He said, "I have come from the Fourth Heaven to deliver sentient beings.

You all must carefully guard the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, diligently practice the six perfections, and perform the rites of repentance so as to avoid falling into the three miserable realms. On the twenty-fourth day, I shall enter nirvana;
my lifespan was seventy-three years. On the seventh day, there was a venerable monk named Fa Meng who brought a woven image of Maitreya, along with Zhong'an Dashi.
On his bed, he wept bitterly and prostrated; suddenly, he was no longer seen.

Previously, when the Great Being was in the world, because the number of sutras was vast and many people were unable to read them all, he went into the mountains and constructed a great multi-storied shrine-casket. It had a single pillar with eight sides, filled with various sutras so that they could circulate without obstruction;
it was called a "Wheel Treasury" (Lun-zang). He further made a vow, saying: "May those who enter the gate of my treasury be reborn [in the Pure Land] life after life."
In every lifetime, one shall not lose the human form. As for those who exhort worldly people and cause them to give rise to the bodhicitta, they are able to promote the *lunzang* (wheel treasury).
Such a person is no different in merit from those who uphold and recite the various sutras. This is why the *lunzang* have been established throughout the world today.
Statues of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) were installed in all of them; this was truly the beginning of such practice.

On the mountain there is an ancient pine tree where the Great Being once made a vow to deliver sentient beings, swearing his oath with an axe. To this day, the axe marks remain upon the pine wood. As for the remains of the food he gave to the tigers:
Rice that had been discarded in the forest was transformed into stone, variegated with shades of blue and white, suitable for making prayer beads;
these are called "rice-stones" (飯石) and remain to this day. How can such traces of spiritual wonder be contained by the limits of thought?

(From the *Benlu*) The Third Patriarch, Great Master Sengcan of the Chen dynasty, came bearing the Dharma robe and, having fled from the Northern Qi, hid himself on Mount Sikong. [At] Yan... of Quanzhou.
Gong was moved by the karmic retribution for releasing [a captured animal]; he donated his fields to create a lake, which is now called Yanhu (Severe Lake).

He further donated his residence to establish a monastery, which is now Guangyan Temple (*Changle Ji*). During the Zhou dynasty, Dharmaruci translated the *Tianwen* (Celestial Omens) in twenty fascicles.
Gengyin (5) & (9) & (2) & (Year 1 of Wuping); Dharma Master Tanyan’s reputation and standing were equal to those of Huiyuan.
Initially, Emperor Taizu of the Qi dynasty followed him to inquire about the Way and provided him with a monthly stipend.
Later, when the Chen envoy Zhou Hongzheng arrived on a mission, high-ranking officials recommended Tanyan to serve as the host for his reception. Zhou Hongzheng relied heavily on his own talent.
Qi Jianyan’s haughty air vanished upon meeting him. Upon his return, he sought out and brought back a portrait of Jianyan along with his commentaries;

the Emperor held him in even greater esteem and promoted him to the rank of Chief Patriarch of the Zhaoxuan Monastery (Biography). The monk Sengwei of the Zhou dynasty dwelt in seclusion among the mountains and marshes.

The Emperor summoned him to the capital and personally received his pure instructions. He issued an edict for the Empresses, consorts, dukes, and ministers to all receive the Ten Wholesome Precepts. That year, he returned to the east, and the Emperor commanded that [he be...].
The Tripitaka Master of Anzhou was further decreed to reside at Tiānbǎo Monastery in the capital. He passed away in the ninth month of the second year of Jiàndé.
