The Emperor composed the "Inscription on the Bell of the Two Teachings of the Great Zhou," which states: "On the Bingyin day of the fifth month, one bell was cast to propagate the two teachings, so that they may together return to the same ultimate principle.
Its resonance shall penetrate the nine palaces and nine earths to reach the profound mystery, and its sound shall be heard afar throughout the three thousand great chiliocosms."
At the edge [of the realm], he invited his dharma companions to partake in offerings at the Silver Pavilion; awaiting the immortal’s cap, the True One descended from the Golden Gate (Hongming ji).
During the Chen dynasty, Emperor Xuan again established a memorial temple for Empress Dowager Xiaoxiao.

It was fifteen *zhang* high, and within it was enshrined a Buddha’s fingernail, two inches long and one inch wide, preserved in various precious caskets. At times, light would fly forth in five colors, and flames would rise a fathom high.
His spiritual transformations were inexhaustible, and those who beheld them gave rise to faith.
On the *xinmao* day (the sixth day of the tenth month, the third year of the second reign period), an imperial edict was issued throughout the realm:
"Those who have newly received the precepts and have not yet completed five summer retreats must all participate in the Vinaya department [of the Sangha] within the capital cities."

At the Great Monastery, he established extensive lecture halls and issued an imperial decree appointing Vinaya Master Yuan to oversee and inspect the proceedings, clearly delineating the disciplinary regulations.

The relevant authorities were ordered to provide him with food and clothing. Within a few years, the study of the Vinaya was revitalized. The Emperor further decreed that Yuan serve as the State Preceptor (Sengzheng).

During the Taizhan era, Fayuan exhorted his disciples to sit upright and passed away. Dharma Master Anlin initially resided in the Wei state for twelve years, where he lectured on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and Mahayana sutras and shastras.
During the Taiching era of the Liang dynasty, he returned to the capital and was decreed to reside at Tian'an Temple, where he lectured on the *Avatamsaka-sutra*.
Emperor Gaozu of the Chen dynasty invited him into the inner palace, where he prostrated at his feet in full reverence and received his precepts and guidance for a long time. By imperial decree...
He resided at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to expound the Dharma. Emperor Wendi, the Founder of the Dynasty, invited him to enter the Zhaode Hall to open a lecture series.

By the time of Emperor Xuan, he was receiving instruction in the Way from the Master at Hualin Garden, where he extensively propagated the transformation of the Dharma. He passed away in the first year of the Zhide era (according to the *Sengzhuan*).
Renchen (the first year of Jiande): [Day] 11; [Month] 9; Chen Xuan Emperor.
He issued an edict to the Vice President of the Secretariat Xu Ling to compose the stele inscription for Master Fu Dashi. The Vice President Zhou Hongzheng [was also involved].

Epitaph for the Upādhyāya Huìhé ○ By the Zhou Dynasty monk Sēngmǐng. Because heterodox and orthodox teachings were intermingled, he composed the *Nàndào Lùn* (Treatise on Difficulties) in eighteen chapters, explaining them through the three categories [of the Abhidharma].
Having thus established the sequence of the sages and saints, the status of the ordinary person became clear. Its preface states in brief:
"Sēngmǐng [observes that] Lǎozǐ and Yǐn Xǐ converted the barbarians to leave the household life; furthermore, the Master Guǐgǔ is said to have composed the *Nánzhōng Jīng*..."
The commentary by Shan Sihao states that this [text] was composed by those who lack discernment and follow heterodox paths.

Nevertheless, because the teachings have both internal and external aspects, giving rise to doubts and suspicions regarding whether individuals are sages or worthies, and because many accounts relate their original nature (*honji*) and manifested traces (*suijaku*), Ban Gu’s *Hanshu* classifies people into nine grades.
It ranks the followers of Confucius as the highest of the high category, considering them all to be sages; it ranks the peers of Laozi as the middle of the high category.
For example, He Xian (何賢) [stated that] He Yan and Wang Bi said, "Laozi had not yet reached the level of a Sage. Emperor Wen of Wei issued an edict stating, "Lao Dan was a worthy man;
he should not be ranked above Confucius. These distinctions between the Worthy and the Sage reveal the inherent superiority or inferiority of their natural endowments.

Now, relying on both internal Buddhist scriptures and external secular classics, I shall distinguish the true from the false so that they may be seen at a single glance. (From the *Sengzhuan*) [The entry for] Zhou Jñānayaśas.
Śīlādharagupta (She) arrived at this time and, together with others, produced six works totaling fifteen fascicles, including the *Sagotrīka-sūtra*.

Yaśakumāra (Ye She Ju Duo) translated three works totaling eight fascicles, including the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*. Later, Jñānagupta (Sha Na Ju Duo) followed Yuwen Jian to Shu, where he translated three fascicles, including the *Samantamukha-gāthā* (from the *Śākyamuni-śāsana*).
Gui-si (2), (12), (5), (4): Emperor Zhou assembled his ministers, monks, and Daoists.
The Emperor ascended the high seat in person to distinguish the sequence of precedence among the three teachings, placing Confucianism first, Daoism second, and Buddhism last (*Tongjian*).
From this year onward, the Emperor had previously been quite devoted to the Buddha-dharma and had constructed [monasteries].

The temple built a pagoda, ordained two thousand monks, and transcribed over one thousand scrolls of sutras. Later, he was flattered by Zhang Bin and became the leader of those who performed unwholesome deeds (local gazetteer).
○ Shi Seng’an resided at Wangwu Mountain. While lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, a female pheasant would crouch down to listen;
when the third fascicle was not yet finished, it suddenly ceased coming. Seng’an said, "The pheasant has been reborn into the human realm. In that year, Seng’an passed away.
In Yuezhou, he arrived at a certain house and called out for a female pheasant. A young girl came running out; she seemed like an old acquaintance and bowed with great joy.
Her parents found this strange and led Hui'an inside to provide him with food. The father said, "When I saw this girl being born, her hair was like the feathers of a pheasant."

He took this as her name. Dao’an laughed heartily and recounted the original circumstances to her. Upon hearing this, the girl wept and earnestly requested to leave the household life; her parents complied with her wish.

He preached the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for her, and she attained understanding upon hearing it. However, when they reached the final three fascicles, she was utterly bewildered and could not comprehend them.
At the age of fourteen, she began to lecture on the text herself, earning the admiration and respect of those near and far. Encouraged by this, many followed her as students.

(Biographies of Eminent Monks) ○ Later Liang: Sengqian served as the Great Sangzheng (Chief Administrator of the Sangha) of Jingzhou. His conduct was so respectful that the seven classes of disciples were brought into harmony and order.
From the establishment of the monastic administration during the Jin dynasty until the present four dynasties, it is rare to find anyone who has fulfilled his duties as he did.
In the fourth month of the fourth year, Sengqian passed away at the age of seventy-nine. When the Master was in his early twenties, he already recited the Lotus Sūtra more than six thousand times.
In meditative concentration, he personally beheld Samantabhadra, who was illuminated by the light of fragrant radiance.
The Bodhisattva then descended and touched his head with his hand, saying (as recorded in the *Benzhuan*): "Jia-wu (3), 13, 6, 5; the fifth month.
At this time, Emperor Zhou Wu was deluded by the demonic words of the Daoist Zhang Bin and others. Fearing the prophecies concerning those in black robes, he—
Wishing to abolish the Buddhist teachings entirely, he assembled his hundred officials and ordered the śramaṇas and Daoist masters to debate their relative merits.
He declared that those who were superior would be retained while the inferior would be abolished. He had the Daoist Zhang Bin prepare deceptive arguments in advance to defeat the Buddhist monks.
Hoping that they would fail in their reasoning and be cast out, at that time Dharma Master Zhixuan confronted the Emperor, responding with eloquence and vigorous speech. The Emperor’s intention—
The guest was unable to restrain him, and he proceeded to display his celestial majesty with indignant words. His attendants shouted at Xuan, commanding him to listen to the imperial decree.

Xuan responded with composure and dignity, and his exposition of the principles became increasingly profound. The Emperor raised an objection, saying: "In the Buddha-dharma there are three impurities: first, the acceptance of the *yelu* (astrological charts) and the birth of Rāhu, which makes the master impure;
second, the eating of the three kinds of pure meat, which makes the Dharma impure; third, when a *bhikṣu* commits a grave offense, the assembly [is defiled]."

"It is impure; such things do not exist in the Way. Xuán said, "What Your Majesty has cited is merely provisional teaching. As for the three evils within the Gate of the Way, they are even worse than this.
First, in the Purple Microcosm Palace of the Celestial Honored One, there are five hundred maidens in constant attendance who preside over impurity."
In the second chapter on "Invoking Blessings through Sacrificial Offerings," it is stated that there are one hundred jin of dried venison and one hundred hu of clear wine.
This teaches impurity. Figures such as the Daoist Yu Ji caused disorder, and Chang Jiangbin committed offenses; such instances have occurred generation after generation. The masses are thus impure.

If the monastic community commits transgressions and seeks to abolish the Dharma, how can they—like subjects who rebel or sons who defy their fathers—seek to empty the position of the Great Treasure? The Great Treasure...

The position [of the Emperor] is certainly not something that can be left vacant due to the rebellion of a subject or son; how could the True and Correct Dharma of the Buddha be abolished simply because the monastic community has committed offenses?
To now wish to abolish Buddhism and preserve only Daoism is like attempting to replace the legitimate heir with a commoner.

The Emperor’s countenance changed with emotion, and among the ministers who descended from their seats, there was none who did not express profound admiration. Since the Emperor could not be swayed, on the seventeenth day, the imperial edict was issued.

Consequently, he abolished both Buddhism and Daoism (according to the *Monastic Biographies*). ○ The Emperor established the "Tongdao" (Way-Penetrating) Academy; all monks and Daoists who were scholars were summoned to serve as Academicians.
○ The Emperor, regarding Shi Dao’an as a man of long-standing reputation, wished to appoint him to an official post, but Dao’an ultimately did not accept.
He subsequently passed away in Zhou. He left behind nine chapters of testamentary instructions, which are preserved in his biography;
they contain many passages of great exhortation, though most of the wording is not recorded here. The Dharma Master Jing’ai first began his lectures on Mount Zhongnan.

Originally there was no water on the mountain, but suddenly a tiger pawed out a spring that gushed forth to provide for his needs. Upon hearing that the imperial decree had been issued, he sighed and said: "I have eaten the grain of Zhou..."

Forgetting these matters—can this be called loyalty? He immediately went to the palace gate to request an audience. The Emperor summoned him for an interview, where he exhaustively expounded upon the calamities of destroying the Teaching and the retribution of karmic rewards.
The Emperor changed countenance at this; yet, seeing that the deed was already done and the issued edict could not be revoked, he thanked him and dismissed him.
Seng’ai withdrew and wept, saying, "The Great Teaching is now strangled and blocked; how can I bear to witness this? Thereupon, he fled into Mount Zhong.
At Nanshan, the Emperor soon wished to appoint him to an official post and dispatched guards to seek out Seng’ai. Upon hearing of this, Seng’ai moved to Mount Taibai;
the guards returned without having found him. Seng’ai lamented the extinction of the Dharma, weeping for seven days with his voice never ceasing at night.

He compiled the *Sanbao lu* (Record of the Three Jewels) in twenty fascicles. Since entering the Dharma, Seng’ai had not worn silk, cotton, or leather, but wore only garments of wool and coarse cloth.
At last, his retribution was exhausted. In the seventh month of the first year of the Xuanzheng era, he told his disciples:

"In my life, I have rendered no benefit to the world; I shall now practice the relinquishment of the body. Thereupon, he sliced his own flesh and spread it upon a stone, drew out his entrails and hung them from the branches of a pine tree, until all five viscera were exposed.
The remaining sinews, bones, hands, feet, head, and face were all torn and broken apart; he cut them with a knife.
He held [the image] in his hands and passed away while sitting upright; no blood remained on the remaining remains, but white milk flowed from its sides, which was mistaken for a stone spring.
At that time, Sun Zhe, the deputy commander of Xiangzhou, destroyed a golden Buddha image at Tanxi Temple; he had not yet finished melting it down when—
Zhe immediately collapsed to the ground, losing his voice; he stared fixedly with his limbs unable to move, and died that very night (*Gantong*).

In the sixth month of that year, a certain Minister of the People’s Department named Ren was feasting with his subordinates when he looked up into the clouds and saw five or six objects vanishing indistinctly.
The smallest one among them hovered in the sky like a banner and suddenly fell.
He entrusted it to Ren, who was permitted to examine it. It was the nineteenth fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which had emerged from amidst the flames without being consumed by fire.
Because of its mystery, he kept it hidden. Later, when Emperor Xuan issued another decree, Ren presented it to him;

the Emperor was then nineteen years of age. In the Qi dynasty, the monk Shi Yuantong resided at Yeshi Temple. He took the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as his primary study. In the summer of the fourth year of the Wuping era...
A visiting monk came to the temple while ill and was taken into Tongyan’s quarters. Tongyan attended to him with medicine and even gave him wine to drink.
When the summer retreat ended and the monk’s illness had been cured, he took his leave, saying, "It was improper for me to have seen you with wine earlier; from now on, you should abstain from it.
Have you ever visited Drum Mountain, the Stone Grotto, or Zhulin Monastery? I shall go to visit you there. That summer, Tongyan ascended the mountain.
Upon first meeting the old man, he followed his companions; however, Tong went alone and saw that amidst the deep and luxuriant forest on the southern ridge, there was the sound of chanting.
The visiting monk then cleared a path through the woods and led him into the temple, where the golden and azure splendors were exceptionally magnificent.
Furthermore, he was introduced to the Great Preceptor (Dàhéshāng) and various other monks, wishing to seek residence with them; however, the Preceptor did not grant permission.
Tōng departed in dejection, and after traveling only one or two *li*, he looked back and saw nothing but peaks and crags (*Sēngzhuàn*).
Yiwei (4), (14), (7), (6). Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Liang.
With civil wisdom he governed and restored the great treasures of the dynasty. He re-established the altars of the Liang state and his brilliance shone upon the common people.
In Jingzhou, he constructed the Tianhuang, Zhiqu, Daming, Baoguang, and Siwang Temples (*Bianzheng*). ○ Chen.
Emperor Xuan established a seven-storied great stūpa. The Chen dynasty śramaṇas Zhizhou and eleven others traveled to the Western Regions to seek scriptures (the *Sambhava-rāja-sūtra*).
Tiantai Master Zhizhe, whose courtesy name was De'an, was surnamed Chen and was a native of Jingzhou.
He had double pupils; at the age of seven, upon hearing the *Lotus Sūtra* being recited, he was able to memorize it. At eighteen, he left the household life. And...

He went to visit Master Si of Mount Dasu, who immediately showed him the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and expounded for him the Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss (*catur-ānanda-caryā*).
The Master entered meditative contemplation for three nights and thereupon attained realization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and the *Dhāraṇī of Revolving*.

When he had completed his studies and came to take his leave, Si said, "You have a karmic affinity with the state of Chen; if you go there, you will surely bring benefit. After Si had departed for Mount Nanyue, Zhiyi then proceeded to Jinling.

Ling was at Waguan Temple, where he first propagated the Dharma of Chan. The Vice President Xu Ling, the Minister Mao Xi, and other eminent figures of the enlightened age all received his instructions on Chan.
From then on, he spread the teachings wherever he went, and both monastics and laypeople turned to him with reverence.
He once dreamed that he ascended a high mountain and saw a monk beckoning to him with his hand; his disciples said, "This is Mount Tiantai. This was in the ninth month of that year.
Leading his disciples, he arrived at Mount Tiantai. Dingguang came out to meet him and said, "Do you remember our invitation from yesterday?
The Master was struck with wonder and prostrated before him. Dingguang said, "This place is a golden land; it is already mine. To the north peak of Fulong is Luoxi, a silver land."
It was a suitable place for practicing the Way. Thereupon, the Master opened the mountain and established a hermitage. Guo Guang said, "For now, settle here as best you can.

When the time comes that the three regions are unified, there will be a person of noble rank who shall establish a temple for you. At North Peak, various spirits and demons caused him constant alarm and distress;
the Master remained steadfast and unmoved, and they were immediately extinguished. Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty appointed the Master as the National...
Wang [Xianzhi] proposed the division of Shifeng County to provide for the expenses of the assembly, and two households of commoners were exempted to supply water and firewood.
During the Master’s summer lecture, the assembly beheld three jeweled staircases descending from the sky; several dozen Indian monks descended upon them.

He entered the hall to prostrate, circumambulated the Master three times, and only after a long while did he depart. Prince Yongyang Baizhi, having been sent out to govern Wuxing, requested the precepts and practiced meditation, vowing to take refuge [in the Triple Gem] for all future generations.
The Emperor of Chen dispatched seven envoys with an imperial decree to summon the Master back to the capital; the Master then set out.

The Chen sovereign welcomed him with formal rites and listened to his Dharma lectures, while all the officials paid their respects. He subsequently moved his residence to Guangzhai Temple, where the Chen sovereign visited him in person.
At the temple, he practiced great acts of giving and lectured on the *Ratnagotravibhāga* (Renwang jing). The Emperor rose from among the assembly to pay him respectful homage with great earnestness;

from the Crown Prince downward, all venerated his model of discipline and requested that he serve as National Preceptor. The Master then went to reside at Linhai. The local people made their living by fishing for oysters.
The fishing nets were interconnected for over four hundred *li*. The Master used his donated gold to purchase this coastal inlet and establish it as a pond for the release of living beings.
Upon reporting this to the throne, Emperor Xuan issued an imperial edict strictly forbidding any further catching or hunting. Furthermore, a stele was erected there (as recorded in his *Biography*).
Bingshen (5) [Year 15] (8) [Year 1 of Longhua]:

Dharma Master Tánqiān of the Qi dynasty studied the *Sūtra of Brilliant Adornment*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, and others.
He thoroughly investigated its profound mysteries. Once, while lecturing on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, he contracted a fever that caused his heart to burn.
Relying solely upon the Triple Gem, he dreamed one night that the moon fell into his lap; he tore it apart and ate it, which was as crisp as ice flakes. Upon waking, his ailment was suddenly cured.
Because he had attained virtue by eating the moon, he privately named himself Yue-de (Moon-Virtue). Later, when bestowing the eight precepts, he would always say: "Before me, Yue-de..."
The Bodhisattva precepts were formally received after three recitations.

The year was Dingyou (the sixth year of the Chen dynasty), the sixteenth day of the ninth month, during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Qi dynasty (r. 482–493). It was the first year of Chengguang (501), when the Zhou dynasty was about to be extinguished.
At Mount Nanyue, Master Sengzhi Daosheng’s reputation for the Way had become flourishing and his fame was heard everywhere. Suddenly, there appeared a Daoist who gave rise to jealousy.

With a malicious intent, he secretly informed the Chen Emperor, falsely accusing the Master, claiming that a monk from the north had received a warrant from the Qi state to "dig up the heart of Mount Yue" and "drive in stakes of stone to stir up demons.
The Emperor then dispatched an envoy to pursue the Master. When the envoy reached Shiqiao, he suddenly saw two tigers pawing at the ground in rage and a great serpent blocking the road.
Startled, the envoy made a vow, saying: "When I see Master Sengzhi, I shall regard him as a Buddha; if I give rise to evil thoughts..."

"Let your heart be as it may; let yourself be wounded. Upon these words, the snake and tiger retreated. The messenger was made to see the Master and prostrate himself before him, then reported the matter to the Master.
Before the messenger had even arrived, the Master saw a small bee come to sting his face; he immediately killed it with a large bee, which carried the carcass back to the Master’s presence.
The Master entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to observe it and knew that this was an old karmic enemy who wished to cause him harm. The Master said to the messenger: "Messenger..."

“[The Emperor] had already departed first; I, this poor monk, followed later. Seven days later, I traveled there by flying my mendicant’s staff. The officials at the gates of the four quarters all reported the Master’s entry.
The Emperor was already struck with wonder and astonishment. When the Master appeared before him for the audience, the Emperor descended from his seat to welcome him. He then asked his attendants:”

When the Emperor saw this monk, he asked his attendants, "What sort of person is this? They replied, "He is but an ordinary monk. The Emperor said, "I saw him treading upon jeweled flowers as he arrived through the air.
He then welcomed the Master into the hall to provide offerings. As for the Daoist priest, the Emperor wished to execute him entirely for the crime of deception.
The Master earnestly petitioned the Emperor, saying, "This is a matter of karmic retribution from past lives. I pray that Your Majesty will grant him amnesty.

The Emperor approved his request and issued an edict for those Daoist practitioners to serve as the Master's attendants. The Master then submitted a memorial to take his leave and return to the mountains. The Emperor saw him off with exceptional honors.
Not long after the Master’s departure, one of the Daoists who had slandered him died suddenly, while another was bitten to death by a dog; thus did the omens of the bees manifest. From then on—

Every year, the Chen Emperor personally attended three audiences to offer his respects and provide offerings that accumulated over time; its splendor was unsurpassed. Yet its divine mysteries were unfathomable:

it remained dry when encountering rain and stayed unstained when treading through mud. At times it manifested in forms both small and large, and at other times it would remain silent and withdraw its body.

In the sixth month of that year, as he was about to pass away, he preached the Dharma for several consecutive days, reprimanding [his disciples] with such bitter urgency that those who heard it were struck with cold dread.

On the twenty-second day, he dismissed the assembly and passed away in stillness. His junior disciple Lingbian wailed and lamented, whereupon the Master opened his eyes and said, "Why do you disturb me?
You foolish man, get out! Having finished speaking, he departed forever. He was sixty-four years of age. The Master had...
Regarding his activities as a writer: he produced five treatises and various verses, all of which remain extant in the world (from his biography).
During the twenty-eight years of the six successive rulers of the Northern Qi dynasty, six translators rendered sixty-two fascicles of sutras and śāstras; there were over two hundred thousand monks.
There were more than forty thousand monasteries. After Emperor Zhou Wu had suppressed [Buddhism], the Qi dynasty occupied the capital at Ye.

He assembled the monks and Daoists and proclaimed his intent to abolish the teachings. The edict stated in brief: "The world propagates the Three Teachings, and their influence has spread far and wide. Yet when examining the ultimate truth, they frequently fail to transform and refine the people.

As for the Six Classics of Confucianism, their texts provide a thorough understanding of the Way of governance and are suitable for the world; therefore, they must be preserved. Furthermore, as for the True Buddha..."
There are no images. To pay distant respect and manifest sincerity while lavishly adorning stupas and temples is of no benefit;

since it is merely a hollow waste of resources, it is not worth preserving. All scriptures and images should be destroyed. The kindness of parents is profound, yet monks and Daoists do not show them reverence;
they should all revert to secular dress to honor filial care. This is my intention. If you have any other principles, you may state them before me.

[The Emperor] withdrew. There were slanderous remarks [circulating]. Dharma Master Huiyuan stepped forward and replied: "Your Majesty presides over the great realm and takes the Three Teachings as your model.

Yet Your Majesty’s clear edict states: 'The true Buddha has no image. This is indeed consistent with the imperial decree. However, the common people rely upon the scriptures to hear of the Buddha and depend upon images to represent the Truth.
If these are abolished, there will be no means to promote goodness. The Emperor said: "The true Buddha is the void."
"Everyone possesses [the Buddha-nature] within themselves; why rely on scriptures and images? Huiyuan replied, "Before the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han, scriptures and images had not yet arrived.

For what reason did people not know the True Buddha? The Emperor had no answer. Huiyuan spoke again, "If one does not rely on the scriptures, then prior to the Three Sovereigns, when written characters did not yet exist, why would people not have known the Five Constant Virtues?
The Emperor again had no answer. Huiyuan further said, "If you claim that clay images lack sentience..."

"It is of no benefit. The seven ancestral temples of the state are likewise a way of reverent obedience; how can they be abolished? Furthermore, the imperial decree orders monks to return to lay dress to honor filial piety and support.
Huiyuan replied, "To establish one's character and cultivate a reputation so as to bring glory to one's parents is itself the practice of filial piety.
Why must one necessarily return home? The Emperor was enraged by Huiyuan’s defiance of his decree, his anger evident in both word and expression; yet Huiyuan remained composed and fearless.

He spoke again, saying, "Your Majesty, though you employ your power to destroy the Great Teaching, the Buddha’s words state that the retribution of the unseen realm does not distinguish between the noble and the lowly.
I, a poor monk, deeply regret this for Your Majesty. The Emperor said, "If it will only bring happiness to the common people, I shall not shrink from the sufferings of hell myself.
Da replied, "Your Majesty employs false teachings to transform the people; you are currently planting the seeds of suffering, and you shall surely share in it with them."

[The Emperor] replied, "Below [this realm], one descends toward the Avīci hell; where, then, is there any joy? His arguments were exhausted, and he could only say, "Let the monks return for now," as he ordered his attendants to escort them out.
Displeased, he concluded the meeting. At that time, the monks and nuns within the borders of the Qi state were all ordered to return to lay dress (*Sengzhuan*).
Originally, the monk Senghu of Lingshi Temple in Jinzhou had vowed to create a stone statue eighteen feet tall. While at the northern valley, he saw a reclining stone.
He then hired craftsmen to construct it. When the front and belly were roughly completed, the back touched the ground; they tried to lift it but could not move it.

At night it turned over by itself, and by morning it was already positioned for construction. It was moved and installed in the Buddha hall. On the day Jinzhou fell, sweat flowed from the image onto the ground.
When the Zhou troops entered the territory and burned various temples and stupas, this image alone did not change color. They then attempted to overturn it, employing six men and oxen.
Ten men pulling could not move it. Suddenly, a strange monk appeared and surrounded it with tiles, wood, and earthen trenches; in an instant, the monk vanished.
Later, the image appeared in a dream to a person of faith, saying, "I suffer from pain in my fingers. When that person examined the image, he found two fingers wounded by wood.
He immediately repaired them. During the Sui dynasty, the image repeatedly manifested miraculous signs.
Wu-xu (the first year of Xuānzhèng): [In the sixth month, the Emperor passed away; Gāozǔ Xuāndì Yūn ascended the throne and changed the era name to Dàchéng. ... [Seventeen] ... [Ten] ...

He passed away without illness. During the reigns of five emperors over twenty-five years, initially Wényuán Tǎi and the Grand Steward Wényú Hù both venerated the Buddha-dharma and, together with more than ten Tripiṭaka masters from the Western Regions, translated over one hundred scriptures.
Scroll. ○ The Yang Clan of the Sui dynasty. Capital: Chang’an. Three rulers. A total of thirty-eight years.

*Xinchou* (the first year of the Kaihuang era of Sui Gaozu). (In the second month of the first year of Dading, Emperor Jing of Zhou abdicated the throne to the High Ancestor [Gaozu] and changed the era name. *Tiānbǎo* 20th year of Liang Shizong. *Tàijiàn* 13th year of Chen.

In the second month, Emperor Wen (Yan) of the Sui dynasty received the abdication from the Zhou and ascended the imperial throne. As the sovereign presiding over hundreds of millions of subjects, he renewed all affairs of state.
He lightened taxes, mitigated punishments, reduced corvée labor, and curtailed service obligations; thus, all who possess teeth and wear hair rejoiced in the Great Peace.

Having purified and cleared the two realms of heaven and earth, he immediately promoted the restoration of the Triple Gem. Consequently, the Sun of the Buddha shone once more, and the Water of the Dharma flowed freely. III.
An imperial edict was issued to establish a monastery for the Sangha at each of the Five Sacred Peaks (*Sānbǎojì*).
Initially, the Emperor was born on the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the seventh year of the Dàtǒng era of the Wèi dynasty at the Bānrě Nunnery in Tóngzhōu.
At that time, a crimson light illuminated his chamber and purple vapors filled the courtyard. A divine nun named Zhìxiān said to the Taizǔ: "This child is a Buddha."
The child was blessed such that his body was like a śarīra, indestructible; thus, the Emperor named him Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, it was said:

"This child’s origins are of a different order than ordinary; the secular home is defiled. He should be raised at a monastery. Thereupon, the Great Ancestor divided his residence to establish a temple.

The child was entrusted to a nun. Later, when the Empress Dowager came to embrace him, he suddenly transformed into a dragon; she fell to the ground in alarm. The nun said, "Why did you recklessly touch my child?
This shall cause you to later obtain the empire. When the boy reached the age of seven, the nun told the Emperor, "This child will later become greatly noble.
He shall come from the East; the Buddha-dharma will temporarily perish, but it shall flourish again because of you. The nun was serene and reserved, possessing few desires.
She spoke of auspicious and inauspicious matters, and there was nothing that did not prove true. When the Emperor reached the age of thirteen, she finally returned home.
Upon the fall of the Northern Zhou dynasty, the nun hid within the Emperor’s household; she passed away shortly thereafter.

It was then that the Emperor indeed entered from Shandong to become the Son of Heaven and greatly promoted the Buddha-dharma, exactly as the nun had foretold. After ascending the throne, he would frequently look back upon his ministers.
The Daoist master Daonian used this as a pretext for his arguments. He further claimed: "The Emperor’s rise was due to the Buddha-dharma, yet he has a fondness for eating hemp and beans;
it seems his previous life must have been among the practitioners of the Way. When young, he stayed in a temple, and even now he delights in hearing the sound of bells and chimes.
Later, [Daonian] erected a statue of a divine nun at a temple pagoda and commanded the court historian to compose a biography for her titled *The Record of the Ailing One* (*Lunheng*).
The Imperial Edict of the Seventh Month: I humbly reflect upon the Great Ancestor, Emperor Wuyuan. Through the vicissitudes of three reigns, he established the foundation of our imperial house.

In reverently contemplating his divine wisdom, my thoughts turn toward the profound and silent truth. Desiring to extensively honor the precious stupas and initiate the construction of monasteries, I wish to increase merit and thereby fulfill his subtle, hidden intent.
Therefore, temples shall be established in each of the following locations: Xiangyang, Suizhou, Jiangling, and Jinyang. One temple shall be founded in each.

A stele was erected to commemorate his virtues, so that this adorned jewel-pagoda might remain indestructible like empty space, and his flourishing achievements might be proclaimed as enduring as heaven and earth.

From then on, every year on the anniversary of the Emperor’s death, official duties were suspended to establish vegetarian feasts, fashion images, perform circumambulations, and conduct the Eight Precepts Repentance ceremony to provide sustenance for the spiritual essence.
In the eighth month, an edict was issued stating: "In years past, during the Zhou dynasty..."
Now that the dynasty has declined, the multitude of rebels has boiled over like a cauldron. I have dispatched my chariots and trained my soldiers to sweep away these demonic and foul creatures.

Among the ranks of those who uphold integrity and righteousness, there are those who disregard their own lives and forget death; beneath the clashing of spears and shields, I constantly hear of their passing. As I perpetually contemplate all living beings treading upon the bitterness of blades and weapons, [my grief is profound].

There are those who cherish the Ultimate Way and undertake the karma of delivering others across [samsara]; they contemplate the establishment of fields of merit, and the power of the Dharma provides silent assistance.

It is my hope that the subjects who died in service may have their *bodhicitta* increase, while their rebellious companions pass from darkness into light, all together investigating suffering and emptiness and being entirely uprooted from birth and death.
May the abode of the great sea monsters be transformed into a subtle and wondrous terrace, and the wilds of dragons and snakes forever become a land of crystal.
A monastery may be established at the site of the battle in Xiangzhou. Furthermore, wherever commoners have violated the law, let them all be executed there.
Let each person take it upon themselves to sponsor a vegetarian feast. The Emperor’s resolve was to propagate the Dharma.

That winter, the śramaṇa Zhizhou and others returned from the Western Regions, bringing two hundred and sixty volumes of Sanskrit scriptures. An imperial edict ordered that they be handed over to the relevant authorities and that people be summoned [to assist with their translation].

*Fanyi* (Kaihuang Lu): Shi Daoshun widely propagated the Dharma and transformed others, yet he alone would not confer the precepts upon a certain woman because her future rebirth as an ox was already manifest.
The assembly doubted his words, so Daoshun stepped onto the empty space behind her skirt and said, "This is the shadow of a tail.
The woman was immediately unable to rise. The assembly, struck with wonder and faith, sought his help; the woman then gave away all her family’s wealth.
Shun performed a ritual for cultivating merit and repentance; his evil karma was immediately extinguished, and he was then able to receive the precepts.
The Sangha Superintendent Tanyan passed away (Tanyan was born with forty teeth already complete).
Ren-yin (2nd year), [Month] 20th, [Day] 14th:
Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty passed away. The emperor had occupied the throne for fourteen years.

He repaired fifty monasteries, constructed fifteen *zhang* high seven-storied great stupas as sacred sites, cast twenty thousand gilded bronze Buddhas, and restored one hundred and thirty ancient images.
Ten thousand images were cast and twelve sets of the Tripitaka were transcribed; ten thousand monks and nuns were ordained.

(The Three Jewels) Initially, Dharmaprajñā (translated as Fǎzhì, "Dharma-Wisdom") served as the Director of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (*Zháoxuán Dū*) at the end of the Qi dynasty. When the Northern Zhou destroyed the Qi, Zhì was appointed as the Governor of Yangchuan Commandery.
Upon reaching this time, the Sui Emperor summoned Zhì back to translate scriptures. Furthermore, Vinitaruci of India (translated as Mièxǐ, "Extinction of Joy") arrived just as the Emperor...
He also summoned the Tibetan translator [Ratnarakṣita]. In the second month, Faxian translated the *Hastikakṣya-sūtra*. In the third month, Zhi translated the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*.
In the sixth month, the Sui Emperor issued an edict that Longshou Mountain was suitable for establishing the capital; accordingly, the site was fortified.

The city was named Daxingcheng (Great Flourishing City), the palace was named Daxingdian (Great Flourishing Palace), and the districts, gates, and gardens were all named Daxing. The monastery was named Daxingsi (Great Flourishing Monastery).

The virtuous monasteries flourished; the compassionate transformation of the Triple Gem was thus greatly promoted. The benevolent wind of the ten thousand nations was extensively propagated through this cause.

Monastic complexes rose majestically, their splendor intermingling with the city walls and moats. Banners and canopies soared aloft, adorning the realm. The Dharma halls and Buddha temples were equal to celestial palaces;
the land of China, the Divine Land, became once again like a Pure Land. Sramanas gathered in great numbers, cultivating the six perfections to perfume their hearts.
The faithful gathered in great numbers, cultivating the ten wholesome deeds as their practice.

Thereupon, those with plump bellies and yellow teeth vied to purchase Jeta’s Grove, while those in blue scholar-garments contended to assemble on King Bimbisāra’s land. Thus, stupas emerged here and there, and precious shrines sprang up.
Suddenly, [the monasteries] were spread out like stars (*Sānbǎojì*). The Emperor issued an edict to the people within his realm, permitting them to leave the household life at will;

furthermore, they were required to pay a tax based on their number of mouths to fund the construction of scriptures and images. Consequently, the common people followed this trend like grass bending in the wind, and Buddhist texts became numerous among the populace.

[The number of followers] reached several thousand times that of the Six Classics (Tongjian). ○ The Dharma Master Tanyan initially encountered the suppression of the teachings and fled into Mount Taihang.
When Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty received the abdication of the throne, he shaved his hair on that very day and went to have an audience as a śramaṇa.

The Emperor was greatly pleased. Consequently, Tanyan was appointed as the Director of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuantong). That winter, he was ordered to participate in the translation of scriptures (Biographies). ○ The Dharma Master Sengmeng possessed both advanced age and great virtue.
[The Emperor] bestowed [upon him] the title of *Dharmabhāṇaka*. He was ordered to reside at Daxingshan Monastery, which was formerly Zhuhu Monastery.
He was subsequently promoted to the rank of Great State Preceptor of the Tripitaka (*Da-tong Sanzang Fashi*) and entrusted with the propagation and protection of the Buddha-dharma.

In the second month of the eighth year of the Kaihuang era, he passed away suddenly. In the seventh month, Faxian also produced the *Zongchi jing* (Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra). In that same month, Narendrayaśas was summoned.
He departed for the capital and was granted quarters at Daxingshan Temple, where he was provided with the highest offerings.

In the twelfth month, he began the manual translation process, assisted by four court officials including Li Daobao, and oversaw the interpretation by more than twenty monks, including Lingzang, the Abbot of Xingshan Temple.

He supervised the management of the Three Jewels. Furthermore, the forty-five provinces through which the Emperor had previously passed during his years as the Crown Prince were all visited simultaneously at this time.

The Daixingguo Temple was established (according to the *Lunheng*). In the ninth month, Emperor Chen convened an Unobstructed Assembly (*anāvaraṇa-pariṣad*) at the Dajidian Hall, where he offered his person, his carriage, and his imperial robes.
A general amnesty was proclaimed.
Gui-mao (the third year) [22] (The first year of Zhide of Prince Changcheng):
Dharma Master Yancong left home at the age of ten and immediately possessed a reputation for wisdom. At twelve, he thoroughly mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
At fourteen, the Qi ruler invited him into Xuande Hall to lecture on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*. At twenty-one, by imperial decree, he was admitted to the Tongdao Monastery to study.
In the second year of the Dàxiàng era, the Buddha-dharma began to flourish slightly; [Seng]cong then expounded and interpreted the *Prajñāpāramitā* for various worthies.

In the first month of the first year of the Dàdìng era, he shaved his head once more. From then on, he regularly attended lecture assemblies. That year, the Emperor saw an image of Laozi converting the barbarians and found it strange;

he consequently convened a debate between the monastics and the Daoists. Cong then composed the "Treatise on Distinguishing the Teachings" (*Biànjiào lùn*) to clarify that the Daoist teachings were delusory and false.
Twenty-five articles. In this year, an imperial edict was issued in advance for translation. ○ The Sui dynasty issued a decree, saying:

"I venerate and honor the holy teachings and cherish their preservation within the realm. Therefore, all temples that were abolished during the Zhou dynasty may be restored. Su Gan, the Governor of Jingzhao,"
By imperial decree, a site of superior topography was selected within the capital city to establish a *gārala* (monastery).

Consequently, throughout the entire city, regardless of whether the space was spacious or narrow, it was permitted to establish temples wherever monks resided (*Bianzheng*). The Emperor issued an edict stating: [text continues].
Valuing life and detesting killing is the foundation of royal governance; the Buddha’s teachings provide a refuge for virtuous karma.
Sentient beings who possess spirit and vitality hold their lives as most precious. You should therefore exhort all under heaven to unite in heart in the protection of life.
In the capital and in the official monasteries of all provinces, from the eighth day until the fifteenth day of the first, fifth, and ninth months each year, [the rites shall be observed].
On the day the monastery held its religious services, no living creature—whether from far or near, among the common people or otherwise—was permitted to be killed (Kaihuang Record).
○ By imperial decree, the Dharma Master Mingzhan was summoned to serve as a court translator and resided at Daxingshan Monastery (Biography).
○ The eminent monk Jingtuo was held in high esteem by the Emperor. Desiring to test the character and capacity of the śramaṇas, the Emperor ordered his guards to brandish swords and pursue the monks.

He was only separated from [the Emperor] by a few paces. When Emperor Xiaowen admired his magnanimity and profundity, he ordered him to ascend the palace hall and bestowed upon him Dharma robes to mark his distinction.
The Emperor often said, "A truly eminent monk. (Beishan lu). ○ Dharma Master Huiyong lectured on the Dharma at Dacanzhong Temple.
In the eighteenth year [of the reign], in the fifth month of this year, he passed away. The monk Faqing had been carving a statue of Śākyamuni when he died before its completion.
After three days, he revived and recounted that he had reached the Hall of the King of the Netherworld. Suddenly, he saw a great image, which said to the people in the hall: [The text ends here.]

"Qingzao, I have not yet finished [eating]; why do you cause me to die? The man hurriedly prostrated himself and called out to those below the steps, saying, "Qingzao should indeed die," but before he could answer, [the deity] said, "Your life is not yet exhausted;
however, your food is finished. He then commanded, "Give him lotus leaves so that he may complete his lifespan. Having spoken, the image vanished from its place.
On the day after Qingzao regained consciousness, she offered some broth and more than ten lotus leaves. She then led a multitude of men and women [to the site].
Thus he completed the image. He passed away at the beginning of the Daye era, at the age of seventy-six. Shi Huiyuan then shaved his head;
the Emperor issued an edict appointing him as the Prefectural Governor of Luozhou.
In the Jiachen year (the fourth year), [the twenty-third day], the second month, the region surrounding the capital suffered from drought.
The Emperor led the people to seek food in Luozhou. Previously, the Vinaya Master Lingzang had been a friend of the Emperor in their private lives.

Upon this occasion, the Emperor ordered Lingzang to accompany him on the journey. Consequently, those who flocked toward Lingzang became extremely numerous. When the Emperor heard of this, he... [held his hand].
The Imperial Edict stated: "I, your disciple, am a secular Son of Heaven; you, Master of Vinaya, are a monastic Son of Heaven.

Should there be those who desire to leave secular life, it is left to you, Master, to ordain them. From this time on, Huizang ordained people by the tens of thousands over the course of his career. Later, when the Emperor was informed of these matters, he was greatly pleased and said:
"The Master of Vinaya transforms people toward goodness, while I, your disciple, restrain people from evil. Though our words differ, our intentions are one."

There was no distinction between them. The Master resided frequently within the inner palace, where he was treated as an equal to the Emperor. When sitting, they shared the same couch; when traveling, they shared the same carriage.

His honor could not have been greater (according to his biography). The Emperor, because [the Master] had been born in a temple in the same prefecture, [regarded him] as [his own] Grand Ancestor, the Martial and Primordial Emperor.
Empress Dowager Yuan Ming, for the sake of Prajñā, founded Daxingguo Temple (Bianzheng).

An imperial edict stated that during the time of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, the Buddha-dharma was destroyed and all images were ordered to be removed. As for those made of gold, copper, and other materials, some had become state property;
if any still exist, they may all be installed in temples. As for images made of wood and stone, the relevant authorities [shall determine their disposition].

He also maintained this intention. Once he knew [the truth], he sent someone to welcome [the relics] and made offerings to them. The reason he aroused his mind and applied his thoughts was to establish a foundation for merit and to spread his teachings;
whenever he spoke, he invariably harbored the intent to provide virtuous guidance (*kāishuáng jì*). *Dán Yán*, the Dharma Master of Hédōng, initially composed a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Fearing that it might not accord with the Sage’s intent, he presented it before the Śarīra stupa and made this aspiration: "If it accords with the Sage’s principles, I pray that..."

As he focused his spirit in response, the moment he finished speaking, the scripture emitted a brilliant light, and the śarīra stupa likewise radiated light, shining intensely for three days (*Gantong lu*).
In the third month of the Chen dynasty, the Monastic Head Baoqiong passed away at the age of eighty-one;

by imperial decree, the relevant authorities were ordered to provide funerary equipment, and the ceremonial insignia of the Son of Heaven’s retinue was lent to adorn the funeral with honor (*Benzhuan*).

Yǐsī (the fifth year of the Kaihuang era). [From the year Gēngxū of the first *yuánshàng* of Tàijí until this year, a total of 143,780 years have elapsed. (24) (3). Emperor Sui invited Dharma Master Jīng to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
Thereupon, he released the prisoners from the jails and issued an edict stating: "I have long been blessed with manifold auspiciousness and have succeeded to the precious mandate.
I am now desirous of taking refuge in the Perfectly Awakened One and reverently honoring the supreme fruits of his realization. Now I invite Master Jīng..."
The Dharma Master received the Bodhisattva precepts in the Great Xingshan Hall.

Now, the teaching of the Bodhisattvas takes liberation as its priority, and the root of ethical conduct begins with compassion. Seeing that the prisons are now dark and secluded, he felt deep sorrow in his heart.

From those who have committed minor offenses downward, all may be pardoned and released. It is calculated that twenty-four thousand light prisoners throughout the realm shall be granted release in advance.
There were over one thousand nine hundred people [pardoned], and those whose death sentences were commuted were over three thousand seven hundred.
All living beings alike understood this as an exhortation toward goodness. In the imperial edict of that year, it was stated: "The Buddha entrusted the True Dharma to the kings of nations.
I am the Honored One among men, having received the Buddha’s entrustment. From this day forward, until the end of my life, I shall regularly invite [the Sangha] for two weeks each month."

The monks took turns, ascending and descending in rank, to recite the scriptures. Four masters of the sūtras and three virtuous elders (bhadanta) read all the sūtras in the Daxingshan Hall (*Bianzheng*).
In the tenth month, Narendrayaśas arrived in the Sui territory in person; he further translated eight works in twenty-eight fascicles.
Later, he moved to reside at Guangji Temple, where he served as the Overseer of Foreign Monks.
Bingwu (the sixth day), [Year] Guangyun 4, Liang Gong (Cao Zong): Shi Zhizao was initially afflicted by illness.
He focused his mindfulness exclusively on Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. One night, he dreamed of a person sucking the essence from his mouth for three nights, after which he immediately recovered.
Furthermore, having received the Way from a wise master, while in meditative concentration, he saw a nine-headed dragon surge upward into the void.
That year, he resided at Baolin Monastery and practiced the Lotus Samādhi. An evil spirit harassed him every night for twenty-one days;
yet Sengzao remained composed and fearless, whereupon the spirit ceased to appear. Shi Fajin possessed virtuous deeds and served as an official for Xiao, the Prince of Shu.

The Consort and her ladies received the precepts; she was able to manifest multiple bodies to attend banquets at dozens of households, her miraculous traces being manifold (according to the *Benzhuan*).
○ Shi Sengjiu compiled the various existing translations of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* into a single collection of sixty fascicles.
○ The Vinaya Master Lingzang of Daxingshan Temple passed away; he was sixty-eight years old (one source says he ended his life at eighteen). ○ Shi Tanxun once [resided on] a mountain...

He once passed through a place where tigers were fighting; when he inquired about it and held out his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) to separate them, the tigers lowered their tails and dispersed. On many occasions he encountered bears and tigers contending with one another, and he would always resolve their conflict.

When he entered his carriage, the horses did not become agitated; even wild beasts regarded him as if they were familiar with him. Whenever he entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), he would only arise after seven days.

His transformative influence spread throughout the region north of the Yellow River, where he extensively propagated the Chan school. The Sui Emperor, who held him in high esteem for his virtue, issued an edict for Yuan Shou, a member of the Court of General Supervisors, to personally present incense and offerings.
It is recorded that he passed away at the end of the Kaihuang era.
Dingwei (the seventh year of the Qi dynasty), the second month (corresponding to the first year of Zhengming during the fall of the Sui);

Vinaya Master Fayan. During the Qi dynasty, he was renowned as a "Tiger of the Vinaya. When the Imperial Sui received the Mandate, he was appointed by imperial decree as the Abbot of Daxingguo Monastery in Bingzhou.
Having repeatedly held high administrative office, he was skilled at guiding the great assembly. His transformation of former practices was truly magnificent and orderly.
In the sixth month of this year, he passed away. The Sui dynasty summoned the Prince of Liang to court, and the Liang state was abolished.

Thus, the Three Princes of the Later Liang reigned for thirty-three years; all of them revered and believed in the Buddha-dharma, extensively constructing stupas and temples. There were two hundred and eight such monasteries.
There were three thousand two hundred monks and nuns (as verified by Bianzheng). Dharma Master Huibu of the Chen dynasty initially studied under Dharma Master Sengquan of Mount She.

He attained a profound understanding of the principles of the *Abhidharma-kośa* Śāstra. He said to the four close friends of Master Quan: "Sili excels in grasping the essence; Yu is skilled in literary composition; Bian is courageous in attaining the meaning.
Huibu once visited Meditation Master Si, who remarked: "The ten thousand miles are empty; there is no one with such wisdom. This was during the Zhide era.
In the central region, he established Xiqia Temple on Mount Sheshan. His fame spread far and wide, and those who came to pay their respects were as numerous as at a marketplace.

The Emperor of Chen and his various princes all received the precepts from him and revered him as a Buddha. On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of that year, he manifested his passing. The earth shook for seven days.
The Grand Astrologer reported, saying, "The star of one who has attained the Way has extinguished. People saw Bodhisattvas coming to welcome him (from his biography).
The eldest son of the Great Being Chen Futai was the Dharma Master Pujian, who that year attained parinirvāṇa through self-immolation (*Dashi lu*).
○ The Dharma Master Tanqian entered the Chen dynasty after the Qi fell; he thoroughly investigated the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, which had not yet been heard of in the northern lands at that time.

Once the Sui dynasty had established the Dharma, Paramārtha took the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* across the Yangtze River. Suddenly, wind and waves surged violently. Paramārtha held the treatise and addressed the deity of the river, saying:
"I now wish to use the Great Dharma to awaken those who have not yet realized it; the Northern Lands must surely hear this Great Teaching. Please cease these winds and waves.

In an instant, all became calm and tranquil, and he reached the shore in a smooth flow. When Paramārtha extensively propagated the *Saṃparigraha-śāstra*, both monastics and laypeople revered and followed his teachings.
[Such masters] were numerous. In that year, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "The Emperor respectfully inquires after the Dharma Master Tanqian of Xuzhou.

We have learned that you are diligent and refined in the Way and its Teachings, bringing benefit to those without limit. Hearing of your reputation and partaking of your virtue, we truly harbor a sense of humble longing. We hope that you will soon come to our court to satisfy our earnest expectations;

we shall join with you, Master, to honorably establish the True Dharma and to edit and determine the scriptures. Furthermore, as the Way and its Teachings have only recently begun to flourish, they encounter obstacles at every turn."

It was initiated [by him]. Its grand establishment and promotion ultimately relied upon a man of great talent. When Huiqian reached the capital, he extensively propagated the Dharma (from his biography).

○ An imperial edict commanded Huìyuǎn to reside at Xìngshàn Monastery. (Yuǎn’s height was nine chi; his eyes were three cun long; his waist measured nine spans; and his voice resounded like a thunderclap.)
On the *wùshēn* day (the eighth), in the third year of the Zhèngmíng era, Lǐ Shìqiān passed away.
Since his youth, Qiān had served his mother with filial piety; for thirty years he distributed medicine and scattered grain. He was naturally fond of Buddhism.
His conduct was restrained by means of precepts and meditative concentration. A guest harbored doubts regarding the Buddhist doctrine of karmic retribution, so Sishen explained to him:

"The accumulation of goodness results in blessings; the accumulation of evil results in calamity—is this not the very sign of auspiciousness and misfortune? The Buddha says that beings revolve through the five realms of existence."
There is no end to them. Jia Xuan also said: "A thousand transformations and ten thousand changes have never had a limit.
For instance, Gun became a yellow dragon; Du Yu became a *tíjué* [cuckoo]; Lord Bao became a dragon; Niu Ai became a tiger; and the gentleman became a crane."
The petty man became a monkey; Peng Sheng became a boar; Ruyi became a large [creature]; Huangmu became a *yuan* (?); Xuanwu became a turtle;

Dengwen became an ox; Xu Bo became a fish; and Yang You’s previous incarnation was the son of the Li family. These are all verifications of the Buddhist doctrine regarding the transformation of forms and retribution.
He was further asked about the relative superiority of the Three Teachings. Shi Qian replied: "Buddhism is the sun; Daoism is the moon."

[He was] also [like] the five stars of Confucianism. The guest was unable to refute him and departed (*Beishi*). ○ Du Qi of Jingzhao died and revived after three days, saying that he had seen King Yan.
The King asked, "What office did your father hold? He replied, "Your servant's father was an Upper Shih of the Zhou Siming.
The King said, "If that is so, you have been summoned in error; he may be released immediately. Do you recognize Emperor Wu of Zhou? Thereupon, he was led away.
In one place, within an iron window, he saw a man with an extremely emaciated body, the color of iron, wearing an iron collar and shackles.

He implored him, weeping, saying, "Master, for what reason are you so afflicted by such suffering? He replied, "Because I, out of faith, protected Yuan Song and thereby caused the destruction and abandonment of the Buddha-dharma, I am now undergoing this suffering.
He further implored, "I pray for my restoration; I shall constantly contemplate matters of the unseen realm and diligently cultivate wholesome deeds. (Biographies of Eminent Monks)

Shi Pu’an specialized in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. During the persecution of the Dharma by the Northern Zhou dynasty, he lived in seclusion in the valleys of Mount Zhongnan. Although he was repeatedly captured and detained, he was released on every occasion.
When Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty restored the teachings, other monks all responded to the imperial summons; only Pu’an remained steadfast in his retreat among the forests and ravines.
As he had already performed many miraculous deeds, in that year he was summoned to the capital by imperial decree to serve as the preceptor for the Crown Prince.
A Princess of the Long clan established Jingfa Temple, and he resided there in Yan’an, though he habitually dwelt among the rocky valleys (according to his biography).
Jiyou (the ninth year), the third [cycle] (corresponding to the fall of the Sui dynasty):

In the fifth month, Chen was extinguished, and the empire was unified. During the reigns of five rulers over thirty-four years, three translators produced more than two hundred fascicles of translated sutras and śāstras.
There were one thousand two hundred and thirty-two monasteries. The state was new.
There were seventeen monasteries built by the imperial court, sixty-eight built by high officials, and more than three hundred large monasteries within the city walls.
There were thirty-two thousand monks and nuns (according to the *Bianzheng lu*). In the eighth month, Ratnayaśas suddenly addressed the assembly, saying:

"The Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter; you should diligently cultivate and study it. A human body is difficult to obtain; take care not to let it pass in vain. Having finished speaking, he suddenly...
Thus he transformed [others]. His lifespan reached a full hundred years. The Master’s physical appearance was magnificent and extraordinary:

his crown was like a *uṣṇīṣa*, his ears were long and upright, and his eyes were perfectly centered—truly the marks of a great virtuous one who transmits the Dharma. For about forty years, the Master traveled through over fifty countries, covering more than one hundred and fifty thousand *li*.
From mountain deities to sea creatures, there were none who did not pay him reverence; his miraculous traces were numerous. [The details are] fully [recorded].
See the Original Biography. ○ Jñānagupta initially translated scriptures during the Zhou dynasty. He returned to the West because the Dharma was being extinguished;

however, the Emperor issued an edict dispatching an envoy to summon him. In the fourth year of the Kaihuang era, he returned once more. In the fifth year, by imperial decree, Jñānagupta was assigned to the Office of the Interior (Neishi Sheng) to translate ancient Indian texts.
At that time, at Guangji Temple, Yashas alone was translating scriptures. In the seventh year, a separate edict was issued for Jñānagupta.
He served as both translator and interpreter. When the work on the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* was completed, an imperial edict was issued for Xuanzang to specialize exclusively in translation.
The dharma seat was moved to Daxingshan Temple, where Dharmagupta and others were again summoned to assist with the translation.

In the spring of the Gengxu year (the tenth year), the Emperor visited Jinyang. He issued an imperial decree for Dharma Master Qian to accompany his retinue. Upon arriving in the Bingzhou region, the Emperor again issued an edict ordering the monk to perform rites in the palace hall until nightfall.
He was then summoned into the inner quarters and shared a couch with the Emperor. The Emperor said, "As your disciple travels on this journey..."
There was a monk named Cheng Da who wished to receive the precepts. Huiqian said, "In the past, when Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Dharma, the assembly of monks went into hiding.

Now that Your Majesty presides over this great destiny, you have further opened wide the gates of the Dharma; there are none who do not sing praises of having found a refuge and come to seek your sagely virtue.
Although they have repeatedly received the opportunity for ordination, they arrived at different times, which has caused a discrepancy in their timing. This morning, Heaven and Earth..."

"Nothing that is covered or supported by Heaven and Earth is not the King’s subject. By the Most Honorable One’s guidance and inspiration, the myriad regions find peace; even a single district receives blessings.
After the Emperor had reflected deeply for a short while, he finally granted his consent. He then issued an edict stating:

"From the fourth month of the tenth year onwards, all monks and nuns who have been privately ordained shall be permitted to remain in the monastic life. Consequently, throughout the realm, hundreds of thousands of people received ordination. [The text continues: "He transferred them..."
It was indeed effective. Shortly thereafter, an imperial edict was issued to establish Shengguang Monastery in the capital for the Fourth Prince, Xiao Xiu, the Prince of Shu.
By imperial decree, the monks were invited to reside within this monastery to receive the Prince’s patronage.

The Chancellor, the high officials, and the nobility, during their leisure from state affairs, all took up volumes of scripture to receive his instructions (from his biography). In the tenth month, Dharmagupta of India (translated as Fami) arrived in the capital.

The Emperor invited him into Xingshan Temple. He served as a co-translator during this period. That year there was a drought, and an imperial decree was issued ordering Dharma Master Tanyan to pray for rain.

When the rain did not fall, the Emperor asked for the reason. He replied, "Your Majesty and your ministers, though you have mastered the principles of governance, still fall short in the profound transformation [of the people].
That it rains or does not rain depends on the conduct of these two parties. The Emperor understood his meaning and commanded the relevant authorities [to rectify their ways].
An auspicious day was selected. A ceremony was established in the main hall, and the Emperor ordered Yan-shou to confer the Eight Precepts upon him.

After the officials had conferred them in succession, the summer heat was as if burning, yet a great rain poured down profusely. The Emperor was delighted; from then on, whenever he entered the court, he would personally serve him with imperial delicacies.
[He] summoned Dharma Master Zhi-zheng to reside at Shengguang Temple; he enjoyed considerable renown (from his biography).
Chan Master Zhishun initially served Master Chou and resided at Bailu for ten years, devoting himself exclusively to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Whenever deluded thoughts suddenly arose, he would immediately stab his abdomen until blood flowed; through this, worldly concerns could not enter his mind, and his resolve became even more strenuous.

Master Chou marveled at him, saying, "In matters of human affairs, you are truly without a heart [for them]. From now on, you may be spoken of as one who understands the Way. Later, he traveled north.

Mount Zhanhuang: His reputation for the Way has spread far and wide. In this year, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "The Emperor respectfully inquires after the health of Chan Master Zhishun of Mount Zhanghong in Zhaozhou.
Your physical well-being is clear and excellent as you instruct the common people, enabling them to achieve realization early. We hold this in high esteem."

I, the Emperor, extensively protect the True Dharma, never flagging in my efforts day or night. I now dispatch Lu Yuanshou, a Grand Marshal of the Palace, to proclaim my former intentions and deliver these incense offerings, as detailed elsewhere (in his biography).
On the *xinhai* day (the eleventh), the Imperial Edict stated:
"The Tathāgata established his teachings with the principle of equality at their core; the Bodhisattva’s application of mind is fundamentally without distinction.

Thus, he is able to serve as a bridge for all categories of beings and to deliver the multitudes of living creatures. I, the Emperor, occupy the station of the King of Men and succeed to the flourishing of the Triple Gem. Reflecting eternally upon this..."

The ultimate truth extensively elucidates the Mahāyāna; all phenomena are suddenly revealed as being, in essence, devoid of self and other. How much more so regarding meritorious deeds—how could there be "public" or "private"?
From this day forward, in all the construction of merit throughout the realm, let it be performed with unified intent according to one's wishes, without giving rise to discrimination.
May all dharma-gates thus return to non-duality, and may the worlds of the ten directions likewise [attain this].
To Bodhi (from the Kaihuang Records): When the capital of Jinling fell into ruin, the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai took up residence at Mount Lu, erasing his traces among the cloud peaks.
While Emperor Yang was still a prince in the provinces as the Prince of Jin, he held command over the Huai and Hai regions and invited the Master to receive the precepts.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of that year, a monastic assembly was convened at the Jincheng Commandery in Yangzhou; the Master was respectfully invited to preside.

He conferred the Bodhisattva precepts. Within his inner quarters, he personally transmitted the fragrance of the precepts and bestowed the dharma of the Vinaya regulations, subsequently bestowing upon him the name Zhizhe (The Wise One).
After some time, he returned to Mount Lu. When the Prince of Jin again invited him to leave the mountain, he composed a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*.
Coincidentally, the Consort Xiao fell ill; the Prince sent a letter requesting his salvation. The Master established a seven-day fast and performed the *Guangming* Repentance. Suddenly, a bird...
It flew into the altar and died after writhing about; a moment later, it flew away. The Master knew that the Consort would recover, and indeed, she was cured the following day.
The King was greatly delighted. Later, the Master returned to Tiantai. As for Dharma Master Sengyu, his learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular texts.

He composed thirty fascicles of treatises, including the *Tao Shen Yin Guo Lun* (Treatise on Cultivating the Spirit through Cause and Effect). In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, he was summoned to an audience, and the Emperor held him in high esteem. Before long—
He requested several times to return home. That spring, he was sent back to the mountains with generous gifts (Biographies).

When the Dharma Master Tanyan passed away—having served as the Imperial Preceptor for three successive reigns—he submitted a memorial to the Emperor at the time of his death to take leave, entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma from abroad. The Emperor mourned him with profound grief.

On the day of his burial, the hundred officials attended in white mourning garments to escort him. The Interior Secretary Xue Daoheng composed a written memorial for the sacrifice, which stated in brief:
"In the past, when the Way fell into ruin and the dark thread of the cosmos slipped from its fastenings, you took refuge in the secluded crags; your resolve was firm and unshakable.

High rank and generous emoluments could not turn your thoughts, nor could stern authority and rigorous laws intimidate your mind. When the Sage Emperor initiated his mandate and the Dharma of the Image Age rose once more, you stood out..."

You, in your black robes, have become preeminent as the foremost of your peers. You have set aside the gravity of the imperial throne to reaffirm the righteousness of the teacher-disciple relationship.

Through you, the Three Jewels are propagated and protected; through you, the Two Truths are proclaimed and spread. Truly, you are sufficient to follow in the footsteps of Fotudeng and Kumārajīva, and to surpass Dao’an and Huiyuan.

As for Vinaya Master Hongzun, by imperial decree in the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, he was appointed to reside at Xingshan Monastery. In that same year, the Emperor decreed that he [should be joined] with Tian...
The monk Zhu Seng [Zhao] and others co-translated the sutras. Zhao Chang, the Vice Director of the Grand Court of Sacrifices, died from illness; after a long time, he revived and said:

"The King of the Netherworld stated that because I had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, my life span ought to have been extended further, and thus he ordered me to be released and returned. I then saw Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty."
With his body bound by shackles and manacles, he said to Chang, "You appear to be a person of my country; I trouble you to convey my regards to the Son of Heaven of the Great Sui.
It was not right for me to have placed my trust in Wei Yuansong’s flattery and treachery, which led to the destruction of the Buddha-dharma.

Now that I am being interrogated before the Lords of the Netherworld, Yuansong has already been cleared of all charges. As for me, I have long remained in this dark confinement and am undergoing extreme suffering; you should perform meritorious deeds on my behalf."

Deji Ba submitted a memorial, and the Emperor issued an edict throughout the realm for every person to contribute one *wen* to perform merit-making rites and repentance for the sake of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou.
(From the *Jingang Zhengyan*) Shi Guanding, whose courtesy name was Fayun, initially studied under Tiantai.

In the first year of the Zhide era, he followed Zhiyi to reside at Guangzhai Temple, where he investigated and refined the *Guanmen* (Contemplation Gate). He subsequently accompanied his master up to Mount Lu on the Yangtze River.
He traveled through Fu and Hengfeng. Later, he arrived at the Jing region and stayed at Yuquan Temple, where he propagated the Dharma and transformed others.

In that year, he followed Zhiyi to Chanzhong Temple in Yangzhou to serve as the presiding superior. He subsequently accompanied Zhiyi back east to Mount Tiantai, and later went out to Chexin Jingshe to deliver lectures.

In the twelfth year, the Renzi year, an imperial edict was issued to search for those who were masters of the three studies (*trīṇi śikṣāṇi*). Throughout the realm, the teachings spread universally. Among the monks, Tan-chong was selected from the community of dhyāna practitioners as the leader of twenty-five men.
By decree, five groups of the fivefold assembly (*pañca-ārya-varga*) were established separately within the city, with one person assigned to each to attend to them day and night.
[He] was instructed and practiced. All four matters were handled by the relevant authorities (Biography). ○ By imperial decree, Dharma Master Zong was summoned to oversee translations.

The Emperor extensively propagated the Three Jewels; whenever he held a great vegetarian feast, he would perform repentance rituals, for which Zong served as the officiant, fully expressing the Emperor’s sentiments (Biography).
○ Chan Master Xinxing was summoned to the capital from the beginning of the Kaihuang era. His Dharma transformation flourished greatly, and he established five monasteries.
In the fourteenth year of Spring, he passed away. ○ Yan Gong of Jiangzhou had others copy the *Lotus Sūtra*, making purity his primary concern.
Once, someone borrowed ten thousand coins from him for the sake of the scripture; against his will, Gong gave it to him. The borrower’s boat capsized and the money was lost, yet the man survived.

When Gong entered the storehouse and saw the coins, they were as damp as if they had been washed with water. Only later, upon hearing the account, did he realize it was a miraculous manifestation. Furthermore—
The deity of Gōngtíng Lake caused people to deliver items for the use of his scriptures. Even at the end of the Dàyè period, his descendants still transmitted the scriptural tradition;
thieves did not enter the village, and the villagers relied upon this (from the *Gǎntōng lù*). ○ Shì Huìyuè resided on Mount Luófú.
He gathered a multitude for the practice of dhyāna and was by nature deeply compassionate. Once, when a pack of wild beasts came before him, he preached the Dharma for them;

a tiger then rested its head upon the Master’s knee, and the Master stroked its whiskers. Later, the Prince of Jin summoned him to enter the palace to propagate the teachings (as recorded in his biography).
In the guichou year (the thirteenth), the Emperor visited Qizhou.
The Master followed him there. By imperial decree, the Prince of Shu was to conduct the spring hunting rites (*chun sou*). While the Prince pursued a wild animal, the Master followed.
He entered a kiln and saw it filled with ancient statues. The King immediately ceased his hunt and reported the matter in detail. Qian memorialized, saying:
"When Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty destroyed the Dao, the sacred icons were scattered. Your Majesty has initiated this project, and we have already succeeded in restoring many;

yet even the fragments of shattered bodies and remaining shadows still fill the wilds. The Emperor was filled with regret and issued an edict stating that all ancient statues were to be sought out by the local authorities in their respective jurisdictions.

He meticulously organized the collection and transported it to a nearby temple. The common people throughout the land each contributed a single coin; he entrusted officials to oversee its decoration (from his *benshen zhuan*).
○ The Second Patriarch, Grand Master Huike, concealed his traces and mingled with the mundane for over thirty years, transforming beings as circumstances required.
In this year, while preaching at the triple gate of Kuangjiu Temple in Guancheng County, his listeners gathered like clouds.
