At that time, Dharma Master Bianhe was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* within the temple; when his disciples heard the Master’s teaching, they gradually drifted away.
Filled with resentment, Bianhe slandered the district magistrate, Zhai Zhongkan. Zhai, deluded by these claims, subjected the Master to unlawful treatment.
He then passed away with a serene countenance, submitting to the natural order. This was on the sixteenth day of the third month. The Master’s age was one hundred and seven years.

During the reign of Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Taizu (according to his original biography). On the eighth day of the twelfth month, Yang Jian, the Emperor of Sui and disciple of the Buddha, respectfully addressed the Triple Gem of the ten directions:
"I look up with reverence to the Tathāgata’s compassion and his propagation of the Way, which delivers and saves all living beings."
Severing the source of evil and opening the path of benevolence and goodness, [this teaching] has been relied upon by all, from the court to the countryside.
However, during the period of disorder under the Zhou dynasty, the sacred traces were insulted and desecrated; stupas and monasteries were destroyed, and scriptures and images were lost.

Consequently, the ignorant had no means to guide those in confusion, and the wise had no way to seek out the numinous and holy. Your disciple, having previously relied upon the causal conditions of the Triple Gem, now receives this flourishing [teaching].
Fate has ordained that I act as the parent of the people, intending to rescue the common folk by once again manifesting the Honored Countenance and further exalting divine transformation.

Where foundations had crumbled and traces were destroyed, I have renewed their solemn adornment; where images were discarded and scriptures left behind, I have ensured they are all carved and transcribed. Though my sincere heart is earnest and diligent, I still fear that nothing may have been fully accomplished;

therefore, I have sought with renewed diligence until these [relics] could now be brought forth. Yet, for many years they lay submerged and neglected, defiled and ruined in improper places, just like...
This matter was brought about by your disciples. Now, before the Triple Gem, we repent with a sincere heart.

During the time when the Zhou dynasty was being overthrown, those high and low, both public and private, defaced images, destroyed scriptures, insulted the Sangha, and demolished monasteries. We now repent for all such grave offenses.
With deep reverence, we offer twelve thousand rolls of silk to all damaged and discarded scriptures and images; the Empress also respectfully makes this offering.

One hundred and twenty thousand rolls of silk were offered. From the princes and dukes down to the common people, they further reverently contributed one million coins, praying that the Three Jewels would bear witness and accept the disciple’s repentance.

At that time, the officials of the Palace Administration and the Ministries, the subordinates and clerks of the prefectures and counties, the monks and nuns of the various monasteries, and the elder residents of the capital all exhorted one another to join in, establishing a vegetarian feast on the following day to offer their service.

To celebrate the scriptures and images, ten thousand people gathered daily. A special imperial envoy was dispatched to each monastery to bathe the images with fragrant water (from the *Kaishuang ji*).

Although the Emperor personally oversaw ten thousand affairs of state each day, he "consumed the flavor of the Dharma" with his ears; every night he practiced the Way, and the Empress and palace ladies personally listened to the reading of the scriptures.

Whenever there were points of doubt, they would consult the Three Great Virtuous Ones (*tridaṇḍin*). Furthermore, by imperial decree, monasteries were established at the foot of famous mountains in various provinces.
One Buddhist monastery was established, along with the granting of manors for its use.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Jia-yin,

when the imperial sacrifice was offered at Mount Tai, Dharma Master Qian submitted a memorial stating that all abandoned mountain monasteries and monks who had fled without official registration should be settled by the Emperor.

Consequently, he issued an edict throughout the realm that all mountain temples with even a single monk or more were permitted to receive official registration (giving them a *e*). Private ordinations were to be registered in the official rolls (*Sengzhuan*).

An imperial edict commissioned twenty great virtuous ones (*bhadanta*) of the Dharma-gate to compile the *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures) in seven volumes, which categorized the scriptures into nine sections and distinguished their various types (it is currently preserved in the canon). Dharma Master Tanchong was highly esteemed for his Way during his time.

At that time, he entered the inner palace to propagate the pure karma; the Emperor received him with every courtesy, calling himself "the Master’s son," while Empress Yeondeok likewise called herself "the Master’s daughter.
All external benefits obtained by the Master were bestowed entirely upon the monastery; he possessed nothing for his personal sustenance beyond his robes and alms bowl.
On the thirtieth day of the tenth month of this year, he passed away without illness. The Emperor was deeply grieved and issued an imperial decree for his funeral rites.

At Nanshan, more than five thousand disciples of both high and low standing escorted him to the mountain site and erected a white stupa for him. Initially, the Master had propagated the teachings of Chan with great success;
Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty issued an edict appointing him as the Tripitaka Master of the Zhou State and concurrently as the Abbot of Zhuhusi.

Later, when the Dharma declined, he returned to lay life and was offered the rank of Jinzi Guanglu and other official titles, all of which he declined. When the Sui dynasty first began its mandate, he was summoned by imperial edict to reside [at the capital].

Xingshan. He subsequently petitioned for the construction of a monastery, and the Emperor established nine monasteries for him. Prince Gaozu of Tang donated his residence to serve as a monastery for him to dwell in.
Prince Jin was deeply reverent; Dinglin and Jiangwei served as his patrons (*dānapati*).

At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict sent fourteen thousand rolls of silk, along with brocades, fine silks, cotton, and cloth. Furthermore, the Empress sent five thousand strings of cash and felt rugs.
The Master then constructed a stupa site. When the Emperor heard of this, he sent five grains of śarīra from within the palace.

The Emperor and Empress also sent more than a thousand garments to assist in the project. It was completed that year, standing eleven stories high, towering and resplendent against the great void (from his *Benzhuan*).

On the day of Yimao (the fifteenth), the Emperor, noting that monks and nuns occasionally committed transgressions, observed that according to the internal Vinaya and the Buddha’s regulations, they were not permitted to be viewed by laypeople. He issued an edict to the relevant authorities:

"In accordance with the Mahayana and Hinayana sutras, extract all passages that contain prohibitions and restrictions concerning śramaṇas, and compile them as a formal code for the various scriptures."

Ten fascicles. Encouraging and guiding those who have left the household life; suppressing evil and propagating good (*Kaishuang ji*). ○ In the second month, the Emperor wrote a letter to Huìzé and others of Shuānglín Monastery in Wùzhōu.
It read in brief: "I, Your Majesty, preside over the world and have caused the Dharma teachings to flourish once more.

I desire that the Three Jewels be eternally honored and that all beings of the four modes of birth receive blessings. I trust that you masters propagate the Holy Way; this must surely cause your virtuous selves much toil."
(*Record of the Great Being*) ○ The Emperor and Empress constructed a multi-storied *stūpa* at the Fajie Nunnery in the capital, enshrining relics within its base.
In the seventh month of that year, a divine light appeared, descending from the base and circling clockwise around the *āmalaka* finial (*lupan*), as brilliant as the flames of a smelting furnace.
○ At Chanju Temple in Xiangzhou, the Śramaṇa Cen engaged in meditative recitation.
Yezhang would regularly go to the kitchen to request gruel. He kept a dog in his room, which, along with dozens of mice within the monastery, would gather every morning to eat together.
Once, when a mouse was missing, he suspected the dog had killed it and immediately rebuked the animal.
The dog then brought the mouse back in its mouth; Yezhang then beat the dog with a staff. Furthermore, when a monk’s robe was gnawed by a mouse, he informed Yezhang. Yezhang summoned all the mice.
He ordered each of them to protect one another; if there was even a single rat that failed to provide protection, Cen would strike it with a staff.
When a rat dared not move, Cen, because the temple was poor, pointed to a certain place beneath a spring to serve as a kitchen and another place to serve as a granary. People laughed at him.
After one night, the water receded and the land emerged. He acted exactly as he had said, thereby causing abundant prosperity.
Emperor [Xuanzong] invited Chan Master Fachun into the palace to confer the precepts upon the Empress (according to his biography).

In the Bingchen year (the sixteenth year), by imperial decree, Vinaya Master Hongzun was invited to serve as the presiding master for the assembly lecturing on the Vinaya. At that time, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* was the only one esteemed;

the Master then propagated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, until gradually everyone adhered to this school. Śramaṇa Fazang was appointed by imperial decree as the head of tonsured monks; the monastery where he resided was...

At Jifa Temple, King Jin offered a miraculous staff of ling-shou wood. In this year, the Prince commissioned an image of Avalokiteśvara, both of which were ordered by imperial decree to be enshrined at Jifa for offerings.
Ding-si (the seventeenth year).
In the first month of the year, the śramaṇa Baogui presented to the Emperor the newly translated scriptures produced since the Kaihuang era; the Emperor personally composed a preface.
Baogui combined the three sections and two chapters of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* into a new edition of eight fascicles (*Neidian lu*).

In the fifth month, a herd of deer came to be tamed at the gate of the Renshou Palace, and the officials of the hundred offices submitted a memorial of congratulation. In the sixth month, an edict was issued.

It is said: In former times, the land was beset by turmoil and disorder, and the holy Dharma was not practiced. Customary habits took root as the norm, and people devoted themselves solely to killing and harming.
I, the Emperor, have followed the holy teachings and made it my duty to cherish and nurture all beings. Through the assistance of you, O Prince, wild deer have come to be tamed.

If officials likewise employ utmost sincerity to transform and guide the common people, then naturally every person within the registered households may become a gentleman. You should therefore maintain a heart of benevolence.

"Excellent! This accords with such auspicious omens" (*Kaishuang ji*). ○ At Xinghuang Temple in Jiangzhou, the Buddha hall was consumed by fire; however, the sixteen-foot gilded bronze statue did not change color at all.
The great assembly marveled and sighed in admiration. Later, when it was moved to Baima Temple, birds and sparrows would not even tread upon it.

Miraculous anomalies were not limited to one (*Gantong lu*). ○ When the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai returned to Mount Tai, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I shall bring my life to an end in this place.
On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of that year, at Shicheng Temple, he passed away.
He lay on his bed facing west and invoked the name of Amitābha Buddha. He then took leave of Prince Jin and left behind seven sheets of writing, entrusting him with the Great Dharma.
He then had the prince chant the title of the *Lotus Sūtra* and listen to the conclusion of the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*.

He asked for hot water to rinse his mouth and spoke of such teachings as the ten suchnesses, the three contemplations, the six perfections, and the fourfold teaching. When someone asked about his own spiritual rank, he replied: "I do not lead a community; [my concern is only that]..."

"Purify the six sense faculties; benefit others while diminishing yourself. This is merely the stage within the five grades [of the Lotus Sūtra]. Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta will both come to welcome me.
The *Prātimokṣa* is that which you revere; the four kinds of samādhi are your clear guides.
Now, each of you remain silent; I shall depart. Having spoken, he sat upright and passed away as if in meditative concentration. He was sixty-seven years of age and had been a monk for four years.

Tenth: During the final years of the Renshou era, he manifested his presence seven times, descending once more upon the mountain monastery. The Master’s stature exceeded seven chi, and his eyes were adorned with an extraordinary radiance.

He established models for the Way throughout the east and west, and his transformative influence extended ten thousand *li*. He repeatedly experienced profound auspicious signs that were truly unfathomable.
He constructed thirty-six great monasteries, transcribed fifteen sets of the Buddhist canon, authored over one hundred scrolls of commentaries, and fashioned [images] of gold and copper.

He fashioned eighty thousand images of clay and wood, ordained fifteen thousand monks, and the number of monastics and laypeople across more than fifty provinces who received the Bodhisattva precepts was beyond counting.
There were thirty-two scholars who transmitted his teachings, and practitioners of Chan meditation dispersed throughout the Yangtze and Han River regions;
they were revered by all in the world and by future generations as the "Four Teachings of Dharma-nature Contemplation."
The School: This is called the Tiantai Teaching (Biography). Shi Guanding received the final letter of Zhiyi and presented it to Prince Jin.
The Prince then dispatched his Generalissimo Wang Hong to escort Guanding back to the mountains. For Zhiyi’s sake, he established a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks and founded Guoqing Temple.
Furthermore, at Fulong Danqiu on the front peak—the very site where Zhiyi had previously marked out the foundation—he constructed a temple.
The Sutra Translation Scholar Fei Changfang was a native of Chengdu. Originally a monk, he returned to lay life when the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Buddhist teachings.

Upon the rise of the Sui dynasty, he remained as a layman while continuing his studies. At that time, he participated in the translation process, receiving the texts and recording their terminology and meaning.

On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month of this year, he presented his work, the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through Successive Dynasties) in fifteen fascicles; an imperial edict was issued for its promulgation. Its...

The *Yijiaolu* (Record of Translated Teachings), fascicle 18, dated the Wumwu year (the eighteenth year of the reign), contains a comprehensive record of the scriptures and dharmas translated throughout successive dynasties,
as well as accounts of the methods and circumstances of their translation by both monastics and laypeople, from beginning to end.

Shi Fachong resided at Huacheng Monastery on Mount Lu to practice meditative concentration. He constantly exhorted the monastic community not to allow women to enter the monastery, arguing that doing so would damage the Buddha’s transformation of beings above and cause the secular world to fall into idle gossip below.
However, because worldly matters of family inheritance and legacy were considered weighty, there were those who did not comply with his advice.
Because his teachings were not being practiced, he threw himself from the base of Mount Xianglu, a height of more than a thousand *tan*. Not even a single hair was harmed.
The monks welcomed him back to the monastery, whereupon he immediately renounced his female form. The Emperor wrote to the śramaṇa Huize of Shuanglin Monastery and others, saying:

"I, the Emperor, have received the Mandate of Heaven to nurture the common people. I hold the Triple Gem in the highest honor, my heart’s intent being deep in its desire to provide protection. I hope..."

May all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, by virtue of these meritorious deeds, together ascend to benevolence and longevity. You all should propagate the holy teachings for the sake of all living beings;
your sincere devotion and ascetic practices deeply comfort my heart. Since the benefits are so manifold, do not decline the labor involved.
(Record of the Great Being)

At the end of the year Ji (the nineteenth year), in the second month, Vinaya Master Zhīwén passed away at the age of ninety-one. The Master’s character was firm and resolute, and his dignified bearing inspired awe in others.
During the Liang, Chen, and Sui dynasties, he widely propagated the Vinaya teachings. Shi Fatong entered the monastic order in his youth; he was extremely frail and weak.

Fatong did nothing but worship Avalokiteśvara, praying for the bestowal of sacred power. Later, he dreamed that someone gave him three donkeys laden with sinews; Fatong ate the sinews from only one donkey.

Suddenly, his mother called out to him and he awoke. From then on, his physical strength became formidable and heroic. Once, he placed a monk’s *kāṣāya* robe beneath a pillar; the monks claimed it was the work of a deity.
Sengtong laughed and lifted the pillar with one hand to retrieve the robe. There was a large stone mortar weighing some five hundred *jin*;

Sengtong went to the Southern Mountain, carried it back, and offered it to the monks. Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty held him in high esteem. At that time, the Western Tubo (Tibet) presented a man as tribute.
It is said that Da Zhuang was skilled at wrestling and there was no one in the kingdom who could match him. The Emperor summoned Baizhang to wrestle with him.

Baizhang said, "How can one who has left the household life engage in such a thing? Nevertheless, we may test our physical strength. He then called Da Zhuang over; Baizhang allowed himself to be seized and grappled by him.
Tong grabbed both of his hands from behind; blood immediately flowed out, and the man lay prostrate on the ground, begging for his life.

Tong released him, saying, "I did not dare to grasp you again, fearing your hands would shatter as they were pulled away. Thereupon, the man submitted completely. The entire court celebrated the event, and the warriors of the time hailed him as the "Celestial Strongman" (Tiānlìshì).
Later, during the final years of Emperor Yang’s reign, he fled the chaos and lived in seclusion in the mountains, carrying a single set of millstones with him. And so forth.
Duzi possessed great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Although his strength equaled that of a hundred men, he never acted in opposition to any being. He was sincere, pure, and lived with frugality.
He passed away at the beginning of the Wude era (according to his original biography).

In the late years of Emperor Gengshen (the twentieth), he placed deep faith in the Buddha-dharma. He issued an edict stating that anyone who defiles Buddhist images shall be charged with the crime of high treason (*Tongjian*).
[The Emperor] summoned five Dharma Masters—Tanqian, Lingyu, Huizang, Sengxiu, and Hongzun—to the Taixing Hall. The Emperor [addressed them].

He observed the rites of a disciple and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma (*Tongji*). ○ Shi Zhikang initially encountered a practitioner of the Way who enticed him with the talismans and registers of the immortals.

Zhikang considered this not to be the true Way; he then requested the method for transcending the world, whereupon [the practitioner] showed him the practice of abstaining from grain, asserting that he would surely reach the Jade Purity (*Yuqing*).

After seven days he was able to fly. When the next period arrived, he did not respond. Daosheng said, "You are still drinking water. After another seven days of abstaining from water, there was again no response.
Daosheng said, "At night you still sleep; that is why you fail to manifest a response. For another seven days he sat constantly without lying down.
When the three-year period was completed, he was unable to ascend to heaven. Later, he encountered a high monk who conferred the precepts upon him, and he became a disciple of the Buddha.
His virtuous conduct moved others, and he gradually began to manifest his hidden traces. Zhang Quan, a member of the second generation of the Zhang family of Jiangling, was blind in both eyes.

Sengkuang said, "The coffin in your family’s tomb rests against an ancient well. If you relocate the grave and open the burial chamber, you will surely obtain relief. They followed these words accordingly, and the blind man regained his sight.
He requested to be ordained, but the assembly was all reluctant to grant it. Only when he was nearly forty years old did he finally succeed in becoming a monk.

Furthermore, at Chengyang, he built Foji Temple. There, a cow gave birth to a calf; the calf emerged from its mother's womb and then disappeared back inside. As the mother cow was about to die, Huikuang said, "This calf is a lay devotee of the temple who misappropriated the property of the Buddha.
It has now come to repay its debt, yet it is ashamed to emerge. He then rebuked and admonished it according to the precepts. Upon this, the calf emerged.
He should have said that he was departing; his divine wonders were exceedingly numerous. In the ninth month of that year, he passed away at the appointed time.
The eight temples he established all possessed miraculous and numinous qualities (as recorded in his original biography).
In the first year of Renshou (the Xin-you year), when the Emperor was still a hidden dragon [a prince], he encountered a foreign monk who presented him with a packet of śarīra relics, saying:

"In the future, you, Dānapati, shall become a compassionate father to all under heaven. These are the remaining sacred remains of the Great Awakened One; therefore, I have left them for you to venerate. After the Emperor ascended the throne, he once...

Together with the Dharma Master Tanqian, they each placed the śarīra in the palm of their hand and counted them; the number varied, sometimes fewer and sometimes more, so that in the end they could not reach a definitive count.
Tanqian said, "The Dharma-body of the Buddhas transcends all numerical measure; it cannot be grasped or fathomed by worldly means.

The Emperor then began to store them in a casket made of the seven precious gems. When the realm attained great stability, the Emperor recalled this event, and thus [he enshrined them] in Qiqiu, Yongzhou, and Taizhou.
In thirty prefectures, including Hua, Song, and Hengzhou, stupas for the *śarīra* relics were each erected. In the sixth month, an imperial edict stated:

"I look up with reverence to the Perfectly Awakened One’s great kindness and great compassion, which rescues and protects all sentient beings and serves as a bridge and raft for all classes of beings. I take refuge in the Triple Gem and have restored the holy teachings.

I contemplate sharing with the four seas the cultivation of meritorious deeds, so that we may forever establish wholesome causes and together ascend to the wondrous fruit. It is fitting [that this be done]."
I invite thirty śramaṇas who are well-versed in the characteristics of the Dharma and capable of acting as guides; each shall be accompanied by two attendants and one official of the lower rank.
With one hundred and twenty *jìn* of frankincense, they shall distribute the śarīra relics along various routes to thirty provinces to erect stūpas.
In each province, three hundred and sixty monks shall perform the seven-day rite for the sake of myself and all officials and subjects, both internal and external.
The Way allows for voluntary offerings, limited to ten coins at most. The money so offered shall be used to provide for the construction of the stupa.

Separately, for the monks and nuns of other prefectures and commanderies, a vegetarian feast shall be established universally for the śarīra relics, limited to the hour of noon on the fifteenth day of the tenth month;

all shall descend together to place the stone casket. From the Regional Commander and Prefectural Governor downward, except for military emergencies, regular duties shall be suspended for seven days to focus exclusively on supervision.

He practiced the Way with a sincere commitment to the utmost reverence. On the thirteenth day of this month, the Emperor personally took a casket made of the seven precious gems containing thirty śarīras and brought them out from within the palace.

He placed them upon the imperial table and, together with various śramaṇas, burned incense and prostrated, vowing that his disciples would always uphold the Three Jewels through the True Dharma and deliver all sentient beings. Thereupon, he took up golden and lapis lazuli vases.
There were thirty of each. Within them, golden jars filled with lapis lazuli held the śarīra relics. The various śramaṇas each received the relics and proceeded.
Upon first entering the borders of the province, the provincial governors, prefects, and various officials lined the roads, leading the way on foot.
The fourfold assembly, their deportment uniform and solemn, all came together to offer worship with banners, canopies, platforms, palanquins, and all manner of music, surrounding [the procession].
They circumambulated him and offered hymns of praise. Thereupon, the Śramaṇa addressed the fourfold assembly, declaring:

"The Most Honored One, through the great compassion of a Bodhisattva, takes pity on sentient beings; for this reason, he has distributed his relics so that all under heaven may together cultivate the causes of merit."
Furthermore, he cites scriptural passages to reprove and instruct [the king] through various skillful means, then recites the text of repentance as follows:
"The Bodhisattva Precept Disciple, the Emperor [Name], respectfully addresses the Triple Gem: 'By the power of the Triple Gem, this disciple has become the sovereign and father of the common people.
I now distribute the śarīra relics and erect stupas; I pray that for the sake of all sentient beings, my manifold transgressions may be repented. At that time...
Upon hearing these words, the great assembly gave away their wealth and clothing in quantities beyond measure. They all made a vow, saying:
"From this day forward, we shall cultivate goodness and sever evil. Even those who were butchers, hunters, or cruel oppressors personally turned their thoughts toward the good.

When the śarīra was about to be placed into the casket, the śramaṇa Gao held the precious urn aloft and paraded it before the assembly; they all beheld a radiant light together and wailed with grief and longing.
He wept, the sound of his voice shaking the earth; wherever he was stationed, it was always thus.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month at the hour of the horse (noon), the Emperor stood holding a jade scepter in the southwest of Daxing Palace.

He invited the Buddha image and three hundred and sixty śramaṇas, accompanied by banners, canopies, incense, flowers, hymns, and music, as they arrived from Daxingshan Monastery and took up residence in the palace.

In the Hall, they burned incense and prostrated themselves. The Emperor descended to the eastern corridor and personally led the civil and military officials to observe a vegetarian fast and maintain ritual purity.
When the enshrinement of the śarīra in the stūpa was completed, the Emperor said, "The Buddha-dharma is being restored; there must surely be spiritual responses.

Subsequently, reports from various locations all recorded auspicious signs (from the *Hongming ji*, Wang Shao’s record). Within the tenth month, whenever the Emperor and the Empress ate, [they would notice something] on their teeth...
The śarīra were obtained. One was placed in a silver bowl and floated upon the water; it was displayed to the hundred officials, and in a brief moment, suddenly two were seen.

In total, nineteen grains were obtained, many of which emitted brilliant light. The kings, dukes, and officials, perceiving that the manifestations of the śarīra were manifold, prostrated themselves and submitted a memorial to offer their congratulations.
Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "Looking up with reverence to the Perfectly Awakened One, who protects and shelters all sentient beings, I, the Emperor..."
With a sincere mind, we dedicate these merits, aspiring to exalt this sublime enterprise so that it may extend throughout the realm, serving as a common cause for goodness.

Therefore, the *śarīra* relics have been distributed and divine stupas erected. Thus, the Great Sage has bestowed his compassion, repeatedly manifesting radiant signs; within the palace, the *śarīra* have descended in spirit.
This is truly a great fortune for all living beings, extending this auspicious blessing. I, together with the princes, dukes, and others, as well as the entire...
All you common people, you ought to redouble your diligent efforts to cause the Three Jewels to flourish. At present, there are still more than fifty relics of the True Body remaining;
the relevant authorities may distribute them throughout the realm according to previous precedents.

In this way, those in the three miserable realms and the six paths of existence may all be liberated from their entanglements, and all sentient beings with consciousness may together ascend to the wondrous fruit of enlightenment. At that time, envoys from the three kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla arrived.
They were about to return. Each requested one *śarīra* (relic) to erect a stūpa for veneration in their own country. An imperial edict granted permission to all.
On the second day of the twelfth month, an edict was issued to send the *śarīra* to Tai Xingshan Temple in the capital.

Ten billion monastics and laypeople escorted it to the temple, where they established an unrestricted great assembly (*anivārita-mahāpariṣad*) and performed rites of repentance and worship. (From the *Hongming ji*) — By Shi Daoxian.
Originally a merchant, he possessed two ships laden with precious goods. His greed remained unsated until he encountered a monk preaching the Dharma;

he suddenly attained a courageous awakening and said, "I shall sink my treasures into the river and leave the household life to distance myself from attachment. To be utterly free from disturbance—would that not be bliss?
He immediately sank one ship, while the multitude stayed by the other, urging him to cultivate meritorious deeds. Xian replied, "In the end, these will only lead to turmoil and toil."
He then submerged himself once more. He went to the temple on Mount Guankou to have his head shaved, vowing that he would not emerge until he had attained the Way.
From then on, he completely severed all human contact and built a dwelling in a mountain cleft. He would often enter meditative absorption for four or five days at a time.

Fellow practitioners of Chan Buddhism all visited him to seek instruction. During a drought, he even went to a dragon’s lair and rebuked its dragon; rain fell immediately. The people all revered him. The Prince of Shu...
Xiu summoned him, but he did not come forth. The King wished to go in person to strike him down. Upon reaching the foot of the mountain, rain and hail fell and waters surged.

The King then returned from afar to repent and prostrate. The sky immediately cleared and brightened. Arriving at the mountain, he paid his utmost respect and invited him to Chengdu, where he honored him with lavish gifts and profound veneration.

The entire city paid him reverent homage, calling him the "Immortal Ācārya. Upon reaching this point, he returned to the mountains and soon thereafter manifested his passing (according to the *Benzhuan*).

In this same year, the Emperor commissioned six life-sized statues of Śākyamuni and issued an edict to station Master Fazang in the temple. When the Prince of Jin succeeded to the throne, [the Emperor]...
When he toured the Tai City (Tai-cheng), Guanding came out from the mountains to pay his respects.

The King again dispatched the Court Gentleman Zhang Qianwei to escort him back to the mountain monastery, where he provided a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks and further renovated the pagodas, temples, terraces, and halls.
In the first month of the second year, the *wuxu* year,
the Emperor again distributed the śarīra relics across fifty-three prefectures, including Qin, Shan, Heng, Hang, and others.

He erected sacred stupas and ordered all officials from the regional military governors (*zongduan*) and provincial inspectors (*cishi*) down to the county magistrates (*xianwei*) to suspend their regular duties for seven days and invite monks [to perform rites].

He performed the ritual circumambulation and offered ten coins of money, exactly according to the previous procedure. It was scheduled for the hour of noon on the eighth day of the fourth month to jointly deposit the stone casket.
In each prefecture, there were various auspicious responses (from the *Hongming ji*). ○ At Shanzhou, light was emitted four times;
within [the light], flowering trees, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth were seen. There were twenty-one such miraculous omens. ○ In the fifth month, at the capital of Yongzhou...
Inside, it rained silver flakes and celestial flowers. In the sixth month, śarīras were sent from various provinces;

after the envoy returned to the palace and was granted an audience of consolation, the Emperor ordered that on the ninth day, a vegetarian feast be held at Jisa Temple to celebrate the auspicious light. Again, it rained silver flakes and celestial flowers.
Regarding the miraculous manifestation of light from the image in Shan Prefecture, a replica of the form was made and presented to Seonggwang Temple, beginning from the last day of the fifth month.
The sun emitted light. Those who came to pay their respects filled the roads, and all gave rise to the aspiration for the Way.

In the various provinces both inside and outside the capital, those who took away silk molds [of the image] also saw them emit light. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, at Yanxing Temple in the capital, a sixteen-foot gilded copper Buddha image was cast;
on that day, rain fell of precious filings and silver blossoms, and the fragrance was most extraordinary (Hongming ji). Śīlanāga.
From the fifth year of the Kaihuang era until this time, he produced the *Rāṣṭrapāla-paripṛcchā* and other scriptures, totaling thirty-nine works comprising one hundred and ninety-two fascicles;
all of these are characterized by the perfect integration of principle and teaching, with both text and meaning fully elucidated, and they circulate in the world today (*Shijiao lu*).
At that time, within the Translation Institute, Ratnarakṣita held the authority, yet regarding profound meanings, he would always consult Dharmagupta.

As for Jñānagupta, his demeanor was profoundly serene, and he devoted himself solely to humility. When Dharmagupta subsequently traveled east on official business, Jñānagupta took sole charge of the translations.
By imperial decree, he was invited to serve as a śramaṇa scholar at Xingshan Monastery to compile the *Catalogue of All Scriptures* in five fascicles;
these were organized into five distinct records, categorized according to their respective types (*Shijiao lu*). The Dharma Master Yuǎnwǎn...
He commissioned a sixteen-foot golden image of Śākyamuni. When the image was completed, he was moved by the descent of heavenly flowers, which resembled mica in appearance.

That evening, celestial music filled the sky, subsiding only at dawn. He further commissioned the four collections of the scriptures (*sūtra-piṭaka*), adorning them all with exquisite magnificence. — *Shì Dàoyōu*.

Suddenly, he dreamed that a celestial being announced, "The Heavenly Emperor invites you to lecture on the sutras. Daoyou did not consent. After a long time, he dreamed again; thus, he complied with the heavenly request.
The deity poured a small amount of incense into Daoyou’s hand and promised to come to welcome him at the appointed hour.

Upon waking, he saw a fragrant scent within his palm that permeated the entire monastery. Later, during a dharma lecture, the monks saw from afar smoke and fragrance filling the area around his seat. Daoyou suddenly...
He then passed away. The assembly saw clouds of vapor emerge from the temple, soaring straight up into the sky before drifting away and vanishing (from his biography).
When Jñānagupta of India arrived at the capital, the Emperor paid him reverent homage. Upon the death of Empress Wenhui, musical sounds resounded from the void.
The Emperor questioned Jñānagupta about this, and he replied: "The Empress has been born into the Pure Land of Amitābha; the various devas are coming to welcome her" (from the Biographies of Monks).

In the third year, on the day of Guihai, the Emperor established Chan-ting Temple to the southwest of the capital following the demise of Empress Hsien. He constructed a seven-story pagoda that rose majestically toward the clouds;

its halls and buildings equaled the imperial palaces, and its groves and gardens resembled the celestial gardens. The entire nation venerated this magnificent establishment as unsurpassed in grandeur.
He further summoned one hundred and twenty eminent and virtuous Chan masters from throughout the realm, all of whom were selected and recommended by Master Xian.

The relevant authorities prepared the proper rites, and Xian was immediately appointed as the abbot of the monastery (*Sengzhuan*). As for Shi Fachun: during the forty-fifth year [of the reign], he constantly resided in a pure precinct.

He took the sutras as his authority to examine his conduct and rectify errors; except for the times of eating and attending to the calls of nature, there was nothing else he neglected or abandoned. He once lit lamps within the meditation hall.
The lamp’s oil did not run out for seven days. Furthermore, the oil jar was suddenly lost, but after one night it returned, and the oil was already full.
He subjected both monastics and laypeople alike to arduous labor. In the fifth month of that year, as he approached his death, a youth appeared, holding a light in his hands.
It was placed to the right of his seat. When a disciple questioned him about it, Hui-chun said, "The Sixth Heaven frequently sent messengers to summon me;

however, because the devas are attached to pleasure, which hinders the cultivation of the Way, I ultimately did not accept. I vowed instead to be born in a place where there is no Buddha, in order to transform sentient beings.
On the twelfth day, he passed away (according to his biography).
In the fourth year, the *jiǎzǐ* year, on the twentieth day of the first month, Emperor Wen passed away and the Crown Prince, Emperor Yang (Guang), ascended the throne.
On the twentieth day of the first month, Master Chishun entered parinirvāṇa. By nature, the Master had little greed or affliction; he would not take hold of wealth with his own hands.
Whenever he saw those who were poor and starving, he would either take off his own clothes to give them away or cut off a portion of his own food to bestow upon them.

Having lived in the mountains for many years, there was no one to shave his hair; he therefore purified it with fire. When someone offered him rice or flour, the Master avoided them and accepted nothing at all.
Someone asked for the reason behind this. He replied, "Living in the mountains, the *kǔlì* (a type of chestnut) is sufficient to ward off hunger;

why trouble others? His simplicity was such as this. Once, a hunter was pursuing a pheasant that flew into the Master’s room. Although the Master earnestly urged him to stop, the man would not desist. The Master then cut off his own ear and gave it to him.

The hunter immediately cast down his bow, released his hawk, and followed the Master to study the Way. Thereupon, he exhorted several villages with great persistence, causing them to abandon [their nets and traps].

Regarding his occupation as a hunter: whenever he saw someone devouring meat, he would invariably assume a sorrowful countenance and admonish them, saying: "The six realms of existence have diverse forms, yet there is none you have not passed through.
All living beings have been your parents; all creatures that possess life have been your own former bodies.
To eat their flesh is to eat your own parents—how can your heart be so callously indifferent? Those who heard this were without exception moved to repentance and reform (from the *Benzhuan*).

The Emperor issued another edict, saying: "I, the Sovereign, reverently receive the initial mandate and cherish the people. I uphold the holy teachings and cause the wholesome Dharma to flourish once more.
Yet, the Tathāgata’s great compassion covers and protects all beings; moved by this, I have beheld the śarīra, which has opened the way for all living creatures.

I have already distributed these relics throughout distant and near regions, erecting spirit-stupas everywhere. However, there are still some provinces where they have not yet reached. I now further request [the Great... "

The Duke respectfully escorted the śarīra relics to various prefectures, instructing them to construct stūpas according to previous precedents so that all common people might share in these meritorious deeds.

He then issued an edict for the Vinaya Master Fazun and others to deliver the śarīra to more than thirty prefectures, including Bozhou and Jiangzhou, to be enshrined in stūpas simultaneously on the eighth day of the fourth month.
In every prefecture, auspicious responses were manifested. (Biographies of Eminent Monks) ○ July.
The Emperor passed away. During his reign of twenty-four years, he had forty-six *piṭakas* of scriptures transcribed, totaling one hundred and thirty thousand scrolls;
he restored four hundred volumes of old scriptures and fashioned more than sixty million images of gold, copper, and sandalwood, while also restoring old images.

There were over one million five hundred and ninety thousand images; within the palace, embroidered and woven icons, as well as painted portraits, and banners of five-colored pearls, were beyond counting. He venerated and constructed more than five thousand temples.
At this time, the four seas were calm and the nine provinces were free from dust. Twenty-four monastics and laypeople engaged in translation produced the following scriptures:

Treatises: approximately five hundred fascicles (including local gazetteers, etc.). In the eighth month, Shi Huishí passed away. Throughout his life, Huishí practiced dhyāna; he never laid his side against anything.
His resolve for purity and austerity grew even more rigorous as he aged. He kept only his robes and alms bowl with him, having no external attachments whatsoever.
He was truly a man of lightness and purity. He was ninety-six years old (according to his biography).

In the year Yichou (the first year of the Daye era of Emperor Yang), Vinaya Master Tongyou passed away while sitting upright on the fifteenth day of the first month. The Master’s observance of the precepts was strictly maintained within himself, while his benevolence was widely extended abroad.
He established four large wells, each equipped with water-strainers. Throughout his life, he never used towels or head-wraps; when his hands became wet, he simply left them as they were.
He dried his own tears and saliva, swallowing them back rather than discarding them within the monastery. Whenever he wished to open a scripture, he would invariably wash his hands up to the wrists;
holding the scripture before his eyes, he did not let his arm hang down. At the time of his death, he instructed his disciples regarding his remaining body, leaving it for birds and beasts.

Śramaṇa Sengshan resided at Mount Mátou. His practice of the Way of Meditation flourished through his teachings. On the eleventh day of the third month, as he was about to pass away, he addressed his disciples.
"Since it is unnecessary to cremate him—lest we harm external life—one may sit him within a jar and bury him. He then passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
The monastics and laypeople followed his instructions and interred him in a cliffside cave. His disciple, Sengxi, happened to be traveling elsewhere at the time.

Upon returning to the cave, he did not know the location of the burial site. As he prepared a memorial assembly, he was overcome with grief; suddenly, a roar shook the valley, and the jar surged up from the ground, revealing the remains.
The bones were like snow; only the tongue remained, glowing with a fresh, crimson luster. He then took both the bones and the tongue and erected two stupas for them (from the *Biographies*).
The Emperor was Emperor Wen; he built Xichanding Temple and also Longsheng Temple in Gaoyang.
The Emperor’s letter to Shuanglin Temple in Wuzhou states in brief: "I reverently receive the precious mandate and nurture the myriad regions. I reflect upon..."
He widely propagated his transformative teachings, which reached far and near... (Record of the Great Being).

In the tenth month, he conquered Silla and Lin’i, obtaining five hundred and sixty bundles of Sanskrit manuscripts, all of which had been transcribed by the *Kunlun* people upon palm leaves (*tāla-patra*). He subsequently attended the Translation Institute.
Śramaṇa Huìkǎn received instruction from Master Hé during his youth. Master Hé took compassionate salvation as his vocation and frequently manifested miraculous wonders.

He saw a pig that had been bound. Huihe said, "I shall liberate you through the Śūraṅgama [Samādhi]. The pig was immediately released, and its owner consequently set it free. Huihe served Sengquan for many years;

later, he served Paramārtha and attained a profound realization of the wholesome Dharma. In his later years, he resided at Xixia. At times he would go to the monastery of Daci Dharma Master in Yangdu.
When he was about to return to the mountain temple, he requested a manifestation of supernatural power. Huike immediately extended his arm out from the window, making it several... [chi] long.
He was over several tens of zhang tall. He removed the plaque from the Buddha hall of Qi-xi Temple and, as he was returning to his room, said:
"I did not do this only for fear that the people of the world would be startled by it. That year, he cast his three robes into the hall, saying:
"The robes return to the assembly of monks; I am now departing. He then returned to his room. The great assembly came in alarm and saw a set of white bones sitting cross-legged upon the bed.
[The Emperor] approached and shook it; it rang out with a clear resonance and did not break. When the Emperor traveled to Jiangdu, Zhi Zhao of Mount Tai came forth to attend an audience.
The Emperor bade him sit and questioned him at length. He then dispatched the Palace Attendant Lu Zhengfang to escort Zhao back to the mountain.

For the sake of Zhizhe, he established a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks, ordained forty-nine people into the monastic order, and bestowed two thousand rolls of temple cloth and three thousand measures of rice.
Shi. Xiangsu, etc. ○ Shi Huizang was skilled in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; the Emperor summoned him frequently to lecture on the Dharma (he was one of the Six Great Virtuous Monks).
In the second year of Bingyin, the Emperor held an unrestricted great assembly at the Daochang Monastery. He ordained one hundred and twenty laymen and laywomen of pure faith.
On behalf of Emperor Wen, he commissioned a seated image of Śākyamuni made of gilded copper. Furthermore, he established Hongshan Monastery in Bingzhou. Beside it...
At Longshan, he commissioned a seated statue of Amitābha one hundred and thirty feet high. In Yangzhou, he established the Huirì Monastery;
in the capital, he founded Qingchan Monastery, Riyàn Monastery, and Xiangtái Monastery.

Furthermore, he donated nine palaces to establish nine monasteries, with one each at the two imperial mausoleums of Taílíng and Zhuànlíng. (Bianzheng) In the sixth month, Dharma Master Yuánjǐng passed away. The Master himself...

During his lifetime, he always maintained this practice. He instructed that his remains be submerged in water, and the community subsequently buried him within the deep, clear waters of the Zimo River.
Three days later, the spot where he had been submerged transformed back into a sand mound, which was exceedingly high and steep, dividing the river into two branches.

Both monastics and laypeople marveled at this sublime omen (from the *Benzhuan*). As for the Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan: initially, when Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou abolished the Buddhist teachings, the Master went...
He came to Sikong Mountain and remained there for over ten years, such that no one recognized him.

In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era (the *renzi* year), he encountered the śrāmaṇera Daoxin, who prostrated to the Master and said, "I beg the Upādhyāya to grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation. The Master asked, "Who has bound you?"

He said, "There is no one to bind me. The other asked, "If there is no one to bind you, why do you further seek liberation? Daixin attained great enlightenment. After some time, [the master] conferred the full precepts upon him.

Later, knowing that his conditions were ripe, he entrusted him with the dharma robe and spoke this verse: "The seed of the flower originally depends on the earth; From the earth, the seed gives rise to the flower.
If there were no one to sow the seed, Neither the flower nor the earth would come to be. The Master then wandered freely through the regions along the Yangtze River.

Having traveled across Mount Luofu and other mountains, he returned once more to his former dwelling. On the fifteenth day of the tenth month, while in the midst of preaching the Dharma, he stood solemnly with palms joined and passed away.
During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Daizong (alternatively said to be Xuanzong) posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Jingzhi (alternatively said to be Jianzhi).

The Master had previously composed the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind), which is concise in expression yet rich in meaning, perfectly exhausting the ultimate essence of the school; it is widely transmitted and recited by the world.
On the twenty-eighth day of the first month of the third year of the Dingmao cycle, the Emperor, Disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, respectfully addresses the Triple Gem: Within the realm,
I have established a superior cause by inviting monks from each prefecture to perform ritual practices for seven days, and furthermore, I have ordained one thousand people in total.
He left the household life. By this merit, may he universally purify the defilements of all sentient beings so that they may together reach Bodhi (*Hongming*).

When the Emperor had established his capital in the Eastern Metropolis (Luoyang), he further established a Translation Institute within the Shanglin Garden and invited Dharmagupta to translate the scriptures.
The Emperor also, for the sake of the Empress Dowager of Emperor Wen, constructed two monasteries and two pagodas in Chang’an, establishing them separately.
There were ten monasteries. They repaired and restored six hundred and twelve scriptural collections, totaling ninety thousand three hundred and eighty fascicles.
They repaired and restored one hundred and one thousand images, and cast three thousand eight hundred and fifty-six new images.
They ordained sixteen thousand two hundred monks.
In the fourth year of the Wucheng era, Yang Hong, the Magistrate of Shiping, led Daoist masters and renowned Confucian scholars to Zhi Cang Monastery.

He requested that a dharma assembly be convened to discuss the Dharma, commissioning the Dharma Master Huijing to debate the principles of doctrine with the Daoist Yu Yongtong. Huijing asked: "The *Laozi* says: 'There was something undifferentiated and complete...'"
It was accomplished. It was born before heaven and earth; I do not know its name, so I style it "the Way" (*dào*).

Now, is the Way mixed because its substance is one, or is it mixed because its substance is different? If it is mixed because its substance is one, then at the very moment of being mixed, it has already been established as one.

This would mean that one is produced from non-duality. If their substance were different, they would be confused; yet even before they were confused, they already constituted two distinct entities, meaning that two could not arise as one.
Tong was utterly bewildered and did not know how to respond; he ceased speaking and withdrew.
(From the *Monk Biographies*) In the fifth month, Vinaya Master Hongzun passed away at Xingshan Monastery; his age was seventy-nine. Shi Faji was proficient in the subtle mysteries.

He was known for his extraordinary powers. During the Chen dynasty and under the two successive rulers of the Sui, he frequently stayed within the imperial palace. He would consecrate water with mantras to cure illnesses, and there were none that he could not heal.
In that year, he took leave of the Emperor and passed away (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
In the first month of the fifth year of the Daye era (the Ji-si year), the Emperor issued an edict stating: "Whenever monks or Daoists have petitions to present, they must first pay their respects;
only then may they state their business. Although this edict existed, the Sangzheng did not enforce it. At that time, there was the monk-translator and scholar Śikṣānanda...

Zōng could not bear this matter and thus composed the *Fútián Lùn* (Treatise on the Field of Merit) to oppose it. It consists of seven sections in total: first, there is no virtue that goes unrewarded;
second, there is no goodness that is not encompassed; third, skillful means are unimpeded; fourth, in nirvana there is no worldly glory;

fifth, ritual decorum must not be transgressed; sixth, vestments must not be disordered; seventh, the causal basis must not be forgotten. His intent was satirical, yet those who spoke of it were without [reproach].

"Sinful! Those who hear this should admonish themselves. (This treatise discusses the lofty protocols for the Three Jewels and exalts the fundamental principle of reverent devotion. Its prose is extremely comprehensive; it is currently preserved in the *Zang Hongming ji*.

Later, when the Emperor had an audience with the various śramaṇas at court, none of them paid him homage. In that year, he went to the Southern Suburban Sacrifice in the capital and displayed a grand array of cultural artifacts.

When the two religious schools appeared before him, he ordered them to prostrate. Upon hearing the command, the Daoist practitioners bowed repeatedly without ceasing. The monks, however, followed [the precedent].
Previously, they had not prostrated. The Emperor questioned them, saying, "The imperial edicts have been promulgated for a long time. Why is it that you monks steadfastly do not obey these commands?
The Dharma Master Mingzhan replied, "Your Majesty extensively protects the Triple Gem; we ought to follow the words of the Buddha.

Since the sutras do not command us to bow to laypeople, we dare not violate the teachings. The Emperor commanded, "Simply prostrate yourselves! The monks stood firm. This was repeated four or five times.
He bowed. The Emperor said, "If you command me to cease my monastic life in accordance with the regulations, I dare not disobey your decree.

However, if you recognize that the Great Dharma is worthy of veneration, then beneath the dharma robes, a monk has no ritual of showing respect to the laity. The Emperor remained unperturbed and ceased his inquiry.
Later, he said to his ministers, "I believed there was no one among the monks; yet yesterday at the Southern Suburb sacrifice, it turned out there was indeed such a person.

He then issued an edict to Xichanding Temple to provide a vegetarian feast for all the monks in the capital. From this point on, the debate regarding the character *jing* (to respect) came to an end (*Hongming ji*).
Shi Dazhi submitted a memorial, wishing that the Emperor would cause the Three Jewels to flourish and manifest. Thereupon, [the Emperor] lit a single...
[The character] "bi" (arm) is used to report [the date]. On the first day of the eleventh month, Dharma Master Puan passed away. The Master exhibited many miraculous traces.

There was a bandit who sought to shoot the Master with a crossbow, but his hand remained drawn and would not relax; his tongue remained locked for an entire night. Only after the assembly had him perform repentance did it release.
Furthermore, Zhang Hui stole an oil jar, but as if bound by something, he could not move it. Only after the assembly offered repentance and apologies on his behalf was he freed.
Furthermore, Cheng Hui was a believer in the Dharma. Two nights after his death, as he was about to be encoffined, he called out several times;

he was then able to sit up immediately and lived for another twenty-odd years. Also, an old woman from Baicun had been mute for one hundred days, but upon seeing Dao’an come to welcome her, she immediately regained the ability to speak.
Moreover, in the village beside the stupa, three pigs were tied up and were about to be slaughtered when Dao’an arrived.
He was unable to redeem it, and the village deity (she) became blind. An then cut flesh from his own thigh, saying, "This is merely flesh, just like that.
When the villagers heard and saw this, they released the pig all at once. Once the pig was freed, it circled An and prostrated itself before him.
Consequently, within fifty li to the southwest of the outskirts, chickens and pigs ceased to breed. His evocation of compassion and kindness was always of this nature. (From the *Benzhuan*)
In this month, Shi Zhixing struck the bell and achieved a spiritual resonance.

A deceased person appeared in a dream to his wife and said, "I was currently undergoing the sufferings of hell, but now, thanks to the monk Zhixing striking the bell, its sound has shaken the hells and I have attained liberation."
On the gengwu day (the sixth), the Emperor habitually had monks, nuns, Daoist priests, and female officials attend him; they were called the "Four Monasteries" (*Tongjian*).
○ An edict appointed the monk Huisheng as the Grand Lecturer. ○ In the seventh month, Yancong of the Translation Institute passed away at the age of fifty-four.
In the eighth month, an imperial edict summoned the Dharma Master Lingrun to the capital, where he was appointed as a Professor at the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu).
During this same month, the monk Huida passed away. Huida had previously restored more than three hundred old temples in the state of Chen.

Furthermore, when a great pestilence spread through the capital city of Yangdu, he established a Great Medicine Treasury to provide relief. During the Renshou era, he constructed a seven-story [pagoda] at Baitasi.
He built wooden pagodas. Furthermore, in various prefectures such as Poyang and Yuzhang, he saw temple towers and sacred images, all of which he encouraged others to construct at his initiative.
He also ascended Mount Lu to the Xilin Monastery to build a seven-bay multi-storied pavilion, vowing to use yellow *nán* wood.

Indeed, he was moved by divine response to find an entire valley consisting entirely of *nán* timber; as the logs were transported on rafts across rapids and eddies, not a single piece was lost. Later, when the pavilion began to lean, a wind blew it back into alignment.
[This is] correct. Furthermore, he went to Changsha to cast bells and create statues; those who offered gold feared only that he would not accept it.

In the seventh year, the *xingwei* (year of the Monkey), Shi Sengzhao first established Shentian Temple in Hu County and later lived in seclusion on Mount Qi. Emperor Wen ordered the Vice President of the Secretariat, Yang...
Fasu was sent with an imperial decree to summon him, but Huizhao did not come forth. The Emperor then issued a second decree; Fasū brought fragrant oil as an offering of deep reverence.
Fasū subsequently donated his gold and silk to expand the temple and its pagodas, yet Huizhao would not accept them. That year, he manifested parinirvāṇa at the age of eighty-three.

From the time he received full ordination until more than sixty summer retreats had passed, he never changed his three robes; though they were repeatedly mended and patched, he continued to wear and maintain them.

**Wuli (Biography)** Shi Senglang (also known as Falang) lived at the end of the Chen dynasty and the beginning of the Sui. He traveled through the regions of Jiang and Ling, where he constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He kept a monkey and a dog, which always followed him wherever he went. At times they would perform the "tortoise-withdrawal," with their heads, hands, and feet all retracted so that they were invisible.
Furthermore, there was once when he sat in a boat; the monkey and dog remained docile by his side as the boat drifted upstream against the current.
A *bhikṣuṇī* was possessed by a ghost and was able to preach the sutras. She scolded a young maidservant named Lang, whereupon the *bhikṣuṇī* ran before Lang and stood there, unable to move.
Only after one hundred days did she return to her original nature. Her spiritual manifestations were not limited to this single instance; she passed away at the end of the Daye period (Biography).
The monk Zhizao of Mount Tai went to Zhuo Commandery to visit the Emperor. The Emperor bestowed gifts upon him, and he returned to the mountain. In total, he made eight such trips.
He had an audience with the Son of Heaven, and was provided with abundant supplies. In the seventh month, Shi Zhen-guan of Tiantzhu Monastery in Hangzhou passed away while sitting upright.
Initially, Hong Yan had prophesied of him: "High cheekbones indicate great wisdom; white ears signify renown.
I possess four excellences, while you possess eight abilities—namely, exegesis, guidance, calligraphy, poetry, discernment of countenances, phonology, and chess."

In the eighth year, on the *renshen* day, the Emperor established two stupas for the two Emperors at the Western Capital. He issued an edict to Huisheng to deliver the śarīra relics to be interred at the sites of the stupas.
On this occasion, the Mahāyāna master and Tripiṭaka scholar Sengcan passed away. At that time, the monk Zhixian was able to know [the future].

Regarding distant events: whenever there was a place of suffering, he would invariably go there to rescue and deliver those in need. Shi Zhuanming came to Luoyang this year and announced that bandits were rising up;
the Emperor ordered him to be detained. The following year, when the wicked and cruel filled the land, his words were proven correct, and an imperial edict was issued to release him.
Later, when the usurper Zheng Shichong was doubly devoted to his faith, he stopped at the capital in the west in the third year of Wude, knowing that Zheng was about to be defeated.
Emperor Gaozu of Tang treated him with great ceremony and respect, yet his ultimate end remains unknown. At that time, the Dharma Master Daoji’s propagation of the Dharma flourished greatly.
Previously, the śramaṇa Baozheng had begun the construction of a hundred-foot Maitreya statue at Pujiao Temple.
When Wangu (Wang Gong) had completed but one-tenth of the work, he passed away. Zhongqing took up the succession. He dreamed of two lions that successively spat out bright pearls;

this was a prophecy that his material offerings would be inexhaustible. Zhongqing then spent ten years in reconstruction, and when the carving and painting were both finished, the clergy and laity rejoiced.
By the end of the Sui dynasty, Yao Su, the Governor of Hedong, proposed that śramaṇas should ascend the city walls to defend it against siege. However—

"Those who offer remonstrance shall be executed. Sengji then led Daoxun up the steps and remonstrated, saying: "The survival or ruin of this city depends on your strategy; the prosperity or decline of the age depends on your destiny.
How could it be achieved by three or five men of empty timidity? In the past, when the Han dynasty honored the Four Recluses, the world flourished in peace;
when the Wei state revered Gan Mu, the entire nation was well-governed. Now, you have detained these Buddhist practitioners..."

"To join the military service and turn against the natural order of Heaven to seek communion with spirits and deities—this I fear will bring about ill-omened portents. I pray you consider this deeply;
do not recklessly cast yourself down in a single day, only to become an object of derision for the world hereafter. Su Zhang stared straight at him with wide-open eyes and said, "How extraordinary!
How robust is this man's spirit and resolve? Thereupon, he left him unchallenged and went instead to visit Ji Chen.
He performed repentance rituals, yet Su was eventually killed by people from the city. Later, he passed away after accumulating [merit] for ten years of Right Contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
Three days before his death, the bell ceased to ring (according to his biography).

In the Guiyou year (the ninth year), Shi Daobian was thoroughly versed in the classics and histories and specialized in the arts of calculation. He observed the topography of the mountain temple and fully understood its signs of prosperity and decline.

Furthermore, he visited various tombs and likewise predicted their fortunes and misfortunes. A layman requested that he design a burial site for him; Daobian traversed the mountain and pointed out a specific location.
He said, "In this location, it is suitable for establishing a tomb; it will provide sufficient food and abundant wealth. At a depth of three feet, one will obtain a sheng of millet;

at a further depth of ten feet, one will obtain stones of five colors. When they dug there, they indeed obtained these things, and thus proceeded to perform the divination for burial. For a long time, the finds remained plentiful.

Furthermore, he was able to calculate celestial degrees and predicted that when the moon approached the lunar mansion of Jing (the Well), people should prepare for floods. Indeed, the Han River swelled greatly, and Xiangyi was flooded.
His foresight regarding his imminent death was as clear as this. *Śramaṇa Huigong* parted from *Huiliang* of the same monastery thirty years earlier.
Liang once asked him, "Have you attained nothingness? Gong replied, "By nature I am dull and have no understanding."
Huiyuan said, "Could you not recite a single scripture? Huigong replied, "I can only recite one scroll of the *Avalokiteśvara Pumenpin*.
Huiyuan said, "I am able to recite them all. Huigong said, "Do not be dismissive; I shall recite it once for you. Huiyuan laughed and said:
"I have lectured on this many times," [Hui]yuan said. "Was it merely to startle people at first? Huigong replied, "I only wished for you to listen with a sincere heart.

Thereupon, he established the ritual altar and ascended the high seat. As soon as he began to speak, a wondrous fragrance filled the room; when the text was entered, the sound of music shook the void, and flowers rained down, covering the ground.
When the sutra concluded, the flowers and music finally ceased. Huiyuan wept and prostrated himself in gratitude (from his *Biography*).
In the Jiashu year (the tenth year), the divine monk Faxi’s speech and silence were inconsistent; yet all of these served as omens of good or ill fortune. Emperor Yang visited Weiyang.

Hearing of his eccentricities, the Emperor summoned him. One day, he wandered about the palace searching for a sheep’s head; the Emperor loathed this and handed him over to the Minister of Justice (Tingwei).

His confinement was extremely strict, yet Huiji begged in the marketplace as if nothing were amiss, eating and drinking with complete composure. When the officials reported this, the Emperor ordered the door opened to inspect him.
He saw only a *kāṣāya* robe covering golden bones, all of which were linked together by chains. He immediately informed the Emperor, who then issued an edict.
The clay was scented mud, and the figure was modeled using the "bones" of trees. That evening, Xī suddenly rose from the clay image and spoke and laughed as usual.

He then released [the monk] from his confinement. It was only when Emperor Yang was assassinated at Jiangdu that [the monk] finally realized this was the fulfillment of Xī’s earlier request for a sheep’s head.
Later, Xī suddenly fell ill; he placed himself upon a wooden frame and had burning coals lit beneath it to roast him. After several days, half of his body was red.
When his body decayed, he entered nirvana and was buried at Xiangshan Temple. Several years later, someone returning from Hainan saw that Huixi was unharmed;
when the man opened the tomb to look inside, there was only an empty coffin. Calculating by this time, Huixi had already lived for over three hundred years.
On the day of Yi-hai (the eleventh), Shi Zhenhui passed away.
Initially, at Magu in Pufan, he first established a hermitage for the practice of dhyāna. At the end of the Renshou era, he was summoned to reside at Xiyan Temple.

At the beginning of the Daye era, he ceased eating grain and subsisted on yellow horseradish (*glehnia*). In the tenth month of that year, he entered nirvana; at the time of his death, there was a wondrous fragrance.

A lotus flower came to welcome him, saying, "I have been born in the Pure Land" (from his *Benzhuan*). Shi Fǎ'ān met the Prince of Jìn during the Kāiyuáng era and subsequently resided at Huìrì Monastery.
Whenever the Prince traveled, Fǎ'ān would invariably accompany him. When the Prince visited Mount Taishān, he looked around but found no water;

Fǎ'ān pierced the rock with a knife, causing a spring to gush forth for their use. Whenever they were about to encounter a calamity, Fǎ'ān would always anticipate it and take precautions, ensuring that none occurred.

His influence was so great that at the very beginning of his great enterprise, the Emperor held him in the highest esteem. His majesty overwhelmed princes and dukes, all of whom bowed their knees upon meeting him.
The attendants and the Three Guards served him as if he were a deity. In the spring of that year, he passed away without illness at the age of ninety-eight (from the *Benzhuan*).

As for Shi Daoxun, his Dharma path flourished greatly, and both kings and ministers turned to him with reverence. Once, while staying overnight at a frontier pass, there was a household there with five sons.
He saw that Xun’s horse was vigorous and wished to steal it for himself. Seeing dozens of stalwart men surrounding him, the crowd retreated.

He went back and forth, seeing them again and again, until the fifth watch when dawn broke; not a single person was to be seen. Realizing this was a divine response, he prostrated himself and returned to repent.
(Bingzi, 12th year) Shi Hui Cheng, at the Eastern Capital, depicted a one-zhang-six-foot sandalwood image of the Buddha from the kingdom of Kucha; it repeatedly manifested auspicious omens.
Shi Hui Xiang, who was diligent in both meditation and lecturing, obtained a śarīra while eating; unable to identify it, he discarded it on the ground.

The [relic] would immediately return to his mouth; suspecting it was the true body, he struck the bell to announce it to the assembly. It did not shatter even when struck with a mallet upon a block, and it emitted light of five colors.
Far and near, all marveled at this wonder. Butchers and hunters changed their vocations, and there were no meat stalls in the market.

Nevertheless, the auspicious day [of the relic's appearance] lasted for only one meal, and the master’s height was eight chi; everyone looked up to him in awe (from the *Benzhuan*). ○ Dharma Master Zhiyue initially served Zhizhe and attained a profound understanding.

Regarding the Chan master Fashi: he once recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, whereupon the water in his pitcher filled itself. When Zhiyi withdrew from public view, the assembly on Mount Tiantai entrusted him with their affairs in Yue for twenty years.
During this time, he was diligent and gentle in his virtuous guidance; the fourfold assembly looked up to him with devotion.

Every year on the anniversary of the Master’s passing, imperial edicts were issued to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks, and Fashi used his own clothing and funds to support these great offerings. In the eleventh month of that year, he passed away lying on his right side.
Dingchou (the thirteenth year; the eleventh month marked the beginning of the first year of Yining under Emperor Gong).
In this year, Wengzhongzi Wang Tong passed away. Tong once composed the *Zhongshuo*, in which the "Duke of Zhou" chapter states:

"The flourishing of the Odes and Documents led to the destruction of the Qin dynasty; this was not the fault of Confucius. The growth of abstruse emptiness led to the chaos of the Jin house; this was not the fault of Laozi."
This was the fault of Zhuangzi. That the state of Liang perished despite his cultivation of fasting and purification was not the fault of Śākyamuni.
Does the *I Ching* not say: "If it is not the right person, the Way will not manifest"? Someone asked: "Is the Buddha a sage?
Furthermore, observing the *Huangji Dangyi*, one sees that the Three Teachings are thus one. ○ The Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, arrived at Ji...
In the province, he encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city. Sengzu instructed the people of the city to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, when the rebel hosts looked toward the city, they saw divine soldiers thereupon withdrawing together. (Wudeng Huiyuan) ○ Shi Fajin initially resided in Yizhou.
He practiced the meditation on water (*āp-kṛtsnāyatana*). His family members saw clear water on his rope bed and threw two stones into it.

That evening, Sengjin felt pain in his back. His family said, "We previously threw stones into the water. Jin ordered them to remove them the next day. When he entered into meditation at dawn, his family again saw the clear water;
they then removed the stones, and his ailment was immediately cured. From then on, he devoted himself to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Eighty years after he left this mountain, during the Kaihuang era, Prince Xiu of Shu governed Yizhou. His consort suffered from a heart and abdominal ailment that no treatment could alleviate.

The Prince sent messengers twice to the mountain to summon the various masters; Master Jin refused to go. The Prince became greatly enraged and entered the mountain himself, intending to inflict punishment upon him with his own hands.
Upon seeing Jin approach, he was unconsciously struck with cold sweat. The Prince then earnestly entreated him to travel [to the capital], and Jin complied.
The King traveled two days ahead and arrived on the following day. He went directly into the Queen’s quarters and saw that Jin was perspiring; immediately thereafter, Jin became well.
Jin then took his leave and returned to the mountain. The King and the Queen observed that Jin’s feet were four or five inches above the ground.
In the first month of that year, he passed away.

Wu-yin (the fourteenth year of Taiye); [Emperor] Gong (the second year of Yining); [Prince] Yue (also changed the era name to Huangtaiyuan); [May, the Tang dynasty] (changed the era name to Wudeyuan).
Dhamagupta, from his initial translation of scriptures until this point, produced a total of nine works in forty-six fascicles.
All are clear in both style and meaning and are currently in circulation in the world (*Shijiaolu*). ○ Shi Minggong resided at Huishan Temple in Zhengzhou. His...

His strength was like that of a deity. Once, while traveling by mountain, he saw a tiger and a pig engaged in combat. As the pig gradually grew weaker, Senggong said to the tiger, "You may release it and let it go.
The tiger refused to comply. Senggong seized the tiger’s head with one hand and gripped its tail with the other, hurling it down the mountainside.
Furthermore, he placed a monk’s robe beneath a foundation pillar. When the monks marveled at this, Senggong smiled and supported the pillar with his hands to retrieve the robe.

Later, when bandits rose up to plunder and reached that monastery, they ordered the temple to prepare food for dozens of large pigs. Senggong invited the bandits to eat; the bandits yielded to him, saying he should go first.
Senggong then took several dozen steamed buns and placed them before the pigs to feed them. In an instant, they were all consumed. The bandit host was struck with awe and submitted.

He was respectfully summoned to serve as a patron (*dānapati*) for the protection of the monastery, and the bandits consented. Consequently, when the armies of the Sui and Tang contended, his territory remained free from the coming and going of marauders;
this was due to the power of [Fajing] Gong’s efforts (from his *Benzhuan*). In the fifth month, Emperor Gong of the Sui abdicated the throne to the Prince of Tang.
During the thirty-seven years of the two reigns of the Sui, more than twenty monastics and laypeople translated scriptures and treatises, producing six hundred works in total.
Volume Thirty-Six.
*The Comprehensive Mirror of the Buddhas and Sages through Successive Dynasties* (Lìdài biānián shìshì tōngjiàn), Volume Six.
*The Comprehensive Mirror of the Buddhas and Sages through Successive Dynasties*, Volume Seven.
Compiled by Shi Benjue of Yian at Kuoshan in Song;
collated by the layman Chan-ti Bi Xizhi of the Ming dynasty.
The lineage of the Li clan of Dū (Cháng'ān) was transmitted through twenty-one patriarchs, totaling two hundred [years].
Ninety years. He established his capital at Houliang (Later Liang).
Emperor Taowu Shendiao Gaozu (Yuan), Wuyin (the first year of Wude):
[Ruled over] Sui (Prince Tong of Yue), Wei (Li Mi), Xia (Dou Jiande), Liang (Xiao Xian), Liang (Li Gui), Qin (Xue Ju), Dingyang (Liu Wuzhou), and Wu.
(Li Shutong) & (Chu) (Lin Shihong). In the fifth month, the High Ancestor ascended the throne.
He then established a universal *dharma-śālā* upon the main thoroughfare south of the Zhuque Gate and convened a Great Unrestricted Assembly (*wu-zhe da-hui*).
In the sixth month, he commanded sixty-nine monks and sixty-nine Daoists each to [perform rites] in the Taiji Hall. Seven...
