Daily Practice of the Way. On the day of dispersing the assembly, a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks was provided (*Bianzheng lun*). At the beginning of the Imperial destiny, the course of Heaven was still precarious:
Xue Ju pointed his forces directly at Bing and Qi, while Wang Chong massed his armored troops at the Yellow and Luo Rivers; as for the remaining subordinate commanders...

Like bees flying away or hedgehogs bristling up, the state maintained its fundamental principles and resolved to eliminate [the Buddhist clergy]. Nevertheless, his reverence for Buddhism remained ever more profound.
Although in his final years he acceded to the request of Fu Yi and issued an edict for the purge of the monastic community, his true intent was actually to protect and sustain it.
Upon the outbreak of the Xuanbu (Jiancheng) rebellion, he immediately suspended that edict; how could this have caused any harm? (From the *Neidian lu*).
Ji-mao (the second year of Wude): [Zheng] (Wang Shichong killed Tong and usurped the throne); [Xia]; [Liang]; [Liang]; [Tang destroyed them]; [King of Liang] (Li Shidu); [Dingyang]; [Wu]; [Chu].
The Fourth Patriarch, Great Master Daoxin, preached the Dharma at Luochuan (*Tongji*). ○ Zheng Yushi Zheng Ting resigned his office to become a monk.
Wang Shichong was enraged and executed him. His poem at the moment of death says: "Illusory birth returns to illusory extinction; the great illusion cannot..."
The body passed away. His mind remained at rest in its own place; though one sought him, no person was to be found (from the *Monastic Biographies*).

In the Gengchen year (the third year of Wude), [Emperor] Zheng (Xia) [of Liang], [the Prince of] Liang, [Mie Dingyang], [Wu], and [Chu]—at the beginning of his reign, the Emperor first founded Lingshan Temple (the epitaph was composed by Li Baiyao, the Attendant Gentleman).
He also founded Huichang Temple and Shengye Temple, as well as Cizhi Temple.
He established the Si Temple, the Zhenguo Temple, and the Jixian Nunnery; he commissioned the carving of statues and the transcription of scriptures to fully cultivate pure merit.

Furthermore, he donated his former residence to establish the Xingsheng Temple, and the Yixing Temple was built in Bingzhou; both feature magnificent halls and pavilions, with sacred images and ritual implements displayed in solemn splendor.
Moreover, for Emperor Taizu Yuanhuang and Empress Dowager Yuanzhen, he commissioned three life-sized sandalwood statues at the Ci... [Temple].

*Beisi gongyang* (Offerings at the Compassionate Temple), from the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing Orthodoxy). The Emperor appointed ten Great Virtues (*daide*) to oversee and lead the monks and nuns.
In the sixth month of the Xinsi year (the fourth year of Wude), following the subjugation of Zheng, Xia, Liang, the King of Liang, Wu, and Chu, there was Fu Yi, Director of the Bureau of Astronomy.
Previously, as a follower of the Yellow Turbans, he harbored deep animosity toward the Buddha-dharma and submitted a memorial proposing the abolition of the Buddhist religion.

The memorial contained eleven points, stating: "The interpretation of the scriptures is preposterous and false; its words are demonic and its matters obscure. It harms the state and ruins families, and I have never heard of it benefiting the world.
I request that the heterodox teachings of the 'Hu' (Buddha) be sent back to India. Let all śramaṇas be released to return to their native lands.
Only then will simplicity and sincerity be restored, and the transformations of Li [Laozi] and Kong [Confucius] will prevail. Although the Emperor believed in Buddhism, he lacked the resolve to act.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, inquiring: "In discarding the hair and beard of one's parents and casting off the ceremonial robes of sovereign and subject, what benefit is there?
We pray you will explain this. Śramaṇa Fali replied: "I, Lin, have heard that the Ultimate Way transcends words; how could the Nine Schools of thought discern it? The Dharma-body is formless;
it is not something that can be expounded by the Ten Wings [of the *Yi Jing*]. Yet, the four realms of rebirth are vast and boundless, drifting and sinking in suffering."

In the ocean of desire, the beings of the three realms wriggle about, tumbling down the mountains of heterodoxy; the sons of men are deluded and burn themselves, while ordinary folk drown and cannot emerge.
For their sake, the Great Sage appeared in the world, and the Perfected One descended with his spiritual power, thereby opening the gate of liberation.
They show them the path of peace and security. Those of the Central Heavenly King’s lineage renounce affection and leave the household life;
the noble youth of the Eastern Lands weary of glory and splendor enter the Way. Thus, they alter their appearance to fulfill their resolve, casting aside their fine hair and handsome features.

They transform worldly conventions to accord with the Way; thus, they discard the ornate robes of ruler and subject. Although outwardly they lack the means to serve their parents, they inwardly cherish filial piety;
although their rites differ from those used to serve a sovereign, their hearts retain that sense of gratitude. Their grace extends to both enemies and kin, thereby achieving great harmony;

its blessings reach both the hidden and the manifest—how could it be restricted by minor deviations? For those of superior intelligence, following the Buddha’s words brings benefit; for ordinary people of inferior capacity...
This is contrary to the holy teachings and thus constitutes a detriment; such is the general outline of the matter. Although the memorial submitted by Mr.

Fu was not acted upon by the authorities, Sengyi then made numerous copies of his petition and circulated them far and wide. Senglin subsequently composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresy) in two fascicles to counter Fu’s arguments, thoroughly exposing all their fallacies.
Both the court and the commonalty recited it with acclaim. Senglin further submitted a memorial to the Crown Prince and the various princes.
The high ministers, dukes, and marquises [were thus influenced]. Consequently, the memorial submitted by Yi was subsequently shelved (*Shijiao lu*).
On the *Renwu* day (the fifth year of Wude), [the states of] Liang, Chu, Handong (Liu Heitai), and Wu were extinguished.

The monk Fayu constantly practiced meditative contemplation and recited the spells of the Seven Buddhas; his acts of rescue and protection were all efficacious, such that the spirits of the local shrines and temples [all responded].

Senggui received the precepts; at this point, he passed away (according to his biography). ○ Li Da'an was killed, but in a dream, a Buddha image rubbed his sword wound, and he immediately regained life (from the *Zhu lin*).
Guiwei (the sixth year of Wude): [Han] Gao Dao and [Wu] Du Fuwei.
At that time, the monk Huilin’s divinations were frequently accurate. He regularly made offerings to a clay statue, which suddenly grew thirty-six whiskers.
Once, he used incantations to cure a person’s illness; the patient sent his daughter to offer a skirt as a gift, but the girl kept the garment and returned the payment.
Falin saw her from afar and said, "Just bring me your skirt; I do not want money. The woman was struck with wonder at his sanctity (as recorded in the *Monk Biographies*).
Jia-shen (the seventh year of Wude): [The Han is extinguished]... [The Wu is extinguished]... [The empire is unified].
The Fourth Patriarch moved his residence to Pòtóu Mountain in Huàixī and took the Fifth Patriarch, Hóngrěn, as a novice monk. Initially, there was a man of the Way.
While planting pine trees on the western mountains of Qizhou, the Fourth Patriarch said, "I wish to transmit the Dharma, but you have already reached an advanced age.
If you come again, I shall still wait for you. The practitioner agreed and went to Huangmei County, where he was conceived by a woman of the Zhou family.
When the woman was first washing clothes by the stream, the practitioner told her he wished to stay with her, and she gave her consent.
The mother conceived and returned home; her parents, loathing her, cast her out. Having no place to go, the woman worked as a hired spinner in the village.
After some time, she gave birth to a son. Considering him an ill omen, she threw him into the water.

The next day, she saw him swimming upstream against the current, so she took him up and raised him. When he was seven years old, the Fourth Patriarch encountered him on the road and, being pleased, questioned him.

[The Master] asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "I do have a surname, but it is not an ordinary surname. [The Master] asked, "What is this surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). [The Master] asked, "Do you have no surname at all?
He replied, "Because its nature is empty (*śūnyatā*). The Patriarch knew that he was not deluded; he then sought him out from his mother and took him back to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*).
(Wudeng Huiyuan) When Chan Master Sengding passed away, the Master had previously suffered from a wind-epidemic illness. He sat in meditation for several years. [...]
His suffering suddenly vanished. His body and head became perfectly pure, and his eyebrows grew several inches long, thus forming extraordinary marks (as recorded in his biography).

In the second month of the year Wuyou (the eighth year of Wude), the Emperor performed the ritual of *xièdiàn* at the National Academy (*guóxué táng*). He established three seats to represent the three schools of thought and summoned three scholars of these teachings.
The assembly gathered like clouds. Shi Hui-cheng ascended the seat and widely spread the net of doctrine; the king and his ministers were delighted and submitted.

Furthermore, a Daoist said, "The Dao can give birth to the Buddha, and the Buddha is perfected through the Dao. Hui-cheng replied, "The Buddha appeared at the beginning of the Zhou dynasty, while Lao Dan was born at the end of the Zhou.
They were separated by some thirty kings and more than three hundred years. How could there have been a Buddha during the time of King Zhao, yet you seek to trace [the origin] back to [Lao] Jing?"
The King then said, "How extraordinary! The Daoist replied, "In the *Lingbao Jing*, it is stated that the Supreme Great Dao was born before heaven and earth;
it mists and billows within the vast void and shines brilliantly above the Jade Purity (*Yuqing*). This is the Teacher of the Buddha.

The Emperor said, "Before the Five Emperors, we had never heard of the Way of the Celestial Honored One (*Tianzun*). Only at the end of the Three Kings did the name Lao Dan first appear. During the reign of Emperor Jing of Han..."
Having returned, he began to promote the study of the Way, investigating the present and scrutinizing antiquity. As for who this "Way" is:
according to the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*), "One Yin and one Yang are called the Way. This is the Way of principle and number; how could it give birth to a Buddha?

How could there be one who wears a golden crown on his head, a saffron robe upon his body, with purple hair hanging down from his temples, holding a jade scepter in his hand, bearing the title "Celestial Honored One," and dwelling atop Mount Dalaru?
"It alone is called the Great Way (Daodao). It governs within the Jade Capital (Yujing), yet it is not detailed in the mountains or seas, nor recorded in the classics or histories.
That 'Great Luo' is already a claim of non-existence; that 'Jade Capital' is fundamentally a tale of what never was. This is an extreme error. Having finished speaking, he descended from his seat.
The entire court turned their eyes toward him, and the assembly of Daoist priests withdrew in silence. (From the *Jiushi* and the *Sengzhuan*)
In the Bingxu year (the ninth year of Wude),
the Fu family, dissatisfied with the destruction of the Buddha [statue], again secretly slandered him and instigated the Yellow Turbans to serve as their faction.
The Daoist Li Zhongqing submitted the "Treatise on the Ten Differences and Nine Delusions," and the Daoist Liu Jinxi submitted the "Treatise on Manifesting the Correct.
Both disparaged the Buddha and the sages, thereby deluding the Emperor's mind. Upon this, Fang Yi successively submitted seven memorials requesting the abolition of the Śākya [Buddhist] religion.
The Emperor was advanced in years and was characterized by indecisiveness and lack of resolve; in the fourth month, he entrusted these memorials to the various ministers for deliberation.
In deliberation, the ministers all stated: "The Buddha-dharma has flourished since successive reigns; it promotes good and restrains evil, providing invisible assistance to the state.
It is unreasonable to abolish it. Only Zhang Daoyuan, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stables, sided with Li Yi, claiming that his proposal was reasonable.
Prime Minister Xiao Yu rebuked Yi in court, saying: "The Buddha is a sage. For Yi to propose such a matter is to act contrary to the Way of the Sage. I request—"

He ordered that severe punishment be imposed upon Yu. Wang Yi said, "Ritual is rooted in serving one's parents. The Buddha left the city to renounce the world, fleeing in order to turn his back on his father.
Yu was not born from an empty mulberry tree, yet he has returned to revere a teaching that lacks a father. I have heard that those who are not filial have no kin; this applies precisely to Yu.
Yu joined his palms and said, "Hell is established exactly for people such as this" (Tang History). The Emperor then [repeated his command].

There is truly a profound reason for both the will of Heaven and human affairs.

He understood transformation; his words were grand and awe-inspiring. He removed delusion and severed the dust of the world; his path was pure and remote, difficult to tread upon.

Unless one refines their essence to examine the true and the false, and contemplates deeply to perceive suffering and emptiness, there is no way to establish a root of faith as firm as rock, nor can one depart from [the mundane].
Regarding the doubts concerning this matter, some have said: "The Three Kings had no Buddha yet their reigns were long; the Two Shi [dynasties] had monks yet their governance was tyrannical.

The decline of transformation stems from the worship of the Buddha; the benefit of the state lies in the abolition of the monks. Such views clarify only partial perspectives and have not yet presented the comprehensive principle.

A broad examination of rise and fall sufficiently proves the nature of superficiality and falsehood. Why is this so? Those who brought about the ruin of Qin did so during the reign of Hu Hai, when there was no Buddha and the empire collapsed like crumbling earth.

Those who caused its flourishing were the world of monks during the era of Emperor Ming of Han, when the state was well-governed. When the Zhou dynasty abolished Buddhist temples, the mandate of Heaven for Yuan did not endure;

whereas when the Sui dynasty propagated the teachings of Śākyamuni, the reign of Kaishuang remained free from peril. Whether a dynasty thrives or declines depends upon the administration of its policies; it is not determined by the presence or absence of Buddhism.

To attribute disorder to the various officials and place the blame upon the Buddhists and monks is truly not a comprehensive argument. Furthermore, the Buddha merely propagates goodness; he does not encourage evil among his subjects.
His precepts are fundamentally for the prevention of wrongdoing; how could they harm the governance of the family or the state?

If every person were to maintain goodness and every household were to uphold the precepts, how could punishments be widespread, and how could calamities and rebellions arise? Though a qíjì horse is magnificent, it is of no use if one does not ride it.
Without this, one cannot travel far. Though medicinal herbs and tonics may be abundant, how can they cure an illness if they have not yet been ingested?
That Fu Jian lost his army was not because Dao’an lacked wisdom; that the Shi clan rose to commit atrocities was certainly not because the Buddha was unkind.

It is simply that [people] bring about violence and chaos by violating [the teachings], never by following them. Viewed from this perspective, it is sufficiently clear. One merely believes according to what one hears.
When it arises, doubt is extinguished through understanding. All those who have been negligent, disparaging, or disrespectful do so because their investigation has not reached its conclusion;

were they to explore the profound and seek out the hidden, they would surely all come to possess deep faith and sincere reverence. I have therefore respectfully composed three treatises: "Discerning Delusions" is the first.

The merits and virtues of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius find no adequate praise in the *Canons* and *Annals*; they were truly revered by distant barbarians rather than being the teachers and scholars of the Central Kingdom.

Beginning with the arrival of Kāśyapa Mātanga in the Han and the travels of Zhu Fashen (Senghui) to Wu, the śarīra relics were manifested in the southern lands and *caityas* (zhāotí) were erected in the eastern capital.

Wherein lies its merit and benefit? Why is its veneration so abundant? It is not equal to the act of melting down images and halting further casting; [the value] of the currency... can [be compared].

Desiring to go to the imperial palace to offer my humble loyalty, I submit this memorial to present this plan, believing it to be truly capable of benefiting the state and the people.
"What do you think of this, my friend? The loyal and upright gentleman replied, "How can such words be considered excessive?
In the past, I was devoted to the groves of Confucian scholars and applied my mind to the gardens of literature; in this regard, my discourse largely coincides with yours.

Yet, because I heard the Dharma so late, I relied upon your guidance to dispel my delusions. Fortunately, I had not yet traveled far astray. If you would examine this extensively and deliberate deeply..."

I shall likewise repent my delusions and know how to return [to the truth]. I have heard that there was a certain Mr. Fu, the Grand Historian (Taishi Ling), whose confusion was even greater than my own former delusions.
I request that you examine Mr. Fu’s confused words in order to release your misguided attachments. Mr.

Fu claimed that the Buddha-dharma originally originated from the Western barbarians (Xihu) and should not be venerated in the Middle Kingdom. Formerly, I shared this same delusion; now I have awakened to it.
This is not so. Now, Youyu came from the Western Rong, yet he assisted Duke Mu of Qin in establishing his great enterprise;

Why must one insist on selecting those of the same customs while discarding those from different regions? A teacher is honored for the greatness of their Way; it does not depend on...
In both [traditions], the Dharma takes excellence through goodness as its standard; it does not take distance—whether near or far—as its measure.

As for regarding benevolence as beautiful and removing desire as lofty, thereby refraining from the lingering calamities of accumulated evil and encouraging the performance of good to seek blessings—this is what all a hundred schools have in common.
The Nine Classics cannot be superseded; yet they are narrow and shallow rather than profound and ultimate, cramped and lacking in comprehensiveness rather than universal and expansive.

As for extending one’s own self to others, how can this compare to the magnanimity of the Buddha? As for discerning the root by observing the branches, how can this compare to the far-reaching insight of the Buddha?
In its exhortation to good and its reprimand of evil, how can it compare to the vastness of the Buddha’s teaching?

In its elucidation of emptiness and its analysis of existence, how can it compare to the profundity of the Buddha’s teaching? Viewed from this perspective, its Way is subtle and marvelous; the virtue of the Sage is unsurpassed.
How could one, born in a foreign land, disparage its Way, or having come from a distant region, cast away its treasure? Indeed, that which transcends all others—
A steed is not merely a product of the central provinces; it is a treasure of many ages. A pearl need not be a thing of China alone;

when the Han sought famous horses from the Western Regions and the Wei dynasty gathered luminous pearls from the South Seas, these objects, though produced in distant lands, were nonetheless treasured here.
If the Way originates in remote regions, how can it alone be discarded? It is like medicinal herbs originating among the tribes of the borderlands or the incantations of prohibitions.
Whether they originate from Hu or Yue, if they can eliminate depravity and dispel illness, how could one refuse to employ them simply because they come from afar?

Now, to extinguish the three poisons and realize non-action (wuwei) is a magnificent way to eliminate depravity; to remove the eight sufferings and attain eternal bliss is a profound way to dispel illness.

Within the thousandfold world-system, it resides in that realm and not in this region. Fu [Daoji] reckoned that because the *Shi* and *Shu* do not mention it, the *Sūtras* were unworthy of esteem;

Indeed, regarding the profound mysteries of celestial astronomy and calendrical phenomena, the extraordinary wonders of terrestrial geography and mountain rivers, and the diagnostic examination of the channels and acupuncture points—[all these are recorded therein].

Nevertheless, when one examines their auspicious and inauspicious outcomes, they manifest their signs at times; when one observes their practice and application, they are frequently effective.

Indeed, when human affairs had not yet flourished in ancient times, the Sages initiated practical innovations for later generations.

Regarding these meals, those used first are not necessarily the most precious, while the merit of fire-refining grain-foods, though established later, is not inferior.

As for their adoption or abandonment and their chronological priority, this is illogical. How can the prevalence or obscuration of a teaching be determined by whether the *Shi* and *Shu* were disseminated early and thus flourished, or whether the *Sūtra* arrived late and thus should decline?
People may have eaten coarse herbs as children yet have a surplus of fine meats as adults; how could one’s youth or age determine the value of what they consume?

To be a commoner in youth and to encounter the honors of a noble rank in old age—how can one claim that having first tasted the coarse herbs of poverty makes them superior in flavor to fine meats? Is it not the case that encountering noble rank late in life is less honorable than being a commoner? Thus, you have praised Laozi while disparaging Śākyamuni, and extolled the Daoist scriptures while rejecting Buddhism. The teachings are diverse, yet their essence is identical. To say they are different is to confuse the source; to say they are the same is to ignore their distinct forms. It is like the sun and the moon: though their light is one, their appearances differ. Or like the ocean and the rivers: though their waters are one, their courses diverge. Therefore, the sages did not compete for fame, nor did they vie for renown. Each followed his own nature and responded to the times.

If one were to judge the depth of their virtue by their outward status, or to measure the loftiness of their principles by their temporal fortune, then surely the humble commoner would surpass the noble official, and the early harvest of wild greens would exceed the late enjoyment of royal robes.

This is why I have come to understand that your former views were mistaken. As for the comparison between the two traditions, let us consider the following: [The text continues: ...if we examine the origins of these teachings, we find that both arose from a desire to save sentient beings. May you reconsider this, and recognize that the ultimate goal of both paths is the same: the liberation of all beings from the cycle of birth and death. Thus, I urge you to abandon your former prejudices and embrace the harmony of these great traditions. This is my sincere hope.
The essential nature of Śākyamuni and Laozi is one and not two. Both alike eliminate the burdens of worldly desire, and both manifest the principle of non-action (*wuwei*).
While the teachings of Laozi are clear yet not fully integrated, those of Śākyamuni reach their ultimate perfection through detailed exposition.

If the Way is indeed correct, then Buddhism is certainly the same in being correct and without error; if Buddhism were indeed incorrect, then the Way could likewise be considered incorrect and without truth. In principle, they are not contradictory.

There are differences between them. People harbor varying attitudes of attraction and aversion; they are as fickle in their joys and angers as the monkeys in the fable, and their love and fear resemble those of Duke Ye.

Furthermore, the principle of the endless conditions of birth and death, and the doctrine of imperishable retribution—these were first elucidated by the Śākya school and were not mentioned even by the Yellow Emperor or Laozi.
I do not know for what reason the present Daoist scriptures are similar to the Buddhist sūtras.

This treatise discusses the three periods of time to provide exhortation and admonition, emerging from the tracks of the nine schools of thought. If one speaks from what is witnessed with the eyes, then one is identical to the Buddha and equalizes his illumination.

if one takes another as a teacher, then that teacher must not be defamed. To praise the Way while slandering the Buddha—what a delusion this is!
How extreme it is! Fu [Xuan] claims that the Buddha is a demonic deity and that monasteries are sites of licentious sacrifice; this is the height of his failure to reflect.

A demon still fears a dog, and a ghost likewise dreads a cat; how then could they subdue the lofty mind of the Heavenly Emperor or crush the divine power of the celestial Māras?
Power. From the Eastern Han dynasty down to our Great Tang, every generation has revered it with awe, and the worthy have honored it with respect.

As for those who served as high ministers and officials—the crowning glory and ceremonial ornaments of human society—such as Wang Dao and Yu Liang, and those like Dai Kui and Xu Xun, they all directed their sentiments toward the realm between Heaven and man and set their traces beyond the mists and clouds;
yet all received the teachings with devotion and took refuge [in the Dharma], placing their minds therein.

Now, the Great Beings and eminent monks have contemplated the principles deeply; the enlightened sovereigns and worthy ministers have deliberated on the state to the utmost.

This is because there is nothing that can surpass the Way of one's nature. Mr. Fu’s contemplation was not as profound as that of the renowned monks, nor was his reflection as refined as that of the sages of old.

He followed only his own mind while turning his back on the Dharma; did he not recklessly sever his blessings and invite calamity? Moreover, the Great Awakened One exhausted his spiritual power to understand transformation;

Life is as constant as a flowing river yet flees like lightning; karma’s ground is vast and enduring, while the heavens stretch on for eternity. The three miserable realms are utterly treacherous and profound, and the four currents are boundless and vast.

It is fitting to transform misfortune into fortune; why then do you harbor thoughts of negligence and act with such madness? As the *Classic of Filial Piety* cites, one should not injure or damage one's body.
They mock the śramaṇas for shaving their hair and beards, claiming that they oppose the Way of the former kings and lose the principles of loyalty and filial piety.
In the past, I shared in this delusion; now I have realized it is not so. As for serving one's sovereign and parents and exhausting one’s devotion—

Though one may sacrifice their life, they are called benevolent; whereas to compromise loyalty and filial piety for the sake of mere survival is to preserve the body in vain, which is contrary to righteousness.

To cut flesh from one’s thigh or offer one’s liver causes injury that is exceedingly grave, yet to shave the beard or pluck out the hair causes damage that is but slight. One who establishes loyalty disregards their own life.
Those who debate the matter do not find fault with him. In seeking the Way, one does not spare even a single hair; why should this alone be considered an error?

Now, the teachings of the sages have diverse paths yet lead to the same destination. In the way of the gentleman, there are times when one may contravene conventional norms yet remain consistent with righteousness—Tai Bo was such a person.
He abandoned his filial duty of providing sustenance at home, feigned gathering medicinal herbs and did not return, and discarded the dress of the Middle Kingdom.
Chapter: [On the Practice of Shaving the Head]. To rely on shaving the head as a form of ornament is to oppose the Classics and subvert the Rites;

nothing is more extreme than this. Yet Confucius praised it as the ultimate virtue (*zhìdé*). Why is this? Although his outward conduct turned his back on his sovereign and parents, his heart remained loyal to the state;

although his physical appearance was altered according to the customs of the Hundred Yue peoples, his virtue was perfected through the three acts of yielding. Thus, although Taibo discarded the regulations for robes and caps, he suffered no loss of ultimate virtue. Therefore—
When a śramaṇa abandons the appearance of a scholar-official, what harm does this do to the sublime Way?

Although he changes his attire and alters his countenance—departing from the ordinary etiquette of a subject or son—he follows the Way with faith and devotes his heart to it, wishing for the many blessings of his sovereign and parents.

By exerting himself in body and mind to cultivate the manifold virtues of the renunciant life, he may leave behind his sovereign and father to extend profound merit through kalpas; how could this not be considered loyalty and filial piety?
That too is much. Fu says: "In the time of Zhao and the time of Liang, there were also monks who rebelled; how much more so now, when the number of monks and nuns who lack discipline is great?
This is a thoughtless statement. If one were to abolish the present monastic community because there were rebellious monks in the past, [it would be a grave error].
How can one take the existence of rebellious ministers and lawless commoners in antiquity as a reason to abandon the scholars and the masses of today?
That those in blue collars commit crimes does not stem from any failing of Confucius; that those in black robes commit wrongs is certainly not the fault of the World-Honored One.
It is simply because people are endowed with natures that are stubborn and ignorant, and fail to transform toward goodness; it is not that the scriptures open the source of rebellion and disorder.
Yet you allow yourself to be defiled by evil; for what reason do you direct anger toward the wicked and extend it to the virtuous? You blame the person and abandon the Dharma.

While a person may have a crime worthy of execution, the Dharma has no fault that warrants its abolition. One should merely prohibit what is improper in order to propagate the Dharma; one must not disparage the Way because of the person.
You should earnestly and sincerely believe in the Sublime Dharma, rather than frivolously forming factions among śramaṇas. As for weeding out the tares and weeds—
"To plant the seeds of auspicious growth and to sternly suppress the wicked and perverse so as to purify the Great Teaching—this is my deepest aspiration.
Fu says, "Before the arrival of the Buddha-dharma, people were all pure and harmonious, and there were no usurpers or rebels in the world. This, too, is a statement made without reflection.

Indeed, when the Nine Li tribes corrupted their virtue, was that not a time before the Buddha? When the Three Miao tribes rebelled against the mandate, was that not during a period after the Dharma existed? [This was under] Xia...
During the decline of the Yin dynasty, how could there have been such pure harmony? During the Spring and Autumn period, were there not usurpations and rebellions?
Yet the Buddha still cautioned against even a hair’s breadth of theft; how could he possibly encourage the chaos of usurpation and rebellion?
He also guarded against the competitiveness of a single word; how could he destroy the way of pure harmony? Indeed, the Buddha’s teaching exhorts ministers to loyalty and sons to filial piety.
They exhort the state toward order and the family toward harmony. They propagate goodness to demonstrate the bliss of heaven and punish transgression to reveal the suffering of hell.
It is not merely for the sake of a single character to offer praise, nor does it stop at the five punishments as a means of admonition.
To claim that this "injures harmony and fosters chaos" is surely an extreme form of slander. How could such a thing harm the Sun of the Buddha? It only causes one to sink further into [delusion].
"In the ocean of suffering, you treat it with such levity that you do not avoid it; how truly lamentable this is! Thereupon, the scholar was humbled in heart and abashed in countenance.
Rising from his seat, he apologized, saying: "I have followed worldly customs and, in my daily life, have habitually strayed from the Way to indulge myself.

I neglected what remains to be investigated and took pleasure only in what has already been recounted. I turned my back on the True Dharma with divergent arguments and accepted false words to share in the same error. Now that I have heard..."
The profound distance of the Buddha’s wisdom allows one to realize the loyalty and substance of the Śākya teachings.

With a sudden and expansive spiritual awakening, the underlying principles are laid bare, sufficient to sweep away delusions and dispel maladies. Although I followed what was erroneous in years past, I now request to return to the correct path today.
As for the essay "On Universal Destiny," that which the Buddha calls *karma* is what Confucianism calls "destiny" (*ming*). Destiny is...
Regarding karma: karma arises from the person; the person receives their destiny according to whether it is in adversity or prosperity, and destiny follows karma in its thickness or thinness.

To examine the beginning and trace the end, synthesizing these to reach a comprehensive understanding, is truly most striking and profound. The chapter "On Emptiness and Existence" extensively clarifies the sudden and gradual [teachings] and thoroughly analyzes form and emptiness, penetrating the subtle and the refined;
as the text is extensive, I have not been able to record it in full (*Hongming ji*).
In the *dinghai* year of Emperor Taizong (the first year of the Zhenguan era), since his accession to the throne,

the Emperor has reverently honored the gate of filial piety and extensively promoted beneficial works; opening the day of the four immeasurables, he has shone his light everywhere upon the world like that of Yao.
Clouds raise the winds of the Six Perfections, and the rains of Shun flow across the land. My intention is to forever empty the prisons and eternally extinguish the smoke of war.
May all living beings, however numerous, together return to benevolence and longevity; may the vast realm of the earth collectively uphold True Suchness (*tathatā*).

This spring, I have ordered the monks and nuns of the capital to perform seven days of ritual practice at their respective temples. All necessities for the offerings and meals shall be provided by the relevant authorities. Dispersed.

On the day of the fast, [the assembly] gathered together at Daxingshan Monastery (*Bianzheng lun*). The Emperor once said to Fu Yi: "The Way of the Buddha is subtle and profound; its sacred traces are worthy of emulation.
Furthermore, its retributions are manifest, having repeatedly been verified by evidence. Why is it that you alone do not realize its principles? Fu Yi replied:
"The Buddha was a clever charlatan from the West who deceived and dazzled his own land. When he entered China, he was a heterodox..."
There was a heterodox man who took the profound discourses of Zhuangzi and Laozi to embellish his own demonic and illusory words; these were of no benefit to the people and harmful to the state.
The Emperor loathed such talk and did not respond to him. From this time on, the man was never spoken of again for the rest of his life (*Jiushi Tangshi*).

The Emperor relinquished the old palace at Taihe in the Zhongnan Mountains to establish Longtian Monastery for the sake of the High Ancestor (later it became Cuiwei Monastery). The Emperor [regarded] the Buddha...

He was brilliant, broad-minded, and skilled in identifying methods of governance. By imperial decree, he was summoned to the inner palace and invited to ascend the imperial throne to partake of a meal.

Upon finishing his meal, he received an audience with the Emperor and extensively set forth the arts of governance employed by past sovereigns, while also presenting the ultimate principles of the Buddhist school, which take compassion and salvation as their core tenet. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
Consequently, an imperial edict was issued on the sixth day of the third month of that year, universally prohibiting slaughter.
It is said that later, temples were established at every military encampment (from his *Benzhuan*). In the eleventh month, the Indian Śīlabhadra (translated as Zuoming Zhishi;
also known as Pōpō, translated as Guangzhi) arrived at the capital. Previously, the Emperor had heard of his reputation and dispatched Prince Gaoping to invite him.
He was invited by Khan Yehu Guo (Khan Yehe). Upon his arrival, an imperial edict ordered him to reside at Xingshan Temple. Monastics and laypeople alike sought his counsel.

The Emperor summoned him for an audience to inquire about the Dharma; his responses were flawless. The Emperor bestowed upon him new garments from the palace treasury, as well as silk fabrics and other gifts.

From then on, he was provided with constant support and consolation, receiving treatment of a most exceptional kind (*Shijiao Lu*). As for Shi Zhi Xi: Initially, he received the Chan teachings of Zhi Zhe and resided at Fulong Mountain.
He practiced dhyāna and founded a monastery. Desiring to construct a sutra-platform, he was moved by the deity of Mount Xianglu, who offered him timber.
On the eighteenth day of the twelfth month of that year, he sat upright and passed away. At the time of his death, he instructed his disciples, saying:
"Since I began my practice of dhyāna forty-nine years ago, my back has never touched a bed" (as recorded in the *Benzhuan*).

In the third month of the wu-zi year (the second year of Zhenguan), the Emperor, reflecting upon his initial pacification of the empire, recalled that he had executed over a thousand people; fearing that their souls might remain obstructed within the dark chambers of the underworld, he [initiated this project].
He immediately bestowed his own imperial robes upon the monks of various temples and performed rites of repentance to dedicate merit for their advancement. He then issued an edict stating:

"Since I first established my righteous cause at the end of the Sui dynasty, my resolve has been to rescue those drowning in calamity. In my northern expeditions and eastern campaigns, every region I have directed toward has been pacified and subdued.

The number of those wounded and slain is beyond reckoning; those executed by my own hand approach one thousand. I reflect deeply that the holy teaching of the Tathāgata highly prizes benevolence and compassion and strictly prohibits..."

Regarding the categories of precepts, the taking of life is the most grave offense. Accordingly, the authorities were commanded to establish a seven-day, seven-night *zhāi* (fasting) and *xíngdào* (ritual practice) at all temples within the capital.
They were to offer sincere worship and repentance, donating all their clothing as alms (*dāna*).

It was hoped that through this, those in the three miserable realms might find liberation and the sufferings of ten thousand kalpas be extensively relieved. (From the *History of the Tang Dynasty*) *Dharma Master Zhiman*, Sui [Dynasty]...

When he first propagated the Dharma, many monastics and laypeople received the Bodhisattva precepts from him. He also traveled to the Yanduan River valley, where he practiced the methods of dhyāna under Chan Master Zàn.
When the Great Tang established its cause, he led his companions into the city; the High Ancestor then issued an edict to have them stay in the residence of Duke Zhixu.

In the first year of the Wude era, an imperial decree established the place where Man resided as Yixing Temple. In the third year, he was commanded to reside in the capital, where several hundred students received instruction from him.
He passed away in the sixth month of that same year. The Master’s pure virtue and lofty integrity are fully detailed in his original biography.

In the ninth month, the Emperor issued an edict stating: "The divine way establishes its teachings with compassion and kindness as primary; its profound transformation permeates all things, sustaining and nurturing the world."
The beginning of prosperity: I, the Emperor, reverently received the Great Treasure and have governed the common people with love. My heart of compassion extends to all things.

Therefore, I have sought divine favor from the unseen and invoked the aid of the manifest spirits, hoping that the nine merits would be properly ordered and the five blessings would respond accordingly.

Yet, as the severe frost fell prematurely and the autumn harvest failed to ripen, I reflect in silence upon my own meager virtue and cannot forget my shame and trepidation. Now, the hundred grains depend [upon the rains]...
The harvest is flourishing; as the myriad treasures are about to ripen, there is still fear that wind or rain may disrupt the season, leaving the nurtured fruits with no place to rest.

I venture to rely upon Your Wisdom and pray for Your external compassion and manifold blessings. It is fitting that for the sake of the billions of beings under heaven, You should look up and grant increased protection.

May the monks, nuns, Daoists, and others in the capital and all the provinces of the empire recite scriptures and perform rites for seven days and seven nights, starting from the first day of the first month each year.

The seventh month of the year follows this same precedent. Since the Emperor’s heart was moved and the power of the sages provided secret support, although there was drought for one year, locusts for two years, and so forth for three years thereafter, he brought about a state of Great Peace through his own presence (as recorded in the *Bianzheng lun* and other texts). Śramaṇa Mingzhan lived in seclusion at Zhiju Temple on Mount Taiyi.
In the tenth month of winter, knowing that his life was drawing to a close, he went to the capital to stay at Xingshan Temple, where he established a vegetarian feast.
Having bid farewell, he immediately returned to his wisdom-torch and applied himself with diligent contemplation. He told his attendant, "Amitābha Buddha is coming.

He then passed away with a serene expression. Once the cremation was completed, his remains were perfectly intact, without any gaps or fissures; at the crown of his head, however, there was a single opening.

A purple radiance shone brilliantly. He was subsequently enshrined in a stupa on the cliff. Dharma Master Yuwan possessed a perfectly pure conduct and a comprehensive mastery of both the Way and the study of wisdom.

In this year, the Emperor issued an edict for him to enter the palace, where he conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the consorts, the imperial princesses, the Crown Prince, and the various princes (according to his original biography).

In the first month of the Jichou year (the second year of Zhenguan), an imperial edict was issued to the monks and nuns of the capital, establishing it as a permanent custom that they should perform ritual circumambulation and recite the *Renwang*, *Dayun*, and other sutras on the second and seventh days of every month at their respective temples (*Bianzheng*).
In the third month, the Emperor [realized] that all conditioned existence is not true happiness. Regarding objects...
"I am entirely empty. Reflecting upon the essential truths, nothing surpasses the Śākya scriptures. Consequently, when Paramārtha arrived at the capital, an imperial edict was issued:
"The relevant authorities shall search for those of eminent virtue who are well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and fully proficient in the ten categories [of Buddhist learning].

Nineteen such individuals were selected, and they began the work of translation at Daxingshan Monastery. The śramaṇa Xuánmù and others served as translators of the vernacular, while the Vinaya Master Kumārajīva acted as the certified translator.
Fali, Huiming, and others took up their pens; Chengzhi, Huisheng, and others verified the meanings.

Furthermore, by imperial decree, the Vice President Fang Yuanling, the Palace Attendant Du Zhenglun, the Minister Li Xiao, and others participated in assisting with the collation and determination [of the text].

Xiao Jing, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness and Director of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, was in overall charge of supervision. The various offices provided all four requisites in abundance. (Record of the Exegesis of the Scriptures) 6.
In the [first] month, Chan Master Mingjing of Mízhōu was summoned to the capital to pray for rain. Dàtōng received an imperial decree granting the ordination of three hundred monks (*Tǒngjì*).

○ An edict was issued stating that Tōngyì Gōng, the former residence of the imperial family, should be converted into a nunnery, named Xīngshèng, so that the Way of the Spirits might have no fixed limit and subtly fulfill the filial longing expressed by the "Song of the Gentle Breeze" (*Hóngmíng*). ○ In the eleventh month, Shèng...

The Abbot of Kuang Temple, Sengzhen, received an imperial decree to proceed to the palace to welcome a set of embroidered images of Śākyamuni, along with images of Bodhisattvas, holy monks, Vajrapāṇi, and others, to be enshrined for veneration at Kuangsheng Temple (Bianzheng). ○ Shi Yuanzang was naturally gifted with early wisdom.

Having delved into the subtle depths of the sūtras and śāstras, he often lamented that although the scriptures already disseminated were stored within his breast, he had not yet been able to behold those scriptures that had not yet arrived.

He therefore resolved to travel to the Western Regions to seek them out in their entirety. That winter, he presented a memorial at the imperial court, but the Emperor issued an edict forbidding him from going.
Xuanzang then secretly fled; departing from Yuanzhou, he passed through the Jade Gate and proceeded toward the kingdoms of Gaochang, the Yehe Kagan, and others.

On the *guichou* day of the intercalary twelfth month, an edict was issued, stating: "The House of Sui lost the Way, and the nine provinces were in turmoil. I personally commanded the vanguard army to inflict this manifest punishment.
Among them were those who, like the dogs of Jie, fell into the nets of Tang; yet they bit their own whiskers in righteous indignation and maintained their integrity to the end.
Each followed what they served, and all are truly praiseworthy. I fear deeply that beneath the nine springs of the underworld, they may still be submerged in cauldrons and boiling pots."
Amidst the eight difficulties, they are forever entangled like ice and fire; with deep sorrow weighing upon my heart, I have not forgotten them whether waking or sleeping.

Therefore, I establish fields of merit to save their wandering spirits. At every site where armies clashed since the inception of the righteous cause, I shall erect monasteries for those righteous men and fierce warriors who lost their lives in battle, inviting eminent companions to reside there.
I hope that when the Dharma drum resounds, [their spirits] will be transformed.
He transformed the blazing fires into blue lotuses—this was heard by those of pure Brahma-sounds—and changed the ocean of suffering into ambrosia.

The relevant authorities were charged with measuring out the sites and establishing monasteries; they submitted a detailed report on these matters to express the Emperor’s intent of compassion (Old History).
In the gengyin year (the fourth year of Zhenguan), the empire was in great order. A bushel of rice cost only three coins.

In the first month, the Emperor issued an edict at Shengguang Temple, ordering forty-nine virtuous monks from various monasteries to perform rites for twenty-one days to celebrate the embroidered images; when the days were complete, a feast was held.

The Assembly for a Thousand Monks: Princes and dukes all came to offer incense (*Bianzheng*). In the fourth month, the Indian master Prajñāvarman finished translating the *Ratnolkā-sūtra* in ten fascicles;

Fali composed the preface, stating that this sutra was preached by the Tathāgata when he had first realized the Way of Enlightenment, delivered Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, subdued the Demon King, and protected the realm. In this year, the walls of the four directions...

At every military encampment, he established monasteries: for example, upon defeating Xue Ju, he established Zhaoren Monastery (in Bingzhou); upon defeating Wang Shichong, he established Zhaojue Monastery (in Luozhou);
upon defeating Liu Wuzhou, he established Hongji Monastery (in Fenzhou); and upon defeating Song Jingang, he established Ciyun Monastery.
At P’ojou, he defeated Huo Laosheng and established Pujise; at Lyjou, he defeated Dou Jiande and established Dengcise;
at Zhengjou, he defeated Liu Heita and established Zhaofose. In each case, the state provided for their sustenance and ordination. Buddhist activities flourished extensively.
By imperial decree, Yu Shinan, Li Boyao, Chu Suiliang, Yan Shigu, Cen Wenben, Xu Jingzong, and others were assigned to collaborate in composing the new [scriptures].
Temple Stele Inscription (from the *Neidian lu*): When the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, was traveling at Mount Niutou, Lanrong resided there.
Upon seeing him, the Patriarch asked, "What are you doing here? He replied, "I am contemplating the mind. The Patriarch said, "Who is it that contemplates?"

"What is this mind? Rong asked, having no further response. He bowed again and requested instruction on the Dharma of the mind. The Patriarch said: "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single principle;
the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are entirely within the source of the mind. Samādhi, wisdom, and supernormal powers are all inherently complete within it."

"There are no three realms from which to escape, and there is no Bodhi to be sought. You need only allow the mind to be free and at ease; do not engage in contemplative practices, nor do you need to suppress the mind.

Whatever you encounter as you look around or meet with conditions is all the wondrous function of the Buddha. Rong asked, "If one does not engage in contemplative practices, what should be done when objects arise?
The Patriarch said, "Objects and conditions have neither good nor evil; it is the mind that conceives of good and evil. The mind..."
If one does not forcefully apply names, from what source would deluded sentiments arise? Once deluded sentiments do not arise, the true mind is free to exercise universal knowledge.
Having received the Dharma transmitted by the Patriarchs, he returned to Shuangfeng (Wudeng Huiyuan). In the tenth month, Master Huicheng died.

Cheng had explained the obscure points and occupied the Way, making the protection of the Dharma his core concern. He served through three reigns and witnessed the transitions of six emperors; he frequently ascended to the inner palace and personally faced the sovereign.

The Emperor’s countenance was radiant, and his noble virtue was held in high esteem; the dukes and ministers all paid him their respects. In the winter, Dharma Master Daoxun (alternatively read as Daosun) was requested by others to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Once the title had been announced, he addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: "How can one, after this verse, request that [the merit] be entrusted to a future life?"
He then proceeded to explain the text according to its wording, passing away upon reaching a verse (one source says he stopped at the "Siṃha-parivarta" until the end of the "Phala-parivarta").
His coffin was carried to the mountains, where suddenly strange flowers sprang up around the corpse, reaching a length of one or two chi and numbering about five hundred stalks (*Biànzhèng zhǔn*).
Shi Faxiang resided at Hailing Temple in Beihang. He was able to foresee calamities and blessings. Once, when a tiger was attacking a person, Faxiang called out to it to stop and let the man go.
The tiger immediately released him. [Daoxuan] preached the Dharma for the tigers, and they all followed him as he departed into the distance.
Previously, in winter, he had manifested his passing into nirvana.

In the year Xinmao (the fifth year of Zhenguan), the Emperor, for the sake of Empress Dowager Mu, constructed Cide Monastery at Qingshan Palace. Furthermore, he established Yaotai Monastery at Shaoling.
The Temple [received] an imperial decree for the Dharma Master Yuǎnwǎn to transcribe the Tripiṭaka for the Empress at Deyè Monastery within the Imperial Garden.

Furthermore, he was commissioned to produce another set of the Tripiṭaka at Yánxīng Monastery; in both instances, Yuǎnwǎn was entrusted with supervision and the detailed verification of the scriptural sections. This practice originated with Yuǎnwǎn.
At Ānyǎng Monastery in Liángzhōu, the disciple Huìguāng’s mother was poor; because of her son, she used his *kāṣāya* robe to make [something for herself].
[He wore] undergarments. Suddenly, thunder struck and he died. On his back was inscribed: "Because of using dharma-robes, it was not according to the Dharma" (from the *Sengzhuan*).
○ Zhao Wenxin of Suizhou died suddenly and revived, saying: "I arrived at the abode of King Yama and was asked about what karma I had committed. He replied: [text missing]
He did not read Buddhist scriptures, but was fond only of the collected works of Yu Xin. The King asked, "Do you know him? Yu Xin replied, "I do not.

The King ordered that Yu Xin be brought forward; there he saw a large tortoise with many heads on one body, which spoke in human voice, saying, "In my life, I delighted in composing literary works and slandered the Buddha-dharma;
therefore, I have received this retribution. Upon awakening, Yu Xin recounted the matter in detail. [This occurred] in Shuzhou.
He was very fond of hunting; therefore, they exhorted and admonished him together to change his occupation and uphold the sutras (from the *Fayuan*).
In the year Renchen (the sixth year of Zhenguan), the Emperor issued an edict to establish the former residence in Taiyuan as Tiangong Monastery, posthumously honoring Empress Dowager Mu at Taicheng.
In the west, within the city of Zhennü, he further built Hongfu Monastery for Empress Dowager Mu (Biànzhèng).
On the fifth day of the fifth month, Wànhuī Fǎyún was born in the Zhāng family at Méngxiāng in Guózhōu. Śramaṇa Guǎndǐng had resided on Mount Tiāntái since the Dàyè era;
he cultivated both samādhi and wisdom, transforming others through both speech and silence. On the seventh day of the eighth month of this year, he passed away.
At Guoqing Temple, his lifespan was seventy-two years. Initially, Huiying transformed the secular world through his spiritual influence, and his divine efficacy spread far and wide.

There was once a villager who fell ill and was on the verge of death; Huiying burned incense for him and recited the Lotus Sūtra. As soon as the sick man smelled the fragrance entering his nostrils, he was immediately healed.
Once, while he was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Changan Shejing Temple, a band of pirates arrived at the temple.
Suddenly, they saw men holding bows and spears, each more than ten feet tall; the pirates were immediately terrified and retreated. His miraculous responses were manifold.

Furthermore, among those who could uphold and comprehend the words and intent of Zhiyi, Zhanjing alone was such a person (*Biographies*). In the tenth month, Prajñāvarman translated the *Prajñāpradīpa*.

The treatise in fifteen fascicles is hereby concluded. Fali composed the preface, which states: "This treatise was composed by the Bodhisattva Vibhūticandra seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
With a mind like an illusion, one discerns that things have no inherent existence;

realizing that things are not [substantial] things, then the nature of every thing is empty. Knowing that the mind has no mind, then the essence of every thought is quiescent. One thus exhaustively realizes non-arising."
Li Jiu Shixiang Yuan (The Principle of Investigating the Source of True Reality). Master Yuwan was renowned for his preceptual virtue.

Among the monastics and nuns who received full ordination under him were over three thousand people; among the princes, officials, and commoners who received the refuges and precepts were over two hundred thousand.

A sorcerer observed that at the time of the conferral of the precepts, spirits and deities were constantly present to receive them. In that year, he established Puguang Temple and issued an invitation.
Wan resided there. Du Ruhui revered Wan’s Way and frequently inquired about the essentials of the Dharma.
When he was approaching death, he summoned Wan, wishing for him to be his teacher for all future generations (according to the *Sengshi*).

In the spring of the guisi year (the seventh year of Zhengguan), Paramārtha completed the translation of the *Vyūha-śāstra* in thirteen fascicles. An imperial edict was issued for Li Boyao, the Junior Secretary, to compose a preface.

Furthermore, an edict was issued to transcribe ten copies each and distribute them throughout the realm. Subsequently, Paramārtha and his colleagues were granted one hundred rolls of fine silk. As the Emperor followed this precedent...

The Wheel-Turning King transforms the world through the ten wholesome paths of action. Within his realm, all markets completely cease the practice of slaughter; he universally prohibits the common people, not permitting the killing of living beings.
In the lands south of the Yangtze River, military camps were established to catch fish across more than thirty states, as well as for breaking dams to harvest them.
[The number of those] was as vast as the sands of the Ganges in hundreds of millions. Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued to abolish them all.

Moreover, as the harvests were abundant and the seasons harmonious, three thousand monks and nuns were universally ordained. Subsequently, because the Crown Prince fell ill and various treatments proved ineffective, an imperial decree invited Śubhakarasiṃha to enter the palace.
After more than one hundred days, the Emperor frequently inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. When the Prince’s illness was cured, he took leave to return to his own monastery;

the Emperor bestowed sixty rolls of silk and other gifts upon him (*Bianzheng*). In the fourth month, Prajñāvarman fell ill and, having distributed his robes and assets, performed various pure deeds before passing away while sitting upright.
The Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang, having departed from the Tang and reached the Great Forest of Kaśmīra...
Upon arriving in the kingdom of Kujūṭa, he crossed the Gaṅgā River with eighty Hu merchants. It was the local custom there to sacrifice humans to their gods;
Xuanzang and the merchants were captured, and they were about to be executed for his sacrifice. Suddenly, a great wind arose, and dust and sand filled the sky until the daylight turned to darkness.
The crowd was struck with terror and, regarding Xuanzang as a holy man, they released him. He then proceeded to Central India, where he encountered...
The Mahāyāna layman [Xuanzang] entered the city of Rājagṛha to open the way for the *Yogācārabhūmi* and stayed at Nālandā Monastery.

The monastery was composed of the seven precious gems, and the monks numbered in the tens of thousands. From the master Śīlabhadra of the Upper Seat, Xuanzang exhaustively explored the secret depths of the Mahāyāna, daily increasing his wisdom and realization.
Shi Dao’ang once gave a lecture at night without a lamp; Dao’ang raised his palm and emitted light.
His radiance illuminated the halls and chambers; thus his supreme path was difficult to fathom. He constantly vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturance (*An-yang*).

In the eighth month of that year, he saw the Dharma-music of the Western [Pure Land] coming to welcome him; he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture (as detailed in his biography). ○ Śramaṇa Fakuang maintained a resolute and upright countenance.
Aside from the three robes and one alms bowl, he accepted or stored nothing else. When people spoke with him, he would say only, "Be free from attachment. At the end of his life...
This is because the faculties of sentient beings are subject to defilement arising from sensory objects. In this year, he cast off his body and passed away (according to his biography).
In the Jia-wu year (the eighth year of Zhenguan), the monk Falin was devoted to the protection of the Dharma;
however, due to Daoists such as Liu and Li, who all composed vulgar writings to slander and defame the orthodox [teachings]...
Fahua then composed the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing and Rectifying) in twelve chapters: 1. The Three Teachings and the Governance of the World;

2. Successive Dynasties’ Veneration of the Buddha; 3. The Chronology of Buddhism and Daoism; 4. The Relationship between Confucius and Laozi as Teacher and Disciple; 5. Ten Similes; 6. Nine Admonitions; 7. Qi as the Foundation of the Dao; 8.
Reciprocal Retribution for Faith and Slander; 9. An Evaluation of Various Texts; 10. The Falsities and Errors of the Daoist Way; 11. Through the Ages...

The tradition continues: there is a work titled *Twelve Returns to the Mind*, which exhaustively investigates the sources of the teachings of Śākyamuni and Laozi and reaches the ultimate depths of their refined principles.
It was annotated by Chen Ziliang, a scholar of the Eastern Palace, who also composed a preface (the treatise is found in the Ming-character volume of the Tripitaka).

The Vinaya Master Huilian deeply understood the essential points; at the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he served as the *upādhyāya* of Yunhua Temple and was subsequently summoned by imperial decree to enter [the capital].
Guang. He took charge of the monastic community. This winter, he passed away (according to his biography). In the tenth month, Dharma Master Zhiyan passed away.

Yan’s conduct was characterized by diligent exertion, and he manifested auspicious omens more than once. Even before the incense burner had been lit at night, fragrant smoke would arise spontaneously; when the evening water jar was just emptied, [the water would refill].
He secretly added water until it overflowed. He also practiced the Sixteen Contemplations of Amitābha. In Mianzhu, Shuchuan, there was the monk Baoqiong;

the local inhabitants followed the Way of the Daoists and did not follow the Buddha. Baoqiong wished to convert them, and upon encountering their assembly, he sat down without performing a prostration. They said:
"Why do you not pay homage to the Celestial Honored One? Qiong replied, "The paths of the heterodox and the orthodox differ, and what each honors is distinct. Even the heavens still pay homage to me;
why then should I pay homage to the Lord Lao? The assembly’s discussion was tumultuous, but Qiong said, "If I were to bow down in homage, I would surely bring disgrace upon myself."
Upon his first prostration, the statue of the Way shook; upon his second, the entire seat toppled to the ground. The assembly then paid homage to Daoyoung, and at once they all returned to the faith.
In that same year, Daoyoung passed away.

In the spring of the Year of Yiwei (the ninth year), the Emperor issued an edict prohibiting killing, beginning in the third month and ending in the fifth. The Dharma Master Yuwan, because his benevolent care encompassed all beings, submitted a petition to extend the period;
the Emperor again granted this special request until the end of the year. In the fourth month, the Vinaya... [text ends]

Master Zhishou passed away. Zhishou was profoundly learned in the Vinaya-piṭaka. Since the Dharma of the Vinaya was first propagated in the East some six hundred years ago, those who have received the transmission of the precepts have largely been confused regarding their essence and characteristics;

the five schools were not distinguished, and two divergent views became intermingled. Zhishou consequently composed the *Wubu qufen chao* (Commentary on the Differentiation of the Five Schools) in twenty-one fascicles.
From the time of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty until his own era, he stood alone as the preeminent authority in the capital, and his fame continued throughout the Tang dynasty.
He was the one who first guided them all. In the eighth year of the Zhengguan era, he was summoned to serve as the *upādhyāya* of Hongfu Monastery.

Upon his passing into *nirvāṇa*, the Emperor mourned him deeply and issued an imperial decree ordering the various offices of state to provide for his funeral rites. From the Sui dynasty until the Tang, there had been no instance of a monk receiving a national burial.

He established the first model for his school, which was highly esteemed by his contemporaries. Fang Yuanling, the Vice President of the Secretariat; Du Zhenglun, the Director of the Imperial Household;

and various high officials all personally expressed their profound grief and lamented that he had passed away, for they held him in the highest regard as a model of discipline. The government granted him ten *mu* of land on the western plains of the capital, where he was buried.
Approximately one thousand pine trees were planted there. Emperor Gaozong composed an inscription for the stele. In the tenth month, Vinaya Master Fali...
He passed away. Sengli was born with his teeth fully formed; until the end of his life, they never decayed or fell out, remaining harder and whiter than ordinary.
He lectured on the Vinaya more than forty times and composed commentaries on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (as recorded in his biography). In the eleventh month, an imperial edict stated:
"The three vehicles govern the path, with salvation as their priority; the eightfold noble path leads to refuge, with compassion as its core. It spreads the ocean of wisdom and provides..."

He moistens all living beings and clears away the forest of afflictions; he serves as a bridge for all things, his actions conforming to the accumulation of goodness and his principles harmonizing with supreme benevolence.

I, the Emperor, reverently emulate the Golden Wheel and humbly receive the precious mandate. The regulations of the Great Sage leave no hidden corner unexamined, and the teachings of Supreme Virtue reach every distant place without fail.

I desire that people may be freed from the entanglements of worldly existence and that every household may attain benevolence and longevity. Recently, however, due to the turmoil of war and disorder, the monks...

In vain has there been a reduction [in their numbers]. The jeweled towers and lotus pedestals have no one to look out from their windows; the dark-blue hair and blue lotuses are weathered by wind and drenched by rain.
Reflecting upon this decay and ruin, I am truly filled with sorrow. Therefore, in all the provinces throughout the empire where there are temples, it is appropriate to ordain monks and nuns.

The number was limited to three thousand. As for the size of the prefectures and the varying numbers of those to be ordained in each location, the relevant authorities were to determine these in detail.
The primary objective was to select those whose virtue and practice were refined and brilliant.

Those who had previously reduced their status or returned to lay life, as well as those who had privately ordained themselves as white-robed laypeople, were included within the quota provided their conduct and practice were praiseworthy, and so forth (Old Tang History).

In the year Bingshen (the tenth), the Crown Prince asked Zhang Shiheng, "What is the response [to one's efforts] when serving the Buddha to cultivate merit? He replied, "Serving the Buddha lies in purity, benevolence, and forbearance.
If one is greedy, arrogant, and tyrannical, then even if one exhausts one's wealth to serve him, it will be of no benefit. Furthermore, as for good and evil..."
Retribution is inevitable, like a shadow following a form. To be loyal as a minister and filial as a son ensures that blessings and prosperity endure; to act contrary to this brings calamity.
At that time, the Crown Prince harbored rebellious intentions, so Liu Shiheng used this response to admonish him.

In the eighth month, an imperial edict summoned the Vinaya Master Huixiu of Xiangzhou to the capital to lecture on the Dharma. Huixiu declined the summons on the grounds of illness. He had once said: "I have seen..."
Among those of great renown who were master craftsmen, there was none who did not revere the Dharma and follow the Way; could one not aspire to emulate them?

Consequently, his practice during the six periods of the day became even more diligent. He did not discard a single pair of shoes for thirty years. He often said, "It is easy to generate a mind of liberation, but difficult to eliminate the defilements of the sensory world.
He passed away at the age of ninety-eight. Shi Daoying, during the Kaihuang era, first entered Mount Taihang.

The Master practiced *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* at the temple. Subsequently, while staying at Shengguang Temple in the capital, he entered meditative absorption and gradually manifested extraordinary signs.

Once, while serving as the temple’s director of affairs (*zhísuì*), he disputed land with a layperson; he suddenly fell prostrate and died. The layperson vowed never again to dispute with him, whereupon the Master immediately rose and sat up.
On another occasion, he entered water to sit in meditation and did not emerge for six nights. Furthermore, encountering thick ice and heavy snow, he remarked, "This place is level and pure."

"How can he not sleep? [he wondered]. He remained lying on his back for three nights before rising. Later, while staying at Puzi Temple in Puzhou, he was lecturing on the *Awakening of Faith* one day;

when he reached the section on the Gate of Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*), he suddenly passed away. Those who knew him said, "This was merely his entry into the meditative state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)."

He did not rise for several days. In the ninth month of that year, he was ordered to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Upon reaching his end, he exhorted [the Emperor] to mind the wholesome realms before passing away.
He was eighty years of age; his spiritual wonders were manifold. The Dharma Master Yuǎn Wǎn sent a letter to the Crown Prince, urging him to diligently practice four essential matters:
first, practicing compassion; second, reducing slaughter; third, following the natural flow of vital energy to nurture living beings; and fourth, [protecting the life of the Emperor].
He observed the fast. The Crown Prince replied: "I have deeply inscribed upon my heart the four categories of the sublime Dharma you have shown me. In the twelfth month, Yuǎn passed away.

In his final testament, he petitioned that sagely emperors and enlightened kings should ensure that rewards and punishments regarding the Three Jewels are not applied indiscriminately, and that they take great pity on śramaṇas who violate the law.
He requested that such individuals be handed over to their proper authorities to be governed according to the monastic code (*vinaya*). Furthermore, he submitted a memorial for peace...

The *Yǎnglùn Sāndé lùn* (Treatise on Nurturing and the Three Virtues) in one volume was graciously accepted by the Emperor. An imperial edict was issued expressing deep sorrow, and the Crown Prince was dispatched to offer condolences.
High ministers and senior officials presented their grief and provided generous funeral offerings. At the time of the cremation, followers gathered like clouds;

for forty li, the roads were filled with those in mourning attire, and the seven assemblies of the Sangha overspread the mountains. With hearts bound in unified grief, they subsequently erected a Buddhist stupa at the site of the cremation.
The epitaph was composed by Li Boyao (according to his biography).

In the dingsyou year (the eleventh year), he was summoned by imperial decree to Luoyang to expound the essentials of the Dharma. By special edict, he was granted permanent residence in the capital, where he was provided with the four requisites.

He was provided with all necessary supplies. Wei Wang, the Governor of Yongzhou, sent a respectful invitation from afar to appoint him as his Preceptor for Precepts (*śīla-ācārya*). Both the court and the commonalty paid him their highest respect.

An imperial edict declared that Laozi is the ancestral progenitor of the state, and that his title and rank should properly precede those of the Śākya clan. The Dharma Master Zhishi and others [submitted a memorial].

He went to the palace gate to present his petition, arguing that the Daoist masters follow the Three Zhangs and that practices such as spirit-water, incantations, and registers do not originate from Laozi;
therefore, they should not rank above the Buddhist monks. Although the Emperor agreed with these words, he desisted because he held his ancestors in high esteem.

In the first month of the twelfth year of the Wuxu cycle (578 CE), Shi Zhi-shi passed away at Zongchi Monastery after bidding farewell to the assembly. Between his eyebrows, he possessed a white tuft of hair several inches long.

His radiance illuminated his jaw and forehead. His three robes, water jar, and alms bowl were never parted from his person. He did not enter the marketplace, nor did he handle money or precious objects.

During that period, because he offended the times by protecting the Dharma, he returned to lay life for two years. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, an imperial edict decreed that he be reinstated as a monk once more.

His will and conduct were solemn and austere; both monastics and laypeople relied upon him. After his death, within a radius of over thirty li around San Yuan, virtuous laymen all erected [memorials] for him.
The Spirit Temple (from the *Benzhuan*): On the eighth day of the second month at the hour of the rat, the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was born.
In the eighth month, the Crown Prince assembled the palace officials and scholars of the Three Teachings at the Hongwen Hall to expound the Dharma.
An edict was issued summoning Dharma Master Huijing to expound the *Lotus Sūtra*. Furthermore, the Daoist Cai Huang was dispatched to debate with the Master.
Huáng asked: "The sutra is titled 'Chapter One: Introduction' (Xùpǐn dìyī). I do not yet understand what portion of the work this 'Introduction' constitutes. Jìng replied:

"The Tathāgata’s emission of light and manifestation of auspicious omens—this is the introduction. 'Chapter' (dì) signifies position; 'one' (yī) signifies the beginning. Huáng said: "'Chapter' (dì) is a homophone for 'younger brother' (dì)."
To call oneself "younger brother" (di) precludes calling oneself "one" (yi); to say "one" precludes saying "younger brother. These two terms are contradictory. How can they be reconciled? Jing said:
"Did I not say before that 'younger brother' refers to one's position and 'one' refers to the beginning?

Since you, Master Xian, do not understand the former principle, yet you falsely raise this latter objection, you are merely creating difficulties for yourself; how can you be said to challenge others? Huang then requested him to explain it again.
Huijing explained, "I am ignorant and deluded and did not understand; please cut and break me several more times. Huiming was filled with shame and stopped.
The Crown Prince laughed heartily, and those present in the assembly leaped for joy. He declared, "I never imagined that the joy of the Dharma would reach such a height.

Huijing frequently entered the palace precincts to engage in unimpeded debate. Shortly thereafter, an edict was issued stating: "The Dharma Master Huijing’s fame and conduct are renowned; we request him to serve as..."

The Abbot of Puguang Temple was revered by both the clergy and the laity. The Vice President of the Secretariat, Fang Yuanling, and the Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Chu Liang, held him in particularly high esteem (*Lunheng*).
Shi Wende, whose secular surname was Xu, could predict future events as if looking directly before his eyes.

Whenever a year was marked by calamities or pestilence, he would invariably urge the people to worship the Buddha and hold vegetarian feasts (*zhāi*). Those who followed his advice were all able to avert disasters; those who did not believe him [met with misfortune].
There was not one whose misfortune did not come to an end. When droughts occurred, he would say, "It shall rain on such-and-such a day," and it invariably rained.
Having been clearly verified as being like a bright mirror, he encouraged and exhorted many. In that year, he manifested his passing into nirvana, and the common people erected a stupa for him.

In the first month of Jihai (the thirteenth year), Yu Shinan, Minister of the Secretariat, passed away. During this year, the Emperor dreamed of Shinan offering him forthright counsel, just as he had done in life.
Consequently, he issued an edict stating: "The late Minister of the Ministry of Rites, Duke Wen-yi Yu Shinan, was pure and complete in his virtuous conduct and resolute in his will..."

Cun Zhongyi has suddenly undergone the transformation of all things; in an instant, the seasons have shifted. Yesterday, due to a dream at night, I suddenly beheld this man, who further offered forth honest and sagacious words as if it were a day from his lifetime.
Recalling his enduring virtues, I am truly moved by grief and lamentation. It is fitting that he be aided by the merit of the afterlife.
Out of my sentiment of cherishing the old, you may immediately go to his home, provide a vegetarian feast for five hundred monks, and have one statue of the Buddha fashioned.
