(Old History, Basic Annals) ○ Shi Tanrong. He served as the presiding master of the Dharma; he lectured on the teachings during the spring and summer, and practiced seated meditation during the autumn and winter.
When the Provincial Governor presented him with three grains of *śarīra*, he made a vow before the assembly to request more, and they obtained a total of over four hundred grains of *śarīra*.

Those far and near were filled with admiration and submission. In the seventh year of the Zhenguan era, while performing the Fangdeng Repentance Rite, the temple monk Sengding beheld a radiance within which—
Seven Buddhas appeared and each declared, "I testify that your sins have been extinguished. The last Buddha said, "I am Śākyamuni.

Because your physical vessel is pure, I have come to bestow this prediction upon you: among the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall be named Puming (Universal Radiance), while I shall be named Puning (Universal Peace).
This was a manifestation of such auspicious response. Tanrong then passed away that winter (*according to the Benzhuan*). In the winter, there was a yellow...
Wearing the cap of the Qin era’s elite, he relied on his occult arts to seek glory. Consequently, he was employed as an official by the Crown Prince.

Having long harbored malice toward the Buddhist community, he secretly submitted Fa-lin’s *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing Orthodoxy), claiming it slandered the imperial lineage. The Emperor became incensed and issued an order to track down Fa-lin’s person.
Upon investigation according to the law, Fa-lin went of his own accord to the public court; disregarding his life to uphold the truth, he was bound in shackles and fetters, and an edict was issued.
Question: In the ancestral alliances of the Zhou dynasty, those of different surnames were placed last; honoring the ancestors and valuing kinship truly stems from antiquity.
Why do you pursue their shortcomings and act like a rat between two ends, extensively citing analogies based on superficial resemblance and setting forth a full array of disrespectful metaphors?

"To offend and destroy my ancestors, to slander and defile my forebears—for such a pursuit of fame, there can be no leniency for the resulting transgressions. Senglin said, "The August Heaven has no partiality;
it assists only virtue. The ancients sided with principle, not with kin. Though one is close, if they have committed a crime, punishment must follow;
though one is distant, if they have performed a service, reward must follow. The Dao and Virtue of Laozi extend to the common people, and its humble radiance manifests in..."
Sihai once said: "The name of my teacher is Buddha; 'Buddha' means one who awakens all people. The Ancient Sovereign of Central India ascended and departed long ago.
Having investigated the Lao Teachings, their beginning and end can be traced. Now, what Liu and Li have written slanders the teacher of Laozi;
therefore, I have composed this treatise, citing historical records alongside [the other texts]. My previous words were certainly not intended to slander the state or the family. Hereafter..."

He presented his case before more than twenty officials, all relying on Senglin’s testimony and submitting a formal petition to the throne. The imperial edict stated: "According to the treatise you have composed, those who invoke Avalokiteśvara are not harmed even when facing the blade.
Grant him a seven-day reprieve so that he may practice invocation himself; let us see whether or not he can remain unhurt by the time his sentence is due.
When the term expired, Senglin suddenly had a vision of a valiant being. When the edict arrived and the matter was investigated, it was found that the period of amnesty had already ended.

When it was time for his execution, [Emperor Yang] asked, "What were you thinking? Did you call upon any spiritual being? Senglin replied, "At the end of the Sui dynasty, virtue was lost and the four seas were in turmoil.
Since the Son of Heaven launched his punitive campaign, the lands and waters have been purified once more; this is precisely the power of Avalokiteśvara’s rescue from distress.
For seven days now, I have not called upon Avalokiteśvara, but only upon Your Majesty. The Emperor then sent another messenger to question Senglin.
An imperial decree was issued, ordering him to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara. [The Emperor] asked, "For what reason do you not recite it? He replied, "I only recite the name of Your Majesty.

Huilin answered, "I have humbly received that Avalokiteśvara is the Most Holy One, who manifests forms within the six realms of existence; from the heavens above to the earth below, all take him as their teacher and model.

Yet, the Great Tang reigns over the four seas, and Your Majesty nurtures all beings like a parent. According to the sutras, Your Majesty is none other than Avalokiteśvara. Since his spiritual discernment thus..."
This memorial is why I think only of Your Majesty. Furthermore, that which I have composed, the *Zhenglun* (Treatise on Orthodoxy), accords with the scriptures and histories;
were there even a single phrase to deviate from them, I would deserve the executioner’s axe. If Your Majesty follows what is loyal and upright, then I shall not lose so much as a single hair.
"If Your Majesty were to inflict excessive punishment upon the innocent, I, Lin, would suffer the pain of a prostrate corpse. He submitted this report, and consequently, no punishment was meted out.
By imperial decree, he was transferred to a Buddhist monastery in Yizhou. The records, treatises, and poems composed by Lin comprise more than thirty volumes;
thus, his surviving writings and past deeds may serve as a guiding model for ten thousand generations. Later, he passed away at Guansi, at the age of... (the text ends here).

69. Regarding the epitaph composed for the funeral arrangements by both monastics and laypeople (Shilu): At that time, the Censor Wei Zong, having investigated Qin Ying’s fraudulent deceptions, memorialized the throne to impeach him.

By imperial decree, he was sent to the Grand Court of Justice, where he was ultimately executed for his madness and wickedness. Both public and private parties marveled that his death had come so late (Lunheng). Shi Hongman:
Initially, while still a layman, he suffered from a chronic ailment that left both his feet withered and crippled; he constantly recited the name of Avalokiteśvara.
After three years had passed, a monk suddenly arrived. When asked where he had come from, the monk replied, "I have come because you, patron, have been constantly calling for me.
Man asked, "What sin did I commit in a previous life that I now suffer from this contraction and lameness? The monk said, "In a former existence, you bound and imprisoned living beings;
the remaining karmic retribution has brought this upon you. Close your eyes, and I shall treat it for you. Man then closed his eyes, and he felt only...
A protuberance on his knee was about six or seven cun high; when it was removed, his eyes opened. Just as he was about to dismiss [the monk], he lost sight of where the monk had gone.

Rising and walking as before, he realized that this was Avalokiteśvara. From then on, he vowed never to marry and devoted himself to the cultivation of dhyāna and contemplation, sometimes for as long as seven days.
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he became a monk; he passed away that year at the age of eighty-three (Biography). ○ Shi Zhiyuan.
He inscribed the scriptures upon stone and stored them within a stone chamber. Intending to construct a Buddha hall, he found that there was no timber on the mountain;
suddenly, a violent rainstorm swept a thousand logs to that spot. In the same year, Fayuan passed away (according to the *Monk Biographies*).
In the gengzi year (the fourteenth year of Zhenguan), an imperial edict was issued stating:
"The images of the Buddha and the Way are of the utmost dignity and solemnity; yet among artisan families, there are many who engage in their casting and manufacture."
Those who make offerings compete to come and purchase [the images] for ransom; they judge their quality, weighing their craftsmanship and estimating their weight.

The buyers disregard cause and effect, seeking only to acquire them at a low price; the sellers originally hope for profit, caring only for a high valuation. Thus, the accumulation of karmic offenses is particularly grave.
When their merit and retribution are both exhausted, they violate the scriptures and teachings; all such instances should be strictly prohibited.

From this day forward, artisans shall not pre-fabricate Buddha images for sale. As for those images already completed, each shall be distributed to monasteries and observatories, and the price shall be paid from the collective funds of the community.
(Old History) ○ Dharma Master Du Shun was held in high esteem by Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty during his youth, and was granted a monthly stipend.
He provided for them. If someone was ill, he would sit facing them in a reverent posture; after a short while, the person would recover.

If there were those who were deaf, when Shun spoke with them, their hearing would immediately become acute. If there were those who were mute, when Shun conversed with them, they were able to speak. If there were those who were insane or deranged...
Huishun sat in meditation facing toward [the river]. He then bowed in thanks and departed. On another occasion, while crossing a stream, his attendant feared he would not be able to cross;
Huishun led him across together, and the water immediately ceased its flow. His divine traces were of this kind, yet Huishun remained humble and unassuming.

At first, he did not take this to heart. He profoundly mastered the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Emperor Taizong held him in high esteem from the outset and frequently invited him into the imperial palace to guide him toward auspiciousness.
The empresses, princes, members of the imperial clan, and various nobles revered him as if he were a living Buddha.

He once compiled the *Huayan fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka). His disciple, the Venerable Zhiyan, transmitted his teachings. In the fifth month of that year, he passed away.
(One account states he passed away in the eighth month of the fifteenth year. ○ Xiangguo Xiao Yu was the son of Emperor Ming of the Liang dynasty.

Since the time of Emperor Wu, his family had maintained a tradition of Buddhist devotion and pure cultivation. Both Xiao Yu and his grandson Mian were exceptionally diligent and rigorous in their practice. When Taizong ascended the throne, Xiao Yu served as Chancellor several times.
He once requested permission to become a monk, but soon desisted because it was deemed impossible. Throughout his career, he served two dynasties and entered the position of Chancellor five times.

He passed away at the age of seventy-four. The *History of the Tang* praises him, saying: "The Liang dynasty of the Xiao clan rose in the region east of the Yangtze River; they truly performed meritorious service for the people.
Their end was not marked by great evil, yet they perished due to their gradual decline. Thus, the remaining blessings extended to their descendants.

From Xiao Yu down to Xiao Gou, there were eight generations of prime ministers whose fame and virtue followed one another in succession, rising and falling with the fortunes of the Tang. Such prosperity among a noble lineage has not been seen since antiquity."

[There was one] named [Shi Hui]leng (from his biography). He was capable of lecturing on the Dharma. Suddenly he dreamed of a person who said, "King Yama has prepared a ritual site (*dōjō*) and invites the Master to lecture on the Dharma.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month, he manifested slight illness. That night, someone informed him, "Dharma Master, rise early and burn incense;
the messenger will arrive immediately. [Hui]leng asked, "Who is it? [The person] replied, "It is King Yama’s messenger to escort you. [Hui]leng then rose and burned incense.

He offered incense and paid homage to the Buddha; then, returning to his room, he passed away suddenly. (The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* [Sengzhuan] states: "In the twentieth year of the Zhengguan era, a person in blue clothing announced that the Heavenly Emperor had invited him to lecture on the sutras;

he then entered nirvana. Far and near, people heard the sound of celestial drums and music accompanying his departure. Śramaṇa Huīyú first entered Mount Yùquán. Beside the temple was a spring, where he built a grass hut and sat in meditation for twenty-three years.
A water-spirit made offerings to him, and he occasionally saw or heard its presence. There was a black snake, many feet long...
It was two *zhang* long. It manifested its form and concealed it as it pleased, appearing like a protective guardian. Although bands of bandits approached, none dared draw near.

When ten bandits arrived, the snake opened its eyes and emitted light, causing all the bandits to fall prostrate. Two days later, Zhou Yu learned of this and went to rescue them; seven of the men had already died.
The snake followed Zhou Yu as he walked, and once he had finished reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-mantra*, three of the men were restored to life. Afterwards—

Monastics and laypeople requested him to come forth to the Shengjue Temple to lecture on the Dharma. In the seventh month of that year, the entire monastery simultaneously saw a cluster of stars enter the well, and they could not fathom the cause.

In the eighth month, he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; when he reached the passage concerning rebirth in the Pure Land, before it was finished, he was holding a *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) in his hand.
He passed away while seated on his mat. Shi Jinglin had been a lay follower since the Wude era;

eminent officials such as the Minister Du Zhenglun all vowed to become his disciples. In the tenth month of that year, he entered nirvana. When his body was cremated, only his tongue remained unburnt.
Throughout his life, the Master was frugal and austere; when his robes were worn out, he would patch them with paper. He spoke neither of the excellence nor the defects of food and drink.

He never allowed saliva or mucus to be visible from his mouth or nose; he was the height of reverence and circumspection. Furthermore, as his spiritual rank was difficult to fathom, lice and fleas did not even crawl upon his body.
When his fame became lofty and his merit profound, the offerings and gifts he received increased daily; yet he entrusted these entirely to his attendants, never asking about them a second time.

This was truly because he took the Way as his sole pursuit and his heart had no involvement with the secular world. These deeds are worthy of being recorded for later generations and serve sufficiently as a mirror for teachers (from his *Benzhuan*).
In the first month of the year Xinchou (the fifteenth year of Zhenguan),
the monk Shi Huizhen once fashioned a stone statue thirteen zhang in height, which was moved by the manifestation of a great white light from the mouth of the image.
In this year, an assembly was held within the temple; lotus flowers sprouted both from beneath the ground and upon the trees.
On the *wuchen* day of the second month, the Emperor visited Hongfu Temple and summoned five virtuous monks, including Daoyi, to take their seats.

He informed them that the founding of the temple was solely for the purpose of honoring Empress Dowager Mu Taihou. As he spoke, tears fell from his eyes; the monks hesitated, and the Emperor personally composed a memorial and bestowed two hundred rolls of silk as offerings.

He who styled himself Emperor and Disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts, having finished the act of dedication, looked toward Yi and the others and said, "Recently, because Laozi was my ancestral progenitor, I ordered his name and rank to precede [the Buddha's]. You all must have felt resentment at this. Yi replied:

Your Majesty has honored the ancestral founders and issued these perfected regulations. We, Yi and the others, having received the grace of the state, shall now dwell in peace and tranquility to practice the Way;

we are all filled with joy at the promulgation of this imperial decree and dare not harbor any resentment. The Emperor said, "As for the Great and Small Vehicles of the Buddha’s Way, I have known them for a long time."
The relative status of Śākyamuni and Laozi is something that those of broad learning reflect upon for themselves; how could one claim superiority based merely on who was exalted at a particular time?
I have placed my ancestors in the position of honor because they are the fundamental source of all living beings, and thus I have prioritized Laozi to distinguish the order of kinship and distance.
This is not a lack of devotion toward the Buddha. Since the founding of this state, I have never established a Daoist monastery; as for those who have rendered service...

Their virtues were such that they both returned to monastic dwellings. Although in the past they had brandished spears and faced the front lines of battle, they never once gave rein to their power or engaged in indiscriminate killing.
Today, at every site where there was a battlefield, a Buddhist temple has been established; even the former residence in Taiyuan is now dedicated to the service of the Buddha.

"This is how I have cultivated my heart," the Emperor said, "and I suspect you have not yet understood this. When Li Yi and the others suddenly rose to hasten toward him in thanks, the Emperor said, "Sit for a moment. This..."

If I do not record my intention here, others will remain unaware of it. As the weather is now turning hot and the temple buildings are not yet complete, the items currently being donated may be used to construct a separate scripture hall, allowing the assembly of monks ample space to practice the Way. (The remainder of the text is largely omitted.

The Venerable Master Baozhang, who lived for a thousand years, traveled extensively through Jiang and Zhejiang. In this year, he returned to the cave of Feilai Peak. There was one who said, "Having traversed all of China..."
"Four hundred states. Among these, the phrase "the path of the man of the Way (daoren) wanders therein" is particularly renowned.

In the year Renyin (the sixteenth year of Zhenguan), the Vinaya Master Huiman devoted himself exclusively to propagating the teachings of the Vinaya, refusing to conform to the sentiments of the age. Whenever monks or nuns committed transgressions, he repeatedly carried out public censures and expulsions against them.
There was frequently a neighboring fire that spread and was about to reach the lecture hall; when Faman sought water and sprinkled it upon it, the fire was immediately extinguished.
In the fourth month of that year, he passed away. When his body was cremated, only his tongue remained unburnt. In the fifth month, the Emperor performed memorial rites for the late Empress Taimu.
He personally drafted a memorial of aspiration and addressed it to Hongfu Monastery, saying: "That which the sages and wise hold in high esteem is filial piety;
that which the benevolent love is their parents. In my youth, I was blessed with the grace of being nurtured; in my maturity, I have received the instruction of being raised within the clan.

How could I ever forget the longing expressed in the *Liaoe* (Sweet Basil) ode? My feelings of boundless grief are such that even the vast heavens cannot repay them. Formerly, Zilu sighed over the 'thousand-jing' salary..."
Lacking the means for sustenance, Yu Qiu lamented that his parents were no longer waiting for him. As he spoke these words of eternal longing, his profound grief was most acute.
Having no way to repay their kindness, he could only rely on the aid of the unseen. He respectfully offers two hundred rolls of silk to the Great Way of Compassion.
If there is a response to this utmost sincerity, I hope to erase the transgressions of my past; if there is a cause for doing good, I pray to obtain the blessings of future conditions. (Hongming)

The Emperor issued an edict to transcribe the Tripitaka for the sake of Empress Dowager Mu. He commanded ten eminent Dharma masters to be selected and summoned from afar to collate and verify the texts.
In this year, Master Xuanzang departed from Rājagṛha and returned to the kingdom of Cīnabhukti.
The king welcomed him at the outskirts of the city and provided elephants and horses to assist Master Xuanzang in carrying the scriptures back on his journey. Śramaṇa Huizhi was six feet tall.
He was seven chi tall. His physical appearance was magnificent and radiant; he maintained a majestic bearing and never cast a casual glance about. At that time, people called him "The Elephant King.
Toward the end of the Sui dynasty, he resided at Hongdao Temple in Yuezhou. For nearly thirty years, he did not step outside the temple gates and remained in a seated posture without lying down.
He preached the Dharma without weariness. In the eighth month of that year, he addressed the assembly, saying, "I wish to go to another realm to teach and transform beings;
you may prepare food quickly. Having finished eating, he returned to his room, sat cross-legged, and passed away. His disciples said he had entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Several days later, when a rare fragrance was perceived, they finally realized he had been transformed for a long time (from his *benzhuan*).

In the year Gui-mao (the seventeenth), an imperial decree was issued summoning the Great Master Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch, to the palace. The messenger went three times, but the Patriarch remained firm in his reclining and did not rise.

On the fourth occasion, the Emperor commanded the messenger, saying, "If he does not rise, then bring his head here. When the messenger arrived at the mountain and delivered this intent, the Master then—

He extended his neck toward the blade, his countenance serene and composed, which left those present in awe. Hui returned and reported the incident to the Emperor, who marveled at it all the more and felt deep admiration.
He bestowed precious silks upon him so that he might fulfill his aspiration. *Śramaṇa Cizang* was a native of Silla.
Once, a deity from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven received the five precepts from him; ever since, he had benefited sentient beings through this Dharma. This continued until the twelfth year of Zhengguan.

In the capital, he was invited to reside at the Shengguang Monastery (Shèngguāng Biéyuàn). There, provisions and wealth were accumulated in great abundance. When a thief arrived intending to take the goods, his heart was struck with sudden alarm;

he returned and confessed his transgression. The Master immediately conferred the precepts upon him. Furthermore, there was a man suffering from blindness who went to the storehouse to offer repentance; later, he regained his sight.
Due to such auspicious responses, those who received the precepts from him numbered in the thousands daily. He subsequently entered Mount Zhōngnán.
He constructed a chamber to dwell in. Those who came to offer their devotion, both humans and spirits, gathered there in great numbers. After three summers had passed, he was about to return east;

he then entered the capital, where he received an imperial edict of consolation and was granted two hundred bolts of silk, as well as a set of patched robes and five hundred pieces of miscellaneous colored fabrics.
The Eastern Palace bestowed two hundred rolls of silk upon him.

Furthermore, because his country’s collection of scriptures and images was incomplete, he obtained a complete set of the Tripitaka, along with various exquisite images, banners, flowers, and canopies—all fit for bringing merit and benefit—which he carried back to his native land.

Upon arriving home, the entire nation came out to welcome him; thus, the Buddha-dharma flourished and became manifest there for the first time in that generation. At that time, there was the Chan Master Fenggan.
Hanshan and Shide appeared one after the other at Guoqing Temple. Fenggan had previously settled in a hermitage in the northwest corner of the Great Canon Library.
While wandering along a pine path, he saw a boy about ten years old; when questioned, the boy said he had neither family nor surname.
The Master brought him back to the temple storehouse to raise him, naming him Shide. Later, there was a poor scholar who came from Cold Rock.
...and arrived there. Consequently, he was called Hanshanzi (Cold Mountain Man). The three men were delighted to find one another. Fenggan departed to travel as a wandering monk.

It happened that Lü Qiu Yin had been appointed to govern Taizhou; as he was about to depart for his post, he suddenly suffered from a headache caused by wind. He summoned renowned physicians, but none could cure it.
Fenggan happened to arrive at his residence and declared himself skilled in treating this ailment. When Lü Qiu heard of this, he went to see him. The Master maintained purity...
He sprayed water upon it, and in an instant, it was completely eliminated. Because of this, he showed him great respect. He asked where he had come from;
[Fenggan] replied, "From Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. He asked, "Are there any sages there? He replied, "Hanshan is Mañjuśrī and Shide is Samantabhadra; you should go there to see them.
When Lüqiu arrived at his post, three days later he personally went to the temple to visit the remains of Fenggan and pay his respects to the two Great Beings.
The temple monks led him to the kitchen area, where Qiu bowed to him. The two gentlemen rose and ran off, saying, "Fenggan is too talkative;
he does not even recognize Amitābha. Why do you bow to us? We shall return at once to the Cold Cliff. The next day, Lüqiu sent offerings of clothing and medicine.
When Hanshan saw the messenger arrive, he shouted, "Thief! Thief! and retreated into his cave, saying, "I inform all of you: each of you must exert yourselves!"
[They] used their strength to enter the cave with Shide, and the cave closed of its own accord. Hanshan and Shide composed poems, which they scattered throughout the mountains and forests;
the monks of the temple subsequently collected them to form a collection that has been transmitted to the world (as recorded in the *Benzhuan*).

On the fourth day of the eighth month, at Hongchi Valley in Songchang, Yuanzhou, five stones suddenly appeared, all of which were blue in substance with white characters forming the words: "Gao Huang emerges from the sea."
Many Sons. Eighty years for King Li Yuan; a thousand years for the Great Peace Emperor, Li Shimin.
Prince Li Zhi, a man of the Yan Mountains, ruler of a great kingdom, whose benevolence surpasses a thousand ages. The kings of the five, six, and seven generations;

the seven Buddhas and eight Bodhisattvas, as well as the Buddhas of the higher fruits, the Son of Heaven of Tian, and others—down to those who performed good deeds in Yuanzhou, they all submitted their petitions to the court.
The various officials drafted characters for it, which were brilliantly clear and manifest. On the *xinmao* day of the eleventh month, there was a sacrificial ceremony at the Southern Suburb.

An imperial decree was issued dispatching an envoy with jade and silk to go to that valley and sacrifice to it. (Zu Xiu’s Commentary states: "The inscription on the auspicious stone emerged spontaneously, manifesting the permanence of the divine mandate.

The old histories listed it in their annals, yet Ouyang Wenchong deleted it and included it in the 'Annals of Portents,' claiming that Empress Wu’s title as 'Compassionate One' (Cishi) and Zhongzong’s title as 'Buddha-Light Prince' (Foguang Wang) were verifications of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas. Now, the Tang dynasty possessed the realm for twenty successive reigns. )

Only Emperor Wuzong’s correct faith was slight; all others were individuals who had attained stages within the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, the Seven Buddhas, the Eight Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas of the higher fruits manifested as world-rulers, appearing according to what was appropriate and sporting within the cycle of birth and death.
How could this apply merely to Empress Wu Zetian and Emperor Zhongzong? (See *Jiaojing Tonglun*).
Jiachen (the eighteenth year):
The Fourth Patriarch, Great Master Daoxin, entrusted the Dharma to his disciple, Great Master Hongren. He spoke in verse: "The seed of the flower possesses the nature of arising;
because of the ground, the flower arises. When the great condition unites with faith, it shall give rise to non-arising. Thereupon, he [Hongren] began his studies.
[The Emperor] merely entrusted [the matter] to them (Wudeng). ○ The Emperor enacted the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Yijiao jing) and issued an edict stating:

"When the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa, because the latter age was degenerate and frivolous, he entrusted kings and great ministers to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma. However, as for monks and nuns who have left the household life, their observance of the precepts must be complete.

If they indulge their passions and abandon themselves to negligence, becoming entangled in afflictions and worldly affairs, they will constantly violate the sūtras and the vinaya. Having already lost [their way]..."

The profound and subtle purport of the Tathāgata has thus been deficient, as has the King’s duty to receive and uphold [the Dharma]. The *Śāsanānuśāsana Sūtra* was spoken by the Buddha at the time of his parinirvāṇa;
its exhortations to his disciples are exceedingly detailed and essential. Yet, among those in the degenerate age—both monastics and laypeople—it is not revered.

As the Great Way is about to vanish and these subtle words are on the verge of being lost, I constantly cherish the Holy Teachings and contemplate how to propagate and expound them. It is therefore appropriate that the relevant authorities be ordered to...
Ten scribes were appointed to transcribe many copies of the sutras, with the aim of ensuring they were fully implemented.
One copy was to be presented to each official of the capital of the fifth rank or above, as well as to the Prefectural Governors (Cishi) of all provinces.

Should they observe that the conduct of monks or nuns did not accord with the text of the sutras, they were to encourage and exhort them both privately and publicly, ensuring that the teachings were strictly observed (*Wenguancilin*). In the winter, Dharma Master Xuanzang returned from the Western Regions. The Master...
After traveling back and forth seventeen times and visiting over one hundred countries,
on the *bingzi* day of the first month of the *yisi* year (the nineteenth year),
Dharma Master Xuanzang brought the scriptures and images back to the capital. The Imperial Resident, Fang Xuanling, provided him with lodging.

At Hongfu Monastery, he submitted a memorial to inform the Emperor. On the *renchen* day, Xuanzang proceeded toward the Eastern Capital; on the *jihai* day of the second month, he was received at the Yiluan Hall.
The Emperor said, "Why did you not report your departure? He replied, "When I was about to leave, I submitted three memorials.

Because my sincere aspiration was humble and shallow, I did not receive your gracious permission. Unable to endure the distance from the Supreme Way, I have ventured to travel privately, acting on my own authority."
...of such a crime. I am deeply ashamed and fearful. The Emperor said, “The Master’s departure from the household life sets you apart from the laity.
That you were able to risk your life to seek the Dharma for the benefit of all living beings is something I greatly admire. You need not feel ashamed at all.

However, I have only wondered how you could reach here, given the vast distances of mountains and rivers and the differing customs of various lands. Thereupon, the Emperor questioned him extensively regarding the regions of India to the west of the Snowy Mountains.

The harmony of the jade-lamp era and its climate, the products of the land and its customs, the ancient sites of the Eight Kings, and the traces left by the Seven Buddhas—these are all things that Zhang Qian [Bo Wang] failed to transmit and which Sima Qian and Ban Gu were unable to record.
Having personally traveled those lands, I, Xuanzang, have committed them to memory without error.
He answered each question with systematic coherence. The Emperor was greatly pleased and said, "The Master has traveled through more than one hundred countries;
it would be no small honor to compile a *Record of the Western Regions* based on all you have observed regarding their mountains, rivers, and customs, to bequeath it to future generations.
When Xuanzang was about to conclude his audience and depart, the Emperor said to his attendants, "In the past, Fu Jian praised Dao’an as a 'divine vessel' (*shénqì*), and the entire nation..."
"Your Majesty, I observe that this Dharma Master’s speech is refined and elegant, and his character and integrity are upright and lofty. He does not merely live up to the ancients;
he truly surpasses them by a great margin. Sireng (Minister) Changsun Wuji said: "Truly so, as Your Majesty’s enlightened decree states.

Although Dao’an possessed noble conduct and vast learning, the merit of propagating the Dharma certainly does not equal that of this Dharma Master, who has personally approached the Holy Realm to deliberate upon the multitude [of teachings]."

"Excellent! You have thoroughly investigated the ultimate essence of our school. At that time, the Emperor was about to launch a punitive expedition against Goguryeo. Upon hearing that the Dharma Master had returned, he invited him for a brief audience.
As they conversed, they were unaware that evening had fallen. The Emperor said, "In our haste, I have not been able to fully express my thoughts.

I wish to travel east with you, the Dharma Master, to inspect the regions and observe the customs. During the intervals between giving commands, may we discuss matters further? Is this acceptable? He replied:

Xuanzang replied, "I have returned from afar and am further afflicted by illness; I am unable to accompany Your Majesty on this journey. The Emperor said, "In the past, you were able to travel alone through remote frontiers;
this current trip is but a mere step compared to that. Why do you still decline? Xuanzang replied, "When Your Majesty undertakes a campaign to the east, the six armies will provide protection.
In subduing the chaotic and executing the treacherous, there will surely be the merit of Muye and the victories of Kunyang. As for Xuanzang, I shall have no role [in such matters]."
It would merely serve as a useless burden upon the expenses of the journey; furthermore, when weapons are clashing in battle, the Buddha’s precepts forbid śramaṇas from observing such scenes.
We pray that Your Majesty will show compassion and grant us leave. The Emperor praised these words, accepted them, and desisted from the plan.

Xuanzang then memorialized that he had obtained six hundred and fifty-seven Sanskrit texts of sūtras and śāstras from the Western Regions, requesting permission to reside at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song to translate them for the benefit of the state. The Emperor...
The Emperor said: "Recently, for the sake of Empress Dowager Mu, I established Hongfu Monastery, and I have invited Xujing to perform translations there.

All that is required shall be deliberated upon with Yuanling. You, Xuanzang, may therefore request an official to guard the monastery gates to prevent any potential conflicts. The Emperor continued: "..."
The Master may be said to have devised a plan for preserving his person; it was appropriate that he should make such arrangements.

Upon his departure, the Emperor issued an edict to retain Fang Yuanling within the palace to exclusively oversee his protection, while all necessary provisions were to be supplied entirely from the imperial treasury. In this month, the Emperor personally led his troops to campaign against Goguryeo.
In the fifth month, Xuanzang entered Hongfu Monastery to translate scriptures. The monk Fachong resided at Kaiming Temple in Hangzhou and Suzhou.
[Daoshi] recorded: In this year, the deity of Gao Wang Temple in Jiaxing County descended to his priest and said, "Request Dharma Master Cong on my behalf to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

Following these words, [the priest] conferred them upon him. The deity further descended and said, "From this day forward, you must completely renounce all alcohol, meat, and the five pungent vegetables.
Should you later seek blessings, you may invite the assembly of monks to perform the *zhai* (fasting) and *xingdao* (ritual practice) within the temple. (From the *Sengzhuan*)

On the Bingwu day (the twentieth), in the first month, Li Siyi, the Director of the Grand Temple, died suddenly. After a day had passed, he revived and said that he had seen an official of the underworld. [The official] said:
"When you were nineteen years old, you once harmed living beings. [Li Siyi] replied: "At that time, I was at the assembly of Dharma Master Min in Anzhou, listening to the *Nirvāṇa*..."
...Pan. For what reason did they harm him there? When the officials went to pursue Master Min, there was a reply: "Min has been born in the realm of Golden Grain (Suvarṇabhasa);

he cannot be pursued. Let him be released and returned home. Once he had revived, a monk named Yuantong performed a repentance rite for him and exhorted him to recite the Diamond Sūtra five thousand times.
By evening, he died again. On the following day, he revived and said: "The official of the underworld said joyfully: 'He has returned home.'"

He performed meritorious deeds. Furthermore, Master Min dispatched a monk to deliver a message, stating that at that time he had committed no killing and had immediately released [the captive] to return home (*Gantong zhuan*).

○ In the third month, the Emperor returned to Chang’an. ○ On the *xinmao* day of the seventh month, Dharma Master Xuanzang presented to the throne the newly translated *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, the *Ṣaṇmukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, and the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra*.

The *Śāsanodbhava-śāstra* (Treatise on the Origin of the Holy Teaching) and the *Mahāyāna-saṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Great Vehicle Compendium Treatise), totaling five works in fifty-eight fascicles. [The Emperor] requested the Master to compose a Preface to the Holy Teaching;

however, in the year Bingshen, he issued a handwritten edict declining the honor and refusing the request. In the year Dingyou, the Dharma Master again submitted a memorial to extend his petition, and the Emperor by imperial decree granted it.
On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month, the Dharma Master Zhikai ascended the seat holding a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem), remaining silent.
He passed away. The Master was a preeminent master of his time; he did not rest his side against a mat and refused offerings or gifts.

The local governor erected a stupa for him. At that time, Shi Zhize resided at Biancai Temple. Although he lived among the monks, his quarters were desolate and simple, leading the community to call him a madman.
Zhize laughed and said, "Those who call others mad do not realize they themselves are mad. To leave the secular world and become a monk is simply—"
He was greedy for food and clothing; whether walking or staying, he was obstructed by them. He locked his doors and cabinets, engaging in all manner of accumulation and toil, never at ease.
Had this not been madness, there would be no one more mad than him—whereupon he clapped his hands and laughed aloud.
Furthermore, he could divide his body into two places to attend to offerings from people, sitting upright throughout the entire night (from the *Monk Biographies*).
In the twenty-first year, the *dingwei* year, the Emperor obtained a secret prophecy which stated:
"Three reigns after the Tang, a female ruler shall possess the empire. He subsequently summoned Li Chunfeng to inquire about the matter.
Li replied, "According to my calculations based on the arts of divination, the omens have already been established; she is currently within Your Majesty's own palace."
It was so. More than thirty years later, the spirit of the Lord of Poyang from Haiyan County descended during a regular sacrifice and said to the officiant:
"For my sake, request Dharma Master Fachong to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The assembly then welcomed the Master to deliver the lecture.
The spirit again descended and said to the officiant: "The divine realm is burdened by karmic obstacles and much suffering. Since hearing the Dharma, my body..."

Within his scales, small insects were devouring him and causing him great suffering; having finally obtained some relief, he prayed, "I beg you to request my teacher to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* once more.
The teacher then lectured on it for him again (*Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
On the twenty-first day of the sixth month in the year of Wushen, the Emperor was at the Yuhua Palace. He summoned Dharma Master Xuanzang and received him in the Yuhua Hall.

The Emperor, considering the Master’s virtue and learning to be profound and vast, wished for him to renounce the monastic life so that he might assist in the governance of state affairs. The Master replied, "Xuanzang humbly observes, O Your Majesty..."

The strategy for weaving together the eight regions of the world and the flourishing of the grand and harmonious enterprise were bestowed by Heaven; they did not depend on man—this is the first point.

To honor Confucianism and exalt virtue, to lighten taxes and mitigate punishments, so that the nine provinces and the four seas all attained peace and ease—this was further the spontaneous transformation through the Sage’s mind;
it did not depend on man—this is the second point. Profound benevolence reached far and wide, and the four barbarian tribes presented their tributes—this was further...
Third, that what is moved by the majesty of Heaven requires no assistance from man. Fourth, that when the Xianyun posed a threat, neither emperors nor kings could subdue them;

yet when Your Majesty took command of the realm and launched a single campaign, their nests were overturned and their lairs destroyed. Thus we know that where there is the Way, success is attained, requiring no assistance from man.
The Goryeo were but a minor vassal state; Emperor Yang returned with his army defeated, whereas Your Majesty led your troops to victory and captured tens of thousands of heads.

Thus we know that success depends on the sovereign and requires no reliance on others—this is the fifth point. Heaven and Earth are in harmonious balance (*tai*), and auspicious omens arrive in response to virtue;
they require no reliance on others—this is the sixth point. Even if Your Majesty were to require further talent, there are currently many who are the equals of Yi Yin and Lü Shang. [End of] Xuan...

"I, Xuanzang, am of humble and inferior capacity; how could I be worthy to participate in this? Nevertheless, to maintain the precepts within the monastic community and to propagate the bequeathed Dharma is my sincere aspiration.

I humbly beseech Your Majesty’s divine compassion to grant that this resolve remain unaltered until the end. The Emperor said, "Since you, Master, desire to spread the wondrous Way, I shall not obstinately oppose your lofty ambition.
The Emperor then asked which sutra he had been translating recently. He replied, "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. The Emperor—
The Emperor asked, "What meaning does it clarify? He replied, "It clarifies the meaning of Maitreya’s Seventeen Stages (Saptadaśabhūmi) as well as sets forth the Great Meanings.
The Emperor was deeply impressed by it and dispatched an envoy to retrieve the treatise into the palace; it consisted of one hundred fascicles in total.

Upon seeing that the phrasing and meaning were vast and profound, the Emperor said to his attendants, "When I examine the Dharma Master’s new treatise, it is like gazing at the heavens or looking out over the ocean; its height and depth are beyond measure. Looking toward the Confucians...
The Nine Schools of the Way are like small marshes and streams compared to the vast ocean.

Consequently, he issued an edict to the relevant authorities to select scribes from the Imperial Library to transcribe nine copies each of the newly translated sutras and treatises, ordering them to be bestowed upon the Governors-General of the Nine Circuits to be circulated and disseminated.

It was hoped that throughout the entire realm, all would together receive this previously unheard Dharma. [The edict was signed by] Minister of Education Changsun Wuji and Chief Secretary of the Chancellery Chu Suiliang.
Liangzou said: "The Buddha-dharma is profound and mysterious; neither devas nor humans can fathom it. Your Majesty’s supreme Way illuminates all, and you have established the Triple Gem.

You dispatched the Dharma Master to traverse perilous paths to seek the scriptures, so that they might be translated upon his return to the kingdom. This is like the initial preaching of Amrapālī, as if the Golden Mouth had opened anew.
All of this is moved by Your Majesty’s sagely virtue; we, your humble and ignorant subjects, are privileged to witness and hear it. [It is] suffering..."

The waves of the sea are vast; yet there is a refuge for ships and rafts. How much more so when Imperial compassion is so broad and far-reaching that it causes this [teaching] to be spread throughout the nine provinces, so that all the teeming masses may partake of the wondrous Dharma.
For us, your subjects, to encounter this after billions of kalpas is a matter of profound gratitude and good fortune.

When the Emperor had completed the *Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka of the Great Tang*, he proceeded to the Palace Hall of Celebratory Fortune (*Qingfu Dian*). He summoned the Dharma Master Xuanzang, who ascended the hall and was granted a seat. An imperial edict was then issued:
Shang Guan Yi, a scholar of the Hongwen Hall, read the text aloud before the assembled ministers. The wording was roughly as follows:

"The two polarities possess form, manifesting their covering and bearing to contain all living beings; the four seasons have no visible shape, secretly alternating cold and heat to transform all things.

Thus, when observing heaven and examining earth, even the mediocre and ignorant may recognize their beginnings; yet when clarifying the Yin and penetrating the Yang, even the wise and sagacious rarely exhaust their mysteries. However—"

Yet Heaven and Earth encompass Yin and Yang, yet they are easily recognized because they possess form. Yin and Yang reside within Heaven and Earth, yet they are difficult to fathom because they have no shape.
Thus we know that when forms are manifest, they can be verified; even a fool is not deluded by them.

But when forms are hidden and cannot be seen, even the wise remain confused. How much more so for the Way of the Buddha, which is profound and empty, riding upon the obscure and controlling the silent—vast and sublime!
It rescues the myriad beings and governs the ten directions; its majestic spirit is supreme above, and its divine power is unsurpassed below.

It remains ever-new throughout ten thousand kalpas, and through the operation of a hundred blessings, it endures eternally in the present. The wondrous Way is concentrated and profound—though one follows it, its limits remain unknown.
The flow of the Dharma is deep and tranquil—though one draws from it, its source cannot be fathomed. Thus we know that the ignorant and foolish are but muddled creatures, and their worldly efforts...
How could one who has humbly surrendered to its essential purpose fail to be free from doubt? Dharma Master Xuanzang directed his heart toward the Pure Land and journeyed alone, staff in hand.
As snow fell thickly at dawn, he lost his way amidst the tracks; as drifting sands rose at dusk, the heavens were obscured beyond the sky.

Having traveled to the ends of foreign lands, he sought out the True Teaching, drawing the clouds of compassion from the Western extremity and pouring down the rain of Dharma upon the eastern borders. O Sage...

The teachings that were deficient have been restored to their fullness; the sentient beings who were burdened by sin have returned to merit. This is like the cassia tree growing on high peaks, whose blossoms are only moistened by the falling dew;

or the lotus emerging from the green waves, whose leaves cannot be defiled by flying dust. It is not that the nature of the lotus is inherently pure; rather, it is because it is situated in such a place.
Yet the substance of the cassia is inherently upright precisely because that which it clings to is lofty; thus, even a minute thing cannot be burdened by it.

When what one relies upon is pure, then turbid things cannot defile it. Now, if even insentient plants and trees depend on the virtuous to achieve goodness, how much more so should sentient human beings rely on auspicious conditions to achieve prosperity?
It is my hope that this scripture shall circulate and spread, enduring as long as the sun and moon.

It is inexhaustible; this merit spreads afar, eternal and vast as heaven and earth. Thereupon, the Emperor personally inscribed a preface with his own brush and appended it to the beginning of the new scripture.

The Dharma Master submitted a memorial of thanks, to which the Emperor replied by hand: "My talent falls short of the refined jade of scholars, and my speech is ashamed of its lack of broad erudition.
As for the Buddhist scriptures (Nèidiǎn), I am especially unacquainted with them. I feel deep shame for the humble composition of this preface yesterday."

I am clumsy. To defile my filthy calligraphy upon the golden tablets and to mark out mere rubble within the forest of jewels—this is truly shameful. Having suddenly received your letter, I have mistakenly been granted such praise;
as I examine my own person and reflect upon my thoughts, my embarrassment increases all the more. My virtues are insufficient to be commended, yet you have needlessly condescended to offer thanks.

At that time, the Crown Prince, having beheld the Sacred Preface, subsequently composed the "Record of the Sacred Text. The Dharma Master submitted a memorial to express his gratitude. The Emperor again examined the new [work].
Regarding the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, its phrasing and purport were so subtle and profound that he consequently issued an edict to the Crown Prince to compose a postscript for it.
The text briefly states: "I have heard that from the time of Fuxi down to Zhuanxu, the essence of the teachings was limited to the patterns on tortoise shells;

from the time of the Yellow Emperor down to Youyu, the elegant mysteries reached their limit in bird-script characters. Even when examining the 'Cinnabar Books' to seek out the hidden, one remains utterly ignorant of the source of ultimate reality."

To recruit and record those who have mastered the subtle workings of reality is indeed the way of extraordinary joy; yet even so, their deeds illuminate the annals and histories, spreading the fragrance of the "Wind of Virtue" across the eight directions, and their benevolence permeates all living beings, stirring the waves of Yao’s legacy for ten thousand generations.
We humbly observe that Your Majesty, while turning the wheel of Dharma with effortless ease, gradually transforms the world as if it were the Garden of the Cock (Kukkuṭārāma);
and while Your Majesty sits with the imperial crown fixed upon the throne of the Victorious Hall, Your Spirit communes with Vulture Peak. You preside over the entire assembly of the Tamer of Men...

These imperial titles are beyond the reach of literary imagination; they exhaust the depths of Prajñā within the imperial edicts. How could the symbols of the *Xiang* and *Xi* hexagrams ever approximate them?
Yet, as the teachings spread across the vast ocean, all have heard the sounds of the Eight Liberations; as the instructions permeate the world, all have trodden the path of the Four Dhyānas.
Thus, throughout the three thousand worlds, every living being is worthy of being enfeoffed, and the ten billion Mount Sumerus are brought into the fold of the Tathāgata.
Sealed as a state guardian, its excellence surpasses that of previous kings; how could it be compared to them in the same breath?
The *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* is the essential tenet of the Great Enlightened One’s doctrinal school.

Once Master Xuanzang had completed his translation, I, during the leisure of my inquiries after his health, purified my mind in the treasure of the wondrous Dharma and respectfully recorded the Imperial decree to briefly express my praise. I have thus commanded the relevant officials to proceed accordingly.
Appended at the end of the volume: From this time on, the Emperor’s personal faith grew ever more profound.

He discussed the principles of the Dharma without ceasing from his lips, and his intimacy with the Master was so deep that there was never a moment’s interval between them. He frequently issued edicts to provide new robes and bedding, treating him as a member of his own family.
In the eighth month, he bestowed upon Xuanzang a hundred pieces of gold for a *mohana* robe and a precious razor. Xuanzang submitted a memorial of thanks.
In brief: The robe of forbearance blends its colors with the flowing clouds; the sword of wisdom is sharper than jade-cutting steel.
I shall reverently wear it to subdue the demons of affliction and fasten it on to sever the net of worldly toil.

After Emperor [Wu] returned from his expedition to Liaodong, his physical strength no longer matched his former vigor, and he harbored anxieties regarding life itself. Upon meeting the Dharma Master, he turned his attention toward the Great Teaching.

His health gradually recovered. Thereupon, [the Emperor] asked, "In what way can one propagate the Dharma so that it may be beneficial? What should be proclaimed first? Xuanzang replied, "Sentient beings sleep in delusion;

without wisdom, there is no way to awaken them. To cause the sprouts of wisdom to grow, the Dharma serves as their nourishment. To propagate the Dharma, one requires people; thus, ordaining monks is paramount. The Emperor was pleased.
In the ninth month, he issued an edict stating: "At the end of the Sui dynasty, the governance was lost and the empire fell into fragmentation. I..."

While suppressing the rebellion, he personally trod upon the front lines of battle, frequently braving wind and frost, and slept upon his horse. Recently, he suffered from illness and took medicine, yet it had not yet been cured;
only in the past few days has he finally recovered. Could this be due to the attainment of merit through good deeds?

[It was decreed that] one thousand persons shall be ordained at each monastery in the capital and in all provinces throughout the empire. In the tenth month, the imperial carriage returned to the capital. Imperial Decree.
The authorities established the Hongfa Monastery to the southwest of the Ziwai Hall at the Northern Gate, and kept Xuanzang within the imperial precincts.
During the day, he accompanied the Emperor in discussion; at night, he retired to the monastery to translate the scriptures.

In the tenth month, a man from Jizhou named You Tianzun performed the Three Sovereigns *zhāi* ritual and submitted its scriptures for presentation. An imperial edict ordered the various officials to deliberate on the matter, and they all condemned it as erroneous.

An imperial edict was issued to collect and burn those scriptures. Those scriptures had altered the "Three Sovereigns" (Sanhuang) to the "Three Caverns" (Sandong), thereby deluding and misleading the ignorant masses;
thus, their falsehoods were eradicated. (From the *Fodao Shilü*) In the twelfth month, the Crown Prince [performed rites] for Empress Wende.
When the construction of the Great Ci'en Monastery was completed, it was requested that Master Xuanzang preside over it, but the Emperor declined.

An edict was issued to select fifty eminent monks (*bhadanta*) instead. In this month, the Crown Prince prepared fifty precious carriages to welcome the eminent monks, with decorated pavilions and jeweled canopies.

Flowers and banners led the way as they entered the various temples within the city. The Prince and his hundred officials escorted them. The Emperor ascended the Anfu Gate tower, holding an incense burner to pay his respects;
only when the scriptures and images had all passed did he cease. The Emperor’s heart was greatly pleased (as recorded in the *Benzhuan*).
In the fourth month of the Jiyou year (the twenty-third year of Zhenguan), the Emperor visited Cuiwei Palace.

Master Xuanzang accompanied the imperial entourage. Whenever they discussed profound and abstruse matters, the Emperor would invariably roll up his sleeves and say, "I regret that my meeting with the Dharma Master came so late;
I have not yet fully realized the intent of propagating the Dharma. [In] the fifth month, the Emperor...
[The Emperor] reigned for fifty-three years. Gaozong ascended the throne.
*Comprehensive Mirror of Buddhism through Successive Dynasties* (Shishi tongjian), Volume Seven;
*Comprehensive Mirror of Buddhism through Successive Dynasties*, Volume Eight.
Compiled by Shi Benjue of Yian at Kuoshan in Song;
collated and edited by Layman Lan Chongqi of Wuhuan in Tang.
In the second month of the gengxu year of Gaozong (the first year of Yonghui),
Shi Mingjun died suddenly. Upon reviving, he said that he had seen two youths dressed in green robes who led him before the King of the Netherworld, who then questioned him.
"What deeds should I perform throughout my life? Xuǎn asked. Tán replied, "Simply recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King said, "Excellent!
If you complete one hundred thousand recitations, next year you will surely be reborn in the Pure Land; I, your disciple, shall not see you again. He then released him to return home.

because of this, both monastics and laypeople took refuge [in him]. Furthermore, at [Pei] County in Mianzhu, he commissioned a great statue three hundred feet tall.

[His prayers] were remarkably efficacious (according to his biography). In the tenth month, [the Emperor] established the Yuhua Palace as a monastery to honor the late Emperor posthumously and issued an edict for Dharma Master Xuanzang to reside there.
Chan Master Shenvu (also known as Dengzhao) of Gengshen (V) was born with white hair. He left home to study under a lecturer and became profoundly adept in contemplative practice (*guanxing*).

He frequently conferred the precepts upon ghosts and spirits, and they all ceased offering meat sacrifices. Consequently, humans and deities alike revered him; butchers and fishermen changed their vocations, and there were no [slaughterhouses] in the market.
[He] established a marketplace. In this year, he passed away while seated in meditation. In the third month, Master Jingzhi of Ximing Monastery passed away.

He had long suffered from a nasal obstruction caused by fleshy growths; despite hundreds of remedies, there was no success. A monk instructed him to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* ten thousand times.

When he reached exactly five thousand recitations, the fleshy rings fell away (from his original biography). Dharma Master Xuanzang translated the *Prajñā[pāramitā] Sūtra* at Yuhua Palace. The Emperor visited the Eastern [Capital].
The Emperor issued an imperial decree summoning the monks Yibao, Hui, Li, and others to Luoyang. They subsequently arrived at Hebi Palace to have an audience with the Emperor;

their discourses were highly commended, and by imperial decree they were stationed at Jingtu Monastery in the Eastern Capital. There, Yibao lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*), his reputation reaching even greater heights.
In the eighth month, the Emperor summoned the monk Jingtai and the Daoist Li Rong to the palace in Luoyang. The Emperor questioned them as follows:
Regarding the origins of the *Senglaoshi huahu jing* (The Scripture on the Monk Laozi’s Conversion of the Barbarians), Tai submitted a memorial stating:

"According to the *Jindai zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) by Pei Ziyè, both state that the Daoist Wang Fu was repeatedly defeated in debate with the śramaṇa Bozu.
Consequently, Wang Fu took the 'Western Regions' chapter of the *Hanshu* and fabricated the *Huahu jing*. Furthermore, the *Shoushen ji* and the *Youming lu* also [record this]."
Yun said, "Your Majesty, this is the fault of Fu for fabricating falsehoods. He then engaged in several rounds of debate with Li Rong, during which Rong repeatedly found himself defeated.
Rong further remarked, "The Great Way and the Lord Lao are what Your Majesty reveres; why have you, originating from the Western Regions, come to disturb the Eastern Xia?"
Tai said: "The Tathāgata appeared in that place as the sovereign among devas; Your Majesty reigns over this realm as the rightful ruler of the earth.

Since the Buddha-dharma has been entrusted to the Emperor and King, there is a necessary resonance between us; how can one speak of 'this side' or 'that side'? Later, he repeatedly posed difficult questions."
The assembly dispersed late at night. The following day, the Emperor ordered the attendant Wang Junde to reprimand Li Rong for his failure in debate.
Li Rong replied that he had acted imprudently because of this; consequently, he was sent back to Zizhou. Among the Daoist community, prestige rested solely upon Rong;

now that he had faltered in his discourse, the entire sect’s reputation was tarnished. At that time, Du Tai was known for his talent and eloquence, and he further distinguished himself by composing a poem.
[The Emperor] praised him highly. The Emperor immediately issued an edict to the relevant authorities regarding Jing’ai Temple, stating that Sengtai could reside there.

When Sengtai entered the temple, he frequently ascended to positions of honor and prestige (Lunheng). As for Shi Fachong: at the beginning of the Zhenguan era, an edict was issued stating that those who privately ordained themselves would be subject to the ultimate punishment.
Fachong vowed to sacrifice his life and immediately shaved his head. At that time, Mount Yiyang had many monks fleeing there to seek refuge.
Hui-chong then divided the monks into two groups, each provided with ten *hu* of rice in a granary.

In one location, there were over forty disciples who studied exclusively the Mahāyāna and practiced the cultivation of dhyāna; after a year, their consumption of rice remained as it was, without diminishing.

In the other location, there were fifty or sixty people; barely two days had passed when their rice was completely exhausted, because they did not practice dhyāna and instead engaged in external studies. Hui-chong said:
This is not to be wondered at. One who is able to practice the Way is merely the grace of the white tuft [of hair between the Buddha’s brows].

At that time, those fleeing the turmoil became increasingly numerous, and there was nowhere for them to seek shelter. On a mountain there was a tiger’s den; Hui-chong went to it and said, “I am now a destitute guest seeking refuge;

may you grant me your hospitality? The tiger then led him away by the hand. When the crisis had passed, Hui-chong propagated the Dharma wherever he went. Although Hui-chong widely proclaimed the scriptures and arts, [the people]...
He specialized exclusively in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and made it the foundation of his family tradition. Du Zhenglun, the Secretary of the Palace Secretariat, frequently sought instruction from him.
At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang did not permit the lecturing on previously translated scriptures. Huizhong said, "You were ordained according to the old translations;

if you do not permit the propagation of the old scriptures, you may return to lay life and be ordained again according to the new translations—only then will I grant your request. When Xuanzang heard this, he [withdrew].
He then ceased [his journey]. This master was truly a man of exceptional strength who propagated the sutras and protected the Dharma for his generation;

he was one whom no one could surpass. Yu Zhi-ning, the Vice President of the Secretariat, remarked: "This Dharma Master is a dhūta monk of the Dharma-realm; he cannot be constrained by the limitations of name and reality."

After [the Emperor] Chong returned, he turned toward the Eastern Xia (China), it is said (according to his biography). ○ An imperial edict was issued to the monk Zhizong to welcome the śarīra from Qishan.
Thereupon, it was moved to emit light and manifest auspicious omens. Xinyou (the first year of Longshuo).
The monk Mingjie of Puguang Monastery in the capital was of keen intelligence. In lute-playing, poetry, calligraphy, and painting, there was no one at the time who could rival him.
However, he was addicted to wine and dissipated his mind. During the Xianqing era, when the Emperor established Ximing Monastery, he ordered Dharma Master Lingrun to select a resident for it.
At that time, several officials came together to Lingrun’s quarters and jointly recommended Mingjie. Lingrun said, "Gentlemen..."

"One ought to seek the training in precepts, concentration, and wisdom to increase one's field of merit. Why then do you propose a wine-drinker and a painter to be entrusted with such a great responsibility?

The officials withdrew in shame, and Mingjie felt deeply resentful. Shortly thereafter, an imperial decree was issued summoning candidates from the four categories of examination, making no distinction between monastics and laypeople.
Mingjie responded to the summons by nominating himself; he took the test, passed the rankings, and his joy was beyond measure. Before long, he fell ill and saw dozens [of figures] before him.
The man held a fierce torch and came to welcome [Ming]jie. As soon as he spoke the words, "You have committed great terror," [Ming]jie passed away; it was the eighth month of that year.
Later, he appeared in a dream to the monk Hui-zheng and said, "Because I did not follow the Inner Teachings in the past, I now undergo great suffering.
I beg for a single meal from you. When Hui-zheng awoke, he prepared food. That night, he dreamed that [Ming]jie came to thank him. This occurred again during the autumn of the second year.
He entrusted his dream to a painter. [The Emperor] said, "I have been addicted to non-Buddhist books; now I am undergoing great suffering. For my sake, write two or three fascicles of scripture.
He further composed a poem to bid farewell. The painter then transcribed the scriptures for him. Later, the Emperor dreamed that the painter came to express his thanks (*Zijing lu*).

In the ninth month, the Emperor visited the old residence of the High Ancestor at Tiangong Temple, where he established a vegetarian feast and ordained monks. The Emperor toured the site, feeling deep sorrow.

He remained sorrowful for a long time (*Tongji*). ○ Shi Yanzong compiled the *Dajiang Jingdilu* (Record of the Temples of the Capital of the Great Tang) in ten fascicles, narrating the miraculous traces of the Triple Gem.
This was in the year of Renxu (the second year of Longshuo).
In the fourth month, a fire broke out at the garrison city of Yuyang County in Youzhou, reducing the private residences to ashes and embers;
only two temples and ten Buddha statues were not consumed by the flames (Zhu lin). The Emperor issued an edict that monks, nuns, and Daoist priests should wear official headgear.

Regarding the matter of paying obeisance to sovereigns and parents: on the fourth month, the monks of Dazhuangyan Monastery, Wei Xiu and others, submitted a memorial stating that it was improper for them to prostrate before laypeople.

It stated in brief: "We monks have received the profound grace of the state; by being permitted to observe the rites of those beyond the mundane world, we are able to propagate our resolve to transcend worldly life."

"Since antiquity, emperors and kings have all adhered to this standard. They have revered the rituals for changing customs and preserved the traces of those who maintained their independent conduct [in relation to the throne] (and so forth).
The Right Minister Xu Jingzong and others proclaimed the imperial decree, saying: 'The Emperor has ordered a detailed deliberation, yet whether one should prostrate or not remains undecided.
You may wait for the next assembly. Thereupon, the monk Daoxuan and others recounted the history of the rise and fall of Buddhism to the various ministers. (5)

On the fifteenth day of the month, the civil and military officials were assembled in a grand gathering; they sat together in the Hall of State to deliberate on affairs. At that time, the discussions among the assembly were tumultuous.
Those who proposed that [the edict] be prostrated before were three hundred and fifty-four people; those who proposed that it not be prostrated before were five hundred and thirty-nine people.

On the eighth day of the sixth month, the imperial decree was proclaimed, which stated in brief: "I have deliberated upon the various opinions and deeply investigated their profound subtleties. However..."
The spirit of Jíyǐng (the sages of Mount Jí and River Yǐng) held their principles in high esteem. Looking back to former ages, such examples certainly existed.

From this point forward, it is not appropriate to perform prostrations [before images]. Let the authorities carry out this instruction. (*Hongming ji*) The Emperor and Empress first visited Tóngzǐ Temple in Bingzhou.
The Great Image there was seventeen *zhàng* in height. In the seventh month of that year, they dispatched an envoy to present a *kāṣāya*. At that time, the image emitted a great light.

*Guangming* (Radiance). The entire city was converted to the good. (*Zhulin*) On the eighth day of the twelfth month, at the Penglai Palace, the Dharma Master Lingbian was summoned to expound the title of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*.
He subsequently engaged the monks in debate. By the fourteenth day, the Daoist Fang Huichang expounded the title of the *Laozi*.
Lingbian debated his doctrine that "the Dao gives birth to the myriad things. Huichang [replied] repeatedly...
Lingbian had no answer to offer. He then submitted a memorial, saying: "I, Lingbian, am an unworthy member of the Buddhist school and truly cherish compassion and forbearance.

Even if I were to encounter a dead sparrow, I would not wish to strike it again with my bow. The Emperor laughed heartily and praised him as excellent. From the reigns of Emperors Xuanzong and Gaozong, Lingbian traveled to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang), where his reputation spread throughout the imperial court.

Subsequently, by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Da Cien Monastery. He frequently entered the palace to debate doctrinal points, and the Emperor always honored and rewarded him. (*Lunheng*)
At that time, Shi Huiming wore but a single robe throughout both winter and summer; his conduct was serene and detached, and he felt no lingering attachment wherever he went.

He constantly recited the *Siyi jing* (The Sutra of Increased Benefit). At that time, the Venerable Shandao entered the capital to widely transform people, leading them to recite the name of Amitābha and cultivate the practice of Pure Land.

While he was preaching the Dharma at Guangming Temple, someone asked him: "If one now recites the Buddha's name, will one definitely be reborn in the Pure Land? Shandao replied: [He spoke as follows: "..."
Entering into meditative concentration after concentration, he then recited the name of Amitābha Buddha with his voice continuing in an unbroken stream.

With each utterance, a Buddha emerged from his mouth. As he exited the temple gate and ascended to the top of a willow tree, he joined his palms toward the west, prostrated himself upon the ground, and passed away (from the *Benzhuan*).
Guihai (the third year of Longshuo):
The Great Being of Sizhou, Saṃgha, initially traveled from the kingdom of Shule to Xiliang, and subsequently manifested his transformative teachings in Luoyang (from his *Benzhuan*).
In the sixth month, Cui Yiqi, a Gentleman of the Court for Minor Ceremonials, did not believe in Buddhism; however, his father-in-law, Xiao Keng, was skilled at reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Qi’s wife died in the fifth month. While the thirty-seven-day *zhāi* (fasting) ritual was being observed for her, a maidservant named Suyu spoke with the voice of the lady, saying:
"I am suffering the torments of hell because you recited the scriptures and lit lamps; I have been granted a brief leave to return. On the twentieth day, I shall come again."
She sent Su-yu away. Su-yu saw the Lady suffering the torments of the fiery cauldron and saw Xiao Keng seated upon a flower dais.
She told Su-yu, "My daughter was full of anger and did not believe in good and evil; she now suffers these torments. When you return, you may tell her husband and son."

To cultivate merit for her sake, Sengjiao Su-yu was commissioned to recite the *Vajra-Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. A maidservant who had been dead for three days then revived.

Later, in the second year of the Linde era, during a vegetarian feast for the monastic community at General Xue’s residence, Su-yu was invited to recite the scripture she had received from the underworld.
The entire assembly marveled at this as a rare occurrence. Xue subsequently reported the matter orally to the Emperor, who sighed in admiration, saying, "The realm of the unseen."
If this is so, how could one not believe it? When the court nobles heard of this, they all conceived great faith (from the *Gantong lu*).
In the eleventh month, Dharma Master Xuanzang completed his translation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, totaling six hundred fascicles (from the *Benzhuan*).

In the sixth year of the Yonghui era, the Tripiṭaka Master Nadi (translated as "Fusheng" in Chinese) arrived at the capital carrying fifteen hundred Sanskrit texts; by imperial decree, he was settled [there].
He was stationed at Cien Monastery. At the beginning of the Xianqing era, he was commanded by imperial decree to travel to the various kingdoms of Kunlun to collect medicinal herbs.

He returned to the capital that year with the intention of widely disseminating the Sanskrit scriptures he had brought back; however, as all of them had been taken northward by Xuanzang, he was able to translate only three sutras.
Soon thereafter, he was requested by the kingdom of Chenla to return. However, Saṃghadeva was a disciple of Nāgārjuna who had profoundly mastered the *tathatā* (the true nature of reality).

His composed treatises on Mahāyāna doctrine were intended to be translated; that he was sent away resulted in the lament of "one who would have embraced the麒麟 (qílín—mythical beast) being lost," a precedent that has occurred throughout history.
How difficult it is to truly know a person! Saṃghadeva had traveled from afar carrying the Way, only to find himself cast into the northern wilderness. Finding no one there to rely upon, he then...

Three times he was poisoned. He served as a laborer in the south for many years, traversing tens of thousands of miles of rugged terrain, yet his original aspirations were not fulfilled. Alas, what a pity! (From the *Monk Biographies*).

In the second month of the Jiazi year (the first year of Linde), Dharma Master Xuanzang commanded his disciple Dachengguang to record the sutras and śāstras he had translated; in total, there were seventy-five.
He compiled one thousand three hundred and thirty-five fascicles. He summoned his disciples to collectively create images and establish a vegetarian feast.
Taking leave of the assembly, he instructed those around him to recite the name of Maitreya Tathāgata. At the fifth watch of the middle of the night, he lay down on his right side and passed away.

He was sixty-five years old. The Emperor suspended court for three days, and the ministers and officials wept with grief. A monk of extraordinary character offered incense to anoint the Master’s body.

In the fourth month, by imperial decree, following the precedent of the World-Honored One, he was enshrined in a golden inner coffin and a silver outer coffin, and his stupa was erected on the eastern plain of the San River.
His disciples Shen Tai, Yuanhui, Yin Hui, Liliang, Mingjun, Yibao, Dacheng, Guang,
and others were all "dragon elephants" (eminent leaders) within the Dharma gate (according to their respective biographies).
In the second year of the Yichou cycle (605), at Faju Temple in Yizhou, there was Zhang Sengyou, who painted an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.

In the seventh month of that year, a monk of the temple obtained a copy of it, which emitted light. Those who successively copied it all likewise had their images emit light. [The monk] Huiyu also made a copy.
He produced miraculous images of the Buddha at Changsha and other locations in Jingzhou. When they reached the capital, they emitted light while at the Duting Hall;

those who heard or saw this were moved to resolve their minds toward enlightenment, each painting an image as an offering (*Zhu lin*). In the second month, the Crown Prince, for the sake of the two sagely emperors, commissioned a bronze bell weighing ten thousand jin at Ximing Monastery.
In the second month of Bingyin (the first year of Qianfeng) and Dingmao (the second year),
Master Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery was at Jingye Monastery when a celestial deity arrived to pay his respects and questioned him.
As for his surname and name, he was styled Wang Fan; he was an official of the Lan-tai (Palace Library) in Wu and served as a messenger under the Heavenly King of the South.
Furthermore, another deity arrived whose surname was Luo; he was a native of Shu and extensively expounded upon the characteristics of the Vinaya. Next, another deity arrived whose surname was Fei;
he paid homage as before and said that General Wei has thirty-two generals, the most prominent among whom is Hong.

Huguang asked about the hidden meanings within the Vinaya, and there was nothing he did not resolve. He further inquired about the famous mountains and sacred sites of this land, and [Huguang] answered them all.
There was also a celestial being named Lu Yuanchang who came to visit the Master;

he inquired about the accounts of those transformed by King Mu and the origins of the various images on Mount Wutai, to which [Huguang] provided detailed answers for each (Fayuan zhulin). In the eighth month, he proclaimed the Vinaya.

When the Master passed away, an imperial edict was issued in mourning for him. A decree was sent to all temples throughout the empire, ordering that his portrait be depicted and an image be sculpted to serve as a model for emulation.
His secular surname was Qian. Initially, when his mother was pregnant with him, she dreamed of a monk who told her that she was carrying the Venerable Yu.
