Upon his ordination, his nature harmonized with the Way; wherever he went, he invariably moved divine beings to provide protection and served him celestial food. Once, while practicing the Way in the middle of the night...
As he was stepping onto the stone steps, he stumbled and fell. A youth in armor caught and supported him, asking who he was.
He replied, "I am Zhang Qiong, a prince of the deva king Pāñcika. Because your master’s precepts and virtue are so sublime, I have come to provide protection.
Xuán then inquired extensively about matters concerning the Buddha-dharma, and Qiong explained them one by one. Upon their parting, Qiong presented Xuán with a Buddha’s tooth relic and a jewel.

He held these two works in his hands, concealing them as tokens of faith. His master compiled the *Neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures), the *Sanbao gantong lu* (Record of Miraculous Responses of the Triple Gem), the *Fudao lunheng* (Weighing of Buddhism and Daoism),

the *Shijia pu* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni), the *Sifen jiemmo* (Quadruple-Part Ordination Rite), the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks), and the *Guang hongming ji* (Extended Collection for the Propagation and Clarification [of Buddhism]),
totaling eighty-one fascicles in eight sections, which remain in circulation today.

In the year Wuchen (the first year of the Zongzhang era), the Emperor summoned monks and Daoists to the Baifu Hall to determine the authenticity of the *Huahu jing* (Sutra on Laozi Converting the Barbarians). The various officials attended as witnesses.
The discussion was tumultuous, until the monk Faming said: "At the time when Laozi converted the barbarians and became a Buddha, he composed the *Huahu jing* in the Hu-language."
"Did you compose it in the Hu language to entice them? If you had composed it in Chinese, the Hu people would not have been proficient in it;
if you had composed it in the Hu language, then having already transmitted it to this land, one would have had to rely on a bilingual interpreter.

I do not know in which generation the *Huahu jing* was translated, nor who served as the scribe for the oral transmission and the verifier of the meaning. Thereupon, the entire assembly was struck with astonishment, and none were able to respond. The high officials and nobles...

Emperor Bì was entirely convinced by its appropriateness; he rejoiced and brought the matter to a close. He issued an edict to search throughout the empire for the *Huahu jing* (Scripture on Converting the Barbarians), ordering it to be burned and discarded so that it would no longer be counted among the Daoist scriptures.
Subsequently, the Daoist priests Bǎi Yàndào and others submitted a memorial requesting that it be retained. The Emperor’s decree stated:

"The three sages have shed their radiance once more, and the Mysterious Origin has presided over the order. How could I forget the teachings of Lǎozi? It is not that I harbor a partiality for the school of Śākyamuni. My resolve is sincere: I seek to return to simplicity."
The intent is to eliminate the false. Those whose principles are contrary and whose actions are aberrant shall be excluded, even if they are kin.

Those whose righteousness accords with their titles and whose names are appropriate shall be recorded, even if they harbor grievances. From this day forward, all records within the various sections of the Daoist scriptures concerning the "Conversion of the Barbarians" (Huahu) shall be expunged.

Let the relevant authorities draft this as a penal regulation. (The *Yinzilun* states: Initially, the Wei Daoists Jiang Bin and others compiled the *Taishang Kaitian Jing*, in which they extensively discussed the matter of the Conversion of the Barbarians.)

He engaged in debate with Tanmuzu, who was forced to acknowledge his own fallacies. Furthermore, the renowned official Zhen Luan composed the *Xiaodao lun* (Treatise on Laughing at the Dao) in thirty-six chapters, refuting the absurdity of Laozi’s transformation into a Buddha; this work is now included in the Buddhist canon. During the Sui dynasty, the Chancellor Yang Su remarked: "Why did Laozi transform the Hu into a Buddha? Why did he not instead transform the Hu into a Daoist?

These words are particularly effective in exposing the error. He further stated: "When Laozi first attempted to convert the Hu, they would not comply. He then ordered Yin Xi to use the words of a Buddha to convert them, and only then did the Hu follow him.
This implies that the Buddha already existed before Laozi, yet it was not Laozi who could convert the Hu, but the Buddha who converted them."
In the year Jisi (the second year), Shi Tongda resided at Lüzang Temple in the capital. He wore a single robe and a single shawl, both patched and double-sewn from coarse cloth.

As for the hemp sandals he wore, they remained so for thirty years; he never adorned his body with silk or fine fabrics. Wearing the same garment through both winter and summer, it did not even become worn or tattered.
Yan. The Palace Secretary Fang Yuanling served him as his father’s teacher. Since the Zhenguan era, he had gradually manifested supernatural wonders.
When he visited people's homes, laughter portended good fortune, while sorrow and distress invariably signaled misfortune. If he requested wealth or goods, they had to be provided accordingly;
if one failed to follow his words, subsequent losses would exceed those incurred previously. General Xue Wanjun welcomed him and made offerings to him for over a hundred days.
When he wished to enter the inner quarters for the night, Xue struck him. Da said, "The blood from my body is impure; you may use it to make broth for washing.
He then stripped off his clothes and entered a boiling cauldron, appearing as if he were in cold water. Consequently, the entire household was struck with awe and offered their devotion.

At that time, grain was expensive, and he wished to host a great vegetarian feast. He ordered the monastery to send out many invitations; by dawn, several thousand people had arrived, yet the provisions remained silent and empty. Suddenly—
There was a meal served, and a carriage arrived carrying it. When the meal was finished, neither the people nor the carriage were seen (according to the original biography).
Gengwu (the first year of Xianheng) and Xinwei (the second year).
The Chan Master Ying of Fahai Temple in the Western Capital was visited by a strange person who said:

"Your disciple knows of the Water and Land Feast, which can benefit both the unseen and the seen worlds. Since the passing of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, it has been neglected and not performed. Now, at Dajue Temple..."

There was a monk named Yiji who preserved these ritual texts. [The Master] wished for the Master to go and seek them, so that on the fifteenth day of the following month, they might be prepared according to the Dharma at Shanbei Temple.
"If my imprisonment is truly released, I dare not fail to repay your kindness. Master Ying soon visited Yiji, obtained the ritual texts, and returned home.
On the appointed day, he prepared the rites at Shanbei Temple. The following day, as dusk fell, he turned toward—
He was not an ordinary man. Accompanied by a dozen or so followers, he came to offer his thanks, saying, "I am the disciple Qin Zhuangxuan Wang.
He then pointed to his attendants and said, "These are Fan Sui, Rang Hou, Bai Qi, Wang Jian, Zhang Yi, and Chen Zhen; they were all ministers of Qin."
They all sit upon their original offenses, imprisoned in the dark underworld. In the profound obscurity of the great night, there is no one able to provide rescue or protection.
Formerly, when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty established this vegetarian feast at Jinshan Temple, the ministers of King Zhou of a previous age were all relieved of their suffering;

at that time, I, your disciple, also briefly ceased my own torment. Yet, because the judgment of my karmic case had not yet been finalized, I was unable to escape. Now, I have received the grace of my Master...
A vegetarian feast was prepared. The disciple, along with this assembly and the various feudal lords of the neighboring states, all relied on the power of their merit to be reborn among humans.

Fearing that the world would change and the nations become distant, they came here to offer their thanks. Having finished speaking, they suddenly vanished. From this time forth, this became the formal ritual procedure.

He traveled throughout the world, bringing great benefit. (From Master Zhe’s *Weijiang ji*) ○ Dharma Master Yijing was thirty-seven years old when he went to the Western Regions to seek Buddhist scriptures.
In the third year, the *wuchen* year, the Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren, was teaching and transforming beings at Póutóu Mountain in Huángméi, Qí Prefecture.
At that time, the Sixth Patriarch was Layman Lu of Lìngnán, named Huínéng; he was thirty-two years old when he came to visit the Patriarch, saying: "I have come seeking to become a Buddha."

The Patriarch said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature. He replied, "People have north and south, but how could Buddha-nature be like that? The Patriarch marveled at this and said, "Go to the granary.
Hui-neng entered the rice-hulling mill and performed manual labor for eight months. The Master then told the assembly, "Each of you compose a verse;
if the words and meaning correspond perfectly, I shall bestow both the robe and the Dharma upon you. The Elder Shenxiu wrote a verse, saying: "The body is..."
"The Bodhi tree; the mind is like a bright mirror-stand. At all times diligently wipe it clean; do not allow dust to gather upon it.
When the Master saw this, he said, "If one practices according to this, one may also attain the fruit of the Way. He who was able to hear this also had someone write beside Xiu’s verse:
"The Bodhi tree originally has no tree; the bright mirror is likewise no stand. Originally there is not a single thing; where could there be dust?"
When Master [Nanyue] saw this, he asked, "Who made this? [Huai]’an replied, "I have not yet seen my nature. That very night, the Master secretly summoned Huai’nan and told him:

"The Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition. According to the capacities of beings—whether small or great—they guide and transform them, resulting in the various teachings such as the Three Vehicles.
Nevertheless, the subtle, wondrous, and secret Treasury of the True Dharma Eye has been entrusted to Kāśyapa."
[The robe] was passed down through successive generations until it reached me. I now transmit it to you. Listen to my verse:
"When sentient beings come to plant seeds, fruits grow back according to the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, that which lacks nature also has no birth.

After he had finished receiving [the robe] while kneeling, [Huineng] further said: "Let this robe remain with your person; do not transmit it further. You must travel far away for now, waiting for the right time to go forth and transform others. When you encounter..."
Huai said, "Stop for now; when we meet again, you shall hide it. Neng took his leave and traveled south through the night. Because of this, the Master did not ascend the hall for three days.
When the assembly questioned him about this, the Master said, "My Way has gone forth. They further asked, "Who will transmit the robe and the Dharma? The Master replied, "Neng will transmit them.
The assembly realized this referred to Layman Lu, but by then he was already gone. They followed one another in pursuit, catching up with him at... [the place where they caught up].
At the summit of Mount Dayu, he was able to place his robe and bowl upon a rock. The Venerable Huiming arrived first and tried to lift them, but could not move them.
He said, "I have come to seek the Dharma; I do not seek your robes.

The Sixth Patriarch then said, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—at this very moment—return to me, Venerable Huiming, your original face. Huiming attained great enlightenment and cried out, "Mimi! (A secret!)
"Is there not further meaning beyond these words? The Sixth Patriarch said, "What I have just told you is not secret.
If you turn back and reflect upon yourself, the secret is right within you. The Sixth Patriarch was commanded to go north to receive disciples.
Later, when he arrived at Caoxi, he was again pursued by malicious people; he therefore concealed his traces between Sihuai and Huaiji. Four...
In his later years, he lived in seclusion among hunters, constantly preaching the Dharma for them; many among the hunters attained enlightenment.
In the fourth year of the Guiyou cycle, there was the divine monk Master Wanhui.
When he was young, he was able to deliver letters to his elder brother from three thousand *li* away, departing in the morning and returning by evening.
For this reason, he was titled Wanhui. The Emperor then ordained him as a śramaṇa.
Jiaxu (the first year of Shangyuan) and Yihai (the second).
The Fifth Patriarch, Master Hongren, suddenly addressed the assembly, saying: "My work is now finished; it is time to depart. He then entered his room, sat upright, and passed away.
His age was seventy-four, and he was interred at Mount Dongshan. Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chan Master Daman.

(According to the *Wudeng lu* and the *Zhengzong ji*, it is recorded that the Master met the Fourth Patriarch at age seven in the Jia-shen year of the Wu-de era; if one were to claim that his age was seventy-four in this [present] year, it must be an error. If [it were true that] his age was seventy-four in this year, then [the date would be... Jia...

This year is the Year of the Monkey, and I am twenty-three years old. If I were seven years old in the Jia-Shen year, then my lifespan would end at fifty-eight this year. (Either the former is mistaken, or the latter is mistaken.)

In the first month of the Bingzi year (the first year of the Yifeng era), the Sixth Patriarch arrived at Faxing Monastery in Guangzhou. There he encountered Dharma Master Yinzong, who was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
At that time, a wind blew and the banners moved; one monk said, "The banners move," while another said, "The wind moves. The Patriarch then said, "It is neither the banners that move..."

"It is not the wind that moves; it is your mind, O virtuous one, that moves. Upon these words, the two men attained great enlightenment. When Yinzong questioned them further, they immediately performed the rites of a disciple.
He then shaved the head of the Sixth Patriarch and invited Vinaya Master Zhiguang to confer upon him the full precepts.

In the second year of the Dingchou cycle, the Sixth Patriarch moved his residence to Baolin Temple on Mount Shuangfeng at Caoxi in Shaoshan. The Regional Inspector Wei Ju invited him to the Dafan Temple to preach the Dharma;
there were over one thousand monastics, nuns, and laypeople in the assembly, as well as the regional inspector’s officials and subordinates. Three...
There were more than ten people present. On this day, he extensively expounded the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*). His disciple Fahai transcribed it for circulation;
this is the present *Platform Sutra*. (3rd year of Wuyin)
The two fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* following the cremation were produced by the śramaṇa Huìníng in the kingdom of Pǎolíng in South India.
Yàonábátuóluó (translated as Zhìxián) brought them from the kingdom of Pǎolíng during the Year of the Qín-fèng (the year of the dragon).
They were sent from South India to Jiāozhōu, and subsequently, they were conveyed to the capital. In that same year, the śramaṇa Línghuì formally requested the imperial favor at the Eastern Palace.

(Xiàozhì jiàolù). In the first month of the Jǐmǎo year (the first year of the Tiáolù era), the lay practitioner Dú Xíngyǐ translated the *Fódǐng shèngzhòu jīng* (Sūtra of the Victorious Dhāraṇī of the Buddha’s Crown) in one fascicle. Xíngyǐ was a native of Jīngzhào.
During the Yifeng era, while serving as the Director of the Dianke Bureau at the Honglu Si, Yan Yi was exceptionally proficient in Sanskrit.

Consequently, through the Kasmirian monk Buddhapāli, he presented the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* to the Emperor, who then issued an edict ordering its translation; it is currently preserved in the canon.

In the year Gengchen (the first year of Yonglong) and Xinsi (the first year of Kaiyao), there was Bodhiruci from South India, who was a preeminent master of the Western Regions. When the Emperor heard of his reputation, he was delighted by it. Consequently...
When the Western Regions were dispatched on an embassy, an imperial decree was issued to earnestly invite Quan Wuer, a scholar of the Crown Prince’s Academy.

He composed ten points of inquiry regarding doubts concerning the Buddhist scriptures to question the Dharma Master Xingshan Fuli. Fuli then compiled the *Ten-Section Treatise on Dispelling Delusions* in two fascicles to explain them;
thus, the collective doubts were instantly dispelled. Although this was a response for a single occasion, it truly serves as a mirror for ten thousand generations.
This is a mirror [of the text] currently circulating in the world.
In the fifth month of the Renwu year (the first year of Yongchun), Rizhao retranslated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (this version contains many errors). [Endorsed by] Master Kuiji of Cien.

Daoci passed away at the age of fifty-one. An imperial edict was issued in mourning for him, and the Emperor composed a eulogy for his portrait. He was granted burial in the North Canal of Fanchuan, near the tomb of Master Xuanzang.

Daoci was of robust appearance and compassionate heart; he once commissioned a jade statue of Mañjuśrī and had the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* transcribed in gold, both of which yielded auspicious responses.
Initially, Vinaya Master Daoxuan had moved the heavens through his propagation of the precepts, such that they provided him with offerings from a celestial kitchen.

Sengji (Sengqi) often treated the trifles of the Three Vehicles with disdain and did not observe the proper rites very strictly. Once, when Sengji visited Daoxuan, it was past noon and the celestial food had not yet arrived.
When Sengji took his leave, the heavenly deity then descended. Daoxuan rebuked him for being late, and the deity replied, "Just now I saw that a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva was here;
his retinue was so formidable that I could not enter of my own accord. Upon hearing this, Daoxuan was greatly impressed.

Everyone was struck with awe; thus, those both far and near increased their reverence for him. Previously, Master Xuanzang had personally transmitted the Yogācāra-bhūmi and the Vijñaptimātra school from the Western Regions to Śīlabhadra, and Ji had mastered all its subtleties.
Consequently, the world designated this as the "School of the Manifest Principles of the Three Vehicle Dharma-Characteristics" (San-sheng Fa-xiang Xian-li Zong), known as the Cien Teaching.
At this time, the hermit Sun Simiao passed away; he was well-versed in the *Zhuangzi*, *Laozi*, Yin-Yang theory, and medicine.
In the art of medicine, he placed particular emphasis on the Buddhist scriptures; thus, the world honored him as "Master Sun.
In the twelfth month of the Guiwei year (843 CE), Emperor Gaozong passed away and Emperor Zhongzong ascended the throne.
Originally, there was a śramaṇa from Kapiśā in the northern Indian region named Buddhapālita (translated into Chinese as Juehu).

In the first year of the Yifeng era, he arrived at Mount Wutai, the Cool Mountain, where he encountered an old man who asked him, "For what purpose have you come? He replied, "I wish to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
The old man asked, "Have you brought with you the *Buddhottamasikhā-tilaka* mantra? He replied, "No. The old man said, "The sentient beings of this land commit the four pārājika offenses."
There were many such [instances]. He was able to retrieve the dhāraṇī and transmit it to this land, thereby performing great benefit.
The disciple then showed the Master where Mañjuśrī resided; suddenly, the old man vanished. Póli then returned to his native country, retrieved the dhāraṇī, and arrived at Cháng'ān.

An imperial decree was issued, ordering Dú Xíngyǐ and the Tripiṭaka Master Rìzhào to translate it. Once the translation was completed, thirty rolls of silk were bestowed as a religious gift (dakṣiṇā).
At this time, Wuxili again brought a Sanskrit manuscript to Ximing Monastery. The monk Shunzheng petitioned for its joint translation, which was titled the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*.
This was the third translation; it is largely identical to that translated by Du Xingyi, though with minor differences.

Compared to all other translations, this one has been the most widely disseminated. Poli then entered Mount Wutai, and nothing further is known of his final destination. [End of] Dharma Master [Wuxili].
Yuánhuī passed away. Huī, whose courtesy name was Dàoshì, compiled the *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín* (Pearl Forest of the Dharma Garden) in one hundred fascicles, which is currently preserved in the canon.
This occurred during the Jiǎshēn year (the first year of Guāngzhái) under Empress Wú Zetian.
In the second month, Zhongzong was deposed as the Prince of Luling, and Empress Wu assumed the regency.
On the day of Yiyou (the first year of Chuigong), Zhongzong was confined in Fangzhou. Empress Wei-yi repaired the Baima Temple.

In the second year, the year Bingxu (626 CE), white lotus flowers suddenly grew from a mulberry tree in the garden of Huang Shugong’s residence in Quanzhou. Consequently, he donated his house to establish a monastery;
this is the present-day Kaiyuan Temple (Fangyu Shenglan).

In the Dinghai year (the third year), Divākara of India (translated as "Sunlight" in Chinese), who had been at the capital since the beginning of the Yifeng era of Emperor Tianhuang, translated the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* and other scriptures.
By this year, he had translated a total of eighteen works in thirty-four fascicles. Empress Wu personally composed a preface, which is extant today.
In the fourth year, the Wuzi year,
the Emperor summoned the divine monk Wan Hui to the palace, bestowed upon him a brocade robe, and ordered palace maidens to attend to his service.
In the year Jichou (the first year of Yongchang),
the Khotanese śramaṇa Tiyun Banya (known here as Tianzhi) arrived at the capital. That year, he had an audience with the Emperor in Luoyang and was ordered to translate scriptures at Dongsi Temple.
On the day of Gengyin (the first year of Tiānshòu;
in the ninth month, the national name was changed to Zhou), ten śramaṇas, including Fámíng and others, went to the palace gate to present the *Dà yún jīng* (Scripture of the Great Cloud).

They extolled at length that Empress Zhètiān was the rightful sovereign of the Tang dynasty over Jambudvīpa. Empress Zhètiān was greatly pleased and bestowed upon the ten śramaṇas purple square-cut robes and silver tortoise-shaped insignia, and she promulgated the scripture.
In every province throughout the realm, a Great Cloud Temple (Dàyún sì) was established.

In the second year [of the reign], on the Xinmão day, an imperial edict elevated the followers of Śākyamuni above those of the Daoist tradition. By this time, Empress Queen Tianzhi had produced six sections of sutras and treatises.
In the *wuchen* year (the first year of the Changshou era), Master Shenjian arrived.
Upon seeing the Emperor, he gazed up at him for a long while and asked, "Do you understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not understand.

The Master said, "This old monk observes the precept of silence," and having finished speaking, he departed (one source says this was in the *yiwu* year of the Tiances Wansui era). On the following day...
He presented nineteen short songs (*tanka*). The Empress examined them and praised them, bestowing upon him generous gifts and rewards.
Today, only one song by Ryōgen remains widely circulated in the world; this master was none other than the Venerable Tōtō.
In the second year, the *gēisi* (Kǐsì) year, the Indian Dharmaruci (translated here as Fǎxī; later changed by Empress Wu to Bodhiruci, translated here as Jué'ài) arrived in the capital.
Initially, the Emperor had sent an envoy to invite him. This year he reached the capital and, at Fóshòujì Temple, translated nineteen scriptures.
Twenty fascicles. The śramaṇa Shi Hui-zhi was of Indian descent; his father was a native of India, so he was conversant with the languages and sounds of both lands.

Whenever there were translations by the Tripiṭaka masters Śīlabhadra, Divākara, Bodhiruci, Yaśogupta, Prajñā, Ratnamati, and others, they all summoned Hui-zhi to serve as a witness and additionally tasked him with interpreting the oral explanations.
In this year, he himself translated one fascicle of the *Guanyin zan song* (Verses in Praise of Avalokiteśvara) (*Shijiao lu*).
In the year Jiawu (the first year of Yanchai), and in the year Yiwu (when the Empress Dowager added the title "Cishi" and changed the era name to Zhengsheng;

subsequently adding the title "Tiance Jinlun Dasheng Huangdi" and changing the era name to Tiance Wansui), she issued an imperial edict to Shi Mingquan and others to collate and finalize the catalogue of the scriptures, compiling it into fifteen fascicles (which still exists today). The Empress reported this to [the Emperor].

In the kingdom of Khotan, there was a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Great Scripture. [Empress Wu] immediately dispatched an envoy to seek it, requesting that one person well-versed in Sanskrit studies accompany them.

Thereupon, the King of Khotan, knowing that Śikṣānanda (which translates as "Joy in Learning") was exceptionally skilled in the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka*, sent him to fulfill the imperial command.
When Empress Wu saw him, she was greatly delighted. In the third month of that year, she issued an edict for him to enter the [capital].
At Biankong Monastery, he translated [the texts] together with Bodhiruci, Fuli, and others. Later, he moved to Foshouji Monastery to continue his translation work.
Empress Wu visited the monastery and personally oversaw the editorial revisions, providing him with offerings of food at that time.
In the fifth month, Dharma Master Yijing returned from the Western Regions; he had traveled through more than thirty countries over a period of twenty-five years.

He obtained four hundred sections of sutras and śāstras, as well as three hundred grains of relics. Empress Wu personally went to welcome them outside the Upper East Gate, with banners and music leading the way.
They were enshrined at Boshouji Temple, where she issued an imperial decree ordering them to be translated. Initially, he worked together with Śikṣānanda.
While the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was being translated [by others], he himself began the translation only after the Jiushi era.

In the year Bingshen (the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era), an imperial edict summoned the śrāmaṇera Kang Fazang to the Taiyuan Temple to expound the fundamental tenets of the newly translated *Avataṃsaka*. This was when he was finally completing the scripture.
Title: An Account of the White Light Emitted from His Mouth. A white light issued from his mouth, forming a canopy that suspended in the air; the myriad crowds marveled at this wonder.

By imperial decree, the ten Great Virtuous Ones of the capital were commanded to confer the full ordination upon Xuanzang, who was granted the title "Xianshou. He was then summoned by edict to enter Dabiankong Monastery.
**Supplement to the Translation of Scriptures (Based on the Original Biography)** An imperial edict summoned the Chan Master Huian of Mount Song to the capital.

He was carried into the palace hall on a sedan chair, where the Emperor personally prostrated before him in worship. The Master was received within the inner quarters, where he was consulted on the Way morning and evening; he was honored as National Teacher.
By imperial decree, Du Men Monastery was established at Dangyang Mountain to commemorate his virtue. At that time, from the princes and dukes downward, as well as the scholars of the capital city...
The common people, hearing of his reputation, vied with one another to come and pay their respects; they prostrated themselves upon seeing even his dust, numbering ten thousand each day (*Jiushi*).

An imperial edict was issued that any foreign monk wishing to settle permanently should be assigned to reside wherever he chose. At that time, the Great Master of Sizhou did not wish to distinguish himself from ordinary monks, so he registered his name at Longxing Temple in Chuzhou.
Just as plans were being made for the construction of a Buddha hall, the Great Master suddenly said, "I shall contribute five hundred strings of cash."

He asked, "How far is it? The man replied, "It is not far. Upon reaching the riverbank, he saw several boats approaching. The Master beckoned them to stop and called out to the last boat, rebuking them:
"To have no heart for saving sentient beings is already foolish delusion; why do you further rob people and inflict harm?

If you do not relinquish [your plunder], you shall surely face the death penalty. The boatmen then surrendered five hundred strings of cash and pleaded for his protection. Immediately, they were seized.
Yangzi County arrested him, and he was imprisoned in a jail cell. Having been interrogated until his confession was complete, he awaited death with a resigned heart.

Thinking only of the Great Master by the river, whom he suspected might be the Holy One Guanyin, he focused his mind and recited the master’s name. Suddenly, the Master appeared amidst the clouds and comforted him, saying:
"Simply know to maintain single-minded recitation; there is no need for other anxieties. When his confession was finalized in the case file, a gracious amnesty suddenly flowed forth.
Throughout the world, he truly caused embers to flare up from cold ashes and flesh to grow upon decayed bones (from his biography).

In the year Dingyou (the first year of the Shengong era), the Great Master of Sishou would sometimes sit in meditation in a deep chamber, or at other times travel along long roads shaking his monk’s staff; he was a master who sprinkled water upon stones.
When she applied it to her mother’s mouth, the mother’s toothache was completely cured. When she threw the jar into the chamber of Lord Pei, Lord Pei’s ailment was instantly healed.
When she offered him a fan, the wind and waves ceased to cause harm. Through her compassion for the young, Lady Zhao’s illness was naturally cured.
Had she not given the fine horse, Officer Sun would have fallen from it and perished; had she not given the bronze cauldron, Lady Pei would have drowned while washing the cauldron.
Later, he vowed with his disciple Huiyan to travel abroad. Upon leaving Shanyang, both monastics and laypeople followed him in devotion.
When they reached Huaiyin, boatmen bowed their heads; none failed to halt their sails to present offerings or stop their oars to burn incense.
He would not descend when requested, yet he arrived suddenly without being invited (from his *Benzhuan*).
In the year Wuxu (the first year of the Shengli era),
the Prince of Luling was summoned back.
In the year Jihai (the second year).

In the tenth month, the new translation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra was completed in eighty fascicles. Empress Wu personally composed a preface and, from the Taiji Hall, proclaimed it to the hundred officials (the original text).
In the gengzi year (the first year of Jiushi), an edict was issued to collect one cash per day from monks throughout the empire to fund the construction of a Great Image at Baima Pass.
Di Renjie and others submitted a memorial urging earnest remonstrance, but Empress Wu did not accept it (*Jiushi*). In the eighth month, the Brahman Li Wuchan translated [the scriptures].
He translated one fascicle of the *Amoghapāśa-sūtra*, which is the essential core of the secret teachings and dhāraṇīs.
In the year of Xinchou (the first year of Chang’an), Empress Wu was about to construct a Great Image.
The Censor Zhang Tinggui submitted a memorial offering earnest remonstrance. Empress Wu summoned him for an audience and bestowed [honors] upon him.

He comforted and consoled him with gold and silk (Tang History). ○ An imperial edict was issued for the Dharma Master Xianshou Fazang to lecture on the *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
When he reached the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," he was moved by a great earthquake.

That very day, he was summoned to the Changsheng Hall, where the Emperor questioned him regarding the meaning of the ten layers of the celestial net and the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*). Fazang expounded these matters with systematic clarity.
Furthermore, when he pointed to the golden lions at the corner of the palace hall to explain [the meaning], Empress Wu attained sudden and complete realization.

Consequently, she compiled his words and titled them the *Jinshizi Zhang* (Treatise on the Golden Lion). [Initially, Master Zhiyan transmitted the Huayan school’s fundamental tenets to Du Shun. Chengguan, who served Zhiyan, received the teachings in their entirety.

When Zhiyan passed away, Chengguan preached the Dharma wearing only a headcloth and cap. Thereupon, the venerable elders submitted a memorial requesting that he be ordained as a monk. Every instance of Chengguan’s tonsure and reception of full ordination was by the special decree of Empress Wu. After Chengguan’s death, National Teacher Qingliang Chengguan transmitted these teachings; scholars took him as their model, and [the work] was titled...]
The school that is perfectly integrated and endowed with all virtues in a single thought-moment is called the Xianshou Teaching.

In the second year, the *wuchen* year (702), when the Duke of Wanhui manifested his spiritual transformations wherever he went, Emperor Xuanzong was still in the frontier regions; he once paid a private visit to Wanhui, who patted him on the back and said:

For fifty years, he was the Son of Heaven during a period of great peace; one may truly admire his sagacity. When Prince Zong served as Chancellor, whenever he was about to go out, he would invariably announce to the market folk, "The Son of Heaven is coming.
After a short while, the Chancellor would arrive. His spiritual anomalies were of this kind.

In the *guǐmǎo* year (the third year), Dharma Master Yìjìng translated twenty scriptures, totaling one hundred and fifteen fascicles, including the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, from the first year of Jiǔshì to this year.
Empress Wùzhōu composed a new preface for the holy teachings. Regarding the expenses for casting the [Buddha] image under Empress Wùzhōu...

[The Emperor] was equipped [with these items]. Li Jiao submitted a memorial of remonstrance, but the Empress did not accept it. That winter, the image was completed; he led the hundred officials to perform rites of worship (Old History of the Tang).

On the Jiachen day (the fourth year), in the first month, Śikṣānanda translated the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in seven fascicles. The work was finished (it is currently in the canon; compared to other versions, this one is particularly detailed and clear).
Śikṣānanda arrived here. In total, he translated nineteen scriptures and treatises comprising one hundred and seven fascicles.
Śikṣānanda took his leave to return to Khotan; by imperial decree, the Censor Huo Siguang was sent to escort him back.

The śramaṇa Maitreyaśānti (translated into Chinese as Jiyou) from the country of Tukhāra had previously collaborated with Śikṣānanda in translating scriptures. In this year, they translated the *Vimalaviśuddhi*.
The *Guang jing* (Sutra of Light), one fascicle, was [composed] when he took leave of the Emperor to return to his home country; the Emperor bestowed generous gifts upon him.
This was during the Yisi year of Zhongzong (the first year of Shénlóng).
In the first month, the high ministers petitioned the Empress Dowager to transfer the succession to the Crown Prince. [The Crown Prince ascended the throne as] Emperor Zhongzong.

The Empress Dowager moved her residence to Shangyang Palace. The Emperor led the hundred officials to bestow a posthumous title upon the Empress Dowager, calling her "Empress Dowager Zetian Dasheng Huangdi.
He further restored the national name to Tang. The Chancellor Fang Rong was exiled to Gaizhou. In the fourth month, Emperor Zhongzong...
An imperial edict was issued, summoning the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi to the capital. The decree stated: "I have invited the two masters An and Xiu to receive offerings within the palace.

In my leisure from the myriad affairs of state, I have frequently investigated the One Vehicle. Both masters, however, declined, saying that there is a Chan Master in the South who secretly received the robe and Dharma from Master Ren;
one should go to him for instruction. I now dispatch the inner attendant Xue Jian to travel at once..."

An imperial edict was issued inviting Master Yuan to come to the capital. Master Yuan declined the invitation with a letter, expressing his illness and his wish to remain in the mountain forests until the end of his days.
Xue Jian said, "The Chan masters of the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must focus on meditation and concentration. I wonder, Master, what kind of Dharma do you teach?
The Patriarch replied, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? Xue Jian said, "I, your disciple, shall return..."

In the morning, the Emperor asked, "I pray that the Master will instruct me on the essentials of the mind so that I may clearly realize the Way. The Patriarch replied, "The Way has neither light nor darkness.
Zanjian said, "Light is a metaphor for wisdom, and darkness is an illustration of affliction. If one does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter affliction," [how can one realize the Way?]
"By what means can one escape from birth and death? The Patriarch said, "If one uses wisdom to illuminate afflictions, this is the capacity of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Jian asked, "What is meant by the insight of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna)? The Patriarch replied, "Luminosity and ignorance are non-dual in their nature."
The nature of non-duality is precisely the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This true nature does not diminish in ordinary beings nor increase in sages.

It remains undisturbed while dwelling amidst afflictions, and it is not quiescent while abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Its essence and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*); this is called the Way (*mārga*). Jian asked:
"When the Master speaks of 'neither arising nor ceasing,' how does this differ from the heterodox paths? The Patriarch said: "The heterodox paths seek to stop arising by means of cessation."
Arising reveals cessation; yet cessation is not truly ceased. Arising is said to be non-arising; I say that it is fundamentally unborn from the beginning and now likewise unceasing.
This is why I differ from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not engage in any deliberation regarding good or evil.
You will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally abiding, with wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges. (End of the Preface)
He returned to the capital and submitted a memorial regarding his grandfather’s words; the Emperor praised them with admiration for a long time.
Shortly thereafter, he dispatched an envoy to bestow upon him a *kāṣāya*, a water flask, an alms bowl, and other items, expressing the Emperor’s own yearning for the Dharma.

The Indian master Prajñāmitra (translated as "Ultimate Measure") resided at the Zhizhi Daochang in Guangzhou. On the twenty-third day of the fifth month, he recited one chapter from the *Abhiṣeka* section.
It is titled the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Mīkhaśakra (translated here as "Cloud Peak") translated it into one work in ten fascicles;

the Chancellor Fang Rong received the text by pen; and the śramaṇa Huaidi verified the translation. When the transmission of the scripture was completed, Amoghavajra boarded a ship and returned to the West (according to the *Yijing tujiji*;

one account states that Fang Rong encountered Amoghavajra bringing the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Śūraṅgama* and requested him to proclaim the translation; once the translation was finished, Amoghavajra took the Sanskrit original back to India). [End of] Yijing’s method.
The Master, at this time, further produced four sections and six fascicles of scriptures, including the *Mayūra* (Peacock) Sūtra;
the Emperor composed a preface, titled "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripiṭaka of the Great Tang’s Longxing Era. In the eleventh month, Empress Wu Zetian passed away at the age of eighty-two.
In the twelfth month, an imperial decree changed the ancient Baolin Monastery in Shaoyang Prefecture to Zhongxing Monastery.
In the Bingwu year (the second year), the divine monk Wanhui was granted the title Dharma-Cloud Master (Fayun Gong). Monks Huifan and others were promoted to the fifth rank.
In the second month, Chan Master Datong Shenxiu passed away; by imperial decree, he was buried at Longmen, with ceremonial insignia and a formal procession provided for the day of the interment.
The Emperor escorted the reliquary stupa to Bianqiao Bridge. Zhang Yue, the Director of the Secretariat, composed the inscription for the stele, which stated in brief:

"The Master attended upon Chan Master Ren, serving him diligently for six years. He then resided on the mountain to the east of Yuquan Temple, where students gathered like a marketplace. During the Jiushi era,"

By imperial decree he was invited to come; he spread his seat and had an audience with the Sovereign. Carried on a palanquin, he ascended the palace hall; the Emperor of ten thousand chariots bowed his head before him, and within the nine layers of the imperial chambers, they sat together in leisure.
Those who transmit the Holy Way do not face north [as subordinates]; those who possess sublime virtue are exempt from the rites of a subject.

Thus, he was promoted to the status of Dharma Master of the two Capitals and Imperial Preceptor of the Three Dynasties. Looking up to the Buddha-sun rising once more, we rejoice that the Udumbara flower has appeared but once.

However, as it was located within the capital city, every time the Emperor shared his seat with him or the Empresses attended his assembly, a retinue of courtiers surrounded him like pairs of mandarin ducks and dragon-elephants circled him thrice;

thus, his sacred reverence increased daily and imperial favors accumulated through successive reigns. At the site of the initial assembly at Dangyang, he established a monastery named Dumon (Gate of Deliverance).

The ancestral residence of his predecessor in Wei County was converted into a temple named Ba’en (Requiting Gratitude). The Master was born at the end of the Sui dynasty and lived for over one hundred years;

it is said his monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera-lakṣa*) reached eighty years, and so forth. At that time, Prince Qi Fan and the Retired Scholar Lu Hongyi both inscribed steles and composed epigraphs for him.
His biography appears in the *Jiushi Tangshu* (Old History of the Tang), as he was the first among monks to be granted a posthumous title (*śrī*). Following this, Master Yijing... [followed].
The Emperor returned to the capital and issued an edict to establish a separate *fanjing yuan* (translation bureau for foreign scriptures) at Dajianfu Monastery to house [the master].
Furthermore, Bodhiruci followed the imperial entourage back to the capital and was ordered to reside at Xichongfu Monastery, where he translated the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* and other scriptures.

On the day the titles were first drafted, the Emperor personally presided over the dharma assembly in the Foguang Hall within the inner palace, recording the essential meanings of the scriptures with his own brush; the Empress and the consorts likewise attended.
[The Emperor] observed that while his hundred officials sat in attendance, there was none who could surpass [the Master] when compared to the ancients.

He bestowed purple robes upon National Teacher Huian and subsequently invited him into the imperial palace to receive offerings. In this year, the Emperor, the Empress, and the princesses extensively established Buddhist temples.
In the eighth month, an edict was issued throughout the realm to test the scriptural exegesis of novice monks; those who demonstrated thorough mastery without impediment were ordained as full monks.
The practice of testing through scriptural recitation for the purpose of ordination began from this time onward.

As for Baosiwei, in this year he translated seven works in nine fascicles, including the *Ārya-śrīmahādevī-vajravidāraṇā-dhāraṇī* and others; from then on, he no longer translated scriptures, devoting himself exclusively to ritual recitation.

In the Dingwei year (the first year of Jinglong), an imperial edict was issued to change the names of Zhongxing Temple and Zhongxing Monastery to Longxing. An imperial decree was sent to the Prefect of Shaoyang Prefecture to grandly refurbish Bao Lin Zhongxing, granting it the name Fajian Temple.
The former residence of the Sixth Patriarch in Xin Prefecture was designated as Guoen Temple. The Emperor summoned [him].
Dharma Master Yijing entered the inner quarters along with the śramaṇas who were translating the scriptures for the same period, remaining there for the ninety-day summer retreat.

The Emperor recalled that in the past, while he resided in Fangbu, he was beset by hidden calamities and had no place of refuge; through his prayers and recitations to Bhaisajyaguru, he subsequently received divine blessings. Consequently, [the ceremony was held] in the Great Buddha Light Hall.
The Emperor commanded Jing and others to translate the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* in two fascicles; while presiding over the Dharma assembly, he personally transcribed it with his own hand.

Shi Zhiyan was the son of the King of Khotan. Having arrived in the Great Tang at a young age, he early on enjoyed high honor and rank, being appointed General of the Great Army and enfeoffed as a Duke of a Commandery.

In the fifth month of the second year of the Shenglong era, he requested to donate his residence to establish a monastery; the Emperor granted his request, and he further earnestly petitioned for [the construction of] a Buddha hall.
He has left the household life. On the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month, an imperial edict in ink stated: "It is the nature of human beings not to fail to cherish rank and position.
Yet, it is your own wish to renounce worldly customs and leave the household life. Having suddenly reviewed your submitted petition, I both admire and cherish this sentiment."
His prayers were thus granted, and his lofty aspirations were fulfilled. On the fifth day of the eleventh month of that year, the Emperor’s birthday, he was ordained as a monk.
He was then invited to reside at Zhongnanshan Zhixiang Monastery, where he cultivated the Way with a humble mind. From then on, he frequently participated in the translation of Buddhist scriptures.

In the fifth year (the Wushen year), an envoy was dispatched with an imperial decree to Khotan for Śikṣānanda, who arrived once more in the capital. The Emperor halted his carriage to welcome him and offer congratulations, receiving him with full ceremonial rites and seating him upon a blue elephant;
he was then installed at Jianfu Monastery. An imperial decree was also issued for the Great Being Śāṇakavāsin of Sizhou.
He entered the palace, where the Emperor addressed him as his "disciple. The Three Ducal Ministers heard the Dharma, and the hundred officials turned their hearts toward it.

He was again lodged at Jianfu Temple. After several months in the capital, a great drought occurred. The Emperor invited the Great Master to the inner palace to request a gift of sweet rain. The Master said:
There is no need for anything else; it requires only the imperial vessel. As soon as the jade nectar is poured forth, a great downpour of sweet rain ensues.
The Emperor appointed Huìyǎn, Huì'àn, and Mùchā as attendants to ordain them.

The Emperor personally inscribed the plaque for their temple, naming it "Puguangwang" (Universal Radiance King), and first sent it back to Huai (according to his biography). ○ Chan Master Yuánguī of Mount Song resided on the mountain.
At Pangwu, one day the Emperor of the Mountains visited the Master. He prostrated himself and requested the precepts.

The Master then conferred upon him the five precepts and further revealed the principle that where there is no mind, there are no precepts, and that there is neither Buddha nor sentient beings. The deity then requested to offer his services according to his capabilities.
The Master said, "I observe that the body is without substance; I observe that all phenomena are impermanent. Being thus clearly realized, what further desire could there be?

The Spirit said, "Master, you must surely command me to perform a worldly deed to display my divine power, so that those who have already resolved their minds, those who have not yet resolved their minds, those with faith, and those without faith may behold my divine traces and know that there is a Buddha and there is a spirit, and that there is the spontaneous and the non-spontaneous."
The Master said, "The area surrounding Dongyan Temple is desolate and treeless; only the northern peak has trees. Can you move those northern trees to the eastern ridge?
The spirit replied, "I have received your command. However, I fear there will be much clamor and commotion during the darkness of night.

I pray that you, Master, do not be alarmed. He then prostrated himself, took his leave, and departed. The Master saw him off at the gate and watched as the procession, solemn and majestic, ascended into the void and vanished.
That evening, wind and thunder shook the earth; at dawn, the weather cleared and grew mild.
Then the pines of the Northern Mountain were all moved to the Eastern Ridge, standing there in dense, orderly rows (from the *Chuan Deng Lu*).

In the second month of the Jiyou year (the third year), the Emperor bestowed a *mona* (patchwork robe) upon National Master Huian. The Master took his leave to return to Mount Song. In the third month, the Master instructed his disciples, saying:
"After my death, place my body in the *śmaśāna* (cemetery) and let it be consumed at will by wild fires. On the eighth day, [the funeral] was completed.

The door was closed and he passed away in silence. His lifespan was one hundred twenty-eight years. His disciples, following his instructions, carried his body to the forest. Indeed, a wild fire arrived and cremated him.
They obtained eighty grains of *śarīra*, five of which were exceptionally large and possessed a red light that dazzled the eyes.

By imperial decree, they were brought in and enshrined within the palace. ○ As for the Dharma-ritual of the Chan Master, he was the son of Wang of Langya. [The Emperor] sought [the teachings of] Lang...
After his release from Xie, the Governor of Fufeng captured him and lodged him in the rear hall. He presented his name to the court.
The Governor’s wife wished to give him her daughter in marriage, but Sengyi firmly refused. When they reached the bathhouse, he severed his own genitals himself.

His maidservant suddenly cried out for help, and the Governor, admiring his integrity, took charge of the matter. Upon arriving at the capital for an audience, the Emperor ordered that he be invested with the title of Langye Marquis.
Regarding the title of "Wicked King," he prepared the formal documents to decline it earnestly based on his original resolve. The Emperor praised him and granted his request.

[The Emperor] summoned the Vinaya Master Dao’an into the palace to confer the *śaraṇa-gamana* (refuge) precepts upon the Empress and other ladies of the court; consequently, he remained within the imperial precincts.

On another day when the Emperor arrived, while all the masters rose from their seats to show respect, Dao’an alone hesitated and merely performed a long bow. The Emperor held his magnanimity in high regard and had his portrait painted at the Lingguang Palace.
The Emperor composed an eight-line eulogy for it (General Discussion).
The Year of Gengxu under the Reign of睿宗 (the first year of Jingyun; June was changed [to the second month]).

The Great Being of Sizhou passed away in the third month; his countenance remained as if alive. By imperial decree, his body was enshrined in a statue at Jianfu Temple and a stupa was erected for him.

Suddenly, a foul odor filled the city. The Emperor prayed for him, and it was permitted that he be sent back to the Huai River region. Immediately, a wondrous fragrance wafted forth, causing the entire capital to marvel.
Thereupon, his whole body was escorted back to Puguangwang Temple in Sizhou, where a stupa was built. The Emperor once questioned Wan Hui.
[The Emperor] asked, "What kind of person was Saṃgha? Huí replied, "He was merely an emanation of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.
The Great Being lived to the age of eighty-three: thirty years were spent in his own land, and fifty-three years here in this region.

Throughout his life, he performed transformative work in twenty-seven locations, and his divine traces were manifold; these are fully recorded in his biography. In the sixth month, Emperor Zhōngzōng passed away. [End of entry for] Míng.
The Emperor executed Empress Wei and others, and [the throne] was offered to Emperor Ruizong for his accession.

At that time, Dharma Master Yijing was translating scriptures and treatises such as the *Bathing the Buddha Image Sūtra* at Da Jianfu Temple; by this point, he had produced twenty works totaling eighty-eight fascicles.

Li Qiao, Zhang Shuo, and others provided literary embellishments, while Vice President of the Department of State Affairs Wei Juyuan and Su Youzhi supervised the translation. [Also present were] Bodhiruci...

The correct title is *Ratnakūṭa*. Upon its arrival, the Emperor again convened a separate assembly at the White Lotus Pavilion in the Northern Garden, as well as in the Gāndhamādana Hall and other halls within the Imperial Palace.
The Emperor himself received the text by hand, while Wang Jin, He Zhizhang, and others provided the literary polish;
Lu Xiangxian and Wei Zhigu of the Secretariat supervised the translation. While the Emperor governed the myriad regions abroad, he internally venerated the Triple Gem. [He] presided over...

He personally composed the preface, which was placed at the beginning of the sutra. In the eighth month, a persimmon tree in the former residence of the High Ancestor at Hyeongseong-sa Temple, which had long been withered, suddenly flourished once more;
consequently, a great amnesty was proclaimed for the realm, and the hundred officials were granted noble titles, while tens of thousands of monks and Daoists were universally ordained.
In the tenth month, Śikṣānanda passed away; his tongue remained unburnt during the cremation, and by imperial decree, it was sent [to the capital].
He returned to Khotan and erected a stūpa.

In the third month of the second year, the *xinhai* year, an imperial edict summoned the monk Yixing of Mount Song to the capital. Yixing declined on the grounds of illness and did not go; he fled instead to Dangyang in Jingzhou.
At Yangshan, he first thoroughly investigated the meaning of the *Taixuan jing*. Next, he transmitted the monastic arithmetic of Tiantai.
Then, he entered Mount Song to study the essential tenets of Chan Master Pujì. Later, while in seclusion at Dangyang, he again followed Vinaya Master Huìwù to study the *Vinaya*.
"A complete list of all scriptures and classics shall never be forgotten throughout one's life" (Jiù Tángshǐ). In the fourth month, an edict was issued stating:

"The Buddhist canon and the profound principles [of Daoism] are equal in their essence though different in their manifestations. In rescuing humanity and transforming customs, their teachings differ while their merits are identical. From now on, when monks and Daoists assemble, they shall be gathered together in equal numbers.
Previously, Emperor Taizong had regarded Laozi as his imperial ancestor and placed him above the followers of Śākyamuni; however, [this policy was subsequently revised].
"In the imperial court, [the monks] were again ranked below the followers of Śākyamuni.

From this point forward, it was established as a permanent regulation that monks should be on the left and the heterodox on the right, with their ranks aligned and assembled together" (Jiu Tang Shu). In the tenth month, an edict summoned the divine monk Wan Hui to enter the palace;
he was housed in the Jixian Yuan (Academy of Scholars) and provided with two beautiful women to attend upon him. In the twelfth month, he suddenly requested river water from Wenxiang. To the left...

The aforementioned [location] was not obtainable. He further said, "The ground in front of the cave hall may be obtained. It was indeed obtained. Having returned and finished drinking water, he passed away in profound stillness.
He was posthumously honored as the Minister (Situ) and Duke of Guo; his portrait was enshrined in the Jixian Academy.

In this same year, Dharma Master Yijing also produced twenty-one fascicles of sutras and treatises, including the *Buddhaguṇa* [Sūtra], under the supervision of Xue Chongyin, the Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Renzi (the first year of Xiantian): In the seventh month, he transmitted the throne to his son, Emperor Xuanzong.
The Great Master Zhenjue of Yongjia was named Xuangjue. He had extensively mastered the Tripitaka and visited the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi.

Upon their first meeting, their words were in perfect accord, and the Patriarch immediately granted him certification. The Master then requested to return home immediately; the Patriarch asked him to stay for one night. Thus, he was known as "The One-Night [Patriarch]."

He attained awakening. When he returned to Yongjia, his disciples gathered like clouds; consequently, he composed the *Song of Realizing the Way* in one chapter to admonish those who had not yet awakened.

The Master further anticipated a profound resonance through spiritual response, and immediately within meditative concentration, he beheld each character of the song transform into golden light, filling the entire realm of empty space.
In that year, the Master entered parinirvāṇa (one source says the second year of the Xiāntián era) and was buried at Mount Sōngtái (now known as Jìngguāng). By Li Yōng.

A stele was erected for him as a monument to his divine path. Later, during the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong, Du Shouben (alternatively said to be Liu Shouben) admired his *Song of Realizing the Way*.

He suddenly excavated the ground to view [the remains] and found the body intact, as if alive. He consequently constructed a stūpa for him. During the reign of Emperor Xizong, the prefectural governor Zhu Bao memorialized these events to the throne;
he was posthumously granted the title of Great Master Wuxiang, and the stūpa was named Jingguang. The Master had a younger sister named Xuán.
Ji also studied under the Sixth Patriarch (who is now the Venerable Patriarch of Jingju).

When the *Song of Realizing the Way* by this Master was transmitted to India by a Brahmin monk and translated there, everyone held him in high esteem and designated him as "the Master of Mahāyāna Sūtras in the Eastern Land.

Furthermore, he composed ten chapters on the "Perfect Meaning of Awakening and Cultivation in the Chan School" and the "Ten Gates of Contemplating the Mind," both of which remain extant in the world. During the Taiping Xingguo era of our Imperial Dynasty, someone presented his collected works to Emperor Taizong of the Tang.

He was pleased with him. He shaved the heads of those who advanced [in the practice] and bestowed one hundred taels of silver upon them, sending them back to establish the community. Furthermore, he granted them tea plantations and permitted them to acquire land of their own to support the monastic assembly. During the Xiangfu era, he was presented with more than one hundred scrolls of imperial calligraphy and landscape paintings (as recorded in the *Yongjia bian* and various other records).
*Comprehensive Chronicle of the Śākya Lineage through Successive Dynasties*, Scroll Eight;
*Comprehensive Chronicle of the Śākya Lineage through Successive Dynasties*, Scroll Nine.
Compiled by the monk Benjue of Yishan Yian during the Song Dynasty.
Edited by the Layman Mingliu Guan, Bi Yanjia, under the auspices of Emperor Taizong of the Tang Dynasty.
In the guichou year (the first year of the Kaiyuan era), Bodhiruci translated the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
Together with previous translations, these were compiled into one collection of one hundred and twenty fascicles;
by this time, his work was complete. From then on, Bodhiruci no longer translated scriptures, but devoted himself exclusively to recitation and the practice of meditative contemplation.
In the seventh month, Dharma Master Yijing passed away at the age of seventy-nine. By imperial decree, his funeral expenses were provided.
He had translated fifty-six scriptures and treatises, totaling two hundred and thirty fascicles, and separately composed nine fascicles on ritual manuals and biographies.

Although Yijing had extensively traversed the entire Tripiṭaka, he specialized particularly in the Vinaya section and instructed his disciples [therein]. In the seventh month, the Sixth Patriarch took leave of his disciples.
The assembly returned to the ancestral home at Guoen Temple in Xin Prefecture. His disciples wept and asked, "When the Master returns, will you come back?
The Patriarch said, "Leaves fall and return to the root; when one comes, there are no words. They asked again, "To whom will your Dharma-eye be transmitted?
The Patriarch said, "He who has the Way attains it; he who is without mind penetrates it. Upon arriving at Guoen Temple on the third day of the eighth month, he addressed the assembly.
He said: "I have received the robe and the Dharma from the Great Teacher of Forbearance. Now I preach the Dharma for you, but I do not entrust the robe to you.
Your roots of faith have already matured, and you are capable of undertaking great matters. A verse says: "The ground of the mind contains all seeds; when rain falls everywhere, they all sprout."
Having suddenly awakened to the nature of the flowers, the fruit of Bodhi was spontaneously realized. He then passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture at the age of seventy-six.

Wei Ju, the Governor-General of Guangzhou, led the officials of the two prefectures of Xin and Shao to receive his entire remains and return them to Baolin Monastery on Caoxi Mountain, where a stupa was erected.
His physical body remains preserved to this day.
In the second year of Jiayin, the Emperor issued an inquiry to Shen Guang, Dharma Master and Chief Registrar of the Left Street, saying:

"What benevolence and virtue does the Buddha possess toward sentient beings, such that one would abandon one's sovereign, parents, wife, and children to serve him as a teacher? If there is reason for this, I shall establish [the Buddhist teachings]; if not, I shall suppress them."
"It is unreasonable; I shall have it expunged. [Kumārajīva] submitted a memorial, saying: "The Buddha’s kindness toward sentient beings exceeds that of heaven and earth;
his clarity surpasses that of the sun and moon; his virtue is weightier than that of parents; his righteousness transcends that of sovereign and subject. The Emperor said:

"Heaven and earth, the sun and moon, possess the power of creation and transformation. Parents and sovereigns possess the virtue of generation and completion. On what basis do you say the Buddha surpasses these? Kālayaśas replied: "Heaven can..."
The heavens can cover but cannot support; the earth can support but cannot cover. The sun illuminates the day but not the night; the moon illuminates the night but not the day.
A father can only give birth but cannot nourish; a mother can only nourish but cannot give birth.

When a ruler possesses the Way, his ministers are loyal; when a ruler lacks the Way, his ministers are sycophantic. By inferring from these principles, it is clear that their virtues are incomplete. As for the Buddha—
The grace toward sentient beings is not like that. As for "canopy," it universally covers the four modes of birth;

as for "recorded in treatises," it is upheld by all six realms of existence. When discussing its illumination, it shines upon the ten directions; when discussing its brilliance, it radiates throughout the three realms of existence. When discussing its compassion, it rescues those from the ocean of suffering;

when discussing its pity, it delivers those in the dark realms of the underworld. When discussing its sanctity, it is the king among all sages; when discussing its divinity, it possesses the six supernormal powers.
"Omnipotent! Thus you save all across life and death, and lead both the noble and the humble. I only pray that Your Majesty will turn your heart to venerate him with reverence.

The Emperor was delighted and said, "The Buddha’s grace is such as this; were it not for you, Master, it could not have been proclaimed. I vow to turn my heart and venerate him with reverence throughout every lifetime."

In the third month of the eighth year of the Yimao cycle (835), the Emperor dispatched Zhang Qia, Director of the Court of Ceremonies, to Mount Dangyang with an imperial edict to summon the śramaṇa Yi-xing to the capital.
By imperial decree, he was installed in the Guangtai Hall. The Emperor frequently consulted him on the essentials of securing the state and governing the people.
Some claimed that Faxing was superior to those who merely memorized and recited the scriptures. One day, the Emperor ordered the palace registers to be brought out and showed them to him.

After Faxing had finished reading them through, he commanded an attendant to hold the text while he recited it back to the Emperor; not a single character was mistaken. Startled and amazed, the Emperor looked at his attendants and said, "A sage!
From then on, he frequently summoned him to inquire about the essentials of the Buddha-mind. Faxing was dignified and composed, serving with reverent devotion. He was a sage.
His influence flourished daily; the Emperor followed him, seeking instruction from him, and addressed him as "Celestial Master" (*Jiù Tángshǐ*).
In the fourth year, the *bǐngchén* year, the Tripiṭaka Dharma Master Vajrabodhi (translated here as Shànwúwèi) arrived at the capital. The Emperor had previously dreamed of a Brahman monk.

His demeanor was extraordinary. Consequently, the Emperor summoned a painter and instructed him on the subject’s physical features to be depicted on the palace walls. When Bhadra arrived and entered for an audience, the Emperor gazed at him intently;
it was the very monk he had seen in his dream. Struck with awe and wonder, he lodged him at Ximing Temple.
The various kings of Ning and Xue all lowered their status to show him courtesy and held him in high esteem (*Jiu Tang Shu*).
○ When Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song passed away, the master had received the Dharma from National Teacher An; he was seventy-one years old.

○ Song Jing served as the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou and entered Caoxi to pay respects at the Patriarch’s stupa, vowing: "I, your disciple, vow to protect the Great Dharma throughout my entire life; I pray for a single auspicious sign."
He presented his credentials. As he finished speaking, a subtle fragrance pervaded the air and sweet rain poured down. Xingjing was filled with joy and departed after composing a poem.

Before long, he was summoned to court and, together with Yao Chong, served in succession as chief ministers. The world praised them as "Yao and Song," calling them the virtuous ministers of the Restoration (Tonglun).
In the fifth month of the Ding-si year, Śubhakarasiṃha translated the *Dhāraṇī for Seeking Hearing and Retention*. In the eighth month, the Vinaya Master Dao’an passed away;

the Emperor commissioned a portrait of him for the Lin’guang Palace. Fang Guan was serving as the magistrate of Tonglu County; he went out on an excursion with the Daoist Xing Hezhuo and passed through Xia.

At the mouth of the village, he entered a Buddhist temple and sat beneath an ancient pine tree. Li Pó had people excavate the ground and discovered letters from Lú Shídé and Yǒng Chánníshī, which had been stored inside a jar.
He smiled and said to Lǐ Guǎn, "Do you recall this? Guǎn was consequently filled with regret, realizing that his previous life had been that of Master Yǒng.
In the *wùwǔ* year (the sixth), the Indian śramaṇa Lekha, having heard from afar of the exemplary conduct at Lushan Donglin [Temple] in Yanmen, traveled the long distance to arrive there.

Once he entered the mountains, he remained for six years from beginning to end, constantly sitting without lying down. With his own hands, he fed the birds; on the northern ridge was the Buddha... [text fragment].
The Dhātustūpa Monastery had stood for over four hundred years; the monks residing there, both past and present, had all suffered from the distance to water.
When the Master arrived and stayed for one year, his refined sincerity moved the profound realm, and a miraculous spring subsequently gushed forth.
Its water was white, light, and delicious, never failing throughout winter or summer (from the *Lushan ji*).
In the year Jǐwèi (the seventh),
on the day Gēngshēn (the eighth),
the Tripitaka Master from India, Vajrabodhi (translated here as Jīngāngzhì), arrived at the capital. By imperial decree, he was invited to enter Dàcí Temple.
At En-ji Temple, he widely propagated the secret teachings and constructed a mandala, which was fashioned according to the ritual precepts;

all were moved by divine portents. Zen Master Ichigyō frequently sought instruction from him. In the fifth month, during a drought, an imperial edict summoned Chih to pray for rain. Chih established a ritual altar and depicted an image of the Seven Koṭis.
He stipulated that rain would fall as soon as the eyes of the image opened. On the third day, the eyes of the image indeed opened, and a substance emerged from the altar.
Clouds spread across the sky, and in an instant, rain fell. The Emperor issued an edict praising him.

On the ninth day of the month, the *xiǎnshū* (辛酉), Shi Zhìyán translated six fascicles of scriptures, including the *Xiūxíng jīng* (Sutra on the Practice). Tiānzhú Bǎosīwéi passed away at the age of one hundred.
In the fourth month of the following year, the court, finding that the *Linde* calendar was no longer accurate, issued an edict for the Master Faxing to revise and compose a new calendar.
Faxing calculated based on the *Dayan* (Great Expansion) number and established a method to correspond with it.
The Daoist Xing Hepu said to Yin Qin, the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy: "Is Faxing not a sage? Formerly, Luoxia Hong, when creating the *Taichu* calendar, once recorded:"
He said, "Eight hundred years hence, the calculation shall differ by one day; there will surely be a sage to rectify it.
Now that the period has elapsed, Yi-xing calculated the figures to correct the errors of several schools; Hong’s words were not false.
Yin also agreed with this.
In the seventh month of the *wuxu* year (the tenth year), there was a drought.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy with an imperial edict requesting the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi to pray for rain.

Vajrabodhi took a bowl filled with water and stirred it with a small knife; after reciting mantras several times, a creature resembling a dragon appeared from the bowl, raising its head above the surface of the water. Vajrabodhi...
Fawei cast a spell to drive it away. White vapor surged up from his bowl, and he said to the imperial messenger, "Return at once;

the rain will arrive immediately. The messenger galloped out, and in a mere moment, wind, thunder, and lightning broke forth. The messenger hurried back in to report that the Emperor’s robes and turban were already soaked through by the torrential rain.

The rain continued for days before finally ceasing. On another occasion, when the heavy rain persisted for over a day, the Emperor feared its end would not come and ordered Fawei to stop it. Fawei kneaded a clay image of an old woman.
The five statues would respond to him in Sanskrit; if he were to revile or scold them, they would immediately become calm. Such was the nature of his divine efficacy.
The Emperor revered him as if he were a deity.
On the *guihai* day (the eleventh), Vajrabodhi translated the *Yogamantra-japa-vidhi* and the *Saptakoṭi-dhāraṇī* (both are currently in the Tripitaka).

In the tenth month, the Zen Master Yi-xing completed the construction of the *Huangdao-yi* (Equatorial Armillary Sphere); the Emperor personally composed an inscription for it and issued an edict to install it in the Wucheng Hall.
This was displayed to the hundred officials. Its form was modeled after the circular heavens, complete with the positions of the constellations and the degrees of the celestial equator.

Water was poured to drive the wheel, causing it to rotate of its own accord; in one day and night, the revolution of the heavens was completed. Two outer wheels were attached, adorned with the sun and moon, allowing them to move in their courses.
As the heaven completed one circuit moving eastward, the sun moved one degree westward, and the moon moved thirteen [degrees].

Dù made a level base using a wooden chest, causing the *yí* to be half-submerged beneath the ground. This provided a standard for the phases of the moon, such as the new moon, full moon, and the first and last days of the lunar month.
He erected two wooden figures upon the level base: one was placed in front with a drum to mark the *kè*; when a *kè* arrived, it would strike itself.
The other was placed in front with a bell to mark the *chén*; when a *chén* arrived, it would ring itself. Both were equipped with rudimentary wheels and axles.
They contended with one another, each claiming it was a divine miracle (both from the *Jiù Tángshǐ*).

On the Jiazi day (the twelfth), Bodhiruci accompanied the imperial entourage into Luoyang; by imperial decree, he was stationed at Changshou Monastery. Śubhakarasiṃha also accompanied the imperial entourage.
He entered Luoyang. At Dafuxian Temple, he translated the *Vairocana-sukṣiti-kalpa* and other scriptures, totaling three sections and thirteen fascicles;
these were all sublime gateways to dhāraṇī. The Chan Master Yixing, the Tripiṭaka Master Baoyue, and others participated in these matters.
Wei was fond of Chan contemplation and constantly exhorted students to practice it. The śramaṇa Niuyun was not wise; he went to...
When she went to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva manifested in the form of an old man. He used a hoe to remove the clotted flesh from her chest;
from that moment, Bian attained awakening and became a teacher for his time. (General Discussion) The nun Xuánjī of Jingjū Monastery in Wenzhou received ordination during the Jǐngyún era.
He constantly practiced meditative concentration within the stone grottoes of Mount Dayi in Pingyang.

Some say that he once studied under the Sixth Patriarch together with his elder brother, Xujue, and consequently composed the *Yuanying Ge* (Song of Perfect Enlightenment), which corresponds closely with the *Zhengdao Ge* (Song of Realizing the Way). Later, he passed away while standing on his head.
His dharma heirs rebuked him for this inverted manner of birth and death, whereupon he fell prostrate at their words. On the evening of his burial, a wind...

The sky was dark with thunder, as if some divine being had moved it. Two days later, someone arriving from Da’i reported that on that evening there was the sound of flutes and chimes in the air, and that the master’s coffin had already been placed upon this peak.
His disciples escorted the śarīra back to the temple for burial and erected a stūpa, which they named the Yuanming Pagoda. Lord Zhao Qingxian erected a stele to record these events.
(Yongning Edition).

In the year Yichu (the thirteenth year), the Venerable Puzhodu of Mount Song resided in seclusion on Mount Song. There was a temple on the mountain that was extremely efficacious; in the temple, there was installed only one...

Regarding the hearth: there was not a single day that its ritual offerings were omitted. When the Master entered the temple, he struck the hearth with his staff, saying, "This is merely a composite of clay and tiles;
from where does the 'sage' come? From where does the 'spirit' arise? He struck it three more times, and the hearth then collapsed and fell apart.

In a moment, a person dressed in blue robes appeared before the Master and prostrated, saying, "I am originally the deity of this hearth. Having long endured the retribution of my karma, I have now received the Master’s teaching on non-substantiality."
The Kitchen God (Zaoshen) was a being subject to birth. Having attained liberation and been reborn in heaven, he came specifically to pay his respects and offer thanks. He bowed twice and departed.

After a short while, the disciples asked the Master, "By what path or principle did the Kitchen God obtain such that he was able to be reborn in heaven? The Master said, "I simply told him that he was composed of clay and tiles;
I had no other doctrine to impart to him. The assembly remained silent. After a long pause, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The assembly [remained silent].
They said, "We do not understand. The Master asked, "Why do you not understand your own inherently existing nature? The monks then prostrated themselves.
The Master said, "Broken! Fallen! Thereupon, the entire assembly realized the profound essence.

On the Bingyin day (the fourteenth), the Japanese śramaṇa Ryōei and others arrived in Yangzhou, bringing ten *saṃghāṭī* robes upon which various landscapes, mountains, rivers, and exotic objects were embroidered.
These had been sent by the ruler of that country as offerings to the śramaṇas of the Middle Kingdom. At that time—
The Vinaya Master Jianzhen received his robe and marveled that people in foreign lands possessed the Buddha-nature (*gotra*), desiring to go there to transform them.
Upon meeting with the entreaties of Huiri and others, he boarded a ship and traveled east to Japan. The King came in person to welcome him and provide hospitality, lodging him in the Vairocana Hall.
Before long, he requested that Jianzhen confer the *śaraṇagamana* precepts upon him; subsequently, the Queen and the ministers all received the teachings in succession. Day by day...
From the beginning, there has been the teaching of the Vinaya.
On the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of the Dingmao year (the fifteenth year), the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci passed away at the age of one hundred and fifty-six. Before and after...
