In total, he translated fifty-three works comprising one hundred and ten fascicles. From the period of the Chángshòu era of Empress Wǔ Tìtiān, he resided in the capital for over thirty years;
such scriptures as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Ratnakūṭa* were all produced through his hands. Both the Emperor and the high officials revered him as if he were a living Buddha.

On the day of his funeral, he was specially granted a ceremonial procession with its full regalia, and his stupa was erected on the western plain of Lóngmén. He was posthumously honored with the title of Hóng... [the text here is incomplete].
He was promoted to the rank of Grand Master of the Second Class (Dàqīng). He was posthumously granted the title "Tripitaka Master Kaiyuan Yiqièbiànzhī" (Kaiyuan All-Knowing Tripitaka).
The height of his fame and virtue had never been equaled since antiquity. In the eleventh month, the Chan Master Yixing bathed, sat upright, and passed away at the age of forty-five.
The Emperor mourned him with profound grief, suspending court for three days and keeping the coffin in its shrine for twenty-one days. Xing’s countenance remained as if alive.
The Emperor personally composed an inscription, which was engraved upon stone. He issued fifty thousand taels from the Inner Treasury to erect a stupa at the site of the Bronze Man.
The master was posthumously titled Chan Master Dahui. The Emperor once asked how long the state’s mandate would endure and whether there would be any obstacles.

Xing replied, "The imperial carriage shall travel ten thousand li, yet the altars of soil and grain will ultimately meet with auspiciousness. The Emperor asked him in astonishment for the reason, but he did not answer. Later, [the Emperor] used small gold...
The casket was presented with the words: "Open it upon reaching Wanli. One day, the Emperor opened the casket and looked inside; there was a small amount of *angui* (a medicinal herb).
When the rebellion of An Lushan broke out and the imperial carriage fled to Chengdu, he suddenly realized its meaning upon reaching Wanli Bridge. Shortly thereafter, the herb indeed returned.

As for Emperor Zhaozong, he was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Ji, yet the Tang dynasty perished because of him; thus it is said that "in the end, there is good fortune" (*zhong ji*). There was also a village matron who had long been...
Fahxing was sitting in prison awaiting execution for his crime. His mother wept bitterly, pleading for his rescue. Fahxing took pity on her and ordered his disciples to capture living creatures.
They obtained seven pheasants and pigs; Fahxing hid one each day inside a jar and performed a *brahma* language incantation over them for seven days.

When the Big Dipper had completely vanished from the sky, the imperial court was struck with alarm. The Grand Astrologer memorialized, stating that a celestial anomaly was imminent and requesting that rites be performed to avert it.
The Emperor asked Xing about this, and he replied, "This is nothing other than a demonic spirit. Generally, a mind of anger destroys all goodness, while a mind of compassion subdues all demons.
If you grant a general amnesty to the empire, then the demon will be unable to act. The Emperor agreed with this and subsequently issued a great amnesty.
Because of this, the old woman’s son was spared. Each day Xing went out, a pig appeared, and with each appearance, a star manifested; this continued for seven days.
The Dipper returned to its former position. His secret arts were mostly of this kind (*Jiù Tángshǐ*).

On the wùchén day (the sixteenth), an edict was issued for Zhang Yue and others to compile and arrange the Daoyan calendar of Xingyī for official use. In the third month, the imperial carriage traveled to the Warm Springs. On the way...
When the Emperor passed by the Yixing Pagoda, he halted his carriage and lingered there.

He ordered an official to visit the pagoda to inform it of his intention to depart on a tour of inspection and granted fifty rolls of silk to have cypress and pine trees planted before the pagoda. Such was the imperial favor shown to it (as recorded in the original biography).
In the year Jisi (the seventeenth), Zhang Yue, Duke of Yan, passed away.
He was a preeminent minister of the Tang dynasty. His literary compositions were refined and powerful; he was particularly adept at the Buddhist scriptures.
He authored a preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* which states: "The myriad practices arise from the mind; the mind is the master of man. The Three Vehicles converge upon..."

First. First is the essence of the Dharma: to know that the mind has nothing to be attained is true attainment; to see that there is nothing that does not penetrate is profound penetration (and so forth).
Furthermore, he composed the *Praise of the Dharma-Pond Courtyard and Dharma Hall*, which says: "This Buddha is the mark of space; this Dharma is the subtle light.
Concentration and wisdom are never separate; this is the meaning of the harmony of the Saṃgha. The person is empty and the dharmas are also empty—this is the twofold emptiness."

They are likewise empty. Abiding in the three jewels of emptiness of mind—this is called the triple refuge. If one sees without being stained by colors and knows without grasping at consciousness, this is called true vision;
it is also called the knowledge of liberation. The Buddha observes that which is free from arising and ceasing;
all phenomena are thus.

On the gengwu day (the eighteenth), Vajrabodhi further brought forth the Five-Syllable Heart Mantra of Mañjuśrī and the Essential Yoga of Avalokiteśvara. Among the monastics and laypeople who transmitted and translated [these teachings] during the Tang Dynasty, there were already thirty-seven individuals by this time.

The number of sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, biographies, and records they produced is as follows: [Note: The original text contains a lacuna indicated by the circle (○). This translation reflects the provided fragment.]
In total, there were three hundred and one works comprising two thousand one hundred and seventy fascicles.

The śramaṇa Zhisheng compiled the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* (Kaiyuan Record of Buddhist Teachings) in twenty fascicles, cataloging and arranging the entire Tripitaka—Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras—totaling five thousand forty-eight fascicles.

(From the volume titled "Heaven and Earth, Dark and Yellow" down to the volume "Sheng," several dozen subsequent volumes consist of transcribed texts and newly translated scriptures from the Tang and Song dynasties.

Xuangao also composed one scroll of the *Continued Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures*, one scroll of the *Continued Record of the Translation of Scriptures*, and one scroll of the *Continued Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism*.
The Emperor summoned eminent masters of the two teachings to the Huaye Pavilion to debate doctrine; the Dharma Master Daoyin engaged in a formal disputation with the Daoist Yin Qian.

After forty rounds of debate, the Master Qianyi was defeated. By imperial decree, the arguments were compiled and included in the Tripitaka, titled *Kaiyuan Fodao Lunheng* (A Weighing of Buddhism and Daoism of the Kaiyuan Era).
The year was Xinwei, the nineteenth [year of the Kaiyuan period].
The *Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra* was promulgated throughout the realm.

In the eighth month of the twentieth year, the Ren-shen year, the Dharma Master Vajrabodhi passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. He was posthumously granted the title of State Preceptor Guanding; the Ministry of Personnel memorialized this.
Du Hongjian composed the *Jide* (Account of Virtue), wherein he records that Zhicong received the Esoteric Teachings from Master Longzhi.

Upon arriving in the Eastern Land, his disciple Amoghavajra transmitted those teachings. Zhicong bestowed upon him the Yoga Five Families and the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*, as well as the *Susiddhikara-vidhi*.
[This concludes] the General Discourse. In this year, Meditation Master Yifu passed away. Fú had received the Dharma from...
Shenxiu was held in high esteem by the Emperor. He propagated the teachings in the capital for twenty years, and all people revered him as their model.
By imperial decree, he was granted the title "Great Wisdom Chan Master" (Dazhi Chanshi).
Guiyou (the twenty-first year):
The fangshi Zhang Guo possessed secret arts for prolonging life and claimed to be several hundred years old. The Emperor summoned him to the palace, where his transformations were unfathomable.

Later, he earnestly requested leave to return to the mountains. An imperial edict was issued granting him the rank of Silver Light Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and the title Tongxuan.
The Master indeed entered Changshan, and his final whereabouts remained unknown.

In the year Jiashu (the twenty-second), the Elder Li Tongxuan was at Mount Shenfu, composing the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka). This began in the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era and continued until the Tai... [year].

Originally, Gao Xiannu hosted him at his residence in Mengxian County. He stayed in the study for three years, then moved to the side of the Ancient Buddha Hall of the Ma family, where he remained for ten years.
Carrying his scriptures and books, he departed; after traveling twenty li, he encountered a tiger blocking the path.
The Elder patted it and said, "I am about to compose a treatise on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; can you find a place for me to dwell? He then placed his scripture bag upon its back.
He turned back and followed them until he reached the front of an earthen grotto at the foot of Mount Shenfu, where he crouched and waited. The Elder then composed his treatise within the grotto;
every evening, white light issued from his mouth to serve as a lamp and candle. There were two women who daily provided water from a spring and lit incense to offer paper and ink for him.
At each mealtime, they would prepare pure food and place it before the Elder; once the meal was finished, they would scatter it [as an offering].
He took his bowl and departed. In this manner, five years passed until the Elder completed his treatise; thereafter, he vanished from sight (as recorded in his original biography).
In the year Yihai (the twenty-third year), the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra passed away at the age of ninety-nine.
An imperial edict was issued appointing Li Xian, Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, to oversee his funeral rites.
The matter is as follows: Shentou Wei left his entire body as a reliquary stupa at Guanghua Temple on the western mountains of Longmen.

Fearing worldly affairs, he renounced the throne to become a monk; his virtue and reputation were preeminent among those of India. Wherever he went to preach the Dharma, extraordinary signs invariably appeared.

Once, while crossing the Dragon River, a camel carrying scriptures fell into the water. Terrified of losing the scriptures, Wei immediately followed it into the water. Thereupon, the Dragon King invited him [to the palace].
He entered the palace to discourse on the Dharma and stayed for three nights before departing; not a single character of the Sanskrit manuscripts he carried was even moistened by the rain.
His miraculous manifestations were numerous and of this kind.
In the Bingzi year (the twenty-fourth), the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra traveled to the Western Regions to seek out masters extensively and broaden his learning.
In the Kingdom of Siṃhala, he received from Ācārya Samantabhadra the Vajra-abhiṣeka and the ritual for constructing the maṇḍala of the Mahākaruṇā-garbha; its king...
A herd of wild elephants was charging wildly along the road; he sat there without moving in haste. When the elephants arrived, they knelt and prostrated themselves.
Consequently, the entire nation came to revere him with divine awe (from his *benzhuan*).
Dingchou (the twenty-fifth year):
Yàowáng was surnamed Wéi, named Gǔ, with the courtesy name Lǎoshī. He was a native of Shūlè.

He wore a coarse woolen robe, carried several hundred gourd flasks at his waist, wore a silk headcloth on his head, and held a cane staff in his hand. He always traveled together with a black dog. At that time, the people...
He suffered from illness and experienced considerable pain. The Master then made a vow to universally provide medicinal remedies, so that none failed to recover.
Those who beheld him were immediately healed. Later, his image was painted for veneration, and the Emperor paid him homage as the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.

Since ancient times, he has manifested five times in transformed bodies to rescue the poor and the sick; on one such occasion, his dog transformed into a black dragon that carried him upon its back, soaring up toward the heavens.

And he departed (*from the Preface to the Bencao and also the Shenxian Zhuan*). ○ Prime Minister Song Jing passed away. Jing had long been a devotee of the Buddha-dharma and regularly took Master Tanyi as his teacher, seeking to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma.

In the twenty-sixth year, the Wuyi Year (738), an edict was issued to all prefectures and commanderies throughout the empire to each establish a major temple, using the name of the current era as its designation: Kaiyuan Temple.

In the year Jǐmǎo (the twenty-seventh), the śramaṇa Fǎxiù dreamed of a strange monk who exhorted him to provide five hundred *kāṣāya* robes and enter Zhōngnán Mountain to offer them to the monks of Huíxiàng Monastery. He subsequently set out to do so;
upon reaching the mountain, he searched everywhere but found no such place as Huíxiàng Monastery. Suddenly, on the road, he encountered one...

The monk said, "I shall lead you to enter Huixiang Temple. Xiu followed him into the mountains. After two days, they reached a place of profound seclusion where nothing was visible but clouds shrouding the rocky caves.
Thereupon, he drilled wood for fire and burned incense in worship. Suddenly, the clouds parted to reveal a lofty vermilion gate halfway up a cliff.
Xiu entered with him and saw that the monks there were all extraordinary and majestic; they produced a *kāṣāya* robe.
He distributed it throughout the monastery as alms. The monks of that temple took Xiu into an empty room and said, "This was the former residence of the Tang Emperor.

Previously, he enjoyed fine music here, and for that reason he descended to become a ruler of men. Before long, he shall return. They then gave him a jade flute and a set of monastic robes, instructing him:
"Take these back and present them to the Tang Emperor. Xiu returned to the capital and submitted a memorial.

The *kāṣāya* robe and jade flute that had been entrusted to him were presented; the Emperor examined them and took up the jade flute to play it, as if he were once again handling it from his former reign (General Discussion).
Gengchen (the twenty-eighth day).

In the third month, Li Changzhe of the Huayan school passed away through meditative transformation within a cave on Mount Shenfu. One day prior, he had left the mountain to bid farewell to the villagers;
when they arrived, he was already in the state of nirvana. He was ninety-five years old.

He authored forty fascicles of the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka), as well as the *Jueyi lun* (Treatise for Resolving Doubts), the *Huishishi men xuanyi* (Comprehensive Explanation of the Profound Meaning of the Ten Gates), the *Yuansheng jie mi* (Resolving Delusion through Dependent Origination), the *Shiming* (Ten Clarifications), and other treatises. [10]

The *Xuanliu xiang baimen yihai jiezan* (Verses Praising the Ocean of Meaning of the Six Phases and Hundred Gates) and other works were all transmitted to the world (as recorded in his biography). In the twelfth month, Chan Master Qingyuan Xingsi passed away. When the Master first met the Sixth Patriarch, he asked what he should apply himself to so as not to fall into stages. The Patriarch asked, "What have you done? He replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch asked, "Into which stage do you fall? [He replied,] "I do not fall into any stage. The Patriarch said, "Then you are one who has attained the Way. The Master then bowed and withdrew. Later, he resided at Qingyuan. His disciples numbered over a thousand; those who attained realization included Nanquan Puyuan, Dongshan Liangjie, and others. He was seventy-eight years old and had been a monk for fifty-three years. His remains were enshrined at Qingyuan. The Emperor bestowed upon him the posthumous title Chan Master Dajian. His stupa was named "Zhaoxian" (Manifesting the Truth). His dharma heirs were many; they include Nanquan, Dongshan, Yunyan, Shishuang, Guizong, and others. The lineage of the Dharma has continued to this day. It is truly a great matter. The Master’s teaching was simple and direct, yet it reached the ultimate point. He did not rely on words or letters, nor did he seek through external forms. He took the mind as the Buddha and took the nature as the Way. He did not establish stages or levels, nor did he speak of gradual cultivation. He simply pointed directly to the human mind, revealing its original face. This is why he is called a true patriarch. His legacy is vast and profound, and his influence extends throughout the world. May all beings study and practice this, so that they may realize their own nature and attain liberation. Ji said, "If one does not even practice the Noble Truths, what levels or stages could there be? The Patriarch [Nanyue Huairang] held him in high esteem. When he resided at Qingyuan, his disciples became quite numerous;
among them, Shitou Xiqian was the one who deeply realized the Dharma (as recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu*). In this same year, Chan Master Pujing of the capital passed away.
Jing had served Chan Master Xiu, who recommended him to Empress Wu Zetian, whereby he received ordination as a śramaṇa. After Xiu passed away...

Those throughout the empire who followed the Śākya clan all took him as their teacher. When Emperor Zhongzong heard of his lofty conduct, he issued an edict ordering Daixiu to succeed him in leading the monastic community.
During the Kaiyuan era, an imperial decree was issued to move Huiji to reside in the capital. Princes, dukes, officials, and commoners vied with one another to come and pay their respects.
Upon his death, all officials and commoners who had ever visited him were required by imperial decree to wear the mourning attire of disciples. The Edict stated:

He was posthumously granted the title of Chan Master Dazhao. On the day of his burial, Pei Kuan, the Governor of Henan, along with his wife and children, all wore mourning garments and took their places among the ranks of the disciples.
The common people and officials filled the city to bid him farewell with wailing; the markets were nearly brought to a standstill (*Jiu Tang Shu*).
In this same year, the Dharma Master Daoyin passed away, and the Emperor issued an edict expressing his grief and lamentation (*Ben Ji*).

In the month of the ninth, on the *xinsi* day (the twenty-ninth) and the *renwu* day (the first year of Tiānbǎo), Yan Tǐngzhī, the Grand Master for Palace Affairs, passed away. Yan Tǐngzhī had himself prepared his funerary epitaph, which stated: "By..."
On a certain day of a certain month, he was buried to the west of the stupa of Master Dazhao, in accordance with the rites.

Initially, Tingzhi served as a disciple of Chan Master Dazhao Huiyi and attained a profound understanding of the Buddhist scriptures. Upon receiving the master’s final testament regarding burial next to Dazhao’s stupa, he demonstrated that he would never forget the master’s virtue (Jiu Tang Shu).
In the second year of the Tiānbǎo era (Guiwei), the Emperor dispatched the palace messenger Yang Tingguang to enter Sīkōng Mountain to gather *chángchūn* (evergreen) vines.

While there, Tingguang visited Wúxiàng Monastery and inquired of Master Běnjìng regarding the meaning of the Buddha-way. The Master said: "If you wish to seek the Buddha, then this very mind is the Buddha."

"If you wish to realize the Way, a mindless state is the Way. Daoguang returned to the palace and reported this to the Emperor. The Emperor immediately issued an edict for Daoguang to take the imperial decree and summon the Master.
That winter, he departed for the capital.
On the first day of the first month of the Jia-shen year (the third year of his reign), he summoned renowned monks from the two monastic districts to the inner palace chapel.
Together with Minister Benjing, a Chan Master, they expounded upon Buddhist principles. There, Chan Master Yuan asked, "What constitutes the Way? The Master replied, "A mindless state is the Way."

Yuan said, "The Way arises because of the mind. How can you say that no-mind is the Way? The Master said, "The Way is originally nameless; it is because of the mind that it is named 'the Way. If the name 'mind' were real, then the Way would not be empty. Since the mind, when investigated to its limit, is non-existent, upon what could the Way rely to be established? Both are equally empty and false; they are all merely provisional names. Yuan said, "Does the Chan Master see the existence of body and mind as being the Way? [The Master] said, "No. Yuan said, "Then does the Chan Master see that there is no body and no mind? [The Master] said, "No. Yuan said, "If there is neither body nor mind, then what is the Chan Master seeing? The Master said, "I am seeing the mountains, the rivers, and the great earth. Yuan said, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "The meaning is that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are themselves the Buddha-nature. Yuan said, "If so, then why do you say that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are the Buddha-nature? The Master said, "Because the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are themselves the Buddha-nature, they are therefore called the Buddha-nature. Yuan said, "If so, then why do you say that the Buddha-nature is the mountains, rivers, and the great earth? The Master said, "Because the Buddha-nature is itself the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, it is therefore called the mountains, rivers, and the great earth. Yuan said, "If so, then why do you say that the Buddha-nature is neither the mountains, rivers, nor the great earth? The Master said, "Because the Buddha-nature is neither the mountains, rivers, nor the great earth, it is therefore called neither the mountains, rivers, nor the great earth. Yuan said, "If so, then why do you say that the Buddha-nature is neither the Buddha-nature nor the mountains, rivers, nor the great earth? The Master said, "Because the Buddha-nature is neither the Buddha-nature nor the mountains, rivers, nor the great earth, it is therefore called neither the Buddha-nature nor the mountains, rivers, nor the great earth. "Monk, body and mind are fundamentally the Way. Yuan said, "Just now you said that 'no-mind' is the Way; now you say that body and mind are fundamentally [the Way].

Are these not contradictory? He replied, "'No-mind' is the Way: when the mind is extinguished, the Way is non-existent. Mind and the Way are one and the same; therefore, it is said that 'no-mind' is the Way.
Body and mind are fundamentally the Way, and the Way is also fundamentally body and mind. Since the fundamental nature of body and mind..."
"This is emptiness; even the Way, when traced to its source, does not exist. Thus, seven distant disciples went back and forth discussing the Way.

The Master’s eloquence flowed like a torrent, and neither the Emperor nor the fourfold assembly failed to praise him before they withdrew. (Five Lamps) The Emperor decreed that the Kaiyuan Temple throughout the realm should enshrine cast gold and copper imperial portraits.
[The Master] wore a Daoist cap, donned monastic robes, and stepped in Confucian shoes. The Emperor himself composed a eulogy for him.
(Tongji) ○ Chan Master Nanyue Huairang passed away. Having received the Dharma from Caoxi, he first resided at Wudang and subsequently came to Nanyue, where he dwelt at Guanyin Daochang;
consequently, he was titled Master Guanyin. Disciples gathered like clouds, and Mazu was his foremost heir who attained the Dharma.
During the Yuanhe era, Zhang Zhengfu composed a stele inscription. (Wudeng Huiyuan) ○ Guoyi of Mount Jing.
Chan Master Qin initially left home under Chan Master Su of Heilin in the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era.

Having attained realization, his daily practice thereafter became wondrous and subtle; he was transcendent, unrestrained, and free from constraints. After he had practiced the Way for a long time, he requested permission to travel south.
Su said, "Go with the flow; stop whenever you encounter a path. The Master took his leave and traveled south to Yuhang, reaching the northeastern path.

The Master silently reflected upon his former words and ascended the hills to seek a place to establish his residence. To the west, past a perilous peak, he found a secluded spot at the edge of a stone cliff.
There he sat cross-legged upon a stone seat. An old man came forward to pay his respects and said, "I pray that you will grant me this site for your dwelling as a place for your stay;
I request that you proceed southward. He then led the Master up to the summit of the mountain and entered among the five peaks.
In the interval, there was a large pond. Pointing to it, he said to the Master, "If my family departs, this pond shall overflow. Leave a single opening for the water and do not fill it in;

I will come at times to assist you. Having finished speaking, he vanished. Thereupon, clouds and mist darkened the sky, and wind and rain burst forth suddenly, continuing without ceasing throughout the night.
When dawn broke and the rain cleared, the waters of the pond had completely dried up, and the sand had surged upward.

The area was subsequently leveled, leaving behind only a single cave known as Longjing (Dragon Well). On the southern slope of the northern peak, there was further a thatched hermitage where the Master could reside;
he thus settled into meditation there. Monks from the four quarters, admiring his lofty way, cleared the weeds and followed the wind to seek him out, building nests and gathering branches.
Before even several years had passed, hermitages were established throughout the crags and valleys, his fame spread through the monastic forests, and his Way filled the heavens.
Below. The foundation of the hermitage still exists today, where no weeds grow (according to the *Benzhuan*).
In the year Yiyou (the fourth year), he summoned the Daoist Ruyun to an audience at Dading Hall. The Emperor inquired about the essentials of the Way and held him in high regard; however, Gao Lishi—
Originally a follower of Buddhism, Lü Yún became critical of the Emperor. Yún subsequently took his leave and returned to reside at Mount Māoshān;
there, in his writings, he severely disparaged the Śākya teachings. Critics lamented this reversal of his former allegiance.

At that time, Chen Shàoyóu, the Regional Inspector of Zhèxī, detested Yún’s conduct and consequently commissioned the Dharma Master Shényōng to compose a treatise refuting him. Shényōng wrote the *Fánmí Lùn* (Treatise on Dispelling Delusion) to rectify Yún’s errors.

Yun’s treatise was consequently discarded. When the Palace Attendant Dou Shao saw Yong’s treatise, he sighed and said: "Yong may truly be called a *maṇi* jewel beyond the mundane world and a lion among treatises" (Old History).

When Chan Master Shenhui of Heze arrived at the capital, he alone determined the path of the Patriarchs, establishing the distinction between the Northern and Southern Schools and describing the gates of sudden and gradual enlightenment.
He composed a work titled the *Xianzong lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the School), whereby that which was transmitted by the Great Mirror [Huineng] was finally established.
The Honored One [ruled] over all under heaven (*Zhengzong ji*).

In the Bingxu year (the fifth year of his reign), the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra returned from the Western Regions. In the fifth month, an edict was issued for the entire realm to ordain monks and nuns, and to command that they all attend to the ancestral shrines.
The issuance of certificates for the various departments began from this point; what is now called the Shibu (Sacrificial Department) originated then.

In the Dinghai year (the sixth year of the reign), an imperial decree summoned the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to enter the palace, where he established a ritual altar to perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for the Emperor. He was subsequently granted the title of National Preceptor Zhizang. At that time...
The court sorcerer Luo Siyuan had gained favor through his arts. An imperial decree was issued ordering him to compete with Amoghavajra to determine their relative skill.

On another day, they met in the audience hall; Siyuan held a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) and directed his discourse toward it. Next, Amoghavajra went to take the gem and threw it to the ground, then commanded Siyuan to lift it.
Although Siyuan possessed great strength, he could not move it. When the Emperor prepared to take it himself, Amoghavajra laughed.
Amoghavajra said, "Sanglang, that was merely a magical shadow. He then raised the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel) in his hand to show him. Siyuan was filled with reverence and submitted.

Whenever Amoghavajra performed prayers, he would invariably set up an embroidered throne and hold a wooden spirit-image in his hand. As he recited mantras and cast it down, the spirit would stand upright upon the throne.
The fourfold assembly gazed around, and they would certainly see the spirit’s eyes and lips twitch and move. No matter how difficult the prayer might be...
The power of transformation cannot be taken away; both the court and the common people revered him as a Buddha.
On the wuzi day (the seventh year), the Grand General Gao Lishi built Baoshou Temple in the Western Capital. When the temple bell was completed, Gao Lishi held a vegetarian feast.
To celebrate this, the entire court assembled. At each strike of the bell, one hundred strings of cash were distributed.
Those who were inclined toward giving continued until twenty strikes, while those who gave less did not fall short of ten strikes (from the *History of the Tang*).

In the year Jichou (the eighth year), at the Tianwang Temple on Nanjian Hill in Fuzhou, there was a massive rock. In the fifth month of that year, a great storm of thunder and rain suddenly broke out;

the summit split open in a spiral pattern, cleaving it right through. Its southern portion collapsed to the ground like fallen leaves, while its northern portion rose toward the heavens like an erected stele. A pavilion [was built there].

He concentrated his mind and manifested a true image from within the hidden depths. Attendants were arrayed in surrounding guard, and the ranks of the awakened ones were established in their proper order.

The solemn adornments and offerings, as well as the ceremonial regalia, were all arranged with perfect regularity. How extraordinary! Indeed, the Buddhas rely upon imperishable materials and depend upon immovable foundations;
since the physical form endures forever, the Dharma may likewise remain eternal. (Recorded by Ouyang Jian)

In the Gengyin year (the ninth year of his reign), the Court Gentleman Wang Wei, whose courtesy name was Mojie, served the Buddha and observed the precepts. After the death of his wife, he did not remarry; he lived alone for thirty years.
Upon the death of his mother, he submitted a memorial requesting that his residence at Wangchuan be donated to establish a Buddhist temple (*Tang Shi*).

In Luoyang, there was a giant serpent that emerged from below Mangshan, over a hundred *zhang* in length; anyone who encountered its breath would die immediately. An imperial edict was issued commanding the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to subdue it with mantras.
Amoghavajra said in alarm, "This creature intends to turn the whole of Luoyang into a vast marsh. After three days of chanting mantras, the serpent perished.
(*Old History of the Tang*, *Treatise on the Five Elements*).
On the *xinmao* day (the tenth year), Chan Master Shitou Xiqian visited Qingyuan and received the Dharma. From the beginning of the Tianbao era, he came to the Southern Monastery on Mount Heng.
To the east of the temple was a rock shaped like a dais; he built a hermitage upon it and was thus known at the time as Master Shitou (Stonehead).

Ghosts and spirits from Mount Nanyue frequently manifested themselves to listen to the Dharma, and the Master conferred the precepts upon them all (*Wudeng Huiyuan*). ○ At this time, Jianana arrived from the Western Regions.

In the *wuchen* year (the eleventh year), Great Master Jingshan Sengyuan of Helin Temple in Runzhou entered parinirvāṇa. Li Hua, the Left Assistant in the Office of Remonstrance, composed his stele inscription, which states in brief:
"The Master spent sixty-one summer retreats within the stage of Bodhi; his life from birth to death spanned eighty-five years. He departed...
As for those in mourning, can their devotion be measured? There were even those who crossed the river to present offerings and wailed facing the temple;

ten *li* away, flowers fell like rain and fragrant clouds gathered from the four quarters. Banners, streamers, parasols, and nets of pearls shrouded the light of the sun and moon. They enshrined the entire body and erected a stupa on the western plains of Mount Huanghe.
The regional governor and the local magistrate observed the rites of a disciple in mourning; thus it was that Qi Han, Zhang Jun, and Liang Sheng [honored him].
Xu Qiao and the others were all disciples of the Bodhisattva precepts; in terms of the flow of the Way and the esteem of the people, none surpassed them.
As for me, a disciple, I have previously heard the Way from Mount Jing, much like Yue Zhengzichun did from the Master Confucius.
In the guisi year (the twelfth year of the reign), the Western Tibetans invaded and besieged Liangzhou. The Emperor commanded the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra to pray for the aid of celestial troops.
Amoghavajra recited the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* mantra several times, whereupon a deity clad in armor appeared. The Emperor saw him personally and asked, "What deity is this?"
Xuankong said, "He is the eldest son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North. Xuankong recited secret mantras and sent him away.

A few days later, a report of victory arrived from Liangzhou, stating that divine troops had arrived with formidable and magnificent prowess; the rebels were terrified and withdrew their armor, departing.
The Emperor was greatly pleased. He issued an edict that military garrisons throughout the realm were all to establish shrines for the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
On the day of Jiawu (the thirteenth year), Chan Master Yuannang of Zuoxi passed away. Initially, Huiren of Nanyue had realized the essential tenets of the *Lotus Sūtra* and transmitted them [to him].
Huisi transmitted it to Zhiyi; Zhiyi transmitted it to Guanding; Guanding transmitted it to Jingyun Wei; and Wei transmitted it to Dongyang Wei.
Lang served Dongyang and received his teachings in their entirety. He dwelt alone in mountain caves for thirty years, sitting in serene meditation at Zuoxi.
He took this as his monastic name. At the age of eighty-two, he had several dozen disciples, including Shen’ung, Xuanjing, Fadeng, Qingbian, and Zhanran, who propagated his teachings.
Li Hua, the Court Editor, composed an inscription for the back of his memorial stele, which states:
"For over forty years, the Master wore a single *uttarāsaṅga*; he never changed his single *niṣīdana* throughout his life. Scholars from near and far flocked to him."
The entry for Sim Tianmen (from his *Biography*): Yuan Deshu died. Deshu’s courtesy name was Zizhi. In his youth, he was filial toward his mother.

When his mother passed away, he lived in a hut by her grave and transcribed Buddhist scriptures with blood drawn from his own body. When he finished writing the final character, he was moved by a wondrous fragrance that wafted forth, lingering for an entire day before subsiding.

Previously, his nephew had lost his mother while still in swaddling clothes; having no means to hire a wet nurse, Deshu nursed him himself. After several days, milk flowed forth spontaneously. He was able...
He would stop eating as soon as he had finished his meal. When he served as the Magistrate of Lushan, he was preeminent in his integrity and purity.

Fang Guan often remarked, "To behold the countenance of Zizhi causes the worldly desires for fame and profit to vanish entirely. Upon his death, his household possessed nothing but a pillow, sandals, a bamboo mat, and a gourd ladle.
His cousin Yuan Jie lamented for him, saying: "The Grand Officer lived for sixty years; in all that time, he never once set eyes on female beauty, nor did he ever possess [worldly wealth]."
On ten mu of land, in a ten-foot house, even a child of ten years has never worn clothing made of finished silk or cloth, nor has he ever eaten food prepared with the five flavors.
I pity them; it is merely to admonish those who are dissolute, lustful, greedy, and sycophantic, and who indulge in fine silks and rich meats (Jiu Tang Shu).
Yiwei (the fourteenth year; in the eleventh month, An Lushan rebelled and captured the Eastern Capital);
Suzong, Bingshen (the first year of Zhide).
In the sixth month, An Lushan captured Chang’an, and the Retired Emperor (Minghuang) fled to Shu. At that time, there was a local official who had rebelled alongside Lushan;
he had previously served as the Governor of Langzhou. A portrait of him was encountered along the road, and the Retired Emperor struck off its head with his sword.
Although the man himself was in Shaanxi, his head suddenly fell to the ground. The Retired Emperor once asked Xingyi, "Why is the destiny of our state so precarious?"

He traveled eastward with a golden casket containing a talisman. Upon reaching Wanli (Ten-Thousand-Li), he opened it; whenever he had previously looked inside, there was always a small amount of *danggui* (angelica).
Now that the imperial carriage had arrived at Chengdu and he was crossing the Wanli Bridge, he suddenly realized the significance of the *danggui* omen.
Thereupon, his sorrows were washed away and forgotten. In the seventh month, Suzong ascended the throne at Lingwu. Within ten days, troops from various commanderies arrived, whereupon...

Fang Guan served as Chancellor and concurrently held the title of Grand Commander. At that time, the calamities of war were still raging. Someone suggested that it would be appropriate to rely on divine blessings.
The Emperor accepted this advice and invited more than a hundred śramaṇas into the mobile palace to establish a *dharmāśālā* (meditation hall), where they chanted sutras morning and evening.
One night, the Emperor dreamed of a śramaṇa with a golden body reciting the name of Ratnasambhava Tathāgata. He questioned his attendants about this, and one replied, "It is Helan Valley."
There was a monk named Wulou who constantly recited this Buddha’s name; he possessed many miraculous powers. The Emperor summoned Wulou, but he firmly declined and did not go.

Soon after, he went to deliver the imperial decree to save Guo Ziyi. Wulou then appeared at the temporary capital (the imperial camp). The Emperor was delighted and said, "He is truly the monk I saw in my dream.
Meanwhile, the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra also appeared at the palace. The Emperor retained them both together and entrusted [them with his affairs].

**A General Discussion on Prayer and Relinquishment** At Longquan Mountain in Wenzhou, the Great Master Wuzhuo resided on the southern slope of the mountain. One day, he sought to relocate his dwelling.

Suddenly, the sky grew dark with lightning, and a dragon appeared at the foot of the mountain in the home of the Zhang family. Wuzhuo consequently requested that they relinquish their fields to build a temple;
however, the Zhangs wished to pay its value in cash. That night, it rained twenty thousand coins from the heavens to purchase them. Thus [the temple was established].
The temple was established in Gunseong, and its affairs were reported to the court. It was granted the name Ryongchon-yeon (according to the *Yeongneung byeon*).

In the first month of the first year of Dingsou (the second year of the reign), An Lushan’s son, Qingxu, assassinated Lushan and usurped the throne for himself. In the ninth month, [the Tang forces] defeated Qingxu and recaptured the capital.
In the tenth month, the Emperor returned to the capital. In the twelfth month, the Taishanghuang (Retired Emperor) arrived from West Shu.

In this year, the Master Chengguan, the commentator on the Avataṃsaka-sūtra, received ordination and the full precepts; he then exhorted himself with ten points, saying: "In body, I shall not discard the outward appearance of a śramaṇa;
in mind, I shall not contravene the regulations of the Tathāgata; in sitting, I shall not turn my back upon the sūtras of the Dharmadhātu."
By nature, he was untainted by the realms of emotional obstruction; his feet never trod upon the dust of a nunnery; his side never touched the couch of a lay devotee;
his eyes did not distinguish between improper colors; his tongue did not savor food past noon; his hands never released the perfectly luminous pearl;
and he never slept apart from his robes and bowl. He followed Chan Master Zhong of Niutou and Chan Master Qin of Jingshan.
When asked about the essential tenets of the Westward Transmission, he bestowed the Perfect Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* upon Chan Master Xuanzhen.
In the year Wuxu (the first year of the Qianyuan era), the monk Wulou manifested his passing within the imperial palace;
his feet remained about one chi above the ground. His attendants reported this to the Emperor, who was struck with wonder and amazement.

The Emperor descended from his carriage to inspect the site. He learned that the deceased had left a final testament requesting to be buried at Jiugou. An imperial decree was issued to protect the site at Jiugou and to construct a stupa there.
Upon reaching Huaiyuan County, [the remains] were immediately enshrined as a whole-body image made of clay and left in the subordinate temple.

Within the inner palace, the Emperor established an Inner Dao-chamber where the recitation of scriptures and the chanting of hymns were conducted with great solemnity. The Chancellor Zhang Gao remonstrated, saying:
"I pray that Your Majesty will take 'non-action' (wuwei) as your core principle and not disturb your sagely reflections with the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The Emperor did not accept this advice.

He subsequently issued an edict to establish monasteries on each of the Five Peaks and selected śramaṇas of high conduct to preside over them. He permitted laypeople who could recite five hundred sheets of scripture to be ordained as monks;
alternatively, those who paid one hundred strings of cash were granted certificates for tonsure and ordination, and were also awarded titles based on their mastery of the Classics.

When the [rebels] in Shenshi and the two capitals were pacified, he again received contributions of money from various prefectures in the Guanzhong region to ordain more than ten thousand monks and Daoists;
the practice of making such offerings began from this point onward.

In the third month of the second year, the Jihai cycle, an imperial edict was issued to all provinces throughout the realm, ordering each to establish a *fangsheng chi* (pond for the release of living beings).

In the tenth month, Yan Zhenqing, the Prefectural Governor of Shenzhou, composed the "Epigraph for the Ponds for the Release of Living Beings Throughout the Realm under the Tang. Its preface states: "Our Sovereign has raised up the entire realm..."

He took this to form a pond, so that all within the realm might receive its blessings. Relying on the power of the *dhāraṇī* empowerment, he exhausted the ocean of afflictions and the fords of birth and death.
Measuring this against antiquity, how could it ever be compared to anything of the past? (From the *Benzhuan*).

In the Gengzi year (the first year of the Shangyuan era), the Emperor dispatched an envoy to Caoxi to welcome the robe and bowl of the Sixth Patriarch and bring them into the palace for veneration (one source states this was the first year of the Qianyuan era).
○ Chan Master Shenhui of Heze entered nirvana; an imperial decree ordered the construction of a pagoda and temple complex, and he was posthumously granted the title Zhenzong Bore.
In the first month of the second year, the *Xin-chou* cycle, the Emperor fell ill.
Empress Zhang drew her own blood to transcribe Buddhist scriptures, while the various officials held vegetarian feasts for the monastic community at various temples (*Tang Shi*).
An imperial edict summoned Chan Master Huizhong of Nanyang to the palace. The edict stated in brief: "I have heard that the Tamer of Men..."
The Supreme Vehicle has long flourished in the Central Land. The Great Hero’s entrustment truly rests upon my person.
I contemplate bestowing the Way upon you, so that you may propagate these secret scriptures and extensively provide the moisture of blessings to reach the great trichiliocosm.

To transmit the mysterious pearl beyond form and to extract the poisonous arrows of delusion—this is indeed a noble opportunity; do not consider it a hardship. Come with your staff in hand; the capital is not far. Purify your mind.
It has been a long time. May you quickly fulfill the hopes of Your Majesty. It is cold in spring; I hope the Master is well. I send this decree without further elaboration.
Initially, Huizhong received the mind-seal of Caoxi and resided at Nanyang for forty years without descending from the mountain gates. Now, he has come to respond to the imperial summons.

At first, he was installed at Qianfu Temple. The Emperor frequently summoned him into the inner palace to inquire about the Way. One day, having purified himself through fasting and bathing, the Emperor presented ten questions to the Master. The first asked:

"After realizing one's nature (*jìng xìng*), is it still necessary to practice giving (*bōshī*) to cultivate merit? Zhong replied: "Giving without signs (*wúxiāng*) is in accord with realizing one's nature.
The second asked: "What kind of practices (*yè*) should one perform to be in accord with this Way? Zhong answered: "To be without effort (*wúgōng*) is to be in accord."

Regarding this path: third, there may be the difficulty of illness; how shall one practice to confront it? One should respond with the realization that the root of karma is fundamentally empty, thereby attaining immovability.
Fourth, at the time of death, how can one attain mastery? One should respond by exerting effort and having confidence in the Way.
Fifth, when afflictions arise, how shall one bring them to rest? One should respond by realizing that the fundamental mind is profoundly still, and thus afflictions...
Returning to the wondrous function is the response. Sixth: After seeing one’s nature, is it necessary to practice *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha’s name) to seek rebirth in the Pure Land?
Zhong responded: Nature itself is the Buddha; nature itself is the Pure Land. Seventh: Once this physical aggregate (*skandha*) has been cast off, where will one be born?
Zhong responded with: There is no casting off and no birth; it is spontaneous birth in sovereign freedom. Eighth: At the time of death, there is a jeweled throne upon a flower pedestal.
[The Master] said, "I am coming to welcome you; can you come? Chō replied, "I do not grasp at appearances.

[The Master] said, "How can one attain supernatural powers like those of a Buddha-land? Chō replied, "Realizing one's nature is like a poor person finding treasure, or like a subject meeting his king.

[The Master] said, "If one practices solely in accordance with this original nature, will one certainly become a Buddha? Chō replied, "One will certainly become a Buddha; yet even a Buddha has no form."
Non-attainment is itself true attainment. These ten pairs all have extensive explanations; here, I have merely paired them according to their topical categories.

Thereupon, the Emperor concentrated his mind on the profound essence (the Emperor had questions regarding the Ten Bodies of the Tamer and the Samādhi of Non-contention; the circumstances are recorded in the *Wudeng Huiyuan*).
In the fourth month of the Renyin year (the first year of Baoying), the nun Zhenru of Longxing Temple in Chu Prefecture was suddenly taken up into the heavens by someone who appeared to her.
There she beheld the Heavenly Emperor, who bestowed upon her thirteen treasures and said to Zhenru: "There shall be calamity in the Central Kingdom; you should use the second treasure to pacify it."
Cui Shen, the Prefectural Governor of Chu State, submitted a memorial to present these to the court: first, the "Mystic Yellow Celestial Talisman";
second, a jade rooster; third, a grain-jade disc; fourth, a Ring of the Queen Mother; fifth, a green-colored gem; sixth, a wish-fulfilling pearl;
seventh, a red mō-mò; eighth, a *langgan* pearl; ninth, a jade pendant; tenth, a jade seal; eleventh, a mulberry hook; twelfth, a thunder-axe; thirteenth—
(The name is lost. When the Emperor examined it, he was greatly pleased and named it the "State-Stabilizing Treasure" (*dingguobao*).

Since the tribute had been presented from Chu Prefecture—the very fiefdom of the Crown Prince—and it was further heard that the Central Plains ought to be secured by this second treasure, the Emperor subsequently issued an edict for the Crown Prince to assume the affairs of government, granted a general amnesty, and changed the era name (*jushi*).
(Old History) In the fifth month, the Retired Emperor passed away. The Emperor was so overcome with inner grief that he fell ill.
He passed away fourteen days later. Daizong ascended the throne.
It was the year of Gui-mao (the first year of Guangde).
In the eleventh month, the Tibetans captured the capital. The Emperor fled to Shan. When Guo Ziyi’s troops arrived, they defeated the Tibetans and recaptured the capital.
While the Emperor was at Huayin, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva of Wutai appeared to him and bestowed secret instructions upon him.

In the twelfth month, the Emperor returned to the capital and issued an edict to construct a Mañjuśrī Hall at Wutai, using copper for the roof tiles and coating them with gold. The cost was... [excessive].
Numbering in the hundreds of millions.

In the second year, the Jiachen year (824), an imperial edict was issued for the Inner Daochang to select three hundred monks, with one hundred serving per rotation. They were permitted to ride horses when entering or leaving the palace and constantly lectured upon and recited the *Renwang jing*.
The King Prajñā Sūtra: The Emperor welcomed National Teacher Zhong, who resided at the Kuangzhai Monastery.

In the first year of Yongtai (the year of Yisi), the Emperor began to favor ancestral sacrifices and did not yet hold the Buddha in high esteem. Yuan Zai, Wang Jin, and Du Hongjian served as Prime Ministers; these three men—
Both were devoted to the Buddha, though Wang Jin was particularly so. He abstained from meat and blood. Together with Li Hongjian, he established the Wufeng Temple.
The Emperor once asked him whether the Buddhist teachings regarding retribution truly exist or not. Wang Jin replied:

"The longevity and prosperity of our state’s destiny could not have been achieved without the planting of meritorious karma in previous lives. Once such merit is established, even if there are occasional minor calamities, they can ultimately do no harm."
This was harmful. Thus, while An Lushan and Shi Siming were still spreading their poison, both met with the calamity of losing their sons;

when Pugu Huaien raised troops to commit internal treachery, he died of illness upon leaving for the Uyghurs; and when the Tibetans launched a great invasion deep into the territory, they retreated without a fight.
All of these events were beyond human power to control. How can one say there is no karmic retribution? The Emperor, because of this, came to believe deeply.

Whenever Zai and his colleagues attended upon the Emperor, His Majesty would often speak of Buddhist matters with composure. Consequently, the worship of the Buddha within the palace was maintained, and the chanting of *brahmā-gāthā* and the offering of incense during fasts never slackened for even a moment.
The ministers followed this exemplary lead, and the people of the four quarters were all transformed by it.

[The Emperor] issued an edict that no government offices throughout the realm shall flog or humiliate monks and nuns. He also decreed that the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) be recited within the imperial palace. [The Emperor] issued an edict.

In the fifth month, Emperor Mingbu summoned the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to retranslate the old version of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*. In the fifth month, the Emperor dreamed that the Sixth Patriarch requested the return of his robe and bowl to Caoxi;

he dispatched an imperial messenger to send them back. In the ninth month, a golden bronze Buddha image was cast at the Guangshun Gate, and the Emperor led the hundred officials to pay their respects and offer sacrifices.
In the tenth month, the Tibetan forces invaded and pressed upon the capital; the Emperor issued the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* from within the palace.

After two days, the scripture was sent to various monasteries in Ximing for exposition. In the eleventh month of the year the rebellion was quelled, an imperial edict was issued to the Dharma Master Liangben to compose a new commentary on the *Renwang jing*.
When the commentary was completed, Ben presented it to the throne with a memorial; the Emperor praised it as excellent.

On the *renwu* day of the seventh month in the *bingwu* year (the first year of Dali), an *ulambana* assembly was held within the imperial palace. Altars were established for the seven successive emperors, beginning with Gaozu and continuing down to Taizong.
Gigantic banners were erected, each inscribed with the respective imperial title at its top. These were escorted from the Grand Ancestral Temple into the inner sanctuary.

The *náo* and *chuī* instruments were played, and the drums and dances performed; banners and streamers reached toward the heavens. On this day, the hundred officials stood in attendance at Guāngshùn Gate to welcome and prostrate before the imperial procession.
From then on, this became an annual custom. On the day of Kǒuwèi, two *língzhī* fungi grew in two chambers of the Grand Ancestral Temple;
the Emperor composed a poem to celebrate them, and the hundred officials all joined in harmony.

In the seventh month of the second year (the Dingwei year), Yu Cha’en memorialized that the manor previously granted to him should be converted into Changjing Temple to provide for the posthumous merit of Empress Dowager Changjing.

The construction was executed with the utmost magnificence and splendor, costing more than ten billion [coins]. Although the Jinshi Gao Ying submitted petitions on this matter twice, both were suppressed.
In the [blank] month of that year, the Chancellor Du Hongjian went out to govern Ba and Shu.

Upon arriving in Yizhou, he dispatched a messenger to Mount Baiya to invite Chan Master Wuzhu into the city. He asked for instruction on the Dharma, saying: "I, your disciple, have heard the Venerable Jin speak thus:"
"The Dharma-gate of the three phrases: 'no recollection,' 'no thought,' and 'do not be deluded. I do not know whether these are one or three. Wuzhu said, "No recollection is named precept;

no thought is named concentration; do not be deluded is named wisdom. However, when the single mind does not arise, one possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom simultaneously—it is neither one nor three.
At that moment, a crow cawed. The Master asked the Teacher, "Did you hear it? The Teacher replied, "Hearing and not hearing..."
"Listen. This hearing is not related to the nature of hearing. When there is sound, it is the object of sound that arises of itself;
when there is no sound, it is the object of sound that ceases of itself. Yet this nature of hearing does not arise following the sound, nor does it cease following the sound.

To awaken to this nature of hearing is to escape the cycle of transmigration through the objects of sound. It is the same for form, fragrance, taste, and touch. You and your subordinates were filled with joy."
Yue praised this as excellent. The Master asked again, "What is meant by 'recognizing the mind and seeing the nature'?

He replied, "All people drift along with their thoughts because they do not recognize the true mind and do not see their original nature. As for the true mind, even when thoughts arise, it does not follow them in arising."
Mindfulness of cessation does not rely on stillness; it is neither fixed nor distracted. It is ordinary and sovereign; everything encountered by the eye is thus.
There is nothing that is not the seeing-nature. Thus, Hongjian settled his mind in the joy of dhyāna (Five Lamps).

In the fifth year (Wu-shen), an imperial edict was issued for the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to establish a *maṇḍala* at Xingshan Monastery. The Emperor commanded his close attendants, high ministers, and generals of the various provinces to all receive the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
The Emperor personally conferred an official title upon Amoghavajra: he was specially appointed as the *Tongzhin* (Special Advance) and *Honglu Qing* (Court of State Ceremonial).
The Emperor summoned National Teacher Zhong to the inner palace and introduced the man from Mount Taibai to him. The Emperor said, "This man possesses considerable insight;

I request that you, Master, examine him. Zhong asked, "What abilities do you possess? The man replied, "I am fortunate enough to recognize mountains, recognize lands, recognize characters, and am skilled at calculation.
Zhong asked, "As for the mountain where you dwell, is it a male mountain or a female mountain? The man was utterly bewildered.

He could not answer. Chong pointed to the floor of the hall and asked, "What is this place? He replied, "Only after my disciple has calculated it will I know. Chong drew a single line on the ground and said, "This is the character '甚' (shèn). He replied, "It is one character. Chong said, "A single stroke upon the earth is the character '王' (wáng). How can you call it 'one character'? Chong then asked again, "Calculate what thirty times seven is. He replied, "National Teacher. Chong said, "I am asking for the calculation; why do you give me the title? The National Teacher was silent. Chong said, "The National Teacher is truly a National Teacher. He then bowed and departed. Chong then said to the assembly, "The National Teacher was like a man who, when asked about the price of a horse, answered with the cost of the saddle. He then composed a verse: "Thirty times seven is twenty-one; The National Teacher is truly a National Teacher. If you ask for the price of the horse, He answers with the cost of the saddle. Later, he composed another verse: "The National Teacher is truly a National Teacher; He is like a man who, when asked about the price of a horse, Answers with the cost of the saddle. If you wish to understand the meaning of this, Look at the character '甚' on the ground. Chong then called out to the assembly: "Do you all understand? If you do not understand, listen to my verse: 'The National Teacher is truly a National Teacher; He is like a man who, when asked about the price of a horse, Answers with the cost of the saddle. If you wish to understand the meaning of this, Look at the character '甚' on the ground. At that time, there was a monk named Daowu. Chong asked him, "How many characters are there in the word '甚'? Daowu replied, "Three characters. Chong said, "You have been following me for so long; how can you still say there are three characters? "Are you playing with your disciples? Are three times seven not twenty-one? Zhong said, "In fact, it is the mountain man who is playing with this poor monk.
Three times seven is ten; why do you say twenty-one? He asked again, "What other abilities do you have? [Zhong] replied, "Even if I, your disciple, possessed such abilities..."
He also did not dare to open his mouth toward the National Teacher. Zhong said, "Even if you possessed such ability, it would still not be correct.
Zhong then said to the Emperor, "To ask about mountains and not know mountains; to ask about lands and not know lands; to ask about characters and not know characters;
to ask about calculation and not understand calculation—where did Your Majesty obtain this hoodwinking fellow? The Emperor said to the mountain man, "I have a kingdom."
"Status is not worthy of being considered a treasure; the Master is truly a national treasure. The mountain man said, "Your Majesty is indeed one who truly recognizes treasure.
In that year, an imperial edict was issued to Chan Master Daoqin of Mount Jing. The edict stated:

"I have heard that in the region south of the Yangtze River there is a Chan practitioner who harbors the Way, whose virtuous nature is as pure as ice and frost, and whose pure conduct dwells amidst the forests and wilds. I gaze upon him with an empty mind, longing for him with deep and constant yearning."

My feelings will surely reach you, and the nation shall likewise share in great celebration. I pray that the Venerable Master will descend from afar to the Central Kingdom, so that I may fully devote myself to you.

Do not disregard the power of your vows; manifest your form in response to sentient beings. I now specially issue this decree to welcome you; please swiftly fulfill my heart's desire. As the spring chill persists, I hope the Master is well.

The Emperor sent this decree, which was not extensive. When the Master arrived at the capital in response to the summons, the Emperor personally paid him homage and offered words of comfort and inquiry.

In a relaxed conversation, the Emperor remarked, "I have heard that the divine dragon of Mount Jingshan offered its pond to establish a precious monastery; were it not for the Master’s virtue and character, such a thing could not have been possible.
One day, while the Master was in the inner court, he rose to his feet upon seeing the Emperor. The Emperor said, "Why must you rise when seeing me?"

The Master said, "Your Majesty, how could you perceive this poor monk within the four modes of deportment? The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him the title National First Chan Master (from the *Benlu*).
In the Jǐyǒu year (the fourth year), the Emperor was once in the private hall.
Pointing to Yú Chá'ēn, he said to National Teacher Zhōng, "Chá'ēn also understands a bit of the Buddha-dharma.
Chá'ēn immediately asked the National Teacher, "What is ignorance (*avidyā*)? From what does ignorance arise? The Master replied:
"The signs of the decline of the Buddha-dharma are now manifest. The Emperor asked, "Why is that? The Master said, "Even a slave knows how to ask about the Buddha-dharma;
is this not a sign that decline has appeared? Zhaoen’s expression turned angry. The Master said, "This very [anger] is ignorance (*avidyā*); from this, ignorance arises.
Zhaoen spoke again, "Some say that you, Master, are now a Buddha—is this so? The Master said, "Some say that you are a god (*deva*)."
"Is it so, my son? Chao'en prostrated himself on the ground and said, "I am guilty of death. The Master said, "My grace is truly not that of a Son of Heaven.

The Master said, "I am not a Buddha. Chao'en said, "Then you shall remain forever an ordinary man; will there never be a time when you attain Buddhahood? The Master said, "In the future, I shall certainly become a Buddha.
But if I become a Buddha, I shall no longer be named Huizhong. And if you, in the future, become a Son of Heaven, you must change [your name]."
The surname [of the monk] was not Mo; it was not Yu or Fou. Zhao’en prostrated himself on the ground again, saying, "I deserve death.
Zhao’en added, "From now on, I truly dare not discuss the Buddha-dharma with you, Master. Zhong said to the Emperor, "I feared that this slave would be put to death.
(General Discourse) Chan Master Qin of Jing Mountain earnestly requested to return to the mountain. Chan Master Daoyi of Jiangxi preached the Dharma at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang.

At the temple, known at the time as Mazu [Monastery], Chan Master Niutou Huizhong passed away. Throughout his life, the Master never changed his single robe, and his only utensil was a single cauldron.
He once had two granaries of grain provided for the monks; when thieves sought to steal it, tigers guarded it for him.

When County Magistrate Zhang Xun entered the mountain to pay his respects and inquire about the Master’s disciples, he asked, "How many disciples do you have? The Master replied, "There are three or five."
The Master struck the meditation bench three times; three tigers emerged with a roar, and Xun retreated in terror.

Later, when he moved to Zhuangyan Temple and was about to construct a Dharma Hall and build a tomb, two divine beings determined the four corners and secretly assisted with the night labor until it was completed in no time.
Consequently, disciples gathered like clouds. When his end drew near, he hung a cauldron before his stone chamber.

The tree and the climbing vine upon which his robes hung withered and died for no apparent reason. After the Master had assembled the community for the *poṣadha* ceremony, he shaved his hair, bathed his body, and sat peacefully until his passing (from the *Wudeng huiyuan*).

In the gengxu year (the fifth year), the Tripitaka Master Dier from the Western Regions arrived at the capital. He claimed to have attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds. The Emperor requested National Teacher Zhong to test him.
Zhong said, "Tell me, where is this old monk now? Dier replied, "The Master is the National Teacher; how could he..."
He went to Tianjin Bridge to watch the monkey performances. Zhaozhong asked again, "Where is he now? Wuzhuo said, "How could the National Teacher go to Western Sichuan to watch the boat races?
Zhaozhong asked again, "Where is he now? After a long while, Wuzhuo was at a loss as to where he had gone.

Zhaozhong rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit! Where is your supernormal power of knowing others' minds? [Regarding] Amoghavajra (Bukong Sanzang): [The text continues: ...Amoghavajra... [The passage concludes with the mention of his name and context.]
He manifested illness as a pretext to decline his audience with the Emperor. An imperial edict was issued dispatching an inner palace messenger to offer condolences and inquiries.

He was subsequently conferred the title of *Kaifu Yitong Sansi* (Minister of State, Peerage) and the Duke of Xiao Commandery; however, he declined this honor four times. The Emperor would not permit it.

On the *guiwei* day of the sixth month, he bathed, changed his robes, and passed away while lying peacefully. The Emperor suspended court proceedings for three days. He was posthumously granted the title of *Sikong* (Grand Minister of Works), and his posthumous name was bestowed as Dabianzheng Guangzhi (Great Discernment and Correctness, Extensive Wisdom).
On the day of the cremation of the Tripiṭaka Master, an imperial messenger was dispatched by decree to carry the prayer for the ancestral sacrifice;
the sagely words were profound and moving, and his rites surpassed all others (this appears in the stele biography, though the *Tongjian* records that the Master passed away in the ninth year).

In the sixth year (Xin Hai), Zhang Ting-shang, the Regional Commander (Jiedushi) of Huainan, submitted a formal petition regarding the life and deeds of the Great Master Sengcan of Shuzhou, requesting a posthumous title from the court.
In the fourth month, he was granted the posthumous title of Chan Master Jingzhi, and his stupa was named Jueji. In the ninth month, an imperial edict was issued...

The relics of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra were enshrined in a stupa at his former residence temple. Yan Ying, the Censor-in-Chief, composed a stele inscription to commemorate his virtues, which states in brief:
"The Upādhyāya was a man from the Western Regions. During the reigns of three emperors—Xuanzong, Suzong, and Daizong—he served as the State Preceptor for Consecration (Guanding Guoshi).
He had fifty summers as a monk and lived to the age of seventy. He translated one hundred and thirty-six fascicles of scriptures. From the Golden... [text ends]
Vajrasattva received the meaning of the Yoga Supreme Vehicle before Vairocana Buddha and transmitted it to Nāgārjuna. Nāgārjuna transmitted it to the master Nāgabodhi.
Nāgabodhi transmitted it to the master Vajrabodhi. Vajrabodhi came from the East and transmitted it to Amoghavajra;
this constitutes six generations. Amoghavajra transmitted it to Huilang and others; these are what the world calls the Esoteric Teachings (Mikkyō). 10.
In the second month, the Vinaya Master Tanyi of Yuezhou passed away. The Master was possessed of profound wisdom and extensive learning; he widely propagated the teachings of the Vinaya.
Renowned scholars such as Lu Xiangxian and Li Yong were all his inseparable friends.
In the seventh year, the *wuchen* year (792), Yan Lugu Gong Zhenqing composed the "Record of the Precept Platform at the Lüzangyuan of Baoyingsi in Fuzhou. It states briefly:

"The prefecture has the 'Scripture Translation Terrace' of Xie Lingyun; the Minister Wei Gong memorialized that it be made into Baoyingsi, and requested that the Vinaya Master Huichin [be appointed there]."

When the Master ascended the altar, he sounded the wooden clapper. From far and near, people rushed forth, filling the precincts of the ritual site. The Dharma of the Image Age underwent a transformation;
all marveled at the power of his transformative influence.

In the eighth year, the *geng-chen* year, the Śramaṇa Cunda from the Western Regions arrived at the capital. At that time he was over six hundred years old. The Emperor summoned him for an audience and questioned him regarding the arts of nourishing life;
he received great respect and admiration. Du Hongjian resigned from the post of Chancellor on account of illness, relinquishing his office after three days.
He passed away. At the time of his death, he was solemnly dressed in court robes with a saṃghāṭī robe added over them; having shaved his beard and hair, he departed.
His final testament was that he be buried according to the dharma of a śramaṇa (Old History).

In the ninth year, the Year of Jiayin (654 CE), the Daoist Shi Hua gained favor through his magical arts. He consequently requested permission to set up a blade-ladder to compete with the śramaṇas in their methods. An imperial decree was issued.
The two streets selected their monks to compete on a set date. The śramaṇa Chonghui regularly recited the *Śūraṅgama-mantra*. He submitted a memorial requesting to defeat [the opponent].
The Emperor led his hundred officials to observe the spectacle. Shi Hua stepped onto a blade and ascended a ladder; he then commanded Chonghui to climb it.

Chonghui stepped upon the blades and ascended, returning and forth without injury. Taking advantage of this victory, he ordered that firewood be piled in the courtyard and a great conflagration ignited. Chonghui—
He entered a mass of fire and called out for the flower to enter. The flower blushed with shame and did not dare look directly at him.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and dismissed the assembly, bestowing honors upon Chonghui and granting him the title "Tripitaka Master Guardian of the State" (*Fodao lunheng*). ○ The śramaṇa Yuanze was on close terms with the hermit Li Yuan.

They encouraged one another to travel to Mount Emei. Sengze wished to go by way of Chang’an, while Fayuan wished to go from Jingzhou; thus, they set out from Jingzhou. As their boat reached Nanpu, they saw a woman wearing a patterned bodice drawing water. Sengze wept and said, "The reason I did not wish to go this way was for her sake. Fayuan asked him in surprise for the reason. Sengze said, "This woman has been pregnant for three years, waiting for me to become her son. He did not finish speaking when he passed away. Fayuan then went to Chang’an, where he met Sengze’s mother. The mother told him, "Your father died while on his way to Mount Emei. He left behind a letter saying that he had been born as a son to a woman at Nanpu who had been pregnant for three years, waiting for him. Fayuan returned to Nanpu and searched for the woman, eventually finding her. He gave her the letter and explained the circumstances. The woman wept and said, "I have indeed been pregnant for three years, but I am not yet married. How could I possibly have a son? Fayuan replied, "Your husband will soon arrive. Later, a man came from afar to claim her as his wife. When she opened the letter, she found it was written in her own hand. She then believed in the Dharma and became a nun. She lived for several decades and only then passed away. It is said that she was reborn in heaven. This is why Sengze wept at Nanpu. His filial piety moved even the spirits. Thus, one knows that the Way of the Buddha is truly profound and vast. It is not something that can be measured by worldly standards. One must simply believe with one's heart and mind. How could it be otherwise? It is like the case of the monk Sengfu, who was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven after dying in the marketplace of Chang’an. Or like the monk Sengshao, who was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven after dying in the marketplace of Xiangyang. Or like the nun Huiming, who was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven after dying in the marketplace of Chang’an. Or like the laywoman Fashang, who was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven after dying in the marketplace of Chang’an. These are all examples of those who, through the power of their sincere devotion, were able to transcend the three realms and ascend to the Pure Land. How much more so for those who, having already received the precepts and cultivated the path, should not be able to attain rebirth in the Pure Land? Therefore, one should know that the Pure Land is the ultimate destination for those who practice the Mahāyāna. It is not merely a matter of seeking a peaceful death in the present life. One must cultivate the path with earnestness and diligence, never ceasing until the end. Only then will one be able to reach the goal. This is what is meant by "the Dharma is not far off; it is only that people do not seek it. One must simply believe with one's heart and mind. How could it be otherwise? If we had met before, that would have been it; now that we have met, there is no way to escape. On the third day after my birth, I wished for you to visit me, taking a smile as my token of recognition.
Thirteen years hence, outside Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou, I shall meet you.
I will have become a bhikṣu through three lifetimes and will reside at Yue-lu Monastery on the western mountains of Xiangxi. There, amidst a grove of massive boulders, I shall practice dhyāna.
Wang Ze was away. After his wife had been nursing for three days, Yuan went to visit her;
the child indeed smiled. Later, as agreed, he arrived at Wu to meet her by the well of Ge Hong. There he heard a cowherd singing: "Upon the Three-Life Stone lies our ancient spirit;
Whether we praise the moon or chant in the wind, let us not debate it. I am ashamed that my lover has come from afar to visit; Though this body differs, its nature remains forever."
Yuan asked, "Is Master Ze well? He replied, "Master Li is indeed a man of true faith. However, his worldly karmic ties are not yet exhausted; do not approach him for now.
Only when you have practiced diligently without indolence shall we meet again. He then sang this song: "The affairs before and after the body are vast and vague;
To speak of their causes and conditions would surely break one's heart. I have searched through the mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue; Now I turn my smoke-smoke boat back upstream."
At Qutang Gorge, [the mountain] suddenly vanished from sight.
In the year Yimao (the tenth year), National Teacher Zhong was about to pass away;
he entered the imperial presence to take leave of Emperor Daizong. The Emperor asked, "After you have entered nirvana, what shall your disciples do?"
The record states: Zhong said, "Inform the donor that you must construct a seamless stūpa. The Emperor asked, "Please show me the model for the master’s stūpa.

After a long silence, Zhong asked, "Do you understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. Zhong said, "I have an attendant named Yingzhen (who later resided at Danyuan) who understands this matter.
On the ninth day of the twelfth month, he passed away in the right side-down posture. His disciples enshrined his entire body.

A stupa was erected for him, and he was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Dazheng (Great Realization). The Emperor soon summoned Yingzhen into the palace and asked him about the previous statement.
After a long silence, Yingzhen said, "Does Your Majesty understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. Yingzhen then recited a verse:
"To the south of Xiang and to the north of Tan, In between lies gold sufficient to fill a nation. Beneath the shadowless tree, the boat is joined together; Upon the crystal palace..."
He lacked knowledge of this.

In the year Bingchen (the eleventh year), Zhou Boyu, who served as the Vice Governor of Weizhou, was a regular reciter of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Suddenly, he beheld a monk from India. Boyu asked, "Who are you?"
He said, "I am Subhūti. For several years I have been reciting the sutras for you, yet you have never ceased eating meat.

If you are determined to seek Buddhahood with a sincere heart, you must certainly abstain from meat. From that time forth, Boyu abstained from meat and subsisted on vegetarian food, increasing his recitation and upholding of the teachings. (From the *Zhengyan fu*).

In the Ding-si year (the twelfth year), Chengguan, whose courtesy name was Daxiu, became the commentator on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Initially, in the third year of the Dali era, he was summoned by imperial decree to enter the palace to serve as a literary editor for the translations of the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra.
After the Great Virtuous One had subsequently taken his leave, Chengguan entered Mount Wutai at the Mahāvaipulya Temple.
He contemplated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* with deep reflection and extensively studied various heterodox doctrines.

In the year Wu-wu (the thirteenth year), he issued an edict to the Vinaya masters of the two capitals to carefully determine the new and old provisions of the Vinaya, categorizing the rules regarding observance and transgression, and to promulgate them throughout the empire. At that time—
The practice of Chan flourished extensively. Mazu Daoyi presided over the school in Jiangxi, while Shitou Xiqian presided over it in Hunan;
travelers came and went in great numbers, all flocking to the gates of these two great masters.
