In the year Jǐwèi (the fourteenth year), Chan Master Chōnghuì of Tiānzhù Mountain first received the Dharma from Níngzōng of Niútóu. A monk asked, "Before Bodhidharma came to this land, was there the Buddha-Dharma?
He replied, "Setting aside for a moment whether it existed before he came, what is the case right now? He also said of him: [text fragment].
He came home looking much like a fortune-teller. Seeing that you did not understand, he pierced through the lines of the divination for you;

as soon as the signs of good or ill fortune arose, they rested upon your own lot, and you must observe them all yourself. This year he passed away; his physical body remained uncorrupted, remaining for several hundred years.
In the fifth month, the Emperor died, and Dezong ascended the throne.
In the Gengshen year (the first year of Jianzhong),
Chan Master Deng Yinfeng burned a monk while heating water for a bath. One day, he called out from an open window toward the heavens, saying, "Return!"
The Master summoned him, saying, "Monk, are you alive or dead? The monk replied, "I am dead. The Master said, "Since you are already dead, who is it that seeks for life?
The monk thanked him and said, "I have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); therefore, I do not see [it]."
In the second year, the year of Xinyou (781), Chan Master Chang of Damei, after having a direct encounter with Mazu, entered Damei Mountain and resided there for twenty years.
When Mazu heard of this, he sent a monk to inquire: "What principle did you realize under Master Ma that caused you to settle on this mountain? The Master replied: "Ma..."
The Master said, "The Way of the Teacher is that the mind itself is Buddha," and he remained settled right here.

A monk said, "Master Ma’s Dharma has recently changed; he now says it is 'neither mind nor Buddha. The Master said, "This old fellow will never stop deluding people! Let him say 'neither mind nor Buddha' all he wants;
I only maintain that 'the mind itself is Buddha. When the monk returned and reported this to the Patriarch (Nanyue), the Patriarch said, "The plum is ripe."
In the third year (the Renxu year), Emperor Dezong dispatched an envoy to summon Làn Zàn.

At that time, Làn Zàn was stirring a fire of cow dung and seeking out roasted yams to eat; with cold tears streaming down his chest, he had not yet responded. The envoy urged him to wipe away his tears, to which Làn Zàn replied, "How could I have the leisure to wipe them for a worldly person?"

[He] wept. In the end, he could not bring [it] and departed. He composed this verse for himself: "A single brazier of fire in the deep night, The whole family sits together in a circle. Having roasted the taro until it is cooked, The Son of Heaven is not my equal.

Furthermore, he inscribed his own portrait, saying: "The dung-fire knows only the yellow beauty; The silver hook does not recognize the fresh purple clay seal. I have no mind even to wipe away cold tears, How could I have the leisure to question worldly men?"
In the tenth month of the fourth year, the *guihai* year, Zhu Ci’s troops rebelled; he usurped the title of state, naming it Qin, and the Emperor fled to Fengtian.

Dharma Master Chengguan composed his commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, dividing the *Avataṃsaka* into four major sections based on faith, understanding, practice, and realization. This work took a total of four years to complete.
The inscription was completed.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day (the first year of Xingyuan), in the fifth month, the capital was recaptured;
in the seventh month, the Emperor returned to the capital. Regarding Chan Master Mingzan of Nanyue: he initially lived in seclusion.

[This was] submitted as a memorial. Prime Minister Li Mi visited him at Mount Heng during the Qianyuan era. As Zhan was reciting the scriptures, Mi said, "Are you not one who has retired in seclusion?
Do you not harbor ambitions for the clouds and the sky? Zhan spat at him, saying, "Do not plot against me. Mi’s expression did not waver.
After a long while, Zhan noticed that Mi remained standing, waiting without ceasing, and asked, "Has it not yet been time for your meal? Mi replied, "Not yet. Zhan pushed [aside the food].
Fire emerged from the yam he was eating. Li Mi conversed with him for a long time before taking his leave. Li Zàn patted his back and said, "You will serve well as a prime minister for ten years.
When Li Mi came to power, he spoke of [Li Zàn’s] noble conduct to the Emperor, and an edict was issued to summon him.

When the messenger arrived at the Stone Cave, he proclaimed the imperial decree, saying, "Venerable One, please rise to express your gratitude. Li Zàn closed his eyes, sat cross-legged in meditation, and remained utterly still. He did not...
He kept this in mind. The messenger did not press him for an answer, but returned to report the matter to the Emperor. The Emperor praised him with admiration four or five times without ceasing.
Zàn once composed a song, which runs roughly as follows: "The affairs of the world are endless; they are no better than mountain mounds.

Lying beneath the wisteria vines, with a block of stone for a pillow, one has no anxieties regarding birth and death—what more need be feared? (Wudeng Huiyuan). ○ Chan Master Zhànrán of Jīngxī passed away.
Liang Su of the Hanlin Academy inscribed the following on the back of the stele: "When the Sage does not appear, there must surely arise one destined for the world.
Since the Venerable Zhi entrusted the Dharma to Guanding, it has passed through two generations to reach Zuoxi. The Way was clear yet appeared obscure; it awaits you, Master, to be revealed.
Mounting this precious vehicle, it flourishes once more in its renaissance. Those who received his instruction and attained mastery number thirty-nine."
Among the people, there were several dozen gentry scholars of high rank and illustrious reputation who humbled themselves to receive his instruction.

As the teacher was revered and the Way honored, those both far and near turned to him with benevolence. Were he not a sage-like figure destined for the world, how could such a state have been reached?

In the year Yichou (the first year of the Zhenguan era), there was the lay practitioner Pang Yun, whose courtesy name was Daoxuan. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. His father served as the Regional Inspector of Hengyang; after he passed away while in office, the family settled there.
From his youth, the lay practitioner was quick-witted and possessed a lofty, pure character. He always mingled with the mundane world and harmonized with the light of common society. He once...
He loaded tens of thousands of household treasures onto a boat and sank them in the depths of Lake Dongting.

When people asked the Layman why he did not practice giving or build temples, he replied, "Since beginningless time, I have been bound by the mutual entanglement of cause and effect and have failed to attain liberation;
from now on, my life shall be as simple as this. He had a son named Genghuo and a daughter named Lingzhao, who daily sold bamboo sieves.
He supported himself by selling them in the market. This year, the Layman went to visit Master Shitou, where they reached a wondrous accord beyond words.
One day, Shitou asked, "How do you conduct yourself in your daily activities? The Layman presented this verse: "In daily activities there is no distinction;

Only I myself am in perfect harmony. At every turn there is neither grasping nor rejecting; In every place there is no discord or conflict. Who assigns the titles 'Red' and 'Purple'? The streams and mountains—"
He cut off all traces of dust; his supernormal powers were coupled with wondrous function. Carrying water and hauling firewood—this was how he acted. Later, he went to Jiangxi to study under Mazu.
He asked, "Who is it that does not take companionship with the myriad dharmas?

Mazu replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single draught, and then I will tell you. At this, the Layman attained great enlightenment. From then on, his spiritual discernment and eloquence [became renowned].
At that point, nothing could resist him.

On the fifth month of the second year, the *lǜshī* (vinaya master) Daocheng was summoned by imperial decree to enter the palace and bestow the precepts upon the consorts, ladies-in-waiting, and eunuchs; he was subsequently granted the title Dayuan.
The Vinaya Master [Daoxuan] established regulations for the preaching of the Dharma in various monasteries and further organized the *Lanpen* (Ullambana) assemblies.

Liang Su of the Hanlin Academy completed his commentary on the *Tiantai Zhiguan Lun* and authored the *Zhiguan Tongli*. It states briefly: "Cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are the principles that guide the myriad transformations and lead one back to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
That things cannot return [to this state] is due to delusion and agitation. To illuminate delusion is called..."

Clarity is called stillness when it abides amidst movement; clarity and stillness constitute the essence of *samatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). In the causal stage, they are termed *samatha* and *vipaśyanā*;

in the resultant stage, they are termed wisdom (*jñāna*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This enables one to be still while moving and clear while still. Through their mutual dependence in the causal stage, phenomena are established;

through their transcendence of dependence, the fundamental source is illuminated. Alas! Are not *samatha* and *vipaśyanā* the treatises for saving the world and clarifying the Way? It is not otherwise.

Noble wisdom is transcendent; who is able to know it? If an ordinary person uses a mind subject to arising and ceasing—wherein the three delusions are vast—to infer the sublime principle from within conventional discourse, this is like a vinegar-fly attempting to speak of the Great Peng, or a summer insect debating the layered ice of winter.
It is clearly impossible for such a person to perceive the light of truth.

In the Dingmao year (the third year), the Dharma Master Chengguan completed his commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. He first lectured upon it for the assembly, whereupon auspicious clouds were moved to gather and linger in the air before the lecture hall.
Furthermore, for the sake of the monk Rui and others, he composed the *Sui shu yanyi* (Explication of the Meaning According to the Commentary) in forty fascicles, providing word-by-word exegesis.
*Mingjing* (Mirror of History), one hundred fascicles.

In the year Wuchen (the fourth year), when there were thirty-six earthquakes in the capital, an imperial decree was issued to welcome the finger bone of the Buddha from the Wuyouwang Temple in Qizhou for veneration within the inner palace. ○ Third month. Jiang...
The Great Master Daoyi of West Mazu passed away. His verse at the time of death read: "The mind-ground is explained according to the occasion;

Bodhi is likewise simply peace. When phenomena and principle are both unimpeded, that which is born is precisely unborn. His disciples enshrined his remains and *śarīra* relics and established a monastic center at Shimen.
Quan Deyu, the Chancellor, composed an inscription for him, and Emperor Xuanzong bestowed upon him the posthumous title of "Da" (Great).
Master Ji had one hundred and thirty-nine disciples who attained the Dharma; each became a patriarch of a particular region, and their transformative influence was inexhaustible.
Thus, the Chan school reached its peak of flourishing in the world at this time.
In the tenth month of the Ji-si year (the fifth year), an imperial messenger was dispatched with an edict to welcome Dharma Master Chengguan to the palace.
Chan Master Qin Guoyi of Mount Jing resided at Longxing Temple; that same year, the Emperor sent an imperial messenger to offer his greetings. Chan Master Lingmo of Wuxie...
The Master first visited Shitou Xiqian. Upon leaving the gate, he returned and said, "From birth until old age, it is simply this. Thereupon, the Master attained great enlightenment.
He stayed there for a long time before entering Tiantai at the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, where he resided at the White Sand Monastery (Baisa Daochang) and later lived at Wuxie.
In the twelfth month of the sixth year, the cyclical year gengwu, Chan Master Xiqian of Shitou passed away at the age of ninety-one; he was posthumously titled the Great Master Wujie (Boundless).
When the Master first read Sengzhao’s *Treatise on Emptiness*, he came across the passage: "Only the sage, indeed, can take the myriad things as himself.

He then experienced a sudden awakening and said, "The sage has no self; there is nothing that is not his own self. Thereupon, he composed the *Cantong qi* (Mysterious Agreement), the text of which runs roughly as follows:

"The mind of the Great Immortal of the land of India was secretly transmitted from east to west. The fact [of this transmission] is like the meeting of a lid and its box; the principle [of the teaching] corresponds to the point of an arrow's tip meeting another. Receiving these words..."
One must realize the fundamental source; do not establish your own rules and regulations. If you do not realize the Way upon meeting it at every turn, how can you know the road while your feet move?

Advancing forward is neither far nor near; delusion creates a barrier as solid as mountains and rivers. I respectfully address those who study the profound mystery: do not let your time and energy be spent in vain.
(Five Lamps) Master Weiyun first studied under Mazu and attained the essential heart of the teaching. At this time, he was traveling to propagate the Dharma in the regions of Wu and Yue.

In the sixth month of the seventh year (the Xinwei year), the Emperor visited Zhangjing Temple to observe the translation of scriptures. The Emperor composed a poem, and the Crown Prince and the various ministers all joined in with verses of their own.
Chan Master Zang of Xitang in Chuzhou had studied under Mazu and attained the Dharma; Mazu had spoken the words, "Zang has a head but no neck. Upon reaching [this point]...
The assembly requested that the hall be opened for the funeral rites.
On the *renshen* day (the eighth year), in the twelfth month, Chan Master Guoyi Qin of Mount Jing passed away. He was posthumously granted the title of Chan Master Dajue. His age was ninety.
12. In the tenth year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong, an imperial decree granted a stone stele for his life account, composed by Cui Yuanhan of the Biubu.
When Chan Master Weiwen arrived at Poyang, the mountain deity requested to receive the eight precepts.

In the ninth year, the *gengyou* year, after Pang Jushi had personally met Mazu and various other masters, he lived with spontaneous ease. He traveled and resided throughout Xiangzhou and Hanzhou, dwelling neither in mountain forests nor cities, his location never fixed.
His daughter, Lingchang, always followed him. The Master had a verse that said: "The mind is like the environment..."
It is also like this: neither real nor unreal, neither concerned with existence nor constrained by non-existence; not a sage or a worthy, but an ordinary person who has finished their business.
The tenth year of the Jiashu era.

Shi Jiaoran (whose given name was Zhou; one source says it was his courtesy name) possessed extraordinary talent. He was held in high esteem by Yan Lugu Gong, Yu Di, Wu Jide, and other eminent figures.
Whenever Lu Yu arrived, they would engage in refined conversation all day long, and the scholar-officials of the realm admired his refined character.
Nevertheless, he felt ashamed to be known for his literary works. He once sighed, saying: "If one were to possess the vast learning of Confucius and the extensive knowledge of Xu Chen..."
To spend one's entire life before one's eyes boasting of the Way and cultivating righteousness is merely sufficient to disturb the true nature;

how could it compare to sitting in meditation amidst the clouds and moon of pine-clad crags, where the Way is harmonized through silence and the nature is unified through ultimate stillness? I shall enter Mount Zhu.
Thereupon, Bao burned the poems and prose he had composed. Later, when Li Hong, the Imperial Censor, was serving as the Governor of Huzhou, he visited Zhaou in person and requested his writings.
Bao said, "I have wielded my brush and inkstone for over twenty years, yet I have gained nothing at all.

My secret investigations into the burdens of worldly objects have only served to give rise to the notions of 'self' and 'other. I have discarded them long ago. Li Hong searched among the common people and managed to recover only ten pieces.

[The work was] completed in ten fascicles. During the day [of its completion], Yu Ti, the Chancellor, composed a preface and presented it to the court. Emperor Dezong issued an edict to enshrine it in the Secret Library (Bige).

On the day of Yihai (the eleventh year), the Vinaya Master Lingche, whose courtesy name was Yuancheng, resided at Yunmen Temple in Yuezhou. At that time, the high officials and nobles were all possessed of great talent and reputation.
Liú Chángqīng, Yán Wéi, and Huángfù Cén all sent their calling cards to him and formed friendships with him. Chè’s poetry was ranked alongside that of Jiǎorán and the monk Biāo.

He authored the twenty-one fascicles of the *Lǜzōng xíngyuán* (The Source of Practice in the Vinaya School). Initially, when Chè traveled to the capital, his fame resounded throughout the imperial city.
Monastics, envious of his success, circulated malicious rumors and slandered him until he was punished by being banished to Tíngzhōu. Upon entering Huìkēi, he subsequently...
He spent his final years in the regions of Wu and Yue. The Chancellor Quan Deyu once composed a preface for his departure, in which he remarked:
"One observes his countenance and examines his words to know his mind; there is no need to wait for external conditions to become still before one attains stillness.
Furthermore, Quan Deyu was on intimate terms with Master Xuan. When Xuan returned to Tianzhu, Deyu composed a preface for his departure, stating in brief: "The *śramaṇa* suffers from being..."
Being entangled with external views is the affliction of having already attained [them], while being bound by internal views is the current state.
Now, Master Xuán dwells serenely between these two views; neither external nor internal, he merges with the ultimate mystery.

Furthermore, as the mountains and waters of Gōngū constitute a supreme realm and Tíānzhú is a pure field for spiritual practice, he has traveled there shaking his mendicant’s staff, his mind vast and expansive. This is surely the arising of inspiration in accordance with conditions.
He transformed those he encountered through his influence, yet was not led astray by external sensory objects.
In the twelfth year, the *bingzi* year,
among the scholar-officials of Wuzhong on the Western Ridge were those such as Li Jifu and Han Huang Mengjian, all of whom were intimately acquainted with him.
He established diplomatic relations with the Western Regions. A saying among the people of Wu was: "The peaks of Hangzhou touch the clouds and the heavens;

the depths of Yue pierce through ice and snow. The scribes of the Xi River possess refined elegance. When Lu Yu of Jingling saw these peaks, he praised them, saying: "They are like the sun, moon, clouds, and mists."

I know that the heavens constitute the mark of Heaven; mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees constitute the mark of Earth; and the ability to defer merit and attribute excellence to others constitutes the mark of Virtue.
To dwell in seclusion and incline toward stillness—is this not the realization that while the name belongs to the public, the reality resides within?

The people of Hangzhou revered him so much that they did not call him by his name, but instead addressed him as "The Monk of the Western Ridge. At that time, Zen Master Tiantai Daowu was first residing in Dangyang, Jingzhou.
Chai Zishan attracted a multitude of disciples who followed him shoulder to shoulder and step after step; men and women from the capital flocked to him, drawn by his reputation.

The Master led them into the city and district, eventually settling at Tianhuang Temple. At that time, the Governor of Jiangling, the Vice President of the Council of State, Lord Pei, sought the Dharma with great diligence.

Although the Master never used the formal rites of welcoming or seeing off guests—regardless of their rank—he would always bow to them while they remained seated. Lord Pei, in turn, increased his devotion and reverence.
[End of] Volume Nine of the *Chronological History of Buddhism* (*Lìdài biānnián shìshì tōngjiàn*).
[Beginning of] Volume Ten of the *Chronological History of Buddhism*. From this point on, the Dharma lineage of Shitou flourished at this seat.
[End of] Volume Nine of the *Chronological History of Buddhism*. [Beginning of] Volume Ten of the *Chronological History of Buddhism*.
Compiled by Shi Benjue of Yian at Kuoshan, Song;
collated by the layman Chan-ti Bi Xizhi of the Ming Dynasty. Tang [Period].
Emperor Dezong (Part II):
On the Jǐmǎo day (the 15th year), in the fourth month,
on the Emperor’s birthday, an imperial decree was issued for the relevant authorities to prepare ceremonial carriages and to welcome the Professor-monk Chengguan into the palace.
The Dharma Hall. To propagate the fundamental tenets of the Avataṃsaka, he ascended the high seat and said: "How magnificent is the True Realm! It is the source from which the myriad dharmas arise.
Encompassing both emptiness and existence, it is free from all signs; entering into words and images, it leaves no trace. Wondrous existence is not existence; true emptiness is not empty."

Our Buddha attained this; he wondrously practiced true awakening and utterly purified the habits of defilement. He remained serene amidst the realm of ten thousand transformations and moved within the midst of a single void.
He merged his body with benefit so that they were mutually contained, and his fame and radiance flowed forth to illuminate the far reaches.

Our Emperor has attained this; his spiritual discernment reaches the ultimate void, and he maintains the great harmony. His sagely writings eclipse those of a hundred kings, and his pure influence fans throughout—
Throughout the myriad nations, he spread the profound transformation to awaken those in their dreams and bestowed the natural truth upon their innate natures.

Thus, the purport of the Avataṃsaka teachings is vast, expansive, profound, and subtle—beyond the reach of thought or calculation. To lose its essential meaning is to labor in vain through kalpas of cultivation;
to find its gateway is to become equal to all Buddhas in a single day (and so forth). The Emperor looked toward his ministers and said: "I, the Emperor..."
The Master’s words were elegant and concise; his expressions were classical and profound. He was able to use the Holy Dharma to cool the Emperor’s mind.

Consequently, "Qingliang" (Cooling) was bestowed as the title of State Preceptor. The Emperor reflected that, from time immemorial, clinging to the selfhood of body and mind, as well as the fixed characteristics of all phenomena, constitutes perversion.
The assembled ministers bowed twice with their heads to the ground and reverently received this enlightened decree. Thereupon, both within and without the realm...
The high ministers of the state’s support all received the Eight Precepts from him and honored him as their teacher.
In this year, the Vinaya Master Xiyi of Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu passed away; Xu Yaozo composed his epitaph, which states in brief:
"The Master’s essence penetrated the Six Arts, and he was broadly versed in the works of the hundred schools. He once [associated with] Lord Lu Yan Zhenqing, Chancellor Zhao Jing, and Censor Lu Qun."
He served as a fellow practitioner for those in meditation. His disciples, including Facan and others, transmitted his teachings.

Fourth, Yu Chengxuan of Mingzhou composed the "Epitaph for the Wugou Jingguang Pagoda in Fuzhou," which states in brief: The Governor Liu and the Military Supervisor Yu said to one another, "There is nothing greater than honoring one's sovereign than promoting merit;
there is nothing greater than promoting merit than planting roots of goodness; and there is nothing greater than planting roots of goodness..."

Within the Buddha’s teaching, is not the foundation of the doctrine found in the *stūpa*? Now, as for the *stūpa*: above, it reaches the various heavens; below, it stabilizes the triple world (*triloka*).
Its shadow provides shelter like the illumination of the sun and moon, dispelling darkness to bring forth light. The ringing of its bells is like the performance of metal and stone instruments;
hearing the sound gives rise to goodness. Thus, all such merits return entirely to the King of Men. Since his plans are thus securely stored, [the foundation is laid].

They looked upon one another with joyful anticipation. Those who partook of the King’s bounty delighted in acts of charity; those who bore the Emperor’s grace were pleased to offer their craftsmanship.
No one complained of the labor, and thus the work was completed. The Emperor praised this achievement and, with his own hand, inscribed the title for the monument, bestowing upon it the name:
"The Stūpa of True Origin, Undefiled and Pure Radiance."
In the Gengchen year (the sixteenth year), the reclusive scholar Liu Ke traveled to Huangshi Rock on Mount Lu. There he encountered a high monk and composed a record for him, which states in brief:

"When Ke arrived at Huangshi Rock, there was a son of the seated-dhyāna (a monk) dwelling there. When asked how many years he had resided [there], he merely pointed with his finger toward the pines and cassias."
He said: "A mere hair’s breadth of self was planted by me; now it encircles the arms of all people. As birds fly and hares run, what more need I take note of?
The world calls this the hook of profit and the bait of fame. Having swallowed the hook and consumed the bait, one's hands and feet are bound in shackles.
How could they possibly leap about here? But the Chan practitioner has cast off these fetters; his four limbs are fully extended, and his movements are as mindless as the clouds."
What mechanism could still the rocks? When things and self are of one accord, the straight path is established and the deviant way is blocked.

It is said that no one but such a person can dwell in such a realm. The Master’s secular surname was Huang and his name was Changjin. Because the Master had resided there for a long time, they subsequently named the cliff after him.
In the year Xin-si (the seventeenth year),
the śramaṇa Huìjù of Jīnlíng and the Tripiṭaka Master Śrīlāta of India compiled and arranged the transmission verses and prophecies of the various patriarchs.
As well as the karmic encounters of the patriarchs, [these were compiled] for the *Baolin Zhuan* (The History of the Baolin Temple).

When Vinaya Master Yunfeng Fazheng of Nanyue passed away, he had ordained fifty thousand students; his lifespan was seventy-eight years. Liu Zhitou inscribed his stupa and further composed a stele for him, which stated in brief:
"In the first year of the Qianyuan era, the Emperor said: 'I desire to cause [the people] to be compassionate, benevolent, joyful, and at ease, thereby governing their lives.'"

"O people! Only the Way of the Buddha is truly followed. Therefore, an edict was issued to the Five Sacred Mountains to seek out those of supreme virtue who could serve as models for the subordinates.
Among them, the one listed first in the *Shangshu* was the Great Master Yunfeng Fazheng.
He served in office for fifty years and passed away in the seventeenth year of the Zhenyuan era. His disciples were named Quan, Yuan, Zhen, Xun, and Su."

There were more than three thousand people in total. To those who came to receive the Vinaya, my teacher displayed a demeanor of dignity and orderliness, clearly categorizing the principles and meanings, so that each person knew what they must not do.

To those who came seeking the Way, my teacher displayed a teaching of loftiness, vastness, and thorough penetration, unifying both emptiness and existence, so that each person knew where they must ultimately arrive.
High ministers and eminent elders bowed their heads in reverence and received [his instruction].

As for the teachings: from the time they were young with their hair in tufts until their teeth fell out, [the disciples] leaped with joy to perform their duties. Thus, those who followed my teacher’s command and attained deliverance numbered fifty thousand in all.
My teacher did not wear warm furs in winter nor eat sumptuous food when hungry; every year he would assemble his followers to read the various scriptures.
Thus, he caused the sacred words to emerge in their entirety, whereby one may perceive their greatness.

Furthermore, he led his followers to fell timber and carry earth to construct Buddhist stupas, temples, and scriptures, whereby the Semblance Dharma was further propagated, and one may perceive its utility (and so forth).
Consequently, his disciples flourished, solely upholding the Great Teaching and strictly observing the sacred precepts; vast and expansive, they were like a great river.
It increased, like the rising of clouds and like a mountain that does not crumble, sustaining [the lineage] through all eternity (from the Liu Ji).
Renwu (the eighteenth year) and Guiwei (the nineteenth year).
The Great Master of Shengshan Temple in the Eastern Capital passed away. Bai Juyi of the Hanlin Academy composed the "Ode on the Eight Gradual Steps" to mourn him.
Its preface states: "I, Bai Juyi, once sought the essentials of the mind from the Master. The Master bestowed these instructions upon me, saying:
'Contemplation, awareness, concentration, wisdom; clarity, penetration, succor, relinquishment. From this, they entered my ears and pierced my heart. Alas! Now the Master’s retribution [has come]."
My body was transformed, yet my teacher’s eight words were not. How ultimate these eight words are! They are truly the gradual gateway to the realization of the Master’s forbearance.
Therefore, I have expanded each word into a verse, calling them the "Eight Verses on the Gradual Path.

This is intended both to manifest the heart-teachings of the Master and to clarify that I, Yiji, shall not allow them to fall into ruin. Thereafter, I ascended to the hall and paid my respects at the bedside.
Kneeling, he chanted; weeping, he departed. (The verse says: "Observe with the eye within the mind the appearances outside the mind. From where do they arise? To where do they vanish?

Observe and observe again, and you will distinguish the real from the delusory. Awakening is only the eternally present reality, yet it is shrouded by delusion. If the real and the delusory are distinguished, awakening arises between them. Without departing from delusion, one attains true emptiness. If the real does not perish, delusion will not arise.

The source of the six sense organs becomes as still as clear water; this is called meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus one is liberated from birth and death. With wisdom (*prajñā*), focus through concentration; yet if concentration remains bound, supplement it with wisdom. Wisdom is then without obstruction, like a pearl on a plate: the plate provides stability while the pearl possesses brilliance."

Concentration and wisdom are unified; only through their union does clarity arise. This clarity perceives all things, leaving no form unmanifested, like a great round mirror. When skillful means (*upāya*) reach their limit, wisdom becomes clear; when clarity reaches its limit, there is penetration. When penetration is reached, there is no obstruction. What is this lack of obstruction?

It is the sovereign mastery of transformation and the power of salvation. This power of salvation is not constant; it changes according to a thought. These two aspects do not exist as separate entities, yet they appear according to what is sought. This is Great Compassion. When one saves the myriad beings, one relinquishes [the self].

Once the multitude of sufferings is relieved, Great Compassion is also relinquished. Since suffering is not real, compassion is likewise provisional. Therefore, among sentient beings, there is in truth no one who is saved. Master Jun returned to Huainan. By Liu Zongyuan.
Yuan Zihou composed a preface for his departure, which stated in brief: "The Way of the Golden Immortal (Buddhism) is fundamentally rooted in filial piety and reverence;

thereafter, it accumulates manifold virtues before returning to emptiness and non-existence. Its teachings are termed Chan, Dharma, and Vinaya, used to guide and support those in a turbid world through the practice of quiescence and non-being.
The Venerable One has exhaustively investigated these esoteric meanings and elucidated the Supreme Vehicle, upholding the three aspects of majestic deportment."
[He was] a thousandfold [in merit]. Although he was always prepared even in moments of haste, he once propagated this Way among the people of the Jiang and Hu regions;

all were delighted by his style and received his grace. Those who clung to the compassionate vessel and gazed toward the other shore numbered in the hundreds and thousands. When the Son of Heaven heard of this, he summoned him to the palace to question him.
He expounded and elevated the fundamental teachings, which greatly pleased the Emperor's mind. The scholars and masses of the capital were then filled with eager anticipation.

He looked up to the grace of the Great Cloud to plant the roots of virtue; yet the Master could not bear the kindness of being cared for and restored, and so he withdrew with thoughts of the etiquette due to his attendants.
He earnestly and persistently requested leave, and in the end, there was no way to dissuade him. Thereupon, leaning on his staff and facing east, he shook out his robes and departed at dawn.
Liu Gong, the Vice Director of the Right Bureau, who was well-versed in the Buddhist teachings, became a companion to the Master in their travels beyond the mundane world.
At first we celebrated his arrival; now we lament his departure. Thereupon, the friends of the clerical office joined together and composed poems to present to him.
I, [the author], have had this youth hold the bamboo slips to record them, and thus append these words: "The Venerable One was single-minded in his observance of the Vinaya;
constant and enduring, it grew ever more firm. Is he not a model for those who follow? He instructs all living beings, and all who encounter him receive blessings. His accumulation..."
Is he one who possesses all virtues? When visiting his dry bone shrine, he perceives the distant as if it were near; is this not because his fundamental nature is filial piety and reverence?

If this is so, then his mind will surely turn toward emptiness and non-existence; having abandoned the raft, he shall ascend to the ground [of enlightenment]. How, then, could one possibly recognize him from such a state? (From the Collected Works of Liu).

In the first month of the Jiashen year (the twentieth year), the Master Banzhou of Nanyue passed away. Liu Zihou composed a second stele inscription for him, the text of which runs roughly as follows:
The Master said, "Daily Awakening. His mind was vast while his conduct was subtle; his person was humble while the Way he embodied was honored.

He held that wisdom must arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and that the Vinaya must necessarily serve as its dwelling place. Consequently, he investigated the profound meanings [of the scriptures] and ascended the ordination platform to preside over ceremonies.
Over thirty-seven years, he ordained approximately one thousand bhikṣus annually, yet his Way never faltered. He held that by departing from the mundane, one immediately [attains the transcendent].
The Sage necessarily took samādhi as his guiding path; he then cultivated and clarified its essential mysteries, thereby attaining focused concentration upon the Buddha’s place of enlightenment.
He knelt upright and circumambulated to the right for a total of one hundred and twenty days, his resolve never flagging.

The Master then constructed a meditation cell on a lofty ridge; all people from the south who specialize in the Nianfo Samādhi (Buddha-remembrance samādhi) must pass through this very place. [He] commanded—
It is called the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the Platform of the Present). Alas, there is nothing that can be cultivated therein. Therefore, mindfulness constitutes the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Because no phenomena are grasped, the Vinaya becomes the Mahāyāna. While the myriad practices are vigorously pursued, the single nature remains eternally as it is.
The limits of quiescent function cannot be apprehended. (From the *Liu Jia Ji*)
In the first month of the Year of Dingshiyou (the first year of Yongzheng),
Emperor Dezong passed away. Emperor Shunzong ascended the throne.
When the Emperor was first in the Eastern Palace, he asked Chan Master Fuguo Rimang: "From what direction does the Buddha come? Toward what direction does he go when he passes away?
Since it is said that he dwells eternally in the world, where is the Buddha now? The Master replied: "The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and goes toward the unconditioned.
The Dharma-body is equal to empty space; it dwells eternally in the state of no-mind. Where there is thought, it returns to non-existence."
Contemplate this: abiding, one returns to non-abiding; coming, one comes for the sake of sentient beings; going, one goes for the sake of sentient beings.
The ocean of pure *tathatā* is profoundly still, its essence eternally abiding. Let the wise contemplate this well and no longer give rise to doubt. The Emperor asked again:
"The Buddha was born in the royal palace and passed away beneath the twin śāla trees. He dwelt in the world for forty-nine years, yet he also said that there is no dharma to be taught."
Mountains, rivers, and the great ocean; heaven and earth, along with the sun and moon—when their time comes, they all return to extinction.
Who would say they are not subject to arising and ceasing? Such is the nature of doubt. The wise distinguish this well. He replied: "The Buddha’s worship is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

It is only through deluded sentiment that one makes false discriminations. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is equal to empty space; it has never undergone arising or ceasing. When conditions exist, a Buddha appears in the world; when conditions are absent, the Buddha [does not appear]."
He entered nirvana, transforming sentient beings everywhere like the moon reflected in water—neither permanent nor annihilated, neither arising nor ceasing.
Having clearly perceived the state of no-mind, he naturally had no dharma to preach. Upon hearing this, the Emperor was greatly delighted.
The Emperor once asked Master Śrī: "How can the sentient beings of this great earth see their nature and attain Buddhahood? Śrī replied:
The Buddha-nature is like the moon in water: it can be seen, but it cannot be grasped. [Emperor Wuzong] once asked Qingliang Guoshi for the essential point of the mind.
The Master answered him, briefly stating: "The ultimate Way is rooted in the mind; the dharma of the mind is rooted in non-abiding.

The essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous awareness that is never obscured; its nature and characteristics are quiescent, encompassing all virtuous functions. To be deluded regarding direct perception (pratyakṣa) is to fall into confusion."

Suffering is chaotic and confounding. When one awakens to the true nature, it is empty, luminous, vast, and penetrating. Although it is said that "the mind itself is the Buddha," only those who have realized it can truly know this.
Yet, if there is realization or knowing, the sun of wisdom sinks into the realm of existence (*bhava*).

If there is neither illumination nor awakening, then the dark clouds of ignorance shroud the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If not a single thought arises, then the boundaries of past and future are severed, and the essence of illumination stands alone.

Standing thus, both self and phenomena are as they are (tathatā). One directly reaches the source of the mind, where there is neither wisdom nor attainment. Yet, delusion and awakening depend upon one another, and the real and the false face each other.

If one seeks the real to eliminate the false, it is like discarding a shadow by exhausting the body. If one realizes that the false is itself the real, it is like standing within a shadow and the shadow vanishing.

If one is without-mind and forgets even this illumination, then all myriad concerns are simultaneously cast off. If one allows the tranquil awareness to function spontaneously, then all practices [are perfected].

Thus it begins: Expansive and unconfined, he allows for coming and going as they may; in tranquil discernment, he awakens to their source and flow. In speech and silence, he does not lose the profound mystery;

in movement and stillness, he never departs from the Dharma-realm. When words cease, both knowing and stillness vanish together; when discussing contemplation, both stillness and knowing are illuminated together.

If one relies on verbal testimony, it cannot be shown to others; yet if one explains the principle, it cannot be understood without testimony. Therefore, awakening to stillness means there is no stillness, and true knowledge means there is no knowing.
By means of this single mind in which knowledge and stillness are non-dual, one accords with the Middle Way where both emptiness and existence have vanished.
In the eighth month, Emperor Shunzong abdicated the throne to Emperor Xianzong and styled himself the Retired Emperor (he passed away in the first month of the following year). 9.
The Grand Commandant of the Moon and Minister of the Secretariat, Wei Gao, passed away. When Gao was first born, his father offered a meal to the monks to pray for blessings.
Suddenly, an Arhat arrived; when the meal was finished, the wet nurse took the infant in her arms to seek a blessing. The Arhat rose and said to the assembly:
"This child is Zhuge Wuhou. In days to come, he shall bring noble governance to Shu. You should name him 'Wu'. Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished.
Subsequently, the general outline of Guo’s official career, his conduct, and his integrity was largely similar to that of Wuhou.
He governed Shu for twenty-one years and was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Nankang. To this day in Sichuan, he is venerated with offerings. (Yaya)
He was fond of the teachings of the Śākya clan. When the stone statue at Jia Prefecture was first completed, Gao wrote an inscription for it, which stated:

"The circumference of its head is one thousand *chi*; the width of its eyes is twenty *zhang*; all other marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa*) are likewise proportionate. Furthermore, he once instructed a myna bird to recite the Buddha’s name;

when the myna died, he performed its cremation according to the traditional rites of the *śramaṇas*. He recovered *śarīra* relics and wrote an inscription for them, of which a brief excerpt reads: "The primal essence..."
The five pneumas bestow upon the myriad classes of beings; though they be scaled, shelled, hairy, or feathered, there must necessarily be a resonance with that which is pure and refined.
Some manifest the brilliance of the fire-element (*li*), while others receive the wondrous essence of the azure-spirit (*cang-jing*). All respond to the patterns of human culture to serve it.

Yet when the administration of the state undergoes change, those avian species who have mastered speech come to understand the mark of emptiness through non-thought, leaving behind their true skeletal remains.

[He] perished. It was likely because the manifestation of the Original Sage moved the hearts of men; though the conditions were diverse, they were employed through the transformation of the One Reality.
(General Discussion).
Emperor Xianzong.
In the tenth month of the Bingxu year (the first year of the Yuanhe era), an imperial edict was issued:

"Let all monks who practice the Way throughout the realm proceed to the capital to propagate the transformation. Regarding this, Xitang Zhizang, when asked by the scholar Zhang Zhuo whether the Buddhas of the three periods and the heavens and hells exist or do not exist, replied to both questions:

[He said: "They exist. [He said: "They do not exist. (Note: The original text indicates that the Master [Zhizang] gave these responses to the questions regarding the existence or non-existence of the Buddhas of the three periods and of heaven and hell.)
"Is there? Zhang said, "I am mistaken. The Master asked, "Whom did you see coming? He replied, "I saw someone who had studied under Baizhang (one source says Jingshan).
He said that there is nothing at all. The Master asked, "What family do you have? He replied, "I have one mountain wife and two stubborn sons. The Master said:
"When you have become like Baizhang, all paths will vanish and you shall attain it. Zhang bowed in thanks and departed.

In the second year [the Dinghai year], an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Dayi of Goose Lake to the Linqide Palace to debate the Dharma. The Emperor attended in person to listen. A Dharma Master then questioned him:

"What are the Four Noble Truths? He replied, "There is but one noble truth; where then are the other three truths? He asked again, "The realm of desire has no dhyāna, and the dhyānas reside in the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Upon what does this [realm of desire] stand? He replied, "The Dharma Master knows only that there is no dhyāna in the realm of desire."
He did not know that the realm of *dhyāna* is free from desire. [The Emperor] asked, "What is the meaning of *dhyāna*? He pointed at the empty space with his hand. The Dharma Master had no reply.
The Emperor said, "The Dharma Master lectures on endless sutras and treatises, yet he cannot even manage this single point.
Daoyi then asked the assembly of masters, "Ultimately, what constitutes the Way? One replied, "Knowing is the Way. Daoyi said, "It cannot be so."
It is known by wisdom; it cannot be known by consciousness. How can it be that "knowing" is the Way? Having an object yet being without discrimination is the Way. The meaning is:
one who is skillfully able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena does not waver from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). How can it be that "non-discrimination" is the Way?
Having an object refers to the four dhyānas and eight samādhis as the Way. The meaning is: the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into [the realms of] existence.
"How could the four dhyānas and eight samādhis be the Way? he asked. Furthermore, there were several people who came forward to debate him;
Huaijiao refuted them all according to their respective capacities. He then cited an instance where Emperor Shunzong once asked Master Śīla, "Can the Buddha-nature be seen?
Śīla replied, "The Buddha-nature is like the moon in the water: it can be seen, but it cannot be grasped. Huaijiao then said to the Emperor, "Since Śīla has already seen the moon in the water..."
"Why do you not seize it? The Emperor then asked Hu, "What is Buddha-nature? Hu replied, "It is not separate from what Your Majesty has just asked.
The Emperor understood this intuitively; consequently, he came to hold the Chan school in even higher esteem.

In the second month, an edict was issued appointing Dharma Master Duānfǔ to oversee the ritual protocols for the inner palace and to serve as the *Sēnglù* (Registrar of Monks) for the Left and Right Streets. The office of *Sēnglù* began with Duānfǔ. [4]

Regarding National Teacher Daowu of Jingzhou: he instructed his disciples that he would pass away before the appointed time. When the final day of the month arrived, the assembly went to inquire after his illness.
The Master asked, "Do you understand? He then picked up his pillow, threw it to the ground, and immediately entered nirvana.
He was sixty years of age and had thirty-five years of ordination. The Master succeeded Shitou as his dharma heir.
In the second month of the third year (the Wuzi year), Chan Master Ruhai of Long’an Temple in Changsha passed away. Liu Zongyuan composed a stele for him, which states in brief:
"The Master resided in Changsha; he remained in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) for fourteen days. People established a dwelling at that very spot, which subsequently became [known as] Bao..."
He went to Ying Temple, located to the west of Xiang. People followed him once more, carrying wood and stone to augment his dwelling, and he established Long’an Temple there.
The Minister Pei [Name], Minister Li [Name], Vice-Minister Li [Name], Yang [Name], and Vice-Prefect Fang [Name] all honored the Master’s Way and observed the rites of disciples.
He lived to the age of eighty-one; he had been a monk for five... [years].
Thirteen years later, his disciples Xuánjué, Huáizhí, and others (the full text is found in the Writings of Liú). ○ Hǎi had a disciple named Hàochū, who was on good terms with Zǐthòu.

Zǐthòu composed a preface for sending Chū off; its wording runs roughly as follows: "The Confucian scholar Hàn Tuìzhī reproaches me for my fondness for the words of the Buddhists and censures me for associating with Buddhists.
Furthermore, he says: 'Having read the Preface for Sending Off Yuánshēng, I see that you do not reject Buddhism.'"
Diagram: It is true that there are aspects of Buddhism that cannot be dismissed. Often it accords with the *I Ching* and the *Analects*.

If one truly delights in it, its essence regarding human nature and emotion is consistent [with Confucianism] and does not differ from the Way of Confucius. Although Tuizhi was fond of Confucianism, he had not yet surpassed Yangzi.
The writings of Yangzi draw upon the teachings of Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, and Han Fei alike.
Yet, as for the Buddhists, are they not even more eccentric, perverse, treacherous, and cruel than Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, and Han Fei?

If one says this is because they are "barbarians" (*yi*) and thus rejects them for being barbarians while disbelieving the Way, then would one instead befriend the likes of E Lai and Dao Zhi, while deprecating Ji Zha and You Yu? This is certainly not what is meant.
Those who discard names to seek reality: what I accept accords with the *I Ching* and the *Analects*. Even if a sage were to be born again, he could not refute this.
What I condemn, Master Tui, is its outward manifestation: shaving the head and wearing black robes; having neither husband nor wife, nor father nor son;
and living off others without engaging in agriculture, sericulture, or mulberry cultivation. Even I would not approve of such a thing.
It is joy. To withdraw from its outward form while violating its inner essence is to know the stone but not the jade it contains.
This is why I delight in the words of the Buddha. Those who associate with such a person need not necessarily master their language;
for all who practice that Way do not crave office nor compete for ability, but instead find joy in mountains and waters and delight in...
Those who find peace and leisure are many. I lament that the world is so frantic, making only the pursuit of official seals and ribbons its sole concern;
if one abandons these, where else can one go? This is why I delight in associating with Buddhists. Now Hao-chu is at ease in his nature and tranquil in his emotions;
he reads their scriptures and is well-versed in the *I Ching* and the *Analects*. His only pleasure is that of the mountains and rivers, and moreover, both father and son are devoted to this Way.

To dwell in contentment and remain detached, seeking nothing, is far superior to those who follow the doctrines of Zhuangzi, Mozi, Shen Buhai, or Han Fei, and who busily pursue only seals and ribbons;
the difference between them is vast indeed (as seen in the *Wenxuan* by Liu Zongyuan).

○ An imperial edict appointed Chan Master Weiyun of Boye Mountain to reside at Zhangjing Temple, where he was summoned annually to the Linde Hall to discourse on the Way. ○ The thirteenth day of the tenth month.

On this day, Chan Master Tianwang Daowu of Jingnan City entered nirvana at the age of eighty-two, having sat in meditation for sixty-three summers (one source states he passed away on the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era).
The Master was a successor of Mazu; his dharma heir was Longtan Xuanzong (also known as Longtan Xin).

[The *Juemeng tang zhongjiao wujia zongpai* states: "The current *Chuan deng lu* erroneously subsumes the Yunmen and Fayen schools under the lineage of Shitou. This is a mistake, because there were two individuals named Daowu who lived at the same time. One was located west of the city of Jiangling... ]

Regarding Tiantaishi Daowu: he was a member of the imperial household who succeeded Mazu. He passed away on the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era. The inscription for his stupa was composed by Qiu Xuansu, a Grand Master of the Right, totaling several thousand words.

It states: "Tiantaishi Daowu of the eastern part of Jiangling City was a native of Dongwang in Wuzhou. He succeeded Shitou and passed away in the second year of the Yuanhe era, the Dinghai year. A stele was composed by the Vinaya Master Fu Cai. Both inscriptions provide very detailed accounts of his origins and life. Zhang Wujin obtained these two records of the stupas and showed them to various quarters, saying:

"I have long suspected that although Deshan and Dongshan both emerged from under Shitou, why is it that their 'extending the hand' (teachings) differ so greatly regarding life and death? Now, having verified this with the two records by Qiu and Fu, everything is clear and evident."

In the fifth month of the Jichou year (the fourth year of the Yuanhe era), an imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities to cast a separate golden seal for the addition of the title "National Preceptor of the Qingliang Temple" to Chengguan, who was also designated as "State Preceptor.

He was entrusted with the affairs of the Imperial Preceptor’s Office. The Prime Minister Quan Deyu composed the "Record of the Seated Meditation of Chan Master Cao Yi," of which the following is a brief excerpt:
It was said: "In Nanyue of Xinzhou, there is a place for seated meditation, and the Chan Master resides there.
He has lived there for thirty years; the people of the prefecture call him 'The Grass-Clothed One. His feet do not touch the ground, and his mouth does not taste flavors.
Regardless of whether it is cold or hot, he uses nothing but a single rope bed. Both his body and his wisdom are utterly pure. Occasionally, one may hear his subtle words and gentle speech."
Whether traversing the far or near reaches of its realm, or according to the high or low capacity of one's faculties, it is like rain moistening the myriad things or wind blowing through the air;

upon crossing its threshold, all are able to enter. Were it not for one who wields the profound mechanism within the boundless and exhausts the source and depth of true reality (*dharmatā*), then the four seasons would assail from without and a hundred ailments would arise from within. As the ancients said: "To cast aside external things..."
"To stand alone apart from men"—the Chan Master has attained this. Alas! The people of the world allow their minds to wander by being moved by external things;
when the mind is shifted by these things, profit and harm arise, and good fortune and calamity take form. They become entangled and fettered, drifting away without returning.

The Perfect Man, however, returns to stillness within movement and restores his nature within the emotions. It is from this that the distinctions between longevity and early death, benevolence and baseness, emerge.
This is merely one explanation according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the Way of the Chan Master, it is like weeds among the grain (from the *Benji*).
○ Da-du, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Dao-hong, the founding patriarch of Bai-lu Monastery in Min County, Fuzhou, led his disciples into Mount Xue-xi this year.
The local elders carried provisions to go and provide him with food. Thus...
He requested to move to the site of his current monastery. There he happened upon a white deer and established a place of practice.
One day, fifty-three buddhas suddenly descended from the sky along with a single staff. Accompanied by a flock of blue ducks, they descended in profusion, each approximately one chi in height.

The Master collected them all and cast them into more than three hundred sacred images. When the Master was about to manifest his passing, he personally selected a site for a stupa at the source of the Xue Stream.
The stream before him flowed with a murmuring sound. The Master remarked, "This water disturbs my meditative concentration.
Taking up his staff, he waded upstream and struck the water several times. As the sound of the staff reached the stream, the current receded and seeped away for over a hundred paces.

A separate spring source gushed forth, whereupon the streambed subsequently dried up. He passed away while seated in meditation on the second day of the twelfth month of the Renyin year of the Changqing era (Changle Ji).

In the seventh year, on the day of Gengyin, the Emperor asked National Preceptor Chengguan: "Regarding that which is expounded in the *Avataṃsaka*, what is meant by the 'Dharmadhātu'? He replied: "The Dharmadhātu..."

This is the fundamental substance of the bodies and minds of all sentient beings. From the very beginning, it has been empty and luminous, vast and expansive, being nothing other than the single realm of ultimate reality.
It possesses no form or appearance, yet it pervades the great chiliocosm; it has no boundaries, yet it contains all phenomena.
Brilliantly manifest within the space between mind and eye, yet its form cannot be seen; radiantly shining amidst the realm of sensory objects, yet its principle cannot be divided.
Were it not for the eye of wisdom that penetrates all phenomena and the clear intelligence free from conceptual thought, one could not perceive such spiritual penetration of one's own mind.
Therefore, when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed: "How marvelous! All sentient beings..."
He was born possessing the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, due to the attachment of deluded thoughts, he had not yet realized them.

Thereupon, in accordance with the nature of the Dharma-realm, he preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, using absolute emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to eliminate emotional attachments and harmoniously integrating phenomena with principle.

All-pervasive, profound, and tranquil, the Emperor listened to this profound discourse and attained spontaneous realization. In the third month, by imperial decree, Meng Jian, the Censor-in-Chief, was appointed [to oversee the project].
The Palace Attendant Xiao Min supervised the translation and editorial refinement of scriptures at Liquan Temple (Old History, Basic Annals).
At Mount Lu, in the Shuiluge Courtyard of Xilin Monastery, Vinaya Master Qilang’s Dharma teachings flourished greatly; he initially traveled from Hongzhou to ascend to Longxing Temple.
Up to the section on *dhūta* practices, there are fourteen assemblies in total. Those who received the *karma-vācanā* numbered in the tens of thousands.

Li Gongbo, Director Extraordinary of the Bureau of Works, and Bai Juyi, Secretary of the Secretariat, both served as administrators of the prefecture and attained a profound understanding of its subtle details.
Every time he reached the place of practice (the *daochang*), he would prostrate himself with deep reverence (*Lushan ji*).
In the *Xinmao* year (the sixth year),
Layman Pang had been residing in Xiangyang since the beginning of the Yuanhe era, dwelling among the crags and caverns (twenty li south of present-day Lumen, there is a Layman’s [Cave]).
At that time, the Prefect, Lord Yu Di, held him in even greater esteem and wonder. He waited for a favorable opportunity and went in person to pay his respects.
From the very first meeting, they circled one another like long-time spiritual friends. Having reached a deep accord in their mutual affection, there was no interval between their visits.
When the Layman was about to enter extinction, he instructed his daughter Lingzhao to observe the sun; when it reached midday, she reported this. Lingzhao hurriedly replied, "The sun..."
While he was in the midst of his meal, an eclipse occurred. The official went out to observe it; as soon as the light returned, he ascended his seat, joined his palms, and passed away.

The official smiled and said, "My daughter is sharp and swift. Thereupon, the period of mourning was extended for another seven days. When the Governor, Lord Yu, heard of this, he went to offer his condolences.
The lay practitioner said, "I only wish to empty all that exists; take care not to reify anything that exists. Do not take pleasure in dwelling in the world; be like [a guest]..."
[The Master] finished speaking. He leaned his head upon the Master’s knee and passed away. When his wife heard this, she said, "These two fools have departed without even bidding me farewell.
Her son was clearing a field by slash-and-burn; his mother went to him and told him, "The old man and Lingzhao have gone.

The son pressed down on his hoe and laughed, saying, "Ha! He too stood there and transformed [passed away]. His mother said, "You are even more foolish than they. After the cremation was completed, [she...]
He traveled throughout his native villages and retired into seclusion; thereafter, nothing further was known of him.
In the seventh year of the Renchen cycle (792), Liu Zhitou composed the Stele Inscription for Master Mituo of Mount Nanyue. Its text states in brief: "During the reign of Emperor Daizong, Fazhao..."
The State Preceptor said, "That master, the Elder of Nanyue, possessed extraordinary virtue; the Son of Heaven faced south to pay him homage.
As his Way could not be summoned [to court], he named his dwelling the 'Prajñā Site' (Bānrě Dàochǎng) to honor his position.

When Emperor Dezong issued an imperial decree to praise and establish it, it became Amitābha Temple. Those who followed him and were transformed by his teachings numbered in the tens of thousands. The Master [Guifeng] acted as...
He served as a monk for fifty-six years and lived to the age of ninety-one (Liu Wen). In this year, the Jingtu (Pure Land) Monastery was completed in Yongzhou;

Liu Zhitou composed its inscription, which states in brief: "Tens of thousands of li to the west of the Central Plains lies a land called Shendu (India), the place where Śākyamuni Tathāgata manifested.
That Buddha said: 'To the west, beyond a hundred thousand koṭis of buddha-lands, there is a world...'"
The realm is called Ultimate Bliss; the Buddha’s name is Amitābha. In that land, there are no three poisons or eight difficulties;
it is adorned with various jewels. Its inhabitants have no ten fetters or nine afflictions; they take the assembly of sages as their friends.

If one can, with a sincere heart and great vow, turn the mind toward this land, provided that the power of mindfulness is sufficient, one shall be born in that realm, forever departing from the triple world and attaining non-retrogression.

His words were never deceptive. During the Jin dynasty, Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu composed the "Eulogy on the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha" (Nianfo Sanmei Yong), which greatly exhorted people at that time.
Later, the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai authored the *Ten Doubts about the Pure Land* (Shijingtu Shiyi Lun) to widely propagate his teachings;
those who were deluded relied upon them. Indeed, there were many who left behind miraculous traces before departing. The Regional Inspector Li Cheng...
Zhi and others established a Pure Land Hall to the west of Longxing Temple. Master Xun further renovated this edifice to initiate future students.
A lay devotee commissioned a Buddhist image, the features of which were most complete. Now, Prefect Feng has constructed a great gate to mark its location.
I, for my part, have surrounded the corridors with painted images of the Great Being (Bodhisattva), along with silk canopies, banners, and streamers.
Thus he brought it to fulfillment. Alas! There are those capable of seeking the birth that is non-arising; they know that the raft exists within this.
Consequently, he inscribed the *Ten Doubts of the Tiantai School* upon the walls of the temple, so that those who behold it might give rise to faith (from the *Collected Works of Liu*).

In the eighth year, the year of Guisi (753), the Dharma Master Zhibian possessed an understanding that was peerless; yet he had few disciples. Occasionally, there were elderly monks who examined Zhibian’s writings.
He then said, "Your realization is supreme and well accords with the Buddha’s intent. That you currently have few followers is merely due to a lack of karmic conditions for others.
Even the Buddha could not save those who lacked the necessary conditions; how much less so a beginner like you? You should prepare food and offer it as alms to all flying and crawling creatures.
Twenty years hence, you shall naturally have a following. Bian followed his instructions; he cooked rice and scattered it outside the city, whereupon he moved a great flock of crows.
He gathered the remaining rice into a ball and departed. Huibian offered a prayer, saying: "May those who eat my food become my dharma companions.
Twenty years later, when Huibian went to the city of Ye to lecture, there were more than a thousand people in the assembly;
they were indeed all young bhikṣus. In that same year, Master Daoshu passed away. He had initially built a thatched hut on Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou, where a hundred strange manifestations appeared.
Sometimes he manifested the forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and the like; at other times, he emitted light or produced sounds.

This continued for ten years before he finally vanished his traces. The Master said: "A rustic man may employ limitless wiles to dazzle and delude people, yet it only takes this old monk not to see or hear them for his wiles to be exhausted.
My own non-seeing and non-hearing are inexhaustible. Because of this, those far and near were filled with reverence and submission.
It is said: "If one does not find strange things strange, the strangeness will naturally dissipate.
On the first month of the Jiawu year (the ninth year), Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai passed away at the age of ninety-five. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dazhi.
The Master left the secular world at the age of seven. He thoroughly refined himself in the three studies and followed Mazu Daoyi, entering the inner chamber together with Xitang Zang.
At that time, there were thousands of students gathered at Mazu’s gate, yet these two great beings stood out as preeminent. Upon Mazu’s passing, the Master went to Mount Baizhang in Xinwu;
disciples flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel converging at the hub. Although the Master was advanced in years, he always joined the community in all daily activities.
He was of the same disposition. He once said, "If one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day.
A monk asked, "What is the sudden enlightenment dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna? The Master replied, "If the mind-ground is empty, the sun of wisdom will manifest of itself.

If both defilement and purity are exhausted, even while dwelling in birth and death, the mind remains sovereign; ultimately, it never again merges with illusory worldly toil, the aggregates, or the elements. Far...

Yet there is no place of reliance; going and staying are unimpeded. If one can, throughout a lifetime, make the mind like wood or stone, so that it is not drifted or submerged by the five desires and the eight winds, then the causes of birth and death are severed, and one attains freedom in going and staying. A monk asked, "How does one attain such freedom?
The Master said, "If you could attain it right now, you would. Facing the five desires and the eight winds, let your mind be free from grasping or rejecting."
When both defilement and purity are extinguished, one is like the sun and moon in the sky, illuminating without depending on external conditions;
or like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, passing over by cutting through the current. This, moreover, is that which neither heaven nor hell can encompass.

Whenever the Master finished preaching the Dharma and the assembly descended from the hall, he would call out to them to turn their heads back. The Master would say, "What is this? Since his youth, the Master had maintained the Chan school.
When Huineng arrived at Caoqi, he mostly resided in Vinaya monasteries while preaching the Dharma. He then established a Chan residence.
Those who possessed the eye of the Way and were virtuous were called "Elders" (Changlao). Among the assembly of students, regardless of seniority, all entered the Sangha Hall together.

Ten administrative offices (liàoshè) were established, each with one person appointed as its head to manage communal affairs. Subsequently, as the monastic groves flourished daily, contemporary masters followed this precedent.
This is expanded upon. What is now known as the *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules of the Zen Garden) is fully contained therein.

In this month, Liu Zhitou composed the Stele for Master Daming of Mount Heng, which states in brief: "The Confucianist establishes benevolence and righteousness through ritual; without it, they perish.

The Buddhist maintains meditative concentration and wisdom through the Vinaya; without it, they are lost. Therefore, one who departs from ritual cannot be spoken with regarding benevolence and righteousness."
Confucians differ from those who distinguish between *samādhi* and *prajñā*; such people cannot be spoken of as Buddhists. Only Master Daming was one who attained this Way.
Whenever the Way of the Buddha declined, his followers would inevitably diminish their observance of the *vinaya* and abandon the *sūtras*. Master Daming feared this;

therefore, he investigated the precepts and regulations so that the Great Dharma might be established, and he mastered the scriptural teachings so that the profound meanings might be cultivated. Regarding all matters of clothing and utensils...
In his conduct, he followed the teachings of his masters; whether in speech or in action, he served as a model for all.
When Dharma Master Beishan Shenqing passed away, Shenqing composed the *Beishan Lu*, which has been circulated in the world.
In the year Yiwei (the tenth year), Ma Zong, the Regional Commander of Nanhai, petitioned the court because the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi had not yet been granted a posthumous title.

The Emperor conferred upon him the title Dajian (Great Mirror) and named his stupa Lingzhao (Numinous Illumination). Ma Zong then commissioned Liu Zhitou to compose an inscription for it, the text of which begins roughly as follows: "From..."

Once living beings exist, they naturally delight in strife and plunder, harming one another. They lose their fundamental reality; their ways become perverse and chaotic, spreading through popular songs and ballads, with none returning to the origin.

Confucius, having held no high office after his death, sustained the world with his remaining words. Yet the doctrines of Yang Zhu, Mo Di, the Yellow Emperor, and Laozi became increasingly mixed and fragmented.
Later, the teachings of the Buddha emerged, which push away the superficial and return to the source, bringing all together. This is what is meant by "nature is originally still."

The Lady Liang delighted in performing conditioned deeds (*saṃskṛta*). Bodhidharma criticized her; thus, the method of Emptiness became increasingly manifest. After six transmissions, it reached Dajian (Huineng).
His Way takes non-action (*wuwei*) as its being, takes the vast emptiness as its reality, and takes the expansive yet non-dissipative as its ultimate goal.

In his teaching of people, he begins with the inherent goodness of nature and ends with the inherent goodness of nature. Without relying on weeding or tilling, he returns to its original stillness. (From the *Liu Wen*) ○ Extraordinary Monks.
Huizhao entered nirvana at Wuling at the age of two hundred and ninety. Chan Master Huitong’s original surname was Wu, and his given name was Yuanqing.
He served as a court attendant (*gongfengguan*). One day he said to the Emperor, “Since my youth, I have not eaten meat;

my vow is to follow the teachings of the Buddha. Within ten days, an imperial decree granted his request. Soon after, his mother fell ill, so he returned to his hometown to visit Niaokuo, wishing to receive the tonsure and become a monk. Niaokuo said:

In these times, those who serve as monks are rarely diligent and austere; their conduct is mostly superficial and excessive. Xitong said, "The fundamental nature is pure, not something to be polished;
the original clarity does not depend on illumination. Xitong asked, "If you realize that pure wisdom is wondrously perfect and its essence is inherently empty and still, that is true renunciation.

After Yuanqing had requested this three times, Xitong then shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him, giving him the Dharma name Huigong. Huigong then suddenly took his leave to depart.
He went to various regions to study the Buddha-dharma. Baizhang said, "The Buddha-dharma is also present here in small measure.
He then picked up a tuft of cloth from his person and blew upon it; Daotong thereupon awakened to the profound principle. At that time, he was known as the "Cloth Tuft Attendant" (Wudeng Huiyuan).

In the Bingshen year (the eleventh year), when Deng Yinfeng was traveling to Mount Wutai, his path lay through Huaiyou. It happened that Wu Yuanji had mobilized troops at Caizhou and was engaged in battle with the government forces.
The Master said, "I shall briefly alleviate their distress. He then shook his mendicant’s staff in mid-air and flew across the battlefield. The two [armies]...
The army looked up in awe and marveled at this extraordinary event; their hearts to fight were instantly stilled, and by this means, the government forces were able to achieve their success.
At Jingyun Temple in Fuzhou, the Vinaya Master Shanghong passed away. Bai Juyi composed his epitaph, which states in brief:

"The Master presided over the Dharma for twenty years, and more than fifteen thousand people received ordination under him. The inscription reads: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Campaka fragrance..."
Decay! Who will reverse this? Great Master Jingyun. With the birth of Jingyun, the Vinaya was revived; with the passing of Jingyun, upon whom shall the Dharma generals rely?
Formerly when Jingyun came, those who entered his room returned [to the path]; now that Jingyun has departed, those who enter his room grieve (as recorded in the *Baizhi ji*).
○ Chan Master Guizong Zhichang had double pupils in his eyes; he subsequently used his medicinal hand to press them.
He rubbed them for a long time until both his eyes and eyelids were red. The world thereafter called him "The One Who Rubbed His Eyes to Return to the Source.

Li Bo, the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou, asked him, "Is it not mere idle talk to say that a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru? The Master replied, "People say you, the Prefectural Historian, have read ten thousand scrolls of books; is this true? He said, "Yes.
The Master said, "From the crown of your head to the soles of your feet, you are no larger than a coconut. Where, then, would those ten thousand scrolls be placed? Li Bo was struck speechless.

He simply lowered his head and remained silent. After the Master passed away, there was a eulogy for his portrait which said: "How lofty is your insight! Wiping your eyes, you avoided the heavenly throne;
turning back to look at those who washed their ears, you have not brought shame upon yourself for a thousand ages.

When Chan Master Bairyam of Zhangjing Temple entered nirvana, an imperial decree ordered his burial at Balingshan, and he was posthumously titled Dajue Chuandeng Ji Shi. This was on the final day of the second month in the twelfth year.
He entered parinirvāṇa. An imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title "Daché" (Great Penetration). Quan Deyu, the Chancellor, composed his stele inscription, which states in brief:

"The Master’s name was Huaiyun. His disciples were Zhi-lang, Zhi-cao, and others. The Master once compiled a single volume titled *Shizi Zhuan* (Biographies of Teachers and Disciples), in which he arranged the accounts of the various patriarchs;

it is the most detailed and authentic. High officials and great ministers all revered and placed their trust in it. Dongxun Dharma Master went to attend the funeral of his paternal uncle, who had passed the civil service examinations.
The request of [Li] Cheng; the preface written by Liu Zhitou, which states that [he] attained the Way of his teacher;
furthermore, Meng Changzhou and Zheng Zhongshu both designated him as their teacher and friend. ○ When the eminent monk Lingche passed away, his collected works comprised twenty fascicles.

Preface composed by Liu Yuxi, Minister of the Secretariat (General Discussion). ○ When Liu Zongyuan served as the Prefect of Liuzhou, there was a Great Cloud Temple (*Dàyún sì*) in the prefecture that had been burned down for a long time.
Zongyuan restored it and personally wrote a record of the restoration.

In the Dingyou year (the twelfth year), there was a monk without a surname named Fajian of Yuezhou, who resided on Mount Lengga; for fifty years, he never stepped beyond the threshold of his dwelling.
In this year, she passed away. Liu Zhitou composed a stele inscription for her (Liu Wen). ○ The "Horse-Spouse" wished to convert those in the region of Shanxi, so she went there.
People, seeing her beauty and refined grace, desired to take her as their wife.

She said, "I also wish to have a home, but only one who can recite the *Bannihuan-jing* (Universal Gate Chapter) in a single night shall have me. By dawn, twenty people had completed the recitation. The woman—
He said, "A woman of my station—how could she be a match for you gentlemen? You should recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; by dawn, those who have mastered it should number at least ten.

The wife further bestowed upon them seven fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, stipulating that they should master them within three days. When the appointed time arrived, only Ma Shi had mastered it. The wife then ordered that the rites for marriage be prepared.
