Ma Shi prepared the rites and went to welcome her; the wife said, "I am currently feeling unwell; wait until I am somewhat recovered before we meet."

He saw that before his guests had dispersed, his wife died; subsequently, her body decayed and putrefied, so he buried her. A few days later, an old monk arrived at the Ma family’s residence, leaning on his staff.
He asked for the reason for his visit, and the Ma family led him to the burial site.

The monk used his staff to push aside the earth, revealing that the corpse had already transformed; only the bones of a golden chain remained. The monk picked up the bones with his staff and said to the assembly: "This..."

The Sage, taking pity on you for the heaviness of your karmic obstructions, has thus employed skillful means to transform you. You should contemplate the causes of goodness so as to avoid falling into the sea of suffering.
Suddenly, he flew into the air and departed. From this time forth, those who venerated the Buddha became numerous in the region of Shanyou. (Master Can of Quanzhou once offered this eulogy:
"Her graceful form and tilted locks deceived all the young men to recite the Lotus Sutra; after she carried away that bundle of bones, one knows not whose house the bright moon now falls upon.")
In the first month of the Wuxu year (the thirteenth year), Chan Master Dayi of Ehu passed away; he was posthumously titled Huijue.
In the third month, Chan Master Lingmo of Wuxie sat upright, burned incense, and after addressing the assembly, suddenly entered parinirvāṇa. In this year, [the] Chan Master Yuan...

Hao entered nirvana. Hao propagated the Tiantai teachings; when the Hanlin scholar Liang Su requested him to compose a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, Hao was moved by a miraculous dream and immediately composed it.
Critics compared Hao’s commentary to that of Wang Bi’s *Yì* and held it to rival Chengguan’s commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

In the Jihai year (the fourteenth year), at Fayun Temple in Fengxiang, there was the Pagoda of the True Body of the Protector of the State. Within the pagoda was a single joint of a finger bone of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Its dharma was that it was opened once every thirty years; when it was opened, the harvests would be bountiful and the people would be at peace. When this year’s first month arrived, [it was opened].

The Emperor dispatched the Palace Messenger Du Yingqi, leading thirty palace women carrying incense and flowers, to welcome [the image] into the Great Inner Palace. The Emperor personally went to Anfu Gate to receive and prostrate before it.
It was kept within the Forbidden City for three days of offerings, during which five-colored light appeared; all the officials offered their congratulations, and the Emperor was greatly pleased.
Thereupon, he sent it on a tour of various temples, complete with the full ceremonial rites of the Buddhist section, as well as those of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and Chang’an Wan...
The music, banners, and drumming resounded along the roads. Princes, dukes, officials, and commoners rushed to prostrate themselves in worship;
they venerated and made offerings, fearing only that they might be too late. Some burned their own arms and heads as offerings; others exhausted their entire fortunes to provide for the donations.
Han Yu, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, submitted a memorial urging earnest remonstrance, asserting that Buddhism is merely one teaching of the barbarians.
[He replied: "From the Yellow Emperor down to Kings Wen and Wu, all enjoyed long lives and the common people were peaceful and happy;

yet at that time, there was no Buddha. It was during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han that Buddhism first appeared. Thereafter, chaos and collapse followed one after another, and the dynastic fortunes did not endure long.
It is evident, therefore, that the Buddha cannot bestow blessings. I beg you to cast these bones into water or fire, so as to end the delusions of future generations."
The Emperor became greatly enraged upon reading the memorial. He showed it to the Chancellor and intended to condemn Miu to death. Pei Du and Cui Qun spoke on his behalf, saying:

"Although Miu’s words were狂 (wild/insolent), they arose from a heart of sincere loyalty. It would be appropriate to show leniency in order to open the channels for public discourse. The various princes of the imperial clan and the former ministers [concurred].

Mou once again petitioned for his release with great sorrow. Consequently, he was demoted to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou. (An ancient worthy composed a poem regarding Han [Yu] that says: "The hundred-year life flickers and soon ends;

who among those setting forth principles recognizes the truth of the Way? He strove to eliminate stale expressions to boast to vulgar customs; alas, his efforts were of no avail and his spirit was exhausted. This is from Wang Jing’s *Collected Works*.

When Yu first arrived at the commandery, he submitted a memorial expressing his grief and gratitude, while simultaneously urging the Emperor to perform the sacrifice of the Eastern Peak (Taishan). After a long time passed without a response, he became despondent and unhappy. Thereupon, he heard that within the commandery...

Chan Master Dadian was renowned for his profound virtue and character. Māṇavaka sent three letters inviting him, and Dadian eventually arrived (the three letters, expressing great courtesy and respect, are found in the Master’s Collected Works).
Dadian’s discourse was transcendent and superior; he stayed for several dozen days, sometimes entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for several days before rising.
Māṇavaka respected him even more deeply. Later, while ascending Mount Ling during a ritual to sacrifice to the sea deity, he visited the Master’s hermitage once again and questioned Dadian.

"How many times [does one recite] in the Spring and Autumn Annals? The Master held up his rosary and showed it to him. Liang Yu still did not understand. The next day he went to the temple again. At the gate, he saw a monk and mentioned the previous conversation.

The monk clicked his teeth. Liang Yu entered the temple and questioned the Master; the Master then clicked his teeth three times. Liang Yu said: (Note: This passage is from the *Wudeng Huiyuan* [Compendium of the Five Lamps], recounting the encounter between the layman Liang Yu and the Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun. The dialogue plays upon the ambiguity of the term "chunqiu" (spring and autumn), which refers both to the historical chronicle and to the seasons. The clicking of teeth is a traditional gesture of realization or agreement in Chan literature.)
The Buddha-dharma is generally like this: the Master would strike a monk and expel him from the monastery. One day, the Duke asked, "My affairs as military governor of Junzhou are many;
what is the essential point? I beg the Master for a single phrase. Dadian remained silent for a long time without looking at him.
The Duke was at a loss. At that time, Sanping was serving as the attendant; he struck the meditation seat once. Dadian asked, "What is this? Sanping replied, "First move with stillness, then..."
He rescued [him] by means of wisdom. Li Yu then bowed in gratitude to Sanping, saying, "The Master’s school of teaching is lofty and steep;
yet, through your attendant, I have found a way of entry. Furthermore, Dadian once asked Yu, "Your countenance is somber, as if you were dissatisfied.
Why is this? Yu replied, "My service in the court has been rewarded with generous stipends. Yet, were I at any time to speak words of loyalty..."
It was not for my own sake. I have been exiled eight thousand *li*, wandering through mountains and seas, losing my wife and children. Poisonous mists and pestilential vapors break out day and night.
Now banished to a land where no human dwells, how can my life be preserved? This is why I, Yu, have come.
On my way out through Guangling, I visited his temple and offered prayers. Fortunately, by his power, I ultimately escaped harm.
Since His Majesty has achieved the merit of restoring the dynasty, I have already submitted a memorial to the Way (the Dao) regarding this.

If the Emperor intends to travel east to Mount Tai to report these achievements to the August Heaven, it would be fitting to summon Han Yu to compose records of these meritorious deeds and offer them at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples. — Yu.
I have waited for you day and night, yet you have not arrived; I hope for your swift return even at the risk of a single chance. How could I possibly feel any joy?
Dian asked, "When you speak directly in court, do you act with loyalty to the sovereign regardless of your own person, or do you still regard your own person and speak forcefully only to pursue fame?
If your words are adopted, you will obtain the reputation for loyalty and uprightness and enjoy its reward; if your words are not..."
If you do not employ what is beneficial and instead pursue that which is certain to happen, why such persistence in your breast?

If you truly fear being pursued [and cast out], then why not simply remain silent? I have heard it said: "One who serves as a minister does not seek comfort regardless of the place, nor act without measuring the circumstances.
Now, you are displeased at being pursued and instead hasten to conform to the times; this is surely not the way of a true minister.
This is the correct course. Furthermore, as for your life and death, your calamities and blessings—do they not depend entirely upon Heaven?
You should simply cultivate yourself within and resign yourself to your fate without; what can Guangling possibly do to bring you fortune?

The Sovereign, finding that a treacherous minister had betrayed the state, was occupied with suppressing him; though he has barely succeeded in pacifying the region, the wounds and sores have yet to heal. At such a time as this—
Furthermore, you now wish to perform the Feng and Shan sacrifices to announce your achievements, thereby agitating the whole world, all while setting your heart on your own desire to return home.
How can you bear to act thus? Moreover, to bring disorder upon yourself through exhaustion and then sacrifice to your own ghost is to be ignorant of fate (*ming*).
To agitate the world without regard for its welfare, seeking only to benefit yourself, is to be ignorant of benevolence (*ren*). To speak with such forced insistence—
"To demonstrate loyalty, yet to be despondent when encountering adversity—this is to be ignorant of righteousness (*yi*).

To take disorder as order and address it to the August Heaven—this is to be ignorant of ritual propriety (*li*). How then could you act in such a manner? Furthermore, regarding your dismissal, what was the matter you spoke of?
Mou said: "The Sovereign welcomed the Buddha’s relics into the inner palace. I, Yu, [considered] that the Buddha is the law of the barbarians."

"Listen. During the Three Dynasties, there was no Buddha, yet their reigns lasted for a long time. The Jin, Song, Liang, and Wei dynasties served the Buddha, yet they did not suffer premature death or chaos.
I fear that Your Majesty may be deluded by this; therefore, disregarding my own person, I have condemned it.
Dian said, "If that is so, then your words are erroneous. Furthermore, the Buddha is the great vessel that covers both heaven and humanity. As for his Way..."

He wondrously transforms all things and speaks of them; his words exhaust the principles of nature and destiny, and his teaching is to abandon evil and pursue good, to discard the false and return to the true. He regards the world as a father regards his son;
for one to destroy him is like a son wielding a blade against his own father. I have heard that those who observe others well observe where their Way resides.
One does not compare them based on the lands where they resided. Kings such as Jie and Zhou, and ministers such as Zhi and Qiao, were all people of the Central Kingdom;
yet they are not to be emulated because they lacked the Way. Shun was born in the Eastern Barbarians, and King Wen was born in the Western Barbarians.
Yong was born among the Rong tribes, and Ji Zha emerged from the Man people. Could those two sages and two worthies be called barbarians for not following [Chinese] laws?
Now, you do not examine the Way of the Buddha, yet you recklessly label it "barbarian. How trivial your words are!
Do you mean that because there were no Buddhas in ancient times, one should not follow the Dharma? Yet Confucius and Mencius lived during the declining Zhou dynasty.
Yet Chiyou and Gusou lived in the High Antiquity. How could one abandon the sages and worthies of the declining Zhou dynasty to emulate the cruelty and obstinacy of the High Antiquity?
You argue that emperors and kings of former ages were long-lived because there was no Buddha at that time. However, the *Book of Documents*, in the "Wuyi" (On Excess), states:
"From that time onward, none were able to live long; some lived for ten years, others for four or three. This refers to the Han...

Chen Ji asked: "If one considers that sovereigns have met with untimely deaths and their reigns were in disorder, then Emperor Ming of the Han was a preeminent ruler of his age, and Emperor Wu of Liang lived to the age of eighty-six;
how could it be said that they all met with untimely deaths and disorder? Yu replied:

'I maintain that the Buddha does not speak the lawful words of the former kings but instead recklessly propounds the doctrine of the cycle of birth and death, and he does not personally practice benevolence and righteousness.'"

While practicing loyalty and trustworthiness, they falsely fabricate the causes of retribution, calamity, and fortune; they lack the righteousness between ruler and subject and the affection between father and son.
They subvert the Way of the former kings—how could I remain silent and fail to refute them? Tian said:
How profound is your lack of understanding! Suppose there were a person here who, throughout the entire day, could recite numbers by the dozens yet did not know that two times five equals ten;

people would surely consider him mad. You spend all day speaking of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and good faith, yet you do not understand the Buddha’s words of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
truly, there is no difference between you and such a person. Moreover, as for your recitation of Buddhist scriptures, your doubts are no different from those of the ancients.
The King asked, "Is there anything extraordinary about them? May you tell me? Yanzi replied, "How could I have the leisure to read their books?
Dian said, "If you have never read their books, how can you know that they do not discuss the legal sayings of the former kings?
Is it not possible that because you have read the books of Confucius, you have consequently come to doubt theirs? Or perhaps you hear others call them wrong, and so you yourself deem them wrong?"
Indeed! If one has ever read the books of Confucius and yet suspects that they are not right, such a person is like the dog of Shun.
Hearing others say something is wrong and then immediately condemning it as wrong, such a person is like a concubine. Formerly, Shun kept a dog; the dog saw only Shun.
One day, when Yao passed by, the dog barked at him. This was not because it loved Shun and hated Yao, but because it was accustomed only to what it had commonly seen.
Shun never met Yao in person. Furthermore, it is heard that when a daughter is married off, her mother sends her with these words:
"When you go to your husband's house, you must be respectful and cautious; do not disobey your husband. Thus, following another is the way of a concubine or a wife;
how can one follow another’s errors without examining the reason why they are in error? Indeed, this is the cycle of birth and death.
This is not a fabrication; it is the ultimate numerical principle of heaven and earth, the subtle truth underlying the realms of the hidden and the manifest.
Viewed through the lens of natural phenomena, when the roots and sprouts of plants wither only to grow again, how should one marvel at their coming and going? As Confucius said:
"Examine the beginning and seek the end; thus one knows the discourse on death and life. Zhuangzi said, "The myriad things emerge from the mechanism and enter into the mechanism.
Jia Yi said, "When one transforms into a different species, what is there to worry about?

These are all discourses on saṃsāra that do not depend upon the Buddha to be clarified. How can they be called false? Furthermore, as for your [objection] regarding retribution for calamity and fortune—
To claim this was a fabrication is all the more sufficient proof of your error. Now, the retribution for good and evil is the natural response of the divine principle.
The *I Ching* says: "Accumulate goodness and there will be abundant blessings; accumulate evil and there will be abundant calamity. It also says:
"The ghosts and spirits harm those who are full and bless those who are humble. Master Zeng said: "Be cautious, be cautious! What goes out from you shall return to you."
These are all explanations regarding retribution and response. Only the Buddha can take deep pity for the misfortunes and blessings of humanity;

therefore, he makes these matters clear and manifest, speaking of the principles that are certain to come to pass, so that people may not sink into such calamities themselves. How could this be a fabrication?
Furthermore, it is said that the Buddha lacks the righteousness between ruler and subject and the affection between father and son; this is certainly beyond what you can comprehend.
There are indeed matters that exist within the realm of the mundane, and there are matters that exist beyond the realm of the mundane.
Those within the realm are what all people together uphold; those beyond the realm, nothing short of the ultimate divinity in the world can reach. Therefore, the Sage—
When people speak, there are those who speak of what is commonly observed and maintained by the multitude, and there are those who speak of the ultimate mysteries of the universe.
Each of these has its own appropriate application. When Confucius spoke of the Way (*Dao*), he pushed it to its limit:
it is without thought and without action, silent and unmoving, yet when stimulated, it immediately penetrates all things. This is not something commonly observed and maintained by the multitude.
These are words that all people ought to contemplate and practice. If the multitude neither contemplates nor practices them, then the principles of the world will almost come to an end.
When the Buddha speaks with a minister, he necessarily relies on loyalty; when he speaks with a son, he necessarily relies on filial piety.
These are words shared and observed by all people. Yet when his words reach their ultimate depth, they arrive at the state of no-mind—not merely being without mind.
Thus, one arrives at non-self; yet it does not stop at non-self, for one further arrives at non-arising.
Once there is non-arising, the sequence of yin and yang cannot be disordered, and the numerical patterns of heaven and earth cannot be manipulated.
Consequently, the roles of ruler and subject, father and son, naturally find their place therein. How could this be something spoken of to those with narrow vision and shallow learning?
Now I shall tell you: according to the principle of the Buddha, it is indeed without fixed form and without substance;
it is the most subtle of the subtle. It may be compared to the heavens: suppose there were someone here who spent all day praising the heavens, yet the heavens would not increase in glory;
or suppose he spent all day reviling the heavens, yet the heavens would not suffer any diminution. Thus, both those who praise them and those who revile them are in error.
Now, from the Han dynasty down to the present, the years that have passed are as numerous as these; the transformations of things and affairs throughout the world are as manifold as these;
the sovereigns, ministers, scholars, and commoners are as vast in number as these; and heaven, earth, and the divine spirits are as impossible to deceive as these.
Yet the teachings of the Buddha have nonetheless prevailed within this realm, such that no one has dared to debate or remove them. This—
There must be something that obscures heaven and earth without shame, and passes through the hundred sages without embarrassment;
the wondrous principle resides within it, and only after this can one reach such a state. Why do you not reflect upon this deeply? Now I shall instruct you:
as a student, you must examine the far-reaching aspects of the Way. That the Way is so far-reaching means that my own will cannot fathom its depths. Thus...
One must personally acknowledge that the person before me is more virtuous than I am.

That they are more virtuous than I means that they take this [principle] to be right, whereas I, on the contrary, see it as wrong; this indicates that there is something my own mind has not yet fully understood.
Therefore, one should reflect deeply upon what that person considers right and strive earnestly to seek it out; in this way, one may perhaps achieve some awakening. Now, you have condescended—
They occupy themselves within the confines of physical forms and rush about amidst sounds, colors, profit, and desire.
When their youthful ambitions are not realized, they become resentful, dejected, sorrowful, and frantic, as if they could no longer endure life.

How are they any different from mosquitoes and gadflies vying for filthy soil amidst a heap of straw? Thereupon, I stared with unblinking eyes, my spirit lost and my breath suppressed; I turned inward to seek...
His response was one of utter bewilderment, as if he had lost his own bearings. After a moment’s hesitation, he said to Dadian, "Are my words exhausted at this point?
Dadian replied, "That which I have told you was spoken according to what you were capable of understanding;
it was not the ultimate truth. Muzai said, "I am unworthy, Master. May I be so fortunate as to hear that ultimate truth? Dadian replied:
"Sincerize your heart, exhaust your nature, fathom the principles of things, and reach the mandate of Heaven; only then may you hear it. You may depart;
I shall not speak further. Mù hurried out. (Wai Zhuan) ○ In the eighth month, during a conversation between the Emperor and his chief ministers...

The Emperor’s illness was cured because of Mocheng’s words, which were truly pitiable. However, Huangfu Bo had long held a low opinion of Mocheng’s character and immediately memorialized the throne, saying:
"Mocheng is ultimately dissolute and reckless; he should be transferred to an internal post. The Emperor accepted this advice and consequently appointed Mocheng as the Prefect of Yuanzhou.
Mocheng again visited the hermitage of Dadian and presented him with two sets of robes, requesting leave to depart and saying: "I am about to leave you, Master; I hope to hear one [verse]..."
He spoke, and they were ultimately cured by one another. Da Dian said, "I have heard that those who easily believe others will surely find their own integrity easily altered;
those who easily praise others will surely find themselves easily slandered. You heard my words and easily believed them;
how do you know that upon hearing a different doctrine, you will not again consider me wrong? He then ceased speaking. Muzhi realized he could no longer hear [the truth] and thus departed.
I went to Yuanzhou. Minister Meng Jian, knowing that I had been associating with Dadian, sent a letter to me expressing his appreciation for my change of faith and new orientation.
In my reply, I stated that Dadian was quite intelligent and understood the principles of the Way;

he was truly able to transcend his physical form, overcoming himself through reason so that he was not disturbed by external affairs. Although I did not fully understand his speech, at the very least—
From within his own breast, he was free of obstruction; it was because of this that he associated with him. ○ In recent times, Huang Shanggu remarked:
"After [Han] Yu met Dadian, his prose became superior in principle, and his polemical writings against Buddhism were also somewhat diminished" (*Hanzi Waizhuan*).
○ In the tenth month, the Prefect Liu Zongyuan passed away. Zongyuan, styled Zihou, once composed the "Farewell to Wenchang. Upon ascending...
The Preface by Ren states: In the past, *śramaṇas* frequently associated with worthy gentlemen.
Since the Jin and Song dynasties, there have been those such as Daolin, Dao’an, Master Yuan, and the Venerable Xiu;

the associates they frequented were figures like Xie Anshi, Wang Yishao, Xi Zuochi, Xie Lingyun, and Bao Zhao. Consequently, the teachings of the True Dharma were employed alongside the Confucian classics. And...
People know how to follow the right direction. Today, there is Shi Wenchang, who has served the Way in the region south of the Yangtze for thirty years.
Treading upon the void, he traveled westward; his staff has been carried beyond ten years. The people of Qin have received benefit from him in great numbers.

The Duke Tianguan, the Duke Xiaguan, the Duke Zheng of the Court of Justice, and the Minister of Personnel Yang—all possess the virtue of Wang Anshi, the loftiness of Wang Xizhi, and the talent of Yao Zaochi.
All [these monks] were deeply devoted to their superiors and inherited their spiritual style (and so forth).

Furthermore, in the "Preface on Sending Monk Chen Southward to Travel" written in Yongzhou, the main point was his resentment toward those who flee from dhyāna and seek quiescence, thereby neglecting the skillful means (*upāya*).
Also, in the "Preface on Sending Master Yuangao," he traced the Way of the Śākya to its origin in filial piety; Master Yao did not deviate from this, and moreover, it harmonized with Confucianism.

Furthermore, he sent the "Method" (Fang) and the Master’s Preface. Its main purport was to criticize those who were pedantic in their literary style yet ignorant of themselves. He also sent the "Preface to the Venerable Xuanjü.

Its main purport was to admonish those who seek complacency while remaining in a state of superficial conformity. Its words run roughly as follows: "The Way of the Buddha is vast and all-encompassing.
Those who have aspirations beyond the mundane world and feel shame at being constrained by worldly norms will consider entering it. Thus, there are those with [certain] appearances..."
Yet they do not act according to their minds; though their names differ, their practices vary, and their types are not uniform.
Nevertheless, they all go about the world with shorn hair and disheveled robes—who among them can truly be known? (From the *Liu Jia Ji*)
In the first month of the Gengzi year (the fifteenth year),
the Emperor passed away (and the Mu-zong ascended the throne).
Mu-zong.

In the third month of the first year of the Changqing era (the Xinchou year), Liu Zong, the Regional Commander of Lulong, surrendered more than twenty commanderies of You and Yan to the court. Liu Zong requested ordination as a monk;
the Emperor granted his request by imperial decree. He was bestowed with monastic robes and titled the Great Master Dajue. His residence was designated as Ba'en Monastery.
Temple.
In the second year, the year of Renyin,
the Emperor dispatched Lingfu, the Supervisor of Monks of the Left Ward, bearing an imperial decree to summon Chan Master Wuye of Fenyang to court.

When Quan Fu arrived and had finished proclaiming the imperial decree, he prostrated himself and said, "The Emperor's gracious intent on this occasion is extraordinary; I pray that you, Master, will rise and proceed.
Fayue smiled and said, "What virtue do I, a poor monk, possess to trouble the Sovereign so often? You may go on ahead; I shall follow shortly."
He then bathed and purified his hair. At midnight, he addressed his disciples Huìyīn and others, saying:

"The nature of your seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing is co-eternal with the great void. All objective realms are fundamentally empty and still from the beginning. Only those who are deluded fail to realize this."
He was immediately deluded by external objects. Once deluded by objects, he transmigrated without end. [The Master replied: "I always realize that all things are empty;

not a single dharma accords with my mind. This is the sphere of activity for all Buddhas. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. Li Fu returned and reported these matters to the Emperor, who sighed in admiration for a long time.
Throughout the two reigns of Emperors Xian and Mu, the Master declined three imperial summons. After his death, he was posthumously granted the title "Great Attainer" (Dada).
Chan Master [Nianchou]. In the tenth month, the Emperor visited Sanyin Temple and bestowed one million strings of cash upon the monks.
Bai Juyi, having initially served as a Secretariat Drafter, was subsequently appointed as the Prefect of Hangzhou. Hearing of the virtue and character of Niaoke, he went to visit him;
Niaoke was dwelling atop a tall pine tree. Bai Juyi asked, "The place where you reside is extremely precarious. The Master replied, "Governor..."
"The danger is even greater. The disciple said, "I hold the position of a regional governor; what danger could there be? The Master said, "Fuel and fire intersect;
the waves of consciousness never cease. Is this not dangerous? The disciple asked again about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. The disciple said, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say that. The Master said, "A three-year-old child..."
"Though the boy may speak well, an eighty-year-old cannot walk as he does. Having expressed this with deep admiration, Bo Juyi departed.

From then on, he frequently followed him to inquire about the Way. By this time, Bo Juyi had become the Prefect of Zhongzhou. In the intercalary tenth month, he composed the inscription for the stupa of Vinaya Master Chou at Xingguo Temple in Jiangzhou.
In it, he wrote: "When the Master passed away, I inscribed four lines of verse as a parting gift; therefore, I have taken [this]..."
The inscription reads: "Originally we formed a bodhisattva society bound by incense and lamps, together lamenting this body of afflictions, as transient as dew or a bubble.

There is no need for lingering attachment; let the Master go as he pleases. We first request the Western Paradise as our host. In the eleventh month, [the Emperor] visited Waguan Monastery to hold a great assembly.
In the twelfth month, the Emperor fell ill; the Empress Dowager and the various officials went to the Buddhist temples to provide offerings for the monks (from the *History of the Tang*).
In the third year, the *guǐmǎo* year, on the eighth month, the Emperor visited Changqing Palace. There he encountered a monk holding an alms bowl and bestowed upon him two hundred rolls of silk.
On the nineteenth day of the eighth month, Chan Master Ruohui of Dongsi Temple passed away at the age of eighty; he was posthumously titled Dashi Chuanchengming. As for the Master’s early life...
He visited Mazu. After Mazu passed away, the Master observed that his disciples were stagnating in the phrase "mind is Buddha.
He then addressed the assembly, saying: "Mind is not Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. The sword has long since been lost, yet you are still marking the boat.
At that time, Dongsi was renowned as a "den of Chan."

In the first month of the fourth year, the Jia-chen year, Emperor Muzong passed away, and Emperor Jingzong ascended the throne. At Yongfu Temple in Hangzhou, the carving of the *Lotus Sūtra* on stone walls was completed;
the Chancellor Yuan Zhen composed a preface for it (*Tonglun*). At that time, there was the Chan Master Shenzan of Guling in Fuzhou.
When he first visited Baizhang and returned to his home temple, he was bathing with his preceptor. The preceptor called for Ling to rub his back;
as Ling stroked the preceptor’s back, he struck him once with his palm and said, “This is a fine Buddha hall, yet there is no Buddha in it.

The preceptor scolded him, to which Ling replied, “Even though there is no Buddha, he still emits light. The preceptor was suspicious of this. Later, while they were reading the scriptures, a mosquito struck the window; Ling said, “The world...”
"The Dharma-realm is as vast as this; why do you need to pore over old papers? The Master said, "Why is it that your speech is so extraordinary? Ling said, "I have a verse:
'Unwilling to exit the Gate of Emptiness, Throwing oneself at the window is truly strange. Poring over old papers for a hundred years— When will one emerge?
The Master was startled and said, 'You have attained the Dharma of a Superior Man (shangrenfa). I wish for you to explain it to me. Ling said:"
After parting from his former preceptor, he took up residence at Baizhang. Upon hearing a statement by Baizhang, the Master suddenly attained enlightenment.

He then wished to return to pay respects to Ling as his teacher for having transmitted the Dharma; however, Ling requested that he instead pay remote homage to Dazhi as his teacher, while regarding himself as a fellow practitioner.
In the fifth month, Hou Gao of Shanggu compiled the epitaph for the Venerable Lishi Xiyi of Donglin on Mount Lu, which states in brief: "The Master..."
He resided at the Yeshé Pagoda Cloister on Mount Lu. His exterior was formal while his interior was tranquil. A divine youth attended him at his side;
though he concealed his form, he remained until Huiyi’s death. When Huiyi cast off his physical form, two crows entered his palm and sought to eat it, yet would not leave.

When he extinguished his mind and became one with all things, two mice made their burrow before the threshold and ate incense, piling it up until it reached his head-cloth. Furthermore, there was a fierce tiger chasing a deer; the deer sought [refuge].
He rescued his master. The master pointed to a deer and entered the room; the tiger then retreated.

Had the master possessed worldly attachments, the divine child would not have attended him, the compassionate crows would not have stayed, the large rats would not have drawn near, and the fierce tigers would not have departed.

When he finally attained the state of quiescent extinction, the white lotuses in his courtyard withered and died, and the trees in the garden decayed and fell. Alas! During his lifetime, the Master witnessed these four anomalies: the crows, the rats, the tigers, and [the deer].
The deer has been caught. When tranquility and extinction (*nirvāṇa*) are manifested through these two wonders, then the lotus and the verdant trees become clear.

(Continued Records of Mount Lu) In the twelfth month, Wang Zhixing, the Grand Secretary of the Palace Secretariat, requested that a *śīla* altar be established at Sizhou to ordain monks during the Month of the Buddha’s Birth.
The imperial decree granted permission. Li Deyu submitted a memorial to prohibit and abolish it, but the Emperor would not accept it. (Old History of the Tang)
In the year Yisi (the first year of the Baoli era), Li Ao,
styled Xizhi, who served as the Prefect of Langzhou, admired the Way of Yaoshan. He entered the mountains to pay his respects to him.
Sansheng was reciting a sutra without looking up. Li said, "To see the person is not as good as hearing of their reputation. Sansheng called out to the Governor, and Li responded.
Sansheng said, "How can you value the ear and despise the eye? Li thanked him and asked, "What is the Way? Sansheng pointed up and down and asked, "Do you understand?
Li said, "I do not understand. Sansheng said, "Clouds in the blue sky; water in the pitcher. Li rejoiced.
Thus it was. He answered in verse: "My body has been refined until it resembles the form of a crane; Beneath a thousand pine trees lie two cases of scripture.
I came to ask about the Way, and there is no other teaching— Clouds are in the blue sky, water is in the jar. He asked again, "What are precepts, concentration, and wisdom?
The Mountain Master said, "There are no such idle furnishings here. Li took his leave. One night, while traveling up the mountain, Yaoshan suddenly—
"The clouds part and the moon appears. He let out a great laugh; the sound fell upon Liyang, some eighty or ninety li away. When Ao heard this, he sent another verse in reply, saying:
"I have chosen a secluded dwelling that suits my rustic heart; All year long, there is neither seeing off nor welcoming. Sometimes I ascend straight to the peak of a solitary mountain;
Beneath the moon, I strip away the clouds and let out a laugh. Li once composed the *Fu xing shu* (Treatise on Returning to Nature) in three chapters. Its...

The first part states: "When the emotions are clouded, the nature is concealed; when the emotions are forgotten, one returns to the nature. Through sincerity comes clarity, and through clarity one exhausts the Way of nature and destiny.
The second part states: "Without thought, there is tranquil illumination; the extension of knowledge lies in the investigation of things. The third part states:
"If one remains in a state of delusion without thinking, one will ultimately not clarify the Way" (from the *Wenji*).

In the Bingwu year (the second year), Pei Su, whose courtesy name was Zhongming, served as the Inspector of Yuezhou. He rebuilt the Great Buddha Hall of Longxing Temple, fulfilling a prophecy made three hundred years prior.
Previously, the monk Tanyan of Yuezhou had collaborated with Xu Xun (courtesy name Yuandu) to construct it.
Regarding the two stupas: while the construction of the stupas was not yet complete, Tanxun passed away. Master Yan lived to the age of one hundred and twenty, still awaiting the rebirth of Tanxun.
He became Xiao Cha, the Prince of Yueyang, who came to govern Yuezhou. Upon arriving at the prefecture, he visited the temple and saw Master Yan.

Through the empowerment of his samādhi powers, Yan caused the Prince to suddenly realize the events of his previous life concerning the construction of the stupas. Consequently, the two stupas were further endowed with magnificent grandeur.
At that time, the main hall of Longxing Temple was in ruins, and the assembly requested its reconstruction. Yan said, "This is not within the karmic power of this poor monk.
Three hundred years hence, a patron in vermilion robes shall come to restore this hall. The monks of the temple carved this record into stone.
When Pei Shou took up his post, he offered his emoluments to repair the hall, which fulfilled Master Xuan’s prediction. Su was the father of Pei Xiu (from the *Chuan Deng Lu*).
In the twelfth month, the Emperor passed away, and Emperor Wen ascended the throne.

In the fifth month of the Dingwei year (the first year of Tahe) during the reign of Emperor Wenzong, the Great Being Shanxin of Taihong Mountain passed away. At that time, Chan Master Longtan Chongxin... [was] profound.
Huahexing’s master originally lived in the alleyway of Wutianwang Temple with Master Wu. Every day, Huahexing would deliver ten steamed buns to him.

After each meal, Master Wu would invariably set aside one bun, saying, "I bestow this upon you so that it may provide shade for your descendants. Consequently, Huahexing requested to leave the household life.

Thereupon, he served at [Baizhang’s] side with diligence. One day, he requested instruction on the essential point of the mind. Baizhang said, "Where have I not already pointed out the essential point of your mind?
The Master bowed his head for a long while. Baizhang said, "If you see it, you see it immediately; if you attempt to deliberate upon it, you are already mistaken.

At that moment, the Master attained realization. He asked again, "How does one maintain this state? Baizhang said, "Roam freely according to your nature; let go and relax in accordance with conditions. Just..."
Exhausting the ordinary mind; there is nothing else but supreme understanding (*viniścaya*) (Five Lamps).

In the year Wushen (the second year), Chan Master Weiyen of Yaoshan in Lizhou, as he approached the end of his life, cried out: "The Dharma Hall is collapsing! The Dharma Hall is collapsing! The assembly...
Everyone supported and held him up. The Master raised his hand and said, "You do not understand my meaning," and then he entered nirvana. He was eighty-four years old.

By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Hongdao, and his stupa was named Huacheng. (The Stele for Yaoshan by Tang Shen states that according to the *Chuan deng lu*, he died in the eighth year of the Dahuang era;

another version says he passed away in the eighth year of Xianzong’s Yuanhe era. The former is incorrect. *Deng Yinpeng of Mount Wutai was quite prominent for his supernatural manifestations; fearing they might cause delusion,* [the Master]... [text continues].
The assembly then entered before the Vajra Cave on Mount Tai. As he was about to manifest his passing into nirvana, he asked the assembly:

"In all places where practitioners have passed away, I have seen them depart sitting or lying down. Is there anyone who has ever manifested the passing while standing? The assembly replied, "There is. The Master said:

"Is there anyone who has ever been cremated while standing on their head? The assembly replied, "Never before. The Master then stood upright and passed away; his robes remained perfectly draped over his body.

The assembly carried the corpse to the cremation ground, but it remained motionless and firm. People from near and far came to pay their respects, marveling at the wonder. The Master had a sister who was a nun;
she rebuked him, saying, "In life you did not follow the laws and regulations, and now even in death you remain so stiff!"
He deluded people; when they pushed him with their hands, he fell over. Thereupon, his body was cremated and the *śarīra* were collected and enshrined in a stupa on Mount Wutai.

In the year Jiyou (the third year of the Taizong era), the stone-wall scriptures were completed at Chongxuan Temple in Suzhou. Bai Juyi composed the inscription for them, which states in brief: "As for revealing and instructing..."

To enter into the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas, there is nothing more venerable than the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which delivers beings through definitive meaning to the limitless and extends the perfect teaching to infinity;

it comprises sixty-nine thousand five hundred and five words. To realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), to compose the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, and to abide in inconceivable liberation, there is nothing more supreme than the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*; it comprises twenty-seven thousand ninety words.

The two texts comprise four thousand two hundred eighty-seven characters and encompass the four modes of birth and nine categories of beings. Regarding entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* without anyone actually attaining deliverance, nothing surpasses the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Sūtra* comprises three thousand twenty characters; for destroying transgressions, accumulating merit, and purifying all evil realms, nothing is more urgent than this. It responds to mindfulness and fulfills one's vows.
To be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, nothing is more urgent than the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, which consists of one thousand eight hundred words.
To contemplate the true aspect through right view, nothing surpasses the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra*, which consists of six thousand nine hundred and ninety words.
To explain self-nature and recognize original enlightenment, nothing is deeper than the *Tathatā-saṃgraha-dharmamudrā Sūtra*, which consists of three thousand one hundred and five words. Emptiness...
Among all teachings based on the Buddha’s wisdom, none surpasses the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. It consists of two hundred and fifty-eight words;
these eight lines of verse encompass the essential tenets of the twelve divisions of the canon and the three vehicles. The secret treasury of the myriad Buddhas is fully contained therein (*Wenji*).

When Chan Master Danxia Tianran was about to pass away, he ordered his disciples to prepare a ritual bath. Once the bathing was completed, he donned a straw hat, took up his staff, and received [the final instructions].

He left one foot dangling from his sandals and passed away before it could touch the ground. He was eighty-three years old. The Master had originally been a Confucian scholar who happened to be taking the imperial examinations when he encountered a Chan practitioner who asked him where he was going.
He replied, "I am going to select an official. The Chan practitioner said, "What is selecting an official compared to selecting a Buddha? He replied:
"Where should one go to choose a Buddha? The Chan practitioner replied, "Mazu of Jiangxi has appeared in the world; that is the very field for choosing a Buddha.
The Master then went to see Mazu and rested his hand upon the forehead of Mazu’s head-wrap (*baku-tō*). Mazu said, "Nanyue Shitou is your teacher.
The Master arrived at Nanyue, where Shitou said, "Go to the fodder shed. Thereupon, he paid his respects and entered the hall of the practitioners.
While he was attending to his duties, later, during a communal work session for weeding grass, the Master (Nanyue) washed his head alone and knelt before a stone.
[The monk] joyfully shaved his head with him. He then preached the precepts to him, whereupon [the monk] covered his ears and departed, immediately returning to Jiangxi.

Upon seeing Mazu again, he did not pay his respects; instead, he entered the Sangha hall, mounted the neck of the Holy Monk statue, and sat there. The assembly was struck with wonder and astonishment.

He informed his master, who entered the hall and saw him, saying, "My son is naturally gifted. The Master immediately descended from his seat and prostrated himself, saying, "I thank you, Master, for bestowing upon me a Dharma name.
After some time, he traveled extensively throughout all quarters. Later, in the third year of the Yuanhe era, he lay across the Tianjin Bridge.

When Lord Zheng, the Regional Commander-in-Chief, came out and rebuked him, he did not rise. An official asked him the reason for this; the Master replied, "I am a monk of no affairs. Lord Zheng [was deeply impressed].
People marveled at this. He provided his own rice and flour, and the people of Luoyang turned toward him with great reverence. In the fifteenth year [of the Dali era], he chose to reside in Dengzhou.
Danxia attracted several hundred followers. The Master once composed two poems titled "Verses on Playing with Pearls," which are still transmitted in the world today.
His posthumous title was Chan Master Zhītōng (the *Chuanjian* states he passed away in the fourth year of the Chángqìng era).
In the fifth month of the gengxu year (the fourth year of Tahe), Liu Ke, Attendant Censor, composed the "Record of the Lotus Sutra Temple at Dongshan Shengquan" in Fuzhou. It states briefly:

"Among the exquisite monasteries throughout the world, those of Min Prefecture are often praised as being most magnificent. There is the Dongshan Fahua Temple, which serves as a hidden retreat for the southeast."
This is the first [instance]. At the beginning of the Jinglong era, the divine monk Huaidao first selected a site to the west of Aitong Peak.
Suddenly, a spring gushed forth, surging upward and spraying out, dividing into two streams as it flowed down. One stream irrigated the washing area, while the other formed a pond.
Later, Huaiyi resided there; after him, Zhichang took up residence. Zhichang was constantly attended by a celestial youth, and śarīras descended in secret. The mountain...
Regarding the *Shéntīng jīng* (Scripture on Divine Listening), inquiries concerning the Buddha-dharma truly began with the three great masters.
This monastery does not harbor women and admits no meat or pungent roots; it is truly extraordinary (*zhūnjué*). (From the *Chánglè jí*) In the tenth month, Chan Master Wúděng of Èzhōu passed away.
He was eighty-two years of age. The Master was a successor of Mázǔ.
In the fifth year of Tàihé (the Xīnhài year), the Emperor had a great fondness for clams.
One day, there was one in the imperial kitchen that could not be split open; it suddenly transformed into the image of a Bodhisattva.
The Emperor was struck with wonder and issued an edict to send it to Xìngshàn Temple, ordering the assembly of monks to gaze upon and pay homage to it. He then asked his attendants, "What is this?"
This was an auspicious sign. At that time, there was the Chan Master Weizheng at Mount Taiyi, who had a profound understanding of the Buddha-dharma.

The Emperor requested an imperial edict to summon him for an audience. When the Emperor questioned him, Weizheng replied: "Things do not respond in vain; it is merely to awaken Your Majesty’s faith. He continued, "The Sūtras state:
'If one is to be saved by means of a Bodhisattva body, the Buddha will manifest in the form of a Bodhisattva and preach the Dharma to them. The Emperor asked, "Bodhi..."
"The form of Śākyamuni is now visible, yet we have not heard him preach the Dharma. Why is this? He replied, "Does Your Majesty regard what you see here as permanent or impermanent?
Do you believe it or not? The Emperor said, "This is an extraordinary omen; how could I not believe it?"

The Magistrate said, "Your Majesty has heard him preach the Dharma to the end. The Emperor was greatly pleased and consequently issued an edict throughout the realm to establish images of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and offer them worship.
At that time, there was Ling Xingpo, who visited Fubei and Zhaozhou; she possesses recorded exchanges [in the *Wudeng Huiyuan*].
In the sixth year, the *renzi* year (892), Chan Master Xiyun first visited Baizhang.
He inquired about the karmic conditions regarding Mazu. Baizhang recounted the story of his second visit to Mazu involving the hanging of the fly-whisk;
upon hearing this, the Master attained great enlightenment. After receiving the Dharma, he resided at Mount Juefeng on Huangbo Mountain in Gaoyang County, Hongzhou.
He descended to Daian-ji Temple, where the assembly of monks flocked to him in great numbers, often exceeding a thousand.
His path was steep, his conduct solitary, his speech concise, and his principles direct; consequently, many among his disciples attained realization of the Way.
On the tenth month of the Gui-chou year (the seventh year),
on the Emperor’s birthday, the Dharma Master Zhixuan was summoned along with Daoists to enter the Linde Hall to debate the Way.
Chan Master Shishuang Qingzhu, having first studied under Guishan and subsequently under Daowu, attained realization of the essential meaning and immediately retired to Liusang.

Taojiafang (Potter’s Lane). Because the monk Xuan visited Dongshan and uttered the words, "As soon as one steps out the door, it is all weeds," Dongshan was startled and said, "Is there an ancient Buddha in Liuyang?
From then on, many monks relied upon him, and it became a center for the Dharma; it was named Shuanghuashan (Frost Flower Mountain).
In the twelfth month of the eighth year, the Year of Jia-yin (824), when Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan was about to pass away, the Head Seat asked him, “After the Master’s passing, where will you go?
The Master replied, “I shall become a water buffalo on the mountain below. The Head Seat said, “I—”
Jiashan asked, "May I follow you, Master? The Master said, "If you would follow me, you must bring back a blade of grass.
He then gathered his disciples and told them, "The metaphors of stars, cataracts, lamps, and illusions have existed for a long time. Do not say that I come and go. Having spoken, he passed away.
The Master had received the Dharma from Mazu; later, he returned to Chiyang and did not descend from his mountain for thirty years.
Nanquan was invited down from the mountain by Lu Xuan, the Grand Master and Inspector of Xuancheng, who requested to extend the rites of a disciple toward him;
consequently, disciples gathered there like clouds (Five Lamps).

On the day of Ding-si in the fourth month of the year Yi-mao (the ninth year), Prime Minister Li Xun submitted a memorial requesting the abolition of the inner monasteries and the purging of corrupt and spurious monks and nuns.
The imperial decree was granted. On that day, as the edict was issued and the sacred images within the Great Palace were being destroyed, a violent storm suddenly arose. The air...

The *chīwén* (ceramic dragon-head ornaments) on the main hall all fell off, and the gates and watchtowers of both the inner and outer walls were destroyed. The officials and commoners were struck with terror.

Because Emperor [Xianzong] believed that Li Xun’s requests had offended the will of Heaven, he immediately issued an edict halting the previous purge and ordering the restoration of the sacred images within the Great Palace;

consequently, the winds ceased abruptly. (According to the *Old History*, Vol. 5, Treatise on Portents, Li Xun was executed that winter. In the eighth month, Bai Juyi presented his collected literary works.
[The work] was compiled into sixty fascicles and included in the Great Canon (Dazang) of Mount Lu’s Donglin Monastery;

he himself wrote the preface, wishing to establish a karmic connection with the two forests for future lives (*Lushan ji*). In the ninth month, Chan Master Daowu Yuanzhi passed away at the age of sixty-seven.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Grand Master Xiuyi.

In the Bingchen year (the first year of Kaicheng), Dàfǎ Master Duānfú—Senior Registrar of Monks for the Left Street, Imperial Attendant, Great Virtuous One for Discourse on the Three Teachings while Leading the Procession, and Recipient of the Purple Robe—passed away.
Pí Xiū, Compiler of the Zhōngguǎn, composed his funerary inscription, which states in brief: "As for those who are men, whether at home..."
In secular life, he would propagate benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music to assist the Son of Heaven, thereby supporting the world and guiding the customs of the age.

Upon leaving the household life, he would exercise compassion, meditative concentration, and wisdom to aid the Tathāgata, thereby expounding the teachings for the sake of living beings within the *kṣetras*. Apart from these, there is nothing by which one may be considered a true man (*puruṣa*).
At the age of seventeen, the Master became a bhikṣu; from that time on, he was unrivaled in the world regarding the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. Emperor Dezong heard of his reputation.

When he was summoned for an audience, the Emperor was greatly pleased upon seeing him at first glance. He frequently entered the inner palace to engage in philosophical discussions with Confucians and Daoists.

The Emperor bestowed upon him a purple cassock and further decreed that he attend the Crown Prince at the Eastern Court. Emperor Shunzong deeply admired his character and treated him with the intimacy of a brother.
They slept and rose together, and the Emperor’s kindness and courtesy toward him were exceptionally profound. Emperor Xianzong visited his monastery several times, treating him as a guest or friend.

He frequently sought his counsel and bestowed upon him singular favor. Through this, the Son of Heaven came to recognize further that the Buddha was a Great Sage and that his teachings possessed great and inconceivable wonders.
At that time, the court was in the midst of pacifying the realm, having bound Wu and subdued Shu.

The waters of Cai and Dang were dammed, and the territory of Yun was pacified, such that the Son of Heaven sat with hands folded in leisure and did nothing. He issued an edict for the Upādhyāya to lead the assembly of monastics to welcome the sacred relics from Mount Ling;
a Dharma assembly was established within the Secret Hall. For the sake of the people, he prayed for blessings, and the Emperor personally attended to the incense and lamps.

Subsequently, punishments were not cruel and the military was not arrogant; the common people raised no cries of sorrow, and the rivers and seas were free of turbulent waves. This was surely because the True Vehicle was employed in conjunction [with secular governance].

His administrative governance was remarkably effective. He presided over the rituals of the inner palace and oversaw the affairs of the clergy in the Left Ward for eleven years, serving as a model for the pure assembly.
On the first day of the sixth month in the first year of the Kaicheng era, he passed away lying on his right side facing west.
Upon cremation, more than three hundred śarīras were obtained.

In the second year, the *ding-si* year, Chan Master Lizong of Zihu in Quzhou first entered the quarters of Nanquan. He then traveled to Matishan in Quzhou, where he settled in a thatched hut for his dwelling.
In this same year, the local resident Weng Qiangui offered the land of Zihu below the mountain and established a monastery there. Later...
In the second year of the Xiántóng era, an imperial edict bestowed upon him the name An-guó (Peaceful Nation). The Master once addressed the assembly, saying: "At Zihu there is a dog;
it seizes people by their heads above, seizes them by their hearts in the middle, and seizes them by their feet below. To hesitate for even a moment is to lose one's body and forfeit one's life."

In the third year, the third month of the Wumu year, the National Preceptor Qingliang Chengguan, the Head of the Sangha, passed away. Throughout his life, he served nine successive dynasties as the preceptor to seven emperors.
He was one hundred and two years of age and had been a monk for eighty-three years. His height was nine chi and four cun.
His hands hung down past his knees; his eyes emitted light at night and did not blink during the day. He could hold two brushes simultaneously, and his voice resonated like a bell.

Because the Emperor Wen-zong revered him as a sage-ancestor, he specifically suspended court for three days, and high officials wore white mourning garments. They enshrined his entire body in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan.
Not long after, a Buddhist monk arrived at the capital and submitted a memorial stating that he had seen two messengers at the Pamir Mountains.
He passed through the air. When questioned, he replied, "I am the deity of Mañjuśrī Hall in North India.

I came here to take the great tooth of the Avataṃsaka Bodhisattva and return to my country for veneration. By imperial decree, the stupa was opened; indeed, one tooth had vanished, leaving only thirty-nine remaining.
He then performed the cremation, and the *śarīra* were brilliant and lustrous; his tongue was the color of a red lotus. Consequently, he was bestowed the title "Qingliang" (Coolness).

The State Preceptor’s stupa was named Miaolan. Under imperial decree, the Chancellor Pei Xiu composed the inscription for the stele, and the Emperor ordered a portrait of the State Preceptor to be painted and enshrined at Daxingtang Temple.

In the fourth year, the fourth month of the Jiwu (1079) era, Liu Ke, Director of the Bureau of Secretaries, composed the stele inscription for the Venerable Baocheng of Donglin, Mount Lu. It states briefly:
"The Master’s name was Zhiman. He lectured on the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) twenty-seven times and presided over the ordination platform on fourteen occasions."
By means of the Vinaya, he saved tens of thousands of people. Among the gentry and scholars who associated with the Master were Bai Shilang Jiyi, Li Binke Bo, Li Zhongshu Zhao, and Pei Xuanzhou Yi;
there were also several dozen disciples, among whom Ke once observed the rites due to a student. How could I dare forget these factual records?
*Comprehensive Mirror of the Buddhas Throughout the Successive Dynasties (Shìshì Tōngjiàn)*, Compiled Chronologically by Dynasties, Volume Ten;
*Comprehensive Mirror of the Buddhas Throughout the Successive Dynasties*, Compiled Chronologically by Dynasties, Volume Eleven.
Compiled by the monk Benjue of the One Hermitage on Mount Kuò during the Song Dynasty.
Edited and collated by the layman Mingzhēnrú (明眞如), Bì Tíngzàn (畢廷瓚) during the Wǔzōng era of the Táng dynasty.

On the sixth day of the first month of the Gengshen year (the fifth year of Kaicheng), Chan Master Zongmi of Mount Gui on Zhongnan Mountain passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Upon cremation, śarīra were obtained, brilliant white and large in size.
He was sixty-two years of age. The fourfold assembly observed the period of mourning, their lamentations resounding through the wilds. Emperor Xuanzong—

He was posthumously honored with the title Chan Master Dinghui. Initially, he attained realization through the *Nirvāṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on Perfect Enlightenment) and became a Dharma heir of Chan Master Daoyuan of Suizhou.
Subsequently, he traveled to the Capital and met the Great Master Chengguan, the commentator on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, to whom he paid the rites of a disciple.

Chengguan said to him, "As for one who can follow me to roam through Vairocana’s Flower Treasury World (*Vairocanābhisambodhi-kusumagarbha*), could it be you? Thereupon, he traveled north to Mount Qingliang.
He returned to reside at Caotang Monastery in Huxian. Not long after, he again entered the hermitage on Mount Gui to the south of the monastery.

During the Dazhong era, he was summoned to the inner court and granted purple robes. The Emperor repeatedly questioned him regarding the essentials of the Dharma, and court officials looked up to him with devotion; among them, none surpassed the Prime Minister Pei Xiu.

He penetrated deeply into the innermost sanctum of the Dharma, receiving its teachings as his external protection. The Master composed the *Cessation and Contemplation Collection of All Explanations* (*Chanyuan zhuquanji*) in one hundred fascicles, with two fascicles of general prefaces.

He further authored commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Flower Garland Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Diamond Sūtra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.

Prime Minister Pei composed an inscription for the Stele of the Transmission of the Dharma, which states in brief: "The Master was resolute and earnest in his efforts to rescue and deliver [sentient beings]."

He was tirelessly devoted to opening and guiding others. Thus, those who encountered his method as a teacher—those who were greedy he would cause to give; those who were violent he would cause to restrain themselves; those who were dull he would cause to awaken;
and those who were indolent he would cause to exert themselves. They came with eager intent and departed with joyful hearts; the places where this occurred were beyond counting.
I do not know the extent of the boundaries of his realm, nor can a mere disputant know the direction in which the Great Way tends. (This is based on the *Guo zhuan* of Pei [Hui]).

This is what is recorded on the Stele of the Dharma. According to the *Chuandeng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), the Master entered nirvana in the first year of the Huichang era. This was the month Emperor Wenzong passed away and Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne.
In the ninth month, he summoned the Daoist Zhao Guizhen and others to enter the inner palace to perform a *Jinlu* (Golden Register) ritual site.

In the tenth month, the Emperor ascended the Xuantan altar and personally received the dharma registers. Wang Zhe, the Left Shiyi, remonstrated, saying: "At the commencement of a royal enterprise, it is not appropriate to exalt [Daoism]."
The Emperor did not accept [the proposal] that faith was excessive.

On the *xinyou* day (the first year of Huichang), in the sixth month, the Daoist Liu Xuanjing was appointed as Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Guanglu Daifu*). In the tenth month, Chan Master Yunyan Cheng...
The Master manifested illness. On the twenty-sixth day, he summoned the administrative monk and ordered him to prepare a vegetarian feast, for a senior monk was departing the following day.
At night on the twenty-seventh, the Master entered nirvana. Upon cremation, over a thousand śarīras were obtained.
He was posthumously titled Great Master Wuzhu, and his stupa was named Jingsheng. His foremost disciple who attained the Dharma was Chan Master Dongshan Jia.

In the second year of the Renxu cycle (842), Pei Xiu was serving as the Governor of Hongzhou. He went from Huangbo Mountain to welcome Chan Master Xiyun to the prefecture, where they stayed at Longxing Temple.
Day and night, the Governor sought instruction from him, presenting him with a poem that said: "Ever since the Great Being transmitted the Mind-Seal, A round jewel has appeared upon his brow."
A body of a single *chi*, he has hung his staff for ten years while dwelling by the waters of Shu; today, with his bowl floating, he crosses the banks of Zhang.

A thousand dragons and elephants follow his lofty steps; from ten thousand *li* away, fragrant flowers form a cause for excellence. If you wish to serve this master as a disciple, you do not know to whom the Dharma will be entrusted.

Guihai (the third year), at Mount Jiuzuo, there was the Great Master Zhengjue, whose name was Zhiguang. A native of Xianyou in Xinghua Prefecture, he manifested birth in the second year of the Yuanhe era.
Initially, he visited National Teacher An of Yanguan and Chan Master Wudeng of Ezhou, whereupon he attained realization. Thereafter, he traveled south.

He returned to Quanzhou and constantly carried an iron alms bowl, accompanied by one hundred dogs. Upon arriving there, he encountered Emperor Wuzong’s impending suppression of the Buddhist teachings, so he fled into the mountain ravines.
When Emperor Xuanzong restored the teachings, he emerged once more from the Southern Mountains, [where] Wang Yu... [and others].
In the third month of the fourth year of the Jiǎzǐ cycle, the Daoist Zhao Guīzhēn was appointed as Professor of the Left and Right Street Gate (Zuǒyòu Shèdào Mén).

At that time, the Emperor was intent on seeking immortality; Zhao Guīzhēn, riding upon this favor, would invariably disparage the Śākyamuni followers whenever he had an audience, asserting that they should be completely eliminated. The Emperor [was deeply...].

The Emperor granted his request. Returning to the True [Daoist] tradition, he again petitioned for a debate with the followers of Śākyamuni. An imperial decree was issued to summon the Buddhist monks and Daoists to the Linqide Hall for discussion.
Master Zhixuan ascended the debating seat; his arguments were swift, precise, and powerful, such that the Daoist practitioners could not defeat him.

Zhixuan subsequently memorialized: "The sovereign’s fundamental domain is ritual and music, the unified system of laws and institutions. As for the practices of breathing exercises and elixir ingestion, these are merely the private pursuits of recluses dwelling in the mountains and forests."

"Regarding these matters, I pray that Your Majesty will not trouble yourself with them. The Emperor’s expression was displeased. The attendant official Feng Xuan urged him to compose a poem to explain himself.
Xuan immediately presented five stanzas, which included the lines: "The crane's back is precarious and the dragon's back is slippery; may the Sovereign remain for another thousand years.
The Emperor understood this as a satirical rebuke and specifically granted him leave to return to his native home (from the *Chuanteng lu*).

In the fifth month of the year Yichou (5), Zhao Guizhen served as a censor and frequently engaged in debate; he subsequently recommended Deng Yuanchao. When Deng was summoned, together with Zhao Guizhen and Liu Xuanjing, they increasingly persecuted the followers of Śākyamuni.
On the first day of the fifth month, an imperial edict was issued to consolidate and reduce the number of Buddhist temples throughout the empire; for the Capital, [each...]
Four temples were retained, with thirty monks remaining at each. One temple was retained in each of the upper provinces, while all temples in the lower provinces were abolished.
In the upper temples, twenty monks were retained; in the middle temples, ten; and in the lower temples, five.
All remaining monks and nuns were ordered to return to lay life. A total of over forty thousand temple buildings were destroyed, and over two hundred and sixty thousand monks and nuns were defrocked.
On the Man (from the *History of the Tang*): At that time, Chan Master Zhizhen of Guishan in Fuzhou had two verses: "The bright moon divides its form, ever new in every place;

How could one clad in white fall away from the person who understands emptiness? Who says that being in the secular world hinders the cultivation of the Way? Kanakamuni once took birth as the body of an elder.
When the Immortal of Patience sat in meditation beneath the forest, He was once maimed by the King of Song; How much more so for me, a holy [being]..."
In the morning there was no such thing; merely to order him to cease his practice of the Way—what sorrow could there be?
(Chuan Deng Lu).
The Xuanzong era, Bingyin year (the sixth year of Huichang).

In the third month, Emperor Wuzong fell ill. Having ingested golden elixirs, he developed carbuncles on his back and malignant sores over his entire body, leading to agitation, loss of composure, and mental derangement.
He was unable to speak for ten days before passing away at the age of thirty-three. The old history praises him, saying:
"Zhaosù abolished the teachings of the Buddhists and punished the ranks of the *śramaṇas*. His ambition was to take a corrective step up the vermilion ladder and seek [the Way]."
Like searching for pearls in red water, you have merely observed the peripheral studies of Xiao Yan and Yao Xing, yet failed to realize the futile quests of Qin Shi Huang and Han Wudi.
It is because you were deluded by the words of heterodox paths that you have one-sidedly disparaged the teachings of foreign lands; how much more so regarding the Dharma that has come from the West!

As the millennium approached, the common people had grown accustomed to these practices until they became established customs; they feared the teachings more than the laws of the state and delighted in its followers no less than in those who have attained immortality.
One morning, the golden images were destroyed and the foreign scriptures were burned and discarded.

They harbored resentment toward those who prostrated themselves and provoked the wrath of even the commonest man. The Emperor praised this as "clear judgment," yet he listened to such a biased account.
(Tang History) In that month, Xuanzong ascended the throne. The Emperor was the thirteenth son of Emperor Xianzong.

Initially, Wuzong had harbored a grudge against him and submerged him in the palace latrines. The eunuch Qiu Gongwu secretly provided protection, causing him to shave his head and become a monk, whereupon he traveled throughout the land.
He once resided within the assembly of Master An of Yanguan. While paying homage at Huangbo, the Emperor questioned him.
The Emperor said, "I do not seek [enlightenment] by clinging to the Buddha, nor by clinging to the Dharma, nor by clinging to the Sangha.

What is the use of performing prostrations? Huangbo said, "I constantly perform prostrations to such matters as these. The Emperor asked, "What is the use of performing prostrations? Huangbo then struck him. The Emperor said, "That was quite coarse.
Huangbo struck him again. Later, Xuedou composed a verse on this: "His majestic wind is chilling, yet he does not boast; Sitting upright, he brings stability to the seas and dragons."
A snake. A Son of Heaven of the Dazhong era once lightly touched it, and three times he personally encountered its claws and fangs.

When the Emperor first arrived at Yanguan, Master An one day warned the administrators, saying, "A person of extraordinary character will arrive here. The next day, several traveling monks came to pay their respects;
Master An recognized them in silence and ordered the *vinaya* master (Weina) to seat them in high positions. Their manner of worship was exceptional.
Whenever Dao’an met with these officials for conversation, they grew increasingly respectful toward him. He then remarked, "The monks of the monastery suffer from a lack of offerings;

I request that you provide a memorial for a single offering. The Emperor composed it for him. Upon reading it, Dao’an was struck with alarm and realized that the document would be taken away to provide for the monks in a most generous manner.
He then said to the Emperor, "The time has come; do not linger like a mud-dwelling serpent. He thus entrusted the Emperor with the final matters concerning the Buddha-Dharma.
He departed. When Yanguan passed into *nirvāṇa*, the Emperor composed a poem of lamentation, saying: "In this age of the Dharma’s semblance, what calamity has befallen the teachings?

The splendor of the Śākya gate has lost its pearl-bearing dragon. I am loath to tread upon the fresh grass of the fragrant steps; With palms struck together, I sorrowfully gaze upon your countenance from another day.

Your jade handle shall forever leave the seat of the Three Teachings; The golden sound [of your voice] shall long remain as a trace for ten thousand years. I know that the causes and conditions of your descent into this world have now ended. It should...
He was the [X]th in the hierarchy of the higher heavens. Later, he emerged and was appointed as the Vice Governor of Jiangling.

Upon the death of Emperor Wuzong, Yang Gong, the Chief Commissioner of the Left of the Shence Army, exhorted the Prime Ministers and the various officials to welcome and install him on the throne. When the Emperor ascended the throne, he received his ministers in audience.
In managing state affairs, both within and without the realm were in unanimous accord; thus, his hidden virtues finally became manifest.

(Zuting shiyuan) In the fifth month, an imperial edict was issued [condemning] twelve individuals, including the Daoist priests Zhao Guizhen, Liu Xuanjing, and Deng Yuanchao, for having deluded and misled the previous reign.
Those who slandered and destroyed the teachings of the Śākya clan were all sentenced by the Imperial Court to receive lashes and banished to the regions south of the ridges.

An imperial edict was issued for each of the capitals, Chang’an and Luoyang, to restore eight great monasteries and grant them new official names. When the Emperor resided in his princely residence, he once had a strange dream similar to that of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.
In the year of the Dragon’s Leap, all were restored as famous temples.
On the intercalary third month of the Dingmao year (the first year of Dazhong), an imperial edict stated:
"During the final years of the Huichang era, monasteries were consolidated and abolished; although it was said that these were teachings from foreign lands,"

Material resources are the source of principle. The people of the Central Kingdom have long practiced this Way; yet, because the reforms were excessive, the resulting state of affairs became distorted.

Regarding the sacred sites of the Spirit Mountain and the monasteries established during the fifth year of the Huichang era, the former resident monks may continue to restore and maintain them as before (*Tang Shi*).
○ When Chan Master Huizhong of Guiyang heard the imperial decree for restoration, he...

He said: "Those who ascend as immortals do not necessarily receive the registers; those who attain Buddhahood do not necessarily require the status of a monk. Consequently, he did not eat after midday and did not dwell within the traces of meditation.
He did not leave the mountains for thirty years. There are three verses that say: "Only after the snowfall does one know the steadfastness of the pines and cypresses;

Only when the clouds are withdrawn does one see the division between the Ji and Huai rivers. Had it not been for the secular ruler’s command to return to lay life, How could one distinguish the solitary bird from the flock of chickens?"
Amidst a flock of cranes for many years, I have drifted through the dust and soil. Though I wear the *kāṣāya*, I am not yet a true monk. Today I return to fulfill my original vow;
there is no harm in keeping my hair while awaiting the transmission of the lamp. Though my appearance has changed, the Way remains ever-present;

though I blend with the mundane, the source of my mind is never clouded. Try reading the verses on Śubhakarasiṃha’s pilgrimage: "How could one from those years be merely counted as a śramaṇa? (From the *Chuan Deng Lu*).
In the seventh month, an imperial edict catalogued the crimes and evils of Li Deyu; he was exiled to Chao-yaya and died there.
In this same year, the Minister of Revenue, Bai Juyi, passed away at the age of seventy-five. He had served as the Left Vice President of the Department of State Affairs.

Initially, having enjoyed the favor of Emperor Xianzong, Bai Juyi was resented by those in power and subsequently suffered banishment and dismissal. Unable to implement his latent ambitions, he gave himself over to literature and wine.
He was able to adapt harmoniously to whatever circumstances he encountered, relying on the Buddhist teachings regarding birth and death as one who had forgotten his physical form.

Later, he maintained a bond of affection with his younger brothers, Xingjian and Minzhong. Residing in Lidaoli, he dredged a pond, planted trees, constructed a stone pavilion at Mount Xiangshan, and excavated the Eight-Section Rapids;

he styled himself the "Madman Who Sings and Recites. In his later years, his devotion to Buddhism became even more intense, to the point that for months at a time he would abstain from eating meat or pungent vegetables.

He formed a "sacred-fire society" with the monk Rumian of Xiangshan. Whenever he traveled back and forth by sedan chair, dressed in lay clothes and carrying a staff with a curved top, he styled himself the "Layman of Xiangshan.
He held banquets with nine others, including Hu Jing, all of whom were elderly men who had not served in office.
People admired them and painted a "Portrait of the Nine Elders. After Bai Juyi passed away, his residence was donated to become a Buddhist temple.
Bai Juyi once painted an image of Amitābha Buddha and worshipped it, composing a record for it himself. It says in brief:
"Our original teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, spoke thus: 'In the west there is a world named Sukhāvatī (Ultimate Bliss), because it is free from the eight sufferings and the four evil realms.
That land is called Pure Land, because it is free from the three poisons and the karma of the five turbidities. As for its Buddha..."
He is titled Amitābha because his lifespan is immeasurable, his vows are immeasurable, and his merit, marks, signs, and radiance are immeasurable.

Contemplate carefully the sentient beings of this Sahā world: whether they be wise or foolish, noble or humble, young or old, should any among them give rise to the thought of taking refuge in the Buddha, raising their hands in palms-joined salutation, they will invariably face the west.
