Should they encounter fear, calamity, or suffering, when they open their mouths—

When one first resolves to attain enlightenment, one must first bring to mind Amitābha. Furthermore, whether casting metal, molding clay, carving stone, embroidering patterns, or even printing on water or gathering sand—among those who play as children, there are none who do not take Amitābha Buddha as their primary object of devotion.
One does not know why this is so, yet it is so. From this we can observe that the Tathāgata possesses great vows directed toward these sentient beings.
It is evident that sentient beings have a great karmic affinity for that land. Otherwise, there are many Buddhas of the past, present, and future in the south, north, and east;

why would it be so exclusively thus? Bai Juyi, Grand Master of the Middle Rank and Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince of the Tang dynasty, in his declining years, having suffered from the ailment of wind-stroke and paralysis, then donated three hundred thousand strings of government stipends and commissioned artisans...

In this painting of the Western World, Amitābha Buddha sits in the center, flanked on his left and right by the two Great Beings, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, while devas and humans gaze up in reverence. May these merits be fully realized.

I, the disciple Ji-yi, prostrate myself and kneel before the Buddha, vowing that these merits be dedicated to all sentient beings. May those among them who are as aged as I, or as afflicted by illness as I, [attain liberation].
All such persons shall alike leave suffering and attain happiness, sever evil and cultivate goodness; without departing from the southern region, they shall behold the Western Land.
There, within the superior grade of blue lotuses, they shall be reborn according to their conditions. In both the present and the future, they shall always remain in close proximity [to the Buddha].

Wishing to reiterate this meaning, he spoke these verses of praise: "In the Pure Land of the World of Ultimate Bliss, There are no evil realms nor any manifold sufferings. I vow that [all beings] shall be like me..."
Regarding those who are aged and afflicted by illness, they shall be reborn together in the presence of Amitāyus Buddha (*Sukhāvatī-vyūha*).

In the second year of the Wuchen era (848), when the Provincial Inspector Pei Xiu was governing Xuancheng, he frequently discussed the Way with renowned monastics. A disciple said to the Master: "I venture to ask—"
Before the term "the three realms" was established, people did not know how to practice cultivation and did not perceive cause and effect.

Those who possessed even a modicum of great fortune did not diminish their efforts. Since this teaching reached the Central Lands, the foolish fear punishment and reduce their evils, while the wise hope for blessings and increase their virtues.
If they continue to increase them without ceasing, then by now they should have attained complete goodness; as for those who diminish [their virtues], [they have not yet done so].
It is so. To this day, there ought to be no evil; yet why is it that delusion, confusion, and tyranny have not diminished since the time of the Qin and Han?
Why is it that merit, wisdom, and the clarity of hearing have not increased since the era of the Wei and Jin? Those who return to it converge from diverse paths like spokes in a wheel;
those who establish it see the myriad dharmas arise like clouds. It is fitting that we all ascend the path of enlightenment; it is not right that the common masses remain as they were from antiquity.
"It is like this. Such delusion arises from being so firmly entrenched in it; is this not indeed a drowning? The Duke smiled and said to him:
'When the Great Illumination first dawned, the Dharma was not yet fully perfected. The Sages appeared in succession, acting as the craftsmen of Heaven. They tied knots and drew trigrams.'"

The patterns of refinement and substance underwent successive transformations; with each Sage established, a corresponding Dharma arose. Thus, the principles of the heavenly way and human affairs corresponded as clearly as matching seals.
Indeed, when the Lord of the Fire-drill had not yet produced fire, there were no celestial fire-stars, humans had no fire for food, and tortoises showed no fire-signs in their shells.
It is certain that there would have been no fires among things had the Lord of Shaohao not yet regulated metal. Then the heavens would have had no golden star;

humans would have had no golden armor; tortoises would have shown no golden omens; and it is certain that things would have suffered no calamities of metal. It was only when the Sage worked the wood and brought forth fire [that these came to be].
As when smelting ore to extract gold, the refined essence takes mastery; it surges and transforms above and below.

Thus we know that in the temporal affairs of the world, the sage acts in accordance with the Way. He probes the source of the spirit and exhausts the manifestation of nature and destiny, creating great skillful means to protect all living beings.
Yet the beings receive these benefits without knowing them, much like the operation of the heavenly way, by which all things flourish and grow.
Everyone claimed it was for themselves; who knew it was truly so? Thereupon, the questioner attained a vast realization, as if tasting the flavor of the Buddha.

When the imperial decree permitted the establishment of a temple, he proclaimed this to the officials and the common people. They encouraged one another with fervor to petition for its construction, first establishing it within the outer walls of Xuan.
He subsequently restored Xinxing Temple. In this year, Pei Xiu again respectfully invited Chan Master Huangbo Yun;
the master arrived at the prefecture and stayed at Kaiyuan Temple, where he received the Dharma morning and evening.
In the third year, the cyclical year Jisi (851), Pei Xiu, the Inspector of Hunan, paid a visit to Chan Master Huilin Jue. Xiu asked the Master, "Do you have any attendants?
He replied, "There are one or two. Xiu asked, "Where are they? Jue then called out, "Dakong! Xiaokong! At that moment, the two...
The tiger emerged from behind the hermitage, and Xiu was greatly startled. Juexian said to the tiger, "Go now; there is a guest here. The two tigers roared and departed.
Xiu asked, "What kind of practice did you, Master, perform to evoke such a response? Juexian said, "Do you understand? Xiu replied, "I do not understand.
Juexian said, "This mountain monk constantly recites the name of Avalokiteśvara. Xiu marveled at this extraordinary event and departed. Juexian remained in seclusion as usual.
Holding his *khakkhara* staff, Wuzhuo went out into the forest at night. Every seven paces he would strike the staff once and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara once.
A monk came to visit him; as the monk was spreading out his sitting mat (*kaṣāya*), Wuzhuo said, "Wait, wait. The monk asked, "What have you seen, Master?
Wuzhuo replied, "It is a pity that you have just knocked over the bell tower. At these words, the monk attained realization.
In the eighth month of the fourth year, the *gengwu* year, Chan Master Huangbo Yun entered *parinirvāṇa*. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Duanjie, and his stupa was named Guangye.
Prime Minister Pei Xiu recorded his words, stating: "The *Chuanxin fayao* (Essentials of Transmitting the Mind-Dharma) contains some ten to twenty chapters; all are the Way of Direct Pointing."

(Chuan Deng). In the fifth year, the Xinwei year, in the fifth month, an imperial edict summoned Chan Master Hongbian of Jingzhao into the palace. The Emperor asked: "In the Chan school, why do there exist the Northern and Southern [traditions]?"
The name was asked. He replied: "The Chan school originally has no north or south. From the various patriarchs down to Master Hongren, there were two disciples:
one was Huineng, who received the robe and Dharma and resided in the region south of the mountains; the other was named Shenxiu, who propagated the teachings in the north.

Although the Dharma they attained was one and the same, their methods of guidance and awakening differed—there being the distinction between sudden and gradual. Thus it is said 'Southern Sudden' and 'Northern Gradual. This does not apply to Chan itself."

The school was known by the names of the Northern and Southern traditions. The Emperor asked, "What are the meanings of precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)? He replied, "To guard against what is improper and cease from evil is called precept.

When the six sense organs encounter objects, the mind does not follow after conditions; this is called concentration. When both mind and objects are empty, one perceives all things without delusion; this is wisdom."

"It is called wisdom. The Emperor asked, "What is meant by 'expedient means' (upāya)? He replied, "The gateway of skillful artifice; to rescue and uplift those of middling and inferior capacities by employing indirect methods of guidance and instruction—this is called expedient means.
If one were to address those of superior faculties, one would set aside expedient means and speak only of the unsurpassed Way."

This, too, is a discourse of expedient means (*upāya*). Even the profound words of the Patriarchs, which transcend all effort and sever all conceptualization, do not go beyond the traces of expedient means.
The Emperor asked, "What is the Buddha-mind? He replied, "Buddha means awakening; that which possesses the wisdom of illuminating awareness is called the Buddha-mind.
The Emperor asked, "If someone recites the Buddha's name, what of it? He replied, "The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma accords with the capacities of beings."
He taught according to their capacities. For those of superior faculties, he opened the way to the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*), whereby they could suddenly awaken to the ultimate principle.

Those of middling and inferior faculties were unable to understand it all at once; therefore, the Buddha opened the gate of contemplation, instructing them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha so as to be reborn in Sukhāvatī.

The Emperor asked: "If one upholds sūtras and mantras to seek the Buddha, what of that? He replied: "The Tathāgata’s various teachings of the Dharma all lead to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It is like [a hundred...]"

"Of the thousands of streams, there are none that do not flow toward the sea as their source. In this same way, all these various differentiated conditions return to the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
The Emperor asked, "Since the Patriarch transmitted the seal of the mind, how is it that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks of 'the dharma of non-attainment'?

He replied, "Throughout the Buddha’s entire ministry, he truly did not bestow a single dharma upon anyone; he merely pointed out that the self-nature of each and every person is identical to the One Dharma."
Zang said, "At that time, when Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata merely sealed Śākyamuni’s fundamental dharma, there was nothing further to be attained; only then did it accord with Dīpaṃkara’s original intent.
The Emperor asked, "Since you, Chan Master, have realized the meaning of the Patriarchs, do you still pay homage to the Buddha and read the sutras?

He replied, "For a śramaṇa to pay homage to the Buddha and recite the sutras is the constant law of maintaining the community. There are four types of retribution; by relying on the Buddha’s precepts to cultivate one's person, one attains these."
He sought out wise teachers and gradually cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), treading the path traversed by the Tathāgata. The Emperor asked, "Why is there sudden realization?
Why is there gradual cultivation? He replied, "One suddenly clarifies one's own nature (*svabhāva*), which is non-dual with that of the Buddha.

However, because of defiled habits from beginningless time, one must rely on gradual cultivation as an antidote to allow the functioning of the nature to arise in accordance with it. It is like a person eating rice: it is not done in a single mouthful."
He was then satisfied. That day, the audience lasted until the seventh watch before concluding. The Emperor was pleased and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Yuanzhi.

On that same day, an imperial edict was issued to increase the maintenance of ancestral pagodas throughout the empire; it was decreed that those who had not yet been granted posthumous titles should be reported by their respective localities, and the Ministry of Rites (Dachang) was to examine their conduct and confer the appropriate honors (*Wudeng Huiyuan*).

In the *wenshen* year (the sixth year), Mount Lu’s Donglin Temple was restored in Jiangzhou. The Regional Inspector, Cui An, composed a stele inscription for it, which states in brief: "The Buddha transforms people through all dharmas;
this is what is meant by rescuing those drowning with one's hands and extinguishing fire with water. His benevolence toward living beings is thus truly vast."
Today, the Son of Heaven has taken up the task of benefiting all living beings and restored the teachings. The decree was respectfully presented by Jiangzhou;
I visited this place and found the pine breezes refreshingly cool, so with joy I returned it [to its former state]. I have often observed the Jin history and read of the deeds of Master Huiyuan:

his discernment was like a flowing commentary and his words were like sharp blades, sufficient to reveal the spirit of that era. Furthermore, during the Six Dynasties in Jinling, each reign was brief and the customs were thin.

The minister fears for his life because of his achievements; the sovereign is distressed by suspicion. [This land] lies at the center of the four quarters and possesses the beauty of rivers and mountains.
Could it not be that Master Yuan has calculated this strategic advantage and observed the conditions of the times? [He has thus]... [acted accordingly].
[The text] is far removed from the three marks [of existence], yet it possesses all excellences for the sake of the world.
Emperor [Wendi] bestowed the posthumous title "Discriminating Enlightenment" (Biànjué) upon Dharma Master Yuǎn (Record of Mount Lú).

In the seventh year, the Guiyou year (853), Chan Master Lingyou of Mount Gui resided at Mount Gui. Students gathered there like spokes converging on a hub. Coinciding with Emperor Wuzong’s suppression of Buddhism, the monastery was consequently emptied.
The Master wrapped his head in cloth and hid among the common people. Later, upon Emperor Xuanzong’s restoration of the teachings, Pei Xiu requested that he come forth.
He then proceeded to his place of residence, which was Tongqing Temple. His disciples came once more, and the situation remained as it had been before.
The Master propagated the teachings and doctrines for over forty years; those who attained realization were beyond counting. He had forty-one disciples who entered his inner circle.
On the ninth day of the first month of this year (the inscription states the eighth year), having washed his hands and rinsed his mouth and arranged his seat, he passed away peacefully.

He was eighty-three years of age and had been a monk for sixty-four years. His posthumous title was Great Perfect (Dàyuán) Zen Master, and his stupa was named Pure and Tranquil (Qīngjìng). Prime Minister Zheng Yú composed the stele inscription.
Briefly stated: Among those in the world who discourse on the Way and its arts, there are many; each takes what they revere as being correct.

Beyond the teachings of the Five Constant Virtues, regarding the realm of spirit and the nature of life, the historians have categorized these as the words of the Daoists; thus, the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi are representative of this school.
However, when it comes to shaking off the burdens of worldly emotions and transcending the boundaries of birth and death within the context of existence and non-existence—
In this interval, he attained a realization that was transcendent and solitary; thus, the teachings on *dhyāna* (meditation) of the Buddhists may be considered nearly exhaustive therein.
One who is not a vessel of brilliant insight and magnificent magnanimity cannot receive its transmission. When it is transmitted, these are all instances of a vast, grand, and peerless measure.

While the Master resided at Mount Mí, he remained tranquil day and night; were it not for one who has cast aside life and death and forgotten anxiety and affliction, how could he have been so compliant?
As for "Great Harmony" (Dàhé), who is capable of participating in this? Furthermore, life and death are the greatest matters of gain and loss for human beings.
Since there is nothing to be gained in life, there must be nothing to be gained in death. Since there is nothing to be gained in gain, there must be nothing to be gained in loss.
Therefore, regarding gain and loss, right and wrong within the realm of the obscure, there is no room for them to be applied; one simply entrusts oneself to transformation.

In this practice of the Way, all the capable affairs of the world are fully realized. Alas! Among the myriad classes of living beings, human life is the most spiritually gifted, yet it takes spirit and consciousness as its foundation.
From childhood to old age, beginning with food and drink, one gradually adds to this the pursuit of fame and achievement, profit and sustenance, and the concerns of right and wrong, day and night.
Bound by fetters, one dwells on thoughts while walking or sitting, and wanders in dreams while lying down.

Driven by the lure of lust, one seeks to employ this aged and withered frame, never knowing how to rest in the shade or cease from activity, nor seeking even a moment’s leisure to cast off anxieties and settle the spirit.
Until at last, one suddenly comes to an end; relatives and friends become no more than mere passersby on a road.

All gains and offerings are left to others, while a sense of shame and debt accumulates before the divine spirits. This disgrace nearly flows down to future generations, as one becomes debauched, dissolute, and profligate, unable to exercise self-mastery.
All of these arise from one’s own mind; they must not fail to be regulated by the Way and its arts (*dào-shù*). There is nothing that surpasses the subtlety of the Way and its arts.

Regarding the teachings of the Buddhist scriptures, my ignorance increases while my spirit yearns for them ever more deeply. Yet their ultimate destination leads entirely to the state of non-existence (the realization of the absence of self).
(*Complete Treatise on Universal Enlightenment*) When Master Dà'ān first visited Bǎizhàng, he asked, "What is the Buddha? Bǎizhàng replied, "Riding an ox, searching for the ox. The Master...

[The Master] asked, "After consciousness, what then? [Dongshan] said, "Riding an ox back home. [The Master] asked, "How does one maintain this? [Dongshan] said, "It is like a herdsman holding a whip, watching over [the cattle] so they do not trample the crops.
After the Master had grasped this meaning, he went with Chan Master Daoyou, who had already established his residence at Mount Mí.
The Master also personally plowed the fields to assist in the Way. When the community requested him to succeed Daoyou as abbot of Mount Mí, he ascended the hall and said: "There is..."
The account of tending the ox at Mount Gui for twenty years (Wudeng Huiyuan).
In the year Jiashu (8), a monk from Zhongnan Mountain was dwelling in a hermitage practicing meditative concentration. One day, the monk lost his *kāṣāya*, and then saw a monkey wearing it.

Yan sat in meditation upon a rock. Later, he saw a troop of monkeys all practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Among them, some even passed away while seated in this state. Today, there is the Five Monkey Stūpa.
Emperor Xuanzong composed a verse in praise of him, which says: "Alas, you monkeys, able to enter meditative concentration; The heart-monkey remains unmoving for thousands of springs.
Cease grasping at the fruits of the red trees through three winters; Desist from playing with the solitary moon-disk in the azure pool. Your two eyes have already followed the blue..."

The mountain barriers close; his two brows still knit like a hundred flowers in frown. Since he passed away while seated at Zhongnan, how many people have awakened to the emptiness of this floating life?
(9th day of the year) Yi Hai.
Chan Master Wuzhuowenxi entered Mount Wutai seeking an audience with Mañjuśrī. Suddenly he saw an elderly gentleman, to whom Wuzhuo bowed and said, "I wish to see the Great Being Mañjuśrī.
The gentleman replied, "The Great Being cannot yet be seen. Have you had your meal? Wuzhuo said, "No."

The old man led him into a temple. Having brought him inside, he ascended the hall and bade him sit. A youth approached with a cup of mother-of-pearl containing a substance like curdled milk or butter, which he was told to drink.
Upon doing so, his mind and spirit felt clear and lucid. The old man asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma being maintained in the South?"
Zhuo said, "In this final age, do few bhikṣus uphold the precepts? He replied, "There are many assemblies. He asked, "How many? He replied, "Sometimes three hundred, sometimes five hundred.
Zhuo asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained here? He replied, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages dwell together."

He asked, "How many people are there? He replied, "Three times three in front, and three times three behind. Their conversation continued until evening. The old man ordered the youth to lead him out. Not long after they had gone, Zhe was moved by a profound sense of sorrow and realized that the old man was none other than Mañjuśrī; he could not see him again. He prostrated himself before the youth and requested a word as a parting gift. The youth spoke these words of the stainless, undefiled, and eternally true: "Stainless and undefiled, this is the eternal and constant. If you wish to see the Buddha, look at your own mind. Zhe attained great enlightenment upon hearing this. He returned to his home village and built a small hermitage. He lived there for twenty years, never leaving. When he finally passed away, he left behind no written testament. Later, when the local magistrate heard of this, he went to the site to investigate. He found only a single footprint, about one chi in length, which remained clearly visible even after the ground had been plowed over. It has been passed down to the present day. This is known as the Footprint of Mañjuśrī. It is located approximately two hundred paces from the temple of the Great Master Huineng. It is said that those who pray with sincere devotion will often hear the sound of the *Heart Sūtra* being recited. Those who hear it are invariably granted their wishes. It is truly a place where the sacred and the profane meet. One must not fail to pay homage to it. Furthermore, the stone image of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is located within the temple grounds. It is said that those who gaze upon it with a pure heart will see the Bodhisattva’s countenance. It is truly a place where the sacred and the profane meet. One must not fail to pay homage to it. Furthermore, the stone image of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is located within the temple grounds. It is said that those who gaze upon it with a pure heart will see the Bodhisattva’s countenance. Having finished speaking, the boy and the temple both vanished. Only the Manjusri riding a golden-maned lion, coming and going amidst five-colored clouds, could be seen;
suddenly, white clouds covered him, and he was no longer visible (from the *Bieji*).

In the Bingzi year (the tenth), Master Bianzhang served as the Head Seat (*śrāmaṇera*) of the Three Teachings. ○ The śramaṇa Sūyan of Daolin Monastery in Tanzhou traveled to the Great [Capital] to seek out the Tripiṭaka.
The eminent scholar Li Jie presented him with a preface, which stated in brief: "As for those who practice the Way of Confucianism..."
Those who take pleasure in disparaging the followers of Śākyamuni invariably argue: "In the eras of Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and Confucius, there were no Śākyas at all;
the Śākya arose during a period of decline and chaos. It should be abolished and severed so that it may not further proliferate.
Such arguments are superficial. They may well recognize that this is so, yet they do not know why it is so. Allow me to explain.
In ancient times, there was a man whose flesh was plump and his complexion serene; his breath was refined and his spirit clear. He never sought out physicians nor did he ever pray to spirits.
Remaining tranquil and preserving harmony, he suffered no afflictions from pestilence or disease—this was indeed a case of goodness. Yet, suppose this one man were to meet with misfortune.

Yet there arose ailments caused by cold, heat, wind, and dampness; thus, the techniques of medical treatment and cauterization were employed, and the rituals for averting calamities and offering propitiations became manifold.
Are these two states merely opposites? It is simply that the conditions of being ill and not being ill differ in their circumstances.

Alas! Before the Three Dynasties, the world was healthy. The virtues and righteousness of Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu were disseminated throughout it, and the canons of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius [were established].
He taught them to uphold it. Although the influence of the Way has declined, its gradual permeation still persists. Deceit does not overcome trust; evil knows how to avoid goodness.

During the final ages of the Three Dynasties, the world was afflicted by illness: the influence of the Way fell into great decay; deceit overturned trust, goodness withdrew through gentleness, and evil prevailed through force.
Superiors and subordinates became mutual enemies, giving rise to a custom of resentment. The teaching of Śākyamuni takes purity and emptiness as its meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
By taking gentleness and humility as patience, resentment and strife can be brought to rest.

By taking frugality and diligent austerity as spiritual practice, and regarding poverty or prosperity, longevity or early death as the workings of cause and effect, one can find peace even in lowliness and obscurity.

Thus, when it is said that "one must experience affliction to perceive the Buddha-nature," this is fundamentally the result of being stirred by the winds of a decadent age. Indeed, such is the nature of a declining era.
In this atmosphere, there is nothing at all to be found that brings joy. Were it not for the followers of Śākyamuni to rescue us from this, where else could we entrust our hearts?

To criticize the rise of Buddhism while failing to hold the customs of this degenerate age accountable is like a man suffering from illness who blames his physician for performing the necessary incantations, treatments, and cures;
such a person knows only that Buddhism arose during a degenerate age, but fails to [understand its purpose].
One knows that in this age of decline, there must be salvation from the Śākya clan. Why is this so?

For when the world is already afflicted and its people are already distressed, if it were not for the Śākya clan to allow them to find peace in their proper lot, the brave would stir up their spirits and think of fighting, while the wise would settle their minds and think of plotting;
thus, the commoners of the fields and roads would rise up in chaotic throngs. Now, as for the Śākya clan—
As for the division of labor, we do not demand it of others; thus, those who are virtuous, wise, and brilliant all set their minds at rest.
Those who cannot reach this understanding are fools, who are merely employed by superiors. It is by relying on this that customs afflicted by chaos can find peace.
How could one possibly eliminate it? Critics fail to consider how the teachings of Śākyamuni support the world.
It is of great benefit to assist in transformation, yet people hasten toward the minor expenses of carving, engraving, and colorful painting. Therefore, I say:
they can know that it is so, but they do not know why it is so. During the final years of the Huichang era, Emperor Wuzong extensively eradicated the followers of Śākyamuni;
the monasteries throughout the empire were demolished as if swept away. At the beginning of the new reign, the Son of Heaven restored the fact that the Śākya teachings could not be abolished.
[The Emperor] issued an edict to restore Xu [Fuzhi]. Alas! It has already been stated how Buddhism assists the world.

Had it not been for our Sovereign’s profound discernment of the source of principle, how could he have restored its establishment? (General Discussion) ○ Initially, monks and nuns were ordered to receive ordination and be granted certificates (*Tongjian*).
Dingchou (Year 11): Chan Master Dongshan Jia.
Initially, he studied under Nanquan and Huishan; subsequently, he studied under Yunyan Cheng.
Upon hearing the discourse on "Inanimate Things Preaching the Dharma," he attained realization and composed this verse: "How wondrous! How wondrous! Inanimate things preach the Dharma."
It is inconceivable. If one were to listen with the ears, it would be difficult to comprehend; only by hearing sound with the faculty of sight can one come to know it.
Later, while crossing water, he beheld his reflection and attained great enlightenment. He spoke a verse, saying: "By all means, do not seek it from another;
To do so is to distance yourself from me. I now go forth alone, And everywhere I encounter him. He is precisely myself right now, But I am not he. One must truly act in this way.

Only when one understands thus can one accord with Suchness (*tathatā*). At this time, at Mount Xinfeng, he gathered and guided students; subsequently, he flourished in his teachings at Dongshan in Gaoyang.
The Master once asked a monk, "What is the most painful thing in the world? The monk replied, "The hells are the most painful. The Master said, "Not so.
To be within the confines of these robes and yet not clarify the Great Matter—this is called the greatest suffering" (Wudeng Huiyuan).

Wu-yin (the twelfth month): Wan Jingru of Luzhou. For three generations his family lived together; he dwelt in a mourning hut beside his parents' graves and transcribed Buddhist scriptures with his own blood. He severed [the ties of] two [families].

[The Emperor] bestowed upon him the title of Duke of the Second Rank. He gave birth in Chuan and changed the name of his residence to Chengxiao Township, Guangxiao Village. Emperor Xuan issued a memorial in his honor.
In his home village of Wenzhou Ruian, at Benji Chan Monastery, there was a monk named Wuyi.

Following the Huichang suppression of Buddhism, he went into seclusion in the northeastern valley, where he built a hermitage for meditation. Ten years passed; vines and creepers entwined around him, yet he remained perfectly still and unmoving.
He was titled the Venerable Tengluo. Later generations established a shrine for him, which is still venerated today (*Yongning bian*).
In the eighth month of the Jimao year (the thirteenth year of Dazhong), the Emperor passed away.
The Emperor was intelligent, benevolent, respectful, and frugal; the world called him the "Little Taizong. [End of] Yidi.
In the year of the Zong reign era, Chan Master Huizhong of Guiyang in Quanzhou passed away while sitting upright with incense burning.
His entire body was interred to the east of the stupa of Chan Master Wuliao. Several years later, the stupa suddenly cracked open.

When the presiding monk was about to open it to look inside, that night, while in a state of meditative stillness, he saw Wuliao say: "There is no need to open it further. It is now for Shen and Chen."
Zhenshen (whose secular surname was Chen; it is recorded that he met Master Mazu).
Yizong gengchen (the first year of the Xiantong era).
In the fifth month, Cai Jing, the Governor of Fuzhou, composed the "Epigraph for the Sūtra Repository of Donglin Temple on Mount Lu. It states:

"Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou, because the three teachings were not identical, issued an edict for the Duke of Xiaoyao to determine their relative superiority and inferiority. [The Duke] replied that although the three teachings differ, they all lead back to goodness;

while their manifestations have degrees of depth, their underlying principle has no gradations. Jing has always believed that the teachings are constrained by their forms and that one becomes mired in their outward traces."
Those who merely observe their differences will remain confused; however, those with profound understanding and penetrating insight will surely realize their underlying unity.

The *zhongshu* (loyalty and reciprocity) of Confucianism, the gentleness and humility of Laozi, and the compassion and forbearance of the Buddha—if one treads these paths, there is blessing; if one violates them, there is calamity. Thus, regarding the three teachings, the gentleman...
Without sinking or destruction, he probes its profound essence to assist the pure truth; by taking this as his governance, his administration will surely flourish.
When Puhua was about to manifest his passing, he asked people for a *zhidu* (a monk’s robe). Whether they offered him a fur cloak or a padded jacket, he would not accept them.
Linji sent someone to present him with a coffin; the Master laughed and said, "Linji, that fellow with the glib tongue," and then accepted it. Thereupon, he took his leave.
A person said, "Tomorrow you will die at the East Gate. When the people of the commandery escorted him out of the city, the Master said, "Tomorrow you will die at the South Gate.
On the second day he said again, "Tomorrow it will be auspicious at the West Gate. On the third day he said, "Tomorrow you will pass away at the North Gate."

On the fourth day, he personally carried his coffin out through the northern gate. Shaking a wooden clapper, he entered the coffin and passed away. The people of the commandery lifted the coffin to look inside;
he was already gone, and they heard only the sound of the clapper fading gradually into the distance from the sky.

Chan Master Da Tong of Touzi in Shu Prefecture first studied under Cuiwei Wuxue. Having attained the essential meaning, he returned to his hometown and resided on Mount Touzi. One day, Zhaozhou arrived there.
At the hermitage, the Master returned carrying oil. Yunzhou said, "I have long admired Touzi; yet upon arriving, you are nothing but an oil peddler.
The Master replied, "You see only the oil peddler, but you do not recognize Touzi. Yunzhou asked, "What is Touzi? The Master said:
Yuyou asked, "What is it like when one attains life within death? The Master said, "Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive by the break of dawn.
From this point on, the Master’s reputation for the Way spread throughout the world.
In the second year of the Xinsi cycle,
Chan Master Caoshan Benji, whose courtesy name was Tanzhang, went to Gaoyang to pay his respects to Dongshan; he remained there for over ten years,
until his reputation became preeminent throughout the monastic community.
In the second month of the third year of the Renwu cycle, Chan Master Huánzhōng of Dàcí Mountain in Hángzhōu passed away without illness at the age of eighty-three.

He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master Xìngkōng (Nature Emptiness). The Master once addressed the assembly, saying: "To speak for ten feet is not as good as to practice for one foot. To speak...

One chi gained is not as good as practicing for one cun. In the fourth month, an imperial edict was issued to establish ordination platforms (*sīlā-maṇḍala*) at four temples in each of the two streets to ordain people for twenty-one days.

His Majesty served the Buddha with the utmost sincerity; he frequently established lecture halls within the palace, personally chanting the essential meanings of the scriptures and transcribing Sanskrit manuscripts by hand.
He visited various temples on numerous occasions, bestowing countless gifts.
On the *guiwei* day (the fourth), by imperial decree, Dharma Master Zhixuan was appointed as National Preceptor Wudao to oversee all matters of the Buddhist teachings.

As for Chan Master Jiaozong, the second patriarch of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou, he initially studied under Wukong of Yanguan to resolve his doubts and delusions; it was at this time that he came to reside at Jing Mountain.

Shan propagated the teachings of Chan. Later, in the intercalary third month of the seventh year of the Xiantong era, he manifested his passing. He was posthumously honored with the title Great Master Wushang.
Jia-shen (5):
Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun left the mountain range to travel as a wandering monk. Having spent a long time attending various Chan assemblies, he visited Touzi three times and [Xuefeng] nine times.
He went up to Dongshan, but the karmic conditions did not harmonize. Later, he attained realization under Deshan’s words;

from then on, he entered the inner chamber [of the master], and his understanding of the profound principles deepened day by day. That year, together with Yantou and Qingshan, he arrived at Aoshan Town in Lishui to stay overnight.
When Yantou woke from sleep, he still saw Xuefeng sitting upright. Yantou said, "Why do you not go to sleep? You look exactly like someone from the seven villages."
Dongshan asked, "Fengdian, are you not yet settled here? Fengdian replied, "I am not yet settled here.

Yunyan said, "I took you for one who had fully received the ancestral seal; why do you still speak such words? Bring forth your view point by point, and I shall either certify it for you or sweep it away for you.
Fengdian then enumerated his various views. Yunyan gave a shout and said, "If you were like this..."
"It is so. Indeed, you have not yet reached the ultimate. Have you not heard that what enters through the gate is not the family treasure?
Hereafter, if you wish to propagate the Great Teaching, every word must flow from your own breast, so that it may cover heaven and earth.
At these words, Feng attained great enlightenment; he prostrated himself and said repeatedly, "Only tonight is Mount Ao finally completed!"
Thus they parted ways. Yantou then established a hermitage at Sleeping Dragon Mountain on Mount Dongting, where disciples gathered in great numbers.
Xuefeng, meanwhile, returned to Minchuan (as recorded in the Complete Collection).

In the sixth month of the seventh year of the Yiyou era (1095), Xuefeng ascended Mount Xianggu and said, "This is truly my dwelling place. He then cleared away the thatch to build a hermitage, and his disciples gathered in great numbers.
This mountain belongs to Houguan County in Fuzhou; it encircles and commands four districts, rising with precipitous peaks ten thousand *ren* high. Before the winter...
It snowed even in the height of summer, and because of this, the mountain was named Xuefeng (Snow Peak). After the Master took up residence on the mountain, he once composed a verse:
"Time passes with such rapidity, a mere fleeting moment; In this floating world, how can one dwell for long?

When I left the ridges, I had reached thirty-two; Entering Min, I was already well past forty. Though there are other matters not to be neglected, they are raised again and again; What has already passed must still be [reconsidered]."
Gradually he was cleared [of charges]. He reported this to the court officials in their crimson and purple robes, saying: "The King of Yama does not fear those who wear the golden fish [insignia].
Later, Emperor Xizong, having heard of the Master’s reputation for the Way, conferred upon him the title of Great Master Zhenjue and bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya*.
As for Chan Master Deshan Xuanjian: initially he resided in Liyang for nearly thirty years. From the beginning of the Dazhong era, the Magistrate of Wuling, Xue Yanwang...

He founded the Deshan Hermitage and invited [the Master] to reside there, where he extensively propagated the style of his school. In the twelfth month of that year, as he was nearing the end, he said to the assembly:
"To grasp at emptiness and pursue echoes is to weary your mind and spirit. When one awakens from a dream, one realizes it was not real; in the end, what event has actually occurred?
Having spoken, he sat upright and passed away. He was eighty-six years old. His posthumous title was Chan Master Jianxing (Realizing Nature). He had nine Dharma heirs. (Complete Record)
Ye Lüláng Hé Chán composed the "Record of the Hall of Heavenly Kings in Huá'ān County, Fúzhōu. It states briefly: "The longing for one's parents is as vast as the heavens and knows no limit.

To provide them with posthumous blessings, one establishes profound causes. The Grand Officer, Duke of Péngchéng, who served as the Military Commissioner of Fúzhōu, has been away from his native land for many years.
Having encountered a favorable time and attained a position of honor, the sorrow of frost and dew constantly envelops him at dawn."
In the evening, he established a shrine for Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North. As soon as a single chant of pure *brahman* was raised, it was as if one had attained the first bhūmi;

the incense smoke did not dissipate, appearing like a succession of clouds of compassion. He donated land to the lower monastery of Lingyan Temple on Mount Sheng and invited the monk Ju Jian from his own temple to serve as its abbot.
Furthermore, he set aside fifty mu of fields in East Lake to provide for the monks' morning and evening meals in perpetuity.
The necessities for sustaining life were entirely provided without lack. Thereafter, morning and evening, he cultivated reverence, chanting praises and performing rites of repentance;
thus his seat became profound, and the merit for the afterlife thereby attained was truly immeasurable.
Bingxu (7): Chan Master Linji Yixuan.
Having received the Dharma from Huangbo, he returned to his hometown and resided at the Linji Chan Garden.
Disciples flocked to him, but he soon departed due to military unrest. The Grand Marshal Mohe donated his residence to establish a temple and invited the Master to dwell there.
He also took Linji as his head preceptor. Next, he went to Hefu, where the Provincial Governor, Attendant Wang Changshi, shared a spiritual affinity with the Master.
Later, he moved to Xinghua Temple in Taizhou, where he lived in seclusion. Chengguan Jian served him closely, and the Master then transmitted the Dharma to him with this verse:

"If you ask how it is when following the current without ceasing, I tell you it is like boundless true illumination. Free from marks and free from names, no one receives it; Only when you have reached the other shore can you see its source."
"When the hair-cutting blade has been used, it must be sharpened again. In the fourth month of that year, he said to the assembly, "After my passing, you must not extinguish my True Dharma Eye.
Sansheng said, "How would we dare extinguish the Master’s Dharma Eye?
The Master said, "In the future, if someone asks you, what will you say? Sansheng then gave a shout. The Master said, "Who knows my True Dharma Eye?"
"Conceal it! Extinguish it before this blind donkey! Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Huizhao.
He had twenty-one successors to the Dharma, the foremost of whom were Sansheng and Xinghua. The Master once addressed the assembly, saying:
"Upon this ball of red flesh, there is a true person of no station who constantly enters and exits through the gates of the faces of all people. You have not yet realized this."
[The Master] looked on. At that time, a monk asked, "What is the true person of no station? The Master grabbed him and said, "Speak! Speak! The monk hesitated.
The Master pushed him away and said, "What is this 'true person of no station'? It is a dried-up shit-stick! The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"It is better not to engage in activities and to go to a state of non-action. Those who have already set out should not continue; those who have not yet set out should not let go."
Arise! You will then surpass those who have practiced for ten years. All people possess the mind that seeks the Buddha and seeks to escape the three realms.
You, foolish person, also wish to escape; where would you go? A single thought-moment of greed is the desire realm; a single thought-moment of anger is the form realm;
a single thought-moment of delusion is the formless realm. These three realms are fully contained within your own house. This one thought-moment of yours—
The place where the mind comes to rest is called the Bodhi tree; the place where the single thought-moment does not come to rest is called the tree of ignorance.
The Master further said: "Followers of the Way, you must first recognize these four kinds of signless realms, so as to avoid being struck down by external conditions."
In a single thought-moment, when the mind is characterized by attachment, it is submerged by water; in a single thought-moment, when the mind is characterized by anger, it is burned by fire;

in a single thought-moment, when the mind is characterized by doubt, it is obstructed by earth; in a single thought-moment, when the mind is characterized by joy, it is blown away by wind. If one can discern in this way, one will not be overcome by external objects, but will employ objects everywhere:
surging in the east and sinking in the west, surging at the edges and sinking in the center. This is because one has realized that the four great elements are like dreams and illusions.
Dinghai (the eighth year), the Great Master Xuansha Zongyi Shibei of Fuzhou. A native of Min, his surname was Xie. His father made his living as a fisherman;
one night, while crossing the river by boat, he fell into the water. Xuansha rowed toward him to rescue him, and upon seeing the moon reflected in the water, he said:

A predecessor once said: "All dharmas are like the moon reflected in water. If one were to kill [a parent] while they were still alive, it would only increase their suffering in the three miserable realms.
Now that they can no longer be saved, one may repay their kindness by renouncing worldly ties and leaving the home life.

Thereupon, he entered the presence of a master and received full ordination. Wearing coarse hemp robes and straw sandals, and taking only enough food to sustain his breath, he sat in meditation all day long with Xuefeng.
Master Yicun approached him, and their minds were in accord through the Way of teacher and disciple. Xuefeng, because of his ascetic practices, called him "Preparer the Dhūta.
Once, carrying his bag, he set out over the mountain ridges, intending to travel throughout all quarters. Suddenly, upon reaching a steep and perilous place, he stubbed his toe;
blood flowed and it was painful. He sighed and said, "This body is not something that exists. From where does this pain come? This body is suffering. It ended there.
In the end, there was no birth. Rest, rest! Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land; the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven.

From this point on, he returned to the peaks of Mount Gong and joined forces with Xuefeng in their construction of the monastery. Disciples of the profound Way flocked to him. The Master entered the inner chamber to seek resolution, never flagging from morning until night.
Furthermore, he studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and realized the mind-ground. Consequently, his responses to the needs of others were swift and nimble, and he [assisted] Xiu...
The *Taraming* (Dhāraṇī) rite was such that whenever scholars from various regions encountered points they could not resolve, they would invariably seek instruction from him.
Even when engaging in rigorous debate with Xuefeng, he never shied away from taking the lead. Xuefeng remarked, "Bai the Dhūta is a man who has returned for a second birth.

Later, he suddenly dreamed one night that his father came to thank him, saying, "Because you have left home to become a monk, I have been reborn in heaven; thus I have come to inform you. (*Tongming ji*)... and so forth.
(5 Lamps). Wuzi (9):
Chan Master Jingcen of Changsha.
Initially, he resided at Lüyuan as its first patriarch; subsequently, he lived without a fixed location.

He merely followed conditions to engage with others and preached the Dharma according to requests; thus, the assembly of that time called him "The Master of Changsha. He once addressed the assembly, saying:
"If I were to exclusively exalt the teachings and the tradition, the weeds in the Dharma Hall would grow ten feet deep.
Having no choice, I tell you: the entire world of the ten directions is the eye of the śramaṇa; the entire world of the ten directions is the whole of the śramaṇa."
The body—throughout the entirety of the ten directions of the world—is within one’s own radiance.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time together with the sentient beings of the ten dharma realms are this light of *mahāprajñā*. Yangshan asked, "Everyone possesses this matter, yet they simply cannot use it.
The Master said, "Precisely; I ask you to use it. Yangshan asked, "How does one use it? The Master then kicked Yangshan down.
Shan said, "Right now he is like a great tiger. Consequently, the world named him "Cen the Great Tiger. In that year, he passed away.
In the third month of the Jichou year (1049), when Chan Master Dongshan Jia was about to pass away, he said to the assembly: "After leaving this shell-and-leak vessel, where shall I go?"
"Come to the place where I shall meet you. The assembly had no reply. Thereupon, he shaved his head and donned the robes, remaining in profound stillness.

At that time, more than a thousand disciples wailed and lamented for a long while. The Master suddenly opened his eyes and said, "As for those who have left the household life, their minds do not cling to things."

"This is true cultivation: exhausting life and resting death. What room is there for sorrow? He then summoned the administrative monk and ordered him to prepare a single midday meal for the 'foolish' (the deceased), thereby rebuking his disciples for their lingering attachment to worldly emotions.
When the seventh day arrived and the provisions were finally ready, the Master joined the assembly for the meal.
After it was finished, he addressed the assembly again, saying: 'In the monastic life, when there is no business at hand—especially on the occasion of a departure—one must not allow clamor.'"
He moved. The next day, after his bath, he sat upright and passed away. He was sixty-three years old. His posthumous title was Chan Master Wuben (Awakening to the Source).

The Master skillfully opened up the five ranks (*wuwei*) and adeptly received those of the three capacities (*sangen*). He extensively expounded the single sound (*yiyin*) and widely propagated it for the myriad species.

Horizontally drawing his precious sword, he cut through the dense forest of various views; wondrously harmonizing with the great penetration, he severed the myriad ends of forced interpretation. Furthermore, he obtained Cao Shan Benji.
The profound intent was clearly realized, and the subtle teaching was further developed. The Way harmonized ruler and minister through the interplay of the biased and the orthodox.
Thus, the mystical wind of Dongshan spread throughout the world; consequently, all quarters honored it as the Caodong School.
As for Chan Master Yuan of Guishan in Ningde, Fuzhou: he first studied under Master Mo of Wuxie and later resided at Guishan, serving as its second patriarch.
In this year, he entered parinirvāṇa at the age of seventy-eight; he was posthumously titled Great Master Xingkong.
In the year Gengyin (the eleventh month), the Chancellor Pei Xiu passed away.
His courtesy name was Gongmei. When he first served as the Regional Inspector of Hongzhou, [he encountered] the eminent monk Huangbo.

At some point, he attained realization through the master’s words and was subsequently invited into the governor’s residence, where he was questioned on the Dharma morning and evening. Later, when the governor was stationed in Xuanzhou, he again ordered him to accompany him.
Through this, he profoundly penetrated the source of the Dharma. Furthermore, his karmic affinity with Chan Master Guifeng Mi was especially deep.

During the Dazhong era, he served as a high-ranking official for six years and subsequently held various regional military governorships. He passed away at the age of seventy-four. As for the Master’s character:
He was refined and possessed a strict and upright character. Emperor Xuanzong once remarked, "This is truly a man of the Confucian scholar type.

In his daily life, he abstained from wine and meat and often wore coarse woolen robes. He would enter the quarters of singing girls with his alms bowl to beg for food, considering himself untainted by worldly passions and thus fit to preach the Dharma for others.
He was particularly skilled at composing prose and authored tens of thousands of words of Buddhist literature. His...
He composed the Preface to the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, the Preface to the *Huayan Dharmadhātu Contemplation*, and the *Exhortation to Generate the Bodhicitta*.
Although there have been authors in later generations, none have been able to surpass him. He also composed the *Verses on the Transmission of the Mind*, which are recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu*.
Furthermore, he wrote the *Preface to the Guifeng Treatises on the Source of Chan*, which is particularly clear and subtle. On the eleventh month, the Emperor’s birthday, he summoned two...
A wandering monk entered the palace to preach the Way; the Emperor was delighted and bestowed purple robes upon ten men, including Tanyuan (Tongji).
Chan Master Jia Shan Shanhui initially resided at Jingkou in Runzhou. When Daowu encountered him while ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the Dharma-body?
The Master said, "The Dharma-body has no form. [The monk asked,] "What is the Dharma-eye? [The Master said,] "The Dharma-eye has no flaw. Daowu was struck dumb.
[The Master] laughed. The Teacher requested me to explain it for him. I pointed toward Huating and told him to go to where Chuanzhi was. The Teacher went to Huating, and because Chuanzhi asked him:
"A fishing line hangs down a thousand feet; its intent lies in the deep pool. It is three inches away from the hook—why do you not speak?

The Teacher prepared to open his mouth, and Chuanzhi struck him with his oar, knocking him into the water. Just as he climbed back onto the boat, Chuanzhi said again: "Speak! Speak! [As the Teacher prepared to speak...]

The Master opened his mouth. The boatman struck him again. The Master had an awakening and nodded his head. The boatman said, "I have fished through the waves of the river until at last I encountered the golden-scaled fish.
The Master covered his ears. The boatman said, "So it is, so it is. From now on, you must leave no trace where you hide yourself;
do not hide yourself where there are no traces. After this, you must not stay in cities, walled towns, or villages. Go only to the deep..."
"By the mattock in the mountains, I have taken up one or half of another. When the Master was about to depart, he looked back repeatedly.

The Boatman raised his oar and said, "You thought there was something else. Thereupon, he capsized his boat and went away into the water. After the Master settled there, his reputation spread, and students flocked to him from all sides.
At this time, the assembly at Hai chose Jia Shan as their site; soon a monastery was established, where the Dharma was widely proclaimed.
(Recorded in the *Wudeng huiyuan*).
In the fifth month of the twelfth year of the Xinmao cycle,
the Emperor visited An Guosi Temple and bestowed upon National Teacher Zhixuan a precious throne made of agallochum and sandalwood, over twenty feet in height.

It was exceptionally rare and magnificent. His surname was Chen, and he was popularly known as "Cen Pusa" (Chen Bodhisattva). He had mastered the three studies (*trīṇi śikṣāṇi*) through and through, and his reputation eclipsed that of his contemporaries;

his miraculous deeds were particularly numerous. At that time, the palace held a midday vegetarian feast for ten thousand monks daily, and the Emperor himself performed the *saṃgīti* (hymns and chants).

The Chancellor Xiao Fang remonstrated, saying: "The Dharma of India involves severing worldly attachments to attain extinction; it is not something for an emperor to personally practice. How much more so regarding the Buddha?"
"It is to be grasped through awakening; it cannot be sought through signs. Although the Emperor did not accept [this advice], he nevertheless praised its excellence (Tang History).
○ Chan Master Daowu Jin of Dongshan attained the essential meaning from Master Jia. When Master Jia passed away, the assembly requested him to succeed him as abbot.
The multitude of disciples were delighted and submitted to his leadership, and the profound tradition was not allowed to decline.
In the *wuchen* year (the thirteenth year), Chan Master Daoying first visited Dongshan and attained realization of the fundamental principle.

Once, referring to Nanquan’s remark that "there is no Maitreya above in heaven and no Maitreya below in the earth," the Master asked Dongshan: "There is no Maitreya above in heaven; [below in the earth...]"
"There is no Maitreya. When asked who had bestowed this name upon him, Dongshan was so struck that his meditation seat shook.
Later, while staying in a hermitage at Sanfeng, he did not attend the hall for ten days. Dongshan questioned him about this, and the Master replied, "Every day a celestial deity brings me food.
Dongshan said, "I thought you were a man of realization; it seems you still hold such a view. That evening, Dongshan...
The Master was summoned by the Abbot of Shaoying. The Master responded with an assent. The Abbot asked, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil, what is this?
The Master returned to his hermitage and sat in silent meditation. The celestial deity could not find him for three days until he finally passed away. The Master had initially resided at Sanfeng.
Although his transformation of others had not yet spread widely, he came once every month to visit Pujia.

Pujia rebuked him for not having forgotten worldly attachments, saying that this was a distraction from the Way, and urged him to go out into the various directions to receive people. Thereupon, he burned down his hermitage and left Haihun.

He ascended the western ridge of Mount Lu on the Oufu plateau—a world-renowned and sublime landscape—where he built a dwelling by binding together trees among the trees. He named it Yunju (Cloud Dwelling), and monastics followed him there as well.
They gathered through seeking; having been scattered among the mountains and beneath the trees, they eventually formed a thatched shelter.
He preached the Dharma beneath it, and by this time, it had become a formal dharma assembly with a following of one thousand five hundred disciples (from the *Wudeng Huiyuan*).
Master Youzhang saw Master Teng Teng of Jiangling and said, "Go to Tiantai and seek a quiet place to dwell. When you encounter peace, then ascend. Zhang arrived at Tiantai.
Tai established Fudang Monastery in Jing’an County; Fu and Teng were his two disciples. Furthermore, he resided at Yinlong Monastery (according to the *Sengbao zhuan*).

In the third month of the year Guisi (the fourteenth year of the Xiántóng era), an imperial edict was issued for the monks of the two monastic districts to welcome the Buddha’s relics from Fǎmén Monastery in Fèngxiáng.

Although a great many ministers offered remonstrances, the Emperor said: "If I am able to see them while alive, I shall have no regrets even in death. He then commissioned the extensive construction of precious canopies, incense-carved boxes, banners, and parasols.

All were adorned with gold, pearls, brocades, and embroidery; the magnificence of the ceremonial escort surpassed even that of the suburban sacrifices. During the Yuanhe era, it had not reached such heights for a long time.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, [the image] was welcomed to the capital. Colorful pavilions lined the roads, and the Emperor ascended the Anfu Gate tower to receive and prostrate before it.
It was then ushered into the inner chapel. After three days, it departed, and an imperial edict was issued to bestow gifts upon all the temples within the capital.
The monks of the two streets were bestowed with gold and silk, and the elders of the capital were all generously rewarded.

In every village and hamlet through which he passed, people gathered earth to erect stupas that lined the roads. Drums were beaten and conchs blown day and night. He issued an edict, saying: "By my meager virtue..."
Having succeeded to the great enterprise, for fourteen years I have occupied the throne with anxiety and diligence, cherishing and nourishing all living beings.

I have thus honored and exalted the Buddhist teachings, regarding the Profound Gate as most weighty; I have invited the True Body [of the Buddha] to pray for the blessing of the common people. Now, the crowds who come to behold it block the roads and crossroads.

As I repeatedly reflect upon the prisons and the fetters, my thoughts remain fixed on them day and night. Alas! My subjects are fallen into the snares of punishment and legal retribution; how much more so...
As the summer heat intensified, those bound in fetters throughout the capital and the various provinces of the empire were each commuted from the death penalty by one degree.
In the seventh month, the Emperor passed away. The Xizong Emperor ascended the throne; in the fourth month of the following year, he issued an edict to send the Buddha’s bone back to Fengxiang.
The elderly citizens of the capital came to bid farewell, all weeping with choked voices and streaming tears.
In the Jiawu year of Emperor Xizong (the first year of the Qiánfú era), Master Ān of Luopu was initially the attendant to Linji. Linji frequently praised him, saying: "Under the gate of Linji..."
"A single arrow—who dares to face its point? Having taken his leave of Jie, Jie praised him as "a single red-tailed carp.

After traveling everywhere, he went straight to the summit of Jia Shan and built a hermitage there, remaining for many years. When Jia Shan learned of this, he composed a letter and dispatched a monk to deliver it.
The Master received him and sat down immediately. The monk turned back and reported this. Jia Shan said, "This monk has been studying the books; he will surely come within three days.
If he has not studied the books, this man cannot be saved. Indeed, after three days, the monk arrived. As soon as he saw Jia Shan, he stood with his hands joined in *añjali*.
Jia Shan said, "A rooster nesting in a phoenix’s nest—it is no match for its kind. Get out! The Master said, "He came from afar to hasten toward [the truth]."
Feng requested, "I beg the Master for a single encounter. Deshan said, "Before my eyes there is no *śrāmaṇera*;
here there is no old monk. Feng then gave a shout. Deshan said, "Wait, wait! Do not be so hasty and precipitate. The clouds and moon are the same; the streams and mountains are each different.
It is not that you cannot cut off the tongues of everyone in the world, but how will you, *śrāmaṇera*, cause a tongueless person to speak? Feng stood there lost in thought.
The Mountain Master (Shishuang Qingzhu) struck him; the Master [Dongshan Liangjie] served him in devotion for several years.
In the year Yiwu (835), the third patriarch of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou, Chan Master Hongyin, first studied under Guishan Zongmi and thereby awakened to the profound essence. From then on—

In the seventh year of the Xiántóng era, he resided at Jìngshān, where his Dharma path flourished greatly. In the ninth month of the fourth year of the Guǎnghuà era, he passed away before the assembly.
He was later posthumously titled Dàshī Fǎjì (Great Master Fǎjì). A monk asked, "What is it like when it is like frost and like snow?
The Master said, "It is still defilement. The monk asked, "What is it like when there is no defilement? The Master said, "Not of the same color."

In the third year, the year Bingshen (796), the Venerable Dao-wu of Guannan in Xiangzhou first visited Master Daochang, whereupon he received confirmation of his understanding. He subsequently visited Deshan, and his realization of the flavor of the Dharma became even more profound.
Whenever he ascended the hall to instruct his disciples, he wore a lotus-patterned hat, donned a monastic robe, and held a ritual tablet while striking [the wooden fish].
He played the drum and the flute, and would call out, "Master Lu Sanlang. At times he would say, "I beat the drum of Guannan and sing the song of Deshan.
At other times, he would take a wooden sword, rest it across his shoulder, and dance, greatly propagating the spirit of the ancestral school.
In the Dingyou year (the fourth year; Huang Chao was raiding Henan, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang), there was an elder from Muzhou named Daoming.
Having first traveled as a wandering monk, he attained the essential meaning under Huangbo.

He subsequently resided at Guanyin Monastery for several decades, where his community regularly numbered over a hundred. Later, he left the assembly and lived in a room at Kaiyuan Temple, where he constantly made mats.
He made sandals and secretly distributed them along the roads; sometimes he would sell sandals to support his elderly mother.

People of the time called him "Chen the Sandal-Maker. Once, the troops of Qiu Fu arrived at the city. The Master placed a large straw sandal at the city gate; when Qiu Fu intended to discard it, he exerted all his strength but could not lift it.
He then sighed, saying, "Muzhou has a great sage. We shall abandon the city and depart," and he did not dare enter again.
Because of this, the people were spared from the turmoil of military incursions and banditry. Master Ji was stern and urgent; those who approached him for instruction were few.

Only Yunmen alone attained accord with the Master’s intent, and he was ordered to succeed Xuefeng. One day, the Master suddenly summoned the assembly, saying, "The conditions here have come to an end;
I shall now depart. He then sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. He was ninety-eight years old, having been in the monastic order for seventy-six years.
In the year Wuxu (the fifth year;
Huang Chao had occupied Fujian), the Monk Luohan of Zhangzhou first attained enlightenment under Guannan. He often sang songs, one of which runs roughly as follows:
A mass of doubt within the mind was like a large wicker basket. When I met the Master, he struck me squarely in the chest with a single blow.

Startled, the delusional mass dispersed like a startled monkey falling from a tree; I looked up and saw the sun newly full. From that moment on, I have been steady and firm, remaining perpetually joyful to this very day.
I hear only my belly growling with fullness; no longer do I go east or west to carry the alms bowl. Furthermore, a verse: Within the universe...
A guest in leisure; among men, acting as a wild monk. Let others laugh at me as they please; wherever I am, I remain carefree and self-satisfied.

In the year Jihai (the sixth year, when Huang Chao ravaged Guangnan, Jinghu, Jianghuai), Chan Master Huiji of Yangshan first visited Mount Gui (Weishan) and attained realization of the fundamental principle. He served [his master] for fifteen years; whatever he said...
His sayings all became models for later generations. While he was leading the assembly at Wangmang Mountain, one day his meditation seat sank into the earth.
A terrestrial deity informed him that this mountain was no longer fit for the Master’s residence, and that there was a great Yangshan to the southeast.
It was truly a blessed land for humanity. He subsequently moved his residence to Mount Yangshan.

In the year Gengzi (the first year of Guangming; it was during this time that Huang Chao captured the Eastern Capital and Tongguan, the imperial court fled, and in the twelfth month, Chao occupied the capital, proclaimed the state of Da Qi, and established the era name Jintong), Master Datong of Touzi Mountain in Shuzhou encountered the chaos and ruin of the empire. One day, there was a madman who, holding—
At Renshan, the Master preached the Dharma according to the needs of the occasion. When the ringleader heard this, he prostrated himself, cast off his robes, offered them as a gift, and departed.
Chan Master Zong of Zihu resided at Zihu preaching the Dharma for forty-five years.
In that year, he passed away peacefully without illness at the age of eighty-one.
In the year Xinchou (the first year of Zhonghe), Emperor Xizong fled to Shu.
The princes and members of the imperial clan all went into hiding. Chan Master Pumen of Longhu was the third son of Emperor Xizong;
he cut off his hair and wandered away, eventually visiting Shishuang Qianzhu. As Qianzhu spoke with him, he marveled at his extraordinary nature and said: "You have..."
"By the power of his vows he has come; he was born into a royal family, yet he left his station to follow me—he is like a lotus blooming from within the fire.

Hearing this, [Nanyue] entered the room at night and asked about the matter of the Patriarchs' separate transmission. Nanyue said, "Wait until Mount An nods its head, and I shall tell you. Thereupon, the Master attained realization.

He remained in attendance for several years and then requested permission to travel extensively among the famous mountains. Nanyue said, "When you meet a dry place, stop there; when you encounter Chen, stay."

He stayed there and traveled far away, passing through Shaowu and arriving at Daqian. Gazing from afar at the mountain peak, which was lush, profound, and beautiful, he asked the elders, "Is there anyone living there?
The elder replied, "There is one named Chen Si who has long been in seclusion within it.

Realizing that this was what his master had meant, he immediately cleared a path through the grass and reached the mountain. As soon as Chen Si saw him, he shared his seat with him and lived together; subsequently, he requested vegetables [for them].
He planted seeds with the hope of reaping bushels and pecks. His son said, "How could there be any bushels or pecks? and gave him a single handful.
Thereupon, he entered the mountains to clear land and sow. Later, the people of the valley mouth said to one another, "The monk who entered the mountains the other day has not come out since;
he must have been devoured by a tiger. They went to look and saw a thatched hut where several practitioners were giving orders and receiving responses from many others.

Amidst the overlapping ridges and layered peaks, the vegetables have already turned green. It appears that those who tilled the soil and sowed the seeds were actually mountain deities, and the traveler was a tiger.
Master Chen Sijue, praising the excellence of the Way, said: "While I lived here, I constantly suffered from the abundance of predatory beasts and venomous insects;
now that you have arrived, they have all vanished. Your virtue and morality are beyond my reach. This is due to the conditions created by these five types of offerings."
"Is he one who belongs to the Duke? Having finished speaking, he vanished with a whirring sound. Today, the site where Chen Sian lived remains on this mountain at Baocheng Chan Monastery;

it is the foundation of the thatched cottage from the days of Yuanjue. On the seventh day of the eleventh month, Chan Master Hui of Jia Shan took his leave of the assembly, saying, "Each of you must protect yourselves well.
At the hour of the rat (midnight), he passed away suddenly. He was seventy-seven years of age.
He was posthumously titled Great Master Zhuanming, and his stupa was named Yongji. After Jia Shan passed away, the assembly appointed Lupu An as the next abbot.
Shortly thereafter, he moved to Mount Lupu in Liyang, where he remained in seclusion for ten years. Later, he relocated to Suxi in Langzhou.
Seekers of the profound flocked to him.
In the second year (Ren-yin), when grain in Chang’an was thirty strings of cash per bushel and Zhong Chuan held Jiangxi, the Emperor fled from the Chao rebels and took refuge in Chengdu.
He dispatched the Censor Guo Zun, carrying an imperial edict, to summon National Teacher Zhixuan.
He proceeded to the imperial encampment for an audience, where he was greatly pleased [by the Emperor]. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title National Teacher Wuda (Wudaguo-shi).
At that time, Chan Master Jiuxing Xuan was residing in Yuzhang. King Zhong of Nanping treated him with the etiquette of a disciple, serving as his master by facing north toward him.
The King purchased Mount Moshan for him and constructed a monastery named Longji to welcome him; students flocked there in droves.
In the Gui-mao year (the third year; Li Ke-yong defeated Huang Chao and restored the capital), National Teacher Zhixuan was returning to Jiulong from the Chengdu temporary palace.
Suddenly, while in a state of meditative concentration, he saw a Bodhisattva touch the crown of his head and comfort him.
Shortly thereafter, a pearl entered his left thigh, swelling up with such intensity that the pain was extreme; upon it appeared the character "Zhao."

Two characters were mistaken. Xuánzhī, having recognized his long-standing karmic debt, lay down on his right side and passed away (the world calls Zhīxuán the reincarnation of the Han dynasty’s Yuán Àng;
Àng had a rift with Cáo [Tàoyīng]. See *Tōnglùn*). In the tenth month, Chán Master Dà'ān of Fúzhōu announced his passing. The Master had transformed through great teaching for over twenty years;
he was posthumously titled Yuánzhì.
In the Jiachen year (the fourth year; Li Kuyong pursued Huang Chao and slew him), there was famine and pestilence in eastern Zhejiang.
Chan Master Youzhang collected and buried several thousand remains in the three prefectures of Wenzhou, Taizhou, and Mingzhou.
Regarding the one known as the Great Being of Increased Compassion: The monk Huisheng of Fakuang Monastery in Wenzhou built a thatched hut on the northern cliff.
He once transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* with such profound devotion that, upon reaching the "Chapter on the Encouragement of Samantabhadra," two śarīras fell from the sky like rain.

The local administration reported this to the court, which granted the monastery the title "Samantabhadra Repentance Monastery. During the Xiangfu era, its name was changed to its current one (*Yongning bian*).
In the year Yisi (the first year of the Guangqi era; in the third month the Emperor returned to the capital;

in the twelfth month, amidst military chaos, the Emperor fled to Fengxiang), Chan Master Lingyun Qin was originally at Mount Guiyang. Having attained enlightenment upon seeing peach blossoms, Mount Guiyang approved his realization.

By this time, he had returned to Minchuan, where disciples gathered like spokes converging on a hub. He subsequently visited Xuansha, and after they had exchanged greetings, Xuansha asked, "Where have you come from?"

"It is like this," said Yunyan, and so forth. "It is simply the mulberry and willow trees; there is no other reason. Sandokai said, "Is it here, or not? Yunyan said, "It is always thus. Sandokai said, "Why do you not speak? Yunyan said, "What difficulty is there? Sandokai said, "Then please speak. Yunyan said, [and so forth]. Sandokai said, "Just speak! Yunyan said, [and so forth]. For thirty years I have been a seeker of the sword; how many times have leaves fallen and branches sprouted?

Since the moment I first beheld the peach blossoms, until this very day, I have had no further doubts. Sha said: "How great is your mastery of the 'sanzhi' (the native tree)! You say that what you point toward is certainly not an external thing.
Sha said: "So it is. You say: "I dare not [claim such mastery]. Sha said: "It is perfectly true, most perfectly true. Do you dare?"
Baofu said, "Brother, you have not yet attained thorough penetration. Yunmen said, "That is exactly it, Master; have you attained thorough penetration yet? Baofu said, "Only then can it be so.

Yunmen said, "Throughout antiquity and throughout the present. Baofu said, "Excellent, excellent! He then composed a verse to send to Yunmen, saying: [Verse omitted] Yunmen said, "Excellent, excellent! He then composed a verse to send [in reply], saying: [Verse omitted]
For thirty years it was just as usual; several times when leaves fell, he emitted rays of light.

From this point on, having emerged beyond the clouds and the sky, his perfect voice and essential nature responded to the Dharma King. (In the *Complete Record of Xuansha*, modern people claim that the preceding verse was composed as a verse of awakening upon Lingyun’s seeing peach blossoms;

this is not so. It is because after Lingyun attained awakening and returned to his hometown, he produced this verse when meeting Xuansha. Furthermore, at the time of their meeting, the phrasing and nuances were such as these; what is recorded in the current *Transmission of the Lamp* is incomplete, and later generations cannot help but [question] it.)

Regarding those who engage in groundless criticism, I have therefore recorded them here in detail. The *Dahui Wuku* states: "In my life, I have been fond of reviling others. However, upon reading the *Recorded Sayings of Xuansha*, I was greatly delighted by his examination of Lingyun. When Xuansha said, 'How perfectly true! How perfectly true!

I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate,' it may be described as standing like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high. Later, when he spoke with Lingyun, he said: 'Only after you have reached such a state will you finally be through; afterwards, however, you will act like this—spitting and urinating. He then asked Yuanwu, 'What do you say? Yuanwu smiled and said:"

"But later on, he acted just like this. I could not understand it either, so I went down and returned to my quarters. Only then did I realize that Xuansha was truly acting strangely. He then recounted this to Yuanguo. Yuanguo laughed and said, "I am glad you have come to understand.
Haitang said, "Nowadays, at most monasteries, there are many who lack this kind of medicine. The Master said, "Be careful that outsiders do not hear such crude talk."
In the sixth month of the Bingwu year (the second year), the Military Governor Xue Zhengji composed the "Record of the Former Causes of Lord Guangping of Mount Lu. It states briefly:

"I have heard that Confucius took Dragon Laozi as his teacher, and Laozi took the Master of Zhugan as his teacher. This Master of Zhugan is none other than Śākyamuni. Although [the traditions of] the Mulberry..."
Though the fields have changed many times, this Way has not perished because its wisdom has spread through transformation.

On Mount Kuang lies Donglin Monastery, founded by the Great Master Huiyuan of the Eastern Jin dynasty. It was there that he established the "Pure Society" (Jingshe) with practitioners from the Western Heaven;
