this is recorded in detail in the historical annals. During the Ren-shen year of the Dazhong era, my late uncle, the Duke of Guangping, once served as the Inspector of Hongzhou.
When Lord An of Qinghe was serving as the Regional Inspector (Mushi) in Jiangzhou, he first established the Prefectural Office (Kaifu). Lord De of Zuo Guangsi followed his example;

following the Huichang era, he restored the former Prefectural Office. Within the inner court, he took the lead in initiating the project, donating three hundred thousand coins for thirty-two large-scale paintings.

Furthermore, he acquired the monasteries of Eastern Lin, Western Lin, and Yiai, along with their gardens and groves from the Ministry of Revenue. Those who came forward to contribute gathered like clouds.
The merit was soon fully realized; this was due to the efforts of the former Marquis of Kaifu. In the year of Xinchou, the realm faced many hardships.
The Duke of Yingchuan came to bring salvation to the eight commanderies, and the Duke of Guangping came to protect the frontier.

In the winter of Jiachen, the clash of arms gradually subsided, providing ample leisure time to visit old acquaintances and causes. Consequently, I read the memorial for the restoration of Donglin Monastery during the Dazhong era, and [proceeded] accordingly.
I examined their names and found them all to be the elite of the court. I wished to re-engrave the records of Master Ji so that those who had contributed would be listed;

yet all these individuals occupy prominent positions, with their grandsons and worthy sons filling their courtyards. Who would have known that every person at Donglin had planted seeds of wholesome fruit?

Thus, I polished the mountain stone and engraved all their names, so that passersby might see them and the achievements of former sages not fall into oblivion. How could this be done merely for the sake of my own family?
...his excellence. Therefore, let us reflect upon him.
In the year Dingwei (the third year;
the royal court was based in Quanzhou), the monk Wei Liang, known as Zhier Na, received the posthumous title Jiekong. He came from Guishan Temple to Changxi in Fuzhou and built a hermitage there.
In front of the Guihu Chan Monastery was a mountain ridge with a lake that rose and fell in accordance with the tides.

Suddenly, a large tortoise appeared, floating and sinking in the lake, wandering and resting about the hermitage. Whenever a monk wished to go somewhere, the tortoise would carry him. The Master saw a starving tiger.
He then cast away his body to feed [the turtle]. The turtle transformed into stone, the hermitage was overgrown with weeds, and the lake likewise submerged it.
Later generations abandoned the site of the old hermitage for the present temple, which has flourished there until now (*Changle ji*). In the fourth month, Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo passed away.
The Master had previously secretly revealed to him the "final word" of Deshan. He later resided at Yantou and said:
The assembly said, "When the old man departs, he will go after letting out one great roar.

Later, when bandits rose up in the Central Plains and everyone fled their lands, the Master remained seated as usual. One day, the thieves arrived and, finding no provisions, proceeded to stab him with their blades.
The Master’s expression remained unmoved; he let out one great cry and passed away. His voice was heard for several tens of *li*. He was sixty-one years old. Hereafter...
The Tang court posthumously conferred upon him the title Great Master Qingyan (Pure and Austere). His successor, Luoshan, was able to perpetuate his lofty legacy.
In the year Wushen (the second month of the first year of Wende; Emperor Wang Jian plundered Xichuan), the Emperor passed away.
Emperor Zhaozong ascended the throne. In the fourth month, Chan Master Shichuang Qingzhu entered nirvana. The Master...
He resided at Shishuang for twenty years. Among his disciples, there were those who practiced long-term sitting meditation without lying down, standing firm like tree stumps;

thus, the world called them the "Dried-Tree Assembly. When Emperor Xizong heard of the Master’s reputation, he once sent an envoy to bestow upon him purple robes, but the Master firmly declined and would not accept them.
He lived to the age of eighty-two and was posthumously titled Grand Master Puhui. His stupa was named Jianxiang (alternatively, it is said he passed away in the second month).
In the fifth month, Chan Master Chunan of Qianqing Mountain in Hangzhou passed away suddenly after bidding farewell to the assembly.

Having received the essential teaching from Huangbo, the Master first arrived at Ba’en Temple in Gusu, where he practiced meditative concentration with great diligence for over twenty years without crossing the threshold of his quarters.
He subsequently resided at Bailin, Zhijian, and Ciyun; although he responded to the needs of others without weariness, he always maintained a solemn and dignified demeanor.
He remained in meditative absorption for either a month or ten days at a time. During the Guangqi era, the King of Qian invited him down from the mountain to receive offerings.

Emperor Zhaozong, having heard of his spiritual transformation, bestowed upon him purple robes. He lived to the age of seventy-six. The Master composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Refuting Heresies), which circulates in the world.
Lungu Yuanjue Chan Master resided in the mountains for several years, eating wild fruits and drinking mountain water. He once encountered a perilous situation...
He sat upon a cedar tree by the roadside and surveyed the strategic terrain. He cast his mendicant’s staff once;
wherever it came to rest, he immediately constructed halls and pavilions. Soon, his virtue and wisdom spread far and wide, and monastics gathered like clouds until it became a great monastery.
Suddenly, an old man knelt and entreated him, saying, "I am a dragon who has made my home on this mountain. Because I have failed in my duty of bringing rain, I have been sent up to heaven."
"There is one who deserves the death penalty; I pray you grant him protection. The Master said, "You have offended the High God; how can I exert my power on your behalf?
Nevertheless, you may come here after changing your form. He was suddenly transformed into a small snake, which the Master then drew into a pure water jar using his mendicant’s staff.

After a long while, wind and thunder shook the meditation platform, and the mountains and peaks trembled. The Master sat in meditation until dawn; when the heavens cleared and the sky was bright, a snake emerged from the jar.

After a short time, it resumed the form of an old man and thanked him, saying: "Had it not been for your reliance on the power of the Dharma, this place would have been defiled by the stench of my flesh and blood.
There is no way to repay your kindness. However, there is no water in the mountains; how can you settle the assembly? I shall—"
He used water to extend the master’s site of practice. He went to the source at the end of a steep valley and scraped the rock to form a cavity.

A spring gushed forth in a single pool; though it began as a mere trickle, it eventually overflowed until it became a lake. It now lies halfway up the mountain. The name "Dragon Lake" (Longhu) likely originated from this.
It does not freeze in the bitter cold and does not run dry in great droughts. Its waters flow out in four directions to irrigate the fields.
It covers several hundred *qǐng*. The local people regard it as divine and have erected a shrine upon it, where they offer sacrifices during the seasonal festivals.

Now, on the occasion of the *Shangyuan* festival—which coincides with the Master’s birthday—the dragon invariably comes to pay its respects, accompanied by responses of auspicious clouds and auspicious vapors.

Consequently, the local people have turned even more toward the Master; the wealthy contribute their wealth and the poor contribute their labor, and thus a multi-storied pavilion has been completed to the right of the monastery.
Fifteen *li* away was the temple of the Sui Dynasty’s Governor of Ōyō, Ginyō, who is now the King Fuzen.
The offerings at this shrine had continued for over two hundred and seventy years by that time. The deity was exceedingly efficacious, bestowing both calamity and fortune upon the region;

the people revered him with such awe that not a day passed without the offering of sacrificial animals and ritual feasts. When Saichō saw this, he felt compassion for them. One day, he set out on foot, staff in hand, to visit the site.
At the shrine, he spoke a verse to reveal his intent and told him: "To awaken to the Way is like death; within death, life is not forgotten.
The tiger submits through non-action; when people come, they are subdued by grace. Killing for sacrifices brings the calamity of ten thousand kalpas of saṃsāra.

To repay the path of humans and devas, the merit of the Unobstructed Feast is most powerful. If you wish to plant the seeds of future birth, in this life you must have sufficient provisions. When he arrived—
The local people were struck with awe and wonder. He observed the fasts and exhorted the Great King, saying, "In years past you were in hell; today you have become a heavenly being.
He further made a covenant with him, saying, "If you can eat vegetarian food and uphold the precept against killing, then we may be neighbors.

That evening, the elders of the village dreamed that a deity said to them, "I have now received the precepts from the Meditation Master. I shall no longer consume offerings of blood. My sacrifices should henceforth be conducted in this manner."

"The Master’s meal is sufficient. Thereupon, he replaced the offerings of blood with pure vegetarian delicacies; this practice has been observed until today, and spirits and men dwell in mutual peace.
From then on, the deity manifested miraculous signs and protected this mountain. Some say that the Master once contended for victory with the deity through the power of the Way.
Beside the temple was a pine tree with a massive trunk reaching to the heavens; the Master raised his hand and snapped it down, circling the Buddha-ground three times.
The deity truly brushed away the two [disciples]. They subsequently yielded and followed him. Vice-Director Huang Lü composed a poem sent to the monk, saying:
"Once at Longhu, I discussed with Youmin (Wang Zeng Youmin), Turning my hands three times beneath the pine branches brushing the ground. Moved by this, I still eat only vegetables today;
Hearing of your solitary purity, I wish to follow and study under you. Later, there was a monk named Shaoxin who wrote a verse: "The ancient tree, the cold crane..."

Day and night, smoke locks the gates; the numinous wind remains constant as kalpas repeatedly shift. Suddenly reflecting on the events of those years at Yuanjue, we spoke only of causes and did not discuss Chan.
Examining this, it appears that the aforementioned claim is likewise not necessarily so. I now record both versions together.
In the Jiyou year (the first year of Longji, 889 CE), Chan Master Jiupeng Qian had long studied under Shishuang Chu.
When Chu passed away, Qian was serving as his attendant; the assembly then requested him to lead the community.
Zuò succeeded various abbots. While they were discussing the succession, Xuánqián addressed the assembly, saying, "It is not yet appropriate;

one must clarify the meaning of our former master before proceeding. The assembly asked, "What was the former master’s intent? Xuánqián said, "It is like this: 'Rest! Cease! A single thought for ten thousand years!

An incense burner in an ancient temple! How do you understand this? Zuò replied, "This clarifies matters on the side of 'one color' (monochromatic unity). Xuánqián said: [This is where the text ends.]

Foguan Qian did not understand the late master’s intent. The Head Seat burned incense and said, "If I had understood the late master’s intent, my body would have cast off its life as soon as the smoke vanished.
Otherwise, the smoke will die out and I shall not be able to depart. As he finished speaking, he passed away.

Qian patted his back and said, "To sit and die, or to stand and die, is not equal to the Head Seat; yet I still do not understand the late master’s intent. Qian then established a mourning hut at Puzhao.
He gathered at the side of the stupa and departed after three years. He practiced walking meditation beneath Mount Moshan and resided at Chongfu Temple.

On the fifteenth day of the first month of the gengxu year (the first year of Dàshùn), after the midday meal was concluded, Master Lìchāo of Shànglán in Hóngzhōu struck the bell and sat upright for a long time.
[He] went to visit Chan Master Caoshan Benji. Initially, he resided at Mount Cao in Fuzhou; later, he resided at Mount Heyu.
At both monastic seats, students gathered like clouds. The lineage of Dongshan reached its peak of prosperity during the time of this master.

[The temple of] Dayun Monastery in Wenzhou had been abolished due to the regulations of the Huichang era; now, the eminent monk Hongchu submitted a petition to the Regional Inspector Zhu Dan, requesting its restoration.

He established Dayun Temple and reported the matter to the Emperor, requesting that the characters "Zhujin" (Wearing Brocade by Day) be added to the temple’s plaque. The imperial decree granted his request.
When Chan Master Chu recited the sutras and preached the Dharma, lotuses grew upon the dry land and a numinous serpent listened to the teaching.
Later, the Prefect Qian Yuangui constructed the Chu Shi Hall. During the Qingtai era, a tall pagoda was erected there.

In the second year of the Xinhai cycle (851), when Yang Xingmi occupied Yangzhou and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wu, Chan Master Huiji of Mount Yangshan one day saw a strange monk arrive through the air. The monk prostrated and stood before him.

The Master asked, "Where have you recently departed from? The monk replied, "I left Western Heaven this morning. The Master said, "Why so late? The monk replied, "I was traveling through the mountains."

[The monk] was playing with water. The Master said, "As for supernatural powers and wondrous functions, you, Venerable Sir, are superior; as for the Buddha-dharma, it must be returned to this old monk.
[The monk] replied, "I came specifically to the Eastern Land to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, yet I have instead encountered a 'lesser Śākyamuni.

He then took out a *pattraka* leaf from West India, paid obeisance to the Master, and ascended into the sky upon a cloud, departing. The Master also once addressed the assembly, saying: "For now, let us set aside matters concerning the Holy One..."
Settle the mind; simply turn toward the ocean of one's own nature and practice according to reality. The three insights and six supernatural powers are merely the peripheral matters of the sages.
For now, you must recognize the mind and reach the root. Once the root is attained, do not worry about the branches; they will naturally be possessed at a later time.
If you have not yet attained the root, even if you apply your emotions and study others, you will not succeed. Have you not seen?
Guishan said: "When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed; when phenomena and principle are non-dual, one is the Buddha of Suchness.
Previously, the Master had given this verse in advance: "At the age of seventy-seven, today I grow old; following my nature, I drift and sink, with both hands clasping my bent knees.
At that time, at Dongping, he passed away with both hands embracing his knees. An imperial edict posthumously conferred upon him the title Zhizheng (Wisdom-Verification).
He visited Master Tong; the master’s extraordinary traces and his prophetic records are fully preserved in the *Shanben Shilu* (Record of the Mountain Monastery).
Regarding Chan Master Guangyong of the South Pagoda: initially, he served Yangshan at Shiting, where Yangshan pointed to him and said to others, "This man is a Buddha in flesh."
He was capable of transforming others. After Seokjeong passed away, he burned his third finger as an offering to the Dharma, and then burned his second finger as an offering to his parents.
This was in the year of Renzi (the first year of Gyeongbok).
The Great Master Chongfu Huiri of Guanhuan in Putian County, Quanzhou, was originally named Wenju.
He served as a jailer in the county prison and frequently visited Shenguang Lingguan and Da'an of Xiyuan. Later, he went to the Chan Master Wansui Tantong to have his hair shaved;
however, he did not don the *kāṣāya* nor receive full ordination, wearing instead a sash made of various colored fabrics. He subsequently returned to Lingguan.
The Master was instructed to go and pay respects at the West Courtyard. Carrying a green bamboo staff, he entered the Dharma Hall of the West Courtyard.
When An Dai saw him, he smiled and said, "Go to the Nirvana Hall. The Master wheeled his bamboo staff and entered. At that time, there were about five hundred monks suffering from an epidemic;
as the Master touched them one by one with his staff, each rose immediately upon being touched. The King of Min treated him with great reverence and established [a monastery for him].
He resided at Guohuan Chan Monastery. Later, many miraculous traces appeared there. He passed away during the Qianning era (894–898). [The year] Gui-chou (the second year of Jingfu, 893):

[At this time, the Wang dynasty occupied Fuzhou and styled itself "Left Protector"; Wang Rong led the armies of Zhending and styled himself "Prince Zhao"; Qian Liu occupied Zhexi and styled himself "King Wu"; and Zhao Rencong served as the Regional Commander of Lulong in Youzhou and styled himself "King Yan"].

Chan Master Zhaozhou Congshen first studied under Nanquan and attained the essential meaning of the Way. Later, he returned to the northern lands, where the assembly invited him to reside at the ancient monastery of Guanyin in Zhaozhou.
His reputation for the Way spread far and wide. One day, the Prince of Yan led his army to the borders of the prefecture of Zhen, intending to seize the city of Zhao.
A diviner of vapors remarked, "There must be a sage residing in Zhaozhou; you will certainly not win the battle."

Consequently, Yan and Zhao entered into peaceful relations. Hearing that Chan Master Shen of Guanyin Monastery possessed clear and penetrating insight into the Way, the two kings considered this to be a divine omen.
One day, they ordered their carriages and went to pay their respects to the Venerable of Zhaozhou. Upon seeing the kings, the Master sat upright and did not rise.

The King of Yan asked, "Between a human king and a Dharma king, which is more honored? The Master said, "Among humans, the human king is honored; within the Dharma, the Dharma king is honored. The King simply acknowledged this and remained silent.
After a long while, the Master asked, "Which one is the Great King who presides over the government? The King of Zhao replied, "I am that one.
The Master said, "This old monk has unworthily occupied a position in the ministry of transformation; I have not had the opportunity to pay my respects. A short while later, the King...
"Please preach the Dharma. The Master said, "Your Majesty has many taboo names. The King said, "Please set aside the taboos and preach the Dharma.
The Master said, "Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, causes sin to be extinguished and merit to arise by the mere utterance of his name once.

Yet Your Majesty’s ancestors would immediately give rise to anger whenever anyone touched upon their taboo names. Zhaozhou thereupon preached the Dharma out of compassion. Both kings were greatly pleased and prostrated themselves in homage.

He then withdrew. When the next day the vanguard general of King Yan entered the monastery, intending to reprimand him for his failure to observe the etiquette due to a sovereign, the Master heard of his arrival and went out to receive him.
The general said, "Yesterday, seeing the two kings, you did not rise; today, seeing me, you have come out."
"Why do you come out to receive me? The Master said, "I will wait until the Grand Steward resembles a Great King; even then, this old monk will not go out to receive him. Feng withdrew in shame.
On another occasion, King Zhao brought his sons to visit Zhaozhou. Upon entering the monastery, the Master sat and asked, "Does the Great King understand?
The King said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Since my youth I have maintained the fasts; now that I am old, I lack the strength to greet people."
He descended from his meditation seat. King Zhao paid him special honors and departed. The following day, he ordered an attendant general to deliver a message.
When the master descended from his meditation seat to receive him, after a short while, an attendant asked: "Yesterday when the Great King came, you did not descend from your meditation seat;
today when the military commander comes, why do you descend? The master said: "This is not something you can understand. It is for those of superior capacity who come."

He received [visitors] on his meditation seat; when those of middle rank arrived, he descended from the meditation seat to receive them; when those of lower rank arrived, he received them outside the triple gate.

[Once], King Zhao invited Master Zhaozhou for a meal offering. When the Master reached the city, the King issued an edict that the entire city should prepare the full ceremonial regalia to welcome him into the palace.

Upon alighting from his carriage, the Master descended, whereupon the King prostrated himself and requested him to ascend the hall and take his seat at the center. They then partook of the midday meal.
[The assembly] ceased. The assembly wished to request that the Master expound the Dharma. The Master said, "I am already seated here; what further Dharma could there be to ask for over there?

Two Honored Ones do not manifest their transformations simultaneously. Thereupon, the King desisted. At that time, the King and his Consort were standing in attendance to the left and right of the Master.

The Emperor later said, "I request that the Master confer the empowerment of touching the crown of my head and grant me a prophecy. The Master touched the Emperor’s crown with his hand and said, "May the Great King live as long as this old monk.
This was the year Jiayin (the first year of Qianning).
The Great Master Guànxiū of Chányuè presented a poem to Qián Lǚ, the King of Wúyuè. It contained the line, "One sword, its frost cold over fourteen prefectures.
The king mistakenly ordered him to change it to "forty prefectures" before they could meet. Guànxiū said, "A poem cannot be altered.
A solitary cloud and a wild crane—what heaven would not be able to fly to? He then entered the Western Mountains of Yùzhāng, later entering [Mount Tiantai].
[The author] visited the King of Shu. The Great King [inquired about] the Shu monk Qiji. At a young age, he renounced the secular life to rely upon Mount Wei.

Later, when Chan Master Huiji of Mount Yang resided at Guanyin Temple in Yuzhang, Master Qiji served as the director of all administrative affairs. He composed a preface for the morning gruel, which said: "Gruel is called a 'fine medicine,' praised by the Buddha.
Its meaning surpasses the three types of giving (*dāna*), and its merit is marked by the ten benefits. I further pray that you, O wise and noble ones, shall each attain fulfillment."
Having fulfilled his vows at dawn, he forever dedicated himself to pure karma. Later, while residing at Jingu on Mount Xishan, he passed away;
his stupa still exists there today. Longpan was his study hall (from *Yunwo Jitan*).

In the second year (the Year of Yi-mao), the ninth seat-holder, National Master Zhengjue Zhiguang, while traveling from the sixth year of the Xian-tong era toward Mount Jiuzuo, suddenly encountered a giant python that intended to swallow him.
The Master’s monk’s staff flew up spontaneously, propping open the serpent’s mouth. The Master entered its mouth and sat cross-legged within it.
He entered samādhi. A deity came to offer an apology, but the Master paid it no heed. When the Master emerged from samādhi, the python had transformed into stone.

Subsequently, thunder and rain surged forth, washing away the sand and forming the foundation of the monastery. The mountain deity shifted the mountains so that the eight directions were shaded and reflected.

In the third year of the Qiánfú era, he manifested his passing. That same year, he was posthumously titled Zhèngjué (Right Awakening). In the fifth month, Chan Master Guǎngxī Zhìxián was about to manifest his passing.

He passed away. He asked his attendant, "Who was it that transformed while seated? The attendant replied, "Sengqie. He asked, "Who was it that transformed while standing? The attendant replied, "Senghui.
The Master then walked six or seven paces, lowered his hands, and passed away.
Bingchen (the third year; Ma Yin occupied Hunan; Qian Liu concurrently governed both Zhejiang regions; Li Maozhen burned the palaces of Chang’an).
In the second month, Chan Master Xuan of Jiufeng instructed his disciples, saying: "Do not let your time pass in vain; do not let the offerings of the faithful go to waste."
Having already left the household life, he walked only upon the Way and was thus called a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Thereupon, remaining in silent meditative concentration, he passed away on the twentieth day of the third month.

In the fourth year, the *ding-si* year (877 CE), when the Min Governor Wang Chao passed away and his younger brother Wang Shenzhi took control of the territory, King Yan of Zhaozhou looked up to him with reverence.
He had previously sent down ceremonial robes from Youzhou; the local government prepared a full ceremonial procession to welcome them and present them to the Master.
The Master firmly declined and would not accept them. His attendants said, "The Great King has done this for the sake of the Buddha-dharma of the Monk."
Therefore, they offered it as a tribute, requesting that he wear this robe. The Master said, "For the sake of the Buddha-Dharma, I, an old monk, shall not wear this robe.
Although the officials petitioned him repeatedly, the Master then took and wore it; the officials prostrated themselves in congratulation, to which the Master merely responded with a nod of assent.
On the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Zhaozhou entered nirvana at the age of one hundred and twenty. He was later posthumously titled the Great Master Zhenji. The Master—
As he was about to pass away, he instructed his attendant to deliver his fly-whisk to King Zhao, saying:

"This is that which this old monk has used throughout his entire life, never exhausting it. King Zhao praised the Master’s true nature, saying: "The moon in the azure pool; the head in the clear mirror.
My teacher, my transformation—Zhaozhou of the world. King Zhao wept for the Master and composed two verses. The first says: "When the Master left Biu Water, the movement..."

O King and Lords: the light of the Mind-Seal has vanished, withdrawn into the whisk. Mists shroud the moon over the pine-clad peaks of the blue void; waves submerge the boat that ferries men across the vast ocean.
When the single lamp is suddenly extinguished, Pāpīyas rejoices; when the two eyes grow doubly dim, the companions on the Path grieve.

Though one may be a traveler beyond the clouds who clearly perceives all, tears still flow whenever they gaze upon the ritual vase and stand. Second: "The Buddha-Sun sinks in the west, the Patriarchal Seal is shattered."

The pearl sinks into the crimson pond; the moon’s radiance fades. Shadows spread across the chamber as the incense smoke grows somber. The wind carries the subtle resonance of pines from the meditation seat.

With a single sandal, he has just arrived, leaving behind traces of transformation. In the Five Indias, where else might we meet him again returning? The disciples who understand emptiness are beyond both grief and joy;
Yet they still sit silently in tears before their snow-white curtains. (From *Canyuan Lianfang*)

In the eighth month of Gwanghwa Year 1 (5th year of King Munjong), on the *wùwǔ* day, Master An of Lopu admonished his disciples, saying: "The dharma of leaving home requires that no superfluous possessions be retained; how much more so for other worldly things!
You must keep this in mind with urgency. Time passes swiftly and the Great Way is profound and mysterious. If you remain negligent and complacent, how will you ever succeed?"
Through his realization, Master Ershan opened the Dharma; his teachings spread throughout all quarters.
On the first day of the twelfth month, he passed away while sitting in meditation (one source says at noon on the second day).

In the Jiwei year (the second year), Chan Master Xuangui of Hua’er compiled the records of the karmic conditions (*jīyuán*) of the patriarchs from the Zhenyuan era onward, titled *The Collection of the Holy Lineage of the Mysterious Gate*.
Chan Master Juyun of Longya first visited Dongshan Liangjie; upon hearing the words "The water of Dong River flows backward," he attained realization.

He attained great enlightenment. He served [his master] diligently for eight years, and his wisdom and realization increased daily. At this time, the Ma family occupied Changsha and promoted the construction of Buddhist monasteries.
They invited Xuedou Chongxian (Dun) to preach the Dharma at Longya Faji Chan Monastery, where he had over five hundred disciples.
A monk asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s intent. The Master said, "Wait until the stone tortoise can speak, and then I shall tell you. The monk said, "The stone tortoise speaks!"
[The Master] asked, "What did I say to you just now? That monk also attained awakening.

In the third year of the Gengshen [era], Chan Master Wenxi of Hangzhou first visited Yangshan. Yangshan ordered him to manage the monastery's permanent assets. One day, there was an extraordinary monk.
He went to seek alms-food. The Master reduced his own portion and offered it to him. Shan Yuhe asked, "Did you provide food for that person of the fruit-stage (phala-sthāna) who came just now?
He replied, "I set aside my own share to give it to him in return. Shan said, "You have performed a great service.

Subsequently, he resided at Qianqing in the region of Zhejiang, and later at Renwang Temple. In the third year of the Guangqi era, the King of Qian invited him to reside at the Longquan Prefectural Office. During the Dashun era...

In the first year [of the Tianfu era], the King of Qian submitted a memorial recommending him, and he was granted purple robes. In the fourth year of Qianning, he again petitioned for a monastic title, which was given as "Wuzhuo" (The Unattached).

In the tenth month of that year, he addressed the assembly, saying, "When the mind within the three realms is exhausted, that is nirvana. Having spoken these words, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away at the age of eighty.
His stupa was erected in the western valley of Lingyin. Later, in the second year of Tianguo, rebel troops destroyed the master's stupa.
Observing that his physical body had not decayed and that his hair and nails had both grown long, King Wusuku marveled at this. He dispatched a subordinate general to re-seal and inter the remains.
(The first year of Tianfu, the Xinyou year.)
One day, the Chan Master Caoshan Benji was visited by a monk known as Zhizhi Daozhe. The Master asked, "What is the matter beneath the paper robe?
The monk replied, "Once the single garment is hung upon the body, all things are entirely as they should be. He asked again, "What is the function beneath the paper robe?
The monk stood with hands clasped in reverence and said, "Yes," whereupon he immediately stripped away his robes. The Master smiled and said, "You merely understand..."
"If you go like that, why do you not come like this? The monk suddenly opened his eyes and said, "If the single, spiritual true nature does not depend on a womb, what then?
The Master said, "That is not yet wondrous. The monk asked, "What is wondrous? The Master said, "Neither borrowed nor not borrowed.
The monk withdrew to sit in the hall and passed away. At that time, Zhong Wang of Nanping, the regional governor of Hongzhou, repeatedly extended the utmost courtesy in inviting him.
The Master did not go himself, but instead wrote a verse on the mountain retreat of Master Damei and gave it to the messenger, saying:
"An withered tree, leaning against a cold forest, Has encountered spring many times, yet its heart remains unchanged. Even when woodsmen see it, they do not even cut it down;
Why, O man of Ying, do you labor so hard to seek it out? In the sixth month of that year, at night, he asked the administrator, "What day is it today? The administrator replied:
On the fifteenth day of the sixth month, the Master said, "Throughout my life as a wandering monk, I have always spent exactly ninety days for each summer retreat.
Tomorrow at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), I shall depart on my travels. When the time arrived, he burned incense, sat upright, and passed away.
He was sixty-two years old. His posthumous title was Grand Master Yuanzheng, and his stupa was named Fuyuan.
In the second year (Renxu), when Qian Liu was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yue, Chan Master Ying of Yunju had resided at Yunju for thirty years, and his Way spread throughout the world.

King Zhong of Nanchang revered him as his teacher and vowed to take him as his master for all generations. On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of the first year, for the sake of the assembly...

He opened the final expedient means and recounted the beginning and end of his departure from the world; the assembly was all deeply moved. On the third day of the first month of that year, he asked his attendant, "What date is it today?
The attendant replied, "The third. The Master said, "Thirty years hence, people will simply say, 'It is just this.

Thereupon, he sat upright and passed away into stillness. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Hongjue, and his stupa was named Yuanji (Perfect Quiescence). (From *Sengbao zhuan* [Monastic Jewel Record]) ○ Yunju.
Chan Master Daojian had long been in the quarters of the late Yunju as the first seat (the head assistant) of the hall.

When the late Yunju was about to pass away, the administrators asked, "Who is worthy to succeed you? Yunju replied, "Jian, the one in the hall. The administrators thought this meant he was to select someone suitable;
they all agreed that the second seat would be appropriate, and so they prepared the formal invitation to invite the first seat.
As he was taking his seat, [the abbot] humbly declined; the Master then firmly requested him to take the second seat.

Having secretly received the transmission of the Dharma-seal, the Master did not decline at all, but immediately took his own ritual implements and entered the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*). He gathered the assembly and expounded the Dharma.

The administrators were dissatisfied with his original aspirations and failed to follow established regulations. The Master perceived their sentiments and quietly departed. That night, the tree deity of Anle wept aloud and questioned him.
At dawn, the head administrator and the assembly rushed to Maizhuang to repent their errors and entreat him to return to the monastery.
As they listened, voices were heard in the air chanting repeatedly, "The Master is coming! In that same year, Chan Master Wei of Tongan passed away.
Guihai (the third year; Wang Jian was invested as King of Shu):
The ruler of Min, Wang Daowang, invited Xuefeng and Xuansha into the palace. The King asked, "Ultimately, what cause and effect must Buddhas and patriarchs cultivate in order to attain Buddhahood?
Xuefeng replied, "One must realize one's nature before one can attain Buddhahood. The King asked, "How [is this done]?"
[The Master] attained the realization of the nature. Feng said: "Awakening occurs in a single instant; non-awakening lasts for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

This matter cannot be pointed out in haste. For the mountain monk has thousands and hundreds of followers who have secretly applied themselves to this matter for twenty or thirty years, yet not even one or two among them has been able to take it up.
How much more so now, O Great King, you who are a secular sovereign and daily serve ten thousand [people]?"
The people judge the mountains and rivers with deluded thoughts; who among them can perceive this true Dharma-gate?
I pray that Your Majesty will serve as the sovereign of the Buddha-dharma and, through the tip of your brush, protect and deliver all living beings. Is this not a most auspicious thing?
The King was greatly pleased. (From the *Yulu*)

Jiazi (the first year of Tianyou): [In the eighth month] the Emperor passed away and Emperor Ai ascended the throne. Qian Liu was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wu; Zhu Wen was enfeoffed as the Prince of Liang.

Chan Master Guangyong of the Southern Pagoda’s reputation for the Way had already become prominent. Zhong Chuan, the South Ping Prince and Regional Commander of Nanchang, received him with ceremonial courtesy and invited him to his headquarters.
Thereupon, he succeeded to the Dharma seat of Shiting. Students flocked to him like clouds. (*Sengbao zhuan*) ○ Ruixiang of Taizhou.
Chan Master Yanshi Yan initially attained the essential meaning under Yantou. He subsequently traveled to Danqiu, where he spent his days appearing as if he were a fool;

the fourfold assembly looked up to him with admiration and requested that he reside at Ruiyan. There he led the community with strict discipline, earning renown throughout the region south of the Yangtze.
The Master would frequently call out to himself, "The Host," and then respond to his own call, saying, "Stay alert! In the future, do not let others deceive you. One day, there was...
A village woman came to pay her respects. The Master said, "Return quickly; you must save the lives of thousands of creatures.
The woman hurried home and saw her daughter-in-law carrying a bamboo basket, gathering field snails to bring back. The woman took them from her and released them by the water's edge.
The Master’s extraordinary traces were numerous (as recorded in his *Yulu*).
In the year Yichou of Emperor Ai (the second year of Tianyou; the Prince of Wu, Yang Xingmi, passed away and his son Wo ascended the throne).
Chan Master Yongguang Zhen of Suzhou ascended the hall and said: "If there is even the slightest deviation at the tip of the verbal spear, one is ten thousand miles from home.
You must let go completely over a precipice and take it up through self-acceptance; only then can you revive after death. This cannot be faked before the Master—it is a most extraordinary principle."
"How can a person hide [their deeds]?
(In the third year, the *bingyin* year, Zhong Chuan of Nanping passed away; his son Kuangshi succeeded him, but was soon captured by the Qin. Gao Jichang governed Jingnan.
Master Youzhang once previously saw the Monk Hanzhan, who said to him: "Forty years from now, there will be one with a turban..."
The Prince descended as a Bodhisattva and ruled over Jiangnan; at that time, my Dharma flourished.

Now, as the Master’s spiritual conduct had become renowned, Qian Wang again dispatched the envoy Tong Jian, carrying robes, incense, and medicinal herbs, to enter the mountains and extend an invitation.

Upon arriving at the provincial seat, he was honored with the title Great Master Zhide and lodged in the Gongchen Yuan. Day and night, the King inquired after the Way, and subsequently established Rui Long Temple.

He was invited into the city, where practitioners of Chan gathered like clouds. This accords with the words of "Dull and Dull" (from *Sengbao zhuan*). One day, the King of Min asked Xuefeng and Xuansha:
"I am now building temples to cultivate merit, practicing charity to ordain monks, and suppressing evil while performing good deeds.
Will I attain Buddhahood as a result of this? The Master replied: "You will not yet attain Buddhahood; for all such things are merely the mind of conditioned effort."

[The King asked about] saṃsāra. The King said, "What karmic retribution is obtained? The Master said, "One obtains the retribution of rebirth in heaven; one obtains the retribution of merit and longevity.

After the King remained silent for a short while, the two masters said to the King, "To see the nature is to be the Buddha. The King asked, "What do you take to be the Way? What practice should be performed?
The Master said, "The entire ocean of karmic obstructions arises from deluded thoughts. If you wish to repent, simply..."
Sitting, he contemplated the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). He wished for the Great King to recognize and grasp the true mark, whereby he would naturally attain Buddhahood.

The Great King rose and paid obeisance to the two masters, saying, "The matter of saving one from birth and death is of great importance. The masters said, "True Suchness (*tathatā*), Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and the twelve divisions of the scriptures—all these are fully present within the Great King’s own fundamental nature;
there is no need to seek them elsewhere. You must urgently save yourself. There was no [need for further instruction].

Human characteristics are merely provisional designations. If one is to become a Buddha, one must first deliver oneself. Once one awakens to the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it does not depend on many words.
The Buddha said that one realizes the Way in the state of non-effort (*anābhoga*). I pray that Your Majesty simply contemplates your own original nature; if you see it clearly, [you will realize it].

All [matters] were resolved through their own realization. Upon hearing the instructions of his two masters, the King gave rise to great faith and vowed to uphold [the teachings], never wavering in his resolve (from the *Xuefeng Lu*).
○ Chan Master Changtong of Xuedou initially studied under Changsha Cen.

At the end of the Xiantong era, the Prefect of Xuancheng County petitioned the throne to establish a Chan monastery on Mount Xiexian, naming it Ruisheng Yuan, and invited the Master to reside there. His fame...

In the middle of the Kaiyuan era, an uprising broke out. The Master led his disciples to Siming. In the second year of Dàshùn, the Prefectural Governor requested that he reside at Xuedou, where his transformative influence flourished magnificently.

In the seventh month of this year, he gathered the assembly, burned incense, and having completed his final instructions, he passed away with palms joined (one source says he manifested nirvana on the day of Yichou).
Chan Master Ling of Changqing attained enlightenment under the words of Xuefeng. This year, he took up residence at Zhaoqing.
The transformation through the Way flourished daily. Later, the Military Governor of Min requested that he reside at the Western Monastery in Changle Prefecture;
the imperial plaque was titled "Changqing," and he was given the title Great Master Chaojue.
This was the Dingmao year (the fourth year of Tianyou).
In the third month, the Emperor abdicated the throne to the Prince of Liang, Zhu Quanzhong.
He changed the era name to Kaiping. *Comprehensive Chronicle of the Buddhas Throughout the Ages*, Volume Eleven;
*Comprehensive Chronicle of the Buddhas Throughout the Ages*, Volume Twelve.
Compiled by Shi Benjue of Yian at Kuoshan in Song;
collated by the youth Biji Huan of Mingshan.
Fifth Generation.
The Later Liang of the Zhu clan. Capital at Bianzhou, later moved to Luoyang. Two rulers; a total of seventeen years.
*Dingmao* year (927): (Liang) Taizu Kaiyuan; (Tang) Li Kelyong Tianyou IV; (Qin) Li Maozhen; (Wuyue) Wusu Wang Qian Liu;
(Chu) Wumu Wang Ma Yin; (Jingnan) Nanping Gao Jixing; (Wu) Jingdi Yang Wo; (Min) Taizu Wang Shenzhi; (Shu) Wang Jian; (Nanhan) Liu Yin.

The founding emperor of Liang was originally named Wén; Emperor Xīzōng bestowed upon him the name Quánzhōng. Upon receiving the abdication of the Táng dynasty and ascending the throne, he changed his name to Huáng.
The founding emperor of Míng invited Xuánshā of Xuěfēng Peak into the palace to seek instruction on the Dharma of the Mind.
The two masters called out, "Great King, listen with a sincere mind: this illusory, empty body is Your Majesty’s *dharmakāya*. All knowing and seeing—"
This, Great King, is the fundamental source and original nature of the True Buddha. Great King, let your mind be as wood or stone; let it be like empty space.
Contemplate the mind as being without mind, arising from delusive thoughts. When your own mind is naturally empty, you will immediately realize the true mark (*dharmatā*).
The hundreds of thousands of samādhis and wisdoms are all present within the Great King’s own mind. Now that you already know your original nature, Great King, release them all at once.
"Below this, one must not allow even a single hair’s breadth of separation. This is called 'the achievement of non-achievement,' where achievement is never in vain.
This is the profound intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. I pray that Your Majesty will give rise to a great, expansive vow to maintain this and proceed toward Buddhahood;
do not undergo further saṃsāra. This is no trivial matter. The King paid homage to the two masters, saying: "In a hundred lifetimes I have been fortunate to encounter such instruction. (2)
The Master said to the King: "If you simply maintain constant emptiness and stillness in every thought-moment, there will be great fruit in your daily life.
Merely practicing giving and extensively performing acts of benefit are both gateways for assisting the Path; do not be bound by views of existence or non-existence. All things are sovereign.
Simply cultivate the path of effortlessness day after day. The King bowed in gratitude and offered twenty bars of gold, but the two masters each declined to accept it.
The King asked Xuan Sha again, "This one true mind is fundamentally without birth or extinction; from what, then, does this present body arise?
The Master said, "This original source of true nature pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

Because of deluded thoughts, a single point of conscious nature arises from the false conditions of father and mother, and immediately transmits life. It undergoes a thousand kinds of suffering, and the body possesses the wheel [of rebirth]."
[The assembly] turned [to leave]. "Buddha" means awakening. Great King, since you have already known and awakened, you shall not fall into the evil realms.

I only ask that the Great King frequently examine his deluded thoughts, return to the truth, and harmonize with the Way. The Great King prostrated himself, accepted it with faith, and practiced accordingly (from the *Xuefeng Lu*).
Wuchen (the second year of Kaiping) [908] (Tang: Li Kuyong was critically ill; Zhuangzong Chen Xun was established as ruler). (5) (Shu: Wucheng Year 1).
In the third month, Chan Master Cunen of Xuefeng manifested illness. The King of Min ordered a physician to examine him. The Master said, "I am not ill," and ultimately refused to take medicine.
On the second day of the fifth month, he traveled to Lantian. Upon returning, he bathed his body. At midnight, he entered *nirvāṇa*. His age was...
[He died at] eighty-seven [years of age], with fifty-nine years of monastic seniority (*varṣa*). The Master resided on the mountain for over forty years;

the prosperity of his Dharma assembly was preeminent throughout the world. His students numbered fifteen hundred in both winter and summer. The King of Min deeply esteemed his Way and expanded the monastery buildings for him.

Statues were installed and bells were cast to adorn the mountain; Youshi was appointed to lead the assembly. At that time, [the Master] was invited to stay at the government office to request a discourse on the Dharma (as seen in the stele).
In the eleventh month, Chan Master Xuansha Shibei passed away (the *Sengbao zhuan* states it was the twelfth month).
The Master first resided at Meixi and later lived at Xuansha. At that time, the monastic communities throughout the realm all admired and submitted to him upon merely hearing his reputation.

The regional governor of Min, Lord Wang, treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher. His disciples numbered nearly a thousand; the doors of his quarters were never closed. For thirty years, he responded to the needs of others and engaged with sentient beings.
The essential points of the Dharma he expounded exist in the world as the *Dali lu* and the *Xiaolu*, which have been circulated for generations. He reached the age of... [years].
Seventy-fifth. Forty-four years of ordination. The Military Governor of Min conferred upon him the title Chan Master Zongyi (Five Lamps).
Jisi (3rd year); (Tang) (Zhuangzong) (6th); (Wu) (Longyang) (2nd). Chan Master Yungai Zhian (one version says Zhian, which is incorrect).
One day, Daozheng of Mount Heng submitted a memorial to the Emperor of Hunan regarding Ma...
"O King, I beg you to allow me to debate the meaning of the Way with the Master. The King then invited the Master to come.
When the tea service was concluded, the Master requested a sword from the Great King. Grasping the sword, he asked Daoweng: "Your original teaching says:
'Vague and indistinct; within it there is a thing. What thing is this? 'Profound and dark; within it there is an essence. What essence is this? Speak!"
He was not executed. It was said that Dao Zheng could not be executed immediately; Dao Zheng remained silent. He prostrated himself and begged for forgiveness.
Seng’an asked the king, "Do you recognize this man? The king replied, "I do. An asked, "Who is he? The king replied, "Dao Zheng. An said, "It is not he.
If his Way were truly upright, he ought to be able to respond to me, a monk. He is merely a masterless, solitary soul. The king was greatly pleased, and because of this, the Way flourished.
No longer further confused (Wudeng). Gengwu (4);
(7); (3); Nan Yue Weijin Touduo collected the机缘 (jiyuan—opportune encounters) of the masters since the Guanghua era and compiled them as a continuation of the Baolin Zhuan.
Volume Four: Chan Master Wensui of Qishan. Initially, Yantou and Xuefeng led the Master on his travels.
Both of these great masters had received the seal of transmission from Deshan. Although the Master repeatedly engaged in vigorous debate and exhortation, he remained ultimately mired in stagnation.
Later, under the guidance of Dongshan, he attained awakening. At the age of twenty-seven, he resided at Qishan. One day, the Master was debating with a Daoist.
The Daoist Master Liyi said, "Coarse words and subtle speech alike all return to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

The Master [Linji] said, "This Daoist is a slave of the Buddha's house. The Daoist said, "A truly coarse fellow! The Master asked, "Where is the primary meaning? The Daoist was speechless (Wudeng Huiyuan).
Xinwei (the first year of Qianhua) &; (8) &; &; &; &; &; (Shu) (Yongping 1) &; (Nanhan) (Liu Yan) &; Chan Master Chongyunhui.
He entered deeply into the stone cliff at Guifeng and saw several pieces of worn-out monastic robes and prayer beads.

Suddenly remembering the ritual implements from his previous life, he proceeded to build a temple there. Just as he was clearing away the weeds, auspicious clouds emerged from among the peaks, whereupon he named it [Chongyun Temple].

Amidst heavy clouds, tigers and leopards all withdrew of their own accord. He also blocked the dragon pool, and the dragon likewise moved elsewhere. Later, Emperor Mingzong of the Later Tang bestowed upon it the name Changxing.
Initially, Daohui resided at Zhongtan in Luoyang, making it his daily practice to distribute water and provide medicine.
There was a leprous bhikṣu who requested the Master to wash and massage him; the Master performed this for him without any sign of reluctance. Suddenly, there appeared divine light and wonders.
Fragrance. Suddenly its location was lost (Five Lamps).
Ren-shen (2); (9); (Nan Han); Chan Master Ru-ne of Daochang Mountain in Huzhou.
Having received the secret instructions from Cuiwei, he then settled at Daochang Mountain and shaved his head.
Caotuo Hermitage. Disciples from all four directions gathered there, and it eventually became a Zen monastery.
In the year Guiyou (the third year of Emperor Qianhua’s reign under King Jun; the Tang dynasty;
the year of the destruction of Yan), the third year, Master Yaoyang of Ruiying Temple in Hangzhou requested the King of Wuyue to establish [an annual ceremony] at Mount Tiantai every year.
The Great Assembly of the Black and White [monastics and laypeople] at the Jinguangming (Golden Light) Dharma-assembly site lasted over a month before dispersing.
This Great Assembly of Radiance originated with this Master (Wudeng Huiyuan).
Jiaxu (the fourth year of the cycle), the sixth day of the fourth month:
Chan Master Datong of Touzi passed away (one source says Yihai). He was ninety-six years old. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Ciji.
Yihai (the twelfth day of the fifth month, the first year of Zhenming):
Master Yun of Shimen, having attained the essential meaning from Qinglin Qian, initially resided at the Huangyue Hermitage. Before long, he moved to Jia Shan.
On his way through Tanzhou, the Prince of Chu, the Ma family, came out of the city to welcome him and asked: "How is it?"
"This is the Great Way of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. The Master said, "Excellent, elder brother! Your carriage drawn by six dragons traverses the elegant jade streets for a thousand ages;
you emerge in ceremonial procession from the Golden Gate. The King was greatly pleased and invited him into the Tiance Palace to provide offerings.
The Master frequently responded to various occasions by saying, "Excellent, elder brother," and thus he was known at the time as Dage Heshang (The Elder Brother Monk).
Bingzi (2nd year) [13th day]; (Shu) [Zhengyuan era]; Pudu Monk of Fenghua County, Mingzhou.
He constantly carried a cloth bag and a tattered mat upon a staff. All the implements for his daily needs were stored within the bag.
Whenever he saw items in the market, he would beg for them—be they vinegar, salt, fish, or pickled vegetables. Just...

He went to the entrance of a shop, took a small amount [of money] and placed it in his bag; at that time, he was called Changtingzi (The One from Changting). When the Master lay in the snow, he remained unstained by it;
moreover, whenever he indicated good or bad fortune, it invariably came to pass. He often stood in the street. A monk asked, "What are you doing here, Master?
He replied, "Waiting for someone. [The monk] said, "I have come. The Master said, "You are not this person. The Master then said, "Give me one coin."

Qian. In the third year (one source says the first year, Dingchou), in the third month, as the Master was about to pass into extinction, he sat upright upon a large rock in the corridor of Yue-lin Temple and spoke this verse:
"Maitreya is truly Maitreya; He manifests in thousands, tens of thousands, and hundreds of millions of bodies.

From time to time he appears to those of the age, Yet the people of the age do not recognize him. Thereupon, he passed away with serene composure. Subsequently, he again manifested in other provinces, likewise carrying [the Dharma].
He traveled while carrying a cloth bag. The fourfold assembly vied with one another to paint his portrait.
The Master composed songs and verses that circulated throughout the world. Dingchou (3): (14) [Shu] Tianhan Year 1; [Han] Qianxiang Year 1. Wuyin (4): (15) [Guangtian] Year 2.
One day, Chan Master Pumen of Longhu gathered his disciples and said, "I am about to depart for another place; I entrust the affairs of the monastery to my two disciples, Cong and Jiao.
He then spoke this verse: "I fled the world's troubles to leave the household life; The Master pointed out to me a place of rest.
For thirty years I have dwelt on this mountain and gathered the assembly; I did not wish to bestow this lightly upon others. Today, I speak it clearly."

"It is as you say. When I close my eyes, listen closely. The assembly of the monastery was moved to sorrow and earnestly entreated him, saying, "Please do this for the sake of the Buddha-dharma remaining in the world.
The Master said, "Do you not know the principle that Bodhidharma returned to the West with only his single sandal, and that Puhua departed entirely with his whole body?
Why do you view me in terms of coming and going, or birth and death? Thereupon, he mounted a tiger and arrived at Xinxiang early in the morning.

The prefectural authorities were to provide the offerings. When he arrived there, the assembly for the monastic feast had just gathered. After the offering was finished, he went to the elder to request another portion for the practitioner.
The elder, thinking the Master was traveling alone, did not grant his request. Thereupon, [the Master] took a bowl of water and fashioned a staff from it to represent a tiger;
mounting it with great authority, he departed. He reached Kaiyuan Temple, while the monks of Longhu Temple arrived there in pursuit of him. He then offered a prayer.
He said, "I shall no longer return to the mountains, for there is already Master Cóng there. Consequently, Longhu has no pagoda for its founding patriarch;
it possesses only the ruins of the Kua-hu Hermitage as a testament to both past and present.

Furthermore, there is a portrait of the master painted by himself while reflecting in water, which remains to this day. He was posthumously granted the imperial title of Chan Master Yuánjué. Whenever prayers are offered to him...

One should regard him as being like an echo. In front of the courtyard stands a cedar tree where the Master used to sit; even today, it occasionally produces extraordinary blossoms (a variant edition states this refers to the one who entered parinirvāṇa, but that is incorrect).
Jǐmǎo (the fifth year of Zhēnmíng; the first year of Wǔyì of the Wú dynasty; the *Shùnzhèng* era of Gōngyǎn of Shǔ; the third year of Qiāndé):
In the first month, Chan Master Lìngzūn of Qīngpíng Mountain in Èzhōu entered parinirvāṇa. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Fǎxǐ.
Gengchen (6), (17), (2), (2), (4): Chan Master Luohan Chen of Zhangzhou.
Initially, he studied under Xuansha and was renowned alongside Huiqiu as the "Two Great Beings."

Fazhen was able to keep the Great Dharma secret and cherished self-concealment. At the request of Governor Wang of Zhangzhou, he resided at Dizang on Mount Shi in the western city for over ten years, where he received three disciples:
Fayan, Shanxiu, and Master Hongjin. Later, he moved to reside at Luohan Monastery;

with its broken walls and dilapidated bedding, others could not endure the hardship, yet none would have reached such a state who were not those who forgot their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma.
Xinsi (the first year of Longde) &; (18) &; &; &; (Wu) (Ruihuang’s biography, the first year of Shunyi) &; (3) &; (5); Chan Master Jiugong Qian.
Previously, after Mazu had passed away at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang, Baizhang and others interred his śarīra at the Baizhang hermitage on the石门 (Shimeng) cliffs in Haihun.
After more than ten years, [Qian] traveled upstream along the Feng River by carriage.
At Lúnfēng, he met the ascetic Sīmātóu, who exhorted him to remain at Bǎizhàng; consequently, he did not return to Shímén.
Jiàn himself traveled from Jiǔfēng to visit him there, whereupon a monastic seat was established. He became the first patriarch of Lètán, continuing the legacy of Bǎizhàng.
In that year, he passed away while sitting in meditation; his posthumous title was Dàjué, and his stupa was named Yuánjì.

Renwu (2): (19) Master Shunde Foyu of Longce Monastery in Hangzhou. Having received the essential teaching from Xuefeng, he first resided at Jingqing in Yuezhou. Students flocked to him in great numbers.
The Vice-Governor Pi Guangye remarked to others: "The lofty discourse of Master Foyu is such that no one can fathom it."
At the height of his influence, King Qian wished to expand the Chan assemblies within the capital and ordered that the Master reside at Tianlong Temple.

Upon first meeting the Master, the King remarked, "Truly a man of the Way," and treated him with profound courtesy and generosity. Consequently, the study of the profound (Buddhist doctrine) flourished throughout Wuyue.
Subsequently, the King founded Longce Temple and invited the Master to dwell there (Wudeng Huiyuan).
Guiwei (the third year) [Tang Tongguang Year 1]: On the thirteenth day of the ninth month, Chan Master Longya Dun passed away while sitting in the lotus position.
He was eighty-nine years old; he had spent sixty-nine summer retreats as a monk.
The master’s verses and hymns circulate in the world. In the second month, Li Cunxun, the Tang Emperor Zhuangzong, ascended the throne.
In Jinyang, in the tenth month, Liang was extinguished. The state of Liang had two rulers for seventeen years before its territory was abolished.
Subsequently, the Later Tang of the Li clan (capital at Ye, later moved to Luo; four rulers for fourteen years).
Jia-shen (the second year of Zhuangzong’s Tongguang era of the Tang): [Wuyue], [Chu], [Nanping], [Wu (fourth year)], [Min], [Shu (sixth year)], [Han (eighth year)].
The Venerable Xiandeheshang of Jingzhao was a man of extraordinary character. He had no fixed abode and, having received the seal of mind from Dongshan, lived among the common people in Minchuan.

He possessed no ritual implements and did not follow the monastic regulations. Wearing a single robe throughout both winter and summer, he would daily gather shrimp and clams along the riverbanks to sustain himself.
At nightfall, he would sleep amidst the paper money offerings at the White Horse Temple on Mount East.
The local residents called him "The Pearl Oyster Monk. When Chan Master Jing of Huayan heard of this, he wished to determine whether the man was genuine or not.
He first hid himself among the paper money offerings. At midnight, when the monk returned, Jing seized him and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The monk immediately replied, "The wine stand and platter before the deity. Jing let go of him and said, "It is no wonder we share the same root."
Shengyan later went to serve Zhuangzong. By imperial decree, he was summoned to Chang’an; the Master also arrived there first.
Every day he sang and played instruments for himself, or would feign madness, coming and going through mud and snow without leaving any trace. His final whereabouts were unknown thereafter.

(Five Lamps) Zhuangzong summoned Chan Master Xinghua Jiang to the inner palace. The Emperor observed the etiquette of a disciple, inquiring into the fundamental tenets of the school. He [the Master] was quite...
There was a profound accord between them. One day the Emperor said, "Since I recovered the Central Plains, I have obtained a single bright pearl, yet no one has offered a price for it.
The Master said, "I beg Your Majesty to let me see the pearl. The Emperor drew back the ends of his *fodou* (head-wrap). The Master said, "This is the treasure of the Sovereign;
who would dare to offer a price for it?"

In the year of Yiyou (the third year of the Qinwang era), Seon Master Hyeomjeong of Huayan Monastery in Jingzhao—having received the imperial decree at Dongshan—initially resided at Huayan Monastery on Mount Dongshan in Fuzhou.
Not long after, Emperor Zhuangzong summoned him to the capital, where he extensively propagated the profound teachings of the Dharma. One day, Emperor Zhuangzong invited him into the inner palace.
During the fast, [the Emperor] saw the assembly of monks studying the scriptures, yet only the Master and his disciples did not look at them.

The Emperor asked, "Master, why do you not study the scriptures? The Master replied, "When the Way prevails, imperial edicts need not be proclaimed; when the times are peaceful, one need not sing songs of great peace.
The Emperor said, "It may be so for you alone, Master, but why do your disciples also not look at them? The Master replied, "In the den of the lion, there are no other beasts."
"The path where the Elephant King walks is utterly devoid of solitary tracks. The Emperor asked, "Why do all the monks recite the scriptures?
The Master said, "The water-jelly has no eyes of its own; to seek food, it must rely on the shrimp. The Emperor asked, "Since he is a junior, why is he addressed as 'Elder'?
The Master said, "A dragon or phoenix cub at three years of age; a veteran court official for a hundred years under Your Highness. Later, the Master...
He passed away at Pingyang; his posthumous title was Chan Master Baozhi (Five Lamps). ○ The Great Master Guanhui of Chan Yue in Western Shu entered nirvana.
○ Chan Master Xinghua Jiang passed away.

Bingxu (Mingzong) [Dǎn] (Tiānchéng Year 1) &;&; (Wuyue Bǎozheng Year 1) &;&;&; (6) (Min Huìzōng) (Shu) [Zhīxiáng] (2) (2); In the fourth month, Zhuāngzōng passed away. Emperor Ming ascended the throne.
○ Chángjué Chánshī of Pǔjìng Yuàn in Dōngjīng initially visited Guīzōng Zhāng.
Upon hearing the Dharma, he attained realization. Thereafter, while traveling to the capital, he resided alone outside Lìjǐng Gate for two years.

At that time, there was a lay devotee from the north, Mr. Zhang, who invited the Master for a meal offering. Having attained a degree of awakening, Zhang prepared a bed and requested the Master to stay overnight.
That night, he and his wife secretly observed the Master; his body seemed to fill the entire bed, with both head and feet protruding from it.

When they ordered their maidservants and servants to look, however, the Master appeared exactly as usual. Their admiration increased manifold, and they said, "We, husband and wife, are now advanced in years. We now wish—"
He divided the front hall to augment the master’s chamber. The Master joyfully accepted it, and by the third year of the Tiānchéng era, it was completed as a large monastery complex.
It was granted the plaque name Pǔjìng (Five Lamps).
Dinghai (2) [Wu Qianzhen Year 8] (3) Month four: Chan Master Ruidong Zhang requested a burial site from the King of Qian.
The King laughed and said, "Does the Master really mean this? He dispatched Lu Renzhang to construct a stupa at Xiguan.
Once the stupa was completed, Zhang went to take leave of the King of Qian, entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma and the care of [the deceased].
The people returned and sat in meditation until their transformation (parinirvāṇa).
His lifespan was eighty-seven years, and he had spent seventy summer retreats in seated meditation. In the year Wuzi (the third year of Tiānchéng;

[equivalent to] the first year of Dàyòu of the Hàn dynasty), Míng Wáng Yánjūn ordained twenty thousand commoners as monks. Consequently, there were many monks in Mín (according to the *Tōngjiàn*). In the autumn, Luó...
Chan Master Han Chen bathed, sat upright, and passed away at the age of sixty-two. Regarding Koushui Zaoguang Gufu:
he first visited Xuefeng, who said, "In the future, you will surely serve as a teacher to a king.

Later, departing from Ehu, he returned to Wenzling to build a hermitage (now Yongfeng Temple) and subsequently resided at General’s Rock, where two tigers attended him. A divine being offered him the land for his dwelling.
At Ruiyan Monastery, students gathered in great numbers. He once said to the assembly, "The practice of the ancient sages must rely upon rigorous austerity.
This summer I shall wear paper robes, and this winter I shall bathe by striking the ice. For this reason, the people of the world called him the "Ancient Buddha Who Strikes the Ice."

Later, he resided at Lingyao. When the year arrived, he was summoned by the ruler of Min, who invited him to dwell in the inner hall. Bowing with reverence, the ruler said, "Thank you, Master, for descending from afar.

During the serving of tea, the Master held up his bag and asked, "Does the Great King understand? The ruler replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The King of Men and the Dharma King each illuminate their own.
He remained for ten days and then took leave on the grounds of illness. On the second day of the twelfth month, he passed away.
Having bathed and ascended the hall, he informed the assembly and passed away. The King, along with the monastics and laypeople, prepared fragrant wood for the cremation.
Auspicious radiance filled the mountains, and relics of five colors appeared. He was enshrined in a stupa at the main chamber of Ruiyan. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Miaoying Fawei Ciji.
From that time until the present, prayers have been offered by those far and near, and its spiritual manifestations have been manifold.

In the year Jichou (the fourth year of the Nanping era, the first year of the Dahuo era of the Wu dynasty), Zen Master Changjue of Pujing Monastery in Dongjing remarked that because the capacities of the times were shallow and dull, it was difficult for them to bear the ultimate meaning [of the teachings]. He then said:

"I would rather not strive to open the Dharma-gate. From this time on, he provided bathing facilities every third and eighth day of the month; the monastics and seekers who gathered numbered in the tens of thousands.
The Master once said to his disciples, "If only the gate of wisdom remains unobstructed, how could blessings ever be hindered?
(Wudeng Huiyuan). At Gaogai Monastery in Yongfu County, Min, there was a mountain that resembled a precious canopy. Formerly, seven siblings of the immortal Xu ascended to heaven together.

During the Jiànyuán era, there was Chan Master Chén Huìjù and his attendant Xiè Zhìzhù. They abstained from grain and practiced seated meditation until they both passed away while sitting in meditation.
Today, the two *dharmakāya* (true bodies) remain. At this time, the King of Mǐn enfeoffed the mountain, naming it Xīyuè (Western Peak). (From the *Chánglè jí*)
Gengyin (the first year of Changxing): [Qin] (Wuyue 5), [Chu] (2), [Yan] (3).
Zen Master Yunmen Wenyan first visited Muzhou. When Muzhou saw him coming, he immediately closed the door. The Master knocked on the door three times.
Zhaozhou asked, "What are you doing? The Master said, "My own matter is not yet clear; I beg the Master for instruction.

Just as Zhaozhou opened the door, the Master pushed his way in. Zhaozhou seized him and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master was so startled that he did not have time to answer. Zhaozhou pushed him out and said, "A wheel-rim from the Qin era!
He then closed the door, injuring the Master’s right foot. From this, the Master attained awakening. Zhaozhou then directed him to see Mazu.
Xuefeng. Having arrived at Xuefeng, he spent a long time making definitive resolutions there. He then traveled extensively throughout various regions before journeying to Guangzhou later in life.

Lingshu Min invited him to serve as the First Seat (Changzuo). Previously, Min had not requested a First Seat; when someone urged him to do so, Min replied, "My First Seat has already left the household life.
After some time, Min requested him again, to which Min replied, "My First Seat has already gone on pilgrimage and realized the Way. After a further period, [Min requested him once more].

Again, he invited [Yanyang]. Yunmen said, "My head seat has already crossed the mountain pass. When the Master arrived, Yunmen greeted him with a smile and said, "I have been waiting for you for a very long time;
why did you come so late? He then ordered him to take up his post. Yanyang accepted without declining and assumed his duties.

Shortly thereafter, the local ruler, King Liu, was about to raise an army and went to consult Yunmen on whether it should be done. Yunmen had foreknowledge of this; he sealed a small casket with his own hand and said to an attendant:

The King arrived and came out to meet him, as had been arranged. [The Master] then sat peacefully and passed away. When the King finally arrived, he was greatly shocked to hear that Hui-min had already passed away.
He asked, "When did the Master fall ill, and why did you pass so suddenly? He replied, "The Master never fell ill.
Just now, he sealed a small casket and instructed me to present it to you upon your arrival. The King opened the casket and found a slip of paper inscribed with these words: "Human and Celestial..."
The Abbot of the Eye Hall (Yanmu Tang) passed away, whereupon the King invited Xian to succeed him on the Dharma seat. He was further welcomed to the provincial seat to propagate the Dharma.
After a long time, he moved to reside at Yunmen Mountain in Shaoyang, where students arrived from afar as soon as they heard of his reputation.

Xinmao (the second year of Changxing) & (the sixth year of Baozheng of Wuyue) & (Chuwang Xisheng) & (Nanping) & (Wu Ruyi Wang) (the third year of Dahan) & & (the fourth year); Chan Master Zhao of Fengxue in Ruizhou.
Initially traveling to study under various masters, he visited Jingqing Fu but did not find accord there. He then traveled north to the regions of Xiang and Mian.
While staying at Huayan, he met Shoukuo, an attendant of Nanyuan. In silence, he attained awakening to Nanyuan’s fundamental teaching.
Shoukuo sent him back to see Nanyuan again; upon seeing him, Nanyuan was delighted. Thereupon, he received instruction with ease and daily heard of his realization of wisdom. Nanyuan said:

That you have come to shoulder the Great Dharma by virtue of your power of vows was no mere coincidence. Six years after Xue had taken leave and departed, in this year [the Master] arrived at Ruizhou.
He saw several thatched huts built against a mountain and asked an old farmer about them. The farmer said, "This is the ancient Fengxue Temple;
due to the famine last year, the community abandoned it, leaving behind nothing but Buddhist statues, drums, and bells. Xue entered and stayed there, begging for alms from the villages every day.
For those who live alone, seven years [are required]. A lay donor renovated it, establishing a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*).
In the *Renchen* year (the third year), [Wang] Xifan, Prince of Chu, [ruled]; (fourth); (fifth);
on the seventeenth day of the fifth month, Chan Master Changqing Ling entered *nirvāṇa*. The Master had propagated the Dharma in two locations, and his disciples numbered one...
[He had] fifteen hundred [disciples]. He traveled and taught in Min and Yue for twenty-seven years. His lifespan was seventy-nine (from the *Chuan deng lu*).
On the sixth day of the eighth month, Lu Yuanhao of Fenghuang Commandery in Wu composed the "Record of the Yong'an Chan Monastery in Xianju Cave on Mount Lu. It states briefly:

"When Yao and Shun were sovereigns, their benevolent transformation reached only within the borders of the realm. When the Duke of Zhou and Confucius established their teachings, their rules and models were merely exhaustive [for that time]."

Within the realm of the world, even for those of a thousand ages, [the Way] has followed the wind, and for a hundred kings, it has been received with reverence. How much more so for the Śākya clan, who appeared in the world;
their wondrous functions are inconceivable, their compassion pervades all living beings, and their vows and practices are widely propagated throughout kalpas as numerous as grains of sand.
It was here that the Tang monk Ruyi established Yong’an Temple. Upon this occasion, the assembly requested the Elder Huicong to come and reside there, and thus the old temple flourished once again.
(Lushan ji). Gui-si (the fourth year):
(Wuyue) [Emperor] Mu Wenwang Yuan-guan. Gui-wu (the fifth): [The first year of] Long-qi of Min.
Gui-wei (the sixth): In the eleventh month, Emperor Ming passed away. Emperor Min Conghou ascended the throne. ○ Chan Master Qieru. Initially, at Xuan...

Shashé attained the essential meaning and subsequently lived in seclusion on Mount Xiàojiè. He hollowed out a large, weathered cypress tree to serve as a small hermitage, just large enough to accommodate his body.
One day, the two elders Qīnghuò and Chōngzhào visited the Master; they were so deeply impressed by his lofty discourse that they did not realize night had fallen.
He saw a jackal and a tiger running to the front of the hermitage, where they naturally circled the two masters in a state of docility.
He subsequently established a hermitage on Mount Dazhang and invited the Master to reside there. Seated alone in both locations, he passed away after fifty-two years.
Jiawu (the first year of Emperor Qingtai’s reign under the Tang dynasty, 935 CE). [6] [2] (The first year of Mingde under the Shu kingdom, 934 CE).
[7]. In the fourth month, the troops of Luwang Congke arrived. Emperor Min fled into exile, and Luwang ascended the throne.
○ The Senior Seat-Holder Jing of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai initially attained awakening through the words of Xuansha. He later resided at Tiantai for over thirty years.
Once there was someone who asked: "When mental thoughts fly about in confusion, I do not yet understand how to subdue them. The Master replied:

"Take this mind that flies about in confusion and investigate the place from which it flies. When you investigate and find no place, then where can the confused thoughts exist? Turn back and investigate the investigating mind itself."
"Then one would be able to investigate this thoroughly—where would the mind rest? (and so forth). The Master, upon observing the meaning of "illusion" within the teachings, composed a verse, saying:
"If you say that all dharmas exist like illusions, then committing various transgressions and evils should entail no fault. How is it that the karma one has created is not forgotten?"
Relying upon the Buddha’s compassion to provide guidance and inspiration, the Elder Xiaojing replied: "An illusory person manifests an illusory Cakravāḍa mountain range;

illusory karma can summon that which is to be remedied by illusion. Failing to realize that illusions arise from illusion, one gives birth to various illusory sufferings. To awaken to the fact that all is like an illusion is itself non-conditioned (asaṃskṛta) illusion.
Now, the ruins of Guoqing Monastery remain here."
Yiwei (2) [Year 1 of Wu Tianzuo] (Year 1 of Min Yonghe); [Shu and Chu]; [Gongxiao Wang Chang, Year 2 of Mingde];
(8): Chan Master Fayan Wenyi. Initially, he met Luohan Chen. Chen asked, "Are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth the same as oneself, or are they different?
The Master replied, "The same. Chen held up two fingers and said, "Two. The Master attained realization and sought further clarification.
Zhe suddenly clarified the Great Matter. After some time, he lived in a thatched hut. Subsequently, he traveled beyond the Yangtze River and arrived at Linchuan.

The local governor requested him to reside at Chongshou Monastery. A monk named Zifang came to consult him; when Zhe raised the phrase, "Among the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed," Zifang attained great enlightenment.
From then on, those from all quarters who possessed intellectual understanding flocked there in droves. At first, his conduct was entirely upright and consistent.
