The Master used subtle means to inspire them, and all gradually came to take his teachings to heart. The assembly of disciples, like those gathered at the sea, often numbered no fewer than a thousand.

Before long, his spiritual transformation became renowned throughout the region south of the Yangtze River. The Ruler of Jinling, who held the Master’s Way in high esteem, invited him to reside at Ba’en Temple, where he was titled Chan Master Jinghui.
Subsequently, he moved to Qingliang (as recorded in the *Wudeng Huiyuan*).
Bingshen (the third year of Qingtai) & & & & (2); (Fujian) (Kangzong Chang, first year of Tongwen) & (3); (9);
In the tenth month, the troops of Shi Jingtang arrived. The Emperor [Li Zhi] committed suicide by fire. In the eleventh month, Jingtang ascended the throne and changed the era name to Tianfu.
The Tang state was extinguished. At that time, Li Yinsun retired to his home village. He initially studied the writings of Han Yu and produced many [works].

He disparaged the followers of Śākyamuni, but later he studied Buddhism and attained enlightenment. He then composed the *Faxi ji* (Collection on the Joy of Dharma) and the *Foguo ji* (Record of the Buddha-land), which circulated in the world.
People of the time called him a flatterer; his integrity was not thorough, as he came to flatter the Buddha (from his original biography).
Later Jin Shi dynasty. Capital: Muke. Two rulers. Eleven years.
Dingyou (the second year of the Tianfu era of Jin Gaozu). [The first year of Shengyuan of Liang Sheng, who succeeded the Wu dynasty]. (2) (4) (10).

On the first day of the first month, Chan Master Zhao of Fengxue was invited with full ceremony by the regional governor, who had heard of his reputation. On the day of Shangyuan, he opened [the assembly].
Dharma. In the eighth month of the year following [the passing of] Nanyuan, the Great Master Shunde Daofo of Longxing Temple in Hangzhou entered nirvana.
Monastics and laypeople alike wailed in grief, and many donned mourning attire. He was seventy-four years of age. The Master taught the Dharma in three locations;
his recorded sayings are contained in the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Five Lamp Compendium).
Wu-xu (3) & & & & (2) & (3) & (Shu Guangzheng 1) & (11); in the summer, Chan Master Guangyong of Shiting passed away without illness.
He was eighty-nine years old and had sat in meditation for seventy summers (one source says the year was Ding-you).
○ Ma Daqing of Wenzhou dreamed that five hundred monks arrived at his home seeking lodging. The following day...
Five hundred statues of Arhats arrived at his gate. Moved by this marvel, Master Ma lent him his house;

at times, extraordinary light emanated from it, whereupon he eventually donated his residence to become a temple called Luohan Temple (in the present dynasty’s Xiangfu era, it was granted the plaque name Chongxin Temple, though the common people still call it Luohan Lane.
This ward was originally named Qingzheng, which was later changed to Congshan, also following the name of the temple—as seen in the *Yongning bian*).
Jihai (4) & & & & (3) & (Fujian) (Jingzong Xi, Yonglong 1) & (2) & (12): Chan Master Yuantong Yuede. Initially, he studied under Qingxi Jin of Xiangzhou.
After a long time, during the days when the Li family held the state in the Jiangnan region, Yuede blended in with the common crowd at Shanglan Monastery in Nanchang.
Lord Song Qiqiu arrived and visited the Scripture Hall, where the assembly of monks hurried forward.
As he was welcomed, the Master continued reading the sutra as usual. The Duke stood by his side and glanced at him, but the Master paid him little heed or response.

The Duke asked, "Elder, what sutra are you reading? The Master held it up for him to see. The Duke marveled at this and earnestly requested that he reside at the monasteries of Sheli, Yougu, and Shuangling.
The Master had no concerns regarding these matters; wherever he went, whether staying or leaving, he would simply sit in silent composure, yet his disciples naturally gathered around him.
Guījù: Throughout his life, he wore a single-layered robe (*śāṭaka*) with its folds fastened by a cord. At night, he would extend the robe to serve as a blanket. (From *Sēngbǎo*).
Dàoyì, a monk of Upper Tianzhu, once saw a brilliant light among the mountains one evening. He went to investigate it and discovered a rare fragrant wood.
He then commissioned a skilled craftsman to carve an image of Avalokiteśvara from it; the white radiance of the statue shone forth so brightly that at night there was no need for rows of candles.
Its radiance eclipsed the brilliance of the sun by day. Once the sacred image was completed, its spiritual resonance became even more magnificent.
In the year Gengshen of the Qianguo era, a monk named Congxun saw it and said, "While traveling in Luoyang, I obtained a relic of an ancient Buddha. I have cherished it for a long time;
I now wish to place it within the *ūrṇā* (hair-treasure) of the Bodhisattva so that it may assist in its divine power. Master [Fahai] followed his request, and it remains so to this day.
Śarīra relics appeared between the crown and the *uṣṇīṣa* (Avalokiteśvara Scripture). Gengzi year (5): [4] [2] [3] [13];
King Xi of Min ordained eleven thousand commoners as monks (*Tongjian*). ○ Xingyin of Foshouyan, Luzhou.
The Chan Master, having truly attained the Dharma at Lumen, subsequently arrived beneath Foxue Rock on Mount Lu.
There was a stone cave there about three zhang in depth, where the Master dwelt in seclusion. Although the Ruler of Jiangnan summoned him three times, he did not rise to comply;

despite earnest entreaties, he only consented to open the hall at Qixian Monastery. Less than a month later, he returned secretly to his rock chamber. Later, manifesting a slight illness, he said to his attendant monk: "At noon..."
"I am departing. When the appointed time arrived, he stepped down from his bed and walked a few paces; then, standing firm, he passed away.
Lord Li prepared fragrant firewood for the cremation and erected a stupa (Wudeng Huiyuan).
Xin-chou (the sixth year); (Wu-Yue) (Wenmu Wang Yuan-gun passed away); (5); (3); (4); (14).
The King of Min built a seven-story stone pagoda on the western mound south of the city wall. Before the work was half-finished, a light like a canopy radiated forth for three nights.
Once it was completed, the radiance shone to the very heavens for another three nights. The King visited to offer his congratulations and subsequently inscribed the title upon it.
Pure Light. Beneath it, he established a monastic residence (Changle Ji).
Year Wenyin (7) [of the Later Wu-Yue period] (Wu-Yue) (Zhongxian Wang Hongzuo) &; Year Liuyi (6) &; Year Wugou (5) [of the Han Dynasty] (Shangdi Bin Guangtian Yuan);
National Teacher Shao of Tiantai first visited Chan Master Longya Dun and the "Short Uncle" of Shushan, seeing his true teacher.
Fifty-four people subjected him to rigorous interrogation, scouring every detail and probing the most hidden recesses until they were exhausted in both body and mind, yet they could find no clue.
Upon reaching Caoshan, he merely followed along with the assembly.
A monk asked Fayan, "During the twelve periods of the day, how can one suddenly bring all conditions to rest? Fayan replied, "Is emptiness your condition? Is form your condition?"
To say that emptiness is the condition means that emptiness is fundamentally without conditions. To say that form is the condition means that form and mind are not two.
In the daily use of things, what object could possibly serve as your condition? When Huishao heard this, he was struck with awe and marveled at it.

Furthermore, someone asked, "What is one drop of water from Caoxi? Baizhang said, "This is one drop of water from Caoxi. Upon hearing this, Huishao attained great enlightenment, and his lifelong doubts were resolved.

His lingering doubts were suddenly dispelled like ice melting; he wept with emotion until his tears soaked his robes. Yuanxian said, "You shall greatly propagate my school. Go now, do not let yourself be hindered.

Thereupon, he traveled to Tiantai to visit the traces left by Zhiyi, which appeared as if they were his own former residence. He gazed upon them with deep affection, his heart resolved to spend the rest of his life there.

Gui-mao (the year of the Gui-mao cycle, the reign of Emperor Chonggui of the Jin dynasty, the eighth year); (Tang) (Emperor Xuanzong, Jingbao Da-yuan); (Min) (Fugong Yiwang Yanzheng, Tiande Yuan); (Han) (Emperor Chengzhong, Chengqian He-yuan): Chan Master Fayan. At the invitation of the Prince of Li of Jiangnan, he was invited into the inner court.
There he beheld peony flowers. When the Prince requested a poem from the Master, the Master composed this verse:

*Clad in coarse wool, facing a fragrant thicket,* *From the start, we have always been far apart.* *My hair has turned white today;* *The flowers, however, remain as they were.* (The Prince asked, "Why do you say so? The Master replied, "Because I am old.")
"The flowers are as red as they were last year. Their brilliance differs with the morning dew; their fragrance follows the evening breeze.
Why wait for them to wither and fall before realizing they are empty? Wang suddenly attained enlightenment to his meaning.

Jiachen (the first year of Kaiyun): A commoner in Shangyuan County, Jiangnan, died suddenly and revived after three days, saying: "I arrived at a palace courtyard and suddenly saw my former lord, who was bound with extremely severe fetters.

Next, the Emperor remarked: "The Study Hall of Mount Lu has already been converted into a monastery. I have heard that when the ancient and sagacious kings of old held the charts and governed the realm, they devoted themselves solely to virtue;

they returned to goodness and remained long within the Way, whereby the world was transformed and perfected. Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges appear in the world to save mundane beings;
relying on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they expound the nature (*dharmatā*). There is no emptiness apart from this nature. To believe is to cultivate and honor it; to awaken is to understand it."
It liberates people, urging them toward the realm of purity and bringing rest to the anxious mind of greed; thus the people become simple and sincere.

The Emperor said to his ministers, "You all should not harbor doubts regarding the destruction of the Buddha. Furthermore, the Buddha regarded both the body and the world as illusory."
He made the benefit of others his primary concern. Had his true body still been present, if it could have benefited the world, he would have wished to cut it into pieces to give as alms;
how much less would he have begrudged this bronze statue, which was as dear to him as his own person, had it been able to save the people.
